title: Crafting a Professional Services Website RFP: A Comprehensive Guide
description:
Crafting a Professional Services Website RFP: A Comprehensive Guide

In the digital age, a well-crafted Request for Proposal (RFP) is essential for professional services firms seeking to build a website that truly reflects their expertise and meets their unique needs. However, many firms fall short by relying on generic templates, which often fail to address the specific challenges and requirements of their industry. This guide outlines why standard RFPs are inadequate and provides actionable insights to ensure your RFP stands out.

Why Off-the-Shelf Templates Fall Short

1. Lack of Customization

Generic RFPs are one-size-fits-all solutions that rarely align with the specific needs of professional services firms. These templates often overlook critical aspects such as showcasing expertise, managing client confidentiality, and presenting complex service offerings.

2. Insufficient Technical Depth

Professional services websites often require advanced functionalities like secure client portals, project management tools, and custom reporting. Off-the-shelf RFPs lack the technical depth needed to address these requirements, potentially leading to underwhelming results.

3. Poor User Experience Focus

The user experience (UX) is crucial for professional services websites, as they aim to inspire trust and professionalism. Generic templates often fail to emphasize the importance of a seamless, intuitive UX, which can hinder user engagement and retention.

Engineering Takeaways for a Tailored RFP

1. Start with User Personas

Begin by defining detailed user personas for your website. This includes potential clients, existing clients, and internal stakeholders. Understanding their needs, pain points, and behaviors will help you craft an RFP that addresses their specific requirements.

2. Prioritize Technical Architecture

Ensure your RFP includes a detailed technical architecture section. This should outline the necessary backend systems, integration points, and security measures. By doing so, you can attract vendors who can deliver a robust, scalable solution.

3. Include Detailed UX Requirements

A professional services website must offer a seamless and intuitive user experience. Specify UX requirements such as navigation structure, content hierarchy, and mobile responsiveness. Consider including wireframes or mockups to provide a clear vision.

Conclusion

title: How I keep a living system map of Mầm Văn — every change, before & after
description:
Hi, I'm Vũ Xuân Toàn (Vu Xuan Toan), a software developer and indie maker from Bắc Ninh, Vietnam, and the founder of Vu Xuan Toan Tech. In my intro post I mentioned Mầm Văn — the literature-learning platform I'm building for Vietnamese middle-school students (React, TypeScript, Supabase, Gemini AI). Today I want to share the part of the project I'm most proud of, because it isn't a feature for users — it's how I keep the whole system understandable while it changes every week.

The problem: the system grows faster than memory

Mầm Văn has two big portals (teacher and student), an AI content studio, a question bank, XP and mastery engines, a knowledge tree, grading workflows, notifications, an admin area… After a few months of intense building, "how does this all connect?" stopped being a question I could answer from memory.

So I built a complete map of every flow in the system — 262 nodes covering every screen, every engine, and the relationships between them (for example: publishing a lesson → notifies students, or rejecting a gift request → refunds the student's total XP wallet). Every node also lists the exact code files and functions that implement it, verified automatically against the codebase.

The rule: the map is part of the code

The map only stays true if it can never drift. So I work under one strict rule:

  1. Before changing any flow, I open the map and identify which nodes and relationships the change touches.
  2. After the change, I update the map, regenerate it, and ship it in the same commit as the code.
  3. The map and a full change history are republished automatically to my website in the same round.

You can see both, live:

  • 🗺️ The system map (interactive, click a node to light up its cluster): https://vuxuantoan.me/so-do-mam-van.html
  • 📜 The change history — every work session: what changed, in which files, with lines added/removed: https://vuxuantoan.me/lich-su-mam-van.html

Before & after, for every flow change

The part I like most: whenever a change modifies a flow, the history page automatically gets two buttons — "flow BEFORE this change" and "flow AFTER this change". Every version of the map is archived immutably, so I can reopen exactly how the system looked before any change and compare. When I recently removed an AI status bar from the question bank, the before-map still shows its node in the tree; the after-map doesn't. That makes design review honest: nothing about the system's shape is ever lost or misremembered.

Why bother?

Because an indie maker's scarcest resource isn't code — it's clarity. The map has already caught wrong assumptions before I wrote a line of code, and it lets anyone (a collaborator, a teacher using the platform, future me) understand a fairly complex product in minutes.

If you build long-lived side projects, I'd genuinely recommend stealing this workflow: one living map, updated in the same commit as the code, with archived before/after versions.

—

I'm Vũ Xuân Toàn. My home on the web is vuxuantoan.me, my code lives at github.com/vut08905, and Mầm Văn itself is live at mamvan.vercel.app. Say hi!

title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.26903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.

title: OpenAI Decisions API now available on AI Gateway
description:
OpenAI’s Decisions API is now available through AI Gateway at /v1/decisions. It uses the same request and response format as OpenAI, so existing OpenAI SDK integrations can switch by changing the base URL, credentials, and model ID.

Decision models answer typed questions about shared input and return structured answers rather than generated text. In one request, you can ask a model to:

  • Estimate the probability that a condition is true with a predicate question

  • Select from supplied options with a choice question

  • Rate the input against an ordered rubric with a score question

Use these answers for tasks such as classification, routing, triage, and rubric-based scoring.

The endpoint works with any decision model on AI Gateway, including Jev, Liquid d1, and Laya. Use openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions model. This is separate from openai/gpt-6-luna, which generates text.

With OpenAI SDK 7.30.0 or later for JavaScript or 3.26.0 or later for Python, point the client at AI Gateway and call decisions.create:

The response returns answers in question order, each with the corresponding question’s name.

See the OpenAI Decisions API documentation for Python and cURL examples. To use decision models with the AI SDK or /v1/evaluate, see the decision documentation.

title: What Android App Testers Actually See in a Google Play Closed Test
description:
When a closed test stalls, most of us debug it from Play Console. Tester count, release status, the Testers tab. If the number sits below what you expected, it's easy to assume people just didn't bother.

Often they did bother. They got stuck on a screen you never see as the developer, usually because of the wrong Google account or a step nobody told them about.

So this post is the tester's side of Google Play closed testing: what your Android app testers actually see, the four screens they go through, where each one breaks, and the message I now send before anyone taps the link.

TL;DR

  • Testers go through four screens: opt-in page, Play listing, install, private feedback.
  • Most "my testers aren't counting" bugs come from the wrong Google account or a Google Group nobody joined.
  • The rule is 12 testers opted in for 14 continuous days. Tell people that in plain words, more than once.
  • There's a copy-paste tester message near the end.

Step 0: check which Google account they're on

Google says a tester needs a Google Account or a Google Workspace account. What the docs don't spell out for testers is that it has to be the same account in two places.

  • The opt-in happens on a web page, under whatever account the browser is signed into.
  • The install happens in the Play Store app, under whatever account is active there.

If those differ, the tester has joined your test with one account and is trying to install with another. They'll often see the app as unavailable, and you'll see one fewer tester than you expected.

Two more things to check before anything else:

  • Google Group on the track? The tester has to join the group first, then opt in. Play Console's help says so, and it's a very common silent failure.
  • Opted in to your internal test before? They aren't eligible for the closed test until they opt out of internal. A user in internal testing only gets the internal version.

Screen 1: the opt-in page

This is the link from the Testers tab of your closed track. The tester opens it in a browser, sees a short explanation of what being a tester means, and taps a button to join. You can't opt in for them. Each person does it themselves.

Things that trip people up here:

  • The link isn't live yet. It only appears once the release is published, and right after the first publish it can take several hours to work. Sending it at midnight and expecting installs by 12:05 doesn't go well.
  • No feedback contact. The feedback email or URL you set on the Testers tab shows on this page. Leave it blank and testers have nowhere obvious to write.
  • Searching instead of tapping. After opting in, the page shows a link to the app on Google Play. Testers should tap it. A closed test app doesn't appear in Play search before you have a public release.


The tester's side of a closed test in five checkpoints, with the thing that most often breaks at each one.

Screen 2: your Play Store listing

From the opt-in page, the tester lands on your listing in the Play Store app. If everything lines up, there's a normal Install button. If there isn't, go back to Step 0 before you debug anything else.

One surprise for paid apps: closed testers have to buy them. Only internal testers get paid apps for free.

Screen 3: install and updates

The install comes straight from Google Play. No APK file, no other store. After that:

  • Their copy updates to your test version automatically.
  • Every new release on the closed track reaches them as a normal app update.
  • They don't have to opt in again.

Google also tells testers that some usage data, like device info and app usage, is shared with the developer during a test. That's why I check Android vitals and crash reports in Play Console every day of the test, not just at the end. Closed testing is still mobile app testing, even if the main goal is the 14 days.

Screen 4: private feedback

Testers can't leave public reviews on a test version. Instead, your Play Store page shows them a "Private feedback to developer" section with a Write feedback button. It asks for a star rating and a short note, and only you can read it.

On your side it lands in Play Console under Monitor and improve > Ratings and reviews > Testing feedback. You'll want a summary of it for the production access form later, so tell testers it exists. Most of them have never seen it.

The 14 days, from the tester's phone

The rule, from Google's Play Console Help page on testing requirements: personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023 need at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before applying for production access.

  • A tester who opts out before 14 days doesn't count.
  • If they rejoin, their 14 days have to be consecutive again.

On the phone, leaving is one tap, and people do it while tidying up their apps. Google's own advice is to tell testers to stay opted in for at least 14 days, so say it plainly.

I also ask testers to keep the app installed. That's my own practice, not a Google rule: I haven't seen anything in the docs saying an uninstall ends the opt-in. But an app that isn't installed isn't being used, and Google can ask for more testing if engagement was low.


Four tester-side mistakes that quietly lower your opted-in count in Google Play closed testing, and the fix for each.

The message I send testers

Copy it, fill in the brackets, send it with the link:

Hi! Thanks for testing [App name] on Google Play. A few steps:

1. Use the same Google account on the link below AND in your Play Store app.
   (Play Store > tap your profile picture to check which one is active.)
2. [Only if you use a Google Group] Join this group first: [group link]
3. Open this link and tap the button to become a tester: [opt-in link]
4. Then tap the Google Play link on that page and install from there.
   Don't search for the app. It won't show up.
5. Please stay in the test for at least 14 days, and keep the app installed.
   If you leave early, Google doesn't count you.
6. Feedback: on the app's Play Store page, scroll to
   "Private feedback to developer" > Write feedback. Or email me at [email].

This week, could you try: [task 1], [task 2], [task 3]?

The tasks at the bottom matter more than they look. "Try the app" gets one session. "Create an account and add your first item" gets a session and usually a bug report.

Quick debug list when the count is low

Before you message anyone, run through this:

  1. Is the release on the closed track actually published?
  2. Does your opt-in link open for a fresh account?
  3. If you use a Google Group, are the missing people in it?
  4. Are any of them still opted in to internal testing?
  5. Did anyone install from a shared APK instead of from Play?
  6. Has anyone left and rejoined, restarting their 14 days?

If headcount is the real problem

The message fixes confusion. It doesn't fix headcount. If how to get 12 testers for 14 days is the part you're stuck on, that's what we built TestMyApps for.

We run 14 Google Play testers on physical Android phones for 16 days, so there's a buffer above Google's minimum. They join through your opt-in link, usually within 6 hours, and you get a production-access report at the end. Plans start from $15. If production access isn't approved, you get a free retest, and if that still isn't approved, a refund. We've tested 400+ apps with a 99.9% approval rate, but Google makes the call, so read that as a track record and not a promise.

Whichever way you find your testers, check the Google account question first. It saves more closed tests than anything else here. Details are on the 12 testers for 14 days page.

title: PACE-MoE: Adaptive Domain Sampling and Domain-Specific LoRA for Medical Visual Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.27656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical visual grounding requires models to align clinical descriptions with spatial evidence across heterogeneous imaging domains. However, existing multi-domain post-training strategies typically rely on fixed domain sampling and shared parameter updates, overlooking the need to adapt both which domains receive training and where their updates are applied. To address this issue, we propose PACE-MoE, a policy-guided framework that jointly performs adaptive domain sampling and domain-specific adaptation for medical visual grounding. PACE dynamically assesses the training value of each imaging domain from current-policy feedback and progressively adjusts domain coverage through domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing. Meanwhile, domain-specific LoRA adapters route updates to the corresponding imaging domains while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder. This coordinated design aligns training-data allocation with parameter adaptation without modifying the original reward formulation or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Experiments across seven medical imaging domains show that PACE-MoE consistently improves grounding performance over fixed-domain training, achieving a 3.64% relative improvement in mean box IoU over the Vanilla baseline. Under matched domain-specific adapter architectures, adaptive sampling alone further improves mean box IoU by 2.07%, demonstrating the benefit of policy-guided domain allocation. These results establish coordinated data-parameter routing as an effective strategy for multi-domain medical visual grounding.

title: Look Before You Reason: Implicit Visual Thinking for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.27341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.

title: Understanding the Benefits of Scaffolds through Computational Separations
description:
arXiv:2610.27157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference-time harnesses, i.e., external procedures that call a model many times and keep state across calls, can substantially improve model capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the benefits of using such harnesses and the extent to which these benefits can be internalized through training. More precisely, we conceptualize a harness $\mathcal{A}$ as an arbitrary wrapper around a base model $M$ and attempt to distill a student model from the harness's traces. Empirically we find that, even with simple scaffolds and small models, the inference-time harness significantly outperforms a distilled student. We then prove that such a gap is due to a fundamental representational limitation: inference-time harnesses can compute a closure of their per-call primitive that is $\NL$-complete even when the primitive is a trivial $\AC^0$ lookup, and that no fixed-depth forward pass can represent under the widely believed conjecture that $\NL\not\subseteq\TC^0$. Our theory suggests that expanding the representational capacity of the student relative to the task at hand, e.g., by enlarging the model, making the task easier, or lengthening its chain-of-thought, is necessary to close the gap, which we verify empirically. Finally, we scale to an agentic harness on competition math, where the same gap reappears. Overall, our results show that a harness confers on the base model a profound gain in representational power, one that training a same-class student on its traces cannot transfer back into the weights.

title: How to compare GPU cloud prices without fooling yourself
description:
"H100 from $X an hour" is the least useful number in a GPU price list. Two offers with the same headline can differ by a factor of two in what you pay at the end of the month, and two offers with very different headlines can come out the same.

We publish GPU prices at Runcrate, and other people's comparison sites read them, so I spend a lot of time looking at how a price turns into a bill. This is the checklist I use. It works for any provider, ours included. I'll use our public pricing endpoint for the examples because it's the data I can show you with a script, not because the method depends on it.

1. Get to one unit: dollars per GPU-hour

Some lists quote the machine, some quote the GPU. An 8x H100 node at a per-machine price looks eight times worse than a 1x H100 at a per-GPU price. Divide by the GPU count first, always.

Runcrate's endpoint already reports per GPU-hour and needs no API key:

import requests

data = requests.get("https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing").json()
print("fetched at", data["fetched_at"])

for g in data["gpus"]:
    s = g["specs"]
    per_gpu = s["num_gpus"] or 1
    print(
        f'{g["name"]:12} {g["vram"]:>6}  '
        f'${g["min_price_hr"]:.2f} to ${g["max_price_hr"]:.2f} per GPU-hr  '
        f'{g["available_options"]:>2} configs  GPUs per machine {g["gpu_counts"]}  '
        f'~{s["vcpus"] // per_gpu} vCPU / {s["memory_gb"] // per_gpu} GB RAM per GPU'
    )

Part of what it printed when I ran it (fetched at 2026-10-21T00:51 UTC):

H100 SXM       80GB  $3.38 to $7.79 per GPU-hr   7 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 8]  ~20 vCPU / 128 GB RAM per GPU
A100 80GB      80GB  $1.76 to $4.26 per GPU-hr  12 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 8]  ~28 vCPU / 120 GB RAM per GPU
L40S           48GB  $1.14 to $1.95 per GPU-hr  10 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4, 8]  ~12 vCPU / 72 GB RAM per GPU
A6000          48GB  $0.65 to $2.51 per GPU-hr  18 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4]  ~28 vCPU / 58 GB RAM per GPU

Notice the ranges. One GPU model can have a dozen configurations with a 2x to 4x spread between them. A comparison that keeps only the minimum hides that the minimum might be one 8-GPU node in one region.

2. Compare the same GPU, not the same name

"A100" is two products (40 GB and 80 GB). "H100" is SXM or PCIe, with different memory bandwidth and interconnect. A "4090" with 24 GB will not hold the model your 48 GB card holds. Before comparing prices, match:

  • VRAM (the endpoint has vram per GPU type)
  • form factor and interconnect for multi-GPU work (interconnect, for example NVLink)
  • GPU count per machine, because you can't split an 8-GPU node

If your model needs 80 GB, the price of a 40 GB card is irrelevant, however low it is.

3. Count what comes with the GPU

A GPU-hour also buys CPU cores, RAM and local disk, and those vary a lot. In the output above, an A6000 can come with about 28 vCPUs, an L40S with about 12. For data loading, tokenization or anything CPU-bound in your pipeline, the "slower" card with more cores can finish first.

So note, per GPU: vCPUs, RAM, local disk, and whether persistent storage costs extra. Runcrate's volumes, for example, are billed separately at $0.03 per GB per month. Your other quotes will have their own line for it, or bundle it.

4. Billing granularity matters more than the rate for short work

This is the one most comparisons skip. Take a 7-minute eval on a $1.14/hr GPU:

  • billed per second: 1.14 x 7 / 60 = $0.13
  • billed per started hour: $1.14, nearly 9x more

For long training runs granularity barely matters. For evals, CI jobs, agent experiments and anything bursty, it dominates. Check three things:

  1. The billing increment (second, minute, hour). Runcrate bills most instances by the second and a few GPUs by the minute; the endpoint's min_price_per_minute flag marks the latter.
  2. When the meter starts: at request, at boot, or once the machine is running. Runcrate starts it when the machine is running, so provisioning isn't billed.
  3. When it stops: only when you remember to delete the machine, or also on its own. Idle shutdown and maximum runtimes turn "I forgot it overnight" from a 12-hour bill into a 30-minute one, which is worth more than a few cents on the rate.

5. Listed is not launchable

A price only matters if you can get the machine. Availability moves by the minute: in the same hour I wrote this, a GPU type showed one configuration on the pricing endpoint while a live launch query showed none. When comparing:

  • try an actual launch, or at least a live availability query, in the region you need
  • note the count of configurations and regions, not just the headline price
  • separate on-demand from spot or interruptible capacity, which is cheaper because it can disappear

6. Date every number

GPU prices change weekly, sometimes daily. A comparison without a date is a guess. Put the fetch time next to every price (the endpoint returns fetched_at for that reason), and re-run your script rather than reusing last month's table.

A template you can reuse

For each offer, one row:

Field Why
GPU model, VRAM, form factor same product?
GPUs per machine can you buy just one?
$/GPU-hour the normalized rate
vCPU, RAM, disk per GPU the rest of the machine
Billing increment, meter start cost of short jobs
Auto-stop options cost of mistakes
Storage and egress cost of data
Region, availability checked at can you launch it
Fetched at how old the number is

Then price your actual workload (hours per run, runs per month, data moved) against each row. The offer with the best headline wins less often than you'd think.

Links

  • Live prices: runcrate.ai/pricing
  • The JSON endpoint used above: https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing
  • Billing details: runcrate.ai/docs/billing/pricing

If your comparison method has a step I've missed, I'd like to hear it. Reply here or write to hello@runcrate.ai.

Written with AI assistance. The script and prices above were run against the live endpoint on 2026-10-21.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

Read more

title: A lab acceptance is a validity range per rule, not a flag on the vendor
description:
Most systems that store test records model laboratory status as a boolean on a vendor row. is_accredited = true. That column is wrong in a specific way: 16 CFR part 1112 grants acceptance per rule or test method, the scope can be extended later, and it can be suspended for one slice of the scope while the rest stands. A boolean cannot represent any of that.

The correct shape is a range table keyed by rule, with the test date checked against it.

The schema 

CREATE TABLE cab (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  legal_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,
  -- independent | firewalled | government, per 1112.11
  cab_kind      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (cab_kind IN ('independent','firewalled','government'))
);

CREATE TABLE cab_acceptance (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  cab_id        BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cab(id),
  cpsc_rule_id  TEXT NOT NULL,           -- the rule, not a product category
  accepted_from DATE NOT NULL,
  accepted_to   DATE,                    -- NULL means currently open
  status        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active','suspended','withdrawn','discontinued')),
  source_url    TEXT NOT NULL,           -- where the listing said so
  observed_on   DATE NOT NULL            -- the day this row was read, not asserted
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX acceptance_one_open_window_per_rule
  ON cab_acceptance (cab_id, cpsc_rule_id, COALESCE(accepted_to, DATE '9999-12-31'));

The observed_on column is the one people skip. Section 1112.19 has the Commission maintain a listing and update it as scopes change, so every row here is an observation with a date attached, not a fact about the world. A pipeline that overwrites observed_on with now() on every write has thrown away the only field that lets you reconstruct what was known on the test date.

The test record 

CREATE TABLE test_record (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  cpsc_rule_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
  tested_on     DATE NOT NULL,
  prime_cab_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cab(id),
  -- 1112.25: subcontracted work must be identifiable in the prime report
  performed_by  JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',   -- [{cab_id, tests: [...]}]
  report_uri    TEXT NOT NULL
);

The gate query

A test result counts only if the body held acceptance for that rule on that date. That is a join with a range predicate, and it has to run before the certificate row is considered complete.

SELECT t.id
  FROM test_record t
 WHERE NOT EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
           FROM cab_acceptance a
          WHERE a.cab_id = t.prime_cab_id
            AND a.cpsc_rule_id = t.cpsc_rule_id
            AND a.status = 'active'
            AND a.accepted_from <= t.tested_on
            AND (a.accepted_to IS NULL OR a.accepted_to >= t.tested_on)
       );

Zero rows is the pass condition. A non-empty result means the file cites a test whose scope line does not cover the rule, or covers it on a date outside the window. Both look identical in a system that stores is_accredited.

The same predicate is what catches a suspension that lands later. Refresh the acceptance windows on a schedule, rerun the query against existing certificates, and a report that was valid when issued can surface as invalid now. That is not a bug in the file. It is the file being current.

Subcontracting

performed_by exists because 1112.25 requires the prime contractor's report to identify which tests a CPSC-accepted body acting as a subcontractor performed. A single PDF from a trading company that consolidated three laboratories does not satisfy that as data. Model it as an array of (cab_id, tests) and let the same range predicate run over each entry rather than only over the name on the cover page.

type Attribution = { cabId: number; tests: string[] };

function unresolvedParts(t: TestRecord, windows: AcceptanceWindow[]): string[] {
  const covered = new Set<number>();
  for (const w of windows) {
    if (w.status === 'active' && w.acceptedFrom <= t.testedOn &&
        (w.acceptedTo === null || w.acceptedTo >= t.testedOn)) covered.add(w.cabId);
  }
  return t.performedBy
    .flatMap((a: Attribution) => a.tests.map((name) => ({ cabId: a.cabId, name })))
    .filter((row) => !covered.has(row.cabId))
    .map((row) => `${row.name}@${row.cabId}`);
}

unresolvedParts().length === 0 is the assertion worth putting in CI for the ingestion job, because the failure mode is silent. A missing attribution reads as a complete report.

Retention, and what it is not

Section 1112.25 makes the laboratory hold its own test reports and technical records for section 14 tests for at least five years from the date the test was conducted. That is the lab's duty on its own copies. It is not a license to delete your side after five years, and it is not a statement that a report older than five years is unusable. The date that starts the clock is the test date rather than the shipment date, so a slow-moving SKU can carry a report whose retention window closed while the goods were still on the shelf.

FulfillNexa by SBT (fulfillnexa.com) runs the inbound scan at three China facilities, floor area 13,000 square meters in Suzhou, 8,000 in Dongguan and 3,000 in Shenzhen, where one carton resolves to one product identifier before it resolves to a test file. That is the same join in the other direction. Whatever the storage layer looks like, the question at the dock is identical to the question in the query above. Which body ran this test, against which rule, on which date.

title: Make your v0 or Cursor app stop looking AI-built in 10 minutes
description:
If you've built a landing page with v0, Cursor, Lovable or Bolt, you've probably had this moment: you put it next to someone else's and it's the same page. Purple-to-blue gradient, centred headline, one font, three feature cards with an icon in a circle, a pricing table, and a "Get started" button that does nothing you can see.

Nothing on that page is broken. It's the average of every landing page the model has seen, and that's what you get when you don't ask for anything specific. Visitors recognise it within seconds, though, and some of them decide the product behind it got the same amount of thought.

Here are the five tells I look for and a fix for each. Every fix is a couple of minutes in a Next.js App Router project with Tailwind CSS v4. I put the result in a free starter (MIT) so you can copy single pieces or start from the whole thing:

  • Repo: https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter
  • Live demo: https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-next-starter/

The five tells

  1. A gradient where a brand colour should be.
  2. One font at one weight for everything.
  3. Everything centred.
  4. An illustration where the product should be.
  5. Buttons that don't respond.

0. Get a page to work on (1 minute)

To try the fixes on a clean page:

npx create-next-app@latest my-app -e https://github.com/teodoravadani/qodesign-next-starter
cd my-app
npm run dev

Or open your own project. The steps assume Next.js 15 (App Router) and Tailwind v4, the setup where globals.css starts with @import "tailwindcss".

1. Swap the gradient for three colours (2 minutes)

Delete the bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-500 to-blue-500 (or whatever your hero has). In Tailwind v4 the palette lives in CSS, and every variable in @theme becomes a utility class:

/* app/globals.css */
@theme {
  --color-ink: #0a0a0d;
  --color-paper: #f3f1ea;
  --color-volt: #c6ff3d;
}

Now bg-ink, text-paper and bg-volt exist. Ink is the page, paper is the text (swap them for a light theme), and the accent goes on one or two things per screen: the main button, a status dot. Once the accent is on every element it does the gradient's job again.

2. Two fonts with some character (1 minute)

Pick a display face for headings and UI and a mono for numbers and small labels. The starter uses Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono. The font @import has to be the first line of the file:

@import url("https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=JetBrains+Mono:wght@400;500;600;700&family=Space+Grotesk:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap");
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --font-sans: "Space Grotesk", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-mono: "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, monospace;
}

One trap I hit while testing this: a project set up with shadcn init (v0 projects use shadcn) already has an @theme inline block with --font-sans: var(--font-sans). That block wins, the variable points at itself, and the page falls back to Times New Roman. Edit the --font-sans and --font-mono lines inside that existing block instead of adding new ones. Also delete any font-family: Arial left on body by the default template, and put font-sans on <body>.

Then use contrast in size and weight: a bold 7xl headline with tracking-tight leading-[1.02], body text at text-lg and 60% opacity, mono at text-xs for the small stuff.

3. Move the hero off centre (1 minute)

Centred layouts are the default because they never look broken. A left-aligned hero with a width limit on the headline looks like someone placed it:

<section className="mx-auto max-w-6xl px-5 pt-28 pb-16">
  <h1 className="max-w-3xl text-5xl leading-[1.02] font-bold tracking-tight sm:text-7xl">
    Know your servers are down before your users do.
  </h1>
  <p className="mt-6 max-w-xl text-lg text-white/60">
    Uptime, latency and deploys on one screen. Set up in two minutes, no agent to install.
  </p>
</section>

Write the headline as one sentence about the visitor's problem. "Supercharge your workflow" is the copy version of the purple gradient.

4. Show the product (2 minutes)

Generated heroes get a blob or a 3D shape because the model has never seen your app. You have. Screenshot your best screen at 2x and put it in a plain browser frame:

import Image from 'next/image';
import shot from '@/assets/dashboard.webp';

<div className="mt-16 overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-white/10 bg-ink">
  <div className="flex items-center gap-1.5 border-b border-white/10 px-4 py-3">
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
    <span className="size-2.5 rounded-full bg-white/15" />
  </div>
  <Image src={shot} alt="The dashboard" priority sizes="(max-width: 1200px) 100vw, 1152px" />
</div>

The static import gives next/image the width and height, so nothing shifts when it loads, and it keeps working if you deploy under a sub-path. priority is there because it's the biggest thing above the fold.

No app to screenshot yet? The starter has a /dashboard route you can use as a placeholder. Swap in your real screen before you launch.

5. Make every button respond (3 minutes)

People feel this one without being able to name it. Click "Start free" on most generated pages and nothing visible happens. A loading state that turns into a confirmation tells the visitor their click did something.

I use the free Toast Stack component for this. It installs from a registry URL with the shadcn CLI, so the source lands in your project and you can edit it:

npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/toast-stack.json

Mount the toaster once in app/layout.tsx:

import { Toaster } from '@/components/toast-stack/ToastStack';

// inside <body>
{children}
<Toaster />

Then wrap your signup call:

'use client';
import { toast } from '@/components/toast-stack/ToastStack';

const start = () => {
  toast.promise(createWorkspace(), {
    loading: { title: 'Creating your workspace…' },
    success: (name) => ({ title: 'Workspace ready', description: `${name} is live. The first check runs in 30 s.` }),
    error: () => ({ title: 'That didn’t work', description: 'Try again in a minute.' }),
  });
};

The spinner stays up for at least 600 ms so a fast request doesn't flash, then turns into a check. Hover the stack and the toasts fan out.

Pricing gets the same treatment. The Pricing Switch component replaces a static three-column table with a monthly/yearly switch whose prices roll like an odometer:

npx shadcn@latest add https://teodoravadani.github.io/qodesign-free/r/pricing-switch.json

<PricingSwitch
  plans={plans}
  header={<h2>Pay for monitors, not seats.</h2>}
  onSelect={(plan, yearly) => startCheckout(plan.id, yearly ? 'year' : 'month')}
/>

Its digits use Saira Condensed, so add &family=Saira+Condensed:wght@700;800 to the font import from step 2.

Bonus: motion that respects people (30 seconds)

If you add scroll-in animations, put them behind prefers-reduced-motion. In the starter the sections fade up with a CSS scroll timeline and no JavaScript:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .reveal {
    animation: reveal-up linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 28%;
  }
}
@keyframes reveal-up {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(28px); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}

Add className="reveal" to a section. The components in the starter check the same setting on their own.

If you'd rather hand it to Cursor

This prompt covers steps 1 to 4. I haven't compared how each tool handles it, so read the diff before you accept it:

Restyle the landing page in this Next.js App Router + Tailwind v4 project.
1. Remove every gradient background. In globals.css add --color-ink #0a0a0d, --color-paper #f3f1ea and --color-volt #c6ff3d to @theme. Use volt only on the primary button and one status dot.
2. Fonts: Space Grotesk for headings and UI, JetBrains Mono for numbers and small labels. Add a Google Fonts @import as the first line of globals.css. If an @theme inline block already defines --font-sans or --font-mono, change those lines instead of adding new ones. Put font-sans on <body>.
3. Left-align the hero: one-sentence headline (max-w-3xl, text-5xl sm:text-7xl, tracking-tight), one supporting line (max-w-xl).
4. Replace the hero illustration with next/image of src/assets/screenshot.webp (static import) inside a simple browser frame.
Don't change any other copy. Don't add dependencies.

What's in the starter

  • /: hero with a product shot, a log upload section with progress and retry (Upload Dropzone), pricing (Pricing Switch), toasts on every action (Toast Stack), and a light/dark switch (Day/Night Toggle).
  • /dashboard: Orbit, an observability dashboard with simulated live data.
  • Next.js 15.5, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion 11. next build passes and every page is static, so it deploys anywhere. The README has a one-click Vercel button.

About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign, so the components in this post are mine. Everything here is free and MIT: the starter and the free components and dashboards in qodesign-free. The paid components are $3 each or $29 for all of them, each with a React + Tailwind version and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools, at qodesign.dev.

If you run the five fixes on your own app, I'd like to see the before and after.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code is copied from the starter repo, and every command above was run in a fresh Next.js 15 app (one plain, one set up with shadcn init) with next build passing before publishing.

title: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.26918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.

title: Timing-Aware and Interpretable Self-Attention for Event-Based Wearable Task Transition Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27549v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task transition detection aims to identify when a person shifts from one task to another, providing a foundation for continuous health monitoring and timely context-aware interventions. While statistical and deep feature representations have demonstrated strong classification performance, they often rely on aggregated or latent features that are difficult to interpret in behavioural terms. Event-based features provide a compact and interpretable alternative by encoding behavioural and physiological patterns as discrete tokens with explicit semantic meaning, making them well suited for behavioural analysis in health informatics. Self-attention offers a mechanism for modelling interactions among such tokens; however, conventional self-attention classifiers primarily rely on token order and do not explicitly incorporate timing or duration information. As a result, informative temporal cues in event representations may not be fully exploited for task transition detection. This study proposes an event-based time-aware self-attention framework that represents behavioural signals as sequences of discrete events augmented with onset timestamps and durations. Event timing is encoded using a parameter-efficient kernel-based representation, while a novel type-aware duration embedding modulates information propagation according to event persistence. Experiments on a semi-naturalistic wearable dataset show that the proposed model outperforms existing event-based approaches, achieves performance beyond or comparable with statistical and deep-learning models with a more compact input representation, and provides improved interpretability through integrated-gradient-based analysis. These results indicate that explicit modelling of event timing and duration enhances both classification performance and interpretability, supporting reliable deployment in biomedical and health informatics applications.

title: Solving the Ho--Nguyen Conjecture for Gaussian Mixtures: Applications to Mixtures of Experts
description:
arXiv:2610.27265v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Over-fitted Gaussian mixtures can contain many parameter configurations with nearly the same density, making the order of density cancellation central to their parameter-learning rates. Ho and Nguyen encoded these cancellations in a polynomial system and conjectured its exact order as a function of cluster size. The key to resolving the conjecture is a common positive-variance shift that turns the coefficient equations into Gaussian moment matching. For every cluster size $\Mhn\ge2$, we prove that the real, nonzero-weight system has order $2\Mhn$: a sharp sign-change bound forces rigidity at that order, while positive Gauss--Hermite quadrature constructs a non-trivial solution through order $2\Mhn-1$. Population-density calculations at 110-digit working precision recover the predicted leading term for two to six components; finite multistart searches recover the same observed powers for two to five components, with smaller finite-scale constants for three to five components. For parameter learning, the exact order gives an explicit pointwise maximum-likelihood exponent and an exact local minimax order on specified shrinking neighbourhoods of a fixed known mixing measure. The same coefficient viewpoint separates high-order cancellation from exact parameter symmetries in mixtures of experts. Synchronized replication preserves the conditional density while keeping the corresponding parameter losses positive in two broad standard-softmax classes, showing why statistical rate arguments must account for exact parameter symmetries.

title: HiQGS: Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Querying for Feed-Forward Gaussian Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.27604v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction from sparse posed monocular frames requires reasoning over observations that vary jointly in viewpoint and time. Existing methods either predict Gaussian primitives from observation-aligned features or aggregate multi-frame information through compact latent queries. However, the former tightly couples Gaussian allocation to individual frames, while the latter does not explicitly structure observed evidence according to its temporal relation to the requested timestamp. Consequently, evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps can be difficult to align and integrate. We present \textbf{HiQGS}, a query-based hierarchical framework for feed-forward Gaussian scene reconstruction from sparse monocular frames. HiQGS introduces a \textbf{Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder} that organizes multi-resolution geometry-appearance visual features according to image location, observation time, and camera pose, thereby preserving complementary appearance and structural cues. Our \textbf{Time-Adaptive Decoder} use target timestamp queries the resulting hierarchical representation to retrieve relevant spatiotemporal evidence and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state. Experiments on static and dynamic scene reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy, validating the effectiveness of hierarchical visual encoding and target-time-aware Gaussian querying.

title: Les di una oficina a mis agentes de IA, y ahora mi equipo puede verlos trabajar
description:
Este artículo es la versión en español de I gave my AI coding agents an office, and now my team can watch them work.

Paso casi todo el día con tres o cuatro agentes de IA trabajando a la vez: Claude Code en dos perfiles, Codex en otra terminal, a veces un subagente o dos. Son buena compañía, pero invisible. La única forma de saber que uno lleva cinco minutos esperando mi permiso es revisar terminal por terminal.

Así que les hice una oficina.

deskmates es una oficina pixel-art donde cada sesión de un agente en tu equipo es un personaje en su escritorio. Entra cuando la sesión empieza, escribe mientras edita, lee mientras busca, levanta un signo de pregunta amarillo cuando necesita tu permiso y se va cuando la sesión termina. Los subagentes se sientan al lado del agente que los lanzó y, cuando terminan, pasan por su escritorio con un documento antes de irse.

Es código abierto (MIT) y se instala con un comando:

npm install -g deskmates
deskmates serve      # http://127.0.0.1:47821
deskmates demo       # agentes simulados, por si quieres verlo antes de conectar nada

Cómo entran los agentes

Cada herramienta le cuenta a deskmates lo que hace a su manera, y todo termina convertido en el mismo evento pequeño:

  • Claude Code, mediante hooks. deskmates connect los agrega a la configuración de un perfil, marcados para que disconnect quite solo los suyos. El hook son unas pocas líneas de shell con un tope de 50 ms que siempre termina con código 0: nunca debe frenar a un agente.
  • Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor y Gemini CLI, mediante los archivos de sesión que ya escriben. Sin configuración.
  • Cualquier otra cosa, mediante una pequeña API HTTP de ingesta o un servidor MCP, para que un script, un job de CI u otro agente también pueda entrar.

Desde ahí los datos van en un solo sentido: eventos, deduplicación, un reducer puro que decide quién está trabajando, esperando, libre, dormido o saliendo, y un WebSocket que alimenta la página. La página es un canvas con una simulación de actores encima: caminan por una cuadrícula de casillas, toman descansos en las máquinas expendedoras, se reúnen cuando dos agentes del mismo proyecto están libres, y hay mascotas que pasean entre las salas.

La privacidad fue la primera regla, no la última

Una oficina que muestra lo que hacen tus agentes podría mostrar demasiado con mucha facilidad. Los eventos llevan solo el nombre de una herramienta y un detalle de 120 caracteres como máximo: un nombre de archivo o la primera línea de un comando. Los prompts, el contenido de los archivos y la salida de las herramientas nunca salen de los adaptadores, y el historial diario guarda conteos, no contenido. Nada sale de tu equipo a menos que lo pidas.

Después terminó en el TV de la oficina

Al lado de mi teclado no era donde la quería. La quería en una tablet, y después en la pantalla de la oficina.

deskmates serve --lan la sirve en tu red detrás de un token, imprime un QR en la terminal, y la página tiene un botón para compartir con el mismo QR y un modo kiosco que llena la pantalla. En un TV eso significó aprender sobre píxeles de dispositivo: la oficina se dibuja a escalas enteras para que el pixel art se vea nítido, y el modo kiosco la estira para llenar la pantalla cuando eso importa más.

La oficina compartida

Ver solo a mis agentes me aburrió rápido. Varios de nosotros usamos agentes de programación, así que la última pieza fue una oficina compartida:

# en un equipo al que todos puedan llegar
deskmates serve --lan --shared

# en cada PC
deskmates serve --relay http://lab:47821 --name "Jesús"

Cada PC envía los mismos eventos pequeños a la oficina compartida, donde llegan al piso Headquarters: seis islas de cuatro escritorios, cada una con el color de su PC, una sala de estar, una mesa de reuniones y un café en el medio. Cuando agentes de PCs distintas esperan permiso al mismo tiempo, se van al café a conversar. Es la función más inútil que escribí este año, y mi favorita.

Lo que aprendí

  • Núcleo puro, bordes visuales. El reducer y la escena son funciones deterministas de los eventos y del tiempo. Eso hizo que casi todo se pudiera probar sin navegador, y las pruebas en el navegador comparan capturas píxel por píxel.
  • El piso tuvo que convertirse en datos. La oficina compartida empezó con la misma sala pequeña repetida una al lado de otra. Un solo piso grande obligó a convertir las constantes de la sala en un valor que los temas pueden declarar. Todas las capturas existentes tenían que quedar idénticas mientras eso pasaba, y esa regla atrapó más errores que cualquier revisión.
  • Los agentes revisan código mejor de lo que esperaba, y leen capturas peor que yo. Construí casi todo esto con Claude Code, con un agente nuevo revisando cada cambio. Encontraron errores reales de concurrencia y de casos límite; las imágenes las tuve que mirar yo, una por una.

Pruébalo

  • Repositorio: https://github.com/Jfernandez27/deskmates?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=deskmates
  • Instalación: npm install -g deskmates, después deskmates serve y deskmates connect
  • Node 22.18 o superior

Si trabajas con varios agentes al día, me gustaría saber qué señal extrañas más cuando trabajan en segundo plano. Eso es lo que decide qué aprende la oficina después.

title: Data Residency vs Data Sovereignty: Cloud Architecture Guide 2026
description:
Data residency is about where data is physically stored and processed. Data sovereignty is about whose laws and whose access apply to it. Meeting both comes down to pinning workloads and data to approved locations, controlling who can reach them, and keeping evidence, while still running in more than one location so an outage does not take you down.

TL;DR

Customers and auditors now ask where the data lives, who can access it, and how it stays available during an outage.

  • Define the requirement first. Residency, sovereignty, and localization are different obligations. Name the framework, the data class, and the jurisdiction before choosing a region.
  • GDPR restricts transfers outside the EEA. It does not by itself require EU storage. Contracts, sector rules, and national laws often add stricter location terms.
  • Primary data is the easy part. Backups, replicas, logs, traces, metrics, keys, support access, and AI inference are where data leaves the approved boundary by accident.
  • One region per jurisdiction answers residency but creates an availability risk. Run active-active across two or more approved locations in the same jurisdiction, so failover stays inside the boundary.
  • Match the pattern to the requirement: single region, multi-region in one jurisdiction, per-tenant cells, on-premises or local-provider locations, or a hyperscaler sovereign offering.
  • Keep evidence current: location configuration, access logs, an audit trail, data flow diagrams, subprocessor lists, and certifications.
  • Confirm obligations with counsel. This guide describes architecture and links primary sources. It is not legal advice.

Control Plane runs each workload active-active in every location of a Global Virtual Cloud, so you build one GVC per jurisdiction and failover never leaves it. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, which can be two regions in the same jurisdiction.

Residency vs sovereignty vs localization

Data residency is a location constraint: a regulation, contract, or policy says a dataset must be stored or processed in a defined geography, such as a country or the EU.

Data sovereignty adds legal jurisdiction and operational control: which country’s laws apply, which authorities can compel access, and who can administer the systems that hold the data. Data can be resident in the EU and still be subject to another country’s legal reach if the provider or operator is based elsewhere.

Data localization is residency required by law rather than by contract, usually national, and it is often stricter than contractual terms, for example by prohibiting offshore copies or processing.

A sovereign cloud is an architecture and operating model built to enforce a named set of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational requirements together. A design that satisfies one public-sector framework may not satisfy a financial-services requirement.

Term What it controls What drives it What it means for architecture
Data residency Where data is stored and processed Contracts, customer requirements, regulations Pin workloads, databases, backups, and logs to approved locations
Data sovereignty Which laws apply and who can compel or perform access Jurisdiction of the provider, operator, and data location Control administrative access, keys, and the legal exposure of every party in the stack
Data localization Mandatory in-country storage or processing National law or sector regulator Use in-country locations, sometimes on infrastructure you operate or a local provider
Sovereign cloud A bundle of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational controls A named framework, data class, and jurisdiction Design placement, isolation, keys, access, telemetry, and operations together, then map each control to evidence

The rules that shape architecture

Each row states what the primary source says. Confirm your obligations with counsel.

Rule What the primary source says Architecture implication
GDPR, Chapter V Article 44 says a transfer of personal data to a third country takes place only if the conditions in that chapter are met. Article 45 allows a transfer where the Commission has decided the country ensures an adequate level of protection, with no specific authorisation required. GDPR conditions transfers; these articles do not say data must be stored in the EU. Map every flow that leaves the EEA and name its legal basis.
Adequacy decisions The Commission’s list includes Canada (commercial organisations), Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States for commercial organisations participating in the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Personal data can flow to those countries without further safeguards. Adequacy can make a transfer lawful. Check that US vendors participate in the framework, and keep a fallback transfer mechanism.
Standard contractual clauses Contractual clauses ensuring appropriate safeguards can be a ground for transfers to third countries. The Commission issued modernised SCCs on 4 June 2021. SCCs govern the transfer; they do not change where data sits.
UK GDPR transfers (ICO) The ICO publishes guidance on restricted transfers, adequacy regulations, and safeguards including the UK IDTA and Addendum. UK customers may need UK-specific transfer paperwork in addition to EU paperwork.
GDPR Article 48 (EDPB Guidelines 02/2024) The European Data Protection Board explains how foreign court judgments and administrative decisions requiring disclosure interact with GDPR transfer rules. Data center location and provider jurisdiction are separate variables.
EU Data Act Applicable from 12 September 2025, with switching charges, including certain data-egress charges, phased out from 12 January 2027 (Article 29). Article 32 requires providers to take all adequate technical, organisational and legal measures, including contracts, to prevent third-country governmental access to non-personal data held in the Union where it would conflict with EU or Member State law. Expect questions about government access controls and switching. Portability planning matters.
US CLOUD Act The DOJ describes the Act, enacted in March 2018, as speeding access to electronic information held by US-based global providers and authorizing bilateral agreements; it lists agreements with the UK and Australia. Sovereignty reviews ask about the legal jurisdiction of every provider in the stack, not only the data center location.
HIPAA and cloud (HHS) A covered entity or business associate may use a cloud service for ePHI with a business associate agreement, and both must conduct risk analyses. A provider holding only encrypted ePHI without the key is still a business associate. Location decisions belong in your documented risk analysis and your BAA.
PCI DSS A baseline of technical and operational requirements to protect payment account data, for entities that store, process, or transmit cardholder data. Validation requirements are set by payment brands, acquirers, or other program managers. Scope the cardholder data environment tightly and ask your acquirer and assessor whether any location requirement applies.
Australia, My Health Records Act 2012, s77 Prohibits the System Operator and registered repository, portal, and contracted service providers that hold My Health Record records, or have access to related information, from holding, taking, or processing them outside Australia, or causing or permitting another person to do so, with a narrow exception for non-identifying data. An example of localization written into health law, applying to the providers the Act names.
India, RBI payment data directive The 6 April 2018 directive requires payment system providers to store the entire data relating to the payment systems they operate only in India; data for the foreign leg of a transaction can also be stored abroad. An example of localization in payments that needs in-country locations.

A requirement to keep data in the EU can apply even where GDPR does not impose it. Customer contracts, public-sector procurement rules, sector regulators, and Member State laws can all set stricter location terms, so read the contract, not just the regulation.

Data residency checklist: what has to stay in region

Teams pin the production database to an approved region and consider the job done. Auditors then find copies in other places. Check each item for every workload covered by a residency requirement:

  • Primary data: databases, object storage, and file stores.
  • Backups and snapshots: backup targets and disaster recovery copies can move regulated data outside the boundary even when primary storage is correct.
  • Replicas: read replicas, cross-region replication, and caches.
  • Logs and traces: application logs, request traces, and error reports often contain personal data, tokens, and query parameters.
  • Metrics and analytics: product analytics, session replay, and metrics with user identifiers.
  • Secrets and encryption keys: where keys are held and who can authorize decryption is a sovereignty question.
  • Support and administrative access: who can reach production, from where, under what approval, and with what logging.
  • Processing: compute location matters as much as storage, including AI inference and embedding calls that send customer data to a model endpoint.

Logs, backups, and observability pipelines are frequent sources of accidental cross-border transfers. A centralized logging or monitoring service in another jurisdiction can create a transfer even when production data never moves, so check where each telemetry pipeline sends data first.

Architecture patterns

Single-region deployment per jurisdiction

Run the full stack in one region inside the approved jurisdiction, with a separate copy for each other jurisdiction.

When to use it. Early-stage products, small footprints, and workloads where a short regional outage is acceptable.

Tradeoffs. The simplest way to prove residency and the weakest on availability: a regional outage takes the whole jurisdiction down, and backups kept in the same region share that risk.

Multi-region within one jurisdiction, active-active

Run the same workload in two or more regions inside one jurisdiction, for example two EU regions, and serve live traffic from all of them.

When to use it. Production workloads with both a residency requirement and an availability commitment.

Tradeoffs. It needs data replication that stays inside the boundary, health-based routing, and headroom in each location to absorb a failed one. Every location serves live traffic, so you are not paying for a standby that serves nothing. The active-active high availability guide covers the design.

Cell-based or per-tenant deployments

Deploy independent cells, each holding a set of customers, and route each customer to the cell in their jurisdiction.

When to use it. B2B software with customers in several regulated regions, where some customers contractually require a specific location.

Tradeoffs. Cells give a clear residency story per customer and limit the blast radius of a failure, but every cell needs deployment, monitoring, and upgrades, and a misrouted request is a residency incident. Run all cells with the same tooling.

Hybrid, on-premises, and local-provider locations

Run the strictest workloads in your own data centers or with a national or local provider, and join those locations to cloud regions under one management layer.

When to use it. Localization laws, highly sensitive data, customers who require infrastructure under their own control, and regions where hyperscalers have no suitable location.

Tradeoffs. You gain control over who operates the hardware and where it sits, and you take on capacity planning unless a provider handles it. The common failure is running those locations as a separate stack; see adding a neocloud without running a second stack and hybrid cloud platforms.

Hyperscaler sovereign offerings

Each major provider publishes sovereignty options, described here from their own pages:

  • AWS: the AWS European Sovereign Cloud is described as a new, independent cloud for Europe for stringent data residency, operational autonomy, and resiliency requirements, alongside Dedicated Local Zones placed in a customer-specified location.
  • Microsoft: the EU Data Boundary commits to processing and storing EU and EFTA customer data in region, and Microsoft Sovereign Cloud includes a Sovereign Private Cloud for hybrid or fully disconnected environments with Azure Local.
  • Google Cloud: Google Cloud’s sovereign cloud offerings include a Data Boundary that stores core customer data in the chosen region with logged administrative access, Google Cloud Dedicated run by a local partner (S3NS in France), and Google Distributed Cloud for on-premises use, connected or air-gapped.

Tradeoffs. These address placement and operations inside one provider’s ecosystem. If you also need other providers or your own data centers, you still need a layer that manages them together; see how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

Data residency and high availability together

A single-region deployment is a residency answer and an availability risk. When that region fails, the options are to wait or to fail over somewhere that may break the residency commitment, and teams under pressure often choose the second. Active-standby inside the jurisdiction helps, but the standby bills for capacity that serves no traffic and is often not tested under real load.

Active-active across two or more approved locations in the same jurisdiction removes that tradeoff. Every location is proven under production load, and when one becomes unhealthy, traffic shifts to locations that are already inside the boundary, so a failover never becomes a residency exception. Keep replication, backups, logs, and keys inside the same boundary. For what each design can deliver, see five nines availability architecture.

Proving it

Auditors and customer security teams ask for evidence, and they ask repeatedly, so build the evidence trail as you build the system.

Evidence What it shows How to keep it current
Location configuration The approved locations each workload can run in Store it as code and review changes like any other change
Access logs Who accessed systems and data, and from where Centralize inside the boundary and set retention to match contracts
Audit trail Every administrative action, tamper-resistant Generate it automatically
Data flow diagrams Where data moves, including backups, logs, and third parties Update with each architecture change and review quarterly
Subprocessor list Every vendor that touches the data and where it operates Review on onboarding and vendor changes, and notify customers as contracts require
Certifications and reports Independent assessment of controls Track expiry, scope, and version, and confirm the scope covers the service you use

Treat the location configuration as the source of truth and generate diagrams from it where you can. Then test the boundary: try to deploy a workload to an unapproved location in staging and confirm it is refused.

How Control Plane helps with data residency and sovereignty

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, on-premises, and bare-metal location into one Global Virtual Cloud (GVC).

  • You choose the locations. A workload deployed to a GVC runs only in that GVC’s locations, active-active in every one, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. Build each GVC from locations in one jurisdiction, and use separate GVCs for separate jurisdictions.
  • Residency and resilience in one design. Every location in a GVC serves live traffic, so you get active-active failover inside your boundary without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be two regions in the same jurisdiction, on one provider or on different providers.
  • Proven in an outage. During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.
  • Infrastructure you control. Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) and Managed Kubernetes let your own clusters, your own servers, on-premises data centers, or a local or national provider join a GVC as locations, managed alongside cloud regions.
  • Use regional cloud services in place. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, so workloads can use databases and key management services you keep in the same jurisdiction.
  • Controls that produce evidence. Mutual TLS between workloads, secrets management, fine-grained access policies, and a tamper-proof audit trail, plus autoscaling, readiness-gated rollouts, automatic TLS certificates, and unified logs, metrics, and traces, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate.
  • Compliance. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant, so the platform layer comes with its own compliance evidence to add to yours.

FAQ

What is data residency?

A requirement that data be stored or processed in a specific geography, such as a country or the EU. It comes from regulations, contracts, or internal policy, and it applies to every copy of the data, including backups, replicas, and logs.

What is the difference between data residency, data sovereignty, and data localization?

Residency is where data is stored and processed, sovereignty is which laws apply and who can compel access, and localization is residency required by national law.

What is a sovereign cloud?

An architecture and operating model that enforces a named set of residency, jurisdiction, access, and operational requirements together. AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud publish sovereign offerings, and you can also assemble one from regional locations, local providers, and infrastructure you operate.

Does a sovereign cloud require dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure?

Not always. The framework, data class, jurisdiction, and threat model decide whether shared regional infrastructure is acceptable or dedicated infrastructure under your control is required.

How do I keep customer data in the EU on AWS, GCP, or Azure?

Choose EU regions for every workload and data store, apply the same rule to backups, replicas, telemetry, and keys, and use each provider’s policy controls to block deployment outside approved regions. On Control Plane, a GVC built from EU locations keeps every workload replica in those locations, across one provider or several.

Does GDPR require data to stay in the EU?

GDPR’s transfer articles set conditions for moving personal data to third countries, such as adequacy decisions and standard contractual clauses; they do not require EU storage. Contracts, sector rules, and national laws can.

Can I have data residency and high availability at the same time?

Yes. Run active-active across at least two approved locations in the same jurisdiction so failover stays inside the boundary. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, which can be two regions in the same jurisdiction.

What data residency requirements apply to healthcare and payments data?

HIPAA guidance centers on a business associate agreement and a documented risk analysis, and PCI DSS sets security requirements with validation set by acquirers and payment brands. Some countries add localization law, such as Australia’s My Health Records Act and India’s RBI payment data directive.

How do I prove data residency to an auditor or customer?

Provide location configuration, data flow diagrams that include backups and telemetry, access logs, an audit trail of administrative actions, a subprocessor list with locations, and current certifications, matched to the framework being tested.

Can I add a region for a new market without rebuilding my application?

Yes, if your platform treats locations as configuration. On Control Plane you add an approved location to a GVC or create a new GVC for that jurisdiction, and the workload definition does not change. Plan data replication and telemetry for the new jurisdiction.

Next step: bring your residency requirements and current architecture, and the Control Plane team will map them to a GVC layout per jurisdiction that stays up when a region fails. Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.
