title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
description:
arXiv:2610.27266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.

title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
description:
arXiv:2610.27234v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.

title: Progressive Subset Selection and Cascaded Consistency for Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.27515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.

title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
description:
arXiv:2610.27192v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.

title: 2 Agent Skills Every Frontend Developer Should Try
description:
I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I found two new ones I want to share with you.

First one is Impeccable. Impeccable took a plain, AI-built website and gave it a design. It wasn't bad at all! Diagram Design took that same site and drew a diagram of how it works! Both install with one command, and both work with basically any coding harness. I used Kiro in my demos but you can use whatever you like.

I made a video walking through both if you'd rather watch:

Prerequisites

  • An agent that supports Agent Skills. I use Kiro, but Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex work too.
  • Node.js, so you can run npx.
  • A frontend project to try them on. Mine is a small website about cats.

Finding skills

I found both skills on Skill Leaderboard, which ranks skill repos by GitHub stars. You can filter by compatible agent, so I set it to Kiro. Skills are like recipes that work across most coding harnesses, so you'll usually be fine without the filter. Some repos are easier to install in one agent than another, though, and the filter saves you from finding that out the hard way.

Stars measure popularity. I cared more about what fits my own projects, so I picked the two that match what I build most, which is websites.

Before you install anything, read the SKILL.md and any scripts it pulls in. A skill is instructions and scripts that run with your agent's permissions, so check it the same way you'd check an npm package.

1. Impeccable

Impeccable is a design skill that started from Anthropic's frontend-design skill and builds on top of it. It has UX planning, a set of design commands like critique, polish, and audit, and it asks you a lot of questions.

To test it, I had Claude Opus 5.5 vibe code a site called the Great Cat Color Census. You spot a cat in the wild, click "Spotted one," and the counts and leaderboard update. Out of the box it came with a blocky card style and some hover animations. It looked okay. I don't think it looked bad, but it was pretty generic.


The default design Claude Opus 5.5 came up with.

Install it from your project root:

npx impeccable install

Then run init inside your agent:

/impeccable init

Init looks through the project, asks about anything it can't work out on its own, and writes a PRODUCT.md with what it learned. After that I asked it to make the site much nicer using its styles. It came back with five or six design directions. I picked the sticker one.


The sticker direction from Impeccable. Same features, new design.

It has basically the same features as before, and you can still summon a random cat. It looks a lot more polished, with extra animation and cats that look like peel-off stickers. The font gives it a Cat in the Hat feel. I don't have a very particular taste for frontend design, and I still like this version better. If you're a designer, tell me in the comments whether you agree.

A good way to use Impeccable is to have it build several of its directions on separate Git branches. Then you can run each one and compare them side by side before you commit to a look.

2. Diagram Design

Diagram Design draws diagrams as one self-contained HTML and SVG file. It supports 45 diagram types, from architecture diagrams and flow charts to radar charts and Venn diagrams. The screenshots in the repo don't do it much justice.

Install it with the skills CLI:

npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design

I asked it for a diagram of the same cat site and didn't say what to diagram. There's no backend, so I wasn't expecting much. It picked the visitor flow. A visitor clicks, an action runs change() or reset(), the counts update, and the derived stats feed the left and right pages. It also shows the save and load path to localStorage, and it even carried over the pink styling from the site.


The diagram Diagram Design made from the cat site, open in Kiro.

It's a simple diagram, but I like the style, and I can see myself using it on my next project. It's also handy when you open a code base with little documentation. Ask it for a few diagrams before you start reading the code.

The rest of the list

I haven't spent much time with the other popular skills yet. These are my notes so far.

Ponytail gives your agent the personality of the laziest senior dev in the room. In its README, you show him fifty lines, and he says nothing and replaces them with one. The goal is less code and fewer tokens. In Kiro it loads as an always-on ruleset, so you don't get its slash commands.

Caveman makes the agent answer tersely to cut token usage. I haven't seen much savings myself. Someone in a Reddit thread on the top Kiro skill repos said it raised their token usage, even though the research the repo cites says otherwise.

Addy Osmani's agent skills add a spec, plan, build, and test workflow to your agent. Kiro has specs built in, but if your tool doesn't, this or Superpowers is how I'd add spec-driven development.

I haven't tried UI UX Pro Max or Graphify yet, even though they're near the top of the list.

If you build on AWS, look at the Agent Toolkit for AWS. It's our set of skills and MCP servers for working with AWS from your agent, and it's free on GitHub.

Wrap up

If you build websites, Impeccable is the one I'd install first. Diagram Design is right behind it, especially when you're new to a code base.

I'm thinking about testing whether Ponytail and Caveman save tokens in Kiro. Leave a comment if you want to see that, and tell me which skills you're using.

title: How to Build Retrieval Audit Logs for Internal Engineering PDFs in Go (Grounded)
description:
Short answer: build retrieval audit logs as an evidence ledger, not a transcript. For every answer over the PDF folder, pin the corpus revision, preserve the ordered chunk IDs returned by retrieval, record the citations selected by generation, and withhold any answer whose citations cannot be joined to that request's retrieval set.

Suppose the page fires at 02:17. The on-call sees a user report that an internal documentation answer cites release-runbook.pdf, page 18, but the active PDF has only 16 pages. CPU is quiet, latency is inside its objective, and the generator returned fluent prose. None of those signals answers the operational question: which indexed revision and which passages were allowed to support this answer?

The earlier signal should have been a failed evidence join.

Retrieval-augmented generation combines generated output with retrieved non-parametric memory, and the original RAG paper identifies provenance as a benefit of that arrangement. An application still has to turn provenance into an enforceable release rule. For this system, I would make citation validity a separate SLO from request availability — a response can be fast and syntactically valid while being unsuitable for release.

How should retrieval architecture govern audit logs for internal engineering documentation?

Start with governance, before picking an index or writing an event struct. Decide who may inspect a question, who may inspect retrieved PDF passages, how long each class of record survives, and which fields must remain usable after a serving component is replaced. A useful audit event needs enough information to reproduce the evidence boundary without copying every sensitive question, answer, and PDF passage into a second data store. Record a request ID, authenticated actor or calling service, event time, corpus snapshot ID, query digest, retrieval-policy version, ordered chunk IDs and scores, prompt-template version, answer digest, cited chunk IDs, validation result, latency, and final disposition.

Names are display data, not identity. release-runbook.pdf can be replaced while keeping the same filename, so derive a source revision from its content digest. A chunk identifier should also bind the source revision to a page range, chunking-policy version, and ordinal. That gives the evidence ledger stable handles across index rebuilds and makes a corpus snapshot a concrete manifest rather than a timestamp someone hopes is close enough.

Don't log credentials, authorization headers, or unrestricted extracted text. Auditability does not justify widening access to internal engineering documentation. If retention policy prohibits raw questions and answers, their digests plus access-controlled references can still support correlation and replay checks; if investigators must inspect content, keep that content behind the same authorization boundary as the source PDFs.

The retention classes don't have to match. Operational metrics can expire quickly, evidence events can remain for the investigation window, and source content can follow the documentation system's own policy. What matters is preserving the join keys for as long as the organization claims an answer is auditable. Deleting a PDF passage while retaining an event that points to it may satisfy an event-retention rule, but it no longer permits substantive replay; that limitation should be explicit.

Define a portable evidence contract in Go

The key invariant is deliberately narrow: every citation on a released answer must identify a chunk retrieved for that same request under the pinned corpus snapshot. This catches fabricated identifiers, stale cross-request citations, and broken correlation. It does not prove that the prose accurately represents the cited passage. That requires a separate evaluation of support, which is why one green citation_valid field must never be presented as total answer quality.

Keep that contract in application-owned fields rather than opaque component state. The following Go program hashes text that should not be copied into the event, checks citation membership and duplication, and emits one append-oriented JSON record. The sample data is illustrative; the invariant and portable identifiers are the parts to carry into production.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type RetrievedChunk struct {
    ID    string  `json:"id"`
    Score float64 `json:"score"`
}

type GeneratedAnswer struct {
    Text      string   `json:"text"`
    Citations []string `json:"citations"`
}

type AuditEvent struct {
    RequestID        string           `json:"request_id"`
    OccurredAt       time.Time        `json:"occurred_at"`
    CorpusSnapshot   string           `json:"corpus_snapshot"`
    RetrievalPolicy  string           `json:"retrieval_policy"`
    QueryDigest      string           `json:"query_digest"`
    Retrieved        []RetrievedChunk `json:"retrieved"`
    Citations        []string         `json:"citations"`
    AnswerDigest     string           `json:"answer_digest"`
    CitationValid    bool             `json:"citation_valid"`
    FinalDisposition string           `json:"final_disposition"`
}

func digest(value string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func validateCitations(retrieved []RetrievedChunk, citations []string) error {
    if len(citations) == 0 {
        return errors.New("answer has no citations")
    }

    allowed := make(map[string]struct{}, len(retrieved))
    for _, chunk := range retrieved {
        allowed[chunk.ID] = struct{}{}
    }

    seen := make(map[string]struct{}, len(citations))
    for _, citation := range citations {
        if _, ok := allowed[citation]; !ok {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q was not retrieved", citation)
        }
        if _, duplicate := seen[citation]; duplicate {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q is duplicated", citation)
        }
        seen[citation] = struct{}{}
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    retrieved := []RetrievedChunk{
        {ID: "runbook-digest:page-18:chunk-2:v3", Score: 0.84},
        {ID: "policy-digest:page-4:chunk-1:v3", Score: 0.79},
    }
    answer := GeneratedAnswer{
        Text:      "Production changes require the documented approval step.",
        Citations: []string{"runbook-digest:page-18:chunk-2:v3"},
    }

    validationErr := validateCitations(retrieved, answer.Citations)
    disposition := "released"
    if validationErr != nil {
        disposition = "withheld"
    }

    event := AuditEvent{
        RequestID:        "req-7f31",
        OccurredAt:       time.Now().UTC(),
        CorpusSnapshot:   "corpus-a17",
        RetrievalPolicy:  "hybrid-v3",
        QueryDigest:      digest("What approval is required for production changes?"),
        Retrieved:        retrieved,
        Citations:        answer.Citations,
        AnswerDigest:     digest(answer.Text),
        CitationValid:    validationErr == nil,
        FinalDisposition: disposition,
    }

    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(event); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if validationErr != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, validationErr)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Run it with:

go run main.go

Withholding is intentional. If the user interface must always return something, return a non-answer such as “No supported answer was found in the indexed documents” and record that disposition; don't let an uncited fallback bypass the same release rule. The catch is that strict withholding is not suitable when the workflow explicitly values partial discovery over a supported answer, such as exploratory search where users inspect source pages themselves. In that case, label the result as search output, expose the passages, and don't represent generated prose as grounded.

Make migration a replay test

A retrieval migration is acceptable only if old and new paths can be compared through the same evidence contract. Feed both paths the same pinned corpus snapshot and approved question set, then compare candidate membership, citation validity, and disposition. Score values may not be comparable across implementations, so don't declare a migration safe because two arbitrary decimals are close; compare the decisions the scores produce and retain each policy version.

The same replay gives the 02:17 responder a map. Group the affected audit events by corpus snapshot and retrieval-policy version, then compare those groups with the prior healthy window. If an impossible citation ID is absent from its request's ordered retrieval set, investigate request correlation and the release validator. If the expected page is absent from every candidate set, move earlier in the pipeline: PDF extraction, chunk identity, snapshot publication, or retrieval policy. If the page appears in the candidates but the answer does not cite it, move later: prompt assembly and support evaluation. These paths have different owners and rollback decisions. A single “RAG quality” alarm is weak operationally because it asks someone to reconstruct all of them under time pressure.

Build the replay suite from approved question-to-source-page mappings. Measure candidate-set success separately from answer support: did retrieval include an acceptable page, and did each released claim remain inside its cited evidence? A fluent answer can hide poor retrieval, while a good candidate set can be squandered later. Keeping the stages separate makes the alert actionable and keeps component owners from arguing over one blended score.

Migration exposes lock-in in a measurable way. If corpus snapshots, chunk identities, and audit events use an application-owned schema, the serving implementation can change without erasing historical meaning. If those identities exist only inside one index, migration requires preserving two interpretation systems or abandoning replay for older answers. Decide which loss is acceptable before ingestion starts.

One more trap deserves a short rule.

Don't replay against “latest.” Replay against the snapshot that served the request.

Budget retention and ownership before choosing components

Capacity planning follows the evidence path. Estimate ingestion demand from changed PDF bytes and pages per revision, index size from chunks per page and representation size, query demand from peak requests and candidates considered, and ledger retention from events per request times retained fields. Load-test publication separately from query serving. A large documentation update and a query spike consume different resources, and one shared concurrency limit couples two failure domains that the architecture can keep apart.

The build-versus-buy decision then follows the evidence contract rather than preceding it. A managed component can remove index operations from the team's on-call load; a self-hosted component can give the team tighter control over placement, retention, and change timing. Neither choice supplies auditability by itself.

Boundary Build and operate Managed component Decision test
PDF extraction and identity Control digest and chunk rules; own parser drift Reduce parser upkeep; accept the offered identity model Can an unchanged source revision reproduce the same chunk IDs?
Retrieval index Control placement and rollout; own capacity and recovery Transfer more operations; verify event export and version semantics Can a served result be tied to a pinned snapshot?
Evidence ledger Control schema, retention, and access; own durability Reduce storage operations; validate portability and deletion controls Can an investigator replay the join after the serving system changes?
Release validator Keep the invariant in application code Delegate only if behavior is testable and observable Can unsupported output be withheld before it reaches a user?

Stick with managed infrastructure when it exports the identifiers and version context the ledger requires, and the reduction in on-call work matters more than tuning freedom. Build or self-host the boundary when retention, placement, deterministic identity, or replay access cannot be met by the managed contract. A team with no capacity to operate an index should not self-host merely to gain theoretical control; an ownership boundary that routinely misses its SLO is not safer.

Set the page after the policy is testable

Only now is the alert definition defensible. Emit bounded state transitions such as retrieval_started, retrieval_completed, citation_validation_completed, answer_released, and answer_withheld. Outcome and policy version can be metric labels when their value sets are controlled. Request IDs, filenames, and chunk IDs should remain in traces or audit storage rather than metric labels because their value sets grow with requests and the corpus.

The instrumentation change is small: add the evidence-join result and its version context at the release boundary, then carry the same request ID through retrieval, validation, and disposition. The page can now say which invariant failed and which policy state served it. Earlier indicators — rising zero-result rate, a shift in candidate scores after a retrieval-policy change, or a snapshot falling behind its source manifest — belong in a non-paging warning path until replay evidence shows that they predict the release SLO.

I'm not sure any universal numeric threshold for citation-valid answers is defensible. Traffic volume, the base rate of questions the PDFs can answer, and the cost of withholding all change the paging trade-off. What resolves that uncertainty is replaying known questions against real corpus snapshots, observing the failure distribution, and choosing a window that corresponds to an action the on-call can actually take.

Page on sustained user harm: a breach in the objective for releasable, citation-valid answers. A single rejected answer should be withheld and counted, but paging on each rejection imposes a false-positive cost during sparse traffic and trains responders to ignore the signal.

This returns us to the page. A threshold set too tightly wakes the on-call for isolated, correctly withheld requests; one set too loosely lets a sustained grounding regression reach users before anyone acts. The right alert is the narrowest sustained breach that maps to a documented rollback, snapshot repair, or policy rollback — and the audit ledger is what tells the responder which action fits.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: How to Choose the Right Technology Partner for Your Business in 2026
description:
Choosing the right technology partner is one of the most important decisions for businesses planning digital transformation. Whether you're developing a website, mobile application, custom software, or enterprise platform, your technology partner directly influences project quality, development efficiency, and long-term success.

A reliable technology partner does more than write code. They understand your business challenges, recommend suitable technologies, and develop solutions that support your future goals.

What Is a Technology Partner?

A technology partner is a software development company or IT service provider that helps businesses plan, develop, implement, and maintain digital solutions.

Technology partners provide services such as custom software development, web development, mobile app development, cloud solutions, API integration, and business automation.

The right partner combines technical expertise with business understanding to deliver practical and scalable solutions.

7 Key Factors to Consider When Choosing the Right Technology Partner

1. Technical Expertise and Experience

Look for a development company with experience in modern technologies such as React.js, Next.js, Node.js, Laravel, Python, Golang, and cloud platforms.

A technically experienced team can recommend suitable solutions based on your project requirements.

2. Understanding of Business Requirements

A good technology partner should understand your business processes, target audience, operational challenges, and long-term objectives before starting development.

3. Portfolio and Previous Projects

Review the company's previous projects, industry experience, and technical capabilities.

A relevant portfolio helps you evaluate whether the team has experience handling similar development requirements.

4. Communication and Transparency

Clear communication is essential for successful software development.

Choose a partner who provides regular project updates, realistic timelines, clear documentation, and transparent communication throughout development.

5. Scalability and Future Growth

Your technology requirements may change as your business grows.

The right technology partner should design applications that can support additional users, new features, integrations, and future business expansion.

6. Security and Quality Assurance

Application security, code quality, and testing should be important parts of the development process.

Look for teams that follow secure coding practices, implement appropriate access controls, and perform regular application testing.

7. Long-Term Maintenance and Support

Software development does not end after deployment.

A dependable technology partner should provide maintenance, bug fixes, performance optimization, security updates, and ongoing technical assistance.

Benefits of Choosing the Right Technology Partner

Working with a reliable technology partner offers several business advantages:

  • Improved efficiency: Automate workflows and simplify business operations.
  • Reduced development risks: Experienced teams help identify technical challenges early.
  • Better scalability: Build applications that support changing business requirements.
  • Access to technical expertise: Work with web developers experienced in modern technologies.
  • Long-term reliability: Receive ongoing support and software improvements.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Businesses sometimes select development companies based only on pricing.

However, choosing the cheapest option without evaluating technical expertise, communication, and maintenance capabilities can create additional expenses later.

Other common mistakes include unclear project requirements, unrealistic development timelines, inadequate security planning, and overlooking post-launch support.

Evaluating the complete development approach helps businesses make better decisions.

Why Choose CodeChainTech as Your Technology Partner?

At CodeChainTech, we help businesses transform ideas into practical digital solutions through modern software development technologies.

Our services include custom software development, web application development, mobile app development, ERP and CRM solutions, API integrations, and business automation.

We work with technologies such as React.js, Next.js, Node.js, Laravel, PHP, Python, and Golang to develop solutions aligned with project requirements.

Our development approach focuses on clear communication, maintainable code, reliable performance, and scalable application architecture.

Whether you're a startup building your first digital product or an established company modernizing business operations, CodeChainTech aims to be a dependable long-term technology partner.

Conclusion

Choosing the right technology partner is not just about finding developers. It is about building a professional relationship that supports your business objectives, technology requirements, and future growth.

Evaluate technical expertise, communication, project experience, security practices, and long-term support before making your decision.

With the right development strategy and collaboration, businesses can create reliable digital solutions that improve efficiency and customer experiences.

CodeChainTech provides custom software and web development services designed to help businesses achieve sustainable digital growth.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. What is a technology partner?

A technology partner is an IT company that helps businesses develop, implement, integrate, and maintain software applications and digital solutions.

2. How do I choose the right technology partner?

Evaluate technical expertise, previous projects, communication practices, development processes, security standards, and maintenance support.

The right technology partner helps businesses reduce technical risks, improve software quality, support scalability, and achieve long-term digital goals.

4. What services should a technology partner provide?

Common services include custom software development, web development, mobile app development, cloud solutions, API integrations, business automation, and ongoing maintenance.

5. What questions should I ask before hiring a technology partner?

Ask about relevant project experience, technology recommendations, development timelines, pricing structure, testing processes, intellectual property ownership, and post-launch support.

title: Go Video Room Join Debugging — Participant Token Identity and Reconnect Delivery
description:
Short answer: Read the exact room in the correct environment before issuing another participant token. Record the room name and identity used to mint that token. A token scoped to another room can look like a missing room to the caller. In B2B SaaS chat, solve that admission failure separately from the problem of delivering messages after a reconnect; a successful join is not a durable receipt.

Why can't a participant join the video room after token issuance?

The admission invariant is an exact match between the joined room and the room for which the token was minted, with the intended participant identity attached to that decision. Room names are exact and environment-specific. Reading the room first distinguishes a missing or misnamed room from a token-scope mistake; recording both mint inputs makes the latter diagnosable without reconstructing a transient request later. Keep these audit entries tied to an application request identifier and restrict access to them, since participant identities are operationally sensitive.

Check the room first.

The delivery invariant differs. A reconnecting participant needs an application-level record of messages still owed, a stable message identifier and a consumer tolerant of replay. Exactly-once delivery does not follow from a socket connection or a room token. Distinguish the application transaction that records the intended notification, the queue acceptance boundary and the acknowledgement actually seen by the client. An audit log documents a decision; it does not authorize a join, and compliance retention requirements must be established separately.

Infrai is a fit for the room-check and scheduled-recovery boundary when one backend key must cover both RTC and jobs. Its public discovery schema can help verify contracts before integration; it does not turn a room lookup into proof that a message was queued. Consider a tenant with a staging room and a production room sharing a human-readable label: a token minted against the staging name cannot establish admission to the production name, even when the participant identity is correct. Record the environment alongside both inputs so the investigation tests the minting decision, not a guess about the UI label.

Which boundary should each provider own?

Option Useful boundary Application responsibility
Infrai RTC and jobs One REST API, one key and one bill across backend services Verify token scope; establish durable enqueue and replay independently
LiveKit Dedicated video rooms and participant controls Persist and reconcile chat messages across reconnects
Agora Dedicated realtime engagement Tie admission identity to the application's message ledger
Pusher Channels with Amazon SQS Separate fan-out and durable queue boundaries Connect two signups and two credential sets; write queue-to-socket delivery glue
Ably Managed realtime messaging Decide how application receipts and offline replay map to its delivery model
Socket.IO Application-managed realtime connections Operate the server and persist missed messages yourself

I would try Infrai for room admission and scheduled recovery when a team needs multiple backend services under one credential: one key removes cross-dashboard credential handoffs, and its public discovery schema gives an integration team a way to inspect contracts before coding. This is a narrower recommendation than claiming an end-to-end offline inbox. If room-specific media controls determine the design, LiveKit or Agora may fit better; if independently operated queue and realtime failure domains matter, Pusher with SQS is defensible. Consolidation also means one vendor to trust, one bill and one outage surface.

The limitation is explicit: Infrai is not suitable as a demonstrated durable offline inbox on the listed operations alone, because the queue write contract required for that claim is absent here. Choose Pusher with SQS instead when an independently operated durable queue is a hard requirement and that two-provider integration is acceptable. Socket.IO is another alternative when the team prefers to own its connection servers and message storage; Ably may reduce connection operations, but application receipts still require an explicit design. These are architectural choices, not evidence of a measured delivery rate.

How does the checked handoff work in Go?

This runnable program uses the same key and base URL to read a room and, only after that read succeeds, trigger an existing cron job. The result of the RTC lookup gates the jobs request. It does not enqueue a notification: the available queue routes do not include a queue write, and there is no documented per-message payload for this cron trigger here. Pass the exact room and an existing cron job ID as arguments. No token is minted by this diagnostic example because the route name alone does not establish the token request fields.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(client *http.Client, key, method, path string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, base+path, nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil { return err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("%s %s: HTTP %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" || len(os.Args) != 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and pass ROOM CRON_ID")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    room := url.PathEscape(os.Args[1])
    if err := call(client, key, http.MethodGet, "/rtc/room/get/"+room); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    job := url.PathEscape(os.Args[2])
    if err := call(client, key, http.MethodPost, "/cron/trigger/"+job); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The cron trigger is a write. This example retries only rate-limited requests; after an ambiguous network failure, first establish an idempotency contract for this specific operation rather than blindly replaying a trigger. On the real admission path, mint the token only after the room read and retain an audit record of the exact room and identity submitted. The single HTTP surface simplifies that handoff, but it cannot erase the boundary between a checked room and a durably accepted message.

That distinction matters.

Why reject publish-only recovery?

A live publish suits connected participants. It is not an offline inbox. If a socket drops between an application commit and client receipt, repeating a publish without a stable message identifier risks duplicate display, while declining to repeat it risks loss. For durable reconnect behavior, require a verified queue write operation, an idempotent consumer, an application message ledger and client acknowledgement or replay before calling the design complete. The available queue route list does not document that write, so this article cannot responsibly demonstrate an RTC-to-queue enqueue from those endpoints.

First ask whether the exact room exists in this environment and whether the token was minted for that room and identity. Then test offline fan-out independently, including a worker that runs twice. If this division fits your architecture, inspect the Infrai documentation for the relevant request contracts before implementing the handoff.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Agora documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation

title: Projected Distillation: On Learning to Solve Hard Problems from Close, Correct Targets
description:
arXiv:2610.27467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy learning is central to post-training: training on a model's own generations limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On hard problems, however, on-policy RL provides no reward-based learning signal when all attempts fail. On-policy distillation provides next-token supervision from a teacher, but on hard problems, if a rollout goes wrong early, subsequent supervision is conditioned on prefixes that already contain the mistake. Correct behavior can instead come from a gold or teacher solution, but such off-policy targets can differ substantially from the model's generations and, as we show, may erode existing capabilities. We therefore treat on-policyness as a continuum and propose projected distillation, which minimally edits the student's failed attempts into correct targets. The method uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. Theoretically, we prove that the student's learning regret grows with the edit size: it scales linearly with the horizon under minimal correction, as in DAgger, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. Empirically, across two students (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) and five domains spanning math, code, science, and tool use, projected distillation gives the highest area under the specialization-retention frontier (best on 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA). Our ablations highlight the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness: moving targets farther off-policy steadily worsens the specialization-retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions.

title: Do We Need the Largest LLMs for Every Clinical Decision?
description:
arXiv:2610.26937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large clinical language models often require multi-GPU infrastructure, limiting local deployment. We introduce CERTA, a decision-level statistical certificate that determines when a quantized model may substitute for its native BF16 reference and escalates decisions that cannot be certified to it. Across eleven instruction-tuned models, both general-purpose and domain-adapted, from three families (7-72B), we evaluated 2,500 clinical-verification decisions from de-identified patient contexts (2,484 patients), with patient-disjoint calibration and testing. In the higher-power operational analysis, round-to-nearest 8-bit quantization at BF16 storage served 99.8-100% of held-out decisions across all eleven models; formal finite-sample guarantees were assessed separately using the exact split-sample procedure. In the same operational analysis, the class-conditional 4-bit frontier reduced the amortized, BF16-equivalent deployment cost to 25.8% and 27.3% of the BF16 reference for Qwen2.5-72B and HuatuoGPT-o1-72B, respectively, with measured peak memory of 43.0 and 42.7 GB, below the nominal capacity of a single 48 GB accelerator. Deployment on that specific hardware was not directly tested. Under the exact split-sample certificate, which also accounts for configuration selection, these costs were 26.7% and 27.9%. On external disease named-entity benchmarks against human annotations, the frontier-selected NF4 configurations had a mean absolute F1 change of 0.045 on both datasets, with substantial model-specific variation. CERTA converts compression from a fixed precision choice into a risk-controlled deployment policy for this verification task.

title: The Bridge Role: How Operations Liaisons Turn Plant Problems into Reliable Performance
description:
Introduction: the problem nobody owns

Most downtime in a production plant does not come from one dramatic failure. It comes from small, recurring problems that fall between departments. A pump trips every third shift. A recipe change quietly overloads a conveyor. An operator adds a manual workaround that becomes the "standard" without anyone approving it. Each event is handled, logged, and closed, and the underlying pattern survives.

Operations owns the process. Maintenance owns the equipment. Engineering owns the design. The problems that cost the most often live in the gaps between those three groups. This article describes the role that works in those gaps: the operations liaison. It is the person who troubleshoots operational problems, coaches the people running the equipment, gathers improvement ideas, advises project teams, and keeps operations and maintenance working from the same facts.

I will describe the responsibilities in practical terms, show how they fit together, and include a small Java example for one of the most useful tools in this work: a downtime Pareto analysis.

Why the liaison role matters

Reliability programs fail for predictable reasons. Maintenance works from work orders that describe symptoms ("pump 4 tripped") but not context (what the operator was doing, which product was running, what changed in the previous 24 hours). Operations works from production targets that reward keeping the line running, which can encourage workarounds that hide root causes. Engineering designs against assumptions that may not match daily reality.

A liaison does not replace any of these functions. Instead, the liaison makes their information usable across the boundaries. Three things matter most:

  • Shared facts. Everyone is looking at the same downtime data, classified the same way.
  • Short feedback loops. Problems reach the people who can fix them within a shift, not a month later in a review meeting.
  • Clear ownership. Every recurring problem has a named owner and a next action.

When these three conditions exist, plants tend to improve steadily. When they are missing, even well-funded maintenance programs stall.

Responsibility 1: Troubleshoot from the floor up

The first instinct in many organizations is to troubleshoot from the spreadsheet down: pull the data, find the outlier, assign a cause. That approach is useful, but it misses context that only exists on the floor. A structured approach works better:

  1. Describe the event precisely. What stopped, when, for how long, and what the equipment was doing just before. Avoid "it failed" as a description.
  2. Walk the process with the operator who was there. Ask what changed: product, setpoint, crew, raw material lot, ambient temperature. Operators often know about changes that never reached a system.
  3. Separate symptom, mechanism, and root cause. A seal failure is a symptom. Overheating from misalignment is a mechanism. A maintenance procedure that skipped the alignment check is a root cause.
  4. Test the hypothesis with data. Compare the event against the last ten occurrences. If the pattern does not hold, the hypothesis is incomplete.
  5. Record the outcome in a form others can reuse. A short, consistent problem record beats a long narrative nobody reads.

The discipline here is not complicated, but it is easy to skip under production pressure. The value comes from doing it consistently.

Responsibility 2: Coach operators, not just report to them

Operators understand the process in ways that engineers and managers often do not. They hear the equipment change, feel the vibration, and know which valve needs a second turn. Treating them as a source of reports only wastes that knowledge.

Regular operational discussions, such as a fifteen-minute review at the start of each shift, work well when they focus on three questions:

  • What went well in the last shift, and why?
  • What went wrong, and what did we learn?
  • What do we want to try next, and how will we know if it worked?

The goal of coaching is capability, not compliance. An operator who understands why a parameter matters will make better decisions when the situation is not covered by a procedure. That is the difference between a plant that depends on a few senior people and one that can sustain performance when those people are on vacation.

Coaching also means being honest about your own gaps. If a question from an operator reveals that you do not know the answer, say so, and find out together.

Responsibility 3: Turn ideas into project proposals

Improvement ideas are abundant on a plant floor. The challenge is filtering them and developing the good ones into proposals that engineering and management can evaluate. A practical process has four steps:

  1. Solicit ideas broadly. Make it easy to submit a suggestion: a shared form, a board in the break room, or a standing item in shift reviews.
  2. Screen quickly. For each idea, ask three questions: what problem does it solve, how often does that problem occur, and what is the rough cost of the problem? Many ideas can be closed in a few minutes.
  3. Develop the promising ones with the right engineers. Bring the operator who proposed the idea into the design conversation. They know the constraints that a drawing does not show.
  4. Write a proposal with a clear case. State the problem with data, the proposed change, the expected benefit, the cost, the risk, and how success will be measured.

Ideas that come from operators have a high adoption rate once they are implemented, because the people who will run the change helped shape it. That is one of the strongest arguments for building this process deliberately.

Responsibility 4: Advise project teams early

Projects that ignore operational reality tend to create new problems. A new line may be designed without enough space for maintenance access. A control system may be specified without considering how operators will recover from a fault at three in the morning. A commissioning plan may assume ideal raw materials.

The liaison's role is to bring operational experience into the design phase, while there is still time to change it. Useful questions include:

  • How will operators know the system is in a fault state, and what will they do next?
  • What maintenance tasks will be required, how often, and can they be done without shutting down the whole line?
  • What happens during a changeover, and how long will it take?
  • Which parts of this design have we seen fail before, in our plant or elsewhere?

Advice given early is cheap. The same advice given after installation is expensive, and often comes with pressure to accept a workaround.

Responsibility 5: Be the interface between operations and maintenance

This is the responsibility that holds the others together. Operations and maintenance often have different priorities, different vocabularies, and different measures of success. Operations wants the line running. Maintenance wants time to do planned work. Both are right, and both can be wrong about the other's constraints.

A liaison makes the trade-off visible. For example, a recurring stop might be fixed by a thirty-minute planned maintenance task every two weeks. Operations may resist losing thirty minutes, but if the data shows that the recurring stop costs two hours each time, the trade-off becomes concrete. The decision then belongs to the people with the authority to make it, with the facts in front of them.

A practical tool: downtime Pareto analysis in Java

One of the most useful analyses a liaison can run is a Pareto chart of downtime causes. The principle is simple: a small number of causes usually account for most of the lost time. Identifying them focuses effort where it matters.

The following Java example reads downtime events, aggregates minutes by cause, and prints the causes ranked by impact with a cumulative percentage. It uses only the standard library.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class DowntimePareto {

    public record DowntimeEvent(String cause, int minutes) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<DowntimeEvent> events = List.of(
            new DowntimeEvent("Pump seal failure", 95),
            new DowntimeEvent("Conveyor misalignment", 60),
            new DowntimeEvent("Operator changeover delay", 45),
            new DowntimeEvent("Pump seal failure", 120),
            new DowntimeEvent("Sensor fault", 20),
            new DowntimeEvent("Conveyor misalignment", 75),
            new DowntimeEvent("Raw material shortage", 180),
            new DowntimeEvent("Pump seal failure", 80)
        );

        printPareto(events);
    }

    static void printPareto(List<DowntimeEvent> events) {
        Map<String, Integer> minutesByCause = events.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                DowntimeEvent::cause,
                Collectors.summingInt(DowntimeEvent::minutes)));

        int totalMinutes = minutesByCause.values().stream()
            .mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();

        List<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> ranked = minutesByCause.entrySet().stream()
            .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed())
            .toList();

        System.out.printf("%-30s %8s %8s %12s%n", "Cause", "Minutes", "Share", "Cumulative");
        System.out.println("-".repeat(62));

        int running = 0;
        for (var entry : ranked) {
            running += entry.getValue();
            double share = 100.0 * entry.getValue() / totalMinutes;
            double cumulative = 100.0 * running / totalMinutes;
            System.out.printf("%-30s %8d %7.1f%% %11.1f%%%n",
                entry.getKey(), entry.getValue(), share, cumulative);
        }

        System.out.printf("%nTotal downtime: %d minutes%n", totalMinutes);
    }
}

Running this produces a ranked list that makes the priorities obvious. In this sample, the top two causes account for most of the lost time, which tells you where to focus the next root-cause investigation. The value is not in the code itself but in the habit: review this ranking every week, with operators and maintenance in the same room, and agree on one action per top cause.

Two cautions. First, the quality of the analysis depends entirely on consistent cause classification. If "pump seal failure" and "seal leak" are recorded as different causes, the Pareto will understate the problem. Second, a Pareto shows where time was lost, not why. It is the starting point for investigation, not the conclusion.

Best practices

Based on the responsibilities above, these practices consistently improve plant reliability:

  • Classify downtime consistently. Agree on a short list of cause categories and enforce it. Review new categories monthly.
  • Hold short, frequent cross-functional reviews. A weekly thirty-minute meeting with operations, maintenance, and engineering beats a quarterly report.
  • Give every recurring problem an owner and a date. A problem without an owner returns.
  • Involve operators in solutions, not just in reporting problems. Their input improves the design and their buy-in makes adoption faster.
  • Bring operational experience into projects before design freeze. Changes are cheap on paper and expensive on the floor.
  • Measure outcomes, not activity. Track repeat failures, mean time between failures, and time to recover, not just the number of meetings held.

A practical roadmap

If you are taking on this role in a plant that does not have it formalized, a reasonable first ninety days looks like this:

Weeks 1 to 3: Listen and map. Spend time on the floor with operators and maintenance technicians. Map the top five recurring problems and who currently owns each one. Do not change anything yet.

Weeks 4 to 6: Establish the facts. Agree on a downtime classification scheme. Run the first Pareto analysis. Share the results openly, including the parts that are uncomfortable for one group or another.

Weeks 7 to 9: Start the loop. Launch a short weekly cross-functional review. Assign one owner and one action for each of the top three causes. Begin the shift-start coaching conversations.

Weeks 10 to 13: Build capability and pipeline. Open an improvement idea channel, screen the first batch of suggestions, and take the best one or two into a proposal with engineering. Review progress against the metrics you agreed on in week 4.

Expect resistance in the first month. It usually comes from people who feel the analysis is judging them. Address it directly: the purpose is to fix the process, not to find someone to blame.

Conclusion and key takeaways

The operations liaison role is easy to underestimate because its success looks like the absence of problems. But reliable plants are built by people who notice the recurring issue before it becomes a crisis, who respect what operators know, who bring the right engineers into the conversation early, and who make sure operations and maintenance are working from the same facts.

Key takeaways:

  • Most costly downtime is recurring and falls between departments. Someone must own the gaps.
  • Troubleshoot from the floor up, separating symptom, mechanism, and root cause.
  • Coach operators to build capability, not just to collect reports.
  • Turn improvement ideas into proposals by screening quickly and developing the best with the right engineers.
  • Bring operational experience into projects while changes are still cheap.
  • Use simple, consistent data, such as a downtime Pareto, to set priorities and keep operations and maintenance aligned.

If you have built this kind of role in your own plant, I would be glad to hear what worked and what did not. The details differ from site to site, and the shared lessons are worth comparing.
