title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing
description:
arXiv:2610.26941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.

title: Build a Faster Photography Portfolio: Convert PNG to WebP (Free, No Upload)
description:
A portfolio gallery is a strange kind of website: it has to look perfect, because the gallery is the product, but it also has to load fast, because nobody waits for a photographer whose site stutters. For years I did what most people do — exported everything as PNG, because PNG is lossless and therefore "safe." It is safe for quality. It is not safe for page weight. A gallery page full of oversized PNGs punishes every visitor on a phone connection, and most of them will never wait for the last row to appear.

I'm the developer of FileOnTap, and here is the workflow I recommend for turning a PNG gallery into a fast WebP one without learning a build pipeline.

Step 1: Separate your masters from your web exports

Keep the full-resolution originals (RAW, TIFF, or high-res PSD) untouched somewhere safe. The PNGs you export for the web are intermediates, not archives. This matters because once you convert to WebP, the WebP is a delivery format — if a client later asks for a print version, you regenerate from the master, not from the WebP.

Step 2: Export web PNGs at the size they'll actually be shown

A gallery grid that renders images at 900 px wide doesn't need 5000 px PNGs. Export at the display size plus a little headroom for retina screens — 2x at most. Every pixel you export beyond that is weight your visitors pay for and never see.

Step 3: Convert to WebP in the browser, no upload

This is where the format swap happens: convert PNG to WebP for your portfolio right in the browser. The files never leave your machine, which matters when a gallery contains client work that isn't public yet — no upload means no third-party server ever holds the images. Convert the whole gallery in one sitting so every image gets the same treatment and nothing slips through as a forgotten PNG.

Step 4: Spot-check what WebP does to your specific images

Don't trust any format blindly. Open a few converted files at 100% zoom and look at the things that matter in a portfolio: smooth gradients (skies, studio backdrops — this is where lossy compression shows banding first), fine text in watermarks, and any transparency in logos. If a gradient bands badly, reconvert from a higher-quality export rather than from an already-compressed PNG.

Step 5: Serve WebP with a PNG fallback

All modern browsers display WebP, but portfolio links travel everywhere — old apps, embedded previews, email forwards. The safe pattern is the <picture> element with WebP first and the PNG as fallback:

<picture>
  <source srcset="gallery-photo.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="gallery-photo.png" alt="...">
</picture>

If your site builder doesn't offer a <picture> element, check its image settings first — many builders now serve WebP automatically once you upload one.

The honest limitations

WebP won't rescue a gallery hosted on a slow server, and it won't fix images that were exported oversized in the first place — resize at export, then convert. Some desktop apps still don't generate WebP thumbnails, which can make browsing your local folder annoying; keep the PNG exports alongside the WebPs during a project, and archive them with the masters when it's done. And don't delete originals after converting: WebP is a delivery format, not an archive.

What I actually do

For a new portfolio batch I export the PNGs once, convert them locally in the browser, spot-check three or four files at 100%, and push. The conversion takes minutes; the painful part was always the waiting — mine and my visitors'. Fixing that is one of the cheapest wins in web publishing.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of FileOnTap, the free browser-local converter linked above. Files are converted on your device — nothing is uploaded.

title: Blueprints, Not Prompts: Using TLA+ to Guide AI-Written Code
description:
Code used to be where a team's understanding of a system lived. Now that LLMs write most of it, that understanding is quietly eroding. Here's why we're exploring formal methods at Mulga, specifically TLA+, to build better systems with AI without losing our grip on what we're building, with a real AWS EBS spec as an example.

The real contribution isn't code

It is my sincere belief that shared understanding and curated mental models are the primary artifact produced by a great engineering team.

For many, the act of sitting down to write the code was the critical step where their understanding of the problem space would SLOWLY be formalized, picked apart, and rearranged. The codebase simply provided a consistent and objective way to distribute the fruits of individual reasoning efforts to the wider team. The design discussions, frantic bug hunts, and PR reviews were core activities that served to deepen a team's understanding of how their particular problem could, and should, be solved.

At the end of it all, yes, the codebase "did the thing" (ideally). Hooray. The more important outcome was that there was now a formalized solution to the original problem, and likely many adjacent issues. Such a repository of distilled technical intent enabled later generations of engineers within the same company/group/project/community to leverage the hard-won mental models of their forebears, and ultimately drive forward the collective understanding.

Where it all went wrong

Since AI-written code became "good enough" to feasibly reach production in early 2026, many of us have been aware of the slow decline of this feedback loop that sustains our industries, livelihoods, and passions. For most of us, days now consist of prompting an LLM to produce code that satisfies a particular business need. Usually via written English. I can't speak for the entire development community, but I can personally attest to this having degraded my ability to write code by hand.

One could play devil's advocate and say something along the lines of: if LLMs can write all the code now, then why does it matter if we lose the ability to do so ourselves? To which I would say: it shouldn't really matter, provided we are able to maintain the cycle of capturing individual understanding in a manner that may be easily consumed by peers.

At last, we arrive at the core of the problem. By degrading/losing the ability to write code, we become disconnected from the act of translating ideas and intent into verifiable formalized logic that is useful to others.

The problem with natural language

How many of us regularly chat to our LLMs using the most horrendous, broken English we can possibly conceive out of sheer laziness? I'm definitely guilty! Even if you are one of the few who maintain a high quality of communication in your prompts, written/spoken language is a famously imprecise method of communication (cough synonyms cough cough).

I challenge you to try to write a system specification in your language of choice that makes explicit all assumptions and ignored details, yet leaves no room for alternate interpretations of the details that are captured. It is unlikely that you will succeed to a degree that allows you to hand that specification to an LLM and get a result that satisfies your intent.

If your system is simple enough that you do achieve an initially satisfactory result, you will inevitably discover some edge case that needs addressing. At that point, you could either adjust the written specification and have AI regenerate the implementation from scratch, which would likely resolve the issue, but also leave you with an entirely different system (unless your written spec is absurdly long and detailed).

Or you could simply ask the LLM to patch the change into the existing implementation via a quick prompt. A prompt whose core ideas are never properly understood, refined, and formalized into the collective human understanding of the project. Even if you do take the time to update the specification, fixing the edge case in isolation from the rest of the system introduces drift that severely degrades (even destroys) the spec's trustworthiness.

To illustrate the hilarity of the current prevailing approach to software specification, imagine an architect giving a construction team nothing more than a written description of the building! If natural language were precise enough to facilitate proper specifications, we wouldn't need lawyers to disambiguate the legal system for us average folk.

Formal methods and TLA+

So what do we do? How do we plug the AI-shaped hole in the bottom of the bucket that used to hold the collective knowledge of our field? Honestly, I don't know. However, my desire for a solution to this conundrum has led me deep into the formal methods rabbit hole over the past year. On my journey, I've picked up a few techniques/tools that have begun to help me address my concerns with LLM-assisted development.

One such tool that has been especially beneficial is TLA+. It was originally created by Leslie Lamport, and proves once again just how far ahead of his time he was. I'm not going to dive into an explanation of TLA+ here as it's already been done far better than I ever could, by the man himself. I highly recommend taking a moment to read Lamport's high-level view of TLA+ over on his website before proceeding. For those of you who will not heed my advice (shame), TLA+ is a language based on formal mathematical notation that allows one to create precise models of anything that can be represented as a state machine (everything, with a bit of creativity). It ships alongside TLC, which can be used to exhaustively explore logical paths within your models, and find design issues.

TLA+ is NOT code; it is mathematics. Before you recoil in disgust, here's an excerpt from Lamport's website that explains why this is so:

TLA+ teaches you that math is inherently more expressive than programming languages because it can describe a value without having to describe how the value is computed.  For example, it can describe the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two numbers as the largest positive integer that divides both numbers. This makes it possible to write a model for a specific purpose, abstracting away irrelevant details such as how to calculate the GCD. (Putting code in a procedure doesn't abstract it away; it just makes you go elsewhere to read the code, requiring that you understand the semantics of procedure call as well as the code.)

In the context of a world in which AI writes the code, this is enormously important. It gives us a language in which we can elegantly capture our intent, without getting bogged down in implementation details that ultimately don't matter to the use case. A well-written TLA+ spec is a human-readable artifact that forces the author to reason through the system they are designing in a constrained and logical format, is easy for peers to digest and iterate upon, and is objectively machine checkable (via TLC) so that LLMs are given a concrete benchmark that implementations may be evaluated against.

The TLA+ model is the architectural blueprint that the design team argues over, iterates upon, and hands to the next generation as learning material, just as the codebase used to be. The code itself becomes a concern of the construction team (coding agents). The details of the implementation can be tied to the spec, preventing drift, with the use of strategies such as trace-checking and refinement mapping. I liken these processes to the surveyor who measures a new build against the numbers in the plans to ensure conformance.

Many readers might be thinking something along the lines of "if TLA+ is so great, why haven't I heard of it before?". TLA+, and the discipline of formal methods as a whole, has largely flown under the radar of the wider software engineering community, with the exception of niche teams within resource-rich industry titans such as Google and AWS. As far as I can tell, this is mostly due to the barrier to entry.

Engineers are trained to write code. Most gave their discrete mathematics classes only the bare minimum attention needed to pass their exams, then promptly forgot the skills once they entered the workforce. From the perspective of an engineering executive: why would I have my team spend time writing a model in TLA+ (or another specification language), when I could have them build the real solution in [insert programming language of choice]? Someone would have to write the code eventually anyway...

At the time, such arguments were perfectly reasonable. No matter how precise your formal spec, someone still has to write the executable code. Or rather, someTHING! Enter LLMs. On February 5th of this year (2026), Anthropic released Opus 4.6. It is widely considered the turning point for AI-assisted development; models could finally write code that was at least somewhat reasonable. We live in a world where, if we can produce testable specifications that sufficiently constrain the details of a system that matter to the use case, we can give AI an "abstract" model and receive a working implementation with very little human babysitting.

This is MUCH easier said than done, but TLA+ is an incredible step in the right direction. And given that so many engineers are no longer writing code themselves, one could argue that improving the quality and accuracy of our specifications is a core part of the job, in a way that it never was before. I have a hunch that this mentality shift will go a long way towards breaking down the perceived "barrier to entry" that has so limited the usefulness of formal methods to the wider software engineering community.

A TLA+ specification of the AWS Elastic Block Store API

My attention at Mulga is largely focused on the storage components of our stack, Predastore (S3-compatible object storage) and Viperblock (EBS-like virtual disks). In such projects, details are extraordinarily important, and ambiguity is to be avoided at all costs. When a user engages with something claiming to be a storage service, they assume that their data is in good hands and won't be carelessly lost. On top of this responsibility, the systems are complex and easy to lose track of under the tidal wave of AI-generated contributions.

I recently used TLA+ to write a specification of the observable behavior of a subset of AWS's EBS API. The intent was to solidify my understanding of the EBS volume lifecycle state machine, so that I can ensure Spinifex (our AWS-compatible control plane) is properly adhering to the behaviors expected by the AWS CLI for the EBS operations it exposes.

For the curious reader, the specification is open source and is available to read in the Viperblock GitHub repository. It's only ~400 lines (as of now), across 4 files! This is rather notable, considering the relevant (English) technical documentation published by AWS for these operations extends across 13 separate web pages, and still manages to leave a vast amount of detail up to the reader to discern. The specification's brevity makes sense as, naturally, a written description of a building would take up far more space than a blueprint capturing the relevant details! Some request/response fields, possible error codes, and features have been abstracted out of this initial version, of course, but the core volume/attachment status state machines are captured very clearly. You do not need to be a career mathematician to make fantastic use of TLA+!

A common question I receive is "can't AI just write the TLA+ too?". Well, yes... technically. However, I'd argue there's not really any value in doing things that way. If an AI writes it, you're right back to relying on prompts that nobody has rigorously thought through, and that are invisible to colleagues and mentees.

TLA+ is ultimately a tool for the communication of ideas, in the same way that the legal system uses a constrained version of natural language to avoid confusion and mathematicians use formal notation. The power in a specification language built upon said mathematical notation is its innate ability to be applied effectively at any level of abstraction. If all you have is a vague idea of how the system you wish to build should appear to a user, that is enough to write a solid specification. There is plenty of room later to refine, and add detail that was missed (or deemed unimportant) on the first pass. This can extend as far down as the electrons themselves, if such detail is relevant to your problem space.

To illustrate this idea, here is the part of my EBS specification that captures the subset of the observable behavior of the CreateVolume operation that I was particularly interested in:

\* A client requested a new volume.
CreateVolume(req, res) ==
  /\ req \in CreateVolumeRequests
  /\ LET PossibleErrors(db) == Errors({})
         PossibleRecords    == [status             : {"creating"},
                                \* After enabling encryption by default, CreateVolume may still
                                \* see a stale value from another replica for a short window.
                                encrypted          : {db.encryptedByDefault : db \in VisibleDBs},
                                multiAttachEnabled : {FALSE}]
        \* The request was accepted.
     IN \/ /\ PossibleErrors(CurrentDB) = {}
           /\ \E vId \in VolumeIds \ usedIds, record \in PossibleRecords :
                /\ Commit([CurrentDB EXCEPT !.volumes = InsertKey(@, vId, record)])
                /\ res = [vId |-> vId] @@ record
        \* The request was rejected, possibly by a stale replica.
        \/ /\ \E db \in VisibleDBs : res \in PossibleErrors(db)
           /\ UNCHANGED vars

Some information to aid in reading this excerpt: /\ and \/ can be read as AND and OR respectively; curly braces represent a set; == is a definition; = is a comparison; the lines that begin with \E are checking whether an element exists in a target set that satisfies the condition after the :. The comments give enough of the gist that the rest of the syntax can be glossed over. Specifics can be found at learntla.com. It helps to think of a TLA+ spec as one big condition in an if statement that you would find in a traditional programming language.

This operator (an action in TLA+ terms) contains very little detail about how exactly a volume is created. In fact, throughout my entire spec, the concept of a "volume" being a virtual disk that bytes can be read from and written to is not captured anywhere! This is because it was not relevant to the control plane operations that I was concerned with at the time. I simply abstracted it away.

A final anecdote: while writing the EBS control plane model, I found myself unable to glean all of the information required to get a good picture of the possible volume status transitions from the AWS docs. This drove me to run some tests myself, and led to the discovery that a volume whose status is "creating" can immediately transition to "deleting" without first passing through "error" in certain cases. This is undocumented behavior that is extremely valuable to me in the design of Viperblock.

What's next?

At the time of writing, the spec only captures a few particularly important EBS API endpoints. I'm currently working on using TLC to trace-check my model against the real EBS API to verify that it is correct. The plan is to then trace-check Spinifex's EBS API implementation against the verified model, and fix the divergences that will inevitably be surfaced! From there I will extend the model to capture all EBS API operations that Spinifex supports, and repeat the trace-checking process.

This was not the article I initially set out to write. I'd intended to cover far more technical detail and dive deeper into the structure of the spec itself, the trace-checking methodology, and my ideas around how formal specification may be feasibly brought into the industry as a standard practice. However, in explaining my experiences to friends and colleagues, I realized that such content would not be very useful to the engineering community if I didn't first attempt to give the "why" behind the methods. Alas, the rest will have to wait for future articles.

If I have sufficiently piqued your interest, rest assured that you will not be waiting long for the next installment in this saga. So stay tuned. Until next time!

Bryn

title: You Are the Trigger: Speaker-Activated Backdoors
description:
arXiv:2610.27210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech models are increasingly used as an interface to AI systems, from transcription tools to voice agents. Existing audio backdoors require an attacker to introduce triggers at inference time. We study a different threat model in which the attacker compromises the model during fine-tuning but has no access to the victim's inference-time inputs. We introduce the Speaker-Activated Backdoor (SAB) setting, in which a target speaker's natural voice serves as the trigger. We develop a two-phase fine-tuning method that first makes speaker identity more accessible and then binds the target speaker to an attacker-chosen payload. Compared with a one-phase baseline with the same training budget, the two-phase method substantially improves selectivity and clean performance, and is especially important for content-dependent attacks. SAB achieves 90.2% and 97.0% backdoor success on Whisper-medium and Parakeet, with false-positive rates of 1.7% and 0%, respectively using as little as two minutes of real audio from the target speaker. We further demonstrate content-dependent semantic rewriting and downstream tool-use attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into 96.9% of target-speaker transcripts. When these transcripts are passed to frontier LLM agents, GPT-4o and Claude (Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku), the injected instruction drives the agent to carry out the harmful action in up to 87.5% of cases. The attack generalizes to held-out recordings, multiple target speakers, and common acoustic degradations. These results establish speaker identity as a practical backdoor trigger that requires no inference-time attacker access and is invisible at the transcript layer.

title: Deep catastrophic-risk-aware reinforcement learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27214v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating extreme risk in reinforcement learning becomes increasingly difficult as the confidence level increases, since only a small number of observations contribute to empirical estimates of Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). In this paper, we extend an Extreme Value Theory (EVT) approach for CVaR optimization to high-dimensional neural-network policies. Using a peaks-over-threshold representation and method-of-moments estimation, we obtain a differentiable tail-risk objective and show that, conditional on the selected threshold, its finite-sample gradient can be computed directly through automatic differentiation. We first validate the approach in a controlled experiment with a known optimal solution and then investigate its performance in a deep-hedging problem with rare extreme market movements. Our results show similar hedging behavior for EVT- and empirical-CVaR-trained policies under normal conditions, while EVT-trained policies exhibit lower hedging losses under the extreme-scenario evaluation across the training sample sizes considered. These results suggest that EVT can provide a practical alternative for training neural policies when the observations relevant to extreme risk are scarce.

title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability
description:
arXiv:2610.26964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with classical planning, but benchmarks rarely distinguish structural difficulty from the difficulty of interpreting symbolic vocabulary. We examine seven STRIPS domains with BFS-optimal plan lengths. For predicting structural difficulty without solving an instance, the zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic $h_{\mathrm{add}}$ outperforms learned alternatives on held-out domains (mean Spearman $|\rho|=0.931$), including ridge regression ($0.707$), object count ($0.657$), and the episodic retrieval architecture ARC ($0.400$). ARC also fails to outperform a linear model using the same features. To isolate semantic effects, we progressively rename predicates while preserving states, transitions, and optimal plans. Valid LLM planning success drops from $67.5\%$ to $40.0\%$ between $0\%$ and $100\%$ renaming, while refusals remain at $0\%$. An LLM supplied with ARC's conditioning information predicts difficulty in context better than trained ARC (mean $|\rho|=0.826$). Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner depends more on calibration to the target LLM's outcomes than on the structural score selected. Thus, established symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty well; improving hybrid planning requires modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than developing more structural predictors.

title: Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition with Bidirectional Audio--Text Cross-Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.26868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) are subtle behavioural states that can be expressed through both what a person says and how it is spoken. This paper presents an audio--text framework for video-level A/H recognition. Full-video transcripts and speech waveforms are encoded using pre-trained multilingual BERT and wav2vec~2.0, respectively, and projected into a shared representation space. Two stacked bidirectional cross-attention blocks allow linguistic tokens to attend to acoustic frames and acoustic frames to attend to linguistic context without requiring explicit temporal alignment. The resulting sequences are aggregated through masked mean pooling and combined using concatenation, element-wise products, and absolute differences for binary classification. We evaluate the model on the subject-independent split of the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) dataset. The proposed system achieves 72.19\% accuracy, 75.00\% precision, 81.13\% recall, 77.95\% A/H F1-score, and 70.16\% Macro-F1 on the test set. These results demonstrate the potential of jointly modelling linguistic and acoustic information for automatic A/H recognition.code at:https://github.com/DorriG/ECCV.

title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
description:
arXiv:2610.27296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

title: How to Build a 3-State Uptime Dashboard from Metrics and Logs (Internally)
description:
Short answer: poll recent health metrics and structured logs, reduce them to green, yellow, or red, and keep the raw evidence one click away. For a small healthtech team, the least complex useful version is an internal page backed by two direct queries. It should expose telemetry cost beside operational status, because a dashboard that hides its own cost is unfinished.

Choice Recovery fit Cost attribution Operating burden
Infrai Recent metrics, logs, and error groups behind one API Per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata Polling and aggregation are yours
Datadog Specialist observability suite Dedicated product billing More platform surface to configure
Amazon CloudWatch Natural fit for AWS workloads AWS billing and log-ingestion accounting Strongest inside AWS
Grafana Cloud Flexible cross-source dashboards Separate hosted-service accounting More choices to own
Healthchecks.io Dead-man monitoring for jobs Separate specialist service Narrow complement for silent jobs

My recommendation is narrow: a team already consolidating backend calls should try Infrai for the recent-status query layer, because one key and one bill reduce credential and invoice glue, while per-call metadata gives the dashboard a direct cost-attribution trail. It is not a full incident-management system.

How should Node.js build an uptime dashboard from metrics and logs?

A checkout page needs a decision rule before it needs charts. I use three states because operators can act on them quickly:

  • Green: recent checks are healthy and there is no matching failure evidence.
  • Yellow: checks are degraded, stale, or mixed; an operator should inspect logs.
  • Red: the recent window shows a failed check, with logs available for triage.

This is deliberately modest. A 0/1 status signal says whether the checkout path worked. Structured logs explain which stage failed, such as eligibility, payment authorization, or order persistence. Error groups can connect an outage window to repeated exceptions for the same service. Do not pretend one signal answers all three questions.

For a healthtech checkout, keep sensitive payloads out of the status document. The UI needs a service name, timestamp, state, correlation identifier, and failure stage. It does not need a patient's name, order contents, or free-form clinical text. The available log interface also has no per-user deletion route, which makes it a poor home for data that may later need selective erasure.

The first trap is averaging. Ten successful checks can hide the one failure an operator cares about. Preserve the latest result and failure count separately, then define yellow and red from explicit product policy. Google's four golden signals are a useful check: errors and latency matter, but saturation and traffic can change how the same error rate should be read.

Keep it boring.

Three colors. Two evidence sources. One written policy.

Two criteria beat a feature checklist

The first criterion is recovery speed. Can an operator move from red status to a small set of relevant events without opening four consoles? Infrai puts recent metrics, logs, and error groups under the same key. Its public discovery surface describes 295 routes across 20 modules, including schemas and runnable TypeScript examples. That reduces client glue, but it does not remove the application work: there is no log subscription or batch export surface, so the admin page must poll direct queries and aggregate returned records itself.

The second criterion is cost attribution. Per-call metadata includes cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request identity across the native API conventions. That is more actionable than a month-end total when a team wants to ask which internal screen or recovery loop generated spend. One wallet and one bill also remove invoice reconciliation across backend capabilities routed through the platform. I care about that more than a transient unit price. Prices move. Plumbing lingers.

There is a hard boundary. These limitations matter: retention and cold-storage configuration are limited, so this design is for recent operational visibility, not long-term compliance reporting. It also has no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route. The polling process below updates an internal view; it is not an on-call system. That trade-off is acceptable for an admin panel only when another system owns paging.

Implement the 3-state poller

The query filters for these surfaces are not declared in discovery, so the client must not guess parameters such as service, from, or window. Query the documented routes as exposed, then inspect the returned schema from discovery before adapting record extraction. This TypeScript program makes both authenticated calls, handles rate limiting, surfaces real error bodies, and prints a compact snapshot.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

async function request(url: string, attempt: number): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      Accept: "application/json",
    },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return request(url, attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`${response.status} ${response.statusText}: ${body}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

async function queryMetrics(): Promise<unknown> {
  return request(`${baseUrl}/metrics/query`, 0);
}

async function searchLogs(): Promise<unknown> {
  return request(`${baseUrl}/logs/search`, 0);
}

const [metrics, logs] = await Promise.all([
  queryMetrics(),
  searchLogs(),
]);

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  checkedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  service: "checkout",
  evidence: { metrics, logs },
}, null, 2));

Run it with Node.js 20 or newer so fetch is available.

INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_your_key_here npx tsx checkout-status.ts

This stops before inventing a response shape. Once discovery confirms the current schemas, add a pure reducer that accepts normalized check records and returns one of the three states. Test it with fixed timestamps. Keep network code out of it. That split makes the red/yellow boundary reviewable and prevents a response change from silently rewriting operational policy.

Polling every few seconds by default is config bloat disguised as responsiveness. Choose the interval from the recovery objective and rate-limit budget. Record the last successful refresh separately; a stale green screen is not green. On 429, the example honors Retry-After when numeric and otherwise uses exponential backoff. A production process should add jitter if several replicas can poll together.

Where does each alternative win?

Choose Datadog when the team wants a specialist observability product, especially if managed alerting, tracing, or richer investigation workflows are requirements. Infrai exposes trace and span identifiers in logs but does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree. It also has no source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. Those are decisive gaps for some teams.

Choose Sentry when checkout exceptions, source-mapped stack traces, and application-error investigation dominate the job. Its specialist focus is a better match than this lightweight query layer when developers need crash context rather than a small service-status view.

CloudWatch is the pragmatic runner-up for an AWS-centered checkout. Keeping telemetry beside the workload can simplify ownership, and its published pricing explains log ingestion as a billed dimension. The trade is tighter coupling to the AWS operating model. Compare the bill using your own retention and ingestion pattern; a generic price table will age badly.

Grafana Cloud makes sense when cross-source visualization is the product requirement. Its flexibility is useful when the team already speaks the Grafana ecosystem. For a three-state admin page, that flexibility can mean more configuration than the decision warrants. Benchmark time-to-first-use with your real schema, not a demo dataset.

Add Healthchecks.io when the failure is silence: a reconciliation task, export, or scheduled payment job never ran. Infrai has no synthetic probe or heartbeat monitor, so ordinary logs cannot prove that a task which emitted nothing was supposed to execute. This is a complement, not a duplicate.

The selection rule is blunt. Use direct queries for recent internal visibility and explicit cost attribution. Use a specialist when alert delivery, deep traces, long retention, compliance export, replay, or silent-job detection belongs in the acceptance criteria.

No single winner.

Ship the recovery path, not just the colors

A status page earns its place when red leads somewhere. Put the correlation identifier and a bounded evidence view beside the state. Link repeated failures to an error group after the query response has been normalized. Give operators a timestamp for both the source event and dashboard refresh.

Then test failure handling. Return a 429 from a local stub and verify backoff. Return a non-JSON 403 body and verify the error remains visible. Freeze time and verify a stale success becomes yellow. These cheap tests target the awkward paths dashboard demos skip.

I would benchmark three numbers before choosing a provider: minutes from empty directory to first authenticated response, lines of adapter code after normalization, and credentials the service must rotate. Those are evaluation criteria, not claimed measurements. They expose integration cost without pretending every team values the same features.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the internal uptime page guide and verify the live schemas before writing the reducer.

Further reading

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing
  • Datadog documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Infrai log ingestion discovery

title: TRACE: Training-aware Robustness and Challenge Evaluation for Text-Vision Embedding Models
description:
arXiv:2610.26993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing benchmarks for text-vision embedding models report aggregate scores that obscure whether performance comes from general capabilities, task-specific adaptation, or robustness to challenging tasks. We introduce TRACE, a Training-aware Robustness and Challenge Evaluation framework that reorganizes 168 tasks from various sources of datasets into three categories: General, Adaptability, and Challenge. Through controlled experiments on two text-vision embedding models, we show that combining general and adaptation data improves Adaptability performance by 7.67 and 7.09 points, respectively, while largely preserving General performance. However, Challenge performance remains below 5.0, with limited improvements from additional training data. Further analysis identifies multilingual and visual-document tasks as major weaknesses. Our findings demonstrate that data adaptation alone is insufficient to address these challenges, highlighting the need for methodological advances beyond data-centric improvements.

title: Getting Started with AWS S3: Creating a Bucket, Uploading an Object, and Understanding Why the Object URL Says Access Denied
description:
Introduction

I'm starting a new series on AWS, and this first article covers Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), one of the most widely used services on AWS. I did this lab in my own personal AWS free-tier account, and I'll explain every term as it comes up.

By the end, you'll know how to:

  • Create an S3 bucket with a consistent naming convention
  • Read the bucket's ARN and properties
  • Upload a file to the bucket
  • Find an object's URL, and understand why opening the image works while opening the Object URL doesn't

What is Amazon S3?

Amazon S3 is an object storage service. Instead of organizing data in a traditional disk with a file system, S3 stores data as objects inside buckets. You can store and retrieve any amount of data from anywhere, and you pay only for what you use.

Three terms to know first:

  • Bucket: a container for your data. Every object in S3 lives inside a bucket.
  • Object: the thing you store. It's the file itself plus its metadata (size, type, last modified date and so on).
  • Key: the object's unique name inside the bucket. For my file, the key is datacenter.png.

Step 1: Open the S3 service

In the AWS Management Console, I typed S3 into the search bar and selected S3 (Scalable Storage in the Cloud) from the results.

This opens the Amazon S3 landing page, where Create bucket is the first thing you see.

Step 2: Create a bucket

I clicked Create bucket, and the only thing I had to provide was the bucket name. The region was already set for me (more on that below), and I left everything else at the defaults to keep things simple.

Region

I didn't pick the region on this page. The Create bucket page shows it as plain text, not a dropdown: Europe (Stockholm) eu-north-1. That's because S3 creates a bucket in whichever region your console is currently set to, and mine was already set to Stockholm. If you want a different region, switch it with the region selector in the top bar of the console before you click Create bucket.

A region is a physical geographic location where AWS runs data centers. Your bucket's data stays in the region it was created in, and the region affects latency (how close the data is to your users) and pricing.

Bucket type

I kept General purpose, which AWS recommends for most use cases. The other option, Directory, is for low-latency workloads that use a single Availability Zone.

Bucket namespace

I kept Global namespace. A namespace is the set of names in which yours has to be unique. In the global namespace, a bucket name must be unique across all AWS accounts, in every region. If someone else already has my-bucket, you can't use it. The console also offers an Account Regional namespace (labelled "recommended"). Buckets created there are unique only within your own account, so no other AWS account can ever claim the same name. I stayed with the global namespace for this lab.

Bucket name and the prefix naming convention

I named my bucket aws-lab1-rahimah.

The aws-lab1- part is a prefix I chose as a naming convention. A consistent prefix gives you three things:

  • It keeps names unique, since adding your own name or project helps avoid clashes in the global namespace.
  • It groups related resources together (aws-lab1-..., aws-lab2-...).
  • It makes resources easy to find and to clean up later.

S3 bucket names must be 3 to 63 characters long, can contain only lowercase letters, numbers, periods and hyphens, and must begin and end with a letter or number.

Default encryption

Further down the page, Default encryption was already set to Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). This means S3 automatically encrypts every new object at rest, using keys that AWS manages for you. You don't have to do anything. I left it as it was and clicked Create bucket.

S3 confirmed with a green banner: Successfully created bucket "aws-lab1-rahimah". The Objects tab shows Objects (0) because the bucket is empty.

Step 3: Look at the bucket's properties and ARN

I opened the Properties tab. The Bucket overview shows three things:

  • AWS Region: Europe (Stockholm) eu-north-1
  • Creation date: October 20, 2026
  • Amazon Resource Name (ARN): arn:aws:s3:::aws-lab1-rahimah

What is an ARN?

An Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is the unique identifier AWS gives every resource. It's how you point at a specific resource in IAM policies, logs and other services. The general shape is:

arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource

For S3 buckets, the region and account sections are empty, which is why you see three colons in a row (:::). The bucket name is the final part.

The Properties tab also shows two settings that were off by default:

  • Bucket Versioning: Disabled. Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object, so you can recover from accidental overwrites or deletions. With it disabled, uploading a file with the same key replaces the old one.
  • Multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete: Disabled. This extra layer of security requires MFA before you can permanently delete object versions.

Step 4: Upload a file to the bucket

Back on the Objects tab, I clicked Upload.

On the Upload page, I clicked Add files and picked an image called datacenter.png from my Downloads folder. You can also drag and drop files, or use Add folder to upload a whole folder.

The page then listed the file as 1 total, 2.4 MB, type image/png, with the destination shown as s3://aws-lab1-rahimah.

Scrolling down, you'll see two collapsed sections:

  • Permissions: where you can grant public access and access to other AWS accounts.
  • Properties: where you can set the storage class, encryption settings and tags.

I left both alone and clicked Upload.

The next page showed Upload succeeded, with a summary of 1 file, 2.4 MB, 100% succeeded and 0 failed.

Back in the bucket, Objects (1) now lists datacenter.png, size 2.4 MB, and storage class Standard.

Storage class controls how your data is stored and what it costs. Standard is the default and is meant for frequently accessed data. Other classes, such as Glacier, are cheaper for data you rarely need to retrieve.

Step 5: Explore the object's details

I clicked datacenter.png to open its details. The Object overview shows:

  • Owner: the canonical ID of the AWS account that owns the object
  • AWS Region: eu-north-1
  • Last modified, Size and Type
  • Key: datacenter.png
  • S3 URI: s3://aws-lab1-rahimah/datacenter.png
  • ARN: arn:aws:s3:::aws-lab1-rahimah/datacenter.png
  • Entity tag (ETag): an identifier for this specific version of the object's content
  • Object URL: https://aws-lab1-rahimah.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/datacenter.png

Two of these are easy to confuse:

  • The S3 URI (s3://bucket/key) is what AWS tools like the AWS CLI and SDKs use to refer to an object.
  • The Object URL is the HTTPS address of the object on the internet, in the form https://bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com/key.

The ARN here is the bucket's ARN with the object key added on the end.

Step 6: Open the image vs. use the Object URL

This is the part that surprised me, and it taught me the most. There are two ways to view the uploaded image, and they behave differently.

Option 1: Click "Open"

Clicking the Open button displays the image in a new browser tab. The address bar shows a very long URL that carries extra parameters such as X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256.

That is a presigned URL. When you click Open, the console uses your own credentials to generate a temporary, signed link that grants access to the object for a short time. S3 sees the signature, confirms that a permitted user created it, and serves the file.

Option 2: Paste the Object URL

When I copied the plain Object URL into the browser, I got this:

<Error>
  <Code>AccessDenied</Code>
  <Message>Access Denied</Message>
  ...
</Error>

Why the difference?

The Object URL is an unauthenticated request. When you paste it into a browser, there's no signature and nothing that tells S3 who you are, so S3 treats you as an anonymous visitor. S3 buckets and objects are private by default, and only the owner can access them unless permissions are explicitly granted. So the anonymous request is refused with AccessDenied.

The error is not a bug. It shows S3's security model working as designed: nothing is public until you deliberately make it so.

Making objects public

If you need public access, for example to host images on a website, you'd have to change two things: turn off the relevant Block Public Access settings on the bucket, and then grant read access through a bucket policy or object permissions. Only do this for data that's genuinely meant to be public. For private files, presigned URLs are a safer way to share something temporarily.

Key Takeaways

  • A bucket is a container and an object is a file inside it, identified by its key.
  • Bucket names must be globally unique, so a naming prefix like aws-lab1- helps keep names unique and organized.
  • The region determines where your data physically lives.
  • An ARN uniquely identifies any AWS resource, and an object's ARN is its bucket's ARN plus the key.
  • The S3 URI is for AWS tools, while the Object URL is the HTTPS address.
  • S3 is private by default. Opening an object from the console works because it uses a presigned URL, while the plain Object URL returns AccessDenied.

Clean up

To avoid unexpected charges, delete what you created. You must empty a bucket before you can delete it:

  1. Select datacenter.png and click Delete. Make sure you tick it, so that the Delete button is not greyed out.


Then confirm deletion.

  1. Go back to the bucket list, select aws-lab1-rahimah and click Delete.

Conclusion

In this first lab, I created an S3 bucket, uploaded an object, and learned why access to it is blocked by default. Next in the series, I'll build on this with more S3 features and other AWS services.

If you're learning AWS, let me know in the comments which service I should cover next.

title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
description:
arXiv:2610.27156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Object:
  Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images.
  Materials and Methods:
  Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction.
  Results:
  Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail.
  Discussion:
  Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

title: LoWAgent: A Low-Resource Multilingual Benchmark for Web Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27205v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated on English-language interfaces, leaving their ability to operate across the world's multilingual websites largely unexplored. This gap is especially significant for low-resource languages, where standardized resources for evaluating web agents remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark (LoWAgent), a benchmark for evaluating web agents across different low-resource languages (LRLs) in comparison to the default, English. LoWAgent evaluates web agents across English and four LRLs: Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic. The benchmark comprises of six fully localized websites, instantiated across five languages to yield 3,000 task instances. We evaluate three closed-source and five open-source models across all five languages on all six websites. Our findings show that both closed-source and open-source models experience performance degradation for LRLs compared to English, with substantially greater performance drops observed among the open-source model agents. We further evaluate the robustness of the models on realistic interface disruptions, such as cookie notices and advertisement pop-ups, and find that these further degrade agentic performance. Finally, we show that post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces can significantly improve low-resource language agentic task performance, demonstrating the usefulness of our benchmark.

title: AI Code Invariant Tests: Catch Regressions That Green Test Suites Miss
description:
An AI coding agent can make every visible test pass and still break the one rule your product cannot afford to violate.

That is the uncomfortable failure mode behind many “safe” agent refactors. The diff looks tidy. Unit tests are green. The new code may even have more coverage than before. But a permission check moves after a database lookup, a retry stops being idempotent, or a list endpoint turns into an accidental N+1 query. Nothing in a happy-path test has to notice.

The fix is not a longer prompt asking the agent to be careful. It is to name the behavior that must remain true, then test it as an invariant. This article shows a practical, framework-neutral way to add invariant tests around AI-generated changes—especially where money, access, state, and latency matter.

Why green tests can still hide an AI-generated regression

Most unit tests answer a narrow question: “Does this example produce the expected output?” That is useful, but it leaves room for an implementation that passes known examples while breaking a rule between examples.

Coding agents amplify that gap. They are effective at repairing the assertion directly in front of them. If a refactor changes a test, they may update the test too. The suite turns green, but the original contract has quietly moved.

Recent developer discussions around agentic refactoring repeatedly describe the same pain: tests can remain green while an agent weakens an alert, rewrites an assertion, or creates a slow query loop. Research and benchmark work on coding agents also points toward specification-first and adversarial validation rather than trusting generated code by default.

An invariant is different from a single expected result. It is a property that must hold across many inputs and implementation paths.

Ordinary example test Invariant test
A member can read their own project. A request can never return a project from another organization.
Retrying this request returns 200. Retrying the same operation never creates a second charge.
A search result is sorted in this fixture. Results are always sorted by the promised key, including ties and empty input.
This endpoint completes quickly in a test. Loading 50 records does not issue more than a bounded number of queries.

The aim is not to replace example tests. Keep them. Invariants give them a harder-to-game companion.

Pick invariants before asking an agent to refactor

Do not begin with “clean up this module.” Start with a short, testable list of things that cannot change. This becomes the acceptance contract for the task and a small map for review.

For a typical application, useful categories are:

  • Authorization: one tenant or role never sees another’s data.
  • State: records move only through allowed states.
  • Money and side effects: retries do not duplicate emails, charges, or writes.
  • Data integrity: identifiers, totals, and ownership stay consistent.
  • Reliability: failures leave the system in a recoverable state.
  • Performance: a refactor does not multiply database calls or network work.
  • Compatibility: a public API preserves its documented shape and meaning.

Write each one in plain language first. A good invariant has a subject, a boundary, and an observable result:

For every invoice event with the same idempotency key, at most one payment record exists.

For every authenticated request, every returned document belongs to the requester’s organization.

For a valid workflow, terminal states cannot transition back to pending.

Avoid vague rules such as “keep the code secure” or “do not change behavior.” They are review intentions, not executable claims.

Turn an invariant into a test oracle

An oracle is the thing that says whether behavior is correct. Existing snapshot tests are weak oracles when an agent can update them. For critical changes, use an oracle the change is not allowed to edit without an explicit human decision.

One practical pattern is to put invariant tests in a protected directory and declare them read-only for the task.

repo/
  src/
  tests/
  safety-contracts/
    organization-isolation.spec.ts
    payment-idempotency.spec.ts
    workflow-transitions.spec.ts

Your task brief can then be concrete:

Refactor src/billing/renewal.ts to remove duplication.

Constraints:
- Do not edit safety-contracts/.
- Run npm test and npm run test:contracts after each logical step.
- Preserve one payment per idempotency key.
- Report changed files, commands, and any failing contract.

That instruction alone is not protection. Enforce it in CI: fail a pull request that changes protected contract files unless a designated reviewer approves it. The important part is separation—an agent should not be able to write both the implementation and the only proof it is safe without making that visible.

Example: protect tenant isolation with generated inputs

Imagine a document query that an agent is about to “simplify.” A normal example test might check that one user can fetch a document. An invariant test should try many organizations and document IDs, then assert that every returned record belongs to the caller’s organization.

Here is TypeScript-style pseudocode using a property-testing library:

import fc from "fast-check";

it("never returns another organization's document", async () => {
  await fc.assert(
    fc.asyncProperty(
      fc.uuid(),
      fc.uuid(),
      fc.uuid(),
      async (requesterOrgId, otherOrgId, documentId) => {
        fc.pre(requesterOrgId !== otherOrgId);

        await seedDocument({ id: documentId, organizationId: otherOrgId });
        const result = await listDocuments({ organizationId: requesterOrgId });

        expect(result.every((doc) => doc.organizationId === requesterOrgId)).toBe(true);
      },
    ),
  );
});

The exact library is optional. You can loop over generated cases yourself. The principle matters: test the rule across values the author did not hand-pick.

For a multi-tenant system, add negative cases too:

  • a guessed ID from another organization
  • an empty role list
  • an admin role from the wrong organization
  • soft-deleted records
  • pagination cursors created by another tenant

These are the cases a polished refactor often fails because the happy path still works.

Example: protect idempotency when an agent changes retries

Retries are a classic regression surface. An agent may correctly add timeout handling but accidentally put the side effect before the deduplication check.

The invariant is simple: repeating a request with the same stable key produces one durable effect.

it("creates at most one payment for the same request key", async () => {
  const key = "payment:order-42";

  await Promise.all([
    createPayment({ orderId: "order-42", amount: 2500, idempotencyKey: key }),
    createPayment({ orderId: "order-42", amount: 2500, idempotencyKey: key }),
  ]);

  const payments = await db.payment.findMany({
    where: { idempotencyKey: key },
  });

  expect(payments).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(payments[0].amount).toBe(2500);
});

Run it with sequential and concurrent calls. Then add a failure injection between “reserve key” and “write payment.” If the invariant cannot survive a timeout, it is not really an invariant—it is a best-case assumption.

Test state machines instead of only endpoints

Many business rules are state transitions disguised as API behavior. A support ticket should not reopen after it is permanently closed. An order should not ship before payment. A deleted user should not receive a new session.

Model the allowed transitions in one small table before the refactor:

From Allowed next states
draft submitted, cancelled
submitted approved, rejected, cancelled
approved fulfilled, cancelled
fulfilled none

Then test every pair, not just the common routes:

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  draft: ["submitted", "cancelled"],
  submitted: ["approved", "rejected", "cancelled"],
  approved: ["fulfilled", "cancelled"],
  rejected: [],
  cancelled: [],
  fulfilled: [],
};

for (const from of Object.keys(allowed) as Status[]) {
  for (const to of allStatuses) {
    const canMove = allowed[from].includes(to);
    await expect(changeStatus({ from, to }))
      .resolves[canMove ? "toBeDefined" : "toThrow"]();
  }
}

Use your test framework’s normal assertion style; the point is to enumerate the system’s real state space. If the agent replaces conditionals, extracts services, or switches an ORM call, this test protects the business meaning rather than its old implementation.

Add performance invariants where refactors hide cost

Correct output is not the whole contract. A coding agent can preserve results while turning one query into one query per row.

For known hot paths, count the work. Inject a database query counter in an integration test, execute with a small and a medium fixture, and set a reasonable ceiling.

it("loads project members without an N+1 query", async () => {
  const meter = trackDatabaseQueries(db);
  await seedProjectWithMembers({ memberCount: 50 });

  const page = await getProjectMembers({ projectId: "project-1" });

  expect(page.members).toHaveLength(50);
  expect(meter.count()).toBeLessThanOrEqual(3);
});

Do not turn every test into a brittle microbenchmark. A query ceiling, outbound-call count, or payload-size limit is usually more stable and more useful than an elapsed-millisecond assertion in CI.

A small contract loop for AI-assisted changes

Here is a repeatable workflow that does not require a formal-methods team.

  1. Name the risk. Identify what can be lost, duplicated, leaked, or slowed down.
  2. Write one invariant. Make it observable in code or a controlled integration environment.
  3. Prove the test can fail. Temporarily introduce the forbidden behavior or use a mutation tool. If the test stays green, strengthen it.
  4. Protect the oracle. Keep contract tests out of the agent’s editable scope for the task, or require explicit review for any change.
  5. Give the agent a bounded goal. Specify files, behavior, test commands, and prohibited changes.
  6. Run the contract suite in CI. Store the command output with the pull request.
  7. Review the invariant, not only the diff. Ask whether the rule still means what the product needs.

The third step is the one teams skip. A test that never demonstrates a failure can be theater. For a payment invariant, change the uniqueness guard in a local branch and confirm the test catches two rows. For tenant isolation, deliberately remove the organization predicate and watch the contract fail.

Give coding agents a task contract they can follow

Clear instructions help, especially when they connect a change to a non-negotiable rule. Here is a concise template:

Goal: extract the notification scheduling logic from src/jobs/run.ts.

Behavioral contracts:
1. A job with the same idempotency key sends at most one notification.
2. A cancelled job never sends a notification.
3. A tenant can never schedule a job for another tenant.

Boundaries:
- Do not modify safety-contracts/.
- Do not add dependencies.
- Keep the public handler signature unchanged.

Verification:
- npm run typecheck
- npm test
- npm run test:contracts
- Summarize any command that fails; do not weaken tests to make them pass.

This is stronger than “refactor safely” because it tells the agent what success means. It is also easier for a reviewer to reject a superficially green change: the contract is visible before the code.

Common mistakes when adding invariant tests

Testing implementation details. A contract should survive a refactor. Assert a durable result—number of writes, access boundary, state transition—not which private helper ran.

Using only random input. Generated input expands coverage, but important named cases still matter. Keep regression fixtures for incidents and known edge cases.

Letting the same change rewrite every oracle. If an agent alters production code, snapshots, unit tests, and contract tests in one sweep, reviewers lose their independent evidence. Separate those changes or require a stronger review path.

Making every rule a blocking invariant. Start with the small set whose failure would cause financial loss, data exposure, irreversible writes, or serious reliability damage. A hundred weak contracts will be ignored.

Mistaking test coverage for behavioral coverage. Coverage reports show which lines ran. They do not show whether the line preserved ownership, idempotency, or a state boundary.

Where this fits in an AI-assisted engineering workflow

Invariant tests sit beside, not above, the rest of your quality system:

  • Types and schemas catch malformed values.
  • Unit tests catch local logic mistakes.
  • Integration tests prove boundaries with real infrastructure.
  • Contract tests protect cross-module promises.
  • Invariant tests protect rules across many inputs and paths.
  • Code review checks intent, readability, and operational consequences.

For AI-assisted work, the practical payoff is trustable speed. You can let an agent make a broad mechanical improvement when the most important promises are executable and independently checked. That is safer than restricting agents to trivial tasks—and safer than trusting a green checkmark with no stated contract.

FAQ

What is an invariant test for AI-generated code?

It checks a rule that must stay true across many inputs and execution paths, such as tenant isolation, one payment per idempotency key, or valid state transitions. It complements example-based unit tests.

Are invariant tests the same as property-based tests?

No. Property-based testing is a useful technique for generating many inputs. An invariant is the behavior you want to preserve. You can test an invariant with generated values, fixed fixtures, integration tests, or all three.

Which invariants should a small team add first?

Start with data isolation, authorization, idempotency, money movement, irreversible deletes, and the most expensive performance paths. Choose rules where one regression would create real user or business harm.

Should an AI coding agent be allowed to edit invariant tests?

It can propose a change, but treat that change as a contract decision rather than routine cleanup. Require explicit review and a reason the product rule itself changed; otherwise the agent can make failing evidence disappear.

How do I know an invariant test is strong enough?

Prove it can fail. Temporarily introduce the forbidden behavior, or use mutation testing, and confirm the contract catches it. If it stays green, it is not protecting the rule yet.

Do invariant tests make refactoring slower?

They take time to write, but they reduce the slowest part of refactoring: diagnosing a production regression after a large, plausible-looking change. Start with high-risk paths and keep each contract narrow.

title: LVMem: Image-Augmented Memory for Long-Horizon Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.27104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable language-guided perception is essential for embodied agents, where questions about objects, events, and their locations must be answered from long observation histories. Unlike conventional visual question answering, realistic robotic settings require reasoning over extended temporal horizons and persistent scene memory. We build upon the view-based memory paradigm and propose an efficient framework for long-horizon spatio-temporal question answering. While existing view-based systems typically store either text captions or visual embeddings, we extend the ReMEmbR-style memory with image paths that link each stored description to its original visual content. To make the stored annotations more informative, we replace uniform sampling during memory construction with an optical-flow-based frame selection strategy (PSFR) and store an object-centric descriptive scene representation instead of plain captions. We further equip a VLM-based agent with an adaptive retrieval tool that returns the image associated with the most relevant caption, allowing the agent to decide when visual inspection is needed. On the OC-NaVQA benchmark, LVMem outperforms ReMEmbR on binary and positional metrics with both backbones and matches or exceeds a 4D scene graph DAAAM baseline on binary accuracy, while operating on a lightweight view-based memory that requires no explicit graph construction.

title: useState vs useReducer: Stop Choosing Tools Before Understanding State
description:
Why React state management needs consistent decision criteria, not another library.

When should you use useState instead of useReducer?

The common answer is straightforward:

  • Use useState for simple state.
  • Use useReducer for complex state.

It's not necessarily wrong. But I think it's incomplete.

Because state management complexity isn't just about how many values we store. It's also about who owns the state, how it changes, which rules govern those changes, and how long that state needs to live.

That leads me to a more fundamental question:

Why do we start by choosing a state management tool before defining the criteria that should guide that choice?

1. The Problem with Tool-First Thinking

Imagine we're building a checkout flow in React.

We have a shipping address, payment method, discount code, and several validation rules.

We could use multiple useState hooks. Or we could combine the logic into a useReducer.

But having multiple state variables doesn't automatically justify a reducer.

What matters is how those values relate to each other.

For example, changing the shipping country might invalidate the selected shipping method.

Now we're no longer dealing with independent values. We're dealing with related state transitions governed by business rules.

And that's where the architectural decision becomes interesting.

2. Introducing a State Management Decision Authority

What if we separated the decision-making process from the tools themselves?

I like to think of this as a State Management Decision Authority.

It's not a new React API, an additional library, or an official design pattern.

It's a proposed architectural approach: define a consistent set of criteria that determines which state management strategy fits a particular problem.

Before choosing a tool, evaluate five dimensions.

State ownership

Who needs access to this state?

Is it owned by a single component, a feature, or multiple independent parts of the application?

Update complexity

Does updating the state involve assigning a new value, or applying several related business rules?

State relationships

Are state values independent, or must certain invariants remain true whenever one value changes?

State transitions

Are there explicit transitions between states, such as idle, processing, success, and error?

State lifecycle

Are we managing local UI state, shared client state, or server state that requires fetching, caching, and synchronization?

The answers should determine the tool, rather than the tool shaping how we define the problem.

3. When useState Is the Right Choice

Consider a simple toggle:

const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);

The state is local, the update is straightforward, and there are no complex transition rules.

Introducing actions and a reducer here would add complexity without providing much value.

The same applies to many inputs, visibility flags, and independently updated UI values.

Importantly, the number of state variables alone is not a reliable decision criterion.

A component with five independent state variables might be better served by five useState hooks than by one reducer.

The goal isn't to minimize the number of hooks. It's to minimize unnecessary complexity.

4. When useReducer Becomes More Valuable

Now consider a payment workflow.

We have several possible states, and transitions between them must follow particular rules.

const initialState = {
  status: "idle",
  error: null
};

function paymentReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "PAYMENT_STARTED":
      if (state.status !== "idle") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "processing",
        error: null
      };

    case "PAYMENT_SUCCEEDED":
      if (state.status !== "processing") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "success",
        error: null
      };

    case "PAYMENT_FAILED":
      if (state.status !== "processing") {
        return state;
      }

      return {
        status: "error",
        error: action.error
      };

    default:
      return state;
  }
}

Inside the component:

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(
  paymentReducer,
  initialState
);

Instead of allowing different parts of the component to independently decide how the state should change, we dispatch actions describing what happened.

The reducer calculates the next state.

This creates a useful separation:

What happened vs. how the state should respond.

But a reducer doesn't automatically guarantee correctness.

We still need to define valid transitions, protect state invariants, and keep side effects outside the reducer.

In this example, initiating an actual payment request is a side effect, not something the reducer should perform.

5. Decision Authority vs. Transition Authority

There's an important distinction here.

Decision Authority determines which state management approach we should use.

State Transition Authority determines how state changes are evaluated and applied.

A reducer can centralize transition logic within a particular state boundary.

But that doesn't mean every state variable needs a reducer, or that every reducer needs a full state machine.

The architectural objective isn't to centralize everything.

It's to make decisions consistently while preserving the simplest appropriate implementation.

6. Beyond React Hooks: Zustand, Redux Toolkit, and Server State

The same decision criteria can extend beyond useState and useReducer.

When multiple components need the same state, we can first consider lifting state up or using Context.

When multiple features need shared client state, tools such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit may become appropriate.

If the primary challenge involves remote data fetching, caching, invalidation, and synchronization, a dedicated server-state solution such as TanStack Query or RTK Query can be more suitable.

These tools aren't necessarily mutually exclusive.

An application might use:

  • useState for local UI interactions.
  • useReducer for a complex form workflow.
  • Zustand or Redux Toolkit for shared client state.
  • TanStack Query or RTK Query for server-state management.

The decision depends on the responsibility of each state boundary.

7. A Practical Decision Framework

Here's a lightweight framework I would use before making a state management decision.

Question Possible direction
Is the state local with simple, independent updates? Start with useState
Are transitions governed by related rules? Consider useReducer
Is state shared within a component subtree? Consider lifting state or Context
Do independent features require shared client state? Evaluate Zustand or Redux Toolkit
Does the state primarily represent remote server data? Evaluate TanStack Query or RTK Query

This isn't a rigid rules engine.

A shared state doesn't automatically require a global store, and a complex state doesn't automatically require useReducer.

It's a framework for asking better questions before committing to an implementation.

8. The Bigger Architectural Principle

State management discussions often become comparisons between libraries.

Which is faster?

Which has less boilerplate?

Which is easier to learn?

Those questions matter, but they're secondary to understanding the problem.

I believe we should first establish consistent criteria for choosing a state management strategy.

Then evaluate available tools against those criteria.

Unify the decision criteria, not necessarily the tools.

That's the architectural principle I'm exploring here.

The real skill isn't knowing every state management library.

It's understanding why, when, and where each one belongs.

Final Thoughts

useState and useReducer aren't competing solutions where one must win.

They're different approaches to managing state, each valuable in the right context.

And the same reasoning applies when we move toward Context, Zustand, Redux Toolkit, or server-state solutions.

Let the problem define the tool, not the tool define the solution.

I'd love to hear how other developers approach these decisions.

Do you follow explicit state management criteria in your projects, or do team preferences and existing architecture usually drive the choice?

Part 1 of the State Management Decision Authority series.

title: Microsoft Decision-1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
