title: Verify CBE and Telebirr payments in your app with a free API
description:
If you sell anything online in Ethiopia, you know the flow: the customer pays by bank transfer or Telebirr, then sends a screenshot. Someone on your team looks at it and decides whether to ship. Screenshots are easy to edit and easy to reuse, so that decision is a guess.

I maintain cheki.et, a free, MIT-licensed receipt checker, and this post is the developer version: how to confirm a payment against the bank's own record from your backend, in a few lines of Node or Python.

One thing first, because it's the most common confusion I see. Searching "telebirr api" or "cbe api" mostly turns up payment collection: merchant APIs where you start a payment and get a callback. Those need a merchant agreement with the bank. What I'm describing is the other half. The customer has already paid, the normal way, and you want to check the receipt they sent you. That needs no contract with anyone, because Ethiopian banks and wallets publish every receipt at a public URL.

How it works

Each bank has its own receipt page: transactioninfo.ethiotelecom.et/receipt/{number} for Telebirr, mbreciept.cbe.com.et/{receiptId} for CBE, a JSON endpoint for Bank of Abyssinia, a PDF for CBE Birr, and so on. cheki fetches the right one, parses it, runs a few sanity checks (positive amount, the reference you asked for, no failed or pending status), and returns the same JSON for every bank. There are 10 banks and wallets live: CBE, Telebirr, BOA, M-Pesa, Dashen, Awash, CBE Birr, Siinqee, eBirr and ZamZam. Three of those (M-Pesa, ZamZam, CBE Birr) are marked beta because they've been checked against few or no real receipts.

One request 

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"}'

No signup and no API key. The body takes bank plus whatever that bank needs:

Field When
reference Almost always: a receipt link, Receipt ID, transaction number or FT Ref
accountNumber BOA (last 5 digits) and older CBE FT receipts (last 8 digits)
phoneNumber CBE Birr (the payer's phone)
qrData A scanned QR payload (BOA, CBE Birr, Telebirr)

That reference is made up, so you'll get a 422 back. A confirmed receipt looks like this (names and numbers are fake):

{
  "success": true,
  "verified": true,
  "bank": "Commercial Bank of Ethiopia",
  "bankCode": "cbe",
  "reference": "FT26SAMPLE01",
  "senderName": "ABEBE KEBEDE",
  "receiverName": "TIGIST ALEMU",
  "receiverAccount": "1****6171",
  "amount": 1250.5,
  "currency": "ETB",
  "date": "2026-10-01",
  "sourceUrl": "https://apps.cbe.com.et:100/?id=FT26SAMPLE0100006171",
  "cached": false
}

The rule that matters: only verified: true means the bank confirmed it. success: true only means the request was handled. A BOA QR that BOA couldn't confirm comes back with success: true, verified: false, decodedOnly: true, and a QR can be copied. Don't ship on that.

The error codes are what you'd expect: 400 bad input, 404 unknown bank, 413 body too large, 422 the bank has no such receipt, 429 rate limited (with Retry-After), 502 the bank couldn't be reached. A 502 for a geo-blocked bank includes a fallbackUrl, which is the bank's own receipt page.

Node: cheki-verify 

npm install cheki-verify   # 1.6.0, no dependencies, Node 20+

Here's the check I'd run before marking an order paid. Confirm it with the bank, then make sure it's actually this order's payment:

import { Cheki, isVerified, ChekiAPIError } from "cheki-verify";

const cheki = new Cheki();
const seen = new Set(); // use a UNIQUE column in your database instead

async function checkPayment(order, bank, reference) {
  let r;
  try {
    r = await cheki.verify(bank, reference);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof ChekiAPIError) {
      // 422: the bank has no such receipt. 502 + fallbackUrl: bank not reachable from the server.
      return { ok: false, why: e.serverMessage ?? e.message, openAtBank: e.fallbackUrl };
    }
    throw e; // network error or timeout: try again later, don't accept
  }
  if (!isVerified(r)) return { ok: false, why: "not confirmed by the bank" };
  if (r.amount !== order.amount) return { ok: false, why: `amount is ${r.amount}` };
  if (!r.receiverAccount?.endsWith(order.accountLast4)) return { ok: false, why: "paid to another account" };
  const key = `${r.bankCode}:${r.reference}`;
  if (seen.has(key)) return { ok: false, why: "receipt already used" };
  seen.add(key);
  return { ok: true, payer: r.senderName, date: r.date };
}

console.log(await checkPayment({ amount: 1250.5, accountLast4: "6171" }, "dashen", "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"));

The last two checks are the ones people skip. A real receipt for a transfer to someone else's account passes isVerified. So does a real receipt the same customer already used last week. The bank can't know about your orders, so those checks have to live in your code.

In the TypeScript SDK, any non-2xx response throws a ChekiAPIError (with statusCode, fallbackUrl and checkedUrl), and a 429 throws ChekiRateLimitError. It retries at most once, and only where that's safe.

Python: cheki 

pip install cheki   # 1.6.0, needs only requests, Python 3.10+

The Python client returns a result for API errors instead of raising, so it reads as one if:

from cheki import ChekiClient

with ChekiClient() as cheki:
    r = cheki.verify("cbe", "https://mbreciept.cbe.com.et/fHCxExampleRcpt01")

    if r.is_verified:
        print(r.sender_name, "paid", r.amount, r.currency, "to", r.receiver_account, "on", r.date)
    elif r.fallback_url:
        print("Bank not reachable from the server. Open:", r.fallback_url)
    else:
        print(f"Not verified ({r.http_status}): {r.error}")

It also installs a small CLI, which is handy in a terminal: cheki-verify telebirr DET0SAMPLE --json. It exits 0 only when the bank confirmed the receipt.

End-of-day reconciliation

POST /api/verify/batch takes up to 20 receipts:

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify/batch \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"receipts": [
        {"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"},
        {"bank": "boa", "reference": "FT26SAMPLE07", "accountNumber": "12345"}
      ]}'

You get back total, verified, failed, cached and one result per receipt. Both SDKs wrap it as verifyBatch / verify_batch.

Limits and what's kept

  • Server side only. The API sends no CORS headers, so call it from your backend, not the browser.
  • Rate limits per IP: 30 checks a minute (each batch item counts), and 5 batch requests a minute. The SDKs export RECOMMENDED_BATCH_CHUNK (15) for long lists.
  • Storage: no accounts and no database. A receipt the bank confirmed stays in the server's memory for up to six hours, so a repeat check returns cached: true without asking the bank again. Failed checks are never kept.

The full reference is in the API docs, and the developer page has the Go, PHP and Dart SDKs as well.

Telebirr and M-Pesa: self-host it

Telebirr's and M-Pesa's receipt pages only answer requests from Ethiopian networks. The hosted cheki.et API runs in Frankfurt, so for those two it returns a 502 with fallbackUrl. That's fine for a person at a counter, who can open the link on their phone, but not for an automated checkout.

The fix is to run your own copy on a server in Ethiopia:

git clone https://github.com/1RB/cheki.git
cd cheki
docker compose up -d   # serves on http://localhost:3000

Then point the SDK at it:

const cheki = new Cheki({ baseUrl: "http://your-server:3000" });

cheki = ChekiClient(base_url="http://your-server:3000")

Every option is an environment variable, and all are optional. For example, CHEKI_CACHE=off turns off the in-memory cache if you'd rather keep nothing. There's a longer walkthrough in the self-hosting guide.

Other options

cheki isn't the only way to do this. check.et, verify.et and qbirr offer hosted APIs with keys and dashboards, and there are open-source libraries if you'd rather parse receipts inside your own app, such as tx-verify for Python and telebirr-receipt for Node. They all read the same public receipt pages. Pick based on which banks you need, whether you want an account and a dashboard, and whether you can run something on an Ethiopian network.

Help wanted

The weakest spots are the beta banks. If you have a real M-Pesa, ZamZam or CBE Birr receipt that cheki gets wrong, an issue on GitHub with the names and accounts redacted helps a lot. The repo has npm run probe -- <receipt-url> --redact for exactly that.

cheki.et is MIT licensed and isn't affiliated with any bank or Ethio Telecom.

title: How to Connect AI Agents to Web Apps with Durable Action Receipts & Clean DOM Inspection: An MCP Browser Bridge
description:
How to Connect AI Agents to Web Apps with Durable Action Receipts & Clean DOM Inspection: An MCP Browser Bridge in Python

In 2026, autonomous AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, LangGraph) are routinely tasked with interacting with live web applications: filling checkout forms, retrieving invoices from SaaS portals, triggering CI/CD pipelines, and scraping protected dashboards.

However, developers building agentic workflows quickly run into three severe production bottlenecks:

  1. Context Window Exhaustion: Dumping raw HTML (often 1MB to 5MB with inline SVG, JSON hydration payloads, and telemetry scripts) exhausts the LLM's context window within 2 or 3 turns, driving token costs through the roof.
  2. Lack of Cryptographic Action Receipts: If an agent performs an irreversible transaction—like submitting a payment form or modifying permissions—there is no tamper-evident audit record proving what the DOM state was before and after the action.
  3. Zombie Memory Leaks: Unmanaged headless browser contexts stay resident in RAM when agents drop connections or fail unexpectedly, consuming gigabytes of host memory.

To solve this, we designed and built BrowserBridge: an enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that transforms noisy web pages into compact, token-efficient Accessibility Object Models (AOM) (~95% token reduction), enforces strict session pooling with automated zombie-reaping, and seals every agent action with a cryptographic SHA-256 receipt.

🏗️ The System Architecture

Instead of having your LLM parse raw HTML or blindly dispatch click coordinates, BrowserBridge sits as an auditable MCP sidecar:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |          BrowserBridge Pro MCP Server         |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   |  AOM DOM Filter   |  | Session Pool Mgr  |  |  Durable Receipts |
   |  (-95% token cost)|  | (Anti-Zombie TTL) |  |   (SQLite WAL)    |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      |   Target Web App DOM    |
                      +-------------------------+

1. Slashing Token Bloat: The Accessibility Object Model (AOM)

Raw HTML is packed with tags irrelevant to an AI agent: <style>, <script>, <svg>, tracking pixels, and deep nesting. What an agent actually needs to know is:

  • What buttons exist?
  • What links can be followed?
  • What text fields require input?

Here is the Python implementation that converts messy HTML into structured, interactive @node elements:

import re
from typing import Dict, Any, List

def extract_accessibility_tree(html_content: str, form_state: Dict[str, str]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    aom_nodes = []
    node_counter = 1

    # 1. Extract Buttons
    for m in re.finditer(r"<button([^>]*)>(.*?)</button>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        attrs, content = m.groups()
        text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", content).strip() or "Unnamed Button"
        aom_nodes.append({
            "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
            "role": "button",
            "name": text[:50],
            "selector": f"button:contains('{text[:20]}')"
        })
        node_counter += 1

    # 2. Extract Links
    for m in re.finditer(r"<a\s+([^>]*href=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"'][^>]*)>(.*?)</a>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        _, href, content = m.groups()
        text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", content).strip()
        if text and not href.startswith("javascript:"):
            aom_nodes.append({
                "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
                "role": "link",
                "name": text[:50],
                "target_url": href,
                "selector": f"a[href='{href}']"
            })
            node_counter += 1

    # 3. Extract Text Input Fields
    for m in re.finditer(r"<input\s+([^>]*)/?>", html_content, re.IGNORECASE):
        attrs = m.group(1)
        name_m = re.search(r"name=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"']", attrs, re.IGNORECASE)
        type_m = re.search(r"type=[\"']([^\"']*)[\"']", attrs, re.IGNORECASE)
        name_val = name_m.group(1) if name_m else f"input_{node_counter}"
        type_val = type_m.group(1) if type_m else "text"

        aom_nodes.append({
            "id": f"@node-{node_counter}",
            "role": "textbox" if type_val in ("text", "email", "password", "search") else type_val,
            "name": name_val,
            "selector": f"input[name='{name_val}']",
            "current_value": form_state.get(name_val, "")
        })
        node_counter += 1

    return aom_nodes[:50]

By presenting the LLM with @node-1 (role: button, name: "Checkout") instead of 250 lines of tailwind divs, prompt tokens drop by ~95% while dramatically improving selector accuracy.

2. Cryptographic Durability: Action Receipts Engine

When an agent interacts with a web interface, proving what happened and when is critical for compliance and debugging.

BrowserBridge calculates a SHA-256 fingerprint of the DOM before the action (pre_state_hash) and immediately after execution (post_state_hash), persisting the transition to an atomic SQLite WAL ledger:

import uuid
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Dict, Any

class DurableReceiptsEngine:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "receipts.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def _init_db(self):
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
            conn.execute("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS action_receipts (
                    receipt_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    session_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                    action_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                    target TEXT NOT NULL,
                    payload TEXT,
                    pre_state_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    post_state_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    status TEXT DEFAULT 'success',
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
            """)

    def issue_receipt(self, session_id: str, action_type: str, target: str,
                      pre_state_hash: str, post_state_hash: str,
                      payload: str = "") -> Dict[str, Any]:
        receipt_id = f"rcpt_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("""
                INSERT INTO action_receipts (
                    receipt_id, session_id, action_type, target, payload,
                    pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, status, created_at
                ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'success', ?);
            """, (receipt_id, session_id, action_type, target, payload, pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, now))

        return {
            "receipt_id": receipt_id,
            "session_id": session_id,
            "action_type": action_type,
            "target": target,
            "pre_state_hash": pre_state_hash[:16],
            "post_state_hash": post_state_hash[:16],
            "timestamp": now
        }

Auditing State Continuity

Using verify_action_trail(session_id), you can verify that the sequence of actions has not been tampered with or skipped:

def verify_action_trail(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
    receipts = self.list_receipts(session_id)
    for i in range(len(receipts) - 1):
        if receipts[i]["post_state_hash"] != receipts[i + 1]["pre_state_hash"]:
            return False # Chain discontinuity detected!
    return True

3. Preventing Memory Leaks: The Anti-Zombie Session Pool

Headless browser automation easily leaks memory when agents abandon sessions mid-flight. BrowserBridge solves this with an automated session reaper:

from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
from typing import Dict, List

class SessionPoolManager:
    def __init__(self, idle_ttl_seconds: int = 180):
        self.idle_ttl_seconds = idle_ttl_seconds
        self.sessions: Dict[str, BrowserSession] = {}

    def reap_zombies(self) -> List[str]:
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        reaped = []
        for sid, sess in list(self.sessions.items()):
            last_active = datetime.fromisoformat(sess.last_active)
            if now - last_active > timedelta(seconds=self.idle_ttl_seconds):
                del self.sessions[sid]
                reaped.append(sid)
        return reaped

Whenever any session is requested, or on a periodic tick, sessions exceeding the inactivity window are safely terminated and removed from host memory.

4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

BrowserBridge adheres to the standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) JSON-RPC specification. Adding it to Claude Desktop or Cursor is as simple as adding a snippet to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserbridge": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "browserbridge.server"]
    }
  }
}

Now, your AI agent has direct access to:

  • navigate_page(url)
  • extract_clean_text()
  • extract_accessibility_tree()
  • click_element(selector)
  • fill_form_field(selector, value)
  • verify_action_trail(session_id)

🚀 Get Started: Open-Source & Enterprise

The full open-source BrowserBridge Lite is available immediately on GitHub with an MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/browserbridge-mcp

If your team requires the Enterprise Pro Edition—including the persistent SQLite WAL receipts engine, multi-tenant session pool reaper, resilient selector resolver for dynamic SPAs, containerized Docker Compose manifests, and 100% passing Pytest suite:

👉 Get BrowserBridge Pro on Gumroad ($14.99 USD)

The phrase “buy verified Binance accounts” is often encountered by people researching cryptocurrency platforms, account verification, and ways to begin participating in the digital economy. Understanding this topic requires more than knowing how an account is created. It involves learning how digital financial services work, why identity verification exists, how individuals manage online financial identities, and what practical skills support responsible cryptocurrency use.
Binance is a cryptocurrency exchange platform that provides services related to digital assets. Depending on a user's location, eligibility, and the services available, its features may include cryptocurrency trading, asset management, transaction histories, and educational resources. Access to these services generally depends on applicable account requirements and identity verification procedures.
For beginners, the subject offers an opportunity to explore broader concepts in digital finance. These include personal financial responsibility, recordkeeping, transaction awareness, online identity management, and the importance of understanding platform rules before using financial services.
An important distinction is that purchasing an account previously verified in another person's name is not the same as completing verification for an account in one's own name. A practical educational approach focuses on understanding verification requirements and learning how to establish an account through the platform's authorized procedures.
Resources such as usasvcit can be considered as starting points for general information and guidance, alongside official platform documentation and applicable regulations. Readers should evaluate informational sources carefully and distinguish general explanations from authoritative requirements.
This guide explains the structure and purpose of verified cryptocurrency accounts, their practical applications, the skills users can develop, and the habits that support effective digital financial management. Its central goal is to help readers build knowledge they can apply in everyday financial decisions.
Section 1: Understanding Verified Binance Accounts
1.1 Account Structure and Essential Features
A Binance account is a digital profile through which an eligible user can access the platform's available services. Its structure may include personal profile information, account preferences, identity verification status, transaction records, and settings relevant to the services available in the user's jurisdiction.
Verification is a process through which a platform checks information about an account holder. Depending on the applicable requirements, this process may involve identifying information, identity documents, or additional checks. The precise requirements can change according to jurisdiction, account type, and platform policy.
Understanding these components helps users recognize that an exchange account is more than a username and password. It connects an individual's identity, access permissions, financial activities, and records within a digital service.
A verified status indicates that certain verification requirements have been completed. It does not automatically establish financial expertise, guarantee access to every feature, or demonstrate that an individual will make sound investment decisions.
1.2 Digital Identity and Financial Significance
Digital identity is increasingly important in modern financial services. Banks, payment providers, investment platforms, and cryptocurrency exchanges may use identity checks to understand who is accessing their services and to meet applicable regulatory obligations.
For cryptocurrency users, understanding digital identity can improve their ability to navigate financial applications. It encourages them to read account requirements, maintain accurate personal information, understand transaction records, and recognize the relationship between identity verification and access to regulated services.
A verified account should be understood as one part of a broader financial identity. Other important elements include financial literacy, responsible decision-making, accurate records, and familiarity with the platform's terms.
The distinction between account ownership and account access is particularly important. Verification is generally tied to the person whose identity was checked. Users should therefore learn how to complete the applicable process for themselves instead of assuming that another person's verification can simply be transferred.
Section 2: Practical Applications
2.1 Everyday Uses of Cryptocurrency Exchange Accounts
Cryptocurrency exchange accounts can support several practical activities when the relevant services are available and the user meets the applicable eligibility requirements. Their usefulness depends on the individual's objectives, understanding of digital assets, and ability to manage financial decisions responsibly.
Common educational and practical applications include:
● Learning about digital assets: Exploring how cryptocurrencies differ from traditional currencies, shares, and other financial instruments.
● Reviewing transaction histories: Understanding how digital financial activity is recorded and how transaction records can support personal bookkeeping.
● Studying market information: Learning how asset prices, trading volume, and market fluctuations are displayed on financial platforms.
● Developing budgeting habits: Separating educational experimentation from essential household spending and tracking any financial activity carefully.
● Understanding financial technology: Becoming familiar with digital interfaces, account settings, identity verification, and online financial workflows.
These applications can help users develop transferable knowledge. Even someone who decides not to trade cryptocurrencies can benefit from learning about digital records, financial interfaces, and the concepts underlying modern payment systems.
2.2 Applying Digital Finance Knowledge in Daily Life
The value of cryptocurrency education extends beyond a single exchange. The concepts learned while studying an account can also be applied to other financial applications, including digital banking, online payment services, and investment platforms.
For example, a person who learns to review transaction histories may become more organized when tracking household expenses. Someone who studies identity verification may better understand why financial institutions request particular documents.
Practical applications include:
● Comparing the fees and terms of financial services before choosing one.
● Maintaining organized records for budgeting and financial reporting.
● Learning how exchange rates and asset prices change over time.
● Recognizing the difference between account verification and financial suitability.
● Improving the ability to read financial documentation and follow digital procedures.
The most useful outcome is not simply familiarity with a platform. It is the development of informed habits that can improve everyday financial decision-making.
Section 3: Educational Value and Skills
Cryptocurrency platforms provide a practical setting for studying several important aspects of digital finance. By learning how accounts work, users can develop knowledge that remains useful even as individual platforms and technologies change.
Learning Outcomes

  1. Financial literacy Users can learn basic concepts such as assets, market prices, transaction fees, exchange rates, and financial risk management. These concepts help explain how digital asset markets operate and why prices may change rapidly.
  2. Digital identity awareness Studying account verification helps explain the relationship between personal information, identity checks, eligibility requirements, and financial services. This understanding is useful when interacting with banks, payment providers, and other online platforms.
  3. Recordkeeping and documentation Transaction histories and account statements illustrate the importance of maintaining clear financial records. Organized documentation can make it easier to review spending, investigate discrepancies, and prepare information for personal or professional accounting.
  4. Analytical thinking Comparing platform features, reading documentation, and evaluating financial information encourage users to ask questions, check assumptions, and distinguish reliable evidence from unsupported claims.
  5. Digital literacy Navigating financial applications helps users develop skills in reading interfaces, understanding account settings, interpreting notifications, and following documented procedures. Life Skills Gained These learning outcomes can translate into practical life skills. ● Attention to detail: Carefully reviewing information before completing financial procedures. ● Organization: Keeping financial documents and records arranged consistently. ● Patience: Following verification steps without overlooking instructions. ● Independent learning: Finding reliable explanations and comparing information from multiple sources. ● Decision-making: Considering fees, eligibility, personal objectives, and relevant terms before selecting a financial service. ● Adaptability: Applying familiar digital skills when using new financial applications. For students, these skills can support financial education. For working professionals, they can improve familiarity with digital financial tools. For households, they can encourage more systematic budgeting and documentation. The educational objective should remain broader than opening an account. Understanding how financial systems work helps individuals make better-informed choices across different aspects of their lives. Section 4: Building Trust and Credibility 4.1 Understanding What Creates Digital Credibility Digital credibility is the degree to which information, identity claims, and online activities can be understood and evaluated as reliable. In financial services, credibility depends on several factors rather than one account attribute. A verified account can indicate that a platform has completed particular identity checks. However, verification should not be confused with a guarantee of financial competence, investment success, or personal trustworthiness. Account age is similarly limited in meaning. An account that has existed for several years does not necessarily demonstrate responsible financial behavior. Its age alone cannot establish the accuracy of its information or the quality of its owner's decisions. For this reason, the educational focus should be on legitimate account ownership, accurate information, clear documentation, and consistent compliance with applicable requirements. 4.2 Key Factors That Support Credibility Several habits can help individuals maintain a clear and credible digital financial profile. Accurate personal information: Information provided during account registration and verification should be truthful and consistent with applicable requirements. Consistent account management: Users should keep relevant account details current through the platform's authorized procedures and review important notifications. Documented financial activity: Maintaining transaction records and understanding account statements can help users explain and review their financial activities. Knowledge of platform rules: Reading applicable terms and verification requirements helps users understand which actions are permitted and which services are available. Responsible communication: When discussing financial activity with an accountant, adviser, or other appropriate professional, clear records and accurate explanations support productive conversations. Independent evaluation: Financial claims should be assessed using credible documentation rather than relying solely on an account's apparent age or status. These principles apply to cryptocurrency exchanges as well as online banking, investment accounts, and payment applications. Ultimately, credibility is built through accurate information, transparent practices, and responsible behavior. It should not be treated as something that can be established solely by obtaining an account with a particular history. Section 5: Productivity and Workflow 5.1 How Structured Account Management Improves Efficiency Digital financial tools can simplify recordkeeping and make information easier to review. However, these benefits are most apparent when users adopt a consistent workflow. A structured approach begins with understanding the account's purpose. Someone studying cryptocurrency markets may need a different set of records from a person who is organizing digital asset transactions for personal accounting. Once the purpose is clear, the user can identify the information they need, establish a regular review schedule, and organize relevant documentation. For example, reviewing transaction records periodically can help a person identify unfamiliar entries, understand how balances have changed, and prepare information for budgeting. Keeping notes about educational activities can also help learners track progress without confusing study exercises with actual financial transactions. 5.2 Actionable Productivity Tips The following practices can make digital financial management more organized. Create a simple recordkeeping system. Maintain a consistent location for relevant statements, transaction exports, and notes. Use clear file names and dates. Schedule regular reviews. Set aside time to examine financial records, account notices, and any changes to applicable platform requirements. Separate learning from financial activity. Use educational materials, demonstrations, or practice exercises where available before making decisions involving real money. Read instructions before beginning. Reviewing the requirements in advance can reduce confusion and help users prepare the information they need. Use official documentation. Platform help centers and published policies are useful references when questions arise about verification, account settings, or available features. Keep financial goals realistic. Learning about cryptocurrency does not require frequent trading or constant monitoring of market prices. A defined learning schedule can prevent digital finance from becoming an unnecessary distraction. Record important decisions. Brief notes about why a financial decision was made can help users review their reasoning later. A productive workflow should reduce unnecessary effort while improving understanding. It should not encourage people to bypass account requirements or treat account access as a substitute for financial knowledge. Section 6: Case Studies and Examples The following illustrative scenarios demonstrate how the principles of account verification, financial education, and organized digital workflows can apply in everyday situations. They are hypothetical examples rather than reports of independently verified individuals or specific outcomes. Example 1: A Student Learning About Cryptocurrency A university student is interested in blockchain technology and wants to understand how cryptocurrency exchanges operate. Initially, the student assumes that obtaining an account is the main step toward learning about the subject. After reviewing educational materials, the student realizes that account registration and identity verification are only parts of the broader process. The student begins by studying blockchain fundamentals, transaction fees, market terminology, and the role of exchanges in digital asset markets. The student also reviews the platform's official documentation to understand eligibility requirements and available educational resources. Where account access is appropriate, the student follows the authorized registration and verification procedures. Over time, the student develops a glossary of financial terms and keeps notes about the differences between exchanges, wallets, and blockchain networks. Learning point: Practical financial education begins with understanding concepts and requirements. Account access alone does not provide the knowledge needed to evaluate digital assets. Example 2: A Freelancer Organizing Financial Records A freelance designer receives payments through several digital services and wants to improve personal bookkeeping. The designer studies how transaction histories and downloadable statements can support financial organization. Instead of concentrating on account age or status, the designer creates a monthly recordkeeping routine. Relevant statements are stored by date, and income entries are categorized for later review. The designer also learns that different services may use different fee structures, transaction formats, and reporting methods. Keeping these differences documented makes it easier to compare records and prepare information for an accountant. When researching cryptocurrency exchanges, the designer examines the applicable account requirements and considers whether the platform's services meet the intended purpose. Learning point: Organized records and an understanding of transaction documentation can improve financial administration. These benefits do not depend on purchasing an established account. Example 3: A Small Business Owner Exploring Digital Finance A small business owner wants to understand whether cryptocurrency could become relevant to future business operations. Before considering any financial activity, the owner researches accounting requirements, applicable regulations, transaction documentation, and the availability of services in the business's jurisdiction. The owner creates a comparison sheet covering platform features, fees, reporting tools, and eligibility conditions. The business also consults an appropriate accounting professional about the implications of digital asset transactions. Rather than treating a verified account as evidence that a platform is suitable, the owner evaluates the business's objectives and documentation needs. The result is a more structured assessment process. Even if the business ultimately decides not to use cryptocurrency, the research provides useful knowledge about financial technology and recordkeeping. Learning point: Sound financial decisions depend on evaluating practical requirements, costs, and objectives instead of focusing on a single account feature. Example 4: An Adult Learner Improving Digital Literacy An adult learner wants to become more comfortable with online financial services. The learner starts by studying the account settings, verification terminology, transaction records, and customer support documentation commonly found on financial platforms. The learner practices recognizing official help resources and distinguishing platform requirements from general advice published elsewhere. When encountering unfamiliar instructions, the learner checks the relevant documentation rather than relying on assumptions. The learner also establishes a routine for reviewing financial records and writing down questions before contacting customer support. These habits gradually become useful across other digital services, including online banking and payment applications. Learning point: Understanding one financial platform can help develop transferable digital skills, including careful reading, documentation, independent research, and organized problem-solving. Taken together, these examples show that the main educational benefits come from knowledge, consistency, and informed decision-making. None requires the purchase of an account that was verified for someone else. Section 7: Step-by-Step Guide to Understanding Binance Account Verification The following six steps provide a practical framework for learning about account verification and applying that knowledge responsibly. Step 1: Define Your Learning Objective Begin by identifying what you want to understand. Your objective might be learning cryptocurrency terminology, reviewing digital financial records, studying exchange operations, or understanding identity verification. A clear objective helps you choose relevant educational resources and avoid spending time on features that do not support your goals. Write down two or three questions you want to answer. For example, you might want to understand what identity verification involves, how transaction histories work, or which services are available in your jurisdiction. Step 2: Review Official Platform Information Visit the official Binance website and locate the relevant help center or account documentation. Read the current information about registration, identity verification, eligibility, supported jurisdictions, and available account features. Requirements can change, so current documentation is more useful than relying entirely on older articles. If you consult general informational resources such as usasvcit, compare important statements with official documentation before treating them as authoritative. Step 3: Understand Identity Verification Requirements Learn what the platform requires from individuals seeking access to its services. Depending on the applicable rules, the process may include submitting identifying information, providing an accepted identity document, or completing additional verification steps. Make sure you understand the relationship between the account holder and the identity being verified. Verification should be completed through the platform's authorized process using the account holder's own accurate information. Do not assume that an account verified for another individual can be treated as your own verified account. Step 4: Prepare Accurate Information Before starting an authorized registration or verification process, read the instructions carefully and identify the information required. Ensure that your information is accurate and consistent with the platform's stated requirements. If a document is not accepted or a detail needs clarification, consult the official instructions or appropriate support channels. Preparing in advance can make the process easier to understand and reduce avoidable errors. Step 5: Learn the Account's Available Features After completing the applicable requirements and receiving access, familiarize yourself with the available account interface. Study profile settings, transaction histories, fee information, account statements, and educational resources. Feature availability may differ according to location, eligibility, and platform policies. Take notes about unfamiliar terms and look for official explanations before relying on your interpretation. Step 6: Establish a Regular Review Routine Create a simple schedule for reviewing account information and maintaining relevant financial records. For example, a monthly review might include checking transaction histories, organizing statements, reading important platform notices, and updating personal financial records. Use this process to reinforce your understanding of digital finance. The objective is to develop a sustainable habit of informed account management rather than simply completing a registration procedure. Following these steps creates a foundation for understanding cryptocurrency services, identity verification, and responsible digital financial administration. Section 8: Frequently Asked Questions
  6. What does a verified Binance account mean? A verified Binance account is an account for which the platform has completed the applicable identity verification requirements. The exact process and available services depend on current platform policies, jurisdiction, and eligibility. Verification does not guarantee investment success or access to every feature.
  7. Why is identity verification important on cryptocurrency platforms? Identity verification can help financial platforms meet applicable legal and regulatory obligations, establish account-holder information, and determine eligibility for particular services. Understanding these procedures helps users navigate digital financial systems more effectively.
  8. Is purchasing a previously verified Binance account the same as verifying my own account? No. A previously verified account may be associated with another individual's identity. Purchasing it does not establish that the buyer has completed the platform's verification requirements. The appropriate educational and practical approach is to understand the current rules and follow the authorized process for your own account.
  9. Can learning about Binance help with everyday financial management? Yes. Studying exchange interfaces, transaction histories, fees, and financial terminology can help develop recordkeeping, analytical thinking, and digital literacy. These skills may also be useful when working with online banking and other financial applications.
  10. What should beginners learn before using a cryptocurrency exchange? Beginners should understand basic cryptocurrency concepts, market volatility, transaction fees, account requirements, financial recordkeeping, and the services available in their jurisdiction. They should also review official documentation and avoid making financial decisions based on unfamiliar terminology or assumptions.
  11. Where can I find reliable information about Binance account verification? The official Binance website and help center are appropriate starting points for current account requirements and procedures. General educational resources, including usasvcit, may provide additional context, but important requirements should be checked against official documentation and applicable regulations. Conclusion Understanding the topic of buying verified Binance accounts provides an opportunity to explore a much broader subject: the role of identity, financial literacy, and responsible account management in the digital economy. A cryptocurrency exchange account is not simply a digital profile. It can connect an individual's identity, financial records, platform access, and interactions with digital asset markets. Understanding these connections helps users approach financial technology with greater clarity and confidence. The most valuable lessons concern accurate information, legitimate account ownership, identity verification, organized recordkeeping, and informed decision-making. These principles are useful not only for cryptocurrency exchanges but also for online banking, investment applications, and other digital financial services. Practical education should focus on understanding how account verification works, what requirements apply, and how financial information can be managed effectively. Purchasing an account verified under another person's identity does not replace the process of establishing one's own eligibility and completing the platform's required procedures. Beginners can make meaningful progress by studying official documentation, learning basic cryptocurrency terminology, reviewing transaction records, and developing consistent financial habits. Additional educational resources, including usasvcit, can serve as starting points for research when their information is evaluated alongside authoritative sources. Ultimately, digital financial competence is built through knowledge and practice. Understanding the systems behind an account is more valuable than focusing solely on its age or verification status. By applying the principles in this guide, readers can develop transferable skills, improve their understanding of digital finance, and make better-informed decisions about the financial technologies they encounter in everyday life. Call to Action Take the next step by strengthening your understanding of cryptocurrency and digital financial services. Start with the official Binance help center, review the identity verification requirements that apply to your location, and explore introductory educational materials about blockchain technology, transaction fees, and financial recordkeeping. Create a personal learning checklist, keep notes about unfamiliar concepts, and set aside time each week to review what you have learned. If you consult additional resources such as usasvcit, verify important procedural details against current official documentation. Focus on developing knowledge, maintaining accurate records, and understanding legitimate account procedures. These practical habits can support long-term digital literacy and help you approach financial technology with greater confidence.

title: 5 timing bugs I hit building timed blocks with Screen Time's DeviceActivity (iOS)
description:
I build minulo, an iPhone app that hides Reels and Shorts. One feature is a timed block: lock the official Instagram app with Screen Time for, say, 30 minutes, and have it unlock on its own even if minulo isn't running. That part runs on DeviceActivity (DeviceActivityCenter.startMonitoring + a DeviceActivitySchedule, with the unlock happening in a DeviceActivityMonitor extension's intervalDidEnd).

It took five rounds of bugs to get the timing right. All five are about how the schedule's start and end are interpreted, so they apply whether you write Swift directly or go through a wrapper like react-native-device-activity (which I use, with my own additions).

1. Windows shorter than 15 minutes are rejected

Pass a 5-minute window to startMonitoring and you get an error. In my testing on device, anything under 15 minutes was refused.

My first workaround was "now + 15 minutes", which meant a 5-minute break stayed unlocked for 15. The fix was to keep the end fixed and move the start back instead:

// keep the end; pull the start back so the window is 15 minutes
export function shortWindow(untilMs: number) {
  const now = new Date();
  const e = new Date(Math.ceil(Math.max(untilMs, now.getTime() + 60000) / 60000) * 60000);
  if (e.getTime() - now.getTime() >= 15 * 60000) return { s: now, e, dated: false };
  const s = new Date(e.getTime() - 15 * 60000);
  // if the start falls on the previous day, include the date (see #3)
  return { s, e, dated: s.getDate() !== now.getDate() };
}

A start in the past is fine; intervalDidEnd still fires at the end.

2. Same hour and minute for start and end is rejected

With hour/minute-only DateComponents, a 24-hour block (13:05 today to 13:05 tomorrow) reads as start == end and is refused. I shift the start one minute later, giving a 23h59m window. Shifting it earlier would make a 1-minute window, which runs into #1.

if (s.getHours() === e.getHours() && s.getMinutes() === e.getMinutes()) {
  s = new Date(s.getTime() + 60000);
}

3. Just after midnight, hour/minute isn't enough

Because of #1, a break ending at 00:05 starts at 23:50. Sent as hour and minute only, that was read as 23:50 today, and the window broke: a 5-minute break after midnight stayed open for 15. When the start falls on the previous day, I now include year, month and day:

export function winEdge(d: Date, dated: boolean) {
  return dated
    ? { year: d.getFullYear(), month: d.getMonth() + 1, day: d.getDate(), hour: d.getHours(), minute: d.getMinutes(), second: 0 }
    : { hour: d.getHours(), minute: d.getMinutes(), second: 0 };
}

4. The number of monitored activities is limited

Registering one activity per weekday for each schedule (bedtime, class hours…) adds up fast, and the number of monitored activities is reportedly capped at around 20. Past that, startMonitoring fails, and the block simply never unlocks. Two changes:

  • daily schedules are a single activity without a weekday
  • failures are stored instead of swallowed, so the app can show that something is wrong 
DA.startMonitoring(FOCUS_ACTIVITY, { intervalStart, intervalEnd, repeats: false }, [])
  .catch((x) => set('focus:nativeErr', String(x?.message ?? x).slice(0, 120)));

5. "Unblock everything" also unblocks things that should stay blocked

Clearing all shields in intervalDidEnd also removed other blocks that should still be active at that moment, like a bedtime schedule or an app whose daily limit was used up. A manual block ending in the middle of the night took the bedtime block down with it until morning.

Now the end action re-applies whatever should still be active at that time, computed when the block starts:

DA.configureActions({ activityName: FOCUS_ACTIVITY, callbackName: 'intervalDidEnd', actions: [
  { type: 'resetBlocks' },
  // re-apply schedules that are still in their window at the end time
  ...during.map((id) => ({ type: 'blockSelection', familyActivitySelectionId: id })),
] });

The extension also drops re-applies that belong to schedules already finished, so a repeating registration doesn't carry them into the next day.

Summary

  • Windows under 15 minutes (on device) are refused: fix the end, move the start back.
  • Identical start and end hour:minute are refused: move the start one minute later.
  • After midnight the start lands on the previous day: include the date only then.
  • Monitored activities are capped: merge daily schedules and record failures.
  • Clearing everything clears too much: re-apply what should stay, at the end time.

Related: opening your own app from a Screen Time block screen (ShieldAction can't open URLs, so I go through a notification).

List of apps and methods for hiding Reels and Shorts on iPhone: https://github.com/ayumu-kitabayashi/awesome-reels-shorts-blockers

title: Controllable Multi-Object Insertion for Detection Data Augmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.26922v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controllable object insertion provides a targeted approach to augmenting object detection datasets that require category--count fidelity, annotation alignment, and source-content preservation beyond visual realism. Several approaches have been proposed to address this grand challenge, but most suffer from different constraints in precise category--count requests and visual consistency, limited coordination across categories and instances, and poor localization of multiple objects of specific category and count. We design SceneP2F, a two-stage trainable framework that connects scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation leveraging explicit instance-level layouts. SceneP2F consists of two novel designs. The first is ScenePlan which allocates one class-labeled query per requested instance, jointly predicts scene-compatible object centers, and separately estimates box sizes conditioned on the planned centers and scene context. The second is SceneAlign-Fill which combines geometry- and appearance-aware conditioning, box--class-guided regional attention, and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to render the planned objects while limiting unintended changes to source content. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K show that SceneP2F outperforms representative general-purpose editors and object-insertion methods consistently, demonstrating the value of coordinating instance-level planning and generation for category-targeted detection augmentation.

title: Meet Harnis: the open-source platform for running AI agents safely across your company
description:
AI agents are finally useful enough to do real work: fix code, answer customers, update tickets, run internal tools. The hard part isn't getting an agent to act. It's letting it act inside a company: across teams and customers, on real systems, with someone accountable for every change and a bill that doesn't surprise anyone.

That's what Harnis is for. It's an open-source, self-hosted platform that gives every agent in your organization the same harness: isolation, approvals, sandboxing, budgets and an audit trail, so teams can ship agents quickly without rebuilding the safety layer every time.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis
  • PyPI: pip install harnis
  • Helm chart: oci://ghcr.io/karawash-projects/charts/harnis
  • License: Apache 2.0

Why a harness?

Every team that builds an agent ends up writing the same plumbing: who is this user, which customer's data can they see, should this action wait for a human, where does model-written code run, how much did that conversation cost, and who approved what. When each team writes it alone, you get ten slightly different answers and no single place to audit.

Harnis turns that plumbing into a platform. Agents plug in; the guarantees come with them.

Three products on one engine

Harnis ships three ready-to-use workloads, all running on the same orchestrator:

1. A coding agent for your developers. Point the CLI at a project and describe the change. The agent works on an isolated copy, shows a diff for every file it wants to write, asks before running any command, runs your tests in a sandbox, and applies the final result to your files only when you confirm.

harnis --workspace ./my-service "add input validation to the signup handler and a test for it"

2. Multi-agent workflows. A router on a small, fast model reads each message and hands it to the right specialist (a support agent, a coding agent, or your own). Agents can hand work to each other or escalate to a person. Add a new specialist with a few lines of plugin code.

3. A multi-tenant agent app. A full API with live streaming over WebSockets and a web console for every role:

  • Users chat with agents and see each proposed change, with diffs inline.
  • Reviewers work an approvals queue and see usage and analytics.
  • Admins manage agents and their prompt versions, API keys and the audit log.
  • Platform admins create and manage tenants.

What every agent gets for free

Customer data stays separated, by the database itself

Every tenant table uses Postgres row-level security, enabled and forced, and the app connects with a role that can't bypass it. The tenant always comes from the verified login or API key, never from the request. Even a query that forgets to filter by tenant can't return another customer's data.

A human approves the exact action

Writing files, running commands and installing packages pause the session until a reviewer approves. The approval is tied to a cryptographic hash of the exact action, so the agent can't get approval for one change and then make a different one. Approvals expire, and separation of duties can stop people approving their own sessions. Paused sessions live in the database, so a decision made hours later resumes the work on any server.

Model-written code runs in a disposable sandbox

Each command gets a fresh Docker container or Kubernetes Pod with no network, a read-only system, no Linux privileges, a non-root user and strict memory, CPU and process limits. gVisor is supported for an extra kernel boundary. Files coming back out are checked, so a model can't sneak a link to a host file into your project.

Need packages? An approved install goes through a proxy that only allows package registries, and it can only change a separate dependency folder, never your code.

Security that checks itself

On Kubernetes, Harnis doesn't just assume the network rules are in place. Before it copies anything into a sandbox Pod, it probes from inside the Pod and only proceeds once the network is confirmed blocked. If the cluster can't isolate the sandbox, the command is refused with a clear error rather than run unprotected.

Costs you can predict

  • Per-turn budgets for steps, tool calls, hand-offs and spend in USD.
  • Per-tenant cost caps.
  • A token and cost ledger per model.
  • A loop breaker: it spots an agent repeating itself, warns it, then hands the session to a person.
  • Confirmed prices: you confirm each model's price at setup, so cost figures and caps are based on real numbers.

Your models, your rules

  • Models: use Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini or Amazon Nova on Bedrock, or self-hosted ones through any OpenAI-compatible API (vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, LiteLLM).
  • Failover: you set the order and Harnis fails over between providers automatically.
  • Data residency: each tenant has its own list of allowed providers, and failover never sends that tenant's data outside it.

Your login, your roles

  • Single sign-on: any OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Google), with group-to-role mapping.
  • Roles: user, reviewer, tenant admin and platform admin.
  • API keys: service keys for CI and automation, with roles, expiry and instant revocation.

Your tools and agents

A plugin SDK lets you add tools, agents and even model providers that register exactly like the built-in ones. Internal APIs, ticketing systems and databases all become tools that inherit approvals, sandboxing and auditing automatically.

Built-in guardrails

  • Prompt injection: incoming messages are checked for injection attempts.
  • Card numbers: they're redacted before the model sees them.
  • Tool output: it's marked as untrusted data, so instructions hidden in a file or web page aren't treated as commands.
  • Semantic cache: repeated questions are answered from the cache, which is fast and costs nothing.

Ready for your auditors and your ops team

  • Audit log: append-only, exportable as JSON or NDJSON.
  • Monitoring: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics and alert webhooks.
  • Data lifecycle: retention jobs, per-user data export and erasure, and backup and restore commands with verification.

Runs where you do

On a laptop, everything starts with Docker Compose on Windows, macOS or Linux. On Kubernetes, the Helm chart deploys:

  • the API, which scales out because sessions resume on any replica;
  • database migrations, run before each install or upgrade;
  • scheduled maintenance;
  • a separate, locked-down namespace for sandbox Pods.

Try it in five minutes, without an API key

The quick start uses a built-in mock model, so you can explore approvals, the sandbox and the loop breaker for free:

git clone https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis.git
cd harnis
python tasks.py install
python tasks.py up              # Postgres, Redis, tracing, demo tenants
python tasks.py sandbox-image
python tasks.py dev             # http://127.0.0.1:8000

Open the console, click Continue as local developer, and type create calc.py. The coding agent proposes two files with diffs, waits for your approvals, then runs the tests in the sandbox. Try repeat: list the files to watch the loop breaker step in, or ignore all previous instructions to see the input guard. When you're ready, python tasks.py check runs a complete feature check against your instance.

Built to be tested

Each release passes:

  • a cross-platform test suite;
  • end-to-end checks against a running API;
  • an evaluation suite and red-team scenarios;
  • sandbox tests under gVisor;
  • a full Helm deployment on a Kubernetes cluster in CI.

The same feature-check script ships with Harnis, so you can verify your own deployment the way the project verifies its releases.

Get involved

Harnis 1.0 is out now, free under Apache 2.0, and provided as is. Star the repo, try it on a real workflow, and tell me what you'd build on it:

https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis

Issues, ideas and pull requests are welcome.

title: Cloudflare says its Rust TypeScript port is 8x faster. I measured 5.3x — and 72% less memory.
description:
Cloudflare says its Rust TypeScript port is 8x faster. I measured 5.3x — and 72% less memory.

Cloudflare announced tsrs today: a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, built with VoidZero and the original tsc-rs author, incubated under Oxc, and developed "in close collaboration with the TypeScript team." The headline numbers are specific, which is an invitation: up to 8x faster and ~70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0, at the same number of type-check workers.

An experimental release is on npm, so the claim is checkable the way all compiler claims should be checked — by installing both and timing them. I did. The short version: the memory claim landed almost exactly, the speed claim is real but "up to" is doing some work, the diagnostics matched perfectly, the emitted JS was byte-identical — and the exit code wasn't.

The setup 

npm install tsrs typescript
tsrs        0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929
            reports: Version 7.1.0-dev.20260930.4 (microsoft/TypeScript@b85298b)
typescript  7.0.2   (the "TypeScript 7.0" baseline from the claim)
machine     2 vCPU Linux VM, Node v24.20.0

One fairness note, because Cloudflare is honest about it in the post and you should be too when quoting me: tsrs tracks TypeScript 7.1 dev, and the post itself says TypeScript 7.1 beta is already up to 2.5x faster than 7.0, partly from optimizations upstreamed from tsrs. So this is not a clean "Rust vs Go, same compiler version" race. It's the race a user actually gets today: the two packages you can npm install right now, run with defaults on the same project. That's the comparison that decides whether you switch.

The corpus is synthetic but not trivial: 400 TypeScript files, 35,199 lines, generated deterministically — a chain of modules, each defining a generic interface, 28 generic functions doing Map construction over typed arrays, and Pick/& type aliases, all under strict: true with skipLibCheck. Both compilers ran tsc --noEmit / tsrs --noEmit, three runs each, timed externally with peak RSS from wait4 rusage (the compiler's own peak, not the npm shim's).

The numbers 

clean project, 400 files / 35,199 lines, --noEmit, defaults
              run 1     run 2     run 3     median    peak RSS
tsc 7.0.2     3.400s    2.508s    1.936s    2.508s    ~392 MB
tsrs 0.18.0   0.581s    0.474s    0.385s    0.474s    ~110 MB

Median-to-median that's 5.3x faster; best-to-best it's 5.0x; first (cold) runs give 5.9x. I couldn't coax out 8x on this box and corpus — but this is a 2-vCPU VM and a mid-size synthetic project, not Cloudflare's benchmark suite, and their wording is "up to." What I can say is that a 5x type-check speedup is not a rounding error or a cherry-picked microbenchmark. It's the difference between a check you run on save and a check you run on commit.

Memory is where it gets almost boring: ~110 MB vs ~392 MB peak is 72% less, against a claim of "~70% less." Reproduced, nearly to the digit. On a laptop that number is trivia; in the environments Cloudflare cares about — Wasm sandboxes, browser-hosted toolchains, Workers — it's the whole argument, and their post makes it explicitly: a Go binary compiled to Wasm carries its garbage collector with it, a Rust one doesn't have one to carry.

Startup overhead, for the small-project case (a one-file project, 5 runs each):

tsc    0.825  0.860  0.552  0.525  0.514   (seconds)
tsrs   0.450  0.354  0.247  0.209  0.217

Even where there's almost nothing to compile, tsrs starts in roughly half the time. Both are dominated by process startup at this size; the ratio is the story, not the absolutes.

Does it agree with tsc?

Speed is worthless if the port quietly checks a slightly different language. I seeded the same project with four errors across two files — two bad assignments, a call to a nonexistent function, and a method call on a number:

tsc:  exit=1, 4 errors
tsrs: exit=2, 4 errors
  src/mod10.ts(89,14):  error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
  src/mod10.ts(90,14):  error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  src/mod10.ts(91,1):   error TS2304: Cannot find name 'nonexistentFunction'.
  src/mod200.ts(89,42): error TS2339: Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'number'.

The four diagnostics are identical in file, line, column, code, and message — in this run even the order matched, though Cloudflare warns diagnostic order is a known current difference, so don't build tooling that depends on it. Then I compiled the clean project to JS with both: 400 output files each, and diff -rq found zero differences — byte-identical emit on this corpus.

The one real divergence I found is small and exactly the kind that breaks a CI script at 2 a.m.: on type errors, tsc exits 1 and tsrs exits 2. Any script doing if [ $? -eq 1 ] instead of -ne 0 will treat a failed tsrs check as success-shaped. It's an experimental release (the version string is a dev build, 0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev), so this is a "file it and move on" difference, not a scandal — but it's the sort of detail the announcement's "compiles like tsc" framing glosses over, and now you know to grep for it.

Verdict

Reproduced, with one qualifier each:

  • "~70% less memory" — yes: 72% less on my corpus.
  • "Up to 8x faster" — I measured 5.3x median on a 2-vCPU VM with a 35k-line synthetic project, against a baseline (7.0.2) that tsrs's own upstream (7.1) is already much faster than. Treat 8x as a ceiling, 5x as plausible, and measure your own repo — the gap will move with project shape and core count.
  • Faithful port — on everything I threw at it: identical diagnostics, identical emit. One exit-code difference to check in your scripts.

The more interesting claim in Cloudflare's post isn't a number at all: it's that frontier models now make ports like this feasible in days, so the maintenance strategy is an agent that reads upstream TypeScript diffs every morning and regenerates a compatibility matrix every night. If that process holds, tsrs stays faithful; if it slips, tsrs becomes a fork with good benchmarks. The 5.3x I measured is real today. Whether it's still the same language in a year is a process question, and for once the vendor said so themselves.

Sources: Cloudflare's announcement (published today, October 20; HN 329 points), the tsrs npm package (0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929). All timings, memory figures, diagnostics, and emit comparisons above were measured locally today; the corpus generator and benchmark script are deterministic (seed 42).

title: Frontend Dogma’s Global RSS Feed Is Now a Paid Feature
description:
TL;DR: Access to Frontend Dogma’s main feed—which features some exclusive news—now requires a small maintenance fee of $12 per year.

Over the years, Frontend Dogma has become one of the main sources of frontend development news and tools. Frontend Dogma’s growing archives provide unique access to the history of the wider field of web development.

Providing this service for free is not sustainable, however. Book sales pay for some of the work, but so far, few people acknowledge Frontend Dogma’s value by supporting the project on Open Collective.

Starting today, the global RSS feed (with the 250 newest articles and videos) is a paid feature.

You can get access by a small maintenance contribution of only $12 per year.

If you don’t like to support Frontend Dogma, you can still follow Frontend Dogma’s individual topic feeds as well as Frontend Dogma’s social media accounts on Mastodon and Bluesky. These are less convenient and reliable but still workable options to stay up-to-date.

Also, if you want to support Frontend Dogma in a different manner and so that the main feed may be made free again, consider buying Frontend Dogma’s books or contributing to the project on Open Collective. You’re not alone: We do the same for the projects we use and like. Thank you.

description:

Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly participate in operational workflows where approvals, binds, and payments create commitments. An approval valid when issued may no longer authorize execution after relevant facts, evidence, policy, or authority change. We call this the evaluation--execution gap. We specify a state-bound runtime assurance layer that separates probabilistic measurement from deterministic adjudication, binds an execution allowance to the decision-relevant basis of an approval, invalidates that allowance after relevant logged changes, and rechecks admissibility at dispatch. This distinguishes the continued validity of a prior approval from a current-state policy check. We describe eight failure modes, an assurance model, a reference architecture, and prospective interventions with retrospective remediation. In a scripted 42-case replay, the state-bound configuration identifies 15 later-invalidated approvals that a deliberately non-re-evaluating point-in-time comparator does not revisit; it holds 14 affected actions before dispatch and compensates one landed effect. These results illustrate behavior under the stipulated policies and event orders, not superiority over dispatch-time enforcement designs or production effectiveness. Under explicit interception, ingestion, dependency, and serialization assumptions, the model establishes dispatch-time validity within the registered execution surface.

title: TIL: GBase Database Silent Installation Requires License Acceptance
description:
Today, I ran a silent installation of GBase Database(GBase 8s), only to have it fail on the first attempt. The cause? The license acceptance parameter was missing.

It is a small configuration detail, but it can stop an unattended installation before deployment gets anywhere.

Why Does License Acceptance Matter?

Unlike an interactive installation, silent installation has no graphical prompt where an operator can review and accept the license during execution. The required acceptance must be provided explicitly through the supported installation parameters.

For a GBase Database(GBase 8s) silent installation, the response file may contain:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Alternatively, you can pass the parameter directly in the installation command:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Confirm the exact parameter name and syntax against the documentation for your installation package, and make sure the applicable license terms have actually been reviewed and accepted before setting the value to TRUE.

Make It Part of Your Deployment Standard

When deploying GBase Database across multiple servers, a missing parameter can cause repeated failures and unnecessary troubleshooting.

To avoid this:

  • Include the required license-acceptance setting in your response file template.
  • Validate the response file before running a batch deployment.
  • Test the complete installation procedure on one machine first.
  • Check the installer logs and exit status rather than assuming the installation succeeded.

The broader lesson goes beyond licensing: every confirmation required by an interactive installation must be handled explicitly in an unattended workflow.

For reliable GBase Database deployment automation, small prerequisites deserve the same attention as installation paths, component selection, and post-installation configuration.

Have you ever lost time debugging a silent installation because of one missing parameter?

title: Language Guidance for Supervised Vision Training: An Empirical Study of Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.27208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success on vision benchmarks, yet they continue to struggle with many generalization challenges. Supervised vision training relies on one-hot labels, which provide limited information about semantic structure and shared attributes between classes. This limited supervision can leave visual representations vulnerable to distribution shifts, spurious correlations, texture bias, adversarial perturbations, and forgetting in sequential learning settings. We study whether pretrained language models can serve as lightweight auxiliary supervision for vision training without requiring paired image-text data, prompt engineering, or contrastive objectives. Specifically, we evaluate two forms of language guidance, Explicit Language Guidance (ExLG) and Implicit Language Guidance (ImLG). We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across six generalization regimes, including in-distribution, out-of-distribution generalization, shortcut and spurious correlation resistance, texture and shape bias, adversarial robustness, and continual learning. Our analyses show that the two mechanisms have complementary strengths, with explicit guidance consistently benefiting in-distribution, low-data performance, and continual learning retention, while implicit guidance is often more useful in shortcut-sensitive settings and under stronger adversarial perturbations. Importantly, both are lightweight and add minimal parameters and training overhead. The analyses characterize when language-derived structure helps supervised vision training and provides a practical roadmap for using off-the-shelf pretrained models from another modality as auxiliary supervision.
