title: Declarative Go CLIs with Commandment
description:
Over the last seven years in IT consulting, I have built more than 50 CLIs for customers and projects. I spent a lot of that time refining workflows around Cobra and Viper, trying to make CLI authoring feel as clean and idiomatic as the rest of the Go around it. I never quite got the workflow I wanted.

There was no single breaking point. The same kinds of friction just kept showing up. I wanted flags and arguments to become ordinary Go values once they reached the application. I got tired of defining the same idea again because help, completion, configuration, or tests needed it. I wanted new capabilities to fit the CLI instead of feeling bolted on. Setup order should only matter when order is actually part of the CLI's meaning.

I also spend a lot of time with Kubernetes and Terraform, so declarative systems were already a natural way for me to think. You declare relationships, validate them, and let the system derive the consequences. After years of trying to improve my CLI workflow, I stopped thinking the remaining friction was another convention I had failed to discover. I thought the underlying authoring model was the constraint.

That line of thinking became Commandment, a declarative CLI framework for Go.

Meet alienctl

I'll use a small fictional CLI called alienctl throughout the article. It has two commands.

$ alienctl scan mars
scanning mars

$ ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH=2 alienctl abduct --beam-strength 4 cow
abducting cow with beam strength 4

BeamStrength has a static default of 1. The host environment can contribute 2 through ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH. The user can contribute 4 through --beam-strength. The accepted value must also be between 1 and 10.

That one value captures the broader problem I kept running into. The flag spelling can live in parser setup, help and completion can need their own description of it, configuration can separately decide whether the flag beats the environment, and tests can encode the same precedence again. Each piece can be reasonable on its own while the same fact ends up with several owners.

Commandment takes a different approach. Application code declares semantic relationships in ordinary Go. Compile validates them and produces an immutable Application, and later operations read from that application instead of rebuilding the CLI's meaning. That's what I mean by declarative here. It does not mean YAML or struct tags, and it does not replace ordinary Go control flow.

Definition -> Compile -> immutable Application

type abductConfig struct {
    Target       string
    BeamStrength int
}

abductCmd := cli.Command[abductConfig]{
    Name: "abduct",
    Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[abductConfig]) {
        cb.Arguments.String(&cb.Config.Target, "target")

        beamStrength := cb.Values.Int(&cb.Config.BeamStrength)
        cb.Values.Default(beamStrength, 1)
        cb.Values.Environment(beamStrength, "ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH")
        cb.Flags.ValueFor(beamStrength).Long("beam-strength")
        cb.Rule.Between(beamStrength, 1, 10)
    },
    Run: func(_ context.Context, cfg *abductConfig) error {
        fmt.Printf(
            "abducting %s with beam strength %d\n",
            cfg.Target,
            cfg.BeamStrength,
        )
        return nil
    },
}

The root also declares a simpler scan command.

type scanConfig struct {
    World string
}

var definition = cli.Definition[struct{}]{
    Name: "alienctl",
    Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[struct{}]) {
        scanCmd := cli.Command[scanConfig]{
            Name: "scan",
            Declare: func(cb *cli.CommandBuilder[scanConfig]) {
                cb.Arguments.String(&cb.Config.World, "world")
            },
            Run: func(_ context.Context, cfg *scanConfig) error {
                fmt.Printf("scanning %s\n", cfg.World)
                return nil
            },
        }
        cb.Subcommands.Command(scanCmd)
        cb.Subcommands.Command(abductCmd)
    },
}

The separate scanConfig and abductConfig types are deliberate. Each command owns the Go state its handler actually needs instead of contributing fields to one universal root configuration. Commandment's declarations stay ordinary, statically typed Go. The design does not depend on reflection-driven struct or tag decoding.

The process entrypoint is ordinary Go too.

app, err := cli.Compile(definition)
if err != nil {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(1)
}

if err := app.RunFromProcess(context.Background()); err != nil {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
    os.Exit(cli.ExitCode(err))
}

For that invocation, the same destination has three candidate values.

static default  -> 1
environment     -> 2
flag            -> 4
resolved value  -> 4

The handler never sees a parser object or a bag of raw strings. It gets an ordinary int. That was one of the things I wanted from the start. The CLI boundary is textual, but application code should work with typed Go values.

int is only the built-in case. An application-defined Go type can use a ValueCodec[T] to define how it crosses the textual CLI boundary. Flags, environment input, defaults, resolution, and inspection can all work with that typed destination instead of inventing separate string representations.

The default, environment variable, flag, and range rule all point at the same typed destination. There is no second BeamStrength definition for configuration or validation.

Help and completion use the compiled application

The compiled application already has enough information to render help.

$ ./alienctl --help
Usage:
  alienctl [flags] <command>

Commands:
  scan
  abduct
  help        Show help.
  completion  Generate shell completion source

Flags:
  --help  Show help.
  -h      Show help.

The abduct command is available through the intrinsic help action as well.

$ ./alienctl help abduct
Usage:
  alienctl abduct [flags] <target>

Arguments:
  <target>

Flags:
  --beam-strength VALUE, --beam-strength=VALUE

I did not define a second command-and-flag model for help. The compiled application already knows the command, positional argument, and flag spelling, so help can present them without another description of the CLI.

Completion uses the same grammar. With incomplete input ab, the application can determine what can legally come next.

completion, err := app.Complete(ctx, cli.CompletionRequest{
    Args: []string{"ab"},
    Cursor: cli.CompletionCursor{
        Argument: 0,
        Byte:     2,
    },
})

For this application, the completion result contains abduct.

abduct

The completion request is not tied to a shell. Shell integration adapts the semantic result for a concrete client without defining another command language.

The compiled application still has the grammar, so execution, help, and completion all use it.

Cobra already does this part well

If you use Cobra, this part should be familiar. Cobra already gives Go applications an executable command model with arguments and flags, generated help, and shell completion.

Viper can sit alongside it as a configuration registry, binding command-line flags and environment variables and resolving multiple configuration sources with an explicit precedence order. In the example above, Cobra + Viper can also resolve the effective value to 4.

Commandment is not a feature-for-feature replacement for Viper. Its boundary is the CLI's semantic model. Broader application configuration can stay in ordinary application code. When external configuration affects CLI semantics, it crosses that boundary as typed input instead of becoming another model of the CLI.

What pushed me toward Commandment was the authoring model. After years of writing CLIs, I was tired of carrying setup knowledge across declarations, follow-up mutations, bindings, lifecycle hooks, and initialization timing. Cobra and Viper can be wrapped and organized carefully. I wanted the relationships themselves to be the source of truth.

Commandment validates those relationships during compilation. Order affects behavior only when order is part of the model. Dependencies between semantic values are declared too, so Commandment can validate scope and cycles and derive evaluation order from the dependency graph instead of callback timing.

A typical Cobra + Viper arrangement separates those responsibilities roughly like this.

Cobra / pflag
    command grammar
    flags
    help
    completion

Viper
    configuration sources
    precedence
    effective configuration

application code
    application-specific policy

             versus

Commandment

BeamStrength destination
    <- default 1
    <- environment ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH
    <- flag --beam-strength
    <- rule Between(1, 10)

             Compile
                |
                v
      immutable Application
                |
       +--------+--------+
       |        |        |
      Run    Inspect   Complete
                |
          semantic tests

Both approaches can produce 4. With Commandment, the application still knows why 4 won.

Inspecting why the flag won 

$ ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH=2 alienctl abduct --beam-strength 4 cow
abducting cow with beam strength 4

A terminal-output test can prove that the program printed 4, but it cannot distinguish normal flag precedence from an ignored environment value, a handler overwrite, or a fallback that happened to produce the same integer.

Because Commandment retained the invocation semantics, Inspect can analyze explicit invocation input without executing the selected handler. The clitest package can assert those observations directly.

func TestBeamStrengthFlagWins(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()

    app := clitest.Compile(t, definition)
    beamStrength := clitest.Command("abduct").Flag("--beam-strength").Value()
    request := cli.InspectionRequest{
        Env: cli.Env{{
            Name:  "ALIEN_BEAM_STRENGTH",
            Value: "2",
        }},
        Args: []string{"abduct", "--beam-strength", "4", "cow"},
    }
    clitest.Inspect(t.Context(), app, request).Require(t,
        clitest.InspectionReady(),
        beamStrength.Text("4"),
        beamStrength.ContributedBy(cli.ValueProducerKindFlag),
    )
}

That test proves both the effective value and the winning producer.

effective value  = 4
winning producer = flag

The default, environment input, and flag are three producers for one semantic destination. Resolution chooses the effective contribution and retains its provenance.

The test does not recreate Commandment's precedence rules. It asks the compiled application what happened.

Parsing does not erase the reason behind the result. Inspect can explain it later without running the handler or inferring semantics from presentation text.

One semantic authority does not mean one representation

One semantic authority does not require one giant data structure or one implementation path for everything.

Help, completion, inspection, diagnostics, schema, reference data, and runtime value state have different consumers and different lifetimes. They deserve different representations.

A semantic fact should still have one authority. Other operations and artifacts can project that fact for their own purpose, but they should not silently redefine it.

Definition
    |
    | Compile
    v
immutable Application
    |
    +-- Run / RunFromProcess --> execution and intrinsic actions such as help
    +-- Complete -----------> semantic completion
    +-- Inspect ------------> invocation-specific observation
    `-- Schema -------------> detached static artifact

Execution, help, completion, inspection, and schema need different representations, but they should agree on the command and value semantics they share.

That is the design I had been trying to get to. Handlers receive typed Go values, each CLI fact has one owner, and help, completion, inspection, and tests reuse the compiled model. Setup order only matters when the model says it matters.

When would I use this instead of Cobra?

Cobra fits well when the main job is an executable command tree with commands, arguments, flags, dispatch, help, and completion. Pairing it with Viper can also provide configuration through environment variables, defaults, files, and explicit precedence.

Commandment is aimed at CLIs where the command tree is only part of the problem. Typed resolution, provenance, and policy may also need to stay coherent across execution, completion, diagnostics, tooling, and tests.

Cobra can implement the behavior shown in this article. The decision is whether a command tree plus configuration registry is enough semantic authority for the CLI you are building.

For a CLI dominated by routing, flags, help, and completion, Cobra is probably the smaller choice. Commandment starts to earn its extra machinery when you need to ask the compiled CLI why a value resolved the way it did, project the same accepted semantics into tooling, or test those semantics without recreating them.

At that point, I would rather have one source of CLI meaning feeding several views than several reasonable systems that can slowly drift apart.

Commandment RC1

Commandment is now in its RC1 review period and requires Go 1.27.1. I am using this release-candidate period to get the API in front of people building real Go CLIs before I finalize v1.0.0.

The source, examples, and documentation are all in the Commandment repository.

If you try Commandment on an existing Go CLI, I'd especially like to hear what gets simpler, what stays awkward, and anything in the API that you think should change before v1.0.0 is finalized.

title: How to Give AI Agents Safe Database Migration Powers Without Locking Production: A Zero-Downtime MCP Guard
description:
How to Give AI Agents Safe Database Migration Powers Without Locking Production: A Zero-Downtime MCP Guard in Python

In 2026, autonomous coding agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, LangGraph, CrewAI) frequently generate full database schema migrations. You ask the agent to "add two-factor authentication support", and seconds later it commits a migration script:

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_users_phone ON users(phone);

In a local dev environment with 10 rows, this executes in 2 milliseconds. But when applied to a production PostgreSQL database with 5 million rows:

  1. ALTER TABLE ... NOT NULL acquires an AccessExclusiveLock, halting every incoming SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE on the users table.
  2. CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) acquires a ShareLock, queuing all user write queries behind it.
  3. Database connection pools exhaust in seconds, triggering widespread HTTP 503 timeouts across your entire web application.

To allow AI agents to safely iterate on database schemas without human babysitting, we built MigrateSafe: an intelligent Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that analyzes migrations for locking hazards, refactors them into non-locking 3-phase Expand/Contract patterns, and verifies rolling upgrades under simulated traffic.

The Architecture: Guarding the Production Database

Instead of letting agents apply unchecked DDL directly, all migration proposals are validated through MigrateSafe:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                         (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |          MigrateSafe Pro MCP Server           |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              |                     |                     |
     (1. Safety Analyzer)   (2. Pattern Engine)  (3. Traffic Sim)
              v                     v                     v
       +-------------+       +-------------+       +-------------+
       | Lock Level  |       | 3-Phase     |       | Live Shadow |
       | & Hazard    |       | Expand &    |       | Concurrency |
       | Detection   |       | Contract    |       | Benchmark   |
       +-------------+       +-------------+       +-------------+
              |                     |                     |
              +---------------------+---------------------+
                                   |
                       (Zero-Downtime Safe DDL)
                                   v
                   +-------------------------------+
                   |     Production Database       |
                   +-------------------------------+

1. Detecting Lock Contention Before Deployment

Different SQL statements acquire different lock levels in relational engines. In PostgreSQL:

  • SELECT acquires AccessShareLock.
  • UPDATE / DELETE acquires RowExclusiveLock.
  • ALTER TABLE / DROP COLUMN acquires AccessExclusiveLock (conflicts with EVERYTHING).

MigrateSafe inspects migration statements and maps exact lock requirements:

def analyze_migration_safety(sql: str, dialect: str = "postgres") -> dict:
    detected_hazards = []
    for line in sql.splitlines():
        if re.search(r"\bADD\s+COLUMN\s+.*?\bNOT\s+NULL\b(?!\s+DEFAULT\b)", line, re.I):
            detected_hazards.append({
                "statement": line.strip(),
                "severity": "CRITICAL",
                "lock_level": "AccessExclusiveLock",
                "message": "Adding NOT NULL column without DEFAULT locks table and fails on non-empty tables.",
                "recommendation": "Use Expand/Contract: Add nullable column, backfill in batches, then add NOT NULL constraint."
            })
        if re.search(r"\bCREATE\s+INDEX\s+(?!CONCURRENTLY\b)", line, re.I):
            detected_hazards.append({
                "statement": line.strip(),
                "severity": "WARNING",
                "lock_level": "ShareLock",
                "message": "CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks all table writes.",
                "recommendation": "Use 'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY'."
            })
    return {"safety_verdict": "CRITICAL" if detected_hazards else "SAFE", "hazards": detected_hazards}

2. The Zero-Downtime 3-Phase Expand/Contract Pattern

When an AI agent proposes a destructive or locking DDL statement, MigrateSafe automatically refactors it into a 3-phase zero-downtime plan:

Phase 1: Expand (Non-blocking deployment) 

-- 1. Add nullable column without exclusive rewrite lock
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);

-- 2. Build index concurrently without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_phone ON users(phone);

Phase 2: Async Backfill 

-- Populate historical records asynchronously in small batches (no long locks)
UPDATE users SET phone = '+1000000000' WHERE phone IS NULL LIMIT 1000;

Phase 3: Contract (Final cleanup) 

-- Add NOT NULL constraint once all rows have been backfilled
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN phone SET NOT NULL;

This guarantees that both the old version of your application code and the new version can run simultaneously during rolling Kubernetes or Docker deployments.

3. Live Shadow Traffic Simulation

How do you prove a migration won't spike query latency before running it in production?

MigrateSafe Pro includes a Live Shadow Traffic Simulation Harness:

  • Spins up an isolated database replica using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL).
  • Spawns concurrent worker threads executing high-frequency read and write transactions.
  • Applies the migration script while traffic is active.
  • Computes average query latency, peak latency spikes, and verifies 0 transaction deadlocks or timeouts. 
migratesafe-pro simulate path/to/migration.sql --threads 4

Output:

=== LIVE SHADOW TRAFFIC SIMULATION ===
Zero Downtime Verified: True
Migration Duration:     14.2 ms
Total Traffic Queries:  382
Failed Queries:         0
Avg Query Latency:      0.82 ms
Max Latency Spike:      4.10 ms

4. Connecting to Claude Desktop & Cursor

In your claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "migratesafe": {
      "command": "migratesafe",
      "args": ["run"]
    }
  }
}

Now, when Claude or Cursor proposes a database change, it can autonomously call:

  • analyze_migration_safety(sql="ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN tracking_code;")
  • generate_zero_downtime_pattern(sql="ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age INT NOT NULL;")
  • simulate_shadow_traffic(migration_sql="ALTER TABLE items ADD COLUMN status TEXT;")

Open Source vs. Enterprise Pro

We have released the open-source MigrateSafe Lite edition:

  • 📦 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/migratesafe-mcp
  • Features: Static AST lock detection, dangerous drop identification, dry-run lock duration estimation, and schema diffing.

For high-availability engineering teams running mission-critical databases, MigrateSafe Pro adds:

  • 🔄 Zero-Downtime Pattern Generator: Automated 3-phase Expand/Contract decomposition.
  • ⚡ Live Shadow Traffic Simulator: Multi-threaded latency spike benchmarking.
  • ⏪ Automated Rollback Verifier: Tests up.sql + down.sql with 100% data preservation guarantees.
  • 🐳 Production Docker & Compose: CI/CD container sidecar.
  • 🧪 100% Passing Pytest Test Suite (15/15 tests passing).

👉 Get MigrateSafe Pro on Gumroad ($14.99 USD)

Conclusion

Letting AI assistants write database migrations doesn't have to be a high-wire act. By incorporating AST lock analysis and Expand/Contract patterns into the Model Context Protocol, your engineering team can move faster with zero downtime.

How does your team safeguard production migrations against locking? Let's discuss in the comments below!

title: Crypto Market Data Is Useful Only When You Understand Its Context
description:
Crypto dashboards can show a lot of information in a small space: prices, daily changes, trading pairs, and lists of popular assets.

At first glance, more data seems like a good thing.

But I think the real challenge is helping people understand what the numbers mean without encouraging them to draw conclusions too quickly.

That's a useful way to think about market interfaces, including the one presented by AviorSwap.

A percentage change doesn't tell the whole story

Imagine seeing a token with a positive daily percentage change.

It's tempting to interpret that as a sign of strength. But the number alone doesn't explain the full market situation.

How liquid is the asset? How much trading activity supports the price? Is the movement part of a larger trend or a short-term fluctuation?

A daily percentage change provides a snapshot, not a complete analysis.

The same applies to assets showing negative performance. A single time window doesn't establish what will happen next.

Context makes a dashboard more useful

AviorSwap's public website presents market information alongside its exchange-related features.

I think this combination raises an interesting product-design question: how can a platform help visitors move from exploring market data to understanding a potential transaction?

A useful dashboard should make it easy to identify the asset, understand the time period behind a statistic, and distinguish market information from an executable quote.

That last distinction matters.

A displayed market price may not equal the price a user receives when swapping a particular amount. Liquidity, route selection, fees, and changing market conditions can all affect the result.

Less noise, more meaning

When designing a market dashboard, I'd prioritize three things.

Clear labels. Every percentage should have an understandable time period and reference point.

Relevant details. Users should be able to find liquidity, volume, and other useful context where those metrics are available.

Honest limitations. Market data can be delayed, incomplete, or different across sources. The interface should communicate relevant limitations instead of presenting every figure as universally definitive.

These details can make a dashboard more helpful without filling every available space with numbers.

Information should support decisions, not replace them

I don't think a market interface needs to tell users what to buy.

Its job is to present information in a way that supports independent judgment.

For example, a clear view of market movements can help someone decide what they want to research next. It shouldn't imply that an asset is a good investment simply because its price has risen recently.

That distinction is important in a market where prices can change quickly and losses are possible.

Final thoughts

Market data becomes more valuable when people understand its limitations.

Exploring the relationship between AviorSwap's market presentation and its exchange functionality highlights a broader principle for financial products: showing information is only the first step. Helping users interpret it responsibly is the harder part.

When you open a crypto dashboard, which information helps you most: price changes, trading volume, liquidity, or historical charts?

title: We pointed AI testing agents at our own apps. 36/100, 79 issues. Here is what they found and what we fixed.
description:
Disclosure first: I'm on the team behind Preetest, an AI website-testing platform built by Yamama Software (Saudi Arabia). This post is about running that platform on Yamama Software's own apps. These are our own apps scanned with our own platform, not an independent audit. Every number below comes from a real report; the report links are public (they open behind a cookie-consent prompt you can decline, so I have also put a screenshot of each report's summary page below). This write-up was drafted by the AI assistant that runs our testing and fixes, from those reports, at the founder's direction.

What Preetest is, in one paragraph

Preetest is a platform, not a company. You give it a URL (and a login if the app needs one). It runs AI testing agents, each with a specialty (accessibility, performance, security headers, mobile layout, SEO, forms, caching and so on; the platform lists 17 specialties, and each of the standard runs below used 9 agents covering 8 of 14 aspects), and writes one report: a score out of 100, every issue with severity and the element it was found on, and a fix prompt per issue that you can paste into Cursor, Claude Code or whatever you build with.

Run 1: our internal office suite

A 10-page signed-in scan of the staff suite we use ourselves (documents, mail, calendar, chat).

Score: 36/100. 79 issues: 0 critical, 3 high, 31 medium, 45 low, 0 info. Known-screen coverage 44 %.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/z1LctGGKyBvPlZIcTkeh4w

The findings that mattered:

  • Every static file was served with Cache-Control: max-age=0. Every visit re-downloaded every script. High severity, and correct.
  • The cross-app sign-in put the user's email and name in a GET ?t= parameter. Medium. Also correct; that lands in server logs and browser history.
  • The "export all my data" action was a plain GET link with no confirmation. Medium.
  • Bottom navigation at 390 px wide cut off the "Mail" label. Low, but it is the first thing a phone user sees.

Run 2: the same app, after two small fixes. The score went down.

We fixed the export confirmation and one accessible-name issue, re-ran with the same settings, and got 29/100. 101 issues: 0 critical, 8 high, 35 medium, 57 low, 1 info (the report's issue card shows 100, because it does not count the info item). Known-screen coverage 51 %.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/AIykp03BiPhDdXf2jn-Lww

Why worse? The second run reached more screens (the calendar, the staff guide, the privacy and download pages), so it found more. Coverage is budget-based: each run stops when its token reservation runs out, and the two runs stopped at different pages. So this is not a clean before/after, and I am not going to present it as one. What the second run added was the most useful finding of the day:

  • The calendar had 49 column-header cells with no role="row" parent, and 42 day buttons using aria-pressed, which their role does not support. Plus text at 4.12:1 contrast where 4.5:1 is required.
  • LCP of 4.7 s on the documents page. The assistant greeting waited on about 1.5 MB of scripts.

Run 3: a small Expo web app

Score: 53/100. 27 issues: 0 critical, 5 high, 11 medium, 10 low, 1 info (the issue card shows 26 for the same reason). 100 % known-screen coverage, 143 tokens used.
Report: https://app.preetest.com/r/BTlW0oUUg-ybJZQxCpPyKA

  • Unknown URLs returned 200 instead of 404 (soft 404). High.
  • No header / main / footer / nav landmarks. High.
  • The onboarding "Next" control was not exposed as a button to screen readers. High.
  • sitemap.xml served as HTML; a JSON data file served with no caching.

What we changed, and how much of it is proven

Plainly: none of the fixes below has been confirmed by a Preetest re-run yet. The only full rescan we did after fixing anything is run 2 above, and it scored lower because it covered more screens. There is no improvement to show, implied or otherwise. What follows is what we changed and how we checked each change ourselves.

Changed, and verified by us (not by the platform):

  • Calendar ARIA: headers and weeks now sit inside role="row", day cells use aria-selected, arrow keys move between days. Verified with axe-core on that page: 92 ARIA violations plus 33 contrast failures before, 0 after.
  • Contrast: the faint purple went from #7c6fd6 (4.12:1) to #5a4cc0 (6.5:1). Verified by computing the ratio.
  • Mobile bar: five apps plus a "More" button. Verified with our own screenshots at 360, 390 and 412 px; nothing cut off.
  • Caching: versioned JS/CSS now sent with a one-year cache header. Verified by reading the response headers; a repeat visit to the documents page renders in under a second in our timing.
  • Expo app: unknown URLs now return a real 404 status, the page has landmarks, "Next" has a real button role, sitemap.xml is served as XML, versioned files get a long cache. Verified with HTTP requests and a DOM check, not with a rescan.
  • A bug the 404 fix exposed: 19 icon font files had been missing from the deploy the whole time. The old catch-all returned an HTML page with status 200 for them, so nothing ever errored. Restored and checksum-checked. Soft 404s hide real breakage; that one finding paid for the run.

Not fixed, or not proven:

  • The documents page first load is still about 4 s. Only repeat visits got faster.
  • We moved the sign-in token out of the URL, but have not yet tested a real signed-in hop between apps with a staff account, so I am not calling it fixed.
  • No Preetest rescan since the bigger fixes, so there is no "after" score. When there is one, I will add it here, whichever way it goes.

Where the agents were wrong

  • It flagged /api/config on the Expo app as "returns private data with no auth". It returns public settings (app name, support links, public client ids). False positive.
  • It flagged a missing aria-current on the docs sidebar. The source already renders it on the active button.
  • It flagged noindex on the internal editor as high. That is intended; it is a staff tool.

So: a sharp junior QA that works at 3 a.m., not an oracle. Read the report, do not paste every fix prompt blindly.

Pricing, honestly

The free plan is 50 tokens. Our smallest real run above used 143, so the free tokens get you a project set up and a look at the flow, not a full inspection. A standard inspection is roughly 1,000 tokens, which is the $29/month plan. The platform also refuses to scan its own domain, so you cannot run it on preetest.com.

If you try it on your own app, I would genuinely like to hear where it was wrong. That list above is the one we work from.

Honest reviews wanted (from the Preetest team)

We are collecting reviews from people who actually used Preetest, good or bad.

Try it on your own site, then write a review on Trustpilot: https://www.trustpilot.com/evaluate/preetest.com. We give one month of the Starter plan ($29) free for a published review. The month is for writing a review, not for a rating: a 1-star review with real reasons gets it exactly like a 5-star one. Please say in the review that you received free access.

To have enough tokens for a full scan, sign up through https://app.preetest.com/register?ref=KJZDCYB4 (adds 300 bonus tokens to the 50 free ones once you confirm your email).

Email preetest.team@mail.tab.bot with the address you signed up with and the link to your review.

title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.27379v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. This can produce inconsistent drafts and reduce acceptance length. Iterative refinement mitigates this limitation by conditioning later predictions on previously committed tokens, though additional passes increase drafting cost. To address this trade-off between draft fidelity and inference latency, we introduce DStill, a two-stage framework that distills a target-conditioned drafter's own multi-step refinement into one-step drafting. We first train the drafter to complete partially revealed blocks, then use its refinement trajectories to train a student to predict the final completion in one pass. Using a curriculum that gradually transitions from partial to fully masked inputs, we successfully transfer the multi-step refinement capabilities into one step. Across reasoning, math, code benchmarks on three model families DStill improves acceptance length by up to 28% and speedup by up to 25% over one-step DFlash, achieving up to 6.45x speedup over auto-regressive decoding.

title: The Second Run Is Where the Lies Show Up
description:
Every agent demo I have ever seen works on the first run. Mine did too. The first run has a clean state, a fresh context, and a demo-friendly task that was probably chosen after a few attempts.

The second run is different, and it is the only run I trust.

What changes between run one and run two

  • The state is no longer clean. Files were created, ports were opened, a lock file exists. Half the failures I logged live in this gap.
  • The context is no longer empty. Yesterday's task file may still be around. A note in the notes file may contradict what I am asking today.
  • The task is no longer chosen for the demo. If it works twice on a task I did not specially pick, it probably works.

There is a fourth difference that took me longer to see: on the second run, nobody is watching. On the first run I am looking at the screen, ready to intervene. On the second I am doing something else. That is the real test, and it is also when I find out how good the failure messages are.

The rules I use now

  • A task is not automated until it has run twice, unattended, on a dirty state.
  • I keep the state dirty on purpose for the second run. Cleaning up before testing cleanup tests nothing.
  • If the second run fails, the bug is almost always in what the first run left behind, not in the task.
  • I read the log of the second run, not the first. The first log is a story, the second log is evidence.

Why this matters for how I judge tools

When I look at a tool now, the question is not "does the demo work". It is "what happens when I run it again tomorrow, with the mess from today still on disk". That question filters out a surprising amount, including things I would otherwise have installed.

The same standard applies to my own work, which is the uncomfortable part. Half the things I call automated have never had a second unattended run. I know which ones they are, and I keep not fixing them.

If you test this way, what does your second run look like? I would especially like to hear from anyone whose second run is genuinely clean, because mine never is.

title: Using Set Learning to Improve Set-Valued Classifiers on Long-tailed Data
description:
arXiv:2610.27443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Set-valued classification (SVC) offers a practical approach to communicating uncertainty while maintaining accuracy by predicting variable-sized sets per input rather than fixed-sized sets (e.g. top-1 or top-5). However, set-valued classifiers (SVCs) exhibit significantly degraded performance on long-tailed and imbalanced datasets, a setting for which they are ostensibly well-suited. This becomes apparent under macro-average evaluation, which weighs all classes equally. SVCs are typically formed during a post-hoc calibration stage, so little is known about how training dynamics affect their behaviour. In this work, we investigate how different neural network training strategies and loss functions impact downstream SVC performance on highly imbalanced data. In addition to methods such as label smoothing and class-balancing, we investigate whether loss functions that operate over sets of examples in a batch, rather than treating all examples as independent, lead to better downstream SVCs. We adapt the recently proposed odd-K-out (OKO) loss function, which learns from sets of training samples, improving its sample efficiency whilst introducing algorithmic modifications that reduce its computational overhead from 3.2x to just 1.36x that of standard cross-entropy training. Experiments on highly long-tailed datasets demonstrate our modified OKO approach significantly improves macro-accuracy across multiple SVC methods - including top-k, average-k, and conformal prediction - while maintaining competitive micro-accuracy. This improved performance on minority classes occurs without substantially increasing prediction set sizes, suggesting that carefully constructed set-based training can produce networks better suited to imbalanced data.

title: Cross-Visibility-Gap Identity Persistence for 4D Scene Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.27505v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding.
  We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity.
  In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.

title: The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent

title: Evaluating Tibetan Speech Recognition Across Dialects and Adaptation Regimes: A Multi-Granularity Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.27002v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tibetan speech recognition is usually evaluated with character or syllable error rates because the writing system does not mark word boundaries. These metrics can rank systems differently and respond differently to adaptation failures. We combine character error rate, syllable error rate, and segmented word error rate in one evaluation framework. We use dictionary-based, neural, and language-model-based segmentation and compare their boundaries with expert annotations. We evaluate five ASR architectures on Lhasa Tibetan, then test zero-shot transfer and target-corpus adaptation on five additional corpus subsets. We also vary LoRA rank and training-data size to examine adaptation failure. The results show that a lower character error does not always lead to a lower syllable or segmented-word error. These ranking differences persist across corpora. Metric correlations also weaken in some unsuccessful adaptation settings. Higher LoRA ranks improve syllable and segmented-word scores but remain worse than full fine-tuning in the tested range. A standardized phonological representation provides another view of spelling errors. These findings support evaluation at several linguistic levels and motivate better segmentation and adaptation methods for low-resource ASR.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, October 12, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent. To use Advanced Analytics, you must also enable whichever Conversational Analytics toggle corresponds to the content that you are querying (Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents). If both the Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents toggles are turned off, then Advanced Analytics cannot be enabled. If either Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents is enabled, Advanced Analytics can be enabled, but it is turned off by default.

The Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents settings inherit the enablement state of the Conversational Analytics setting in previous versions of Looker.

Conversational Analytics preview features can still be enabled selectively under the Enable Trusted Tester Features setting.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

Conversational Analytics data agents for both user-defined dashboards and LookML dashboards are now generally available.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

You can now apply themes to Looks in addition to internal dashboards.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where duplicating a scheduled plan could fail to retain the custom message value. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table visualizations now proportionally scale left-pinned columns during automatic sizing, which prevents unnecessary horizontal scrollbars. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where enabling subtotals on table visualizations did not automatically disable the Cell Visualizations option. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where previews for Looker charts in Slack integrations could fail to be displayed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where editing and saving a dashboard could cause the dashboard to reload indefinitely, forcing users to refresh the page. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table cell visualizations that included both positive and negative values could display unwanted scrollbars and hide value labels. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the BigQuery JDBC driver could fail to properly parse certain data types, such as BYTES, STRUCT/RECORD, and nested ARRAY structures. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where linked filters on a dashboard could fail to display autocomplete suggestions even when a parent filter is selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to ensure that phase timings (such as connection acquisitions, execution runtimes, and optimistic pivot fallback retry loops) are successfully captured for queries that fail or time out. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity Dashboard Diagnostics dashboard has been updated to fully support statistics, tile run counts, and performance recommendations for LookML dashboards. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the color palette popover in visualization settings failed to dynamically reposition when it expanded, causing controls to overlap or truncate. This feature now performs as expected.

Breaking

title: Why Security Reviews Stall Procurement — and How to Answer Them Faster
description:
A Toronto-based SaaS vendor gets within one signature of a six-figure enterprise deal. Then procurement routes the contract to security review. Three weeks later, the champion who fought for you internally is fielding questions about data residency, database access, and audit trails that nobody on your team can answer without pulling an engineer off the roadmap for a day. The deal doesn't die — it just stalls, quarter after quarter, until the buyer moves on.

This is the quiet tax on growth at mid-size Canadian software and services firms: the product sells itself, but the security questionnaire doesn't. And the questions are rarely about your roadmap. They're about whether a vendor's AI or support tooling can reach a live production database, and whether you can prove, in writing, what happened during an incident.

Why security reviews stall procurement

Most review delays come down to one unanswerable question: can this system touch our data, and if something breaks, can you show us exactly what changed and who approved it? Vendors who rely on broad database access for support or diagnostics have no clean answer. Vendors who can say a tool never connects to a live database at all — and that every fix is logged as a reviewable pull request — end that conversation in one meeting instead of three.

This matters more in regulated and semi-regulated Canadian sectors — finance in Toronto, health tech in Montreal, logistics and natural resources in Vancouver — where procurement teams are explicitly trained to ask for a data-flow diagram before they ask for a demo. If your production-support process depends on a developer or AI tool holding live credentials, that diagram becomes the reason the deal sits in legal for another month.

The real cost of a stalled review

The slow procurement cycle isn't the only cost. When a production incident does hit, the clock is just as unforgiving — industry estimates put the median cost of downtime for large enterprises at roughly US$9,000 per minute. A security review that takes weeks because nobody can explain your incident-response architecture is bad enough; an incident that takes hours to diagnose because the same architecture lacks a clear root-cause trail is worse, and it's the exact scenario a sharp-eyed procurement reviewer is trying to screen out.

Layer on the talent market: skills gaps are reported by around 90% of organisations in the Gulf and an estimated 57% of firms in Europe can't find qualified developers. Canadian teams are competing in the same global hiring pool, and senior engineers who can trace a production bug to the exact file and line under pressure are the scarcest, most expensive hires on the team. A lean Canadian operation — ten developers instead of thirty — cannot afford to keep that kind of diagnostic depth on call around the clock, and procurement teams increasingly know it, which is part of why they ask so many questions about your support model in the first place.

How to answer security reviews faster

Corporate AI 365 is built around the sentence that ends most security reviews early: it never hosts your code and never connects to a live database. It reasons over your source code and a scripted database schema — not live rows, not a connection string. When a genuine need for live data comes up, it writes a read-only query for your own developer to run; the result never leaves your environment and never comes back to us. That's not a policy promise buried in a contract appendix — it's the architecture, and it's the line that lets a reviewer check the box and move on.

The rest of the workflow is built for the same scrutiny. Anyone in the company — not just engineers — can describe a problem in plain language through the Employee support portal. The AI diagnoses root cause down to file, class, and line, with a confidence score and a proposed fix, and the analysis is reproducible: cached against a hash of the issue, the code snapshot, and the model, so the same report always produces the same answer. That reproducibility is what makes an approval gate meaningful instead of theatrical.

From there, the fix moves through real git branches and pull requests — Developer, QA, approval, production — each gate a permission, each transition an audit record, with a one-click revert if something still goes wrong. Your own CI confirms what shipped. When procurement asks for an audit trail, you hand them one that already exists, rather than reconstructing it from Slack threads.

Across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps, with 41 composable permissions and a real org hierarchy, the same governed pipeline works whether you're a ten-person team in Vancouver or a 200-person department in Toronto. Face Off then scores delivered work across developers, teams, and departments, with an AI umpire naming the actual bottleneck — useful internally, and a credible answer when a buyer asks how you keep a lean team accountable without a stack of senior hires you can't find.
