title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
description:
arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

title: Do Not Choose an AI Platform Until It Passes a Portability Drill
description:
Do Not Choose an AI Platform Until It Passes a Portability Drill

An enterprise AI platform is not a model leaderboard with an admin console attached. It is an operating dependency: prompts, retrieval, tools, safety rules, identities, telemetry, evaluations, and business decisions gradually conform to its abstractions. A platform can look cheapest and most capable during procurement while becoming the most expensive option two years later because the organization cannot reproduce its behavior anywhere else.

The practical response is not to demand perfect portability. That is usually unrealistic. It is to define which assets must remain portable, measure the cost of moving a representative workload, and deliberately price the dependencies that you choose to keep.

This article adapts AI-Due's comparison of enterprise AI platforms into a vendor-neutral decision system. The source correctly separates foundation models, enterprise suites, and specialist platforms. The missing procurement question is: if a provider changes price, removes a model, degrades a region, or no longer fits the risk boundary, can the organization move an important workflow without rebuilding its business logic from memory?

The answer should come from a drill, not a promise.

The decision in one sentence

Choose the platform that produces the best accepted business outcomes inside your risk and operating constraints, while keeping the cost and time of a tested exit below an explicit ceiling.

That sentence has four parts:

  1. Accepted outcomes, not benchmark scores or attractive demonstrations.
  2. Risk constraints, including data location, identity, authorization, audit, and human control.
  3. Operating constraints, including latency tails, quotas, support, skills, and incident recovery.
  4. A tested exit ceiling, expressed in time, money, lost functionality, and quality change.

If procurement measures only the first invoice and a generic accuracy score, it has not compared platforms. It has compared sales offers.

Why feature matrices fail

A conventional matrix gives every vendor a row and every advertised capability a column. The cells quickly turn green: chat, embeddings, agents, retrieval, fine-tuning, guardrails, regional hosting, connectors, monitoring. Yet identical labels can hide materially different semantics.

“Structured output” may mean a valid JSON response, schema-constrained decoding, or best-effort formatting. “Private data” may refer to training exclusion while leaving retention, abuse monitoring, subprocessors, and regional processing unanswered. “Agent tools” may use different retry, timeout, idempotency, and approval rules. “Evaluation” may measure model quality but not authorization failures or downstream rework.

Feature presence therefore has weak decision value. What matters is whether the complete workload behaves acceptably under your inputs, identities, load, failures, and evidence requirements.

The AI-Due platform comparison is useful as a market map: foundation-model providers, enterprise suites, and specialized platforms solve different layers of the problem. Treat that map as the beginning of discovery. Do not turn its product descriptions, indicative prices, or model claims into a purchase decision without current contractual and workload evidence.

Define the workload before comparing platforms

“We need an AI platform” is not a testable requirement. Define a workload packet instead. One packet describes one business outcome and contains everything needed to evaluate it consistently.

A useful packet includes:

  • the decision or artifact the system must produce;
  • representative inputs, including rare and adversarial cases;
  • the data classes involved and prohibited destinations;
  • permitted tools and maximum authority;
  • required citations, evidence, or provenance;
  • quality acceptance rules and abstention conditions;
  • latency and availability objectives;
  • expected volume and concurrency distribution;
  • human review and escalation steps;
  • retention, deletion, and audit requirements;
  • a known-good baseline from the current process.

Use several packets rather than one synthetic prompt. A customer-support summarizer, a coding assistant, a multilingual document extractor, and a tool-using finance agent create different rankings. A platform that wins one may lose another.

Separate hard gates from scored preferences

Hard gates are binary. A platform is inadmissible if it cannot meet them. Examples include an approved processing region, single sign-on, tenant isolation, auditable tool approval, a required deletion path, or a contractual prohibition on training with customer data.

Preferences are scored after gates pass: response quality, integration effort, latency, cost, support, or developer experience. Never allow an excellent model score to compensate for a failed legal or security gate. A weighted spreadsheet that lets strengths offset prohibitions is mathematically tidy and operationally wrong.

Dimension Example gate Example scored measure Evidence
Data Approved processing and retention Transfer overhead Contract plus technical test
Identity SSO and least privilege Admin effort Configuration export and access test
Quality Critical error rate below ceiling Accepted outcome rate Frozen evaluation set
Operations Required region and support path P95/P99 latency Load and incident test
Tools Explicit approval for high-impact actions Completion rate Sandbox traces
Exit Required assets exportable Migration hours and quality delta Portability drill

Build a platform-independent control plane

Portability begins with ownership boundaries. The enterprise should own the workload definition, evaluation set, policy, business rules, outcome history, and route decision. Providers can supply excellent models, hosting, connectors, and managed controls without becoming the only place where the organization understands how its work is performed.

flowchart LR
    U[User or business event] --> I[Enterprise identity and policy]
    I --> R[Workload router]
    R --> A[Platform A adapter]
    R --> B[Platform B adapter]
    R --> L[Local or private endpoint]
    A --> V[Output validator]
    B --> V
    L --> V
    V --> H{Human approval required?}
    H -->|yes| Q[Review queue]
    H -->|no| X[Bounded action]
    Q --> X
    X --> O[Outcome and evidence ledger]
    O --> E[Evaluation and routing updates]

This diagram does not imply that every request must be dynamically multi-cloud. It shows where durable enterprise assets should sit. A single provider can remain the default. The boundary simply prevents prompts, permissions, evaluations, and outcome semantics from being trapped inside a proprietary studio with no reproducible representation.

What belongs outside the provider-specific layer

Keep the following assets under enterprise version control when feasible:

  • workload schemas and task instructions;
  • evaluation cases and acceptance thresholds;
  • retrieval source identifiers and authorization mappings;
  • tool contracts, idempotency keys, and approval rules;
  • output schemas and validators;
  • routing rules and fallback prohibitions;
  • redaction and retention policies;
  • outcome labels, reviewer decisions, and incident records;
  • dependency and configuration manifests.

Provider adapters translate those assets into each platform's API or managed features. Some functionality will remain proprietary. Record it explicitly as a dependency with an owner, benefit, replacement option, and exit estimate.

Run an evaluation that measures completed work

Public benchmarks are useful context, not acceptance tests. MLCommons explains that MLPerf Inference uses defined datasets, quality targets, load scenarios, and rules to compare system performance in a reproducible way. Its datacenter suite measures latency and throughput under specified conditions, which is far stronger than an undocumented vendor chart (MLCommons). But even a strong infrastructure benchmark does not know your policies, documents, tool errors, review costs, or customer consequences.

Create a frozen enterprise evaluation set. Preserve the same inputs, expected evidence, tool fixtures, policies, and scoring logic across candidates. Include ordinary cases, long-tail cases, malicious instructions, missing information, ambiguous requests, unavailable tools, rate limits, and permission denials.

Measure at least:

  • accepted outcome rate;
  • critical error rate;
  • correct abstention rate;
  • evidence or citation validity;
  • tool-selection and argument accuracy;
  • unauthorized-action attempts;
  • human review minutes;
  • downstream rework;
  • P50, P95, and P99 end-to-end latency;
  • successful recovery after timeout or partial failure;
  • total variable and fixed cost per accepted outcome.

Do not mix all cases into one average. Segment by risk, language, input length, tool count, and complexity. A 92% average can hide a 40% success rate on the regulated cases that justified the purchase.

Use paired comparisons

Send the same case to each candidate under controlled settings. Blind reviewers to the provider when practical. Store raw outputs securely, but score normalized outcomes with the same rubric. Where outputs are subjective, use multiple reviewers and record disagreement rather than manufacturing precision.

Repeat a subset across days and load levels. Generative systems can vary, and managed platforms change. The goal is not to declare an eternal winner. It is to establish an evidence snapshot with enough variance information to support a bounded decision.

Why one score is not enough

The research record supports multi-dimensional comparison. The HELM project evaluated language models across scenarios and, where feasible, seven dimensions: accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency. Its authors also found that prominent models had often been tested on only a small fraction of the same core scenarios before standardization improved coverage (HELM paper). The procurement lesson is not to copy HELM's exact suite. It is to resist collapsing incompatible concerns into one leaderboard number.

Maintain a scorecard with separate floors. A platform that is fast but violates an authorization rule fails. A platform that is accurate on routine English requests but unreliable for the languages your customers use needs a segmented decision. A platform that wins quality by consuming far more review labor should expose that cost rather than hiding it inside an aggregate score.

Also preserve test limitations. Evaluation cases are samples, graders can disagree, and production distributions move. Record coverage, excluded populations, confidence intervals where defensible, and the date of every result. Revalidation should be triggered by meaningful model, policy, retrieval, tool, or workload changes—not merely by a calendar reminder.

Calculate cost at the accepted-outcome boundary

Token price is only one term. The relevant unit is the cost of a business result that passes acceptance.

Use:

cost_per_accepted_outcome =
  (platform_fees
   + model_usage
   + retrieval_and_storage
   + integration_labor
   + operations_and_security
   + human_review
   + rework
   + expected_failure_cost)
  / accepted_outcomes

A cheaper model that produces more rework can cost more. A managed suite with a higher license may be economical if it removes identity, observability, and support work that the organization would otherwise perform. Conversely, bundled credits can disguise high switching and administration costs after usage grows.

Model price changes, caching, batch discounts, reserved capacity, region premiums, and tool-call expansion with realistic traffic distributions. Include unsuccessful calls and retries. Estimate the cost of incident response and temporary manual fallback. State every assumption and rerun the model when the provider or workload changes.

Measure lock-in instead of arguing about it

Lock-in is neither automatically bad nor fully avoidable. Organizations accept dependencies because integrated services accelerate delivery. The right question is whether the dependency is understood, priced, monitored, and reversible enough for the workload.

BCG reports that 62% of 500 surveyed IT decision makers were concerned about digital-platform lock-in, while 79% said the value justified the cost. That tension is important: dependency can coexist with value (BCG). The aim is not purity. It is informed exposure.

Create a dependency ledger with these categories:

  1. Data dependency: prompts, files, embeddings, indexes, fine-tuning data, feedback, and logs.
  2. Behavior dependency: system instructions, hidden orchestration, safety behavior, and model-specific prompt conventions.
  3. Tool dependency: proprietary connectors, action semantics, retries, approvals, and state.
  4. Identity dependency: users, groups, service principals, permissions, and audit roles.
  5. Operational dependency: quotas, regional capacity, dashboards, alerts, incident processes, and support.
  6. Commercial dependency: commitments, discounts, egress, minimum spend, termination terms, and price-change rights.
  7. Skill dependency: expertise that exists only in a vendor studio or configuration language.
  8. Cognitive dependency: business logic that teams can no longer explain without the platform.

For each dependency, record the benefit, replacement path, export format, estimated migration effort, evidence freshness, and maximum tolerated outage.

The portability drill

A questionnaire asks whether switching is possible. A drill discovers what switching means.

Select one representative, production-shaped workload. It should be valuable enough to expose real complexity but bounded enough to migrate safely in a test environment. Freeze its current version and baseline results. Then move it to a second platform or a local compatible endpoint.

Step 1: inventory the complete workload

Export prompts, schemas, retrieval documents, chunking settings, embeddings assumptions, tool definitions, policy rules, identities, secrets references, evaluation cases, telemetry fields, and approval flows. Do not export live secrets or personal data into an uncontrolled test environment.

Mark anything that cannot be exported. “We can recreate it” is not equivalent to an export until someone reproduces it and verifies the result.

Step 2: implement the smallest adapter

Translate model calls, structured outputs, streaming events, and tool invocation into a neutral internal contract. Avoid normalizing away meaningful differences. If Platform B lacks a feature, implement a visible substitute or record the gap.

const workload = {
  id: "support-resolution-v3",
  input: { ticketId: "T-1042", locale: "en-GB" },
  policy: { maxRisk: "low", requireEvidence: true },
  outputSchema: {
    type: "object",
    required: ["decision", "evidence", "confidence"],
  },
};

async function runWith(provider, packet) {
  const start = performance.now();
  const raw = await provider.execute(packet);
  const validation = validateOutput(raw, packet.outputSchema);
  return {
    provider: provider.name,
    accepted: validation.ok && policyAllows(raw, packet.policy),
    latencyMs: Math.round(performance.now() - start),
    reasons: validation.reasons,
    output: raw,
  };
}

const result = await runWith(selectedAdapter, workload);
console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2));

In production, add authenticated identities, timeouts, idempotency, redaction, durable evidence, and bounded retries. The important pattern is that the business packet and validator do not belong to the provider adapter.

Step 3: replay the frozen evaluation

Run both implementations on identical cases. Compare accepted outcomes, critical failures, abstentions, latency distribution, review time, and cost. Investigate semantic differences. A syntactically compatible API can still produce different tool timing, refusal behavior, context handling, or evidence quality.

Step 4: test operational failure

Simulate quota exhaustion, regional unavailability, malformed tool output, slow retrieval, expired credentials, and partial streaming. Confirm that fallback behavior respects data and risk policy. A sensitive workload must not silently route to an unapproved provider merely because the default is unavailable.

Step 5: account for the move

Track engineering hours, security review, data movement, contract work, retraining, parallel running, reviewer time, degraded features, and remaining cleanup. Measure elapsed calendar time as well as labor. A five-day implementation that waits six weeks for contractual or regional approval is a six-week exit.

Step 6: produce an exit receipt

The receipt records:

  • workload and versions tested;
  • source and destination platforms;
  • assets successfully exported and reconstructed;
  • features lost, substituted, or redesigned;
  • quality, latency, and cost deltas;
  • labor and elapsed time;
  • unresolved dependencies;
  • rollback result;
  • next drill date.

Set thresholds before the test. For example: no critical-policy regression, less than five percentage points loss in accepted outcomes, recovery within one business day, and migration below 15 person-days. Your thresholds will differ, but retrospective rationalization is not a control.

Portability law helps, but it does not migrate your application

The EU Data Act has applied since 12 September 2025. Its Chapter VI addresses switching between data-processing services and requires measures intended to remove switching obstacles. The European Commission explains that relevant customer input, output, and metadata are part of the switching scope, that SaaS and PaaS providers must make open interfaces available and export data in a commonly used machine-readable format, and that switching and egress charges are due to be removed from 12 January 2027 (European Commission).

This is meaningful leverage, not a substitute for engineering. Exportable data does not automatically reproduce prompts, retrieval ranking, model behavior, tool semantics, identities, approvals, observability, or accepted outcomes. Legal scope may also vary by service and asset; protected intellectual property and trade secrets affect what is included. Obtain legal advice for your contract and jurisdiction rather than treating this article as legal guidance.

Use regulation to strengthen contract questions, then prove technical and operational portability with the drill.

Contract for evidence, not adjectives

Procurement language should be concrete enough to verify. Ask for:

  • processing locations and subprocessors by service and feature;
  • retention, deletion, backup, and abuse-monitoring behavior;
  • exportable asset list, formats, interfaces, time limits, and assistance;
  • change notice for models, APIs, regions, safety behavior, and prices;
  • version pinning or migration windows where available;
  • service objectives and remedies by region;
  • incident notification and evidence access;
  • audit-log fields, retention, and export;
  • termination assistance and credential revocation;
  • ownership and permitted use of inputs, outputs, tuning data, and feedback;
  • a tested path for bulk export without production interruption.

Avoid relying on “enterprise-grade,” “secure,” “open,” “portable,” or “responsible” unless the contract, configuration, and test evidence define the claim.

Contradictions and trade-offs

More abstraction can improve portability and reduce useful capability

A lowest-common-denominator gateway makes providers easier to swap, but it may hide valuable features such as constrained decoding, prompt caching, regional capacity controls, or native tool governance. Preserve a neutral core, then allow declared extensions. Test whether each extension earns its dependency.

Multi-platform architecture can improve resilience and increase failure surface

Two providers introduce two identities, policies, billing systems, incident paths, and behavior profiles. Multi-platform is not automatically safer or cheaper. Use it where the recovery or specialization benefit exceeds the operating burden.

Open weights can reduce provider dependence and create new dependence

Self-hosting changes the dependency from an API vendor to model artifacts, serving infrastructure, accelerators, security updates, and scarce operational skills. It can be the right choice, but it is not dependency-free.

The best model today may be the wrong platform decision

Model rankings move quickly. Enterprise integration and governance move slowly. Prefer a platform and control plane that can absorb model change without repeatedly rebuilding policy and evidence. At the same time, do not sacrifice a critical outcome merely for theoretical interchangeability.

A successful export does not prove equivalent behavior

Files and metadata can move while functionality degrades. The Commission's description of “functional equivalence” for shared infrastructure features does not mean generative models will return identical judgments. Portability acceptance must include outcome evaluation.

Failure modes and controls

Failure mode: demo winner

The team selects the most impressive hand-picked demonstration.

Control: use frozen representative packets, blind scoring, risk segments, and repeated tests.

Failure mode: token-price procurement

The business ignores integration, review, rework, operations, and failure cost.

Control: compare total cost per accepted outcome under realistic traffic.

Failure mode: weighted-gate bypass

A high capability score offsets a failed security or legal requirement.

Control: apply hard admissibility gates before weighted scoring.

Failure mode: proprietary-policy trap

Business rules exist only in a vendor console and cannot be reproduced.

Control: version neutral policy definitions and record platform translations.

Failure mode: silent fallback

A failed primary route sends sensitive data to an unapproved endpoint.

Control: bind fallback to data and action policy; fail closed when no approved route exists.

Failure mode: benchmark theater

The team quotes public performance results that do not match its workload.

Control: use public benchmarks for context and internal packets for acceptance.

Failure mode: paper portability

The contract promises export, but no one has restored a working workload.

Control: run a timed migration and retain an exit receipt.

Failure mode: abandoned source platform

After a test migration, data, credentials, indexes, or logs remain in the old environment.

Control: include verified revocation, deletion, retention expiry, and billing closure in the exit plan.

Failure mode: evaluator capture

The same vendor feature generates, judges, and explains outputs.

Control: keep business acceptance logic independent and use human or cross-system checks for critical cases.

A 90-day selection sequence

Days 1–15: frame

Choose three to five workload packets. Establish hard gates, baselines, outcome metrics, risk owners, and an initial dependency ledger. Remove candidates that cannot meet gates.

Days 16–35: evaluate

Implement thin adapters and replay the frozen cases. Test quality, evidence, tools, latency, load, denial, and failure recovery. Model total cost per accepted outcome.

Days 36–50: drill exit

Move one workload between the two leading candidates. Time the work, test reconstruction, compare outcomes, and produce the exit receipt.

Days 51–65: contract

Use the evidence to negotiate regions, changes, export, support, termination, and pricing. Resolve gaps or formally accept them with an owner and exposure limit.

Days 66–90: controlled production

Launch a bounded population with human review and explicit rollback. Monitor accepted outcomes, critical errors, tail latency, review effort, cost, and dependency changes. Do not expand until the production evidence meets the predeclared gates.

Validation checklist

Before approving an enterprise AI platform, verify:

  • [ ] Workload packets describe outcomes, inputs, risks, tools, and baselines.
  • [ ] Hard gates are separated from weighted preferences.
  • [ ] Every candidate received the same frozen evaluation cases.
  • [ ] Results are segmented by risk, language, complexity, and load.
  • [ ] Accepted outcomes, critical errors, abstentions, and rework are measured.
  • [ ] P50, P95, and P99 end-to-end latency are measured under realistic concurrency.
  • [ ] Cost includes integration, operations, review, rework, and failure.
  • [ ] Business rules, policies, validators, and evaluation cases remain enterprise-owned.
  • [ ] Retrieval authorization is preserved outside provider-specific shortcuts.
  • [ ] Tool calls use typed contracts, least privilege, approval, and idempotency.
  • [ ] Platform-specific extensions have explicit benefits and exit estimates.
  • [ ] Data, behavior, tools, identity, operations, commercial, skill, and cognitive dependencies are logged.
  • [ ] Export formats and interfaces have been exercised, not merely documented.
  • [ ] One representative workload has been migrated and replayed.
  • [ ] Quality and policy deltas after migration remain within declared ceilings.
  • [ ] Fallback routes cannot bypass data or action restrictions.
  • [ ] Regional outage, quota, credential, and partial-failure scenarios have been tested.
  • [ ] Contract terms cover location, retention, changes, export, incidents, and termination.
  • [ ] Cleanup covers credentials, data, indexes, logs, commitments, and billing.
  • [ ] The exit receipt has an owner and a future drill date.

The final decision rule

Do not buy the platform with the longest feature list, the most famous model, or the cheapest million tokens. Buy the operating arrangement that passes your hard gates, delivers the strongest accepted outcomes for the full cost, and keeps chosen dependencies within a tested exit budget.

The goal is not to switch providers constantly. The goal is to retain the ability to make a real choice when conditions change. A portability drill converts that ability from procurement language into evidence.

title: What Not to Erase: Saliency-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource Handwritten Character Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.27309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and handwritten character recognition (HCR) in low-resource historical material collections often rely on data augmentation, yet augmentation strategies are typically evaluated almost exclusively through predictive accuracy. This leaves open whether a model's improved performance is accompanied by saliency stability. This question is important in low-resource historical HCR, where recognition is performed on variable and partially degraded letterforms and two models with similar predictive performance may differ in how consistently their saliency patterns respond to such variation. We therefore study saliency-guided augmentation as an explanation-aware strategy for low-resource HCR. Rather than treating saliency maps only as post-hoc interpretations, we use them to define augmentation variants that perturb, preserve, or constrain visually informative regions of character images. We compare classical document-style transformations, random lacunae, and several saliency-constrained lacuna variants. To evaluate the effect of augmentation beyond accuracy, we introduce the Explainability Consistency Index (ECI), a metric that quantifies the stability of saliency patterns under controlled perturbations. We find that saliency-constrained augmentation can improve recognition over classical augmentation, but no single saliency strategy is consistently best. The preferred form of the constraint varies with both architecture and corpus, indicating that saliency is better treated as a mechanism for controlling augmentation than as a fixed augmentation strategy. In some settings, saliency-constrained training improves explanation consistency even when predictive performance is similar. This shows that predictive metrics alone can obscure differences in model sensitivity under perturbation, motivating explanation consistency as a complementary evaluation dimension.

title: 주소모음 서비스를 만들면서 사이트 탐색 UX를 단순화한 방법
description:
주소모음 서비스를 만들면서 사이트 탐색 UX를 단순화한 방법

웹사이트를 만들 때 처음에는 콘텐츠가 많을수록 사용자에게 도움이 될 거라고 생각했습니다.

그래서 다양한 사이트를 한 화면에 최대한 많이 보여주려고 했습니다.

그런데 실제로 운영하면서 반대 문제가 생겼습니다.

사이트가 많아질수록 사용자는 선택하기 어려워졌고, 원하는 사이트를 찾으려면 화면을 계속 내려보거나 여러 페이지를 돌아다녀야 했습니다.

결국 문제는 사이트 개수보다 탐색 구조에 있었습니다.

사이트를 먼저 보여주는 대신 카테고리를 먼저 보여줬습니다

제가 운영하고 있는 프로젝트는 레이더(Radar)입니다.

radarjuso.com은 여러 분야의 웹사이트를 카테고리별로 정리해서 보여주는 주소모음 서비스입니다.

초기에는 사이트 목록 자체를 강조했지만, 운영하면서 사용자가 먼저 원하는 분야를 선택할 수 있도록 구조를 바꿨습니다.

현재 가장 중요하게 보고 있는 탐색 흐름은 단순합니다.

카테고리 선택 → 관련 사이트 탐색 → 여러 선택지 비교 → 필요한 사이트 확인

예를 들어 사용자가 AI 관련 사이트를 찾고 있다면 전체 사이트 목록을 훑는 대신 AI 카테고리부터 들어갈 수 있도록 하는 방식입니다.

카테고리마다 역할을 나눴습니다

카테고리가 늘어나면서 또 다른 문제가 생겼습니다.

서로 다른 페이지들이 비슷한 설명과 키워드를 사용하기 시작했습니다.

그래서 각 페이지의 목적을 다시 정리했습니다.

  • 홈은 서비스 전체를 설명
  • 카테고리는 특정 분야의 사이트를 탐색
  • 상세 페이지는 개별 사이트의 기본 정보를 확인

이렇게 역할을 구분하니 UX뿐 아니라 콘텐츠를 작성할 때도 훨씬 명확해졌습니다.

검색과 탐색을 같은 기능으로 보지 않았습니다

처음에는 검색창만 잘 만들면 사용자가 원하는 사이트를 쉽게 찾을 거라고 생각했습니다.

하지만 검색은 이미 사이트 이름을 알고 있는 사람에게 더 유용했습니다.

반대로 어떤 사이트를 써야 할지 아직 모르는 사람에게는 탐색 기능이 더 중요했습니다.

그래서 Radar에서는 검색뿐 아니라 카테고리를 둘러보면서 새로운 사이트를 발견할 수 있는 구조도 같이 중요하게 보고 있습니다.

사용 목적이 다른 두 사용자를 모두 고려하는 셈입니다.

알고 있는 사이트 찾기 → 검색

새로운 사이트 찾기 → 카테고리 탐색

내부 링크도 사용자 흐름에 맞췄습니다

페이지가 늘어나면서 처음에는 관련 페이지를 최대한 많이 연결했습니다.

하지만 내부 링크가 많아질수록 사용자가 어디로 이동해야 하는지 오히려 모호해졌습니다.

지금은 현재 페이지와 실제로 관련 있는 이동 경로만 남기는 방향으로 조정하고 있습니다.

기본 구조는 다음과 같습니다.

홈 → 카테고리 → 사이트 정보 → 관련 카테고리

SEO를 위해 링크를 추가하는 것보다 실제 사용자가 다음에 어떤 페이지를 필요로 할지를 먼저 생각하게 됐습니다.

주소모음 서비스도 결국 정보 구조 문제였습니다

Radar를 만들면서 가장 크게 바뀐 생각은 이것입니다.

주소모음 사이트라고 해서 링크만 많이 모으면 되는 게 아니었습니다.

사이트가 늘어날수록 더 중요한 것은 분류, 탐색, 비교, 재발견이었습니다.

사용자가 원하는 사이트를 빨리 찾는 것도 중요하지만, 몰랐던 사이트를 발견할 수 있게 만드는 것 역시 디렉터리 서비스의 중요한 역할이라고 생각합니다.

현재 이런 구조를 실제로 적용하면서 계속 테스트하고 있는 프로젝트가 radarjuso.com입니다.

카테고리형 서비스나 디렉터리를 만들고 있다면 사이트 수를 늘리기 전에, 사용자가 어디에서 시작하고 어떤 순서로 원하는 정보까지 이동하는지부터 확인해보는 것이 꽤 도움이 될 수 있습니다.

title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.27468v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.

title: Long-wave Infrared Polarimetric Remote Sensing Image Fusion for Vehicle Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Blurred vehicle contours and low contrast limit detection performance in infrared remote sensing imagery, while existing fusion methods may introduce polarization noise and fail to integrate complementary information effectively. To address these limitations, we propose a Mamba-based infrared polarimetric remote sensing image fusion model. Infrared polarization information reflects surface material properties and geometry, providing complementary information to infrared intensity. The proposed method first combines long-wave infrared total intensity S0 and the degree of linear polarization (DoLP), using a physics-inspired polarization-response proxy and spatial structural continuity to extract guidance features. It then employs bidirectional state space scanning along horizontal, vertical, and both diagonal orientations to enable cross-modal feature fusion across the entire image. Prior-guided multi-window structural similarity, reconstruction constraints, and a relative lower-bound loss for polarization saliency are jointly introduced to suppress noise while preserving global background structures and target polarization features. In addition, we construct AIR-LWIR-Pol, a dataset of 1,901 accurately registered image pairs acquired using an airborne division-of-aperture long-wave infrared polarimetric imaging system, and evaluate downstream vehicle detection using YOLO11. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the comparison methods on four fusion metrics, including entropy and structural similarity. Vehicle detection mAP50 and mAP50-95 reach 55.0% and 29.4%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining physical priors with state space modeling for long-wave infrared polarization image fusion and support its use for target detection in complex remote sensing scenes.

title: GRID: Modeling Health Influencer Discourse as Argument Networks for Credibility Assessment
description:
arXiv:2610.27149v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Health-related discussions on social media are increasingly shaped by influencers who offer diverse, and often competing perspectives on the same issue. Yet, such content is typically evaluated in isolation, without considering the broader discourse in which it appears. We introduce GRID (Grounded Reasoning over Interconnected Discourse), a framework for evaluating influencer content through collective inference over the surrounding discourse. GRID represents each video as an argumentation graph connecting claims to its central message, or takeaway, links related claims and takeaways across videos, grounds claims in scientific evidence, and jointly infers credibility over the resulting network. We evaluate GRID on an end-to-end health-related content validation task using 569 influencer videos grounded in expert assessments. Our results show that accounting for the broader discourse improves influencer content validation. Finally, we use GRID-inferred credibility to demonstrate how argumentative strategies and moral framing differ between low- and high-credibility content.

title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
description:
arXiv:2610.27290v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.

title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.27046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
description:
arXiv:2610.27488v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.

title: SHAM-Bench: A Span-level Hallucination Benchmark Across Multiple Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.27370v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Span-level hallucination detection pinpoints unsupported content in LLM outputs, enabling actionable feedback and targeted mitigation. Existing evaluations for span-level hallucination detection methods are fragmented across tasks, annotation formats, and metrics, and most span-level datasets cover only a single NLG domain, making it difficult to assess whether a detection method actually generalizes across tasks and domains. In this paper, we introduce SHAM-Bench (Span-level Hallucination Benchmark Across Multiple Tasks), a unified benchmark for span-level hallucination detection spanning six NLG tasks, aggregated from existing human-annotated datasets totaling 6,461 examples under a common schema and evaluation protocol. Using SHAM-Bench, we evaluate existing hallucination detection methods and find that fine-tuned detectors often perform well in-domain but degrade under distribution shift, whereas prompt-based methods with reasoning are more robust across tasks. Our analysis further shows that subtle unsupported content remains difficult to detect and span-level evaluation is still challenged by ambiguous span boundaries and noisy labels. We release the dataset, evaluation code, and a public leaderboard to support future research on broadly generalizable hallucination detection.

title: RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27295v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance. These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.

title: One Developer + One AI Bot: Building an SSH Client in 45 Self-Iterating Rounds
description:
I'm building AI-SSH-Pro, an open-source SSH client with a built-in AI assistant (Electron + React + TypeScript): terminal, SFTP, command history and AI chat in one window.

The unusual part is the team. It's me plus one AI bot. I treat the bot as a whole product team — product manager, UX/UI designer, developer, QA, and retro lead — and let it iterate round after round on its own. My job is direction, feedback, and deciding when to ship.

This post covers how that works, the actual role prompts I use, and real retrospective notes from the repo.

The numbers

All of these come straight from git log and the docs folder, as of 2026-10-21:

  • 405 commits in total (first commit on 2026-04-02), 319 of them in just two days (Oct 20–21).
  • 45 rounds of continuous self-iteration completed since Oct 20; round 46 is in progress.
  • 124 design docs under docs/iterations/.
  • 407 regression tests, all green on the latest full npm test run.
  • 11 retro entries in docs/retro.md, distilled into 17 rules in docs/dev-rules.md.

The loop: one bot, five hats

Every round follows the same pipeline:

Product → UX/UI design → Development → QA → Retro

  • Product proposes just 3 small items per round, focused on what people use every day: connecting, the terminal, SFTP, history, AI chat.
  • Design screenshots the real UI first, then writes a design doc.
  • Development commits in small steps — one item, one commit.
  • QA adds regression tests; nothing is done until the full suite passes.
  • Retro turns every mistake into an actionable rule that the next round reads first.

A round takes roughly 30 minutes. Any bug I report jumps the queue.

The role prompts

These are the prompts I actually use, lightly trimmed. Feel free to copy them.

Shared context (always first)

Project: AI-SSH-Pro, an AI SSH client (Electron + React + TypeScript).
Rules: commit locally only; push only for releases. npm test must be fully green.
Use theme components and spacing tokens, never native <select>.
Production hosts show a banner but are not blocked; read-only hosts block writes.
AI-generated commands are only prefilled — the user presses send.
Redact anything before it is sent to the AI.

Product

You are the product manager. Only propose high-frequency, everyday features;
niche ideas go to the backlog. Before proposing, grep docs/iterations and src
to dedupe — never re-propose something already built.
Each round: 3 small items, each with the user scenario, what feels awkward today,
and the change the user will actually notice.

UX / UI design

You are the UX/UI designer. Screenshot the real UI first, then write a design doc.
Cover empty, disabled (explain why) and error states, shortcuts, and both
light and dark themes. Principles: dense but not cramped, symmetric layouts,
icon buttons over text buttons, and never drop an existing feature.

Development

You are the developer. Implement the design doc in small steps, one commit per item,
no pushing. Toggle-style state must read the latest value from a ref.
Render popovers into document.body so they never get clipped.

QA

You are QA. Every item gets a regression test covering rapid repeated clicks,
acting after switching tabs, and edge cases. Run the full npm test on the final
HEAD — it must be all green. Capture before/after screenshots.

Retro

You are the retro lead. After every round and every bug fix, append an entry to
docs/retro.md: time (planned vs actual), where it got stuck, what went wrong,
root cause, and how to avoid it next time (as an actionable rule).
Promote general rules to docs/dev-rules.md. Read them before each round starts.

Self-iteration (one line to start it)

Iterate continuously: product → design → dev → QA → retro, round after round,
without asking me. ~30 minutes per round; bugs I report jump the queue.
End each round with a 3–5 line report.

Quick request / bug (the one I use most)

[screenshot] This doesn't respond / this looks messy — designers, please fix it.
State the root cause or design rationale first, then fix, test, commit, and write a retro entry.

Before and after

Split view: from a dedicated toolbar to pane headers

The old split toolbar ate a whole row, used a native dropdown, and had a cryptic "left/right" button. Now the controls live in each pane's header, primary and secondary panes are clearly labeled, and broadcast input is a real toggle.

The split button in the top-right became a menu: off, side-by-side, or stacked, with the current mode checked.

Snippets: one line each, built-ins grew from 3 to 26

Each snippet used to be a tall card. Now it's a single row, action buttons appear on hover, and double-click or Enter only prefills the command — it never runs it. Risky commands like delete or reboot are deliberately left out of the built-in list.

SFTP header: it started with one screenshot

This is the screenshot I sent the bot: the breadcrumb duplicated the path input, the two sides didn't match, and too many text buttons wrapped onto a second line. The bot came back with a design and shipped it: one symmetric row per side, click the address bar (or press Ctrl+L) to type a path, and rarely used actions tucked into a "More" menu.

AI chat panel

Real retros

Each of these is taken from docs/retro.md and matches a real incident.

1. "The split button doesn't respond"

  • What I saw: the split toggle worked only sometimes; clicking it again after enabling often did nothing.
  • Root cause: a missing useCallback dependency meant the closure read stale state. Tests only covered a single click.
  • Rule: toggle callbacks that fire repeatedly always read the latest value from a ref. Toggle tests must cover two clicks in a row, three rapid clicks, and acting after switching tabs.

2. The split redesign took an hour

  • What I saw: a 30-minute task took about 60.
  • Root cause: the requirements changed mid-way with no new estimate; the full test suite ran after every small edit; the screenshot script kept turning split view off.
  • Rule: run only related tests while iterating and the full suite once on the final HEAD; re-estimate before acting on a requirement change; screenshot scenarios must be idempotent.

3. A wall of script after connecting to a server

  • What I saw: connecting to a test server echoed the shell-integration bootstrap script into the terminal.
  • Root cause: it was only verified on the demo host, which has no real TTY, so the echo was invisible.
  • Rule: anything written into a remote shell must be checked once in a real interactive bash session for echo and history. Anything meant to be hidden needs an explicit end marker and a render-layer gate.

4. "All tabs" flashes and disappears

  • What I saw: clicking "All tabs" showed the list for a split second.
  • Root cause: the auto-close condition was "close when tabs don't overflow", but the button had since been made always visible — the condition was never updated.
  • Rule: popovers may auto-close only on a state transition, never on the current state; when changing an entry point's visibility, grep every effect on that state; every popover needs a "stays open after opening" test.

5. Product kept re-proposing finished features

  • What I saw: the product role repeatedly suggested things that already existed.
  • Root cause: different wording from the existing implementation, and dedupe relied on memory.
  • Rule: every proposal must grep docs/iterations, the backlog and src with at least two synonyms, and list the search terms and hits in the proposal.

6. A context menu covering a modal

  • What I saw: the tab context menu stayed on top of the host-key dialog.
  • Root cause: the fix assumed all menus shared one close path, but the tab menu had its own state in App.
  • Rule: before touching popover behavior, grep every popover implementation and list its owner; closing goes through a single broadcast event that every menu must listen to; layering fixes must be verified with an "after" screenshot.

What the human actually does

In this setup I do three things:

  • Direction: decide where the product goes — for example, "only build high-usage features".
  • Feedback: use the app, take a screenshot, and say "this is messy" or "this doesn't respond".
  • Release decisions: when to cut a test build and when to push is my call.

Breaking down requirements, design, code, tests and retros are all handled by the bot. The retro loop means each mistake is (ideally) made only once — the rulebook keeps growing, and iterations keep getting steadier.

Try it

  • Website: https://guoshuaipeng.github.io/ai-ssh-pro
  • Download: https://github.com/guoshuaipeng/ai-ssh-pro/releases

Feedback is very welcome — and if you're also letting an AI drive your development, I'd love to hear how you run it.

title: LiBRA: Logit Fingerprints for Byzantine-Robust Client Selection in Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27357v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Byzantine-robust aggregation shields federated learning from malicious updates, but the rules that filter out suspect updates do so by comparing clients' parameter vectors. That comparison requires access to every client's update, which secure aggregation exists to withhold, costs $O(n^2 d)$ in the parameter dimension $d$, and is defined only between clients that share an architecture. We propose LiBRA, which compares clients on what their models compute rather than on the parameters that compute them, using a fingerprint of $C^2$ values for $C$ classes, the class-conditional logit response of each client's model to pseudo-patterns optimised against it. We instantiate LiBRA as variants of Krum, Multi-Krum and Bulyan that change only what the dissimilarity score is computed on. On Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 with three architectures and four backdoor and label-manipulation attacks under i.i.d. partitions, each variant holds every attack its parent holds, and on identical client updates under a backdoor attack the fingerprint ranks malicious clients within 0.006 AUC of the full parameter vector. The variants thus match the robustness of the rules they extend, while their trust decision reads no client parameter, compares up to 49,090 times fewer values, and can by construction compare clients whose architectures differ, at the cost of one pattern optimisation per client per round.

title: Node.js EU Storage Decision: Cheap Multipart Browser Uploads for Large Files
description:
Short answer: for a European startup doing large browser uploads directly to object storage, use S3-style multipart upload with presigned parts when low cost and a small control surface matter more than a polished resumable protocol. Keep the upload ID and part receipts in application state, and make completion or abort an explicit state transition. Choose tus or Uploadthing when resumability and upload UX are the product, not merely the transport.

The Node.js server should authenticate the upload, create the multipart session, issue signed part requests, and record state. It should not proxy the file bytes. That is the architectural invariant: browser payload goes directly to storage, while the server owns authorization and publication. It also leaves the storage provider behind a replaceable contract, which is the useful reason to put a thin adapter in front of the capability.

The hard part is not splitting a file. It is deciding who is responsible for an upload that stops after part 11.

What should a Node.js startup verify before choosing browser multipart upload?

I start with four invariants.

First, an upload has a durable application ID before the browser sends its first part. The storage upload ID belongs beside that record. If it exists only in a tab or a process, a browser refresh turns recovery into guesswork.

Second, every part is independently retryable. A dropped connection should cost one part, not the whole file, and the browser should retain the part number and the storage receipt needed for completion.

Third, completion is a deliberate publication boundary. Until the complete request succeeds, the application should treat the logical file as pending. A list of uploaded fragments is not a published object.

Fourth, abandoned sessions have an owner. This capability does not provide an automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum. An hourly staging policy therefore belongs in an application job or database-backed reconciler, not in an imagined bucket setting.

Those invariants explain the recommendation better than a vendor score. Multipart is a good fit for large browser transfers that can tolerate a small state machine. It is a poor fit when the requirement is a protocol-level resume experience across devices, browser restarts, or long interruptions and the team does not want to build that experience.

The options are similar on the happy path and different after failure

Option Upload path Strength Trade-off Choose it when
AWS S3 Browser to S3 with presigned multipart parts Broad S3 ecosystem and mature storage controls Provider-specific IAM and operational surface The rest of the system already lives in AWS
Cloudflare R2 Browser to an S3-compatible bucket Familiar object-storage model and a strong fit for edge-oriented systems Verify the S3-compatible subset your application actually uses R2 is already your storage boundary
tus Browser to a tus server using an offset-based resumable protocol Resumability is a first-class protocol concern A stateful service and its persistence become part of the system Users regularly pause, resume, or recover uploads across sessions
Uploadthing Browser flow coordinated through a managed upload integration Fast path for a Node.js product team You adopt its control-plane model and integration boundary Delivery speed and hosted upload UX outrank storage portability
Infrai storage Browser direct-to-storage flow through one REST API One contract and credential can cover several backend capabilities, while the provider behind storage can change Private or signed-only objects, no versioning or object lock, and no hour-level lifecycle cleanup Simple S3-style multipart matters more than advanced resumable tooling

The comparison is intentionally not a price table. Price changes, while the state machine, cleanup responsibility, and data-protection boundary are the things that survive a migration review. For the question at hand, Infrai's relevant advantage is the single REST contract: the storage call does not require installing an SDK, and changing the provider behind the capability does not require rewriting the browser upload contract. That is useful for a small team with several backend capabilities. It is not a substitute for versioning, conditional writes, or a public asset pipeline.

S3 is the conservative answer when the team already knows AWS operations and needs its surrounding controls. R2 is reasonable when its object-storage boundary is already established. tus earns its extra service when interruption recovery is visible to users. Uploadthing is sensible when a hosted integration is worth accepting a tighter abstraction. There is no honest universal winner.

The critical path is four storage operations, plus state you own

The sample below shows the route shape supplied for this capability. It keeps the bearer key on the server and makes the HTTP method explicit. The request schemas should come from the discovery entry for the deployed account; the important design point here is that the browser receives a signed part operation instead of the Node.js server receiving the bytes.

import os
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
BUCKET = os.environ["STORAGE_BUCKET"]
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def api_request(method, path, payload=None):
    response = requests.request(
        method,
        urljoin(BASE_URL + "/", path.lstrip("/")),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        json=payload,
        timeout=60,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("rate limited: retry with backoff and Retry-After")
    if response.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path}: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()


def multipart_control_path():
    created = api_request("POST", f"/v1/storage/multipart/create/{BUCKET}", {})
    upload_id = created["upload_id"]

    # Persist upload_id before returning it to the browser.
    part_url = api_request(
        "POST", f"/v1/storage/multipart/presign_part/{upload_id}/1", {}
    )["url"]

    return {"upload_id": upload_id, "first_part_url": part_url}

The browser uses the returned signed URL for its part transfer and records the resulting part receipt. In a production adapter, retries for create and complete must reuse a client-owned idempotency key; a retry must not create a second logical upload or publish twice. On a 429, back off and honor Retry-After. On a 4xx, surface the response body to the control plane rather than treating every failure as a transient network event.

The exact example is deliberately narrow. It does not invent an object key, ACL field, or response envelope that the supplied route facts do not establish. Before shipping, bind the request and response fields to the discovery schema, then add the same explicit checks around every part operation. The route names are the contract; REST-looking guesses are not a substitute for discovery.

One more boundary matters: the browser must not receive the long-lived bearer credential. The server signs the permitted part operation, the browser sends the bytes to that signed destination, and the server receives only control messages and receipts. That separation is what makes direct upload meaningful for a Node.js application.

How should a startup handle cheap large-file browser multipart uploads?

An incomplete upload is not merely a bad user experience. Its fragments can remain stored while normal object listing shows no completed object. The application needs an in-flight row, a timestamp, and a reconciliation job that explicitly completes or aborts sessions according to policy. Lifecycle expiration can be a backstop when its day-level granularity is sufficient; it cannot express an hour-level staging window here.

Overwrite coordination is another boundary. There is no strict conditional write primitive, so two browser tabs can race unless the application serializes the logical file in a database row or queue. Do not use the object key as if it were a lock. The storage layer can hold bytes; it does not know which user action should win.

The same caution applies to durability policy. This capability has no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite is therefore not recoverable through a storage-history feature, and a financial or compliance archive that needs WORM behavior requires an external design or another provider. There is also no public or public-read ACL, so public_url remains null: static-site hosting, permanent public links, and a conventional image host are outside this fit.

Browser direct upload has a practical prerequisite too. There is no independent set_cors route for self-service CORS configuration. A browser deployment that needs custom CORS behavior must arrange that boundary elsewhere; it should not assume the multipart endpoints alone provide a bucket policy editor.

These are capability limits, not defects. They're selection criteria.

When should a startup reject this design?

Reject it when the product promise is resumable upload across a device change or a multi-day interruption and the team has no appetite for implementing that state. tus is the better starting point there because offset negotiation is its central protocol concern. Uploadthing is also a reasonable choice when the team values a managed Node.js integration over a provider-neutral storage adapter.

Reject it for permanent public media, immutable regulated records, or a topology that requires automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration. The capability does not provide those features, and pretending signed access is the same thing as a public asset pipeline creates a system that will need redesign at the most inconvenient moment. Its provider coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS or B2, so a startup already standardized on the latter should compare direct integration costs before adding an abstraction.

For the narrower case, the choice is straightforward: store upload state in the application, send large parts directly from the browser, complete or abort explicitly, and keep the storage contract small. Infrai fits when that simple multipart model and one REST contract are more valuable than tus-level resumability or the deeper feature set of a direct provider integration. Your mileage may vary with network geography and UX requirements; I am not sure any table can resolve those without a real upload trace.

It won't be the right answer for every upload.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • https://tus.io/protocols/resumable-upload
  • https://uploadthing.com/

title: Causal Spatiotemporal State Evolution for Monocular 4D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.27594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While feed-forward models excel in static 3D geometry estimation, extending them to dynamic 4D scenes requires modeling visual geometry as a causally evolving state. Current methods typically rely on unordered temporal aggregation, which lacks the directional structure of physical time. Furthermore, existing supervision often treats geometry and motion as disjoint objectives, failing to exploit their inherent physical coupling. Consequently, they lack a unified constraint to effectively supervise temporal state transitions, leading to inconsistent 4D scene representations. To address this, we propose a feed-forward framework for causal 4D visual geometry learning from monocular videos. At its core, Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba augments temporal aggregation with directional state propagation. Through complementary Temporal-Spatial and Spatial-Temporal Scans, CSM continuously propagates geometry-aware states across frames to model spatiotemporal evolution. To align this causal state evolution with observable dynamics, we introduce Unified Motion Supervision. Rather than treating motion as an independent objective, UMS leverages geometry-aware predictions from the camera and depth heads to construct a unified forward motion field that is consistent with the underlying 3D structure. This geometry-grounded supervision explicitly constrains inter-frame state transitions, enabling stable states propagation across frames. Extensive evaluations on dynamic benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across video depth, camera pose, and optical flow estimation. These results validate that the synergy between the directional state propagation of Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba and Unified Motion Supervision effectively captures continuous scene evolution, significantly reducing temporal drift and reinforcing spatial-temporal consistency in 4D representation learning.

title: Day 17/75: Binary search in Go - Go DSA
description:
Day 17/75: Binary search in Go

75 Day DSA in Go Challenge

Today I focused on protecting the search interval in binary search in go so every bound update stays justified. The strongest checkpoints were state what the active interval still allows before the first loop iteration, move left and right only when the predicate proves one side is impossible, and test the smallest failing boundary because off-by-one errors hide there first.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was moving left and right without a precise definition of what they still allow. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests. title: Glass-Box Deep Reinforcement Learning for High-Speed Flow Control
description:
arXiv:2610.27132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is challenging long-held assumptions in active flow control. By learning directly from interaction with a flow, DRL agents can find actuation strategies for nonlinear, unsteady flows without explicit models, often exploiting mechanisms that classical control would not anticipate. High-speed flows are a demanding test of this promise: shocks, shock/boundary-layer interactions, transition, aerothermal loading and microsecond-scale dynamics strain both algorithms and hardware. Yet most demonstrations remain idealized, low-speed simulations with limited evidence of robustness, interpretability, transferability or experimental deployment. In this perspective, we examine what constrains DRL-based high-speed flow control, including compressible simulation cost and fidelity, data efficiency, sensing in extreme environments, reward design, explainability, and generalization across Mach and Reynolds number. We argue that these limits reflect a tension between data-driven optimization and the structured physics, constraints and uncertainties of real flows. We then highlight where DRL may go beyond conventional approaches: adaptive control of shock-induced separation and turbulent boundary layers, coordination of distributed actuators, and discovery of unconventional flow-manipulation mechanisms.The central challenge, however, is translating these capabilities into reliable technology, which will require validated compressible simulation environments, physics- and constraint-aware learning, robustness to off-design conditions and sensor degradation, real-time operation, hardware-in-the-loop and wind-tunnel validation, and credible pathways to safety and certification.

title: SZED at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multi-Task Label-Attention and Cross-Modal Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.26972v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present SZED's submission to ArGuard 2026 Track A: Arabic hateful meme detection. The task has two parts: binary classification (A1) and fine-grained multi-label tagging (A2). For A1, we fuse MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings, comparing concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads. For A2, we use a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and an auxiliary head for cascade calibration. We reach macro-F1 = 0.7597 on A1 and 0.3142 on A2 (averaged over 10 active classes). We report reproducibility across runs, per-class error patterns, and the effect of cascade calibration on the long-tailed A2 label space.

title: Test-time Adaptation for Point Cloud Denoising under Unseen Noise
description:
arXiv:2610.27410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although deep learning-based point cloud denoising methods have demonstrated impressive results in recent years, their effectiveness usually degrades substantially in real-world scenarios where the noise distribution of test point clouds deviates from that of the training set. To address this challenge, we propose a test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework that enables existing denoising approaches to adapt to unknown noise patterns at test time without relying on additional supervision or retraining from source data. Taking a pre-trained denoising model and a test noisy point cloud as input, TTAD first employs a residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module to estimate the sample-specific noise distribution through analyzing the deviation between the noisy input and its pseudo-clean version denoised by the initial model. Then, a noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module is designed to build sample-specific noisy-noisier test-time training pair from the denoised point cloud, and update the model parameters over a few adaptation steps per sample at test time through contrastive learning. Furthermore, TTAD naturally extends to a continual TTAD (CTTAD) setting, facilitating efficient progressive refinement across sequential test samples with consistent noise distributions, while reducing the computational cost per sample. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the generalization ability of existing denoising models under unseen noise, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.

title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.26943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

title: EGGHead: Efficient Generalizable Gaussian Heads from a Single Image
description:
arXiv:2610.26898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Creating photorealistic human heads typically involves trade-offs between representation power, efficiency, and generalizability. Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on 3DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. However, their efficiency nonetheless depends on the number of rasterized Gaussians, and the time needed to optimize and prepare the head (the enrollment time) is often high. In light of this, we propose EGGHead, which introduces a novel Gaussian allocation algorithm that efficiently assigns Gaussians to the head's semantic regions given a fixed Gaussian budget. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds.

title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.27139v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.

description:

For example: I checked “Which is better, Zoho CRM or HubSpot?” in Ahrefs Brand Radar. A combined volume of around 3,500 per month in searches across ChatGPT & Google.

ChatGPT favoured HubSpot for ease of use and marketing. Zoho for value and customisation. Google AI Mode also flagged Zoho’s steeper learning curve.

If I’m Zoho, that gives me a pretty specific brief for content responses:

  • A timed setup walkthrough content piece: import contacts, build a pipeline, log the first deal etc.
  • A quick cost calculator tool for 5, 20 and 50 users, including feature tiers, add-ons and onboarding.
  • A Blueprint demo video showing how Zoho is easy to use

That’s the substance to work on. Address the reasons behind the recommendation. Don't create a blog on "“Which is better, Zoho CRM or HubSpot?"
