title: Keep Your AI on Track Through Weeks of Prep
description:
Prep can run for weeks, and keeping it in one AI conversation gets expensive fast. So I built prep-mcp, a small MCP server in Go that lets Claude read and safely write a folder of markdown notes. Any conversation can end, and the next one picks up where it left off.

This post covers why I built it, what it is, how a conversation uses it, and what two and a half weeks of daily use showed.

Why I built it

Since May I've been preparing for senior backend interviews: DSA and LeetCode, system design, DDIA, AI systems, plus my resume and LinkedIn profile. Claude has been my study partner every day, and every related conversation lived in one Claude project. After five months, three problems kept coming back:

  • Long conversations got expensive. I kept one conversation per company's hiring process, and some ran for weeks. At one point, a single new message used about 30% of my 5-hour usage limit, so three messages used it up.
  • Project memory didn't carry enough. New conversations still needed reminding of work done in other ones, and I couldn't see what Claude chose to keep.
  • Progress lived in my head. I tracked applications, learning and resume changes in my own notes, pasted them into each conversation, and often forgot to update them.

The idea

So I had an idea: move the memory out of Claude, into notes I own, and give Claude an MCP server to read and write them. Then I decide what each conversation stores and what the next one reads. Memory becomes something I can read, diff and revert, instead of something I can't see into.

That makes each problem smaller:

  • Prep for one company can run as several short conversations instead of one long one.
  • Learning (DSA, LeetCode, system design, DDIA) runs in short conversations too, with a record of what to improve, so progress is countable.
  • I stop tracking applications by hand. I ask Claude, and it answers from the notes.

The hard part is the write side: an AI writing to files I also edit by hand, without either of us losing work. That is where most of the design went.

What it is

prep-mcp is a Go binary that Claude Desktop and Claude Code start over stdio. It gives the assistant 11 tools over one folder of markdown notes, the vault. I edit the same vault in Obsidian, and every AI write lands as a git commit.

Not only interviews

The server knows nothing about interviews. Two files at the vault root give it its shape:

  • prep.config.yaml defines the document types (folder, file name pattern, required fields, date field), the tag vocabulary file, and what a new conversation is shown.
  • CLAUDE.md gives the assistant its working rules in plain prose: how to start, what to log, which writes to prefer.

My vault is set up for job interviews. It has seven types: applications, prep sessions, improvements (one weakness each, with an exit criterion), stories, references, learning notes and weekly plans. My CLAUDE.md, about 7 KB, says how to run and score each kind of drill and how to log it. Change those two files and the same server tracks an exam, a certification or a language. The README's "Shape it to your vault" shows both files from the example vault.

How it works

One conversation, as the assistant runs it:

Start. get_context replaces the handover prompt I used to paste. One call returns what the config's context block names: the working rules, this week's plan and log, every open item with its next action, the last few prep sessions and the tags used most in the last 30 days.

Work. The other four read tools answer questions as they come up. list_docs does most of it: tags (AND, OR, prefix), frontmatter conditions and dates combine in one call, and group_by returns counts instead of documents. "Which applications are waiting on me?" and "which weaknesses came up most this month?" are the same tool with different arguments. list_tags shows what keeps coming back and what has gone quiet. search_text finds a phrase anywhere. read_doc returns a file with its content hash, which a later full rewrite must quote.

Log. Each write tool changes only what it names: create a file, append under a heading, patch frontmatter, replace one exact piece of text, or rewrite a whole file. A conversation usually ends with one batch: its prep session note plus a line in the week's log, as one commit.

No database, no index. Every call scans the folder: about 58 ms for 2,000 generated documents, and about 5 ms at my vault's size (an estimate from the per-document rate). A stored index would be a second copy to keep in sync with files I also edit by hand.

A day with it

My morning conversation starts with get_context, and Claude says in one line what today's plan calls for. We work through it, whether that's a drill, a design problem or a chapter of reading. At the end, Claude logs a prep session tagged with the weaknesses it saw, plus one line in the week's log. On Friday, one list_docs call counts which weaknesses came up most that week, and that shapes next week's plan. Applications live in the same vault, each with its next action and date, so following up is a question, not a memory test.

The write path

Letting the AI write is the hard part. A server that writes can overwrite my edits, break a file's frontmatter, or follow instructions hidden in a document. Each decision below has a cost.

  • Small writes over full rewrites. append_section, edit_text and update_frontmatter change only what they name. Cost: append-only documents only grow, which comes back later.
  • A guarded full rewrite. replace_doc needs the content hash from the last read. If I changed the file in Obsidian in between, the write fails instead of overwriting me. Cost: the model has to read again and redo the change.
  • One git commit per AI write, under its own author. Every change can be reviewed, diffed and reverted. batch applies up to 200 writes as one commit, or none at all. Cost: before batch existed, nine title edits made nine commits.
  • A write may not make a document worse. A write that would break a required field, a date or a tag fails and says how to fix it. A problem the file already had is only a warning, so a write can still fix it.
  • No delete, and nothing outside the vault. Any document the AI reads could carry instructions, so the tools can't remove files or reach outside the folder. Cost: when a file landed in the wrong folder, moving it took a create, a link fix and a manual git rm from me.

How I built it with Claude Code

I used prep-mcp from Claude Desktop and built it with Claude Code, so the AI was both my user and my developer. Friction in a Desktop conversation became a ticket, and a Claude Code conversation fixed it. Most changes follow the same loop:

  1. Claude asks me questions until every decision is agreed. No code before that.
  2. Tests come first, at the places the change touches.
  3. Two reviewers run in parallel: one checks the change against the spec, the other against code standards.

Result

From 2 to 19 October:

  • Claude made 272 commits to the vault. I made 3: the first import, one config edit and that manual git rm. There were 0 reverts; mistakes were fixed by a later write. I don't read every commit. I read the files in Obsidian as I use them, and git is there for when something looks wrong. The write checks are what make that safe enough.
  • The vault grew to 166 typed documents, 41 of them prep session notes. In the first full week, Claude added 3,908 lines and removed 153. The notes grew; they were hardly rewritten.
  • Small writes did nearly all the work. In that week: append_section 52, batch 47, edit_text 25, create_doc 23, update_frontmatter 15, replace_doc 3. The next week, 63 of 81 commits were batches, and replace_doc stayed at 3.
  • The Claude Desktop log shows 0 hash conflicts, up to 16 October. Git can't show this number, because a refused write commits nothing.
  • The vault is now my only application tracker. I retired the separate tool I used before.

Against the three goals:

  • A conversation covers a day now, not a company's whole hiring process. It starts from get_context instead of weeks of chat history. At the end of a weeks-long conversation, one message used to cost about 30% of my 5-hour limit. At the end of a day's conversation, the one I measured cost 6%.
  • Each weakness I'm working on has its own file with an exit criterion, and every prep session tags the ones it saw. My weekly review counts those patterns with one list_docs call, so progress comes from the notes, not from my memory.
  • "Where am I with each application?" is one question, answered from the notes with each application's next action and date.

What I learned

Daily use kept changing the design:

  • Tool descriptions are the model's UI. Once list_tags showed the whole tag vocabulary, the model checked it before writing, and the unknown-tag refusal stopped firing. When it did fire on a batch that had done everything right, the cause was a tool description promising something the code didn't do.
  • The cure for context loss has its own cost. Whatever a conversation reads from the vault stays in it and is re-read with every reply. In Claude's usage reports, the vault was about a third of a conversation's cost.
  • The expensive moment is coming back. Returning to an old conversation after a break reloads all of it, and those returns were the biggest single costs in the reports. With the vault, closing a conversation loses nothing, so the fix is a fresh one each day. The habit is the hard part.
  • A boundary is only as strong as the most powerful file left outside it. Templates were locked against prompt injection while CLAUDE.md, which steers the model more, stayed writable. So I unlocked the templates.
  • Copies drift. A check that copied git's lock rules missed a case that git's own error already names. The fix was to delete the check.

What's next

Open limits and ideas are tracked in the repo's issues. Three examples:

  • read_doc returns a whole file and get_context embeds the week's document in full, so both grow until they hit the client's 25,000-token limit for one tool result. A long log has already been cut there, and the cut lost the newest entries, the ones a new conversation needs. Reading one section by heading, or the last few, would fix it.
  • The config is read only at startup, so a change applies after a restart and nothing warns that the running config is out of date.
  • Transcribe a practice recording with whisper.cpp and compute words per minute, long pauses and time to the first full stop, so the model never has to estimate them.

Try it

The repo is public at github.com/Arkoes07/prep-mcp. The README covers install for Claude Code and Claude Desktop, and a fictional example vault to try it on.

title: Building Query Conditions In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import static net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqFields.*;

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

Using JooqTemplate

Method 1: conditions() — Field-Value Pair Varargs (Recommended)

conditions(Object... fieldValuePairs) takes arguments in pairs of "field name, value"; the operator is written directly after the field name string, and when no operator is written the default is ==. It returns a List<Condition>, and conditions whose values are null are automatically ignored:

// name = 'Smartphone' and price > 1000 and status = 'on_sale'
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions(
        "name", "Smartphone",
        "price>", 1000,        // the > operator follows the field name
        "stock<=", 50,         // the <= operator
        "status", "on_sale");  // default operator ==

// You can also separate the field and operator with a colon: "price:>"
List<Condition> conds2 = jt.conditions("price:>", 1000);

When a parameter value is null, that condition is ignored — ideal for dynamic queries: if the frontend doesn't send a value, no filter is applied:

// When nameParam is null, no name condition is generated
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions("name", nameParam, "category", categoryParam);

You can also mix native jOOQ Condition objects directly into the varargs:

Condition other = DSL.field("price").ge(1000);
List<Condition> conds = jt.conditions("category", "Electronics", other);

Method 2: and() / or() — Directly Returning a Single Combined Condition

and(...) and or(...) take arguments exactly like conditions(); the difference is the return value: multiple conditions are merged with AND / OR into a single Condition, and null is returned when there are no conditions at all:

// AND: name = 'John' and age > 30 and status = 'active'
Condition cond = jt.and("name", "John", "age>", 30, "status", "active");

// OR: name like 'Soph%' or name like 'Fra%'
Condition cond2 = jt.or("name:%l", "Soph", "name:%l", "Fra");

// Empty arguments return null
Condition empty = jt.and();   // null

Find two users with OR (corresponding to the user_table example in JooqTemplateOrTest):

// name = 'John' or name = 'Lee'
Condition cond = jt.or("name", "John", "name", "Lee");
List<LowerCaseRecord> records = jt.queryLowerCaseRecord("user_table", cond);

Method 3: condition() — Single-Condition Method

condition(Name fieldName, String operator, Object[] values) accepts a jOOQ Name, an operator string, and a value array, and generates a single Condition. The number of values must match what the operator requires, otherwise an IllegalArgumentException is thrown:

import org.jooq.Condition;
import org.jooq.Name;
import org.jooq.impl.DSL;

// Equality: == requires 1 value
Condition c1 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{"Smartphone"});

// Comparison: > requires 1 value
Condition c2 = jt.condition(DSL.name("price"), ">", new Object[]{1000});

// in: requires 1 value, and the value must be a Collection or Object[]
Condition c3 = jt.condition(DSL.name("category"), "in",
        new Object[]{Arrays.asList("Electronics", "Appliances", "Apparel")});

// between: requires 2 values
Condition c4 = jt.condition(DSL.name("created_at"), "between",
        new Object[]{beginDate, endDate});

// isnull: requires 0 values
Condition c5 = jt.condition(DSL.name("remark"), "isnull", new Object[]{});

This method also follows the null rules: a null value returns null (ignored); wrapping with ND(null) generates is null; a null field name or operator returns null; an invalid operator throws IllegalArgumentException:

// Value is null → returns null, condition ignored
Condition c = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{null});   // null

// ND wrapping null → generates name is null
Condition c2 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{ND(null)});

// Value count mismatch → throws IllegalArgumentException("Operator require value count is 1")
Condition c3 = jt.condition(DSL.name("name"), "==", new Object[]{});

not() — Negating a Condition

not(Condition) negates an existing condition and returns null when the input is null:

Condition original = jt.and("status", "disabled");
Condition notDisabled = jt.not(original);   // not (status = 'disabled')

orOne() — Multiple Fields Matching the Same Value

orOne(Object... sameOneValues) starts with several "fields" (single-value operators), and the last argument is the shared value, generating field1 op value or field2 op value .... A typical "global keyword search" scenario:

// name = 'Apple' or nick_name = 'Apple' or remark = 'Apple'
Condition cond = jt.orOne("name", "nick_name", "remark", "Apple");

Null Fallback for between

between / notbetween take 2 values; when either end is null, it automatically falls back to a one-sided comparison, and when both ends are null the whole condition is ignored:

// Both begin and end are non-null: price between 100 and 500
jt.conditions("price:between", 100, 500);

// begin=100, end=null: price >= 100
jt.conditions("price:between", 100, null);

// notbetween fallback: begin=null, end=500 → price > 500
jt.conditions("price:notbetween", null, 500);

Operator Reference

Condition operators (written after the field name or passed to condition(); all are case-insensitive):

Operator Value Count Meaning
== (default) 1 Equal to
<> 1 Not equal to
> >= < <= 1 Comparison
% / like 1 Contains %value%
%l / llike 1 Prefix match value%
%r / rlike 1 Suffix match %value
in / notin 1 Value is a Collection or Object[]
between / notbetween 2 Range; a null end falls back automatically
isnull / isnotnull 0 Null check

Sort operators (only used in the order part of a query or in orders()): asc, ascnf (nulls first), ascnl (nulls last), desc, descnf, descnl.

Null handling rules:

  • In queries (conditions() / and() / or() / condition()), a null value → the condition is ignored.
  • A value wrapped with ND(null) → generates field is null.
  • In UPDATE / DELETE, a null value → generates field is null.

title: How DeepInfer Slashed Latency by 2.4 and Cut Costs by 45% – The Future of AI on Edge
description:
DeepInfer × DeepSeek – What the “breaking‑news” rollout means for high‑performance inference

Lead

“Half‑the‑latency, double the throughput – on the same silicon.”

DeepSeek’s chief architect announced this claim at the June 2026 launch, and the benchmark data backs it up. By open‑sourcing DeepInfer, DeepSeek has delivered a new suite of low‑precision kernels, a unified kernel‑ABI, and a speculative MoE scheduler that together cut end‑to‑end latency by 2.4× and lift throughput by roughly 30 % on flagship GPUs.

The headline grabs attention, but the deeper story lies in the engineering trade‑offs and market dynamics that will determine whether DeepInfer reshapes inference‑as‑a‑service or remains a specialist library.

A real‑time chatbot on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin

A startup wants to embed the 671‑billion‑parameter DeepSeek‑R1 model in a voice‑assistant device powered by a Jetson AGX Orin (204 TOPS, FP8/INT8/INT4 support).

Before DeepInfer

  • Proprietary runtime required FP8 weights and a custom CUDA stack.
  • Model load consumed 12 GB of GPU memory, leaving only 4 GB for activations.
  • A 256‑token prompt responded in 78 ms; cold‑start time was 1.2 s.
  • To meet a 100 ms SLA the startup ran two GPUs in parallel, doubling power draw and cost.

After DeepInfer

  • Switching to deepinfer.run(model, prompt) automatically selected the INT4 path, activated the Ozaki integer‑matrix‑multiply unit, and enabled activation‑recycling.
  • Memory fell to 8 GB, freeing room for a larger activation buffer.
  • End‑to‑end latency dropped to 33 ms, comfortably under the SLA with a single GPU.
  • Cold‑start time halved to 0.6 s thanks to lazy loading of MoE expert weights.

Result: hardware cost down ≈45 %, power consumption down ≈30 %, and on‑device personalization became feasible.

Hard numbers from the first week

Metric Baseline (DeepSeek‑only) DeepInfer on NVIDIA A100 DeepInfer on Ascend NPU SuperPOD
End‑to‑end latency (512‑token) 78 ms 33 ms (2.4× faster) 41 ms (1.9× faster)
Throughput (tokens / s per GPU) 5.2 k 7.8 k (30 % up) 7.0 k (35 % up)
Memory footprint (model + activations) 12 GB (FP8) 8 GB (INT4) 9 GB (Ascend‑optimized)
Cold‑start time (model load) 1.2 s 0.6 s 0.7 s
Power draw at full load 350 W 260 W 240 W

Key stat: DeepInfer earned >200 k GitHub stars and 30 k forks in its first week, making it the fastest‑growing inference engine of 2026.

Kernel‑level innovations that drive the gains

1. Ozaki integer‑matrix‑multiply

Packs INT4 values into 8‑bit lanes and runs a fused multiply‑add on tensor cores, cutting memory traffic by 45 % and doubling arithmetic intensity.

2. Speculative MoE token pre‑scheduling

Predicts which experts will fire, pre‑loads their weights, and pipelines execution, shrinking expert‑selection latency from 12 ms to under 3 ms.

3. Unified kernel‑ABI (v1.0)

A binary interface that abstracts vendor specifics; NVIDIA, AMD, and Huawei ship drop‑in libraries (libdeepinfer_cuda.so, libdeepinfer_hip.so, libdeepinfer_ascend.so) without touching the model graph.

4. Activation‑recycling

Reuses activation buffers across layers of identical shape, reducing fragmentation and improving cache locality.

Together these advances collapse into a single‑line Python call, a JSON config, and a compiled backend library.

Compatibility matrix

Model family Supported precisions Special kernels Accuracy loss
DeepSeek‑R1 (671 B) FP8, INT4, INT8 Ozaki integer‑MMU, speculative MoE < 0.3 % BLEU drop
DeepSeek‑V3 (1.2 T) FP8, INT4 Mixed‑precision fused kernels, checkpointing < 0.5 % perplexity rise
DeepSeek‑V4‑Pro (1.6 T) FP8, INT4, INT8 Hybrid CSA/HCA attention, Ozaki MMU < 0.1 % quality change
DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash (284 B) FP8, INT4 Same as V4‑Pro + speculative token pruning < 0.2 % quality drop

DeepInfer treats each model as a graph of operators; the runtime swaps in the optimal kernel based on target precision and hardware, requiring zero code changes from the user. Future MoE or sparse‑attention models fit the same ABI without recompilation.

Market reaction

  • Stock rally – DeepSeek’s parent (NASDAQ: DSK) jumped +12 % on announcement day, the biggest single‑day gain since the V4‑Flash launch.
  • Cloud beta programs – AWS rolled out g6e instances with DeepInfer‑optimized drivers; Azure announced NDv5 VMs exposing the Ascend backend; Alibaba Cloud unveiled GN5 instances for the China market.
  • Ecosystem adoption – NVIDIA now lists “DeepInfer support” under its CUDA toolkit; AMD’s ROCm roadmap includes a DeepInfer‑HIP shim slated for Q1 2027.
  • Developer buzz – Within 48 hours the repository logged >200 k stars and 30 k forks, outpacing TensorRT and ONNX Runtime growth in 2024.
  • Competitive positioning – OpenAI’s CTO warned that “proprietary inference stacks risk isolation,” hinting at pressure to open their own kernels. Anthropic called DeepInfer “a compelling alternative for high‑throughput workloads,” signaling a possible shift in the inference‑as‑a‑service market.

Risks and unanswered questions

  1. Non‑DeepSeek models – Early adopters report kernel mismatches with third‑party checkpoints (e.g., LLaMA, GPT‑4). Community contributions are needed to close the gap.
  2. Quantization accuracy – INT4 introduces a 0.2–0.5 % drop in BLEU/perplexity. DeepSeek’s upcoming calibration tool (Q4 2026) has yet to prove its robustness across domains.
  3. IP friction – The kernels overlap with patents held by NVIDIA and Huawei, raising the possibility of licensing disputes that could delay commercial rollouts.
  4. Hardware‑specific extensions – The Ozaki MMU relies on a microcode extension present only in recent NVIDIA and Ascend GPUs, forcing early upgrades for full speedup.

Outlook

  1. Standardization pressure – Continued cloud support could push the ABI toward a de‑facto industry standard. ONNX may adopt it as an optional “high‑performance inference” extension, compelling other runtimes to comply.
  2. Edge‑AI expansion – The Jetson Orin case shows DeepInfer’s viability on low‑power devices. OEMs in automotive, robotics, and smart speakers are likely to bundle the engine, creating a new revenue stream via enterprise support contracts.
  3. Cross‑modal inference – DeepSeek’s roadmap includes a Vision‑Language MoE that will share the same kernel stack. If DeepInfer can handle dense vision backbones without extra code, it could become the universal inference layer for multimodal services.
  4. Competitive response – OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta will accelerate their own open‑source inference projects. A future “breaking‑news” headline may feature a joint benchmark pitting DeepInfer, TensorRT, and TVM on a unified MoE workload.
  5. Monetization via support – While the core engine stays free, DeepSeek can sell enterprise‑grade plugins (security‑hardened kernels, compliance logging, SLA‑guaranteed cloud images), mirroring the successful Linux ecosystem model.

Call to action

DeepInfer has already proved that sub‑50 ms latency for 512‑token prompts is achievable on a single GPU, turning real‑time AI from a cloud‑only fantasy into an on‑device reality. The next step for engineers, product leaders, and investors is clear:

  • Test the ABI on your own workloads and contribute missing kernels to broaden model support.
  • Watch the standardization debate—early alignment with ONNX or a similar body could lock in long‑term compatibility across clouds.
  • Plan for hardware upgrades if you need the full Ozaki MMU boost, but weigh that against the cost savings DeepInfer already delivers.

If the community rallies around the open‑source stack and the ABI matures into an industry standard, DeepInfer could become the backbone of inference‑as‑a‑service for the next generation of low‑latency AI. The question now is not whether it will, but how quickly the ecosystem can coalesce around it.

title: October 05, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Change

The BigQuery JupyterLab plugin is now enabled independently of the Dataproc plugin: it is enabled by default and can be turned off with the new disable-bigquery instance metadata key, while disable-mixer now controls only the Dataproc plugin.

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Security

Security fixes for the integrated portal and API specs in the Apigee Edge management UIs.

The Apigee Edge UIs for managing integrated portals and API specs were updated to patch vulnerabilities in underlying libraries and serving components. Functionality is unchanged, but some pages might show minor styling differences.

Application Design Center

Feature

Use the recommendeIAMroles API to identify a list of required APIs and Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles that you must configure before you deploy your application.

BigQuery

Feature

Iceberg external tables and Iceberg managed tables now support flexible column names by default. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The gemini-embedding-2 model works well for embedding long strings, including multilingual and unstructured data. It supports a mix of text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. You can use this model in the AI.EMBED, AI.SIMILARITY, and AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING functions. This model is generally available.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

This feature is in Preview.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports Assured Workloads control packages to help you meet regulatory, data residency, and data sovereignty requirements.

Specifically, the Cloud Workstations API (v1, v1beta, and v1alpha) supports the following Assured Workloads control packages:

  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP High
  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP Moderate
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 2 (IL2)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5)
  • US Data Boundary and Support (AW Regional Controls - Premium)
  • EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications

For more information about compliance-supported regions for each control package and API fields that aren't intended for sensitive data, see Regulatory support in Cloud Workstations.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Z3 machine types that have 8 to 44 vCPUs can use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes to synchronously replicate data across two zones.

For more information, see About Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (260900) is available.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Deprecated

Starting on July 1, 2026, Identity Service for GKE is deprecated in GKE version 1.36 and earlier. This feature is also unavailable in organizations that were created on or after July 1, 2025. GKE version 1.37 and later don't support Identity Service for GKE. Before you upgrade clusters to 1.37 and later, disable this feature and migrate to Workforce Identity Federation.

For more information, see Identity Service for GKE deprecation.

Feature

GKE support for using the c4-standard-* machine types (up to 192 vCPUs) as Confidential GKE Nodes with Intel TDX is generally available. For more information, see the following pages:

  • To use this feature with GKE , see Encrypt workload data in-use with Confidential GKE Nodes.
  • To learn more about the feature from Compute Engine, see Confidential VM overview.
  • To see supported configurations, including machine support, see Supported configurations and its "Machine types, CPUs, and zones" section.

Google SecOps

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Terraform and client libraries for multiple features using Chronicle API

Terraform providers and Google Cloud client libraries are now available for several Google SecOps features using Chronicle API including Feeds, Parsers, Rules, Findings Refinements, Retrohunts, Dashboards, Data Tables, Watchlists, Custom Lists, Environments, Environment Groups, Data Export, SOAR Domains, and SOAR Networks. For more information, see Terraform reference.

Terraform providers enable programmatic provisioning and management of Google SecOps resources as code, while Client Libraries enable developers to build custom integrations and automate Google SecOps workflows in their preferred programming languages. For more information, see Client libraries.

Guest Environment

Feature

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following features:

  • The managed workload identity certificate refresher is now a locally bundled extension. For more information, see Managed workload identities overview.
  • The guest telemetry extension is updated to version 1.1 and polls every 15 minutes instead of every 24 hours. However, it will only send data to the API every 24 hours, unless it detects a change in the system since the previous poll. The extension supports the following capabilities:
    • Running a command as the user associated with a discovered process.
    • Configuring regular expressions to match against the version command output.

Fixed

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following fixes:

  • The NetworkManager setup now no longer reloads the primary NIC when it applies changes to the network configuration of secondary NICs, unless necessary.
  • If the core plugin successfully rolls back any configurations, then it force-reloads the configurations to make sure that the instance re-obtains DHCP leases for secondary NICs.
  • The core plugin now respects the address-manager configuration flag and the corresponding metadata attribute.
  • The extensions manager now ignores install and remove requests from ACS for the core plugin and locally bundled extensions.
  • The extensions manager no longer logs that there are no local plugins to install when it's installing local plugins.
  • The metadata script runner now respects the sysprep_specialize configuration flag.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog now support Looker (Google Cloud core) assets. You can package, govern, and share Looker (Google Cloud core) dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, Explores, and LookML projects, models, and views in a data product using Google Group mirroring and IAM access controls. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see About data products and Create data products.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Change

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Users may now specify short template names when creating a serverless session.

Network Intelligence Center

Feature

Flow Analyzer displays packet drops, allowing you to analyze packet loss in your traffic flows. For more information, see Display flows in packet drop mode.

Network Service Tiers

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier in Preview. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

title: Think Before You Transcribe: Context-Steered Reasoning for Hotword-Aware Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.26986v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contextual automatic speech recognition (ASR) improves rare-entity recognition by supplying candidate hotwords, but retrieved candidates may be incomplete or incorrect. A reliable system must therefore exploit a relevant candidate without allowing unsupported alternatives to override the acoustic evidence. We propose a context-steered reasoning framework that generates a short, audio-grounded caption before transcription. This task-specific representation lets the model assess candidate relevance before making a lexical decision. Supervised fine-tuning establishes the structured caption-to-transcription behavior, while targeted trajectory injection strengthens group relative policy optimization when difficult utterances yield only unsuccessful rollouts. Experiments across diverse context conditions show that the proposed method consistently improves both transcription quality and hotword recognition while remaining robust to irrelevant candidates.

title: Node.js PDF Retrieval for Course Tutors: Precision Gates Before Release Checklist
description:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an online course tutor answering questions from a folder of PDFs, that usually means measuring recall and precision before optimizing latency, then keeping ingestion, querying, and citations as separate observable stages.

I run a one-person SaaS, so my release rule is practical: every retrieval decision must either protect answer quality or reduce future maintenance. Anything else steals time from shipping weekly. The checklist below is deliberately boring. Boring is good when a wrong citation teaches a student the wrong thing.

The decision matrix

Approach Retrieval quality Latency control Operational shape Best fit
One giant index with broad queries Uneven across courses Hard to bound Simple at first, opaque later A prototype with one tenant
Per-course collections plus metadata filters Predictable and auditable Query scope is explicit More ingestion bookkeeping Most multi-course tutors
Hybrid keyword and vector search Strong on names and concepts Two paths to budget Needs score fusion and tests PDFs with exact terms and prose
Hosted retrieval service Depends on vendor defaults Vendor-specific limits Fast to start, less control Teams buying time over control

My default is the second row, with a small hybrid path when the documents contain lots of identifiers, formulas, or proper nouns. A collection is a boundary, not a folder name: include tenant, course, document version, page, and access-control metadata on every indexed chunk.

What should an online course tutor release checklist test?

Start from the answer a student should see and write a retrieval contract for it. The contract says which collection is eligible, the maximum number of chunks, the score threshold, and the citation fields that must survive to the final response. It also states what happens when evidence is missing: ask a clarifying question or say that the course material does not establish the claim.

Then build a small evaluation set from representative documents and failure cases. Include a clean definition, a question spanning two pages, a table, a scanned page, a stale syllabus, and a question from the wrong course. Label the expected source pages. Track recall (did we retrieve the needed page?) and precision (did the returned pages actually support the answer?).

Do this before changing chunk size. Otherwise a latency improvement can quietly become a citation regression. I learned to keep one deliberately awkward case in every release candidate; the awkward case catches assumptions that happy-path PDFs hide. For example, take a 70-page PDF whose glossary defines “momentum” differently from the general physics text, then ask a question that uses both meanings. A useful test records the expected pages, the retrieved rank for each page, the final citation, and the elapsed time for each stage. If the glossary page is absent, the answer should fail closed. If it is present but a page from another tenant ranks higher, the metadata filter has failed even when the vector score looks excellent. That single fixture exercises chunk boundaries, version labels, tenant isolation, and citation rendering together, so it earns a permanent place in the release suite.

Keep one ugly test.

A staged pipeline that stays observable

Ingestion should parse, normalize, chunk, attach metadata, and record a document version. Querying should resolve the tenant and course, apply access checks, and issue a bounded retrieval request. Answering should receive source ids, page numbers, and snippets rather than an undifferentiated blob. Log a request id and stage timings for each step, while avoiding raw student content in logs.

The boundaries make failures diagnosable. If recall drops, inspect chunking and indexing. If precision drops, inspect filters and the query contract. If citations disappear, inspect the handoff into answer generation. This is the kind of undifferentiated plumbing I prefer to outsource to a consistent API surface so I can spend my revenue-per-hour budget on tutor behavior.

For a small Node.js service, an API that describes itself can shorten that plumbing. Infrai's public discovery response exposes the request schema and runnable examples for each capability, so wiring a new retrieval operation starts with reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. Infrai also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key and one bill, which removes a separate credential and reconciliation step when the tutor adds storage or scheduled ingestion. That breadth is a workflow convenience, not evidence that retrieval quality is automatic; your data and tests still decide that.

Here is a minimal bounded query. The collection id and tenant filter are application values; the route and method are the documented vector query surface.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const response = await fetch("/v1/vector/query", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    collection: "course-physics-v3",
    query: "How does conservation of momentum apply to the lab?",
    top_k: 5,
    filter: { tenant_id: "tenant_42", course_id: "physics-101", acl: "student" },
  }),
});

if (response.status === 429) {
  throw new Error("Rate limited; retry with exponential backoff and Retry-After");
}
if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Vector query failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
}

const payload: unknown = await response.json();
console.log(payload);

In production I would wrap that call in bounded exponential backoff, honor Retry-After, and make any write-side retry idempotent. A query should also carry enough context to render a citation: document id, version, page, and the chunk text selected by the contract.

Where the alternatives win

There is no universal winner. Pinecone is a sensible choice when a managed vector database and its operational tooling are the product requirement. Weaviate fits teams that want an open-source-first database with hybrid retrieval features. pgvector is attractive when Postgres is already the system of record and joins over tenant metadata matter more than a separate service. Elasticsearch remains strong when lexical search, filters, and existing cluster operations dominate.

Option Strength Trade-off for this tutor
Pinecone Managed vector index and straightforward scaling Adds a separate data service and vendor-specific controls
Weaviate Open-source deployment and hybrid search More cluster decisions for a solo maintainer
pgvector SQL joins, transactions, and familiar Postgres operations Vector tuning competes with the primary database
Elasticsearch Excellent lexical matching and filtering Heavier operational surface if you only need course retrieval
Infrai vector API Self-describing REST discovery and runnable examples You still own collection design, evaluation, and citation policy

Stick with pgvector when your tenant permissions already live in Postgres and a second control plane would slow releases. Choose Pinecone or Weaviate when dedicated vector operations are worth the service boundary. The catch is that a unified API does not make weak source documents or missing labels disappear; if your team needs deep index internals, a specialized store may be the better fit.

Release gates I would sign

Before release, I want every indexed item to retain tenant and access-control metadata, every query to have a bounded top_k and an eligible collection, and every answer citation to point to a versioned page. I also want a replayable test set with recall and precision thresholds, plus a latency budget measured separately for ingestion, retrieval, reranking, and generation.

One more gate: query the wrong course on purpose. The correct result is no supporting context, not a confident answer from a neighboring syllabus. Your mileage may vary on thresholds because chunk size, language, and document quality change the curve; record the evidence behind the threshold instead of treating it as a universal number.

That is enough structure to ship a tutor without turning retrieval into a six-month platform project. Keep the contract visible, keep the stages observable, and revisit the matrix when the documents or tenancy model changes.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html

title: Project Scheduling Software Explained: Features, Benefits and Selection
description:
Delivering a project on time requires more than setting deadlines and assigning tasks. Project managers must understand dependencies, estimate activity durations, balance workloads, track progress, and respond to unexpected changes. When several teams work toward the same goal, even a small delay can affect the entire delivery plan.
Managing these activities through spreadsheets and manual updates may work for simple projects. However, as projects become more complex, keeping schedules accurate and communicating changes becomes increasingly difficult.
Project scheduling software helps teams organize activities, visualize timelines, assign resources, and monitor deadlines in one place. It gives project managers a clearer view of what needs to happen, when it should happen, and which activities could delay completion.
This guide explains project scheduling software, its essential features, popular tools, scheduling techniques, and practical ways to build more reliable project plans.
What Is Project Scheduling Software?
Project scheduling software is a digital tool that helps project managers define activities, arrange them in the correct sequence, estimate durations, assign resources, and track progress against planned dates.
It turns a project plan into a structured schedule that teams can update as work progresses.
Depending on the platform, common features include:
Gantt charts and visual timelines.
Task dependencies and milestone tracking.
Critical path analysis.
Resource allocation and capacity planning.
Baseline schedules and progress tracking.
Notifications and automated workflows.
Project dashboards and reports.
Multi-project and portfolio scheduling.
For example, imagine a company preparing to launch a new software product. The schedule may include requirements gathering, design, development, testing, security reviews, user acceptance testing, and deployment.
Some activities can happen simultaneously, while others depend on earlier work. Scheduling software helps teams map these relationships and understand how a delay in one activity could affect the release date.
Why Do Teams Need Project Scheduling Software?
A project schedule is useful only when it reflects the actual work, available resources, and dependencies. Dedicated software helps teams maintain this information as circumstances change.

  1. Create more realistic timelines Manual planning can overlook dependencies, holidays, resource constraints, and approval delays. Scheduling software helps project managers organize activities and calculate dates using the relationships and calendars configured in the system. A realistic schedule gives stakeholders a more reliable basis for planning and making commitments.
  2. Identify delays earlier A task that falls behind schedule may affect several dependent activities. Visual timelines and progress reports help project managers identify these changes before they become larger delivery problems. For example, if a design approval is delayed, the project manager can assess whether development, testing, and deployment dates need to change.
  3. Improve resource utilization Employees often work across several projects. Without a shared view of assignments, managers may allocate the same specialist to multiple tasks during the same period. Resource planning features help identify over-allocation, compare demand with availability, and adjust assignments where necessary.
  4. Strengthen communication A shared project schedule gives team members and stakeholders a common reference point. Instead of relying on separate status spreadsheets and email updates, teams can review task ownership, milestones, deadlines, and current progress in a centralized workspace.
  5. Support better decisions Scheduling software can help managers compare planned and actual progress, identify bottlenecks, and evaluate alternative timelines. These insights support decisions about changing priorities, adding resources, adjusting scope, or revising delivery commitments. Best Project Scheduling Software to Consider Different tools suit different project environments. Some focus on detailed scheduling and critical path analysis, while others emphasize collaboration, flexible workflows, or spreadsheet-style planning. The following options are worth evaluating according to your requirements. Features and pricing can vary by plan, so confirm current capabilities directly with each vendor. Software Best suited for What to evaluate Celoxis Complex projects, resource planning, and portfolio scheduling Dependencies, critical paths, workload management, financial tracking, and portfolio reporting Microsoft Project Detailed schedules and structured project planning Scheduling depth, resource planning, reporting, and integration with your Microsoft environment Smartsheet Teams familiar with spreadsheet-style workflows Timeline views, automation, cross-project reporting, and dependency management Wrike Cross-functional teams coordinating multiple workflows Gantt charts, collaboration, workload visibility, and configurable dashboards monday.com Teams that prefer visual work management Timeline views, workflow customization, automation, and multi-project visibility Zoho Projects Teams looking for general project planning and collaboration Task dependencies, milestones, reporting, integrations, and resource requirements

How to choose the right tool
If your team primarily needs a visual task list and basic deadlines, a lightweight work management platform may be sufficient.
If you manage complex dependencies, multiple projects, shared specialists, or cost-sensitive delivery commitments, prioritize advanced scheduling, critical path analysis, and resource planning.
For organizations with established reporting and business systems, integration capabilities should also be part of the evaluation.
Essential Features of Project Scheduling Software
Not every project requires advanced scheduling functionality. The right feature set depends on project size, delivery approach, team structure, and the consequences of missing deadlines.

  1. Gantt charts and timelines A Gantt chart represents activities as bars across a calendar. It allows users to see when tasks begin and end, how long they take, and where activities overlap. Useful capabilities include: Start and finish dates. Task duration and progress indicators. Milestones and key deadlines. Visual task dependencies. Baseline comparisons. Timeline adjustments. Gantt charts are particularly useful for projects involving multiple phases, approval stages, external vendors, or tightly connected activities.
  2. Task dependencies Dependencies define the relationships between activities. They help the schedule reflect the logical order in which work must happen. The four common dependency types are: Dependency Meaning Example Finish-to-Start (FS) Task B starts after Task A finishes Testing begins after development is completed Start-to-Start (SS) Task B starts after Task A starts Documentation begins once development starts Finish-to-Finish (FF) Task B finishes after Task A finishes Final review cannot finish before the deliverable is complete Start-to-Finish (SF) Task B cannot finish until Task A starts A rare handover arrangement where a new shift begins before the previous shift ends

Most project schedules rely heavily on finish-to-start relationships, but other types may be appropriate for overlapping activities.
Accurate dependencies make it easier to understand the impact of changes and avoid unrealistic deadlines.

  1. Critical path analysis The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities that determines the earliest possible project completion date under the current schedule assumptions. Activities on this path generally have no scheduling flexibility without affecting the final completion date. Critical path analysis helps project managers identify where delays need immediate attention. It can also support schedule compression decisions, such as adding resources to selected activities or performing some work in parallel. However, compressing a schedule may increase cost or introduce additional risk, so changes should be evaluated carefully.
  2. Resource allocation and capacity planning Resource management helps project managers assign work according to availability, skills, workload, and project priorities. Look for features that show: Current and future assignments. Resource availability calendars. Workload by person or role. Over-allocation warnings. Capacity across multiple projects. Options for adjusting assignments. This is especially valuable for organizations where specialist employees support several projects simultaneously.
  3. Milestones and baseline schedules Milestones mark important events, approvals, or deliverables, such as completing a design review or releasing a product. A baseline is the approved version of the project schedule used to compare planned performance with actual progress. Together, milestones and baselines help managers measure schedule variance and explain whether the project is progressing according to the agreed plan.
  4. Progress tracking and reporting Scheduling software should make it easy to update task status, record actual dates, review overdue activities, and understand changes to the expected completion date. Useful reports may include milestone status, delayed tasks, resource utilization, schedule variance, and overall project health. The most valuable reports are those that help people decide what to do next, rather than simply presenting large amounts of information.
  5. Collaboration and notifications Notifications can alert team members when assignments change, deadlines approach, or a dependency is affected. Comments, shared documents, and activity histories can also help teams understand decisions and reduce the need for separate updates. Before enabling automation, define which events deserve notifications. Too many alerts can make important messages easier to overlook. How to Build a Project Schedule Step by Step A reliable schedule begins with a clear understanding of the work. Software can organize a plan, but it cannot compensate for missing activities, unrealistic estimates, or unclear responsibilities. Step 1: Define the project scope Document the project's objectives, deliverables, boundaries, and acceptance criteria. Clarify what must be completed and what falls outside the project's scope. This reduces misunderstandings and makes it easier to identify missing work. For example, a website redesign might include user research, interface design, development, testing, content migration, and launch. Defining the scope helps ensure that these activities are reflected in the schedule. Step 2: Create a work breakdown structure A work breakdown structure (WBS) divides the project deliverables into smaller work packages. These can then be broken into activities that are easier to estimate, assign, and track. For example: Website redesign Research and requirements User experience and design Development Testing and review Launch and handover Each work package should contain enough detail to help the team identify the activities required for completion. Step 3: Identify and sequence activities List the individual tasks needed to complete each work package. Consult the people responsible for performing the work to avoid missing technical steps, reviews, or approvals. Next, determine the logical order of activities. Some tasks must finish before others can start, while some can run in parallel. Record these relationships in the scheduling tool so the plan reflects how the project will actually be delivered. Step 4: Estimate task durations Estimate how long each activity will take using relevant historical information, expert judgment, and the complexity of the work. For uncertain activities, three-point estimating can provide a more balanced forecast by considering optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations. The PERT weighted-average formula is: [ \text{Expected duration}=\frac{O+4M+P}{6} ] Here, (O) is the optimistic estimate, (M) is the most likely estimate, and (P) is the pessimistic estimate. For example, if an activity could take 2 days in the best case, 4 days under normal conditions, and 8 days in the worst case, the expected duration is approximately 4.3 days. This is an estimate, not a guarantee. Add appropriate contingency where uncertainty or project risk warrants it. Step 5: Assign resources Assign a responsible owner to each task and confirm that the required people or equipment will be available. Consider holidays, existing assignments, specialist skills, and competing priorities. Avoid planning as though every team member is available full-time for a single project. If a resource is over-allocated, consider shifting non-critical work, changing priorities, or arranging additional capacity. Step 6: Set milestones and calculate the critical path Identify important review points, approval gates, and delivery dates. Use the scheduling tool to calculate the critical path where supported. Review the activities that have little or no scheduling flexibility and establish how delays will be monitored. This helps the team focus attention on activities that could affect the final deadline. Step 7: Review and approve the baseline Before finalizing the schedule, validate it with the project team and key stakeholders. Confirm that the scope is covered, durations are realistic, dependencies are correct, and resources are available. Once approved, save the baseline. It becomes the reference point for tracking progress and evaluating schedule changes. Step 8: Monitor and update the schedule As work progresses, update task status and actual dates. Review the difference between planned and actual performance and investigate important variances. If a task slips, assess the impact on dependent activities and the final deadline. Document approved changes so the schedule remains a reliable representation of the current plan. Project Scheduling Techniques Every Manager Should Know Software becomes more useful when project managers understand the techniques behind the schedule. Critical Path Method The Critical Path Method (CPM) identifies the sequence of activities that determines the earliest possible completion date. Use it when tasks have clear dependencies and durations can be estimated with reasonable confidence. It is particularly useful for construction, product launches, implementation projects, and other initiatives with several connected stages. Resource leveling Resource leveling adjusts the schedule to address resource conflicts. For example, if the same engineer is assigned to two tasks at the same time, the manager may move one task to a later date. Leveling can extend the overall project duration when resources are limited, so its effect on the deadline must be reviewed. Resource smoothing Resource smoothing aims to reduce workload fluctuations while keeping the project within its existing completion constraints, where possible. It often involves shifting activities that have scheduling flexibility to create a more balanced distribution of work. Fast-tracking Fast-tracking means performing activities in parallel that would normally be completed sequentially. For example, a team might begin preparing training materials while final testing is still underway. This can shorten the schedule, but it may create rework if the earlier activity depends on information that has not yet been finalized. Crashing Crashing shortens selected activities by adding resources or spending more to accelerate the work. Examples include assigning additional specialists or paying for extra shifts. Crashing should focus on activities that affect the critical path. Accelerating a task outside the critical path may not improve the overall completion date. Best Practices for Effective Project Scheduling
  6. Build the schedule with the team Project managers should involve the people who will perform the work when estimating durations and identifying dependencies. Their input can reveal hidden activities, technical constraints, and resource conflicts that might otherwise be overlooked.
  7. Use realistic assumptions Avoid committing to dates simply because they are desirable. Consider the availability of resources, approval times, supplier commitments, and uncertainty in the work. A realistic plan is more useful than an optimistic schedule that must constantly be revised.
  8. Review progress regularly Choose a review frequency that matches the pace and risk of the project. During reviews, focus on overdue activities, upcoming milestones, changes in the critical path, and risks that require decisions. Updating the schedule consistently is essential to keeping forecasts meaningful.
  9. Manage changes through a defined process Changes to scope, priorities, or resources can affect both the schedule and the budget. Before approving a major change, assess its effect on dependent tasks, resource capacity, cost, and delivery commitments. Record the decision and update the plan only when the change has been authorized.
  10. Communicate delays early When a milestone is at risk, communicate the issue along with its likely impact and proposed response. Stakeholders need time to make decisions, adjust expectations, or provide additional resources. Waiting until a deadline has already passed limits their options.
  11. Use dashboards that match stakeholder needs Team members may need detailed task lists, while executives may need milestone status, schedule variance, and forecast completion dates. Create views that provide the right level of detail for each audience. Keep reporting focused on actionable information. How to Choose the Right Project Scheduling Software Before purchasing a platform, evaluate it against your actual working environment. Understand project complexity. Determine whether you manage simple task lists, detailed dependency networks, or multiple interconnected projects. Identify essential capabilities. Decide whether you need critical path analysis, workload balancing, baseline tracking, financial controls, or portfolio-level reporting. Check integration requirements. Confirm that the tool works with your existing collaboration, finance, development, and reporting systems. Evaluate usability. Ask project managers and team members to complete common scheduling tasks during a trial. Review security and deployment. Check permissions, data handling, hosting options, and any organizational security requirements. Compare total cost. Consider licensing, implementation, training, support, and ongoing administration. Test realistic scenarios. Use an actual project plan to verify how the software handles dependency changes, delayed tasks, resource conflicts, and reporting. A structured comparison is more reliable than selecting a tool based on its interface or feature count alone. How Celoxis Supports Project Scheduling Celoxis is a project and portfolio management platform that supports project planning, Gantt charts, task dependencies, critical path analysis, resource management, and project reporting. It may be worth evaluating for organizations that manage complex schedules or need visibility across several concurrent projects. Its scheduling capabilities include interactive Gantt planning, inter-project dependencies, resource assignments, and baseline-based tracking. These functions can help project managers assess how changes in one task or project affect other activities. Celoxis also provides dashboards and reporting capabilities that can help teams monitor project status and review performance. Organizations should evaluate these features using their own project data and reporting requirements. For teams considering a scheduling platform, the best approach is to test a representative project, check resource and dependency behavior, and confirm that the reporting meets stakeholder needs. You can explore the Celoxis project management platform or book a demo to assess whether it fits your scheduling and portfolio management requirements.

Conclusion
Effective project scheduling depends on clear scope, realistic estimates, accurate dependencies, available resources, and consistent progress reviews. Project scheduling software brings these elements together so teams can manage timelines, identify potential delays, and make informed decisions.
The right platform should match the complexity of your projects, support the scheduling techniques you use, and provide useful information without making the process unnecessarily complicated.
Start by understanding your scheduling challenges, define the features that matter most, and test shortlisted tools against a real project. With the right process and software, project schedules can become practical tools for coordinating work and managing delivery, rather than static timelines that quickly fall out of date.

title: I broke an Elementor site on purpose, then built a tool to find the bugs
description:
The night I broke my own site

I'm 53, I work in a factory, and in the evenings I build things in vanilla JavaScript.

Lately I've been looking at freelance WordPress jobs. Almost every one of them says the same thing: "Elementor site, layout is broken, fix it."

So I did something a bit crazy. I took an empty test site, installed Elementor, and asked an AI to break it for me — 5 hidden CSS bugs, packed into an encoded script so I couldn't just read the answer.

Then I tried to find them.

It was humbling. The page looked wrong, but the console said nothing. Of course: CSS doesn't throw errors. A bad rule is still a valid rule, so the browser applies it silently. That's exactly why clients say "everything moved and I don't know why."

I found the first bug the slow way — DevTools, Styles panel, unchecking rules one by one until I saw it:

.elementor-section, .e-con { margin-right: -60px !important; }

Twenty minutes for one line. I thought: there must be a faster way.

So I built one: CSS hunt

🐞 BeeLadybug is my zero-dependency debugging overlay. You paste one line in the console and it attaches to any page — WordPress dashboards, Elementor pages, mobile viewports. It already showed element size, classes, display type, FPS and memory.

Version 0.5 adds a new mode: CSS hunt (press F6).

When you hover an element, it tells you what's wrong with it:

  • !important rules that match the element, and where they come from (<style> inline or the stylesheet URL)
  • Overflow causes: which element actually leaves the viewport, plus negative margins
  • Invisible text: color: transparent, opacity: 0, or text the same color as its background
  • Click blockers: what sits on top of the element's center, including fixed ::before / ::after on html / body
  • Stretched images: natural ratio vs rendered ratio, when object-fit is fill

Press S to scan the whole page. Click a line and the element gets a red outline.

The hard part: telling the truth without noise

My first version was technically right and practically useless.

One card overflowing the screen produced ten red lines: the card, its article, its p, its h2… All "overflowing", because they inherited it. A fixed overlay blocking clicks? One warning per element underneath it.

A real developer doesn't want ten alarms. They want the culprit.

So the scan now:

  1. Reports the cause, not the containers. An ancestor is skipped if a descendant overflows by the same amount (±2px).
  2. Groups by cause. Instead of 12 lines you get: 
▾ body::after blocks clicks on 12 elements
    div.elementor-element-629ef32
    img#1301
    summary.elementor-element-3925463
    …
  1. Separates bugs from info. Red = bug. Grey = info, like unreadable sheet: fonts.googleapis.com (cross-origin stylesheets can't be read — that's a browser rule, not a problem on the page).
  2. Keeps the log calm. Hover and DOM-mutation lines are hidden unless you turn on verbose mode (F3). Each issue is logged once per element every 5 seconds. Press P to pin the panel on an element and read it in peace.

The real test

The demo page bugs are easy — I wrote them. The real test was the broken Elementor page, with Elementor V4 "atomic" widgets, Google Fonts, Altervista ad scripts and all the usual mess.

Result: CSS hunt found the click blocker, the negative margin overflow, the invisible button text and the stretched image on a live page I didn't build the bugs for.

Try it

Open any page, press F12, paste this in the console:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.5.3/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Then press F6, hover, and press S.

No build step, no framework, no dependencies. Just vanilla JavaScript.

What I learned

  • CSS bugs are silent. The console won't help you. You need to look at computed styles and geometry.
  • The right answer is not enough. A debugging tool must point to the cause, or it's just another wall of text.
  • Breaking things on purpose is the best teacher. I recommend it to anyone who wants to do WordPress fixes for clients.

I'm still learning. If you try CSS hunt on a broken page and it misses something, tell me in the comments — that's how the next version gets better.

🐞 npm: bee-ladybug

title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.26951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks- MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K-1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
description:
arXiv:2610.26932v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.
