title: Build-as-Code, CI Integration, and Build Doctor
description:
• Why treat builds as code: eliminate drift and make builds a pure function
  • CI integration patterns for hermetic builds and remote cache clients
  • Designing and implementing a Build Doctor diagnostics tool
  • Rolling out at scale: onboarding, guardrails, and measuring impact
  • Practical checklists and runbooks for immediate action

Treat every build flag, toolchain pin, and cache policy as versioned code — not a local habit. Doing so converts the build from a mutable ritual into a repeatable, auditable function whose outputs are pure and sharable.

The pain is specific: slow pull requests because CI redoes work, “works on my machine” debugging, cache-poisoning incidents that invalidate hours of developer effort, and onboarding that takes days because local setups differ. Those symptoms trace back to one root cause: build affordances (flags, toolchains, cache policy, and CI integration) live as handwaves instead of code, so behavior diverges between machines and pipelines.

Why treat builds as code: eliminate drift and make builds a pure function

Treating the build as code — build-as-code — means storing every decision that influences outputs in version control: WORKSPACE pins, BUILD rules, toolchain stanzas, .bazelrc snippets, CI bazel flags, and the remote-cache client configuration. That discipline enforces hermeticity: the build result is independent of the host machine and therefore reproducible across developer laptops and CI servers.

What you get when you do this correctly:

  • Bit-identical artifacts for the same inputs, eliminating “it works on my machine” debugging.
  • A cacheable DAG: actions become pure functions of declared inputs, so results can be reused across machines.
  • Safe experimentation via branches: differing toolchain or flag sets are explicit commits, not env leaks.

Practical rails that make this discipline enforceable:

  • Keep a repo-level .bazelrc that defines the canonical flags used in CI and for canonical local runs (build --remote_cache=..., build --host_force_python=...).
  • Pin toolchains and third-party deps in WORKSPACE with exact commits or SHA256 checksums.
  • Treat ci and local modes as two configurations in the build-as-code model; only one (CI) should be allowed to write authoritative cache entries in the early rollout phase.

Important: Hermeticity is an engineering property you can test for; make those tests part of CI so the repository encodes the build’s contract rather than relying on implicit conventions.

CI integration patterns for hermetic builds and remote cache clients

The CI layer is the single most potent lever for accelerating team builds and protecting the cache. There are three practical patterns you will choose from depending on scale and trust.

  • CI-as-single-writer, developers-read-only: CI builds (full, canonical builds) write to the remote cache; developer machines read only. This prevents accidental cache poisoning and keeps the authoritative cache consistent.
  • Combined local + remote cache: Developers use a local disk cache plus a shared remote cache. The local cache improves cold-starts and avoids unnecessary network trips; the remote cache enables cross-machine reuse.
  • Remote execution (RBE) for speed at scale: CI and some dev flows offload heavy actions to RBE workers and take advantage of both remote execution and the shared CAS.

Bazel exposes standard knobs for these patterns; the remote cache stores action metadata and the content-addressable store of outputs, and a build consults the cache before running actions.

Example .bazelrc snippets (repo-level vs CI):

# .bazelrc (repo - canonical flags)
build --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.corp.example:9090
build --remote_download_outputs=minimal
build --host_jvm_args=-Xmx2g
build --show_progress_rate_limit=30

# .bazelrc.ci (CI-only overrides; kept on CI runner)
build --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.corp.example:9090
build --remote_executor=grpcs://rbe.corp.example:8989
build --remote_timeout=180s
build --bes_backend=grpcs://bep.corp.example   # send BEP to analysis UI

CI example (GitHub Actions, illustrating integration with existing cache steps): use the platform cache for language deps and let Bazel use the remote cache for build outputs. The actions/cache action is a common helper for pre-built dependency caches.

name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Restore tool caches
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/bazel
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-bazel-${{ hashFiles('**/WORKSPACE') }}
      - name: Bazel build (CI canonical)
        run: bazel build --bazelrc=.bazelrc.ci //...

Contrast of caching approaches

Mode What it shares Latency impact Infra complexity
Local disk cache per-host artifacts small improvement, not shared low
Shared remote cache (HTTP/gRPC) CAS + action metadata network-limited, large benefit across team medium
Remote execution (RE) executes actions remotely minimizes dev wall-clock time high (workers, auth, scheduling)

Remote execution and remote caching are complementary; RBE focuses on compute scaling while the cache focuses on reuse. The protocol landscape and client/server implementations (e.g., the Bazel Remote Execution APIs) are standardized and supported by several OSS and commercial offerings.

Practical CI guardrails to enforce:

  • Make CI the canonical writer during pilot: developer configs set --remote_upload_local_results=false while CI sets it true.
  • Lock who can clear the cache and implement a cache-poison rollback plan.
  • Send BEP (Build Event Protocol) from CI builds to a centralized invocations UI for later troubleshooting and historical metrics. Tools like BuildBuddy ingest BEP and provide cache-hit breakdowns.

Designing and implementing a Build Doctor diagnostics tool

What a Build Doctor does

  • Acts like a deterministic, fast diagnostics agent that runs locally and in CI to surface misconfigurations and non-hermetic actions.
  • Collects structured evidence (Bazel info, BEP, aquery/cquery, profile traces) and returns actionable findings (missing --remote_cache, genrule calling curl, actions with nondeterministic outputs).
  • Produces machine-readable results (JSON), human-friendly reports, and CI annotations for PRs.

Data sources and commands to use

  • bazel info for environment and output base.
  • bazel aquery --output=jsonproto 'deps(//my:target)' to retrieve action commandlines and inputs programmatically. This output can be scanned for rogue network calls, writes outside the declared outputs, and suspicious commandline flags.
  • bazel build --profile=command.profile.gz //... followed by bazel analyze-profile command.profile.gz to get the critical path and per-action durations; the JSON trace profile can be loaded into tracing UIs for deeper analysis.
  • Build Event Protocol (BEP) / --bes_results_url to stream invocation metadata to a server for long-term analytics. BuildBuddy and similar platforms provide BEP ingestion and a UI for cache-hit debugging.

Minimal Build Doctor architecture (three components)

  1. Collector — shell or agent that runs the Bazel commands and writes structured files:
    • bazel info --show_make_env -> doctor/info.json
    • bazel aquery --output=jsonproto ... -> doctor/aquery.json
    • bazel build --profile=doctor.prof //... -> doctor/command.profile.gz
    • optional: fetch BEP or remote cache server logs
  2. Analyzer — Python/Go service that:
    • Parses aquery for suspicious mnemonics or commands (Genrule, ctx.execute) that contain network tools.
    • Runs bazel analyze-profile doctor.prof and correlates long actions with aquery outputs.
    • Verifies .bazelrc flags and remote cache client presence.
  3. Reporter — emits:
    • a concise human report
    • structured JSON for CI pass/fail gating
    • annotations for PRs (failed hermetic checks, top 5 critical-path actions)

Example: a tiny Build Doctor check in Python (skeleton)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, subprocess, sys, gzip

def run(cmd):
    print("+", " ".join(cmd))
    return subprocess.check_output(cmd).decode()

def check_remote_cache():
    info = run(["bazel", "info", "--show_make_env"])
    if "remote_cache" not in info:
        return {"ok": False, "msg": "No remote_cache configured in bazel info"}
    return {"ok": True}

def parse_aquery_json(path):
    with open(path,'rb') as f:
        return json.load(f)

def main():
    run(["bazel","aquery","--output=jsonproto","deps(//...)", "--include_commandline=false", "--noshow_progress"])
    # analyzer steps would follow...
    print(json.dumps({"checks":[check_remote_cache()]}))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Diagnostic heuristics you should encode (examples)

  • Actions whose command lines contain curl, wget, scp, or ssh indicate network access and likely non-hermetic behavior.
  • Actions that write to $(WORKSPACE) or outside declared outputs indicate source-tree mutation.
  • Targets tagged no-cache or no-remote deserve review; frequent no-cache usage is a smell.
  • bazel build outputs that differ across repeated clean runs reveal nondeterminism (timestamps, randomness in build steps).

A Build Doctor should avoid hard fails on first rollout. Start with informational severities and escalate rules to warnings and hard-gate checks as confidence grows.

Rolling out at scale: onboarding, guardrails, and measuring impact

Rollout phases

  1. Pilot (2–4 teams): CI writes to cache, developers use read-only cache settings. Run Build Doctor in CI and as a local dev hook.
  2. Expand (6–8 weeks): Add more teams, tune heuristics, add tests that detect cache-poisoning patterns.
  3. Org-wide: Make CANONICAL .bazelrc and toolchain pins required, add PR checks, and open the cache for a broader set of write clients.

Key metrics to instrument and track

  • P95 build/test times for common developer flows (changes to a single package, full test runs).
  • Remote cache hit rate: percent of actions served from the remote cache vs executed. Track daily and by repository. Aim high; a >90% hit rate on incremental builds is a realistic, high-leverage target for mature setups.
  • Time to first successful build (new hire): measure from checkout to successful test run.
  • Number of hermeticity regressions: count CI-detected non-hermetic checks per week.

How to collect these metrics

  • Use CI BEP exports to compute cache-hit ratios. Bazel prints per-invocation process summaries that indicate remote cache hits; programmatic BEP ingestion gives more reliable metrics.
  • Push derived metrics to a telemetry system (Prometheus / Datadog) and create dashboards:
    • Histogram of build times (for P50/P95)
    • Time-series of remote cache hit rate
    • Weekly count of Build Doctor violations per team

Guardrails and change control

  • Use a cache-write role: only designated CI runners (and a small set of trusted service accounts) can write to the authoritative cache.
  • Add a cache clear and rollback playbook to respond to cache poisoning: snapshot the cache state and restore from a pre-poisoned snapshot if necessary.
  • Gate merges with Build Doctor findings: start with warnings and move to hard failure for core rules once false positives are low.

Developer onboarding

  • Ship a developer start.sh that sets up the repo-level .bazelrc and installs bazelisk to pin bazel versions.
  • Provide one-page runbook: git clone ... && ./start.sh && bazel build //:all --profile=./first.profile.gz so new hires produce a baseline profile that CI can compare to.
  • Add a lightweight VSCode/IDE recipe that reuses the same repo-level flags so the dev environment mirrors CI.

Practical checklists and runbooks for immediate action

Baseline measurement (week 0)

  1. Run a canonical CI build for the main branch for seven consecutive runs and collect:
    • bazel build --profile=ci.prof //...
    • BEP exports (--bes_results_url or --build_event_json_file)
  2. Compute baseline P95 build times and cache-hit rate from BEP/CI logs.

Setup remote cache and clients (week 1)

  1. Deploy a cache (e.g., bazel-remote, Buildbarn, or managed service).
  2. Put canonical flags into repo .bazelrc and a CI-only .bazelrc.ci.
  3. Configure CI to be the primary writer; developers set --remote_upload_local_results=false in their per-user bazelrc.

Ship the Build Doctor (week 2)

  1. Add collector hooks to CI to capture aquery, profile, and BEP.
  2. Run Analyzer on CI invocations; surface findings as PR comments and nightly reports.
  3. Begin triage for top findings (e.g., genrules with network calls, nonhermetic toolchains).

Pilot & expand (weeks 3–8)

  1. Pilot with three squads and run Build Doctor in PRs as info-only.
  2. Iterate on heuristics and reduce false positives.
  3. Convert high-confidence checks into gating rules.

Runbook snippet: respond to a cache-poison incident

  • Step 1: Identify corrupted outputs via BEP and Build Doctor reports.
  • Step 2: Quarantine suspect cache prefixes and flip CI to write to a fresh cache namespace.
  • Step 3: Roll back to last-known-good cache snapshot and re-run canonical CI builds to repopulate.

Quick rule: make CI the source of truth for cache writes during rollout and keep destructive cache administration actions auditable.

Sources

Hermeticity | Bazel - Definition of hermetic builds, benefits, and guidance on identifying non-hermetic behavior.

Remote Caching - Bazel Documentation - How Bazel stores action metadata and CAS blobs, flags like --remote_cache and --remote_download_outputs, and disk-cache options.

bazelbuild/remote-apis (GitHub) - The Remote Execution API specification and list of clients/servers implementing the protocol.

JSON Trace Profile | Bazel - --profile, bazel analyze-profile, and how to generate and inspect JSON trace profiles for critical-path analysis.

buildbuddy-io/buildbuddy (GitHub) - An example BEP and remote-cache ingestion solution that demonstrates how build event data and cache metrics can be surfaced to teams.

actions/cache (GitHub) - GitHub Actions cache action documentation and guidance for dependency caching in CI workflows.

The Bazel Query Reference / aquery - aquery/cquery usage and --output=jsonproto for machine-readable action graph inspection.

Treat the build as code, make CI the canonical actor for cache writes, and ship a Build Doctor that codifies the heuristics you already reach for in the hallway — those operational moves convert day-to-day build firefighting into measurable, automatable engineering work.

title: The Supabase Security Checklist to Run Before You Launch
description:
If you built something on Supabase with a lot of AI help and you're about to ship it, this checklist is for you. Supabase is secure by default in the sense that the tools are all there — but "vibe coding" tends to skip the boring parts, and the boring parts are exactly where data leaks live. Every item below is a one-line check plus the fix. Run them in order. It's maybe 30 minutes, and it's the difference between a launch and an incident.

1. RLS is enabled on every table in the public schema

The single most common Supabase mistake: a table exists, the anon key can reach it over PostgREST, and Row Level Security was never turned on. With RLS off, the table's GRANTs are the only gate — and because Supabase exposes the public schema to the anon role by default, that means anyone holding your (public) anon key can read it.

Check — run this in the SQL editor to list every public table with RLS off:

select tablename
from pg_tables
where schemaname = 'public'
  and rowsecurity = false;

Any rows returned are exposed. Fix each one:

alter table public.your_table enable row level security;

Enabling RLS with no policies is deny-all — a safe default. Now add the policy you actually want.

2. Every table has owner-scoped policies (not using (true))

Enabling RLS isn't enough if your policy waves everyone through. The classic leak is using (true) with no to clause. A SELECT policy like that is world-readable, anon included. Two facts to keep straight: a policy with no TO clause applies to all roles, and for anon, auth.uid() is NULL — so any check that compares against it silently fails open or closed depending on how you wrote it.

Check — list every policy and read it:

select tablename, policyname, cmd, roles, qual, with_check
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public';

qual is the USING expression; with_check is the WITH CHECK expression. A bare true in qual on a SELECT policy is world-readable. (It's only world-writable if a permissive INSERT/UPDATE/ALL policy also allows it — reads and writes are separate policies.) Fix with owner scoping:

-- users can only read their own rows
create policy "own rows are selectable"
on public.todos for select
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

-- and only insert rows they own
create policy "insert own rows"
on public.todos for insert
to authenticated
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Two things people get wrong here:

  • USING vs WITH CHECK. USING filters which existing rows a role can see, and which it may update or delete. WITH CHECK validates rows being written. An INSERT policy has WITH CHECK only — there are no existing rows to filter. UPDATE uses both. If you protect reads but forget WITH CHECK on writes, users can insert or update rows they shouldn't own.
  • A policy and a grant. A role needs a matching policy and the table GRANT. Multiple permissive policies OR together; restrictive policies AND. If access feels "too open," look for a second permissive policy widening things.

3. You're using the right key in the right place

Every Supabase project has two keys, and confusing them is catastrophic.

  • anon / publishable (role: anon, new format sb_publishable_...) is public by design. It's meant to ship in your browser bundle. It is not a secret, and it does not need rotating. RLS is what protects your data when this key is used.
  • service_role (role: service_role, new format sb_secret_...) is a server-only secret that bypasses RLS entirely — full read/write/delete across every table, plus Storage. It must never appear in a browser, a public repo, or a client config file.

Not sure which is which? Decode the JWT payload — the middle segment, base64URL — and read the role:

# paste your key; this prints the payload
echo 'PASTE_KEY' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null; echo

"role":"anon" is the browser key. "role":"service_role" must never leave your server.

The trap in frontend frameworks: any env var prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, or EXPO_PUBLIC_ is inlined into the client bundle at build time. That's correct and safe for the anon key and project URL. Putting the service_role key behind one of those prefixes ships your master key to every visitor. Check your env files:

grep -rE 'NEXT_PUBLIC_|VITE_|EXPO_PUBLIC_' .env* | grep -i 'service\|secret'

Anything returned is a bug. The service_role key belongs only in server-side env — API routes, edge functions, backend — never behind a public prefix.

4. No secrets in the repo — or in git history

Deleting a secret file doesn't help if you already committed it once. A committed secret lives in git history forever. AI tooling makes this worse by scattering config files people don't think to check.

Check the working tree, including the easy-to-miss ones:

grep -rnE 'service_role|sb_secret_|eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}' \
  . --include='*.json' --include='*.env*' --include='*.ts' 2>/dev/null

# the ones vibe-coders forget:
git ls-files | grep -E '\.env|\.claude/settings\.local\.json|\.cursor/mcp\.json'

.claude/settings.local.json, .cursor/mcp.json, and .env.local love to hold live keys and DB connection strings. Then check history:

git log --all --full-history -p -- '.env*' '**/mcp.json' '.claude/settings.local.json'

Fix, in this order:

  1. Rotate first. If a service_role key (or DB password) was ever committed, treat it as compromised. Regenerate it in the dashboard under Project Settings → API. Deleting the file does not un-leak it.
  2. Purge history with git filter-repo (or BFG), then force-push: 
git filter-repo --path .env.local --invert-paths
  1. Add the patterns to .gitignore so it can't recur: 
.env*
.claude/settings.local.json
.cursor/mcp.json

Order matters: rotate before you spend time rewriting history, because the old key is public the moment the repo is.

5. Storage buckets have real policies

Storage is Postgres too — access lives in storage.objects and obeys RLS. A public bucket means the files are readable by URL to anyone. A private bucket with no policy means no one can read it, which is usually not what you shipped either.

Check your buckets and their object policies:

select id, name, public from storage.buckets;

select policyname, cmd, roles, qual
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'storage' and tablename = 'objects';

Decide per bucket: are these files meant to be world-readable (avatars, marketing images) or private (invoices, uploads)? For an owner-scoped private bucket, a common pattern keys access to a per-user folder:

create policy "users read own folder"
on storage.objects for select
to authenticated
using (
  bucket_id = 'user-uploads'
  and (select auth.uid())::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]
);

6. Do a real self-audit before you trust the checklist

Reading policies by hand is exactly where over-confidence creeps in — a policy can look scoped and still leak because of a second permissive policy or a missing TO. So verify empirically.

I keep a small free repo for this: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. It's a minimal reproduction of the classic RLS leak plus read-only audit SQL you can paste into your own SQL editor to list tables without RLS, policies with no TO clause, and using (true) permissive policies in one shot. It changes nothing in your database — it just tells you where you stand.

The most honest test, though, is to hit your project the way an attacker would: with nothing but the public anon key.

curl "https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/rest/v1/your_table?select=*" \
  -H "apikey: <ANON_KEY>"

If that returns rows you expected to be private, RLS is not doing what you think. Fix it before launch, not after.

Run all six and you've closed the failure modes behind almost every "Supabase leaked my data" post-mortem: RLS off, using (true), the wrong key in the bundle, and a secret buried in git history.

If you'd rather not assemble this by hand, I packaged the whole thing — the audit queries, owner-scoped policy templates for the common table shapes, the Storage patterns, and a printable pre-launch checklist — into a $29 RLS Audit Kit. The free demo repo above is genuinely enough to secure your project; the kit just saves you the afternoon of writing the SQL yourself. Either way, ship it locked down.

title: Day 17/60: Testing HTTP handlers - Go Backend Engineering
description:
Day 17/60: Testing HTTP handlers

60 Day Go Backend Engineering Challenge

Today I focused on making testing http handlers feel like request flow design rather than just handler boilerplate. The strongest checkpoints were name the request boundary, validation step, and response contract before writing handler code, keep routing and middleware explicit enough that ownership of each concern is obvious, and make serialization and status codes follow the service contract rather than handler convenience.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was mixing validation, orchestration, and transport formatting in one handler. The day felt better once the service boundary stayed visible and each component had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next service still feels related to the same design idea. I also want to keep tracing one request path end to end because it exposes weak assumptions faster than a larger demo.

title: CorteXforge: Scenario-Based RF Dataset Generation on Real Testbeds
description:
arXiv:2610.26999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep learning for radio frequency (RF) signal analysis relies on large annotated datasets, yet synthetic datasets trade physical realism for controllability, while uncontrolled over-theair measurements offer realism but limited reproducibility. We present CorteXforge, a scenario-based framework for generating realistic and reproducible RF datasets on programmable software defined radio (SDR) testbeds. High-level RF scenarios are automatically translated into synchronized experiments executed on the SLICES-RI/CorteXlab platform, producing fully annotated Signal Metadata Format (SIGMF) datasets that capture hardware impairments and propagation effects. We validate CorteXforge through automatic modulation classification using ModForge, an over-the-air (OTA) dataset generated with the framework. Cross-domain experiments reveal a synthetic-to-real performance gap and show that synthetic pretraining remains beneficial for adaptation to OTA data. CorteXforge provides a practical foundation for reproducible RF dataset generation and future research on domain generalization.

title: Fixing "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" from dates in Next.js (tested repro, Next 16 + React 19.3)
description:
If your AI-built (or hand-built) Next.js app throws Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client in the browser, a common culprit is a date formatted with toLocaleDateString() or toLocaleString() and no locale or time zone. The server and your visitor's browser print different text, and React refuses to hydrate.

We reproduced it on a small synthetic app, applied the smallest fix, and checked it in headless Chrome set to a different locale and time zone than the server. Below: the exact error, the cause, the fix, how we verified it, and what we did not test.

The exact error

In development (next dev), from our headless-browser run:

Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client. This can happen if a SSR-ed Client Component used:

- A server/client branch `if (typeof window !== 'undefined')`.
- Variable input such as `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` which changes each time it's called.
- Date formatting in a user's locale which doesn't match the server.
...
<time id="placed" dateTime="2026-01-13T23:30:00Z">
+  14.1.2026
-  1/13/2026

The + line is what the browser rendered; the - line is what the server sent.

In production (next build + next start) the same problem shows only as:

Minified React error #418; visit https://react.dev/errors/418?args[]=text&args[]= for the full message

Older React/Next versions word this differently, for example "Text content does not match server-rendered HTML" (the title of the official Next.js page). We did not run those versions.

Versions we used

Item Version
Node.js 20.19.2
next 16.4.2 (Turbopack)
react / react-dom 19.3.1
Browser Google Chrome, headless, via playwright-core 1.64.1
Server time zone UTC
Browser locale / time zone de-DE / Europe/Berlin
OS Linux, single machine

Cause

Even a "use client" component is rendered twice: once on the server to make the HTML, and again in the browser to make it interactive ("hydration"). React requires the two results to match.

new Date(x).toLocaleDateString() with no arguments uses whatever locale and time zone the current machine has. Our server was in UTC with US English, so it printed 1/13/2026. The browser was in Berlin with German, where the same moment (2026-01-13T23:30:00Z) is already 14 January, so it printed 14.1.2026. Same code, two answers, hydration error.

The same thing happens with Date.now(), new Date(), Math.random(), or typeof window checks used during render. We reproduced only the locale/time-zone date case.

Smallest working fix

Pass an explicit locale and time zone, so the server and every browser format the date identically.

Before (hydration error): app/OrderRow.js 

"use client";
import { useState } from "react";

export default function OrderRow({ id, createdAt }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return (
    <div>
      <span>Order {id} placed </span>
      <time id="placed" dateTime={createdAt}>{new Date(createdAt).toLocaleDateString()}</time>
      <button onClick={() => setOpen(!open)}>{open ? "Hide" : "Details"}</button>
      {open && <p id="details">Synthetic details</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

After (no hydration error)

Change the <time> line to call formatDate(createdAt) and add this at the bottom of the file:

// Same locale and time zone on the server and in every browser,
// so the first browser render matches the server HTML.
function formatDate(iso) {
  return new Date(iso).toLocaleDateString("en-US", { timeZone: "UTC" });
}

Pick the locale and zone that fit your business (for example "en-US" and "America/Phoenix"). The trade-off: every visitor sees that same zone's date. If you need each visitor's own local date, the usual pattern is to render a neutral value first and switch to local formatting in useEffect after hydration. That is documented on the Next.js hydration page, but we did not test that variant.

Prompt for your AI coding tool 

My Next.js App Router app shows "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" in the browser console. Find every place that formats dates, times, numbers or prices during render using toLocaleString, toLocaleDateString, toLocaleTimeString or Intl.DateTimeFormat/Intl.NumberFormat without an explicit locale and timeZone, and every place that uses Date.now(), new Date() with no argument, or Math.random() during render. For the formatting cases, pass an explicit locale and timeZone (use "en-US" and "UTC" unless I tell you otherwise). For the clock/random cases, compute the value on the server and pass it as a prop, or set it in useEffect. Do not change anything else, and show me the diff.

Review the diff yourself. We did not test this prompt in any AI tool.

How we verified

All runs on 2026-10-20 on a small synthetic app. Server started with TZ=UTC; headless Chrome set to locale de-DE and time zone Europe/Berlin.

  1. Both builds pass: npx next build exited 0 for before and after. The bug does not show at build time.
  2. Before, production (next start): the browser threw Minified React error #418 ... args[]=text. Server HTML had 1/13/2026; after hydration the page showed 14.1.2026.
  3. Before, dev (next dev): the browser threw the full "Hydration failed ..." message with the + 14.1.2026 / - 1/13/2026 diff shown above.
  4. After, production and dev: no hydration error or React error in the console; server HTML and the hydrated page both showed 1/13/2026.
  5. Button still works: in every run, clicking "Details" showed the details paragraph.

Both runs also logged one unrelated 404 resource error, most likely the missing favicon; we did not confirm which file it was.

Not verified

To be upfront about the limits:

  • Other browsers (Firefox, Safari), real phones, and real visitors' settings; we simulated one locale/time zone in headless Chrome.
  • The useEffect "show local time after load" variant.
  • The other causes in the error message (Date.now(), Math.random(), typeof window, invalid HTML nesting, browser extensions). Same family, not reproduced.
  • Other Next.js/React/Node versions, including older "Text content does not match" wording, and the Pages Router.
  • Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare or other hosts (host server time zones may differ from ours).
  • Code generated by Cursor, Lovable, Bolt or v0; our app is hand-written and synthetic. We did not measure how often AI tools produce this pattern.
  • Whether the AI prompt produces a correct diff in any tool.

Quick troubleshooting

  • Only see "Minified React error #418": run npm run dev and open the page; the dev overlay shows the full message with the +/- diff that points to the exact text.
  • Error goes away on your machine but users report it: your computer and server may share a time zone. Test with a browser set to a different time zone or language.
  • The diff points to an attribute, not text, or you have a password manager/translate extension: try a private window with extensions off; extensions can cause this too (not tested by us).
  • Prices like 1,234.50 vs 1.234,50: same cause; pass a locale to toLocaleString / Intl.NumberFormat.

Security: no secrets are involved. Don't "fix" this by disabling server rendering for whole pages without understanding the SEO and performance cost.

The original guide, with the before/after files, is on The Agent Ledger: Hydration mismatch from date locale: Next.js fix.

AI disclosure: This article was written with the help of AI. The reproduction and the before/after browser runs described above were actually performed and checked against the logs before publishing.

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox
description:
A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

Snapshot restoration time now counts toward creation instead of the first operation. Creation is about 50 ms longer at p50, with a larger increase possible for uncached snapshots. The total time through the first operation remains the same.

This change applies automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. See the Sandbox.create() documentation for details.

title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
description:
arXiv:2610.27045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

title: Decomposed Relation Extraction from Aviation Accident Narratives: Evaluating Transformer-Based Safety Knowledge Discovery under Relational Sparsity
description:
arXiv:2610.27013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relation extraction from aviation accident narratives is challenging because genuine safety relations are sparse among possible concept pairs. This study evaluates a decomposed framework separating relation classification from concept identification. A benchmark of 300 National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) narratives containing 2,524 unique concept-text nodes was expanded into 21,038 ordered candidate pairs, with only 248 (1.18%) representing RESULTS_IN or CONTRIBUTES_TO relations. A TF-IDF Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) and weighted RoBERTa classifier were developed using an independent graph-annotated resource with hard-negative sampling and frozen before sealed evaluation. Development Macro-F1 scores of 0.4738 (SVM) and 0.4809 (RoBERTa) declined to 0.2741 and 0.2420 under exhaustive evaluation, with Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.0128 and 0.0197. False positives dominated: the SVM recovered 96 reference relations but generated 7,018 false positives, while RoBERTa recovered 125 but generated 9,824. Post-test diagnostics revealed overlapping RoBERTa confidence distributions and false positives even within valid relation-category directions. Complementary end-to-end SmolLM2 evaluation identified missed and unsupported relations alongside malformed outputs. These findings demonstrate that known concept endpoints do not guarantee reliable relation extraction and that sampled-negative development performance may poorly reflect exhaustive evaluation. Controlling false positives and managing candidate-space sparsity remain essential for aviation safety knowledge extraction.

title: Unknown Is Not Zero: Modeling Evidence in a Fan-Made Game Wiki
description:
Most game wikis I've used have the same failure mode: every cell is filled. Drop rate? A precise percentage. Pet speed? A precise number. Codes? A long list, all "working". Half of those numbers came from one video, a Discord screenshot, or a guess that got copied enough times to look like a fact.

While working on a fan guide for the Roblox game Ride A Pet, we took the opposite approach: a value is only shown if we can say where it came from and when. That sounds like an editorial rule, but it turned out to be mostly a data-modeling problem. Here's what that looks like in practice and what we'd do the same way again.

1. Give every fact an evidence status, not just a value

The eggs reference doesn't have one "source" column. Each row carries a label for how we know it:

  • Recorded screen: the name is visible in gameplay footage we can rewatch (e.g. an Aurora Egg growing at a ranch nest).
  • Reported: a dated third-party source says it (e.g. Blackhole and Cherub Eggs being searched for around the Giant Tree and a waterfall cave).
  • Official artwork: the name appears in promotional art (Flame Egg, Dragon Egg). That proves the name exists, not that it's buyable today.

The UI consequence is small but important: a "Reported" row reads differently from a "Recorded" row, and a reader can see why the page is hedging.

A sketch of the shape:

type Evidence =
  | { kind: "recorded"; source: string; timestamp: string }   // e.g. "SpaceQT", "2:57"
  | { kind: "reported"; source: string; checkedOn: string }   // ISO date
  | { kind: "official-art"; source: string }
  | { kind: "unknown" };

interface Fact<T> {
  value: T | null;          // null when unknown, never 0
  unit?: string;            // "$/s", "stock", ...
  evidence: Evidence;
}

2. null is not 0, and the UI should say so

The pets page has a line I like a lot: an unmeasured stat remains unknown; it should not be entered as zero.

That's a classic data bug wearing a game costume. If a comparison tool defaults an empty field to 0, every pet nobody measured looks terrible, and readers draw conclusions from your defaults. So:

  • Missing values render as "Unknown", not as 0 or -.
  • A number is always shown with its unit. The game shows a lightning label, a clover label, and a dollar-per-second label next to pets; a big number alone doesn't tell you whether it's movement, luck, or income.
  • Comparisons only happen between the same field on two pets.

The same idea shows up in the game-pass table. Four passes (Instant Hatch, Infinite Radar, Infinite Backpack, Auto Collect) have a known purpose from published guides, but the exact rules and prices aren't confirmed. Instead of guessing, the table has a column literally called "function detail still needed for a purchase decision". Writing down what you don't know is more useful than a confident row that's wrong.

3. Snapshots get a date and a source timestamp

Shop data in a live game is volatile. A recorded Gears shop frame shows Royal Radar marked Legendary at $20K with x3 stock, and Magic Radar out of stock. That's useful for recognizing the row, and useless as a price list a week later.

So every snapshot keeps:

  • the creator and video timestamp it came from (SpaceQT at 3:07, ItzVexo at 5:45),
  • a note that "$" is the game's own price display, not US dollars,
  • and a page-level "Checked" date plus a separate "last substantive edit" date.

Two dates sound redundant until you need them. "Checked" means "we re-read the sources on this day." "Edited" means "the content actually changed." Mixing them hides whether a page is stale or just stable.

4. The best page on the site is an empty list

Codes pages are where game wikis lose the most trust. The fan guide's answer is a page whose main content is: no verified codes, with a timestamp (24 September 2026, 03:07 UTC), the official page that was checked, and two dated third-party reports that also found none.

What makes it work as a data page is that "verified" has a definition. A code record needs four fields before it's published:

  1. the exact string,
  2. the announced reward,
  3. a redemption control that actually exists in the current game,
  4. a successful redemption check.

If any one is missing, the record doesn't exist yet. A failed attempt can't tell you whether a code expired, was mistyped or never existed, so on its own it doesn't move a row anywhere. You can see the whole structure on the Ride A Pet codes checklist; it's a nice reference if you're designing any "status" page where the honest answer is often "nothing yet".

5. Separate states that look the same

Another modeling lesson from the eggs page: a world listing, a radar target, and an egg in your basket are three different states, even though a player might call all of them "my egg". The page maps each screen to the one question it answers:

Screen Question
Track What is listed in the world?
Radar marker Where is this search's target?
Egg Basket What am I carrying?
Hatch screen What stage is this egg at?
Index: Eggs What have I collected?

If you've ever debugged an order system where "in cart", "paid" and "shipped" got collapsed into one boolean, this will feel familiar.

6. Keep personal state on the client, and say so

The egg-locations page has a small run-notes checklist: an optional target name (up to 60 characters) and seven checks, from "prepare a rideable pet" to "place it in a nest and confirm hatching". It's one checklist per browser, not synced to a game account, and the page states that the component doesn't send notes to analytics.

The "report a problem" form is similarly scoped: it sends the page address and a category (outdated, unclear, video problem, missing info), and nothing else. Writing the data boundary next to the control costs one sentence and removes a whole class of "what are you collecting?" questions.

What I'd take to any reference site

  • Model evidence explicitly. A value without a source is a draft.
  • Default to null, render "Unknown", keep units attached.
  • Store "checked" and "edited" dates separately.
  • Define what "verified" means as required fields, and let the empty state be a real, dated page.
  • Put the privacy boundary of a widget right next to the widget.

None of this needs a fancy stack. It's mostly refusing to let a table cell be filled just because the layout has room for it.

title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
description:
arXiv:2610.27605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg

title: FocusOVD: Geometric and Contextual Feature Refinement for Open-Vocabulary Small-Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27479v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to detect both seen and unseen categories by leveraging the semantic knowledge of vision-language models. However, existing methods often struggle with small objects due to insufficient preservation of high-resolution details, ineffective information aggregation across feature levels, and limited region-level discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose FocusOVD, an open-vocabulary object detector that enhances small-object representations without modifying the frozen VLM backbone. FocusOVD introduces three complementary components: a Reweighted Cross-scale Feature Fusion module, which learns normalized level-wise weights to adaptively balance shallow appearance details and deep semantic cues during feature pyramid aggregation; a Residual Pinwheel-shaped Gated Convolution module, which strengthens local geometric responses in high-resolution features; and a Residual Convolutional Gated Linear Unit module, which suppresses background-dominated activations and enhances RoI discriminability before prediction. Extensive experiments on COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD demonstrate the effectiveness of FocusOVD. On COCO-OVD, FocusOVD achieves a novel-category AP of 36.3%, outperforming CORA, UniDetector, and SAMP by 1.3%, 1.1%, and 1.5%, respectively; on LVIS-OVD, it achieves an overall AP of 33.7%, surpassing the strongest competing method by 0.6%. These results demonstrate the strong generalization ability of FocusOVD for open-vocabulary small-object detection.

title: Predictive Closure: A Set-Level Characterization of JEPA's Feature Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.27364v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), an encoder and a predictor are trained together to produce a representation that minimizes the error in predicting the representation of the next observation. Because the representations of both the current and the next observation are learned, it is unclear which features they will include. Earlier characterizations describe the features JEPA selects in terms of their individual predictability, raising the concern that unpredictable features, like a traffic light, will not be encoded into the representation. However, the prediction error is also affected by the relationships between features, e.g., the light's color helps predict whether the traffic will stop. We propose the predictive closure characterization, which accounts for these relationships. Based on a reformulation of the JEPA training objective, we show that selection depends on properties of feature sets. This view agrees with earlier works when features evolve independently, but makes new predictions when they do not, for instance that a feature like the traffic light can still be retained. We test this characterization in controlled experiments, which show that unpredictable features can become better represented when they help predict other features, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships can affect how well others are represented. We also demonstrate implications for steering feature selection: targeting one feature with an auxiliary objective, or supplying it to the predictor as side information, can strengthen the representation of another feature whose future values it helps predict, so steering can be indirect.

title: Node.js Broadcast Polls: Aggregate Votes into a Reconnect-Safe Interval Tally
description:
Short answer: keep vote ingestion separate from interval publication, assign every published tally a monotonic revision, and let a reconnecting viewer request the newest snapshot after the last revision it applied. For a live media poll, the least complex dependable design is one authoritative aggregator per poll, a durable vote log or database behind it, and disposable realtime connections in front of it. The five-second ticker is presentation cadence, not correctness.

The page that should fire is tally_revision_stalled, scoped to one poll and accompanied by the last accepted vote position, the last published revision, connected viewers, and publish age. The on-call does not need a bright chart saying connections are down 8%. They need to know whether votes are still being accepted while viewers are seeing an old result, because that is the split-brain experience an audience will notice during a broadcast.

This design also answers the Node.js implementation question without tying correctness to an Express process timer. Express can validate and accept a vote; a serialized poll worker owns aggregation; a scheduler asks that worker to publish; and the transport delivers a versioned snapshot. If a process restarts or a viewer reconnects, both resume from durable positions instead of guessing what happened during the gap.

What should page the on-call?

Imagine the alert arriving with only WebSocket disconnect rate high. That signal is noisy by construction: mobile viewers roam between networks, laptops sleep, and browsers close. A disconnect is an event, not yet an incident. The actionable failure is narrower: accepted votes have advanced beyond the input position represented by the most recent published tally, and that gap has remained open longer than the promised publication interval plus a small scheduling allowance.

The alert payload should make the failure legible without dashboard archaeology:

  • poll and broadcast identifiers
  • latest durable vote position
  • input position included in the latest tally
  • tally revision and publication timestamp
  • worker lease owner, if ownership is leased
  • publish attempts and delivery failures

Ask one blunt question: what page fired? If the answer is merely CPU, open connections, or queue depth, the team still has to infer user impact. Page on a sustained publication lag while votes are arriving. Ticket or graph the rest.

The earlier signal is accepted_position - published_position, measured per poll. Publication age alone cannot distinguish a quiet poll from a stuck worker. Vote throughput alone cannot show that viewers are stale. The position gap joins the two sides of the contract, so it should fire before audience reports arrive.

How should Node.js aggregate votes and publish each interval tally?

A vote command needs a stable identifier, poll identifier, selected option, and an authoritative position assigned when the command becomes durable. Reject choices outside the poll definition before appending. Deduplicate by the stable vote identifier according to the product's voting rule; a rule allowing one active choice per account requires an identity and replacement policy, while an anonymous multiple-choice poll has a different state transition. Do not pretend those policies are interchangeable.

The aggregator consumes commands in position order and produces a complete snapshot. A snapshot carries the poll identifier, counts, the highest included input position, and a monotonic tally revision. Complete snapshots cost more bytes than deltas, but they make reconnect recovery bounded: the client can replace local state after verifying that the revision is newer. Deltas demand gap detection and replay, and one lost increment can poison every later display. For a small option set, the snapshot trade-off is easier to operate.

That is the invariant.

The state transition below is Go because the important part is ownership and revision, not a framework API. A Node.js service should preserve the same single-writer semantics through one queue partition, a database transaction, or another explicit serialization boundary.

package tally

import (
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Vote struct {
    ID       string
    Option   string
    Position uint64
}

type Snapshot struct {
    PollID           string         `json:"pollId"`
    Revision         uint64         `json:"revision"`
    IncludedPosition uint64         `json:"includedPosition"`
    PublishedAt      time.Time      `json:"publishedAt"`
    Counts           map[string]int `json:"counts"`
}

type Aggregator struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    pollID   string
    allowed  map[string]bool
    seen     map[string]bool
    counts   map[string]int
    position uint64
    revision uint64
}

func (a *Aggregator) Apply(v Vote) error {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    if !a.allowed[v.Option] {
        return errors.New("unknown poll option")
    }
    if a.seen[v.ID] {
        return nil
    }
    if v.Position <= a.position {
        return errors.New("non-monotonic input position")
    }
    a.seen[v.ID] = true
    a.counts[v.Option]++
    a.position = v.Position
    return nil
}

func (a *Aggregator) Publish(now time.Time) Snapshot {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    a.revision++
    copied := make(map[string]int, len(a.counts))
    for option, count := range a.counts {
        copied[option] = count
    }
    return Snapshot{
        PollID: a.pollID, Revision: a.revision,
        IncludedPosition: a.position, PublishedAt: now.UTC(),
        Counts: copied,
    }
}

The mutex makes this sample internally coherent, but it does not make two processes one writer. That trap matters. If every Express replica runs its own interval and holds its own counts, viewers can receive alternating realities; adding a distributed transport spreads the contradiction faster. Elect or partition one owner for a poll, persist the consumed position and snapshot atomically, and treat publication as retryable delivery of already committed state.

Timers are not authority.

How does reconnect and backfill stay boring?

A client stores the greatest tally revision it has applied. On connection, it sends that revision as resume metadata. The server returns the current snapshot when the stored revision is absent or older; if the client already has the current revision, no tally transfer is necessary. A late message with a lower revision is discarded. An equal revision is idempotent. A higher revision replaces the displayed counts.

That rule is intentionally dull.

WebRTC data channels are one possible transport, and the WebRTC specification defines data channels for bidirectional arbitrary data, but transport choice does not remove the application-level revision contract. The same contract can sit above WebSocket, server-sent events for downstream delivery, or periodic HTTP retrieval. Keep vote submission on an authenticated request path with explicit acknowledgement rather than assuming a transient viewer connection proves a vote became durable.

Backfill does not need to mean replaying every five-second publication. A viewer wants the latest correct tally, so one current snapshot is enough unless the interface exposes historical movement. Analytics is different: if producers need the full time series, retain committed snapshots or derive them from the durable vote log under a stated retention policy. Do not overload reconnect recovery with an analytics requirement most viewers never use.

Incoming revision Client action Operational meaning
lower than applied discard delayed or reordered delivery
equal to applied ignore safely duplicate delivery
exactly one higher replace snapshot normal interval update
more than one higher replace and record a gap reconnect or missed delivery

Recording a gap is useful telemetry, but a gap between complete snapshots is not a reason to freeze the UI. The newer snapshot is authoritative. This distinction keeps recovery fast while leaving evidence for investigation.

Instrument the contract, then test failure

Start with four measurements: accepted vote position, aggregated position, committed tally revision, and delivered revision acknowledgements sampled from clients. The first three locate a server-side stall. The last reveals an audience segment that is connected but not advancing. Include broadcast and poll identifiers in logs, but avoid attaching voter identity to high-cardinality metrics.

Emit one structured record at each boundary using the same poll identifier and positions: vote committed, vote applied, snapshot committed, publication attempted, and client revision observed. This creates an alert-to-action trace. An operator can move backward from a stale client revision to a failed delivery, an unpublished committed snapshot, a stalled aggregator, or an ingestion gap without correlating unrelated panels by eye.

Test the trace with failures. Kill the aggregation owner immediately after snapshot commit and before delivery. Deliver revision 42 after revision 43. Submit the same vote identifier twice. Disconnect a client for three publication intervals, then resume it with revision 39 while the server holds 43. Restart an Express replica and verify that its local timer cannot create a second authority. Each test should assert displayed counts and positions, not merely that a callback ran.

Deployment needs the same discipline. Introduce revision fields as optional readers first, then publish them, then require them after old clients age out. During rollback, a previous server must not emit an unversioned message that a newer client mistakes for fresh state. Schema compatibility belongs in the incident plan because reconnects surface older client builds.

The threshold can create its own incident

A five-second publication interval should not translate into a page at 5.001 seconds. Runtime pauses, scheduler jitter, and temporary delivery retries exist, while a quiet poll can legitimately publish no changed tally if that behavior is documented. Define the alert around a sustained position gap across more than one expected publication opportunity, and validate it under the slowest supported deployment conditions. The exact allowance is a service objective decision, not a universal constant.

Too loose, and viewers watch stale numbers while votes accumulate. Too tight, and every brief pause wakes someone who can take no useful action; repeated false positives train the team to distrust the one page that matters. Track how often the alert corresponds to an actual breached viewer-freshness objective, then revise either the threshold or the instrumentation when it does not.

The operational conclusion is compact: make vote acceptance durable, serialize aggregation per poll, publish complete versioned snapshots, and recover reconnects by revision. The interval controls how often the picture changes. It must never be the only place the truth lives.

Further reading

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Issue

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.
  • Container-Optimized OS with containerd (cos_containerd) node pools on GKE versions 1.33 and earlier, 1.34 versions earlier than 1.34.6-gke.1154000, and 1.35 versions earlier than 1.35.3-gke.1389000.

Workaround: For cos_containerd node pools, upgrade the node pool to a version with the required kernel support (for example, 1.34.6-gke.1154000 or later, 1.35.3-gke.1389000 or later, or match the control plane). For ubuntu_containerd node pools, a fix is in progress. Alternatively, downgrade the control plane to a version earlier than 1.36.3-gke.1244000.

title: Joint Constraint Aggregation for Qualifier-Sensitive Retrieval-Augmented QA
description:
arXiv:2610.27114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented QA can fail even when the correct answer is in the retrieved evidence. This can happen when a competing answer satisfies some, but not all, of the question's requirements and is mentioned frequently in the retrieved documents, which can make it appear to be the best-supported answer. To test whether this retrieval skew actually affects the decision, we manipulate it directly: increasing the prevalence of passages that favor the competing answer makes the model more likely to select it. This points to a decision problem that candidate-level support alone cannot resolve. We therefore introduce Joint Constraint Aggregation (JCA), which compares candidates against the same question-derived requirements using the retrieved evidence. Across three evaluation settings and three instruction-tuned backbones, JCA improves overall accuracy, and its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer. Together, these results suggest that when partial matches and retrieval prominence pull models toward a competing answer, comparing candidates against the question's full requirements can make selection more reliable.

Announcement

On September 21st, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-4, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-4 within the next seven to 21 days. Key characteristics and requirements include:

  • Administrator only: Only users with the Gemini Enterprise Admin role (roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin or roles/discoveryengine.admin) can transfer agent ownership. Agent owners cannot transfer ownership unless they are also administrators.

title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.27103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

title: PRIMFLOW: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.27146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher's sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose \method, which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, \method learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that \method achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.

title: HierDTA: Hierarchical Structure-Aware Representation Learning for Drug--Target Affinity Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.27001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Drug--target affinity (DTA) prediction plays an important role in computer-aided drug discovery, where reliable computational models can help prioritize compound--protein pairs before experimental validation. A key challenge in DTA prediction is to effectively mine multi-level molecular information from drug structures while accurately modeling the binding-site environment of target proteins. To address these issues, we introduce HierDTA, a hierarchical structure-aware framework for DTA prediction. \textcolor{black}{HierDTA represents each drug as an atom--motif heterogeneous graph and introduces an augmentation module that propagates functional-motif semantics to the corresponding atoms. For proteins, kinase-domain structures are converted into residue interaction graphs. The resulting atom and residue representations are integrated using cross-attention to capture pair-specific relationships, while molecule fingerprints and pretrained ESM-2 embeddings provide complementary global information. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HierDTA achieves superior performance on the Davis dataset across all metrics and attains the highest \(r_m^2\) of 0.791 on KIBA. It also exhibits strong generalization under cold-start settings, particularly on KIBA, where MSE is reduced by 21.7\% in the unseen-protein scenario. Ablation study and interpretability analysis supported the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components.} Case studies further showed that HierDTA provided early enrichment of candidate bioactive compounds. These results indicate that HierDTA is an effective framework for affinity prediction and target-specific virtual screening.

title: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning for Dual-Use Concepts in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27490v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding).
  In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace.
  We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.
