title: Test Your Supabase RLS Policies Locally: A Free SQL Harness
description:
Row Level Security is the thing standing between your Supabase tables and the whole internet. Your anon key ships in the browser bundle on purpose — that's fine, that's by design, it isn't a secret — but it means any row your policies fail to lock down is a row a stranger can read with curl. So the real question isn't "do I have RLS on?" It's "do my policies actually do what I think they do?"

The good news: you can answer that in a local Postgres, deterministically, without touching production or hitting a rate limit. The trick is that Supabase's auth.uid() and the anon / authenticated roles are just Postgres primitives you can reproduce. This is a walkthrough of a small harness that impersonates anon and any logged-in user right in psql.

Everything here is packaged as a ready-to-run repo: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. Clone it if you'd rather run than copy-paste.

How Supabase auth maps to plain Postgres

Two facts unlock the whole thing:

  1. When PostgREST handles a request, it does SET ROLE anon (or authenticated) and stuffs the decoded JWT into a session setting called request.jwt.claims.
  2. auth.uid() is just a SQL function that reads sub out of those claims.

The service_role key is different in kind — it's a server secret that bypasses RLS entirely (full read, write, delete, plus Storage). It never belongs in a browser, a public repo, or a client config, and it's not what we're testing here. (Reflex check: a NEXT_PUBLIC_ / VITE_ / EXPO_PUBLIC_ prefix inlines a value straight into the client bundle — safe for the anon key and project URL, catastrophic for service_role. Tell the two keys apart by decoding the JWT's middle segment as base64URL: "role":"anon" vs "role":"service_role" — or by the newer sb_publishable_ vs sb_secret_ prefixes.) We're testing the role that is exposed: anon.

So to reproduce a request locally, we set the role and set the claims. That's it.

Step 1 — a minimal shim

If you run the full stack with supabase start, the auth schema and roles already exist and you can skip this. On a bare Postgres, create them:

-- roles PostgREST switches into
do $$
begin
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname = 'anon') then
    create role anon nologin;
  end if;
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname = 'authenticated') then
    create role authenticated nologin;
  end if;
end $$;

-- the same auth.uid() Supabase gives you
create schema if not exists auth;
create or replace function auth.uid() returns uuid
language sql stable
as $$
  select nullif(current_setting('request.jwt.claims', true)::jsonb ->> 'sub', '')::uuid
$$;

The true argument to current_setting means "return NULL instead of erroring if it's unset" — which is exactly the anonymous case. For anon, auth.uid() is NULL. Keep that in mind: any policy written as auth.uid() = user_id silently denies the anon user, because NULL = anything is never true. That's usually what you want.

Step 2 — a table with a policy to test 

create table if not exists documents (
  id       bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  owner_id uuid not null,
  title    text not null,
  body     text
);

alter table documents enable row level security;

-- owners can read their own rows
create policy "owner can read"
  on documents for select
  to authenticated
  using (auth.uid() = owner_id);

Note the to authenticated. A policy with no TO clause applies to all roles, including anon — a common way to leak data by accident. Being explicit about the role is half the battle.

Step 3 — impersonate anon and a real user

Wrap each check in a transaction with SET LOCAL so the role and claims reset automatically on ROLLBACK. That keeps tests isolated and non-destructive.

-- as an anonymous visitor (no JWT)
begin;
  set local role anon;
  select count(*) as anon_sees from documents;
rollback;

-- as a specific logged-in user
begin;
  select set_config(
    'request.jwt.claims',
    json_build_object(
      'sub',  '11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111',
      'role', 'authenticated'
    )::text,
    true                       -- is_local: scoped to this transaction
  );
  set local role authenticated;
  select id, title from documents;      -- only their rows
rollback;

Set the claims before switching role, then switch. Now you can assert concrete numbers. With the policy above, anon_sees should be 0, and the authenticated block should return only rows whose owner_id matches that sub. If anon_sees is anything but zero, you have a leak — go look at your TO clauses and USING expressions.

The two mistakes worth internalizing

USING vs WITH CHECK are not interchangeable. USING decides which existing rows a role can see, and which it's allowed to scan for UPDATE / DELETE. WITH CHECK validates the new row values on INSERT / UPDATE. INSERT policies have WITH CHECK only. Getting these backwards is how people write an "owners only" update policy whose USING guards the old row but whose missing WITH CHECK lets anyone reassign a row to themselves.

USING (true) means world-readable for SELECT. A SELECT policy with USING (true) simply lets everyone read — genuinely fine for a public catalog. It only becomes a write hole if a permissive INSERT / UPDATE / ALL policy also opens that path. Permissive policies OR together, so one stray using(true) with no TO widens access to anon in whatever command it targets. And a role needs both a matching policy and the table GRANT: RLS with the grant missing fails closed, while a grant on a table with RLS still disabled fails wide open.

Step 4 — audit the whole schema at once

Before you write per-table tests, get a bird's-eye view. Two read-only queries surface most real problems.

Tables where RLS is off entirely:

select n.nspname as schema, c.relname as table
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind = 'r'
  and not c.relrowsecurity;

Every policy, with the fields that matter — roles, cmd, and the actual expressions:

select tablename,
       policyname,
       roles,          -- {public} = applies to anon too
       cmd,            -- SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / ALL
       qual       as using_expr,
       with_check as check_expr
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
order by tablename, cmd;

Read it like a reviewer: any row where roles is {public} and using_expr is true on a table with private data is a red flag. Any table in the first query's output that isn't meant to be fully public is a bigger one. The demo repo ships this audit SQL as a single file plus a seeded leak you can watch the harness catch — a fast way to confirm your setup works before you point it at your own schema.

Wire it into CI

Because the whole thing is SQL against a throwaway database, it runs anywhere Postgres does. A pg_prove file or even a plain script that fails when anon_sees > 0 will do:

psql "$DATABASE_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f test/rls_anon_readonly.sql

Run it against supabase db reset output on every push. Now a policy regression breaks the build instead of leaking rows in production.

Where to go from here

You now have a repeatable way to prove — not hope — that anon sees exactly what you intend. Clone github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo, run the audit against your schema, and fix whatever the pg_policies query lights up.

If you'd rather not hand-roll the assertions, I keep a small RLS Audit Kit ($29) — the same harness plus a checklist of per-command policy tests (insert-as-other-user, update-reassignment, delete-scope) and copy-paste pg_prove cases. Entirely optional; the repo above is enough to secure your project today. Either way, go run the anon check before you ship.

title: TIL: How to Record a Response File for GBase Database Silent Installation
description:
Writing a response file manually for GBase Database(GBase 8s) can be error-prone. A misspelled parameter or an unsupported value may cause problems when you automate the installation.

Fortunately, the installer can record your choices during an interactive installation and save them to a response file.

Record Your Installation Choices

Run the following command from the directory containing the installer:

./ids_install -r /opt/bundle.properties

Follow the interactive installation prompts as usual. The installer records the supported installation settings in /opt/bundle.properties, which you can then review and reuse for silent installation.

Depending on the installer version, the recorded settings may include the installation directory, selected components, and other installation options.

Why Record Instead of Starting from Scratch?

This approach offers three practical benefits.

1. Fewer manual errors

You don't have to guess every parameter name or construct the entire response file from memory.

2. A useful starting point

The response file is generated from an actual installation workflow, giving you a practical configuration to review before automating deployment.

3. Easier customization

After recording the file, you can inspect it and adjust the settings required for your target environment.

One important caveat: a recorded response file is not automatically guaranteed to work on every server. Review the parameters, confirm any required license-acceptance setting, and check for paths or options that differ between environments.

A Practical Workflow for GBase Database

For batch deployment of GBase Database(GBase 8s), use this sequence:

  1. Record a representative interactive installation.
  2. Review the generated response file.
  3. Adjust and validate the required parameters.
  4. Test silent installation on a single target machine.
  5. Reuse the validated configuration for additional servers.

The key idea is simple: record first, review second, automate third.

This workflow reduces unnecessary manual editing and provides a more reliable starting point for repeatable database deployment.

Have you tried recording an installation response file, or do you usually build yours manually?

title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
description:
arXiv:2610.27304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.

title: Architectural Breakdown: Integrating ByteDance deer-flow: Vector Memory Persistence Patterns for Lon
Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
description:
arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

title: A Hybrid TFT-NBEATS Framework for Robust Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.27155v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate multi-horizon photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for grid stability, energy scheduling, and the efficient operation of PVbatterygrid systems. However, existing models often fail to jointly capture short-term variability and long-term temporal patterns, while lacking unified multi-horizon capability and interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel hybrid deep learning framework that integrates a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and N-BEATS within an attention-based fusion architecture. The proposed model leverages TFT to learn short-term temporal dependencies and dynamic feature importance, while N-BEATS captures long-term trend and seasonal components through interpretable basis decomposition. An adaptive attention mechanism dynamically fuses both branches, enabling balanced multi-scale learning. The framework simultaneously generates forecasts for 30-minute, 2-hour, 6-hour, 12-hour, and 24-hour horizons within a single unified pipeline. The model is evaluated using multi-year real-world datasets from the Desert Knowledge Australia Solar Centre (DKASC). Experimental results demonstrate superior performance over statistical, machine learning, and deep learning baselines. The proposed model achieves RMSE values of 42.35, 46.27, 52.29, and 48.11 across the 20162017, 2023, 2024, and 20252026 datasets, respectively, corresponding to a 3540% reduction compared to the best baseline (TFT). Additionally, MAPE remains below 5% across all datasets, indicating high predictive accuracy and stability. The model also provides interpretability through attention visualization and trendseasonality decomposition, and is deployed on a cloud-based platform for real-time forecasting. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework is robust, interpretable, and suitable for practical renewable energy applications.

title: Unsupervised Tool Evolution for Coding Agents in Data-Lake Analytics
description:
arXiv:2610.27327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents can answer analytical questions over a data lake by discovering, cleaning, and joining the relevant data. However, they discard this work after each question and redo it from scratch for the next one. Tool evolution, which automatically builds and refines reusable tools across tasks, is a natural fit for this repetition. Since a ground-truth label for a data-lake question requires an expert to solve it first, we consider the unsupervised setting. We propose TEAL (Tool Evolution for Analytics over data Lakes), which evolves a library of tools and usage skills for a given Worker agent without labels. Two agents propose tools from complementary evidence, an Explorer from the data lake itself and a Critic from Worker trajectories. A proposed change is kept only if the Worker adopts the tool on a rerun without extra steps and any changed answer is supported by trajectory evidence. We also introduce TEAL-Q, which generates synthetic questions for tool evolution when real ones are unavailable. We evaluate on KramaBench and LakeQA with four Worker LLMs under step budgets, which cap the number of steps the Worker may take per question. With a tight budget of 10 or 15 steps, TEAL improves every Worker on both benchmarks, lifting Sonnet-5 at 15 steps by 9.3 points on KramaBench and 21.7 points on LakeQA. A tighter budget also yields better feedback for evolution. For example, Sonnet-5's LakeQA library evolved at 20 steps and deployed unchanged at 30 steps scores 68.3, above both the baseline (59.6) and a library evolved directly at 30 steps (64.2). Additionally, a library evolved on synthetic questions performs comparably to one evolved on real questions. These results show that useful tools can be evolved without labels, and hopefully inspire future work on what to evolve and how to obtain feedback in unsupervised agent evolution.

title: TokenFlow: Latent Token Rectified Flow Matching for 3D Point Cloud Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.27418v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D point clouds generation requires capturing both part-level layout and surface detail while preserving permutation equivariance. Existing latent generative models often encode an entire shape into a single vector, which limits their ability to retain part-level structure. We propose TokenFlow, a hierarchical flow matching framework that represents each shape as a set of latent tokens and couples a rectified flow over these tokens with a conditional flow over points. A bottleneck of $M \ll N$ learnable tokens aggregates global context through cross-attention at $O(NM)$ cost. On ShapeNet, TokenFlow achieves the best MMD and coverage across airplane, car, and chair, while obtaining 1-NNA comparable to the strongest baselines. On ModelNet, its learned latent set reaches the best reported linear-evaluation accuracy on ModelNet10. These results show that representing a shape as a set of latent tokens, aggregated at $O(NM)$ cost, provides an effective representation for 3D point cloud generation.

title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27406v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: We're fed up with Rust's borrow checker. It's time to break free.
description:
I like Rust. I also dread the moment the borrow checker says no and the compiler refuses to
explain what it assumed.

That is not a complaint about competence. Rust's borrow checker is one of the most valuable
things to happen to systems programming. It is a complaint about posture: the compiler stands
outside your program, announces a verdict, and the burden of proof lands on you. When the verdict
is wrong, there is often no receipt to inspect.

We built Loment around a different posture. It keeps the
checks; it moves the burden. This post is about what that means precisely, because "we removed the
borrow checker" would be a lie, and the interesting part is not the removal.

What Loment keeps

Loment is a systems language with a Rust-flavoured surface. It still checks the ownership
mistakes that matter most:

  • use after move (E006),
  • a mutable borrow alongside another borrow (E007),
  • a dangling reference (E012).

It also adds capability domains (capability disk[0..4] plus guard), compiles to a native
ELF/PE artifact with no runtime by default, and has two implementations — a Python reference and
a self-hosted one — that must emit byte-identical IR.

What it does not do is pretend to be Rust's borrow checker. The boundary is written down in
the repository: it proves three things and explicitly does not prove four others (no lifetimes, no
cross-function reasoning, no field-level moves, no branch-sensitive move sets). Keep that in mind
for the rest of this post.

From verdict to receipt

The change is a seventh choose dimension called LSPE — Loment Safety Police Espace. It does
not change any verdict. It changes what a verdict leaves behind.

With lspe_open_admin (the default), every allowance is recorded in the artifact's Potato v16
ledger: the site, the obligation, the evidence, and what is still unproved. With
lspe_close_admin, the recording is turned off; the LMS, runtime and capability decisions are
unchanged. The audit is not a second checker bolted on top — it is a ledger of the compiler's own
decisions, answerable offline.

The design document puts it more bluntly than I can:

Rust's borrow checker is a god. LSPE is a shop assistant.

A god stands outside the transaction and says "no". An assistant stands inside it, has to name the
price, and gives you a receipt. Concretely, LSPE has three outcomes instead of two:

  • PROVED — here is the evidence;
  • UNDECIDED — here is the site where my proof has a hole;
  • REFUTED — here is a counterexample, so this is a hard no.

"Undecided" is a first-class result. In strict mode it becomes E034; the ledger's own consistency
failures are E035–E037. The point is not that the compiler is always right. The point is that when
it is wrong, you can point at the site and the obligation instead of arguing with a verdict.

"Gentle" is a measurable claim

It is easy to say a checker is friendlier. We tried to make it falsifiable:

  1. Same verdicts. Compile the same corpus with the audit open and closed: the set of decisions is identical. The audit changes the ledger, not the language.
  2. No silent permit. Every allow has a source, or an explicitly recorded assumption. An allow with neither is an error in the ledger.
  3. No overclaiming. LSPE does not claim to prove more than Rust. What it adds is accountability, not completeness. The remaining cases are UNDECIDED and labeled.

That is the sense in which it is "gentler with nearly the same safety": not that it catches
everything Rust catches, but that the same checks no longer arrive as an unaccountable verdict.

Loment also has a memory-safety ladder, lms, with seven levels and four tiers
(lms_full, lms_forensic_admin, lms_daily_admin, lms_manage_only_admin). The default is
full; writing a lower tier is a downgrade and carries _admin. The literal-out-of-range check is
E028; use-after-free is E029.

What it looks like

The defaults, written out:

module demo
choose runtime
choose lms_full
choose lspe_open_admin

capability disk_slots : disk[0..4] revocable

fn write_slot(slot: u32) -> u32 {
    guard disk_slots(slot);
    return slot;
}

fn _start() {
    let xs: [u32; 3] = [1, 2, 3];
    let i: u32 = 5;
    if i < 3 {
        xs[i] = 7;          // a runtime index: you guard it, the language does not guess
    }
    syscall4(60, 0, 0, 0);
}

Two details matter here. guard bounds the index, not the subject — it is not authorization.
And the array write is still your responsibility: Loment refuses a literal out-of-range index
at compile time (E028), but a runtime index is not silently checked.

What this does not mean

I would rather say this before the comments do:

  • Loment is early. 0.1.5 is the release where LSPE lands; the packaged front end is still being finished. Do not rewrite your service in it this weekend.
  • It is not Rust. The borrow checking is a subset. No lifetimes, no cross-function reasoning, no field-level moves, no branch-sensitive move sets.
  • "No receipt" is not the same as "no bug". LSPE records the compiler's decisions; it does not make the compiler omniscient.
  • Defaults are not free. lms_full is the default and it changes the emitted artifact (inline bounds checks on alloc(<const>)-derived accesses). That exception is documented, not hidden.
  • The benchmark is a pilot. We measured an LLM agent writing Loment from the guide alone: three tasks, one attempt each, Rust and Python as controls. It is a direction, not a confidence interval.

The reason I care about the receipt is not abstract. Rust's own tracker has a soundness bug
(#164250) where an obligation was not rechecked after substitution, and it stayed invisible for
years — not because Rust's team is careless, but because a verdict-only compiler leaves nothing
to audit when the verdict is wrong. LSPE's answer to that shape is a record with a site id
(Q004 stale_wf), readable offline. That is the part I want other language designers to steal,
whether or not they like Loment.

Try it, then tell us where the receipt is wrong

  • Source: https://github.com/Loment-Lang/Loment

We are not asking you to believe the slogan. We are asking you to compile something, read the
ledger, and tell us which line is wrong. That is the whole point of moving the burden.

Disclosure: I'm one of Loment's authors. This draft was prepared with an AI assistant and
reviewed before publishing.

title: Partner commissions on serverless Node and Postgres, with no server to run
description:
I run a small software company in Malaysia. We sell through referral partners and agents, and we pay them a share of what customers pay, not once, but for as long as the customer keeps paying.

That sounds simple until you try to do it. A customer pays on the 3rd. You promise the partner 25%, but only after a 30-day hold, in case the customer asks for a refund. In month 13 the rate drops to 20%. A refund arrives for half of one payment. The partner quits, and now you owe their unpaid commission to the house. Every one of those is a place where money can be wrong.

Of course, there are many existing tools in the market that does this out of the box, some even self-hosted. However, most tools that do this want their own server. A hosted CRM, or a self-hosted one with a Docker container, a background worker and a queue. We run on a serverless stack: Next.js functions on Vercel and one Postgres database. There is no machine of ours that stays switched on, and we felt like the cost vs benefit doesn't justify maintaining one just to pay partners.

Since we could not find a tool that did this and ran as a library inside our stack, we built one. It is called Tandem CRM, it is open source (MIT), and this post is about how it works and what I learned.

The idea: a CRM that is just a library and a schema

Tandem is an npm package plus a set of SQL migrations. You point it at a Postgres database you already have, and it adds a tandem schema with leads, agents, partners, commissions and payouts. There is no separate server and no container to run.

That is the part that matters for serverless. Each call is just a function that opens a database connection, does its work inside one transaction, and returns. Nothing holds state in memory between requests, so it does not care how many function instances you have or how often they start and stop. The state lives in Postgres, and Postgres is what keeps two requests from stepping on each other: the code locks the lead's row before it writes, so two payment webhooks arriving at the same moment cannot both win. Hold periods and releases are plain SQL, so a scheduled job (a cron route on Vercel works, and is how we do it) calls one function, release_due_commissions(), and that is the only background work there is.

npm install tandem-crm
npx tandem-crm init --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" --sample-data

init applies the migrations, runs a health check, and can seed a small demo workspace so you have something to look at.

Every payment gets its own commission line

Here is a lead being created and a payment being recorded. Everything goes through one shared writer, so the rules apply the same way whether the call comes from your app, a webhook or the admin screen.

import { defineTandemConfig } from "tandem-crm";
import { createTandemPool, withTandemSession, createLead, recordPayment } from "tandem-crm/db";

const pool = createTandemPool(process.env.DATABASE_URL);

const config = defineTandemConfig({
  commission: {
    holdDays: 30,
    rateSchedule: [
      { fromMonth: 0, basisPoints: 2500 },   // 25% for the first year
      { fromMonth: 12, basisPoints: 2000 },  // 20% after that
    ],
  },
});

const { leadId } = await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  createLead(client, {
    workspaceId,
    companyName: "Aman Logistics",
    contactPhone: "+60 12-345 6789",
    qualificationMetric: 8,
    productTag: "starter",
    partnerId: "rajesh",
    config,
    source: "signup",
    sourceEventId: "signup-1042",
  })
);

await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  recordPayment(client, {
    workspaceId,
    leadId,
    config,
    source: "stripe",
    payment: {
      paymentId: "inv_001",
      amountMinor: 30000,          // RM300.00, always whole sen
      currency: "MYR",
      confirmedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
    partnerStatus: async (id) => ({ id, active: true }),
  })
);

Each payment produces one commission line with its own rate and its own 30-day hold. A scheduled job releases lines once they are due. If a refund comes in, the matching line is reduced or clawed back. If a partner is deactivated, their unpaid lines move to a house account. That policy is something you configure, not something we decide for you. We just decided to set ours up this way.

Why events

Tandem stores what happened, not just the current state. A lead is a stream of events: created, qualified, converted, paid, refunded. The current status is calculated by replaying them.

The practical benefit is that every decision is saved in the event it was made in. The rate that applied, the qualification result, who the beneficiary was. If you change your commission settings next year, old payments do not quietly change. And when a partner asks "why did I get this amount?", you can answer with the actual history.

Row-level security, so one tenant cannot read another

Tandem uses Postgres row-level security. Every query runs as a role called authenticated, and every row belongs to a workspace. Agents can only append three kinds of event (lead.lost, lead.stage_changed, conversion.confirmed). Anything that moves money needs an owner or admin, and the database enforces it, not just the application code.

The one setup step people trip on: the role you connect with must be able to grant authenticated. init explains this clearly if it cannot.

What two audits found

I am not a programmer by training, and I built this with quite a bit of help from AI and learning each step of the way (I make sure I understand at least fundamentally what the code is supposed to do). That is exactly why I did not want to trust it on my own. I had two independent audits run over the money code, and I wrote tests against a real Postgres instead of mocks.

The audits found real problems. A scheduled release job that could crash part way through. A case where a payment could silently produce no commission at all. Writes that were not safe if two requests arrived at the same moment. All of them are fixed, and each fix has a test that fails without it.

The rules we now follow for anything that touches money:

  • Money is integer minor units. No floating point anywhere.
  • Every write to a lead locks the lead row first, replays the history plus the new events, and only then inserts.
  • Retrying a request with the same source id returns the existing result and never creates a duplicate.
  • A fix needs a test that fails without it.

Where it is tested

The test suites run against real Postgres 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 in CI, on Node 20 and 22, and also as a limited, non-superuser admin account, which is what most managed hosts give you. I have also run it by hand on Neon, Supabase, Layerbase and Aiven. Aiven needs its own certificate file, and the docs say how.

What it is not (yet)

It is early and pre-1.0, and it has not been proven at scale. It has run the partner commission ledger for our own product, Utuh, since 20 October 2026, and I checked it end to end on the live Stripe account, with a real card payment from an outside account and a real refund. No outside developers use the package yet, and we still pay partners by hand, by bank transfer. It is one Postgres and an append-only events table, which should be fine for small and medium use, but I have not load tested it.

Try it, and tell me what breaks

  • Repo: https://github.com/angkutdigital/tandem-crm
  • Docs: https://tandemcrm.dev

The most useful thing you can do is run it against your own Postgres host and open a "Postgres host report" issue, whether it worked or not. If a guide confused you, that is a bug in the guide, and I would like to know.

title: Automated Brick Schema Knowledge Graph Completion Across Buildings
description:
arXiv:2610.27339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Brick schema represents building equipment, sensors, spaces, and the relationships between them as typed, multi-relational graphs, providing machine-readable metadata that supports generalizable control applications. Current methods for producing complete Brick models require extensive manual examination of building schematics and point lists. We observe that as Brick models are knowledge graphs, inferring missing relations is naturally posed as a knowledge graph completion problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of knowledge graph completion to Brick model generation. We compare three methods, gradient-boosted trees, Pairwise Brick Relation Ranking, and CompGCN, on the relations feeds, hasPart, and hasPoint, which account for the majority of the schematic-reading work in building a Brick model by hand. Models are evaluated on held-out MORTAR buildings and out-of-distribution Kaggle and Building Time Series data. Although CompGCN is the strongest performer on held-out buildings under metrics resistant to class imbalance, leading macro-F1 and AUPRC, no method generalizes uniformly across datasets or relations.

title: Predicting Linear Relational Decodability Without the Relation
description:
arXiv:2610.27241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear relational embeddings (LREs) approximate a language model's subject-to-object mapping with an affine function. Their faithfulness varies enormously across relations, from near zero for person_father to the ceiling for country_capital_city. We investigate the factors that contribute to this variation and demonstrate that it can be significantly predicted from a readout that is not aware of the underlying relation. To do so, we propose a novel form of the Jacobian lens, the entity lens. Whereas the Jacobian lens is estimated across all tokens and concepts, the entity lens EL_t is trained to predict what the model will output for an entity of type t under the neutral prompt "{} is known for"; e.g., we train ELs for countries and persons. After estimating an entity lens, we measure how highly it ranks the model's answer for a relation without using any relation-specific information in estimation and prediction. Across 28 relations of the LRE dataset on Olmo-3-7B this relation-agnostic score correlates with LRE faithfulness at \rho = 0.7355 (p < .01). This suggests that linear decodability is largely a property of what a subject's representation already carries, rather than of the relation being decoded. Moving the unit of analysis from the relation to the individual fact, we conclude that new relation datasets and analysis methods are needed to address several problems in existing datasets, most prominently semantically weak first tokens (e.g., most predicted universities' first token is "University") and reference competition (e.g., the LLM confuses obscure actor names with competing non-actor entities that have the same last name). Our full pipeline is available at https://github.com/jonasrohw/entity-lens

title: Reproducing Olmo 3 7B Pre-training in MaxText: case study of large scale training on TPUs
description: The MaxText team successfully reproduced Ai2’s Olmo 3 7B language model from scratch on Google Cloud TPUs using JAX/XLA, precisely matching the original PyTorch-on-GPU reference across pre-training and mid-training stages on all held-out evaluations. The implementation achieved up to 57.4% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) and demonstrated robust infrastructure portability by surviving mid-run cluster resizes and cross-generation TPU shifts without requiring recipe alterations. Crucially, the exercise proved the necessity of comprehensive held-out validation by catching a silent data-loader memorization bug that artificially depressed training loss and would have otherwise faked a performance win.

title: Day 13/75: HashMap patterns in Java - Java DSA
description:
Day 13/75: HashMap patterns in Java

75 Day DSA in Java Challenge

Today I focused on using a stable invariant so hashmap patterns in java feels like a process instead of a trick. The strongest checkpoints were name the exact window, prefix, or pointer region each variable owns, reuse prior work instead of recomputing the same range each iteration, and test boundary sizes first because they expose weak invariants quickly.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was moving boundaries before stating what region they actually represent. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests. title: The Router Already Knows
description:
arXiv:2610.27421v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models already make a sparse choice for every token: which experts should process it. We ask whether a sparse dictionary should reuse that choice. NR-SAE gives each routed expert a small dictionary and opens only those the frozen router selects. At block 15 of Gemma 4 26B-A4B, after ten million C4 training tokens and across three seeds, the expert-aligned autoencoder explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs on a fixed evaluation capture. A rank-addressed control with the same parameters but sixteen times as many candidates reaches 0.481, a candidate-matched control 0.458, and an architecture-matched control with randomized expert identity 0.387. A transcoder variant also leads all three controls: 0.432, against 0.347, 0.371, and 0.118. Part of this advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert names the subspace. How much it explains, we have not measured. At this layer and budget, the router already knows something a dictionary would otherwise have to learn. Our implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.

title: Stop Storing Tracking Numbers as Numbers: a float64 Bug Hiding in Your CSV Pipeline
description:
If any part of your stack reads a shipping CSV, this one is probably already in your data and nobody has noticed. A tracking number is a label, but almost every tool in the chain is happy to treat a long run of digits as a quantity - and quantities get rounded.

The failure, in two shapes 

9214490424550000386431   ->  9.2144904245500004E+21
9400150206217912         ->  9400150206217910

The first is loud. The second is the one that costs you a week: same length, no exponent, no warning - the final digit is now a zero. Every downstream lookup returns "not found" for parcels that are completely fine, and the first instinct is to blame the carrier's API.

Why

IEEE-754 double precision carries about 15-17 significant decimal digits. Look at what common formats need:

Format Length All digits? Survives a float?
USPS IMpb 22 yes no
FedEx Ground 15 yes borderline
DPD parcel number 14 yes yes, but still reformatted
UPS 1Z + 16 18 chars no safe
S10 postal (AA999999999CC) 13 chars no safe

The pattern that matters: the formats that survive are the ones containing letters, because a letter forces the value to stay a string. The all-digit formats are the exposed ones - and that includes the single most common barcode in the world, the 22-digit USPS IMpb.

This is also why the bug feels intermittent. A column of 1Z... numbers round-trips perfectly, someone concludes the pipeline is fine, and then the first USPS batch of the month is silently mangled.

In code

Pandas will do this to you by default:

# wrong - pandas infers int64/float64 and your 22-digit numbers are gone
df = pd.read_csv("shipments.csv")

# right - say it explicitly
df = pd.read_csv("shipments.csv", dtype={"tracking_number": "string"})

# or, when you do not want to name every column
df = pd.read_csv("shipments.csv", dtype=str)

The same rule in the other languages:

  • JS/TS: never Number(tn) or parseInt(tn). A 22-digit value is already past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991, 16 digits), so the damage happens before you can validate it. If you need a numeric type, use BigInt - but you almost never do, because you never do arithmetic on a tracking number.
  • SQL: VARCHAR, not BIGINT. Leading zeros are real and significant in several postal formats, and a numeric column eats them without comment.
  • JSON: quote it. An unquoted 22-digit literal is a double in most parsers.
  • Excel/Sheets exports: format the column as Text before the first paste. Formatting a column that already holds broken values does not recover the digits - that information is gone, not hidden.

Validating a column you inherited

Cheapest checks first:

s = df["tracking_number"].astype("string")

s.str.contains("E+", regex=False).sum()   # loud corruption
s.str.len().value_counts()                # a USPS column should be all 22s
s.str[-1].value_counts(normalize=True)    # an implausible pile of "0" = rounding

That last one is the useful one. If a column has the right lengths but an unreasonable share of values ending in 0, you are looking at rounding, not coincidence.

The validation rule that actually helps

Do not validate tracking numbers with a numeric range or a length-only check. Check the shape: a letter-anchored prefix plus a fixed length is both cheap and specific. ^1Z[0-9A-Z]{16}$ identifies UPS exactly. ^[A-Z]{2}\d{9}[A-Z]{2}$ is the S10 international postal form, and the last two letters are the issuing country - not the destination, which is a different and equally common mix-up.

And if the number survives shape validation but returns nothing, check whether the label was merely created before you conclude anything is lost - "we have the order details but not the parcel" is a legitimate state, not an error.

Written by the team behind 24hTrack, a free package tracker for 3,200+ carriers - paste any tracking number and the carrier is detected automatically, no sign-up. Shape and format notes come from the carrier formats we maintain at package-tracking-guide (CC BY 4.0).

title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.27043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. Task 1 (cheque extraction) and Task 2 (Mintaka QA with pinned evidence across nine languages and nine model-effort configurations) test whether accuracy and effort settings transfer; Task 3 (FinanceBench pilot, 50 items over SEC 10-K filings in four languages) validates whether these patterns generalise to financial content. Accuracy reusability is broadly confirmed: Gemini 3.5 Flash achieves 95.2-97.6% extraction accuracy across prompt languages, and FinanceBench per-language means span 5.8pp (77.1-82.9%), though the language-difficulty ranking reverses between domains (Hindi is worst on Mintaka, best on FinanceBench at 82.9%). Effort reusability is domain-dependent: higher reasoning effort yields marginal gains on general-knowledge QA but up to 8pp on financial content, and effort configurations that help in English help proportionally in other languages. Behavioural reusability holds: citation-set overlap with English averages 77-79% Jaccard, with no single language consistently worse. Together, these results support qualified reuse of English-built pipelines, but per-domain, per-language validation remains necessary--neither semantic similarity nor self-reported confidence reliably predicts cross-lingual accuracy.

title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
description:
arXiv:2610.27550v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth-order methods scale to high-dimensional tasks such as language model fine-tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We show that they cannot. We study finding $\varepsilon$-stationary points of $L$-smooth nonconvex functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ from exact function values, assuming that below the starting value the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix with trace at most $LE$; this is the effective rank condition used to explain zeroth-order fine-tuning. When $ET\le d$, the Gaussian two-point method that such fine-tuning uses needs only $O(ET)$ calls if it rejects steps that raise $f$, where $T=L\Delta/\varepsilon^2$ is the iteration count of gradient descent from initial gap $\Delta$, and we prove that every randomized method needs $\Omega(ET)$ calls, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In contrast, every deterministic method needs $\widetilde\Omega(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls, and adaptive subspace search attains $O(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$: a deterministic method pays about $d$ calls per discovered direction, and the trace budget allows about $\sqrt{ET}$ directions. Determinism thus multiplies the cost by a factor of order $d/(E+\sqrt{ET})$ up to logarithmic factors, which grows linearly with $d$ for fixed $E$ and $T$; once $E$ exceeds $T$ by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods need $\Omega(dT)$ calls, as without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for $C^\infty$ functions with the matrix bound on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, even when each call also returns gradient projections priced by rank.

title: "Design a Calendar System" Looks Easy. Here's Where Candidates Fail in the Interview
description:
"Design Calendar System" sounds simple. Create a meeting, invite people, show a grid of boxes.

It isn't. Underneath sit some of the most interesting problems in system design: a read-heavy workload with a fan-out on every write, notifications that must reach every invitee, reminders that must fire at an exact minute for hundreds of millions of people, and recurring events that never really end.

This walkthrough follows the structure we coach for a 45–60 minute interview: requirements, estimates, APIs, data model, high-level design, then the deep dives where the real signal is, and finally the AI follow-up more interviewers now ask.

1. Requirements

Functional

  • Create, read, update and delete meetings.
  • Invite people by email, including people who don't use the product.
  • Show a user's calendar for a day, week or month.
  • Notify invitees when a meeting is created or changed.
  • Remind participants a few minutes before a meeting (e.g. 15 minutes).

Nice to have: find a free slot across several people (free/busy), recurring meetings, time zones.

Non-functional

  • Highly available: 99.99%. A calendar that's down means missed meetings.
  • Low latency: calendar views in well under 500 ms (p99).
  • Read-heavy: people look at their calendar far more often than they change it.
  • Scalable: hundreds of millions of daily users.
  • Consistency: eventual consistency is fine for invitees, but the organizer must see their own change immediately (read-your-writes).

Interview tip: say why each requirement matters. "Eventually consistent, except read-your-writes for the organizer" shows judgement; "eventually consistent" alone is a buzzword.

2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Assumptions:

  • 2B users
  • 500M daily active users (DAU)
  • 20% of DAU create 2 meetings a day, and 30% create 1
  • New meetings / day → 0.2 × 500M × 2 + 0.3 × 500M = 350M
  • ~4 participants per meeting → ~1.4B invites per day
  • Calendar views / day → ~10 opens per DAU → 5B

QPS planning:

  • Write QPS → 350M / 86,400 ≈ 3.5K/s average, ~10.5K/s peak
  • Read QPS → 5B / 86,400 ≈ 50K QPS average, ~150K/s peak
  • Read : write ratio ~15 : 1, so read-heavy

Capacity planning:

  • 1 KB meeting + ~100 Bytes per participant ≈ 1 KB + 4 × 100 Bytes = 1.4 KB
  • 1.4 KB × 350M ≈ 0.5 TB/day ≈ ~180 TB/year before replication (no media)

Interview tip: The numbers tell us where to spend effort: optimise reads, make writes reliable, and design the fan-out carefully.

3. APIs 

POST   /meetings                      create (title, start, duration, tz, invitees)
                                      + recurrence?, Idempotency-Key header
GET    /users/{id}/calendar?start&end  meeting summaries for a day/week/month (paginated)
GET    /meetings/{id}                 full details
PATCH  /meetings/{id}                 update only the changed fields (If-Match: version)
DELETE /meetings/{id}                 cancel
POST   /meetings/{id}/invitees        add invitees
DELETE /meetings/{id}/invitees/{uid}  remove an invitee
POST   /meetings/{id}/rsvp            accept / decline / maybe
GET    /free?users&start&end          free blocks only (for slot finding)

Two details interviewers notice:

  • The calendar view returns summaries, not just IDs. Returning IDs and then fetching details is an extra round trip on the hottest path.
  • Updates carry a version (optimistic locking). Even if only the owner can edit, they can edit from two devices at once.

How an update works. The client sends only the fields that changed, never the whole meeting row. Moving a meeting 30 minutes later looks like this:

PATCH /meetings/m_123
If-Match: "7"
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json
{ "start": "2026-10-20T10:30:00Z" }
  • Partial update. Fields that aren't sent stay as they are, and null clears a field. The payload is tiny, and a client can't accidentally overwrite a field it never touched.
  • Version check. If-Match: "7" means "apply this only if the meeting is still at version 7". The Meeting Service runs a conditional write: UPDATE meetings SET start_utc = …, version = 8 WHERE meeting_id = 'm_123' AND version = 7. If another device changed the meeting first, nothing is updated and the API returns 412 Precondition Failed. The client refetches, shows the user the newer meeting, and lets them retry. The response to a successful update returns the whole updated meeting with its new version (ETag: "8").
  • Invitees have their own endpoints. Adding or removing people writes participant rows and sends notifications, so it isn't hidden inside a generic PATCH.

4. Data model

Users

  • user_id (PK) → Shard Key
  • email (unique)
  • metadata

Meetings

  • meeting_id (PK) → Shard Key
  • owner_id
  • title
  • description
  • start_utc
  • duration
  • version
  • metadata
  • list

Participants

  • user_id → Shard Key
  • meeting_id
  • start_utc
  • duration
  • status (invited / accepted / declined)
  • PK(user_id, start_utc, meeting_id)

Why two tables? The two hottest queries want different partitioning:

  • "Show my week" → all of one user's meetings in a time range → partition by user_id, sort by time. One range scan on one shard. Once you get meeting_id, you can easily fetch meeting details based on meeting_id from meetings table.
  • "Change this meeting" → one meeting and all its participants → partition by meeting_id.

The participants table denormalises the start time so the calendar view never has to join. The cost: moving a meeting rewrites one participant row per invitee. Writes are rare and reads are hot, so that's a good trade.

Interview tip: Tables in the same DB can have different shard keys.
To fetch meeting details for a user, don't perform join between participants and meeting table, instead first fetch all the meeting Ids for the user within a day/week and then issue a separate query to DB to fetch meeting details. The Calendar Service does this server-side, so the client still gets summaries in one call.
Optimization → Cache meeting details for the current and next week. Older meetings are rarely read, so caching them wastes memory.

5. High-level design


Async path for notification. Every change in the participants table is captured with change data capture (CDC) into an event queue. Downstream consumers react to it:

  • Event Subscriber Service subscribes to a change and put notifications in a queue.
  • Change notifications (new invite, time changed, cancelled) are sent with immediately delivery to the delay queue. Delay queue with immediate delivery behaves as a FIFO queue.
  • The Reminder Notifications are scheduled with delay delivery.

Using CDC instead of having the Meeting Service publish events directly is deliberate. The database is the single source of truth, so an event can't be lost because a service crashed between "write the DB" and "publish the event".

What if the Participant table can't be updated in the same transaction as meetings table.

Use CDC to update participants table asynchronously.

6. Deep dive: keeping invitees up to date

When a meeting changes, invitees should see it if online. Two options:

Pull (periodic refresh)

  • Simple to build.
  • Wasteful: most refreshes return nothing new, and at 500M DAU that's a lot of empty requests.
  • Changes appear late.

Push

  • Precise and cheap on the network.
  • The server sends a tiny message, "meeting X changed", over Server-Sent Events or WebSocket to open web clients.
  • The client then fetches only what changed.

Use push, and keep a light pull on app open as a safety net (pushes can be missed when a device is offline).

7. Deep dive: reminders 15 minutes before

This is where strong candidates separate themselves. We need to fire hundreds of millions of reminders a day, at the right minute, exactly once, even when meetings move or get cancelled.

8. Where agentic AI fits, and where it doesn't

Interviewers now often add a follow-up: "How would you use AI here?" In agentic AI system design rounds it's sharper: "Which parts of this would you hand to an agent?" The strong answer starts by drawing a line.

Keep the core deterministic. The Calendar DB, CDC, the event queue, fan-out and the delay queue must be exact, fast and cheap. An LLM call takes a second or more, costs real money per request, and can answer the same input differently twice. Nobody wants a reminder that fires "probably around 9:45", or a fan-out that decides which invitees deserve a notification. None of these components should be replaced by an agent.

Put agents at the edges, where the input is human. The good fits are jobs that today need a person to read, judge or negotiate:

  • Finding a time: open everyone's calendar, compare, propose. With Agent → "Find 30 minutes with Priya and Alex next week, mornings, not Friday" → it checks free, ranks slots and drafts the invite
  • Rescheduling after a decline or a new conflict With Agent → Proposes new times to everyone, collects the replies and books the slot that works.
  • Empty meeting descriptions With Agent → Drafts an agenda from the email thread or last meeting's notes.

9. Common mistakes

  • One table for everything, so "show my week" becomes a scatter-gather across shards.
  • Not creating Participants table and read fetch meetings created but not invited. Participants table is required and Invitees, organizer both should be added as participants.
  • Relying on Redis key expiry for reminders.
  • Doing the maths and not using it. Estimates should drive decisions (read-heavy → denormalize data).
  • Putting an LLM in the core path, for example letting an agent decide who gets notified, or giving it direct database access.

Wrapping up

A great answer isn't the biggest diagram. It's a clear story: the numbers say it's read-heavy, so we shape the data for reads; writes fan out asynchronously through CDC; and reminders use a delay queue that survives retries and reschedules. AI belongs at the edges, where people talk to the system, not inside its core. Then you show you know where it breaks.

title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
description:
arXiv:2610.27465v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off.
  Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.

title: Persist the practice stop before sending it
description:
Ending a piano practice session sounds like one POST. The tricky case is a lost response: the server may have accepted the stop while the client still sees a timeout. Retrying with a new event ID could turn one user action into two logical events.

In Pianory's account-backed practice flow, we persist the intent before sending it. queuePracticeStop writes both the session snapshot and the pending stop into one IndexedDB readwrite transaction. The pending record contains an ordered list of tick and stop events; each event keeps its ID and seconds. If a tick request had an uncertain response, we keep that same ID for replay.

The replay path sends the events in order. It rejects a failed HTTP response, validates that the stop acknowledgement belongs to the same session and contains a nonnegative integer duration, and only then calls completePracticeStop. That final method updates the session and removes the pending record in another IndexedDB transaction.

The useful invariant is small: an uncertain network result leaves a durable pending record. A later retry refers to the same logical event, rather than inventing a fresh one. The in-memory replay guard also coalesces concurrent sync requests within a client namespace.

A focused test covers replay and retry ordering. The end-to-end check uses a mock endpoint. This does not prove live D1 behavior, exactly-once delivery, or that every elapsed second survives every possible device failure. The contract is limited to account-backed sessions; guest sessions do not queue server practice stops.

This pattern applies beyond music practice: if the user says 'done', save that intent locally before treating the network as reliable.

AI assisted with drafting this article; I checked these claims against the repository and focused tests. I make Pianory, the piano-learning app behind this example.

title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.

title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
description:
arXiv:2610.27400v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.
