title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.

title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
description:
arXiv:2610.27301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $\tau$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.

title: Run a ByteChef workflow like a CLI command (no server, no database)
description:
Most automation platforms are built to stay up. ByteChef is no exception: the server stores your projects, fires triggers, listens for webhooks, and records every execution in PostgreSQL.

That's great until you look at where a lot of real work runs:

  • a nightly batch sitting in a Kubernetes CronJob next to twenty others, with alerting on failed pods
  • a CI step that should go red when something breaks
  • one task inside an Airflow DAG
  • a product with its own job runner that just wants to execute a workflow

In each of those, a standing server plus a database plus a message broker is overhead. You need the engine for the length of one run, and then you want it gone.

That's what the Runtime Job app does. You pass it a workflow name, inputs as JSON, and credentials as JSON. It boots the full Atlas engine in one JVM, runs the workflow to completion, and exits 0 or 1. Nothing to provision, nothing to clean up.

The Runtime Job app is part of ByteChef's Enterprise Edition. Source: server/ee/apps/runtime-job-app.

Same engine, different packaging

This isn't a lightweight interpreter. The coordinator, workers and task dispatchers are all there. What changes is everything around them:

ByteChef server Runtime Job app
Execution state PostgreSQL In memory, gone on exit
Message broker Redis, Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ, JMS… In-process
Connections Encrypted store in the DB JSON passed at launch
Triggers Scheduler, polling, webhooks None. The run starts with the process
UI / API Yes No
Record of a run Execution history Exit code + log

The workflow JSON is identical in both, so the loop is: build and test in ByteChef, export, hand the file to the Runtime Job app.

A real example

A daily sales report: take a date, total the paid orders for that day from PostgreSQL, log a summary.

{
  "label": "Daily Sales Report",
  "inputs": [
    { "name": "reportDate", "label": "Report date", "type": "string", "required": true }
  ],
  "triggers": [
    { "label": "Manual", "name": "trigger_1", "type": "manual/v1/manual" }
  ],
  "tasks": [
    {
      "label": "Sum paid orders",
      "name": "postgresql_1",
      "type": "postgresql/v1/query",
      "parameters": {
        "query": "SELECT count(*) AS orders, coalesce(sum(total), 0) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at = CAST(:reportDate AS date)",
        "parameters": { "reportDate": "${reportDate}" }
      }
    },
    {
      "label": "Log summary",
      "name": "logger_1",
      "type": "logger/v1/info",
      "parameters": {
        "text": "Sales for ${reportDate}: ${postgresql_1[0].orders} paid orders, revenue ${postgresql_1[0].revenue}"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Save it as ~/bytechef/data/workflows/daily-sales.json (the default lookup location). Note the task name postgresql_1 and component name postgresql; both matter for connections later.

Build and run:

./gradlew :server:ee:apps:runtime-job-app:bootJar

CONNECTIONS='{"postgresql": {"host": "localhost", "port": 5432, "database": "shop", "username": "etl", "password": "..."}}'

java -jar runtime-job-app.jar \
  --workflow=daily-sales.json \
  --parameters='{"reportDate": "2026-10-14"}' \
  --connections="$CONNECTIONS"

echo $?   # 0

On a laptop the whole thing took about 10 seconds, roughly one of which was the workflow itself. That's the trade: a few seconds of boot for zero standing infrastructure. Fine for a nightly batch; for a thousand calls a minute, use the server.

The flags

Flag Required What it does
--workflow=<file> yes File name, e.g. daily-sales.json. A lookup key, not a path.
--parameters=<json> no Workflow inputs as a JSON object.
--connections=<json> no Connection name → parameters. Repeatable; objects are merged.
--timeout=<duration> no 30s, 15m, 1h. Exit 1 if exceeded.
--outputs-file=<path> no Write the workflow's outputs as JSON on success.

Any Spring Boot property works too, e.g. --logging.level.com.bytechef=DEBUG.

Gotcha: --workflow is not a path

The app drops the directory, strips the extension, and Base64-encodes the rest into an id (daily-sales → ZGFpbHktc2FsZXM=). At startup it indexes every file in the enabled workflow repositories the same way, then looks the id up. So these are identical:

--workflow=daily-sales.json
--workflow=/anything/at/all/daily-sales.json

…and pointing at a file outside the repositories won't work. Repositories available: filesystem (default, ~/bytechef/data/workflows), classpath (workflows/ inside the JAR), and Git (off by default).

# read workflows from somewhere else
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN='/opt/workflows/*.json'

# or straight from Git, so a merge to main is a deploy
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_GIT_ENABLED=true
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_GIT_URL=https://github.com/acme/workflows.git
BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_GIT_BRANCH=main

Tip: export workflows from the editor rather than hand-writing them. Component defaults are written into the JSON when you add a node, not at runtime, so a hand-written file can fail mid-run with Unknown value for : <property>.

Connections

No credential store means credentials arrive as JSON. Keys are connection names; values use the same property names as the component's connection form in the UI.

Before each task runs, its connection is resolved like this:

  1. By task name (postgresql_1) — applies to that task only.
  2. By component name (postgresql) — shared by every task of that component.
  3. No match — the task runs without one (fine for logger, fatal for a database).

Task-name keys let two tasks of the same component use different credentials, say a read replica and a primary. And you can split credentials across secrets by repeating the flag:

java -jar runtime-job-app.jar \
  --workflow=daily-sales.json \
  --connections="$OPENAI_CONNECTION" \
  --connections="$POSTGRES_CONNECTION"

Two caveats worth knowing up front:

  • Connection JSON is logged at INFO on startup. Treat the log as credential-bearing: restrict access and set retention.
  • Not every connector works this way yet. Database components (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and LLM providers that take an API key work. SaaS connectors whose auth is applied as an HTTP header by the platform (bearer, API key, OAuth2) don't get that header from --connections. Test before relying on them.

Exit codes are the API

Code Meaning
0 Job COMPLETED
1 Job FAILED or STOPPED, or --timeout hit
other non-zero Couldn't start: missing flag, bad JSON, unknown workflow
143 Killed by SIGTERM (eviction, drain, docker stop)

That's all a scheduler needs. A Kubernetes Job retries per backoffLimit, Airflow marks the task failed, CI goes red. Nobody parses logs.

Always set --timeout. Without it the app waits forever, and a stuck process is never retried because it never fails. This matters doubly for JavaScript/Python script tasks, which have no CPU or heap cap of their own.

Make writes idempotent. A 143 leaves no trace in the log, and a retry starts from scratch. Prefer upserts or check for an existing result.

Getting results out

Declare outputs in the workflow as usual:

"outputs": [
  { "name": "orders",  "value": "${postgresql_1[0].orders}" },
  { "name": "revenue", "value": "${postgresql_1[0].revenue}" }
]

They're logged as one JSON line on completion. For programs, use --outputs-file:

java -jar runtime-job-app.jar ... --outputs-file=/tmp/daily-sales.json
jq .revenue /tmp/daily-sales.json   # 1540.50

The file is only written for a completed job, so check the exit code first. Keep outputs small (counts, ids, a status); write anything big to where it's used and return a pointer.

Docker 

docker build -t registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16 server/ee/apps/runtime-job-app/

docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)/workflows:/workflows" \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN='/workflows/*.json' \
  registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16 \
  --workflow=daily-sales.json \
  --parameters='{"reportDate": "2026-10-14"}' \
  --connections="$CONNECTIONS"

The image is about 2 GB (GraalVM base + a ~770 MB JAR with ~100 components and the polyglot runtime). Use immutable tags with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent so each node pulls it once. Use the prod profile; local builds default to dev, which logs at DEBUG.

Kubernetes CronJob

This is where it fits best: a pod starts, runs one workflow, exits, and the exit code decides whether Kubernetes retries.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-sales
spec:
  schedule: "15 6 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: runtime-job
              image: registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16
              imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
              args:
                - >-
                  exec java -jar /opt/bytechef/runtime-job/runtime-job-app.jar
                  --workflow=daily-sales.json
                  --parameters="{\"reportDate\": \"$(date -d yesterday +%F)\"}"
                  --connections="$POSTGRES_CONNECTION"
                  --timeout=20m
              env:
                - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
                  value: prod
                - name: BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN
                  value: /workflows/*.json
                - name: POSTGRES_CONNECTION
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: daily-sales-connections
                      key: postgresql.json
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 768Mi }
                limits:   { memory: 1Gi }
              volumeMounts:
                - name: workflows
                  mountPath: /workflows
          volumes:
            - name: workflows
              configMap:
                name: daily-sales-workflow

Why it looks like this:

  • restartPolicy: Never + backoffLimit — exit 1 fails the pod; each retry is a clean process.
  • --timeout — backoffLimit only retries failed pods, not stuck ones. (activeDeadlineSeconds works too, but it kills the pod with a silent 143.)
  • Memory — a small workflow used ~370 MiB. Measure a real run and size from that; OOMKilled exits 137.
  • sh -c + exec — computes yesterday's date, and exec keeps the JVM's exit code as the pod's.
  • Secret + ConfigMap — credentials stay out of the manifest; updating the workflow is a kubectl apply, not an image rebuild.

CI

Exit codes make it a normal CI step. GitHub Actions, generating release notes on every tag:

name: Release notes
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  notes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: registry.example.com/bytechef-runtime-job:2026-10-16
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Generate and publish release notes
        env:
          SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
          BYTECHEF_WORKFLOW_REPOSITORY_FILESYSTEM_LOCATION_PATTERN: ${{ github.workspace }}/.bytechef/*.json
          OPENAI_CONNECTION: ${{ secrets.BYTECHEF_OPENAI_CONNECTION }}
        run: |
          java -jar /opt/bytechef/runtime-job/runtime-job-app.jar \
            --workflow=release-notes.json \
            --parameters="{\"tag\": \"${GITHUB_REF_NAME}\"}" \
            --connections="$OPENAI_CONNECTION" \
            --timeout=10m

The workflow lives in .bytechef/ in the repo it automates and gets code-reviewed like everything else. Same idea works in GitLab CI, Jenkins, or Airflow's KubernetesPodOperator.

What's in, what's out

In: ~100 components — HTTP client, script and Bash, helpers, CSV/JSON/XML/XLSX, PostgreSQL and MySQL, the major LLM providers, Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 basics, Slack, GitHub, Jira, HubSpot, Shopify — plus control flow (branch, condition, each, loop, map, parallel, fork-join, subflow, approval). Check the app's build.gradle.kts before depending on a specific one.

Out, on purpose: triggers, the UI and REST API, execution history (ship your logs somewhere), and scaling within a run (launch more processes instead).

Quick troubleshooting

Symptom Fix
Workflow with id: <base64> does not exist File isn't in a configured repository (or the volume isn't mounted). The directory in --workflow is ignored.
Unknown value for : <property> Re-export the workflow from the editor.
Auth error on a task Connection key doesn't match task/component name, or property names are wrong.
Process never exits Add --timeout.
Exit 143, nothing in log SIGTERM from outside. Check pod events.
Exit 137 / OOMKilled Raise the memory limit (and -Xmx).
No outputs file The job didn't complete. Check the exit code.

Server or Runtime Job?

Use the server when you need triggers, webhooks, a UI, run history, RBAC, a central credential store, or always-on/high-frequency processing.

Use the Runtime Job app for nightly batches, CI steps, and anything whose schedule already lives in Kubernetes, Airflow or GitHub Actions.

They're not competitors. A common setup: people build and test on a ByteChef server, and CronJobs run the exported, reviewed versions in production. Same JSON, unchanged.

Full reference: Runtime Job Runner docs. Originally published on the ByteChef blog.

title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.

title: Supabase RLS with auth.uid() not working? Causes and fixes
description:
You wrote a tidy Row Level Security policy, something like auth.uid() = user_id, and now one of two annoying things happens: your query returns no rows at all, or it returns everybody's rows. Both are common, both are fixable, and neither means RLS is broken. It means the policy isn't seeing the identity you think it's seeing.

Let's walk the actual causes, in rough order of how often they bite people, with copy-pasteable SQL you can run against your own project.

First, what auth.uid() actually is

auth.uid() reads the sub claim out of the JWT attached to the current request. No JWT, or a JWT without a user, means auth.uid() returns NULL.

That single fact explains most "no rows" bugs. A policy like auth.uid() = user_id becomes NULL = user_id, which evaluates to NULL (not true), so the row is filtered out. Every row. Silently.

So the first debugging question is never "is my policy wrong?" It's "who does the database think I am right now?"

Cause 1: You're on the anon key, so auth.uid() is NULL

Every Supabase project ships two keys, and they are not interchangeable:

  • anon / publishable (role: anon) — public by design. It's meant to sit in your browser bundle. It is not a secret and does not need rotating. RLS is what protects your data when this key is used.
  • service_role (role: service_role) — a server-only secret that bypasses RLS entirely. More on why that's dangerous below.

If you initialize the client with the anon key and the user hasn't logged in, there's no user JWT, so auth.uid() is NULL and auth.uid() = user_id matches nothing.

Confirm which key you're holding by decoding the middle segment of the JWT (base64url-encoded JSON):

echo 'PASTE_KEY_HERE' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool

Read the role field: "anon" or "service_role". The newer key formats make it obvious without decoding: sb_publishable_... is public, sb_secret_... is the secret one.

Then confirm you're actually authenticated. In the browser:

const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser()
console.log(user)   // null here means auth.uid() will be NULL server-side

If user is null, fix sign-in first — no policy change helps until the request carries a user JWT.

Cause 2: RLS isn't actually enabled, so you get everything

The opposite symptom — you see all rows — usually means RLS isn't switched on for the table. Policies are ignored entirely until you enable RLS:

select relname, relrowsecurity
from pg_class
where relname = 'your_table';

If relrowsecurity is false, turn it on:

alter table your_table enable row level security;

One gotcha: the table owner and superusers still bypass RLS. To apply the rules even to the owner, add alter table your_table force row level security;.

Cause 3: You're testing with service_role, so it "works" (misleadingly)

The sneakiest one. Your test passes, data comes back exactly right — because the test client is using the service_role key, which bypasses RLS completely. You're not testing your policies; you're testing with the guard switched off.

service_role belongs only on a trusted server. Never in a browser, never in a public repo, never in a client .env that gets bundled. Anything prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, or EXPO_PUBLIC_ gets inlined into the client bundle at build time — perfect for the anon key and project URL, catastrophic for service_role.

And if service_role has already been committed to a repo: deleting the file is not enough. A committed secret lives in git history forever. Rotate the key in the dashboard and purge history (git filter-repo or BFG). Rotation is the part that actually revokes the leak; history-scrubbing stops the old value from being fetched back out.

Test policies with the anon key plus a real logged-in session, the way your app runs. To check directly in SQL, impersonate a role and a user inside a transaction:

begin;
-- become the anon role
set local role anon;
select * from your_table;   -- honors your anon policies

-- now simulate a logged-in user
set local role authenticated;
select set_config(
  'request.jwt.claims',
  '{"sub":"11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111","role":"authenticated"}',
  true
);
select * from your_table;   -- auth.uid() now returns that sub
rollback;

If it returns rows here but not in your app, the difference is your app's auth state, not the policy.

Cause 4: Missing GRANT

RLS policies do not grant access — they restrict it. A role needs both a matching policy and a table-level privilege. If anon or authenticated was never granted SELECT, no policy will save you; the query errors out regardless of the rows.

select grantee, privilege_type
from information_schema.role_table_grants
where table_name = 'your_table';

Supabase's default setup grants the API roles broad privileges, but if you've been locking things down by hand you may have revoked them:

grant select, insert, update, delete on your_table to authenticated;

Then let RLS decide which rows each user actually touches.

Cause 5: Missing (or wrong) TO clause

A policy with no TO clause applies to every role, including anon. That's a frequent source of "why can logged-out visitors read this?"

Scope policies explicitly:

create policy "Users read own rows"
on your_table
for select
to authenticated                       -- <- this line matters
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Multiple permissive policies are OR'd together, so a broad one you forgot about widens access. List what's really on the table:

select policyname, cmd, roles, qual, with_check
from pg_policies
where tablename = 'your_table';

Read the roles column. If you see {public} where you expected {authenticated}, that's your leak — public means every role, anon included.

Cause 6: Comparing a uuid to a text column

auth.uid() returns a uuid. If your user_id column is text, Postgres resolves uuid = text by casting the text to uuid — which throws invalid input syntax for type uuid the moment any value isn't a well-formed uuid, and adds a per-row cast even when it isn't. Check the type:

select column_name, data_type
from information_schema.columns
where table_name = 'your_table' and column_name = 'user_id';

The clean fix is a real uuid column referencing auth.users:

alter table your_table
  alter column user_id type uuid using user_id::uuid;

If you can't change the schema right now, cast inside the policy so both sides match:

using ( (select auth.uid())::text = user_id )

Prefer fixing the column type — a uuid that references auth.users(id) indexes better and is harder to get wrong later.

The policy pattern to standardize on

Notice I keep writing (select auth.uid()) instead of bare auth.uid(). Wrapping it in a select lets Postgres evaluate the function once per query instead of once per row — a real, measurable win on larger tables, and the pattern Supabase now recommends. A complete per-user set:

alter table documents enable row level security;

create policy "read own documents"
on documents for select
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

create policy "insert own documents"
on documents for insert
to authenticated
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

create policy "update own documents"
on documents for update
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Mental model for the two clauses: USING filters which existing rows a role can see (and which rows an UPDATE/DELETE may touch); WITH CHECK validates the new values being written. INSERT policies have WITH CHECK only. UPDATE usually wants both — USING to pick the row, WITH CHECK so a user can't reassign user_id to someone else.

A 60-second self-audit 

-- tables in public with RLS still disabled
select c.relname
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind = 'r'
  and c.relrowsecurity = false;

-- policies with no role restriction (they apply to anon too)
select tablename, policyname, cmd, roles
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
  and roles = '{public}';

If you want a reproducible sandbox where each failure mode fires on demand — anon-key NULL, missing GRANT, service_role bypass — plus a fuller read-only audit query to paste into the SQL editor, I put a small demo repo together: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. Clone it, run the SQL, and watch the "no rows / all rows" behavior flip as you toggle each cause. It's the fastest way I know to build the intuition.

The takeaway

When auth.uid() "doesn't work," it's almost never that RLS is broken. It's that the request isn't carrying the identity you assume: you're on the anon key with no session, RLS was never enabled, a test used service_role and hid the bug, a GRANT is missing, the TO clause is too wide, or a uuid is being compared to text. Walk the six checks in order and you'll find it.

If you'd rather not hand-audit every time you ship a new table, I maintain a $29 RLS Audit Kit — ready-to-run policy tests and a checklist that flags exactly these six failure modes across your whole schema. Entirely optional; the queries above will get you unstuck today either way.

title: Dark Mode Design Best Practices: What Google, Apple, and the Research Say
description:
Dark mode is a table-stakes feature now, and most teams still build it the laziest way possible: take the light theme, flip the colors, ship it. The result is an app that looks like a photographic negative — gray text on black soup, brand colors that scream, cards you can barely tell apart from the background. Google and Apple both wrote detailed specs explaining why that approach is wrong. And the battery story that justifies half of it? For most users it's 3–9%, not the headline numbers.

The battery myth: 47% is real, and it almost never applies to you

The strongest battery claim comes from good science. Purdue researchers Pranab Dash and Y. Charlie Hu built a per-pixel OLED power profiler and tested four phones (Pixel 2, Moto Z3, Pixel 4, Pixel 5) across six Google apps. Switching from light to dark mode saved 39–47% of display power — at 100% brightness. That's the number everyone quotes.

Here's the part that doesn't fit in a headline: at 30–50% brightness, the saving was 3–9%. Most people use auto-brightness, which sits around 30–40% indoors. The researchers' verdict was blunt: the saving is so small at normal indoor brightness that most users wouldn't notice. On LCD screens — budget phones, most laptops, older iPads — it's essentially zero, because the backlight stays on regardless of pixel color.

Dark mode is a real battery feature outdoors at max brightness, where the 39–47% shows up. Everywhere else it's a comfort and aesthetics feature. Stop selling it as battery management and start designing it as what it is.

Don't invert — rebuild: what Google's spec actually says

Google's Material Design dark theme guidance reads like a direct answer to the invert-and-ship crowd. The baseline surface is #121212, not pure black. Text comes in two tiers: white at 87% opacity for high-emphasis text, 60% for medium. The big idea is elevation: since dark shadows are invisible on a dark background, depth is communicated by making higher surfaces brighter — thin white overlays on top of the base surface, getting stronger with elevation. In Google's codelab, a bottom app bar gets the base #121212 plus a 12% white overlay. Cards, dialogs, and sheets all follow the same logic.

Color gets a rule most teams skip: desaturate. Saturated brand colors vibrate against dark backgrounds, so Material tells you to pull them back and use them sparingly — "limited color accents," preferring the surface color over the primary color in most chrome. Even your error red needs a dark-mode version: the same fire-engine red that reads fine on white vibrates on black, so the guidance is a dustier, dimmer red. If your red is still shouting at the same volume in dark mode, nobody adjusted it.

Apple took a different path — and both agree on one rule

Apple's approach is semantic instead of numeric. iOS (since 2019's iOS 13) and macOS define colors as roles — label, secondaryLabel, systemBackground — that automatically adapt to the trait environment. Use UIColor.label and dark mode mostly handles itself; hardcode a hex for your text and you've broken dark mode before you tested it. Apple's actual values show the same discipline as Material's: label text is white at 85% opacity, elevated cards step up through dark grays (#1C1C1E, #2C2C2E) to signal depth, and community measurements put dark-mode systemBlue slightly brighter than its light-mode counterpart to hold its contrast.

One disagreement worth noting: Apple's base system background is pure black (#000000), where Material explicitly avoids it. The honest reading: Apple's black maximizes OLED savings and contrast for content; Material's dark gray is friendlier for long sessions and makes elevation layering visible. Both are defensible. What neither defends is a theme nobody designed.

Contrast doesn't retire when you go dark

A common assumption is that dark mode is automatically more accessible. The opposite can be true: light text on black at full strength causes halation — text that seems to bleed into the background — which is why the platforms cap text opacity at 85–87% instead of pure white. WCAG's 4.5:1 ratio for body text still applies; it just gets harder to eyeball on a dark canvas, especially for saturated accents.

Practical checks that catch the most failures: view the whole UI in grayscale to expose contrast problems instantly; re-check every accent color against its dark background (your light theme's accessible blue is often a failing blue in the dark); and never trust the simulator — test on a real OLED screen outdoors, where dark interfaces lose legibility fastest. For contrast science beyond the old 4.5:1 rule, the perceptual color work in my OKLCH and APCA guide applies here too.

Type, images, and the ten small things

The details that separate a designed dark theme from a flipped one: bump font weights slightly — thin type that was elegant in black-on-white turns spindly in white-on-black; small text may need a size bump too, since the readability gap between modes grows as type gets smaller. Images and logos need dark-mode variants or at least transparent backgrounds, or you'll ship white boxes around every logo. QR codes are a real gotcha: an inverted QR code won't scan. Interactive states (hover, pressed, disabled) must stay distinct without relying on brightness alone. And animate the theme switch with a subtle transition — a hard flash at midnight is the kind of detail users feel even if they never name it.

Respect the user: give them the switch, then listen to the data

Ship both modes, default to the system preference via prefers-color-scheme, and always offer a manual toggle that persists. A Nielsen Norman Group survey of 115 mobile users found opinion split exactly three ways: a third want dark, a third want light, a third switch. There is no default everyone loves.

And here's the finding every designer should sit with: in NNGroup's summary of the German readability research (Piepenbrock and colleagues, Institut für Experimentelle Psychologie Düsseldorf), light mode won on every measured dimension — visual acuity and proofreading, for young and old adults — and produced no difference in fatigue. Yet participants reported no difference in readability. As NNGroup puts it: don't listen to users. Measure the reading task.

The takeaway isn't "ship light mode only." It's that the mode that looks good in a screenshot and the mode that performs in a reading test are different problems, and a designed dark theme accounts for both.

What to do this week

Audit your dark theme with five checks: is your base surface dark gray rather than pure black (or pure black with a deliberate reason)? Does elevation make cards brighter instead of relying on shadows? Is your loudest accent color desaturated relative to light mode? Does body text clear 4.5:1 on the actual dark background? And can a user override the system default? If any answer is no, you don't have a dark theme yet — you have an inverted light one.

References

  • Nielsen Norman Group — "Dark Mode vs. Light Mode: Which Is Better?" — summary of Piepenbrock et al. readability studies; 115-user preference survey (1/3 dark, 1/3 light, 1/3 mixed)
  • ScienceDaily — "Dark mode may not save your phone's battery life as much as you think" — Purdue Dash Hu OLED profiler study (MobiSys '21): 3–9% savings at 30–50% brightness, 39–47% at 100%
  • Google Codelabs — "Design a dark theme with Material and Figma" — #121212 surface, 87%/60% text opacity, elevation overlays, limited color accents
  • Android Developers — Material Design 2 in Compose — elevation overlay behavior, primarySurface limited-accent guidance
  • Median.co — "Apple's Human Interface Guidelines: Dark Mode do's and don'ts" — semantic colors, vibrancy, base/elevated backgrounds
  • AppCherish — "Dark Mode Isn't Optional Anymore" — iOS semantic-color checklist, hardcoded-color pitfalls since iOS 13

title: AnomalyJev: Towards Evaluating Image Anomaly Explanations via Claim-Level Verification
description:
arXiv:2610.27565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based anomaly detection (AD) methods can generate textual explanations that help interpret their predictions. However, reliably and efficiently evaluating these explanations remains challenging. While LLM judges can assess explanations through structured rubrics, they often require substantial token generation, making evaluation costly and difficult to scale. We instead propose to anchor evaluation in the available ground truth by extracting verifiable claims from each explanation and verifying them against the corresponding annotations. We instantiate this idea as AnomalyJev, a lightweight framework that extracts verifiable claims from contextualised representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer based heads, without token generation. The claims are then verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness. For evaluation, we construct a human-annotated set of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings. Despite its compact design, AnomalyJev achieves stronger agreement with human annotators than most open MLLM judges and approaches that of flagship MLLM judges, at a fraction of their runtime and resources.

title: Rate as a Feature, Not a Nuisance: Curriculum FiLM Training for Event-Based Graph Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.26933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An event camera emits events at a rate given by the scene motion, object texture, illumination, its own contrast thresholds, and other settings. Across the N-Caltech101 dataset, recorded by a single event camera, the event rate varies by roughly 26x. Standard event-based Graph Neural Network GNN pipelines do not make use of the variable event rate. They either normalize each event's timestamp into a fixed window or train the network to be invariant to the event rate. We argue that both choices lose information that could instead be used to improve the performance of a pipeline. Per-recording normalization is non-invertible, incurring about 6pp (percentage points) of natural-rate accuracy loss in our setting. And invariance training trades accuracy for robustness to shifts in the event rate. We instead take a different path and condition on the event rate directly. We add a per-recording log-rate scalar that modulates every stage of a PointNet++ backbone through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), initialized to identity, so that training begins at the unmodified baseline. A two-stage curriculum (natural event rates first, then rate-augmented fine-tuning) reaches 67.2% on N-Caltech101 (+6.3pp) and 82.5% on DVS128 Gesture (+14.0pp) with an additional ~0.2M parameters. A matched-capacity control experiment shows that the gain is not from the increase in model capacity but from the rate conditioning. We will make the implementation publicly available upon acceptance of this work.

title: VPFlow: Value-Predictive Planning with Imperfect World Models for Offline Goal Reaching
description:
arXiv:2610.27280v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning enables skill acquisition by reaching any goal from any state without dense rewards. Model-based methods allow for planning by scaling test-time compute to solve complex tasks. Combining both holds appealing promise for pre-training on suboptimal demonstrations and zero-shot adaptation via goal specification and planning. Yet existing methods assume effective planning requires accurate next-state prediction in pixel or latent space. In this work, we show that value prediction is more useful for planning, whereas accurate state prediction is often unnecessary. Our key insight is that offline goal reaching naturally admits a closed-form Monte Carlo return, enabling value regression to replace temporal-difference bootstrapping. We use this return as the sole supervision for latent world models: imagined latents are trained to predict goal-reaching value rather than match future states, implicitly preventing representation collapse. These planning-oriented representations let imperfect world models imagine on the level sets of value field beyond dataset transitions. We then present VPFlow, a value-predictive planner that pairs the world models with a one-step flow policy and plans in its noise space via evolutionary search. It enables policy improvement with imagined generalized advantage and reduces out-of-distribution queries common in action-space planning. On 30 state and pixel OGBench datasets, VPFlow surpasses model-free baselines by at least 30.3 and 10.1 percentage points in success rate, respectively, and outperforms latent planners LeWorldModel, PLDM, and TD-MPC2. It achieves this despite a latent prediction error orders of magnitude larger than with state prediction, while minimizing this error lowers success rate. This demonstrates that value-predictive representations, not exact state prediction, are what offline planning requires.

title: Benchmarking Autonomous API Onboarding and SaaS Grants: An Empirical Audit of the Sourcey Open Datasets
description:
When autonomous software agents provision cloud infrastructure or evaluate vendor credits, they face two structural bottlenecks: undocumented onboarding friction (CAPTCHA gates, manual sales loops, opaque billing) and unverified promotional claims. Using the deterministic open datasets published by Sourcey, we audited 105 probed API readiness profiles in agent-readiness.json and 557 vendor records in startup-credits.json anchored to the 2026-10-21 cryptographic release (sha256:95a216ee10b539d5c46c9788448b4962d91d0b92b9f48091deff6a9d46bce5e9).

1. Cryptographic Provenance of the Audited Snapshot

Every observation in this analysis is reproducible against the live public JSON endpoints:

  • Unified Release ID (release_id): sha256:95a216ee10b539d5c46c9788448b4962d91d0b92b9f48091deff6a9d46bce5e9
  • Artifact Digest (artifact_sha256): sha256:a80cde0e54161d2b74ede25fa29015f6470729012eae2b52b3eb56e119d12fa2
  • Registries Examined:
    • Sourcey Agent Readiness Registry (sourcey.agent-readiness-dataset/v1alpha1, 105 probed service jobs under policy kind-2026-10-12)
    • Sourcey Startup Credits Registry (sourcey.startup-credits-dataset/v1alpha1, 557 verified companies)

title: You Committed .env to GitHub: What to Rotate (Supabase + Next.js)
description:
You pushed, then your stomach dropped: .env is in the commit. Maybe a bot already emailed you. Take a breath — this is recoverable, and panicking into random git commands usually makes it worse.

The single most important thing to understand: deleting the file does not fix anything. Once a secret is in git history, assume it is public forever. The real fix is rotation — making the leaked value useless by replacing it upstream. Purging history is cleanup you do after rotating, not instead of it.

Let's go value by value through a typical Supabase + Next.js .env, sort out what's actually a secret, and rotate only what matters.

First: which of these is actually secret?

A typical .env looks like this:

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://abcdxyz.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJhbGciOi...        # role: anon
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=eyJhbGciOi...            # role: service_role
SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET=super-secret-signing-key
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:PASSWORD@db.abcdxyz.supabase.co:5432/postgres
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
RESEND_API_KEY=re_...

Here's the part that saves you hours of unnecessary panic.

Safe by design — do NOT need rotating:

  • NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL — your project URL is public. It's in every network request the browser makes.
  • NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY — the anon (publishable) key is public by design. It ships in your client bundle on purpose. Any NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable is inlined into the browser JavaScript at build time, so it was never a secret to begin with.

The anon key's role is anon. It has no special power on its own — it's just an identity meaning "an unauthenticated (or logged-in) user of this project." What protects your data when that key is used is Row Level Security (RLS). If your tables have RLS enabled with correct policies, a leaked anon key is a non-event. If they don't, that key was already exposed to every visitor of your site — the git commit changed nothing.

Actually secret — rotate every one of these:

  • SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY
  • SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET
  • DATABASE_URL (the Postgres password inside it)
  • Every third-party key: Stripe, Resend, OpenAI, etc.

The service_role key is the scary one. Its role is service_role, and it bypasses RLS entirely — full read, write, and delete on every table, plus Storage. It's a server-only secret. It must never appear in a browser, a public repo, or anything with a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix. If it leaked, treat it as a full database breach until rotated.

How to tell the two keys apart

Both are JWTs, so they look identical at a glance. Decode the middle segment (base64URL) and read the role claim:

# paste your key in place of PASTE_KEY
echo 'PASTE_KEY' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python -m json.tool

You'll see either "role": "anon" (safe, public) or "role": "service_role" (secret, rotate now). Newer Supabase projects use clearer prefixes instead of JWTs: sb_publishable_... (public) vs sb_secret_... (secret). The prefix tells you everything — no decoding needed.

Rotating each secret

The Supabase keys

In the dashboard, go to Project Settings → API Keys. How rotation works depends on which key system your project uses:

  • New keys (sb_publishable_ / sb_secret_): these are independent of each other and of the JWT secret. Revoke the leaked sb_secret_ key and create a new one; the publishable key is unaffected because it wasn't a secret.
  • Legacy JWT keys: both the anon and service_role keys are JWTs signed by your project's JWT secret. Rolling that secret regenerates both keys at once, because both are signatures over it.

Either way, after rotating the secret:

  1. Copy the new service_role / sb_secret_ key into your server environment (Vercel project env vars, .env.local, etc.).
  2. If you rolled a legacy JWT secret, also grab the regenerated anon key and redeploy so the fresh key ships in your bundle.

One consequence to expect on the legacy path: rolling the JWT secret invalidates every JWT signed with the old one, which logs out all existing user sessions. That's the correct, safe outcome after a leak — do it anyway.

Database password

Project Settings → Database → Reset database password. This changes the password embedded in your DATABASE_URL / connection string. Update that string everywhere it lives (Vercel, CI secrets, local .env.local, migration tooling). Anything still using the old password starts failing — that's your checklist of places to fix.

Third-party keys

Each provider has its own flow, but the pattern is identical: generate a new key, deploy it, then revoke the old one. Don't skip the revoke — a new key does not disable the leaked one.

  • Stripe: Developers → API keys → roll the leaked secret key.
  • Resend / OpenAI / etc.: create new key, swap in env, delete old.

Now purge git history

Rotation makes the leaked values worthless. Purging history is about hygiene and not re-leaking on the next clone. Deleting the file in a new commit is not enough — the old commit still contains it.

The clean tool is git filter-repo:

pip install git-filter-repo

# remove the file from all of history
git filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths

Or with BFG:

bfg --delete-files .env
git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive

Then force-push the rewritten history:

git push origin --force --all
git push origin --force --tags

Two honest caveats: force-pushing rewrites history for every collaborator (they'll need to re-clone or reset), and GitHub caches commits — forks and cached commit views can retain the blob even after your push. That's exactly why rotation is the real fix and history-purging is secondary. Then add .env to .gitignore so this can't recur:

echo ".env" >> .gitignore
echo ".env.local" >> .gitignore
git rm --cached .env      # stop tracking without deleting your local copy

The part everyone skips: is your RLS actually protecting you?

Here's the uncomfortable truth. If a leaked anon key genuinely exposes your data, the anon key wasn't the vulnerability — your RLS was. That key is public to every visitor regardless of any git leak.

A few things worth checking on every table:

  • RLS is enabled on the table. Enabling it with no policies denies all access through the API — that's fail-safe, not broken.
  • A role needs both a matching policy and the underlying table GRANT.
  • A policy with no TO clause applies to every role, including anon.
  • USING (true) on a SELECT policy makes the table world-readable. It's only world-writable if a permissive INSERT/UPDATE/ALL policy also exists (INSERT policies gate rows with WITH CHECK, not USING).
  • For an anonymous request, auth.uid() is NULL — so USING (auth.uid() = user_id) correctly returns nothing to anon.

Quick audit of what's exposed:

-- tables with RLS OFF (guarded only by GRANTs, no policy gate)
select relname
from pg_class
where relkind = 'r'
  and relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
  and not relrowsecurity;

-- every policy, so you can eyeball no-TO and USING(true)
select schemaname, tablename, policyname, roles, cmd, qual, with_check
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
order by tablename;

If reading those results makes you nervous, I put together a free, read-only repro and audit kit here: github.com/cekuu35/supabase-rls-leak-demo. It has a deliberately leaky schema plus copy-paste SQL that flags world-readable tables and no-TO policies, so you can see exactly what an anon key can reach in your own project.

The 60-second recap

  1. Don't panic, don't just delete the file.
  2. Anon key + project URL + NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars: safe, no rotation needed.
  3. service_role, JWT secret, DB password, third-party keys: rotate now, revoke the old ones.
  4. Purge history with filter-repo/BFG and force-push — but only after rotating.
  5. Audit your RLS, because that's what actually stands between the public anon key and your data.

If you want to go deeper than the free audit — a full policy-by-policy checklist, the common false-positive traps, and fix templates — I keep a $29 RLS Audit Kit that packages it all up. Totally optional; the free demo repo above is enough to check and fix most projects on your own. Either way: rotate first, breathe second, and get RLS right so the next leak is a shrug instead of a scramble.

title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
description:
arXiv:2610.27227v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present \textbf{GRSE}, \textbf{G}roup-\textbf{R}elative \textbf{S}kill \textbf{E}volution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent--skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions ($+6.7$ and $+3.2$ F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library ($+6.3$ points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27119v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

title: One panic shouldn't kill the scan: isolating rules with catch_unwind
description:
Cloud Cost Analyzer runs 92 rules against your cloud account in a single scan. A rule is a real unit of work: it pulls a resource's config and metrics, evaluates them against a cost model, and maybe emits a finding. They're independent, and every one of them leans on libraries I don't control: cloud SDKs, response parsers, date and math crates.

Any of that can meet an input it didn't anticipate and panic: an unwrap() that couldn't fail until some resource shape I'd never seen, an index out of bounds deep in a dependency, an overflow on a field that's normally small. Usually nobody wrote bad code. A library just hit an edge case nobody dependency-audited for.

The question isn't whether a rule will panic. It's what happens to the other 91 when rule

57 does. A cost report that dies two-thirds of the way through because one rule met one weird EBS volume isn't much use to anyone.

"So handle it with Result"

The obvious objection: this is Rust, so model the failure as a Result and there's nothing to catch. The rules do exactly that for every failure they can see coming. Can't reach the metrics API? Result. Missing a field the check needs? Result. Expected failures travel the normal error path and always have.

A panic is the failure I didn't foresee. You can't write ? for a bug you don't know exists, and you certainly can't for one buried three crates deep in a dependency that panics on input its author never tested. Result handles the errors you anticipated. catch_unwind covers the ones you couldn't, and it only exists in my code because Result can't reach into code I didn't write.

std::panic::catch_unwind runs a closure and hands you back a Result instead of letting the panic tear through your stack. Here's the real dispatch, one rule at a time:

let mut eval = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
    rule.evaluate(resource, metrics, costs)
}))
.unwrap_or_else(|_| {
    tracing::error!(
        rule_id = rule_id,
        resource_id = %resource.resource_id,
        "rule panicked during evaluate; skipping its finding"
    );
    None
})?;

A rule panics, we log which rule and which resource, return None for that one finding, and the loop moves on to the next rule. One panic costs one finding.

What AssertUnwindSafe actually promises

The compiler demands that wrapper, and it's worth understanding why before reaching for it.

catch_unwind only accepts a closure that's UnwindSafe. The idea: if a panic unwinds through the middle of your closure, any state it shared with the outside could be left half-updated, and UnwindSafe is the marker that says there's no such state to observe. My closure captures &rule, &resource, and friends by reference, so the compiler can't prove that on its own and refuses to compile.

AssertUnwindSafe is me telling the compiler I've checked, and that catching this panic won't let anyone observe a broken invariant. That holds here for a concrete reason: on panic I throw the result away. I return None and never read a partially-built finding. There's no torn state to see because I don't look. That's the bar for reaching for AssertUnwindSafe. You should be able to point at why the post-panic state is unobservable.

The setting that silently turns all of this off

catch_unwind only works if panics unwind, which is why it isn't a try/catch. Rust has two panic strategies, and you choose per build:

# Cargo.toml — a size-optimized profile
# Inherits all release settings, adds panic=abort to remove unwind tables
panic = "abort"

Under panic = "abort", a panic doesn't unwind the stack. It calls the abort handler and kills the process immediately, so catch_unwind never gets a chance to run. Every one of those careful per-rule guards becomes a no-op, and rule #57 takes the whole process down with it. That happens in the exact build you ship to production, because panic = "abort" is something you turn on to drop unwind tables and shrink the binary.

So panic isolation is a whole-binary decision rather than a library feature you add. If you want one bad rule to cost one finding, you have to keep the unwinding runtime, and eat the binary size, on purpose. No assert or catch_unwind call can buy that back for you. It's the trade you make once, in the profile, and it's invisible in the code that depends on it.

One more edge: poisoned locks

If a rule panics while holding a Mutex or RwLock, that lock is poisoned and the next rule to touch it inherits the panic. The isolation above holds partly because the shared data these rules read is immutable and lock-free, so there's no lock to poison. If yours mutates shared state under a lock, catching the panic isn't enough. You have to decide what a poisoned lock means.

Where it landed

Rules and the second-stage analyzers both run inside that catch_unwind, under an unwinding profile. When a rule, or a library it leans on, meets an input nobody anticipated, the cost is one missing finding and a log line naming the culprit. The isolation works because the binary is built to allow it, and I can say exactly why the post-panic state is safe to ignore: I never read it.

This is part of a series on building Cloud Cost Analyzer in Rust.

title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control
description:
arXiv:2610.27446v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.

title: Batch Deploying GBase Database with a Response File
description:
Deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s) across multiple servers can become repetitive if every installation requires manual interaction. A response file provides a more consistent approach by defining installation parameters once and reusing them across deployment targets.

Combined with shell scripts and remote execution tools such as SSH, silent installation can become part of a repeatable database deployment workflow.

The goal is not simply to install software faster. It is to make the deployment process easier to validate, maintain, and reproduce.

1. Prepare the Response File

Start by preparing a bundle.properties response file using the template supplied with your GBase Database installation media or by recording a supported interactive installation.

Review the installation directory, selected components, license-acceptance settings, and any other required parameters.

Before deploying to multiple machines, test the response file on one representative server. Confirm that the installation succeeds and that the resulting database instance can be configured and started correctly.

Keep environment-specific settings separate where necessary. Different servers may require different paths, resource configurations, or connection definitions.

2. Create a Reusable Installation Script

The following Bash example checks for the response file and installer before starting silent installation.

#!/bin/bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

RESP="/opt/bundle.properties"
INSTALLER="/opt/ids_install"

# Verify required files
[[ -f "$RESP" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing response file: $RESP" >&2
    exit 1
}

[[ -x "$INSTALLER" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Installer is missing or not executable: $INSTALLER" >&2
    exit 1
}

# Run silent installation
"$INSTALLER" -i silent \
    -f "$RESP" \
    -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

echo "Silent installation command completed."

Save the script as install_gbase.sh and make it executable:

chmod +x install_gbase.sh

The script uses set -Eeuo pipefail to help detect command failures and prevent certain errors from being silently ignored.

The installer command shown here is an example. Confirm its supported options and license-acceptance requirements against the documentation for your specific installation package.

Also note that a successful installer exit does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for application connections. Post-installation configuration and validation remain necessary.

3. Execute the Installation on Multiple Servers

For a small environment, SSH and SCP can distribute the response file and execute the installation script remotely.

For example:

#!/bin/bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

RESP="/opt/bundle.properties"
SCRIPT="/opt/install_gbase.sh"
HOSTS=(node1 node2 node3)

[[ -f "$RESP" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing response file" >&2
    exit 1
}

[[ -f "$SCRIPT" ]] || {
    echo "ERROR: Missing installation script" >&2
    exit 1
}

for host in "${HOSTS[@]}"; do
    echo "Deploying to $host..."

    scp "$RESP" "$SCRIPT" "root@$host:/opt/"

    ssh "root@$host" \
        "bash /opt/install_gbase.sh"

    echo "Installation command completed on $host."
done

This example processes the hosts sequentially, which makes execution easier to follow and failures easier to isolate.

Before using it, ensure that SSH authentication, host-key verification, remote permissions, and installation prerequisites are configured correctly.

The example also assumes that the installer is already available at /opt/ids_install on every target server. If it is not, include distribution and verification of the installation media in the deployment workflow.

Important: Running the installer as root should follow the supported installation procedure. Instance initialization may require switching to the designated database account, such as gbasedbt. Do not assume installation and initialization use the same account.

4. Add Post-Installation Configuration and Validation

Batch installation should not stop when the installer exits.

A complete GBase Database deployment workflow should also address:

  • Environment variables: Configure the required instance-specific environment.
  • Configuration files: Review onconfig and sqlhosts for the target server.
  • Instance initialization: Run the documented initialization procedure using the appropriate operating system account.
  • Service validation: Confirm that the instance starts and client connections succeed.
  • Logging: Record the host, installation result, and relevant diagnostic output.

These steps should be implemented according to the selected installation method and the requirements of your environment.

Avoid reporting a server as successfully deployed until the required validation checks have passed.

5. Make Batch Deployment Reproducible

For larger deployments, consider a few additional safeguards.

Version-control the response file and scripts. Review changes before they are used in production.

Protect sensitive configuration. Do not store passwords, private keys, or other secrets in ordinary response files or source repositories.

Control deployment concurrency. Start with sequential execution. Introduce parallel deployment only after validating resource requirements and failure handling.

Make reruns safe. Check whether a target already has an installation or running instance before executing the installer again. A failed deployment should not automatically trigger an unsafe reinstall.

Maintain a recovery procedure. Record installation logs and define how failed or partially completed deployments will be investigated and corrected.

For larger fleets, configuration-management tools can provide better inventory management, controlled concurrency, and centralized execution reporting than a collection of ad hoc shell commands.

Conclusion

Batch deployment of GBase Database(GBase 8s) starts with a validated response file and a reliable installation script. SSH and SCP can extend that workflow across multiple machines, while configuration management and automated checks help maintain consistency as the environment grows.

The essential principle is simple: standardize the installation inputs, validate the results, and make failures visible.

How does your team manage database deployments across multiple servers: shell scripts, SSH automation, or a configuration-management platform?

title: Skip sending request bodies to Routing Middleware

Enable this option only if your Routing Middleware doesn’t read request bodies. Vercel Functions and rewrite targets still receive the body, so you can read and process it there.

Set skipMiddlewareRequestBody to true in your project’s JSON configuration file, vercel.json:

If you use a TypeScript configuration file, add the same setting to vercel.ts instead. This example assumes @vercel/config is installed:

Redeploy your project for the change to take effect. The option defaults to false, so existing projects are unchanged unless you enable it.
