title: PerQ: Inverse Generative Modeling for Neural Image Compression via Quantization Error Compensation
description:
arXiv:2610.27374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural image codecs face a fundamental trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality. Distortion-optimized codecs preserve pixel-wise fidelity but produce blurred reconstructions at low bitrates, whereas generative codecs leverage learned priors to improve perceptual quality but tend to exhibit saturating PSNR at higher bitrates and require separate models for different bitrate targets. We propose PerQ, which reframes perceptual reconstruction as inverse generative modeling with bounded support. Specifically, we define the quantization cell as the set of latents that yield the same transmitted symbols and derive a transport bound showing that reconstructions from this cell remain within a rate-determined radius of the codec output. This motivates performing generative reconstruction within the codec-induced quantization cell, rather than sampling from an unconstrained image prior. PerQ implements this principle by attaching a rate-conditioned flow-matching compensator to a frozen, multi-rate distortion-optimized backbone, enabling perceptual enhancement while preserving the backbone's coding performance. Experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 show that PerQ achieves perceptual performance comparable to generative codecs such as MS-ILLM in LPIPS and FID, while maintaining competitive PSNR relative to distortion-optimized codecs such as ELIC. A single model checkpoint supports a wide bitrate range with fast decoding, and the compensator provides consistent gains across three different backbones. The implementation is available at https://jasminepp.github.io/PerQ/.

title: Node.js Background Worker HTTPS Push Subscriptions — Receiving Queued Logistics Jobs
description:
Short answer: a Node.js background worker can receive queued jobs through a public HTTPS push subscription, but it should authenticate every request and acknowledge only after an idempotent reservation transition.n that expires after a fixed hold window, use an authenticated HTTPS push endpoint, acknowledge only after an idempotent state transition, and make retries boring.

Keep the edge boring. It is not glamorous, but it is where auth belongs.\n\nThe useful mental model is a conveyor belt. A scheduler puts an expiry job on the belt; a public worker endpoint receives it; a database decides whether the reservation can still move to expired. Delivery is at-least-once in most practical queue systems, so duplicate messages are normal input, not an exceptional path.

What should a Node.js worker check before accepting queued jobs securely?

Start with the message contract, not the framework. The payload needs a stable jobId, reservationId, holdUntil, and an event type such as reservation.expire. The producer should include an expiry timestamp, while the worker uses the database clock for the final decision. Client-supplied time is useful context, not authority.

Delivery choice Pick this when Main cost
HTTPS push to a worker Jobs are irregular and you want low idle overhead Public ingress, signature verification, and replay controls
Long polling Your network cannot accept inbound HTTPS Open connections and slower scale-out behavior
Pulling from a broker You need consumer-controlled rate and ordering More worker state and operational plumbing
A cron sweep The job is naturally periodic and lateness is acceptable Coarse timing and repeated scans

For a reservation hold, push is a good fit when the queue can retry delivery and the worker can answer quickly. A cron sweep remains reasonable for a small system that can tolerate a few minutes of delay. The choice is about failure handling, not fashion.

A retry-safe expiration path in Express or Fastify

Treat the HTTPS handler as an adapter. Authentication, schema validation, and a short transaction belong at the edge; business work belongs behind a function that both Express and Fastify can call.

type ExpiryJob = {
  jobId: string;
  reservationId: string;
  holdUntil: string;
  event: "reservation.expire";
};

type ReservationStore = {
  expireIfHeld: (reservationId: string, now: Date) => Promise<"expired" | "already_done" | "not_due">;
};

export function makeExpiryHandler(store: ReservationStore, verify: (raw: string, signature: string) => boolean) {
  return async (request: { body: string; headers: Record<string, string | undefined> }, reply: { code: (n: number) => { send: (v: unknown) => void }; send: (v: unknown) => void }) => {
    const signature = request.headers["x-queue-signature"];
    if (!signature || !verify(request.body, signature)) return reply.code(401).send({ error: "unauthorized" });

    let job: ExpiryJob;
    try {
      job = JSON.parse(request.body) as ExpiryJob;
    } catch {
      return reply.code(400).send({ error: "invalid_json" });
    }
    if (job.event !== "reservation.expire" || !job.jobId || !job.reservationId) {
      return reply.code(400).send({ error: "invalid_job" });
    }

    const result = await store.expireIfHeld(job.reservationId, new Date());
    // A duplicate delivery gets the same successful acknowledgement.
    return reply.send({ accepted: true, outcome: result });
  };
}

The transaction should look like UPDATE reservations SET status = 'expired' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'held' AND hold_until <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Check the affected-row count. One row means this delivery won the transition; zero rows means another attempt already handled it or the hold is not due. Put a unique constraint on jobId if you retain a delivery ledger, but do not use that ledger as a substitute for the conditional state change.

I once started with a boolean processed flag in a design review. It sounded tidy until two workers read false before either wrote true. The repair was to make the reservation transition itself the idempotency key. That small change also made metrics honest: duplicates are counted, while inventory is changed once.

Return a 2xx only after the durable decision is complete. Return a retryable status for a transient dependency timeout, and make the queue's backoff bounded with jitter. A five-second first retry and a maximum delivery age are easier to reason about than an infinite storm.

Making public HTTPS delivery observable

Log one structured record per delivery: jobId, reservationId, attempt number, outcome, and latency. Never log the signature or full customer payload. Emit counters for accepted, duplicate, rejected, and expired-too-early jobs; alert on a rising rejected rate and on age of the oldest queued job.

A trace should connect enqueue, delivery, database transition, and acknowledgement. The useful dashboard is a before/after: queue age and held reservations before the worker change, then the same two measures after. Your mileage may vary when traffic is bursty; use a 95th-percentile age window rather than a single average.

Test the ugly cases deliberately. Send the same jobId twice in parallel, deliver a job before holdUntil, replay a valid signed body after its maximum age, and kill the process after the database commit but before the response. The expected result is one expiry, a successful duplicate acknowledgement, and a retry that cannot create a second side effect.

A useful failure drill follows one reservation from enqueue to reconciliation. Imagine reservation R-1842 with a 15-minute hold. The scheduler emits one job at minute 15, the queue delivers it twice because the first acknowledgement is delayed, and a deploy restarts the worker between the SQL commit and the HTTP response. The first transaction matches status = held and hold_until <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, changing exactly one row. The duplicate sees zero affected rows and returns a normal success response. After the restart, the redelivery sees the same zero-row result. Metrics show two deliveries, one state transition, and no inventory double-release. Now move the clock to minute 14: the conditional update changes nothing, and the handler returns not_due; the queue should treat that as a completed delivery only if the job policy allows early delivery to be discarded. Otherwise, schedule a delayed retry based on the remaining hold window. This is why a single processed flag is weak: it records a message, while the reservation row records the business truth. The same test works against an in-memory store in unit tests and a real transactional database in an integration test. Keep both.

Limits and a practical decision rule

The trade-off is clear: this limitation matters. Public HTTPS push is not suitable when policy forbids inbound traffic or when work routinely exceeds the queue's acknowledgement deadline. Choose a pull-based consumer in that environment. Long polling is also a better boundary when signatures cannot be verified at the edge.

This pattern does not provide ordering across different reservations, and it cannot make a non-transactional downstream API idempotent by itself. Use an outbox or a downstream idempotency key when expiry triggers a carrier call. Keep a cron sweep as a reconciliation path, but make it issue the same conditional update instead of inventing a second expiration rule.

The rule is simple: select the delivery mode your team can observe, authenticate, retry, and replay safely. For fixed-window logistics holds, that usually means a small HTTPS adapter wrapped around one database transition.

References

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://nodejs.org/api/http.html

title: SuperClip Pyramid for Video Temporal Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.26925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.

title: Limit agent permissions and spend in AWS Transform custom
description: AWS Transform custom runs an autonomous agent with shell access over your source code, using your AWS credentials. This post bounds it with three controls: a scoped trust allowlist, an execution identity separate from the one that authors, and a per-run agent-minute cap backed by an account budget.

title: LAMB: Latent Multi-Hypothesis Beliefs for Long-Horizon Large Language Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.26955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon language agents require compact memories that retain interaction evidence while preserving competing hypotheses about unobserved states. Although effective, many belief-state methods encode memory in discrete natural language, where repeated compression can omit evidence or prematurely discard plausible alternatives. We introduce LAMB, a recurrent framework for latent multi-hypothesis beliefs. A Common--Delta factorization combines a shared Common state for interaction evidence with weighted Delta components for competing hypotheses. Relative evidence from action-outcome predictions guides recurrent hypothesis updates without generating textual memory. A context-conditioned readout exposes hypotheses separately to the policy through a fixed-token belief prefix in the default configuration. The belief modules and policy are jointly trained using action imitation and auxiliary state, outcome, and observation-discrimination objectives. Across ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, LAMB matches or outperforms PABU, improving ALFWorld SR@30 and ScienceWorld success by 6.0 and 22.0 percentage points, respectively, and Crafter achievement progress by 26.37 points. On ALFWorld, it also reduces the redundant-action rate by 17.70 percentage points. These results support latent multi-hypothesis beliefs as compact memory for effective long-horizon decision making

title: SciFigBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Method Figure Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.27087v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper's methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse-grained tasks, such as context-based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine-grained content and inter-module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real-world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question-answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training-free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow-induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method-figure reasoning. Experiments across open-source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.

title: Implementing DDD and Hexagonal Architecture in NestJS: A Complete Practical Guide
description:
1. When a service starts doing everything

A NestJS application often begins with a controller, a service, and a few Prisma calls. That structure is easy to understand when the business operation is “save these fields.” Then the requirements change.

An order needs a technician before work can be registered. Required tasks must be completed before finalization. A visit must fit the technician's schedule. Closing an order must record a business event together with the updated state.

When all those decisions live in services that also handle HTTP responses and database records, changing one rule means navigating several technical concerns. Testing the rule can require constructing much more of the application than the rule itself needs.

In this guide, we will follow a service-management API built with TypeScript, NestJS, Prisma, and PostgreSQL. We will use Domain-Driven Design (DDD) to express business behavior and Hexagonal Architecture to control dependencies around it.

You should be comfortable with TypeScript classes, interfaces, async functions, and basic NestJS controllers. You do not need previous DDD experience. The goal is to understand where each responsibility belongs and how the pieces fit together.

The complete example is available in nest-ddd-hexagonal on GitHub. The snippets below are selected from that project; excerpts omit unrelated code and imports where indicated. This is an educational implementation with concrete limits, which we will discuss alongside its benefits.

2. Start with the business and its language

Imagine a company that sends technicians to customer sites. A service order captures the work commitment: customer, contract, address, service level, required tasks, performed activities, and materials used. A visit captures a scheduled appointment with a technician.

The project organizes those concerns into two modules:

Module Main concepts Responsibilities
service-orders ServiceOrder, activities, materials, required tasks Record work, enforce the order lifecycle, finalize and close orders
visits Technician, Visit, TimeSlot, TechnicianAvailability Register technicians, schedule visits, check availability, cancel appointments

These modules are candidate context boundaries within a modular monolith. They run in the same process and share PostgreSQL, while maintaining separate models and application contracts. A directory alone does not establish a bounded context; the useful boundary comes from ownership of language, rules, and integration.

Several requirements make this example useful beyond basic CRUD:

  • Service level determines order priority.
  • A technician must be assigned before activities or materials can be registered.
  • Finalization requires at least one activity and no pending required tasks.
  • Closing requires prior finalization and records a domain event.
  • Visits last between 30 minutes and four hours and cannot start in the past.
  • Scheduling checks technician activity, overlapping visits, order status, and assignment.

DDD helps us turn these sentences into named operations. order.finalize() communicates a business decision more directly than assigning a status field in an HTTP handler. Those names also give tests a useful vocabulary.

3. Dependencies point toward the core

In Alistair Cockburn's original Hexagonal Architecture article, the application can be driven and tested independently of its external interfaces. Ports describe interactions with the application; adapters connect those interactions to particular technologies.

This repository implements that idea through three layers:

Layer Owns Depends on
Domain Business concepts, invariants, behavior, domain errors Its own model and standard runtime APIs
Application Use cases and contracts for external capabilities Domain and application ports
Infrastructure HTTP, DTO validation, persistence, integration adapters Application, domain, and technical libraries

The core consists of domain and application. In this project, neither imports NestJS or Prisma. It does use standard Node.js APIs such as randomUUID, so framework independence does not imply independence from every runtime.

The following arrows represent source-code dependencies:

HTTP controller ----------> Use case ----------> Domain model
                               |
                               v
                        Application port
                               ^
                               |
Prisma adapter ----------------+
       |
       v
Prisma client / PostgreSQL

Nest module: selects adapters and constructs use cases

At runtime, the use case calls an adapter through the port. The dependency direction remains inward because the use case imports the interface, while the adapter implements that interface.

The repository places outgoing ports in application/ports, where the use cases consume them. Putting ports in the domain can also be reasonable when that layer owns the contract. Hexagonal Architecture does not require one universal folder location.

Incoming operations are exposed through use-case methods. Controllers call them directly; there is no additional interface for every incoming port. The important question is whether the core can execute independently of HTTP and persistence.

4. Organize by capability, then by layer

Here is a shortened view of the project:

src/
├── main.ts
├── app.module.ts
├── shared/
│   ├── domain/
│   └── infrastructure/
└── modules/
    ├── service-orders/
    │   ├── domain/
    │   │   ├── model/
    │   │   ├── events/
    │   │   └── errors/
    │   ├── application/
    │   │   ├── ports/
    │   │   └── use-cases/
    │   ├── infrastructure/
    │   │   ├── http/
    │   │   └── persistence/
    │   └── service-orders.module.ts
    └── visits/
        ├── domain/
        ├── application/
        ├── infrastructure/
        │   ├── http/
        │   ├── persistence/
        │   └── integration/
        └── visits.module.ts

prisma/    # Schema and SQL migrations
test/      # Domain, application, HTTP, and adapter tests

Grouping by business capability keeps related work close together. Within each module, the three layers explain responsibilities. This follows the feature-first organization often associated with vertical slicing, although the repository also retains explicit layers within each module.

The result is easier to navigate than global folders containing every controller, every service, and every entity. It does not make modules automatically independent: visits integrates with service-orders, so extracting one would still require addressing that integration and the shared database.

The shared directory contains small mechanisms such as DomainError, DomainEvent, and AggregateRoot, plus infrastructure support. Business models remain in their owning modules. A shared generic repository would add little value when each module has different persistence needs.

5. Model rules inside the domain

5.1 An aggregate protects a consistency boundary

ServiceOrder is the aggregate root for the order and its child collections. Code changes the order through operations such as assignTechnician, addActivity, completeRequiredTask, finalize, and close.

An aggregate defines a boundary within which related state and rules are managed together. In this implementation, the repository persists the root, activities, materials, and required tasks as one transactional snapshot.

The main lifecycle is:

CREATED -> ASSIGNED -> IN_PROGRESS -> FINALIZED -> CLOSED
             ^              |
             |              +-- activities or materials start work
             +-- technician assignment can be changed before work starts

Finalization additionally requires:
  assigned technician + at least one activity + all required tasks completed

The aggregate implementation has a private constructor and separate factories for creation and rehydration. Creation derives priority from service level and starts the order in CREATED. Rehydration reconstructs an existing order and validates snapshot consistency without replaying business operations.

Here is the actual finalize method, shown without the surrounding class:

finalize(now = new Date()): void {
  this.ensureOperationallyMutable();
  this.ensureTechnicianAssigned();

  if (this.activitiesValue.length === 0) throw new ActivityRequiredError();

  const pending = this.requiredTasksValue
    .filter((task) => !task.completedAt)
    .map((task) => task.id);

  if (pending.length > 0) throw new PendingRequiredTasksError(pending);

  if (this.statusValue !== ServiceOrderStatus.IN_PROGRESS) {
    throw new ServiceOrderInvalidStateError(
      `Only an in-progress service order can be finalized; current state is ${this.statusValue}`,
    );
  }

  const latestWork = Math.max(
    this.createdAtValue.getTime(),
    ...this.activitiesValue.map((activity) => activity.performedAt.getTime()),
    ...this.requiredTasksValue.map((task) => task.completedAt?.getTime() ?? 0),
  );

  const finalizedAt = validDate(now, 'finalizedAt', new Date(latestWork));
  this.statusValue = ServiceOrderStatus.FINALIZED;
  this.finalizedAtValue = finalizedAt;
}

The operation validates its prerequisites before changing status. Registering material alone moves an assigned order into progress, but still does not satisfy the activity requirement for finalization. The timestamp must also be consistent with the recorded work.

These rules apply whether a controller, a test, or a future batch adapter invokes the model. They remain meaningful without any knowledge of status codes or database columns.

5.2 Encapsulation requires protecting references

The aggregate is mutable through its methods. Its getters return frozen child snapshots and copied dates, preventing callers from modifying internal collections indirectly.

That detail matters in JavaScript: readonly is a compile-time restriction, and a Date can change even when its containing property cannot be reassigned. Copying dates on input and output protects the aggregate from those reference mutations.

The implementation also validates rehydrated metadata, child identifiers, lifecycle dates, and state consistency. This is a deliberate safety choice with extra validation cost. Persisted data still crosses a boundary and must be converted into a valid model.

5.3 A value object gives time intervals a meaning

Technician and Visit are entities: their identity persists as their state changes. TimeSlot is a value object: it describes an interval through its values, without a separate identifier or lifecycle. Its role is to represent a valid interval and answer questions about it. The complete source includes date-validation and duration helpers; this excerpt contains its main behavior:

export class TimeSlot {
  private constructor(
    private readonly startsAtValue: Date,
    private readonly endsAtValue: Date,
  ) {}

  static create(startsAt: Date, endsAt: Date): TimeSlot {
    if (!isValidDate(startsAt) || !isValidDate(endsAt)) {
      throw new InvalidTimeSlotError('Start and end dates must be valid dates');
    }

    const durationHours = getDiffHours(startsAt, endsAt);

    if (durationHours < 0.5 || durationHours > 4) {
      throw new InvalidTimeSlotError('Duration must be between 30 minutes and 4 hours');
    }

    return new TimeSlot(new Date(startsAt), new Date(endsAt));
  }

  get startsAt(): Date {
    return new Date(this.startsAtValue);
  }

  get endsAt(): Date {
    return new Date(this.endsAtValue);
  }

  overlaps(other: TimeSlot): boolean {
    return this.startsAt < other.endsAt && other.startsAt < this.endsAt;
  }
}

Intervals that touch at their endpoints are allowed: 10:00–11:00 and 11:00–12:00 do not overlap. The strict comparisons encode that boundary explicitly.

Whether an interval starts in the past belongs to Visit.schedule, which receives now. An interval can be valid in isolation even when it is unsuitable for a new appointment. Separating those concepts makes each rule easier to understand.

5.4 Use a domain service for rules across objects

Availability depends on a technician, a requested interval, and existing visits. TechnicianAvailability receives those objects and rejects inactive technicians or overlapping scheduled visits.

It does not fetch records. The application supplies the information, and the domain service evaluates it. Cancelled visits do not block the interval, and visits belonging to other technicians do not cause a conflict.

This is a useful distinction when naming services: the domain service makes a business decision, while the application use case coordinates the data and steps needed to reach that decision.

Domain failures use typed errors derived from DomainError. They express concepts such as PendingRequiredTasksError and TechnicianUnavailableError without choosing their HTTP representation.

6. Let use cases coordinate the work

6.1 Define the capability the application needs

The service-order repository port exposes three operations:

import type { ServiceOrder } from '../../domain/model/service-order';

export const SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY = Symbol('SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY');

export interface ServiceOrderRepository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<ServiceOrder | null>;
  insert(order: ServiceOrder): Promise<void>;
  save(order: ServiceOrder): Promise<void>;
}

The contract speaks in domain objects. It does not expose Prisma arguments, SQL transactions, or HTTP responses. Separating insertion from saving also allows the adapter to distinguish a new aggregate from an existing one.

The finalization use case is correspondingly small. Imports are omitted here:

export class FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase extends ServiceOrderUseCaseBase {
  constructor(repository: ServiceOrderRepository) {
    super(repository);
  }

  async execute(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    const order = await this.loadOrThrow(orderId);
    order.finalize();
    await this.repository.save(order);
  }
}

The base class only loads the order and raises ServiceOrderNotFoundError when needed. The use case owns the sequence; the aggregate owns finalization rules; the repository owns persistence.

No Nest decorator is needed. A unit test can construct this class directly with a repository double.

6.2 A more involved example: schedule a visit

ScheduleVisitUseCase depends on four collaborators:

// Constructor excerpt from ScheduleVisitUseCase.
constructor(
  private readonly technicians: TechnicianRepository,
  private readonly visits: VisitRepository,
  private readonly serviceOrders: ServiceOrderLookup,
  private readonly availability: TechnicianAvailability,
) {}

Its command contains serviceOrderId, technicianId, startsAt, endsAt, and now, with dates represented as Date objects. HTTP string parsing happens before entering this boundary.

The use case creates the interval, loads the technician and order information, and checks that the order is CREATED or ASSIGNED. If the order already has an assigned technician, that technician must match the request. It also rejects an existing scheduled visit for that order.

Next it loads the technician's scheduled visits, asks the availability service to evaluate them, constructs Visit, and inserts it. Scheduling a visit does not automatically assign a technician to the service order; those are separate operations in the current model.

The split is practical: rules using the order information available to scheduling stay in the application, interval rules stay in TimeSlot, appointment lifecycle rules stay in Visit, and availability rules stay in the domain service.

Passing now makes scheduling deterministic in tests. The HTTP adapter currently supplies new Date(). Other order operations still use default timestamps, and there is no shared clock abstraction in this repository.

7. Connect HTTP and persistence through adapters

7.1 HTTP adapts request data to a command

The HTTP layer owns route decorators, Swagger metadata, DTOs, and request validation. Nest's global ValidationPipe uses whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted, and transform.

For visit scheduling, DTO validation checks UUIDs, strict ISO date strings, and explicit timezones. The controller converts those strings into dates and supplies the current time:

// Method excerpt from VisitsController; imports and constructor omitted.
@Post()
@ApiCreatedResponse({ description: 'Visit scheduled' })
async schedule(@Body() dto: ScheduleVisitDto): Promise<{ id: string }> {
  const id = await this.scheduleVisit.execute({
    serviceOrderId: dto.serviceOrderId,
    technicianId: dto.technicianId,
    startsAt: new Date(dto.startsAt),
    endsAt: new Date(dto.endsAt),
    now: new Date(),
  });

  return { id };
}

Another useful translation occurs when creating an order: the HTTP DTO accepts requiredTasks as objects with name, while the application receives an array of strings. A transport shape does not have to become the domain's shape.

Boundary validation and domain validation serve different callers. An invalid request should fail early, while direct application calls must still respect business invariants. A structurally valid date string can describe an interval that the business rejects.

7.2 Translate domain errors at the boundary

DomainExceptionFilter catches DomainError and maps its code to HTTP. For example:

Domain condition HTTP status
Technician or service order not found 404
Invalid interval or pending required tasks 422
Technician unavailable or invalid order transition 409
Optimistic concurrency conflict 409

DTO and pipe failures return 400. Domain failures produce a JSON body with statusCode, error, and message. Unmapped domain codes become 500 and are logged by the filter.

The domain can therefore evolve its rules without importing HttpException, and a future non-HTTP adapter can translate the same errors differently.

7.3 Persistence converts records into models

PrismaServiceOrderRepository implements the application port. Its findById loads the root and child records, maps database enums, converts nullable values, and calls ServiceOrder.rehydrate.

For writes, it stores a complete snapshot in a transaction: the root is inserted or updated, previous child rows are deleted, and the current collections are inserted. Pending domain events are written to the Outbox within that transaction as well.

This approach is straightforward for an educational aggregate with moderate collections. Its write cost grows with collection size because even unchanged children are replaced. A larger workload might justify tracking child changes or revisiting the aggregate boundary.

The Prisma schema represents persistence relationships. The domain model represents behavior. Keeping both explicit costs mapping code, but prevents a generated database record from becoming the only representation of the business.

8. Use NestJS as the composition point

TypeScript interfaces disappear at runtime. Nest therefore needs a runtime token to identify each outgoing dependency. This project uses symbols and factory providers.

The following is an excerpt of the providers in ServiceOrdersModule:

providers: [
  {
    provide: FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase,
    inject: [SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY],
    useFactory: (repository: ServiceOrderRepository) =>
      new FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase(repository),
  },
  { provide: SERVICE_ORDER_REPOSITORY, useClass: PrismaServiceOrderRepository },
],

The adapter can use @Injectable() because it lives in infrastructure. The factory creates the plain application class and supplies its dependency. This is the connection between compile-time contracts and runtime objects, using Nest's custom provider facilities.

Modules are allowed to know concrete implementations: assembling those implementations is their job. The application itself does not select a repository or create a Prisma client.

In tests, the same use case can receive an in-memory adapter or a mock. Replacing an adapter remains subject to its contract and semantics; a remote store would introduce failure and consistency concerns that wiring alone cannot solve.

9. Integrate modules through a local contract

Visits needs a small amount of order information to decide whether scheduling is allowed. It declares its own contract rather than importing the complete order aggregate:

export interface ServiceOrderSchedulingInfo {
  id: string;
  status: 'CREATED' | 'ASSIGNED' | 'IN_PROGRESS' | 'FINALIZED' | 'CLOSED';
  assignedTechnicianId?: string;
}

export interface ServiceOrderLookup {
  findById(id: string): Promise<ServiceOrderSchedulingInfo | null>;
}

export const SERVICE_ORDER_LOOKUP = Symbol('SERVICE_ORDER_LOOKUP');

The ServiceOrderLookupAdapter calls the exported GetServiceOrderUseCase and maps its result to that local shape. It translates a missing-order error to null and propagates unexpected errors.

Visits application        Visits infrastructure       Orders application

ScheduleVisitUseCase
        |
        v
ServiceOrderLookup <----- ServiceOrderLookupAdapter --> GetServiceOrderUseCase
 (local contract)            (translation)                (exported by module)

The concrete cross-module dependency is concentrated in the adapter and module composition. The scheduling use case knows the local port, while VisitsModule imports ServiceOrdersModule to wire the adapter.

This is synchronous communication within one process. The order-closed event does not drive visit scheduling in the current implementation. Moving the integration to messaging would require new behavior around delivery, stale information, and retries.

10. Advanced concerns: reads, concurrent writes, and events

10.1 Shape reads around their consumers

Loading a complete aggregate makes sense when enforcing a state change. A list page usually needs a smaller view. service-orders separates ServiceOrderRepository from ServiceOrderQuery, whose methods return application views.

PrismaServiceOrderQuery maps records directly to those views without rehydrating an aggregate. List results are ordered by createdAt and id, both descending. The cursor carries both values so equal timestamps still have a deterministic order.

The adapter fetches one extra record to determine whether a next cursor exists. The use case validates limits between 1 and 100, with a default of 25, and validates filters and cursor data.

This is a pragmatic separation of reads and writes within one application and database. There are no command buses or asynchronous read projections. The visits module uses its repositories for reads; the example does not force both modules into identical abstractions.

10.2 Detect stale aggregate writes

Suppose two requests load order version 3. Both change their local object. Without a version check, the second save could overwrite the first request's work.

On update, the repository performs this check inside its transaction. The excerpt omits the surrounding persistence work:

const result = await tx.serviceOrderRecord.updateMany({
  where: { id: order.id, version: expectedVersion },
  data: { ...updateInput, version: { increment: 1 } },
});

if (result.count !== 1) throw new ServiceOrderConcurrencyError(order.id);

Only a matching version can advance. A stale write fails before replacing children or storing its events. New objects start at version 0 in memory and are inserted at version 1.

After the transaction commits, acknowledgePersistence advances the in-memory version and clears only the persisted event IDs. If persistence fails, the object keeps its previous version and pending events. The code does not automatically retry a stale business operation; the caller receives a conflict.

The repository also maps relevant Prisma errors to a concurrency error. See the complete adapter for its transaction and error handling.

10.3 Persist domain events atomically with state

Closing an order records ServiceOrderClosedEvent, named service-orders.service-order.closed.v1. Its payload includes order and contract IDs, worked minutes, materials, and the closure timestamp.

The repository copies pending events before entering the transaction and inserts each into outbox_events:

// Inside the same transaction that persists the aggregate.
for (const event of events) {
  await tx.outboxEventRecord.create({
    data: {
      id: event.eventId,
      eventName: event.eventName,
      aggregateId: event.aggregateId,
      payload: event.toPrimitives(),
      occurredAt: event.occurredAt,
    },
  });
}

The intended database guarantee is that the order state, children, and Outbox rows commit together or roll back together. This avoids a separate database write followed by a publication attempt that could be lost between the two steps.

There is currently no publisher worker, broker, or event consumer. publishedAt exists in the schema, but nothing in the repository marks events as delivered. Reliable publication would need a worker, retry behavior, and consumer idempotency. Outbox storage alone does not provide exactly-once delivery.

This is also different from Event Sourcing: the repository stores current aggregate state and selected events, rather than rebuilding orders from an event history.

10.4 Know where the guarantees stop

Visit scheduling reads availability and then inserts a visit. Two concurrent requests can both observe a free interval and both proceed. The schema has indexes for these queries, but no exclusion constraint or equivalent mechanism preventing overlaps or duplicate scheduled visits per order.

The service-order version check does not protect scheduling, technician deactivation, or cross-module reads. Those guarantees would need a separate design using appropriate database constraints, locking, or transaction isolation. Defining a rule in the domain and enforcing it under concurrency are related but distinct engineering tasks.

11. Test the behavior at each boundary

11.1 Domain tests require only the model

This test from the aggregate suite demonstrates the finalization rule. Imports and the createOrder fixture are omitted; the fixture creates an order with one pending required task:

it('cannot finalize while required tasks are pending', () => {
  const order = createOrder();
  order.assignTechnician(randomUUID());
  order.addActivity('Inspection', 30);

  expect(() => order.finalize()).toThrow(PendingRequiredTasksError);
});

No Nest module or database is involved. Other domain tests cover lifecycle transitions, snapshot integrity, copied dates, duration boundaries, overlapping versus adjacent intervals, and cancellation rules.

11.2 Application tests substitute outgoing ports

The finalization suite uses a real aggregate and a repository double. This is its successful path, without imports:

it('persists the finalized aggregate', async () => {
  const order = ServiceOrder.create({
    customerId: randomUUID(),
    contractId: randomUUID(),
    serviceAddress: 'Plant 1',
    serviceLevel: ServiceLevel.STANDARD,
  });

  order.assignTechnician(randomUUID());
  order.addActivity('Repair', 60);

  const repository = {
    findById: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(order),
    insert: jest.fn(),
    save: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  } satisfies ServiceOrderRepository;

  await new FinalizeServiceOrderUseCase(repository).execute(order.id);
  expect(repository.save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(order);
  expect(order.status).toBe(ServiceOrderStatus.FINALIZED);
});

The missing-order test also verifies that nothing is saved. This checks orchestration while leaving persistence mechanics to adapter tests.

11.3 Be precise about what integration tests prove

The current suite uses Jest, ts-jest, and Supertest:

Test level Real behavior exercised Replaced dependency
Domain Invariants and state changes None of the domain objects
Application Finalization coordination Repository
Visits HTTP Nest routing, DTOs, filters, real use cases Persistence and lookup ports
Module integration adapter Mapping and error translation External use case
Persistence and queries Prisma call contracts and mapping Prisma client

The HTTP tests open a local port and need permission to bind it. The persistence tests verify calls and application behavior around transactions using doubles; they do not demonstrate real PostgreSQL rollback, isolation, or races.

Run the suite and build with:

npm test -- --runInBand
npm run build

CI generates the Prisma client, runs tests, and builds on Node.js 22. It does not start PostgreSQL. A useful next validation layer would exercise migrations, transactions, and concurrent requests against a real disposable database. Existing coverage is useful without implying that every use case has exhaustive tests.

12. Run the project and follow an order

Use Node.js 22 or newer, npm, and Docker Compose. The project uses NestJS 11 and Prisma 6, with PostgreSQL 16 in Compose. Follow the repository's versions when reproducing these examples.

From a fresh checkout:

git clone https://github.com/Carlosgmdev/nest-ddd-hexagonal.git
cd nest-ddd-hexagonal
cp .env.example .env
npm install
docker compose up -d --wait
npm run prisma:generate
npm run db:deploy
npm run start:dev

db:deploy applies committed migrations; db:migrate is for creating migrations during development. The default database connection and port are in .env.example.

Swagger is available at http://localhost:3000/docs. The routes use /api, and GET /api/health returns a static application status rather than checking database connectivity.

First, register a technician:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/technicians \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ana Martinez"}'

Create an order without required tasks for a shorter walkthrough:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "customerId":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
    "contractId":"22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
    "serviceAddress":"Industrial Avenue 1200, Plant 2",
    "serviceLevel":"PREMIUM",
    "requiredTasks":[]
  }'

Both endpoints return { "id": "..." }. The customer and contract UUIDs are illustrative: this example has no customer or contract module validating their existence. Use the returned order and technician IDs in the next requests.

Replace <order-id> and <technician-id> in the following commands:

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/technician-assignment' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"technicianId":"<technician-id>"}'

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/activities' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"description":"Electrical inspection","workedMinutes":30}'

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/finalize'

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>/close'

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/service-orders/<order-id>'

The mutation endpoints above return 204. The final read shows CLOSED, the activity, and lifecycle timestamps. The closure also persists an Outbox row, which can be inspected with npm run db:studio.

To explore visits, use a new order that is still CREATED or ASSIGNED, then call POST /api/visits with its ID, the technician ID, and future startsAt/endsAt values containing a timezone. Try a 15-minute slot, adjacent appointments, an overlap, and cancellation through POST /api/visits/:id/cancel. Swagger documents the request shapes.

13. Choose the structure when its benefits justify the cost

This approach makes business behavior easier to locate and test. Nest handles transport and composition, Prisma handles database access, and the core expresses the work the company performs. New entry points can reuse application operations, while adapters contain technology-specific translations.

The costs are real: more classes, mapping code, provider definitions, and contracts to maintain. A small application with simple data operations may be clearer with fewer abstractions. Business complexity, expected change, and testing needs provide better reasons for this structure than a desire to draw a hexagon.

The most useful lessons from this project are concrete: name operations in business terms, keep rules with the model that owns them, make external needs explicit through ports, and compose implementations at the edge. Test those boundaries and document exactly which consistency guarantees the current code provides.

If you extend the example, start with one new business rule and follow it through domain behavior, application coordination, adapters, and tests. Improvements such as real database integration tests, scheduling concurrency protection, and an Outbox publisher should each solve a specific observed need.

References and related reading

  • Complete NestJS example and README
  • Hexagonal Architecture — Alistair Cockburn
  • Custom providers — NestJS
  • TypeScript classes
  • My related guide: Implementing Hexagonal Architecture in React

What rule in your application currently requires a framework or database to test? That can be a useful place to begin applying these boundaries.

title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

title: Less is More: Concise Retrieval and Critic-based Re-ranking for Composed Image Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2610.27538v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image based on a reference image and modification text. Recent approaches commonly rely on large vision-language models to generate target image captions for retrieval. However, these captions may include redundant semantic details, introducing noise when retrieving the target image and leading to suboptimal retrieval results. To address this issue, we propose Less-is-More CIR, a two-stage training-free framework that combines Concise Retrieval and Critic Re-ranking. In the first stage, concise target-oriented captions are generated that preserve only the most discriminative modification semantics, thereby reducing semantic noise in the retrieval. In the second stage, a critic re-rank module further evaluates the retrieved candidates from the perspectives of modification consistency and reference preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework for the ZS-CIR. Our code is available at: https://github.com/dxlabskku/LM-CIR.

title: CoASFL: Coupled Consistency Optimization for Asynchronous Split Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.26992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training large-scale deep models on resource-constrained edge devices. Although asynchronous SFL alleviates the straggler bottleneck caused by system heterogeneity, it inevitably introduces two coupled dimensions of inconsistency: horizontal inconsistency across clients and vertical inconsistency between clients and the server. These inconsistencies, further exacerbated by statistical heterogeneity, result in biased activation representations, model divergence, and severe client drift. To address these challenges, we propose CoASFL, an inconsistency-aware asynchronous SFL framework that incorporates a dynamic activation merging mechanism and a consistency-aware model aggregation mechanism. Specifically, CoASFL constructs more consistent activation sequences from heterogeneous clients to alleviate horizontal inconsistency, and dynamically adjusts aggregation weights according to client participation frequencies and progress gaps to mitigate vertical inconsistency. By jointly coordinating activation-level and model-level consistency, CoASFL effectively suppresses inconsistency propagation during asynchronous training. Extensive experiments on an 80-device heterogeneous edge testbed demonstrate that CoASFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SFL approaches, accelerating training by 1.61$\times$ to 3.74$\times$ and improving final model accuracy by up to 3.26\% under heterogeneous scenarios.

title: EviDial: When Correct Depression Predictions Lack Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.27541v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Depression dialogue benchmarks commonly assess models by comparing predicted symptom labels with clinical scale scores. However, a prediction may agree with a benchmark label even when the dialogue lacks enough evidence to justify it. We introduce EviDial, a benchmark that distinguishes label agreement from evidence-grounded assessment. EviDial comprises 382 depression dialogues from three sources and 2,744 participant-symptom cells, each classified as having absent, partial, conflicting, or sufficient evidence. Because evidence sufficiency lacks a directly observable gold standard, we derive calibrated evidence references from multiple judgments using generalizability theory, many-facet Rasch measurement, and random-effects latent class analysis. Our audit reveals that 82.8% of participant-symptom cells lack sufficient textual evidence for the corresponding symptom assessment, with substantial variation across sources. Across model families and prompting strategies, 69.2%-96.9% of predictions judged correct by benchmark labels are nonetheless unsupported by sufficient dialogue evidence. Further analyses show that strong agreement among LLM evaluators need not reflect independent evidence judgments, underscoring the need to calibrate automated reference panels. These findings demonstrate that label-based evaluation can overestimate evidence-grounded performance by conflating agreement with clinical labels and support in the observed dialogue. EviDial provides a measurement layer for separating these constructs and auditing LLM-based depression assessment more faithfully.

title: Day 17/420: Packages and project layout basics - Python in production
description:
Day 17/420: Packages and project layout basics

420 Day Python Production Track

Today I wanted packages and project layout basics to feel like a real engineering decision, not a syntax demo. The useful shift was turning packages and project layout basics into something I can explain from the code instead of memorizing from a tutorial.

The checks that mattered were data shapes that stay obvious at a glance, control flow that makes valid states visible, and small units of logic that remain easy to test.

The failure mode I was actively trying to avoid was letting convenience hide where state changes actually happen. I treated it like a build day, where the only useful explanation is one that survives contact with an actual repository and a real set of constraints.

That is the bar I want from this track: code that stays readable when requirements move, not just code that runs today. I also want to keep tracing one concrete path through the code because that exposes weak assumptions faster than a larger demo.

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
description:
arXiv:2610.27099v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.27220v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.

title: Robustness of Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When given an image and a text prompt, vision-language models (VLMs) can produce seemingly sophisticated text responses. However, they are also prone to hallucinate objects in their output, which can have detrimental consequences in safety-critical applications. To detect these hallucinations, certain methods interestingly leverage internal signals from the VLM as it generates the text response; potentially, these methods use the same signals that led to a hallucination to detect it. We conduct an in-depth analysis to understand the robustness of these detection methods. First, we show that a naive baseline of a generated word's token position in the VLM text response achieves competitive performance. Further, we reveal how some detection methods rely on token position and use this heuristic as a shortcut. Second, we explore detection methods' sensitivity to language and vision modalities. Our experiments suggest that strong detection performance is often driven by detecting language-based hallucinations, and when methods rely on token position, they tend to be less visually grounded and exhibit reduced robustness when hallucinations occur earlier in a text response. Lastly, we demonstrate that different detection methods can carry complementary signals; when ensembling methods together, adding weaker methods to an ensemble of higher performing ones still offers performance improvements. Altogether, while there may be useful internal VLM signals to detect hallucinations, our investigation reveals important limitations of the current methods that try to leverage them.

title: MatchCityLoc: Aerial Localization in LoD City Models via Surface Normal Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.27110v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments requires precise pose estimation. Because Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are often unreliable in cities, visual localization serves as a crucial complement. Within this domain, textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a lightweight and privacy-preserving substitute for heavy 3D textured meshes. However, localizing against abstract geometry is challenging. Existing pipelines typically score 2D silhouette overlaps, which can suffer from severe geometric ambiguities. We present MatchCityLoc, a framework that shifts this paradigm to direct feature matching from a noisy 6-DoF pose prior. By extracting surface normals from the query image using a zero-shot foundation model and matching them against rendered LoD normals, we establish explicit 3D-to-2D correspondences. This enables a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) pose solve, which we iteratively refine through a render-and-match loop. Experiments demonstrate strong pose recall and accurate translation and rotation among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods with very few renderings. By bridging the modality gap between aerial imagery and texture-free geometry, MatchCityLoc enables accurate localization using lightweight, privacy-preserving city models.

title: OmniVLoc: Topo-metric Visual Localization for Omnidirectional Cameras
description:
arXiv:2610.27522v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omnidirectional cameras provide surround-view information, significantly overcoming the field-of-view constraints for traditional visual localization systems. However, existing localization systems fail to fully exploit the characteristics of omnidirectional cameras, struggling to deliver accurate and robust localization performance amidst scene content variations and illumination-induced appearance changes. In this work, we propose OmniVLoc, a surround-view localization system based on a topo-metric framework. By integrating state-of-the-art global place recognition and monocular depth estimation methods, we introduce a multi-constrained visual localization paradigm. By solving a scale-aware pose graph and performing precise spherical bundle adjustment, we accurately recover the metric-level pose for each query frame.Furthermore, a hierarchical verification mechanism is designed to filter out erroneous outputs across different stages, effectively bolstering the overall system robustness. Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets validate the superior accuracy and reliability of OmniVLoc. To benefit the community, our source code and dataset will be made publicly available upon publication.

title: Sample-efficient learning with Dense Associative Memories
description:
arXiv:2610.27384v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We analytically study the evolution of the energy function of Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) as they train on randomly sampled codewords of random expander low-density parity-check codes (a.k.a. solutions of random XORSAT problems). We identify two distinct regimes and a transition between them, reminiscent of grokking in neural networks. A regime of small training set size is where the model memorizes a few training examples but cannot discover the underlying rules of the entire codeword dictionary generative process. The opposite regime, corresponding to a larger training set size, is where the model has uncovered the sparse constraints that generated the entire data set after seeing only polynomially many patterns. We also design a novel class of DenseAMs with a thresholding learning rule, and show that any amount of thresholding enables the model to perform simplified sparse Hamiltonian learning, which exponentially reduces the number of training examples needed to learn the true underlying data set. In this regime, the model learns how to discover $\exp[\mathrm{O}(n)]$ solutions from only $\mathrm{O}(\log n)$ training samples, which is asymptotically optimal for any learning algorithm. When training on codewords of certain random codes, the model can even learn the underlying code when a small O(1) fraction of bits are latent variables. These latent variables are not shown to the model during learning, but will be discovered by sparsifying observed higher-order correlations. For certain random codes, we show that a simple and conservative algorithm learns a minimal latent representation for the data set. This provides a transparent, physics-motivated, and analytically tractable toy model for how deep latent representations emerge in an associative memory training.

title: WordPress Memory Exhausted Error: Fix It at the Right Layer
description:
If your WordPress site shows Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 268435456 bytes exhausted, a PHP process asked for more memory than the server allows. The fix is usually quick. The catch is that the common fix, one line in wp-config.php, fails on many sites because it changes the wrong layer.

Decode the number first

The limit is reported in bytes:

Bytes Limit
33554432 32 MB
67108864 64 MB
134217728 128 MB
268435456 256 MB
536870912 512 MB

The end of the message gives a file path. The folder after /wp-content/plugins/ or /wp-content/themes/ is your first suspect.

Three layers decide the limit

  1. Host or php.ini memory_limit is the real ceiling.
  2. WP_MEMORY_LIMIT in wp-config.php is only a request, capped by layer 1.
  3. Per-folder overrides such as .user.ini or .htaccess.

The smallest value wins. Ask WordPress for 256M on a 128M host and you still get 128M.

Fix 1: wp-config.php

Back up the file first, then add this above the "That's all, stop editing" line:

define( 'WP_MEMORY_LIMIT', '256M' );
define( 'WP_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT', '512M' );

Fix 2: php.ini, .user.ini or the hosting panel 

memory_limit = 256M

Most panels expose this as a PHP settings or INI editor page. On PHP-FPM hosts, a per-site .user.ini is usually the file that is read, and it can take a few minutes to apply.

Fix 3: .htaccess (Apache with mod_php only) 

php_value memory_limit 256M

On PHP-FPM or FastCGI this directive causes a 500 error. Remove it immediately if that happens.

If nothing changes

Open Tools → Site Health → Info → Server and read the PHP memory limit. If it still shows the old value, the change did not reach the right layer. Also check that you edited the right wp-config.php, that the line sits above the stop-editing comment, and that no cache is serving the old error.

Find the real culprit

Raising the limit hides the problem. To find it, log errors without showing them to visitors:

define( 'WP_DEBUG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_LOG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY', false );

Repeat the failing action, read wp-content/debug.log, and note the plugin path. Rename that plugin folder over SFTP to deactivate it and retest. A diagnostic plugin like Query Monitor, run on staging, shows memory per page and per plugin.

FAQ

Is it safe to raise the memory limit? Yes, going from 64M or 128M to 256M is routine. Avoid extreme values on shared hosting, and fix the cause if you keep needing more.

Why does the error only show in wp-admin? Image processing, updates and imports need more memory than front-end page views.

Will more memory speed up my site? No. Memory prevents crashes. Speed comes from caching, lighter plugins and good hosting.

The full guide, with a symptom-to-cause table and prevention checklist, is on my site: WordPress memory exhausted fix.

title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics, with intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations evaluated across open-weight and closed-source models. Editing substantially increases judge-rated severity over the seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fall in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase. Among 219 prompts that pass model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit responses containing unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, although pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only $\rho=0.0387$ to $0.1897$. Curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the failures they expose in each model.

title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.

title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.

title: Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training for Long-Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.26910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.

title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
description:
arXiv:2610.27142v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

title: Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.27571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.

title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
description:
arXiv:2610.27140v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.
