title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
description:
arXiv:2610.27027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
description:
arXiv:2610.26915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.

title: African Languages AI Safety Readiness Report
description:
arXiv:2610.27269v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) across languages and domains, AI safety has emerged as a critical global concern. However, due to resource constraints, research and development efforts tend to prioritize a limited number of high-resource languages, leaving many others, especially those spoken in Africa, underrepresented. While existing research on language "resource-ness" has largely examined whether sufficient resources are available to develop language technologies, the question of whether languages are adequately represented in AI safety research has received attention only more recently. This report examines the readiness of African languages for inclusion in AI safety discussions, drawing on existing literature and data. It considers four factors: the availability of AI-relevant resources, including text data; national AI policy support; performance on established text benchmarks; and speaker population. Based on these factors, languages are grouped into four readiness categories: fully ready, mostly ready, emerging, and foundational support needed. This classification is intended to inform the inclusion of African languages in AI safety benchmarks, highlight varying levels of preparedness, and guide strategic investment in data development, policy, and community engagement for underrepresented languages.

title: Designing Internal Service Status from Metrics and Logs (For AI Agent Loops)
description:
An uptime page for a media AI agent loop has a stricter constraint than a general monitoring console: an editor needs to know whether a publishing job can finish correctly, while an operator needs enough evidence to reconstruct why it did not. Displaying every metric and log line satisfies neither need. The right first version is a small, read-only projection built from bounded metrics, correlated terminal events, and an explicit freshness rule.

TL;DR: model the loop as a state machine, expose one aggregate snapshot to the internal admin UI, and keep raw logs behind drill-down links. Show availability, end-to-end latency, error ratio, and an estimated usage unit for each workflow class. Mark stale data as unknown rather than healthy. This preserves the distinction between service reachability and completed editorial work, which is where many simple status pages become misleading.

How should a Node.js uptime dashboard combine metrics and logs?

A media workflow may accept a story brief, retrieve background material, call one or more models, run a policy check, and persist a draft. A process-level health check can succeed while that sequence repeatedly times out or produces no publishable result. For an internal page, the unit of health should therefore be the completed workflow, not the HTTP process.

Start with four questions derived from the latency, traffic, errors, and saturation signals described in the Google SRE monitoring chapter: are workflows finishing, how long do they take, how much work is arriving, and is a constrained dependency accumulating pressure? The dashboard can present those questions without pretending that one green badge captures them all.

For each workflow class, such as article-draft or caption-rewrite, define a terminal success event and a terminal failure event. Require both to carry the same opaque run identifier, policy version, and workflow class. The identifier is the audit key. It also makes retries visible: a retry is another attempt attached to the same logical run, not a second successful publication.

Exactly-once processing is not something a dashboard can confer on the underlying pipeline. Its projection can still adopt an exactly-once mindset. Deduplicate terminal events by (run_id, attempt_id, terminal_state), reject contradictory duplicates from the aggregate, and retain enough evidence for reconciliation. If a success counter says 100 while the terminal-event ledger contains 99 unique successful runs, the page should report an integrity discrepancy instead of averaging the disagreement away.

Retries lie.

Unknown matters.

A snapshot older than the agreed collection interval is not evidence of availability. It is unknown, with its observation timestamp shown plainly. That single rule prevents a frozen collector from leaving a reassuring green panel on screen.

Derive the projection before choosing storage

The status view needs a compact contract. The example below uses a 5-minute window for fast operational feedback and a 24-hour window for context; those are example policy choices, not universal thresholds. The response separates observed values from decisions so a later threshold change does not rewrite history. A Node.js admin application can consume the same JSON contract even when the aggregation worker is written in another language.

package status

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Window struct {
    DurationSeconds int64   `json:"duration_seconds"`
    Completed       uint64  `json:"completed"`
    Failed          uint64  `json:"failed"`
    P95LatencyMs    float64 `json:"p95_latency_ms"`
    UsageUnits      float64 `json:"usage_units"`
}

type Snapshot struct {
    Workflow      string    `json:"workflow"`
    Status        string    `json:"status"`
    ObservedAt    time.Time `json:"observed_at"`
    FreshUntil    time.Time `json:"fresh_until"`
    Recent        Window    `json:"recent"`
    Daily         Window    `json:"daily"`
    IntegrityGaps uint64    `json:"integrity_gaps"`
}

type SnapshotReader interface {
    Read(r *http.Request) (Snapshot, error)
}

func Handler(reader SnapshotReader, now func() time.Time) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        snapshot, err := reader.Read(r)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "status snapshot unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }
        if now().After(snapshot.FreshUntil) {
            snapshot.Status = "unknown"
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-store")
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(snapshot); err != nil {
            return
        }
    })
}

UsageUnits should use the stable unit the pipeline actually records, not a currency estimate silently mixed across model contracts. Currency conversion belongs in a separately versioned rule with its effective time and source. This is the same discipline a ledger projection needs: preserve the immutable observation, then apply a reviewable interpretation.

The aggregate store may be a relational table, a time-series database, or an in-memory cache backed by durable events. The status contract does not depend on that choice. What does matter is atomic publication: calculate a complete snapshot off to the side, validate its counts and timestamps, then replace the visible version in one operation. Readers should never see the five-minute latency from one calculation paired with the daily failure count from another.

This design has a clear limitation: a precomputed projection favors predictable reads and auditable states over open-ended exploration. It is not suitable as a replacement for a metrics explorer or restricted log-search system. The trade-off is deliberate because an incident-facing status page must remain cheap to read and easy to reconcile, while deeper diagnosis can tolerate a separate, slower path with tighter access controls.

Join metrics and logs without turning the page into a log viewer

Metrics answer trend questions efficiently. Logs explain individual runs. Joining them on the page is useful only if the join is deliberate: an aggregate row links to a filtered set of terminal events for the same workflow and time window, and an individual run links to its attempts. Do not ship raw prompts, generated copy, credentials, or personal data into a broad admin view. Retention and access must follow the organization's compliance policy, and access to the status page should itself leave an audit record.

The useful event is small. A terminal record needs the run and attempt identifiers, workflow class, terminal state, start and finish timestamps, policy version, usage unit, and a bounded error category. Free-form error text belongs in restricted logs, not in a label or aggregate key. Unbounded labels create noise and make the metric series harder to reason about.

This division also controls ingestion volume. Log services commonly charge according to ingestion volume; the CloudWatch pricing page, for example, documents per-GB log ingestion dimensions. The architectural response is not to make price the main criterion. It is to emit fewer, higher-value events, keep high-cardinality evidence out of metrics, and choose retention according to investigation and compliance needs.

A compact admin table can then carry the information operators actually compare:

Workflow State Last observed 5m completions 5m failures p95 latency Integrity gaps
Article draft Healthy 14:05 UTC 82 1 18,400 ms 0
Caption rewrite Unknown 13:54 UTC 0 0 - 0
Policy review Degraded 14:05 UTC 77 9 6,200 ms 2

These values are illustrative data, not benchmark claims. Notice that zero traffic is not automatically an outage, and stale observation is not converted into zero. The integrity column also remains separate from runtime failure: a workflow may finish while its evidence trail is incomplete.

Set decisions that resist alert noise

A dashboard and an alert have different jobs. The page can show every supported workflow class; a page-worthy alert should represent an actionable breach sustained for a defined window. One failed run may deserve a visible count and a drill-down link without waking anyone. Conversely, an integrity gap may require immediate investigation even while the completion ratio looks normal.

Use a decision table owned in version control. For example, a team might classify a workflow as degraded when its error ratio breaches a reviewed threshold in two consecutive five-minute windows, or when its p95 latency exceeds a workflow-specific objective with enough completed samples to make the percentile meaningful. The exact threshold must come from the service objective and traffic profile. No source can supply it generically.

Three distinctions keep the signal honest:

  1. Separate unknown from healthy; missing telemetry cannot prove success.
  2. Separate logical runs from attempts; retries must not inflate throughput or erase the original failure.
  3. Separate operational errors from audit-integrity gaps; each has a different owner and response.

Test those rules with deterministic fixtures before testing the HTML. Feed the projector duplicate terminal events, late arrivals, a retry that succeeds, contradictory terminal states, an empty window, and a snapshot beyond fresh_until. Assert both the aggregate and the retained reconciliation record. Then load-test the read path independently, because an internal page that runs expensive ad hoc log queries can compete with the collection path during the incident it is meant to explain.

Roll out the view without losing audit continuity

Begin in shadow mode. Produce snapshots, compare their completed and failed counts with the terminal-event ledger, and publish the discrepancies only to the implementation team. Once reconciliation remains within the team's explicit acceptance rule, expose the page read-only to operators; alerting can follow after the display has earned trust.

During migration, version the snapshot schema and keep the prior projector available until consumers have moved. Deploy decision-rule changes with an effective timestamp, record who approved them, and annotate the page when a rule changes. A latency graph that crosses a newly changed threshold is then explainable rather than mysterious.

The final acceptance test is intentionally plain: given a run identifier, an operator can trace every attempt to one terminal outcome, reproduce the aggregate row for its window, and explain the displayed state from a versioned rule. If any link is missing, the page is decoration, not an operational control.

title: Designing a Smarter Dog Breed Discovery Experience: UX, Data and AI
description:
Designing a Smarter Dog Breed Discovery Experience: UX, Data and AI

Choosing a dog breed is more complicated than it first appears.

People often start with appearance, popularity, or recommendations from friends. But finding a suitable dog requires considering several factors: lifestyle, available space, activity level, grooming requirements, and previous experience with dogs.

This creates an interesting challenge for anyone building a digital discovery platform.

1. Turning Complex Information Into Better Decisions

A dog breed directory can contain hundreds of pages, but more information does not automatically mean better decisions.

The challenge is organizing information so that visitors can compare breeds and understand which characteristics matter to their situation.

Useful design principles include:

  • Clear navigation and structured breed categories
  • Consistent presentation of breed characteristics
  • Mobile-first interfaces
  • Accessible descriptions and comparison tools
  • Transparent explanations of recommendations

2. The Potential of AI-Assisted Discovery

AI can help users explore large collections of information through more natural interactions.

For example, a breed discovery system could consider:

  • Daily activity and exercise preferences
  • Apartment or house living
  • Experience with dog ownership
  • Household composition
  • Time available for training and care

However, recommendations should never be presented as guarantees of compatibility. Individual dogs vary, and responsible decisions require more than a matching score.

3. Structured Data and Search Experience

From a web development perspective, structured content creates opportunities for better navigation and discovery.

A well-organized breed platform can benefit from semantic HTML, descriptive internal links, accessible components, and relevant structured data.

Performance matters too. Fast-loading pages and responsive layouts make complex information easier to explore across devices.

4. A Real-World Project:

One project exploring this space is Hunderacer.dk, a Danish website focused on dog breeds and helping people explore their options.

The project illustrates an interesting product-design challenge: combining breed information, intuitive navigation, and decision-support experiences in one accessible platform.

The broader lesson applies well beyond pet websites.

Whether building a product comparison engine, an educational platform, or a recommendation interface, the goal should be the same: help people make better-informed decisions without hiding complexity or overstating certainty.

5. What Would You Build Differently?

For developers and UX designers, several questions are worth exploring:

  • How should recommendation systems explain their results?
  • When should rule-based matching be preferred over machine learning?
  • How can structured content improve both usability and search discoverability?
  • How do we design interfaces that communicate uncertainty responsibly?

These questions are especially important when recommendations influence long-term decisions.

Final thought: Good discovery experiences do more than return results. They help users understand why those results matter.

Disclosure: I am associated with Hunderacer.dk. This article was prepared with AI writing assistance and should be reviewed before publication.

title: Mixture of Phonetic Experts Based Low-Rank Adaptation of Conformer Models for Accented English Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.26888v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Mixture of Phonetic Experts based Low-Rank Adaptation (MoPE-LoRA), a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for accented English speech recognition. Recent mixture-of-experts approaches typically allocate experts per accent, implicitly treating accent identity as the primary axis of variation. In contrast, we organize adaptation along phonetic categories, motivated by the observation that accent differences are often expressed as systematic distortions of phoneme realization. MoPE-LoRA introduces a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes and performs frame-level routing through a hybrid mechanism that combines phoneme supervision with learned acoustic gating. Because the expert set is shared across accents, the model does not require accent-specific modules and naturally extends to previously unseen accents. Experiments on L2-ARCTIC show that MoPE-LoRA consistently improves over single LoRA and full fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation where one accent is held out during training, the proposed method yields a 12.3% relative improvement over single LoRA. These results indicate that phonetic-category-based decomposition offers a scalable and transferable alternative to accent-level adaptation.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

title: LEAF: LUT-aware Efficient Attention on FPGAs
description:
arXiv:2610.27078v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Lookup-table (LUT)-aware Efficient Attention on FPGAs (LEAF). LEAF is the first nanosecond-scale LUT-aware transformer for FPGAs. Deploying transformers that are large enough to perform well, small enough to fit on an FPGA, and fast enough to meet the sub-microsecond timescales required by real-time systems such as those at CERN remains difficult, since the same attention mechanism that gives these models their high expressivity also makes them costly to implement in hardware. LEAF converts the query, key, and value projections and the final output feed-forward layer into FPGA-native layers with LUT-aware training, creating the first LUT-aware transformer and linformer layers built for ultra-low-latency inference. Attention resists LUT-aware training because it multiplies two activations where the method needs a constant weight to tabulate; LEAF tabulates the attention block's constant matrix-vector multiplications and leaves the rest in arithmetic form. On a standard jet tagging benchmark this improves accuracy by 1.8 percentage points while using 2.9 times fewer LUTs than the previous state-of-the-art sub-microsecond transformer at the same input size. Our most efficient LEAF-based linformer with 64 input particles reaches 80.4% classification accuracy at 28k LUTs and 35ns.

title: Accelerating Spatio-Temporal Attention for Video Diffusion on TPUs
description: To address the quadratic latency bottleneck of self-attention in high-resolution video diffusion models, developers implemented Sparse VideoGen (SVG) to dynamically route attention heads to highly structured spatial or temporal sparse masks. Translating this algorithmic sparsity into physical hardware speedups on TPUs required optimizing the Splash Attention kernel by bypassing empty memory tiles, restricting exact coordinate masking strictly to boundary tiles, and permuting token memory layouts into temporal-major order for contiguous access. By aligning these sparse masks with actual hardware tile execution, the combined optimizations significantly reduced wasted matrix operations and achieved up to a 1.69x end-to-end inference speedup for 1440p video generation.

title: CityPaint: A Free Lunch from 2D Diffusion for City-Scale 3D Texturing
description:
arXiv:2610.27564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating high-fidelity, city-scale 3D environments plays a crucial role in applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and urban digital twins. However, the scarcity of real-world city-scale 3D training data forces existing methods to either stitch independently generated assets or learn from synthetic urban corpora, often sacrificing realism and global consistency. In contrast, 2D image data and their corresponding generative models are abundant and encode rich visual priors. To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a novel framework that leverages 2D diffusion models to generate globally consistent city-scale 3D textures without relying on city-scale 3D training data. Specifically, CityPaint integrates geometric priors with the generative power of 2D diffusion models, introducing a robust top-$K$ camera baking strategy for iterative texture projection. To address the artifacts of 2D-to-3D projection, we further propose a decoupled refinement mechanism that separately optimizes terrain and building textures. Extensive experiments show that CityPaint produces globally coherent textures with fine local details and achieves favorable results against strong baselines in both visual quality and cross-view consistency.

title: VitronEdit: Universal Visual Editing across Images, Videos, and 3D Scenes
description:
arXiv:2610.27049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data-scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry-aware post-training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera-pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi-view consistency. The project page: https://vitron-llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.

title: I wrote a 10,000-line Windows security suite in one Python file. Here's how the crypto container works, and ₹50 if you can break it
description:
Most small encryption tools fail in boring places, not in the cipher. They fail on what happens with a wrong password, a doctored header, a rolled-back state file, or a corrupted chunk.

I spent a long time on those boring places for ATLOCK v5, and this post walks through the design. At the end there's a challenge for you.

1. The container format

Files, folders and Quick Lock items all use one container (v3.1):

magic(8) | salt(16) | kdf_packed(6) | chunk_size(4) | nonce_base(8)
| commitment(32) | plain_len(8) | header_hash(32) | chunks...
  • Chunked AES-256-GCM. Every chunk is authenticated independently, so a single flipped bit is caught at that chunk and nothing gets decrypted blindly.
  • Per-seal chunk subkey. v3.1 derives a fresh subkey for each seal instead of encrypting everything under the raw master key.
  • Header-bound AAD. The header is mixed into authentication, so you can't swap parameters around without detection.
  • Optional Padme padding. The true file size is hidden by padding to a Padme bucket with random bytes, at no more than about 12% overhead.

2. Key commitment before any plaintext

AES-GCM alone doesn't commit to a key, which is why partitioning-oracle attacks exist. ATLOCK stores HMAC-SHA256(enc_key, "atlock-commit-v3") in the header and verifies it with a constant-time compare before a single byte of plaintext is produced. A wrong key is rejected at the header, and it never reaches the decryption loop.

3. KDF: Argon2id, and a parser that doesn't trust its own header

  • File floor: Argon2id, t=3, m=64 MiB, p=4
  • Vault and recovery: t=4, m=128 MiB, p=4
  • All sub-keys come from HKDF-SHA256 with per-purpose info strings (vault-enc, vault-verify, totp-wrap, backup-enc, and so on), so no key is ever reused across purposes.

The KDF parameters live in the header, which means an attacker can edit them. So the parser clamps untrusted values to hard ceilings (t≤6, m≤512 MiB, p≤8). A doctored file can't make ATLOCK burn gigabytes of RAM or minutes of CPU.

4. Sealed local state

Settings, guard list, vault index, lockout counters and logs are never stored as plain JSON. Every record goes through a SealedStore: AES-256-GCM with a key derived via HKDF from a DPAPI-protected state key (with extra entropy). A separate rollback anchor catches someone restoring an old state file to reset attempt counters.

There's also an optional hardware mode, where the state key becomes HKDF(DPAPI root || TPM secret) and every sealed file is re-sealed under it. If the TPM key is enabled but unusable, ATLOCK fails closed.

5. Public-key mode

Ephemeral X25519 for encryption (HKDF over the shared secret, salted with the ephemeral and recipient public keys), plus Ed25519 for signatures. Signatures can be pinned, so a file signed by a different key than the one you expect is rejected. There's also Shamir M-of-N splitting for recovery keys, FIDO2 hardware keys, TOTP and Windows Hello.

6. The unglamorous hardening

  • SetDefaultDllDirectories runs before any other import, against DLL planting.
  • Every child process is launched by full System32 path, never through a shell, with a rebuilt minimal environment (fixed COMSPEC/PATHEXT, no inherited PATH or PSModulePath).
  • PowerShell scripts are fixed strings, and variable data goes in over stdin as JSON, never interpolated.
  • Symlinks and junctions are refused. Data-folder ownership is checked, and anything inside OneDrive/Dropbox/Drive is detected so decrypted working copies never get synced.
  • Environment variables that influence paths (like the Nuitka onefile parent PID) are only honoured if they match the actual process layout.
  • Log output goes through a redaction filter for keys and tokens.

7. Detection layer

Ransomware canary decoys in Desktop/Documents/Pictures/Downloads, a startup-item watchdog with a baseline and allow-list, an audit log with its own verify command, and intruder photo/video capture after failed unlocks.

8. Testing

ATLOCK.exe --selftest runs against a throw-away data folder and registry key, so it never touches a real install. --fuzz N throws N random corruptions at the container parser.

Now the actual point: break it

I can't find my own blind spots, which is why I'm posting this here.

  1. Download ATLOCK_v5.zip: https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/ATLOCK/releases/download/v5.0.0/ATLOCK_v5.zip
  2. Extract ATLOCK.exe. It's unsigned, so Windows SmartScreen will warn you. Click "More info → Run anyway", but do it in a VM or Windows Sandbox. You should treat any random exe from a stranger this way, including mine.
  3. Use it, then try to break it. Recover a protected file without the password, bypass lockout, forge or roll back state, or get plaintext where there shouldn't be any.

Reward: ₹50 via UPI for a valid break, ₹60 for a major one. Send a reproducible write-up in the comments or DM me, and I'll judge what counts.

I'm not rich, so that's what I can afford. Because my parents didn't give me money 💵 and in my fampay account I've only 110rupees 😂 The real reward is that every break you find gets fixed in v6, and your name goes in the credits.

I'm Anmol. I'm 13 and I build under Akhouri Systems. Yes, really. Tear it apart.

title: Fluent but Fallible: Benchmarking Hallucination and Factual Reliability in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27034v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced natural language processing and artificial intelligence applications through their capabilities in reasoning, text generation and knowledge retrieval. However, LLMs are still vulnerable to two important challenges: hallucination, generating factually incorrect or fabricated content, and response deviation, meaning systematic deviations from ground-truth responses. These limitations raise serious concerns regarding reliability and trustworthiness in academic and research environments. This study offers a thorough comparative analysis using a variety of metrics of ten advanced LLMs ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude~3.5~Sonnet, LLaMA~3, Mistral, Grok, Perplexity, DeepSeek~V3, Falcon, and Gemma based on a benchmark consisting of 70 carefully designed academic prompts across four complexity levels: Basic, Explanation, Advanced, and Tricky, evaluated in February 2025 on specific model versions. Each response was independently evaluated by three reviewers using five metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Response Deviation Index, and Hallucination Index. Perplexity and DeepSeek~V3 achieved the highest overall accuracy, while Gemini demonstrated strong recall and a well-balanced performance profile across all five metrics. LLaMA~3 showed strong resistance against hallucinations through a conservative method of generation. Advanced-level prompts proved most challenging across all models, while Tricky prompts were handled more reliably owing to their binary true/false structure. Falcon achieved perfect precision and zero hallucinations, but at the cost of the lowest recall and the highest response deviation. The results show a fundamental trade-off between response completeness and factual reliability, intensified by prompt complexity.

CodeMender updates (v0.14.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Better pull request scans: cm find --diff now catches removed security controls and gives large files more time (configurable with --diff-job-timeout).
  • Unified sessions: --deep and --diff scans now appear as a single session in cm session list, cm report, and cm stats.
  • Moved code in cm verify: cm verify now finds code that moved since cm find and updates the finding's location.
  • Guided activation: cm now opens the activation page and waits for activation instead of exiting.
  • New cm find flags: --deep-max-turns limits exploratory steps per file in --deep scans, and --enable-bash allows shell commands during scans.
  • Improved detection: More distinct findings per file and more precise CWE classification for weak hashing and randomness.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed scans of repositories reached through nested symbolic links.
    • Fixed findings for nonexistent files and over-merged findings.
    • Shell scripts created by cm verify are now executable.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

Google SecOps now includes the Response Health Hub curated dashboard, a central location for monitoring playbook performance, execution latency, automation effectiveness, and integration health across environments.

  • Automation effectiveness metrics: Compare automated versus manual case closure rates and Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR).

title: What Stays Intact When the Model Changes? Paper 2 on Externalized Intelligence
description:
I have published the second paper in the Artificial Deterministic Intelligence research series: Externalized Intelligence and Model Substitution.

The question is deliberately narrower than “are smaller models as intelligent as larger models?” They are not assumed to be. The question is whether a bounded operational contract can remain intact when authoritative task state is maintained outside model weights and the inference model changes.

In synthetic first-party studies, a frozen governed package was tested across 8B to 35B, 35B to 8B, and same-model restart controls. All 120 confirmatory handoff trials retained the measured policy contract and task correctness. The study also compares governed scoped context, authorized metadata-filtered lexical retrieval, and an oracle authorized-context ceiling. Each completed 90 of 90 trials under the shared frozen contract; conventional lexical retrieval had the lower measured retrieval-component time.

Those findings do not establish general model equivalence, production readiness, universal continuity, a universal safety guarantee, or retrieval superiority. The companion retains non-acceptances, timeouts, an incomplete scoped study, and a non-confirming cross-environment replication attempt.

Read the Version 2 preprint and evidence companion: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23523687

The public-safe supplementary evidence package provides aggregate outcomes, claim boundaries, hashes, and a verifier without disclosing Cortex, HOPE OS, raw prompts, worker packages, or private implementation.

I welcome technical criticism, alternative experimental designs, and independent work that can challenge these bounded findings.

title: How to Deliver SaaS File Export Downloads with Signed URLs (Without App-Server Storage)
description:
Short answer: for most healthtech SaaS exports, write each completed report to private object storage and return a short-lived signed GET URL; keep authorization, retention, and deletion decisions in your application database. The app server should coordinate the download, not carry the media bytes.

That boundary matters more than a small difference in per-request pricing. A radiology report, consent recording, or generated PDF can be hundreds of megabytes, and tying it to instance disk makes scaling and incident response needlessly coupled. The design below keeps access control in the system that knows the patient and tenant, while storage handles delivery. Infrai is a candidate at this boundary when a team wants storage alongside other backend capabilities under one REST contract; it is not a reason to weaken tenant authorization.

The second advantage is a self-describing discovery surface: the public schema and runnable examples make the storage contract inspectable before credentials reach a developer laptop. That matters when a healthtech team adds notification, scheduling, or observability around the same export workflow, because the platform has 295 routes across 20 modules behind one consistent set of conventions rather than a new SDK shape for every capability.

Start with the trust boundary, not the bucket

An export has two identities: the business record (tenant_id, report_id) and the object key. Generate the key in application code, for example exports/tenant-42/report-0187.pdf, and store it with an authorization record. A download request first checks that record, then asks storage for a signed URL. The client receives a URL with a short expiry and downloads directly from storage. The REST surface is plain HTTP, so a Node.js service, a Python worker, or a small Go utility can use the same contract without installing a storage SDK; the public discovery document also exposes schemas and runnable examples before a key is issued.

This is simpler than streaming through a Node.js process. The process handles a small control request instead of buffering or piping the entire file, so a slow browser cannot consume an application worker. It also avoids assuming that a particular app instance will still have the file on its local disk after a deploy.

There is a sharp edge: private signed delivery is not the same as a permanent public link. The storage capability has no public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. That is a good fit for protected reports, but it is the wrong tool for a public image host or static website. Use a provider with public hosting semantics for those cases.

How should cheapest, simplest file export delivery use signed URLs and object storage?

Treat the export as a state machine: generating, stored, available, and expired. A worker claims one (tenant_id, report_id) in a database transaction, writes a unique object key, and marks the row stored only after the write succeeds. The API issues a presigned GET only from the available state, after checking the caller's tenant and role.

Consider a real retry sequence. A report worker receives a queue message, reserves tenant-42/report-0187, and starts uploading a 640 MB PDF while the user's browser is still waiting on a job page. The worker loses its network connection after the storage service has accepted the final bytes but before the response reaches the process. A second delivery of the queue message must not create report-0187-copy.pdf, and it must not overwrite latest.pdf either. The worker asks the database whether the deterministic claim is already stored; if it is, it records a reconciliation event and returns the existing key. Only an available row can mint a signed URL, and only an authorization check tied to tenant-42 can request that mint. When the URL expires, the bytes remain governed by the retention row, not by a browser cache. This is the boring machinery that prevents a transient network ambiguity from becoming a cross-tenant disclosure or an unexplained duplicate in a clinical export ledger.

Do not replace exports/tenant-42/latest.pdf. There is no object versioning or object lock here, so an overwrite is not recoverable from this storage layer. Unique filenames make retries and audits legible. There is also no If-Match conditional write; if two workers can produce the same report, coordinate the claim in your database or queue before either worker writes bytes.

Here is a small Python adapter. It uses only the documented object write and presign routes, reads the key from an environment variable, sets methods explicitly, and retries a 429 without a tight loop. The database remains responsible for the idempotency record; the object key is the deterministic identity for this example.

import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def request(method, path, body=b"", content_type="application/octet-stream"):
    for attempt in range(4):
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            BASE + path,
            data=body,
            method=method,
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
                "Content-Type": content_type,
                # The application derives this from tenant_id + report_id.
                "Idempotency-Key": "tenant-42:report-0187",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                return response.status, response.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)


def put_export(bucket, tenant_id, report_id, pdf_bytes):
    key = f"exports/{tenant_id}/{report_id}.pdf"
    status, _ = request("PUT", f"/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", pdf_bytes)
    if status < 200 or status >= 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"object write returned HTTP {status}")
    return key


def presign_export(bucket, key):
    presign_url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    status, payload = request(
        "POST", presign_url.removeprefix(BASE), b"{}", "application/json"
    )
    if status < 200 or status >= 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign returned HTTP {status}: {payload.decode(errors='replace')}")
    return payload

The application should persist the returned key and state transition before exposing the presigned response. If a retry occurs after a timeout, the same key and idempotency identity let the worker reconcile the result instead of inventing a second report. Your mileage may vary on expiry defaults, so set the URL lifetime in the request according to the live discovery schema and your policy; never make a clinical download effectively permanent.

Compare the real delivery options

Object storage is a family of trade-offs, not a single product. AWS S3 is the broadest specialist choice for lifecycle controls, replication, and compliance integrations. Google Cloud Storage is a natural fit when the rest of the system and residency controls already live in Google Cloud. Cloudflare R2 can be attractive when egress economics and Cloudflare delivery are central. Infrai covers storage backends including S3-compatible, R2, OSS, and COS through one REST surface, but it does not cover GCS in this capability set.

Option Access and delivery Data-handling strengths Where it is a weaker fit
AWS S3 Mature private objects and presigned URLs Lifecycle, object lock, and multi-region patterns More provider-specific IAM and account surface
Google Cloud Storage Signed URLs with Google IAM Strong GCP residency and governance integration A poor match if the rest of the stack is outside GCP
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible private delivery Cloudflare edge integration and egress-focused design Compliance and replication choices need careful review
Infrai storage One REST contract for put and presign Broad backend capability behind one key and consistent discovery examples No public ACL, versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or GCS coverage

Infrai is worth trying when the team wants breadth behind a simple surface: adding storage to an existing backend integration is another documented endpoint rather than another SDK and credential set. The supporting benefit is operational consistency; discovery exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which reduces the integration-specific glue around a small export adapter. I would recommend it for private export delivery when those boundaries are acceptable, not as a substitute for a specialist's compliance controls.

In concrete terms, Infrai exposes a plain REST API with no SDK required, so any language can serve the export writer, its notification hook, and the audit job with the same Bearer authentication and HTTP conventions. That keeps a Node.js SaaS from growing a second client library just because a worker was written in Python.

Retention, deletion, and processor boundaries

A signed URL controls who can fetch an object for a period; it does not decide how long the processor retains the object or where the bytes are replicated. Put region and retention commitments in your contract with the storage provider, and record deletion intent in your own audit log. Lifecycle rules can remove old exports, but the shortest lifecycle granularity here is one day, not an hour. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup policy.

Deletion should be a two-step job: mark the export expired in the database, then call the object deletion operation and record the result. A failed deletion is a reconciliation item, not permission to issue another URL. Metadata is not server-side searchable beyond prefix listing, so keep patient, tenant, and report attributes in your database rather than trying to query them from object metadata.

The catch is regulatory immutability. If a financial or clinical retention rule requires WORM storage, version history, or automatic cross-region replication, choose S3, GCS, or another specialist system that provides those guarantees and keep the application adapter narrow. If browser-direct uploads need configurable CORS, this surface does not expose an independent CORS route for self-service policy changes; route uploads through a service with that control instead.

Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes, so production-like export storage needs a billable account. That is a deployment prerequisite, not a reason to put files back on app disks.

A rollout that can be audited

Start with one report type and a private bucket. Add a database uniqueness constraint for (tenant_id, report_id), emit an audit event for each state transition, and make the signed URL lifetime shorter than the user session. Measure object bytes, download bytes, expired rows, and deletion lag separately; those numbers tell you whether the storage boundary is working.

Keep the storage adapter behind one interface so a specialist provider can replace it without changing authorization code. Run a migration that copies existing files to unique keys, verifies checksums, and flips reads only after the new object is confirmed. Then remove the app-server copy according to your retention policy.

If your system needs public links, WORM guarantees, browser-configurable CORS, GCS, or cross-region replication, stick with a specialist provider. If it needs private SaaS exports and a consistent REST contract across backend capabilities, Infrai is a reasonable storage boundary to test first.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability index and verify the live request schema before wiring the adapter.

title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
description:
arXiv:2610.27439v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.

title: Idempotent Email Verification for REST APIs
description:
Email verification is often implemented as a single request: create a user, send a message, and wait for a click. That model breaks down when the client times out after the server has already accepted the request. A retry can create a second token, send a second message, or attach the wrong result to the user.

The fix is to make verification intent idempotent. The API should treat repeated requests as a lookup for the same operation, while PostgreSQL enforces the uniqueness that application code alone can miss.

This matters in both production authentication flows and automated tests that use a free throwaway email or a throwaway email address. A test mailbox is useful only when the API can explain which verification attempt produced the message.

Why verification retries create duplicate work

Suppose a client sends POST /verification-requests and waits six seconds. The server commits the request, but the response is lost. The client sends the same request again without an idempotency key.

The server cannot know whether this is a new request or a retry. It may issue two tokens and deliver two emails. The first retry is mostly harmless; the second one is where things gets confusing. A user clicks the older link, while the database considers the newer token to be current.

Email delivery makes the timing less predictable. A provider can queue messages, a worker can restart, and an inbox can expose messages in a different order than they were created. The REST API needs its own record of intent instead of using inbox arrival time as the source of truth.

For integration tests, a run-scoped email contract is a useful companion to this design. Each run should know which verification request and mailbox it owns.

Define the idempotency contract

Require the client to send an Idempotency-Key header when it starts verification. Scope that key to the authenticated user and operation, then persist the request fingerprint with it.

The endpoint contract can be simple:

  • The first request creates a verification intent and returns 202 Accepted.
  • A retry with the same key and the same payload returns the existing intent.
  • The same key with a different payload returns 409 Conflict.
  • A new key creates a new intent only when the account is allowed another attempt.

That last rule is important. Idempotency prevents accidental duplicates, but it should not bypass rate limits or account security policy. The API still needs a separate decision about how often a user may request a new message.

Store intent and delivery separately

The verification intent describes what the user asked the system to do. Delivery attempts describe what a worker tried to send. Keeping them separate makes the states less ambiguous:

verification_intent: pending -> sent -> consumed
delivery_attempt:   queued  -> accepted -> delivered
                                  \-> failed

An intent can remain pending while a delivery attempt is retried. It should not be marked verified just because a provider accepted a message. Verification happens only after the user presents a valid, unexpired token.

The database record should include a user ID, an idempotency key, a hash of the request parameters, an expiry time, and a token hash. Do not store the raw token in logs. A test can assert the resulting state without exposing a credential in CI output.

Enforce uniqueness in PostgreSQL

Application checks are not enough when two workers or two HTTP requests run concurrently. Use a unique constraint for the idempotency boundary:

CREATE TABLE verification_intents (
    intent_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id uuid NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key text NOT NULL,
    request_hash text NOT NULL,
    status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'sent', 'consumed', 'expired')),
    token_hash text NOT NULL,
    expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key)
);

On conflict, fetch the existing row and compare request_hash. If the hash differs, return 409; if it matches, return the existing intent. The transaction should not send the email itself. Commit the intent first, then let an outbox worker handle delivery.

This separation also supports operational controls. Deployment workflows can use email failure budgets in deployment workflows to decide when provider failures should stop a rollout rather than making every API request wait for the provider.

Return useful states from the REST API

The client needs a stable status resource instead of guessing from a button spinner:

{
  "intent_id": "3d1d0fb8-0b6a-4b91-ae49-7a3559e0bf2e",
  "status": "sent",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-21T06:00:00Z"
}

Keep provider details out of the public response. A sent status means the delivery workflow accepted the intent, not that the user has read the message. An expired status should be terminal for that intent, while a new request may create another intent if policy allows it.

The API response are easier to debug when each state has one meaning. In local notes, someone might search for temp gamil com or tempail mail; those phrases can appear as plain text, but they should never be used as identifiers or routing logic.

Test the failure paths

The most valuable tests are not the happy-path click. Test a lost response followed by an identical retry, a reused key with a changed email, concurrent requests, an expired token, and a delivery worker that fails after the intent commits.

For an automated test, assert the intent ID and state, then inspect a message matched to that intent. The test does not need to knows the provider's internal timing. It only needs evidence that the right message belongs to the right request.

A useful checklist is:

  • Require and persist an idempotency key.
  • Hash request parameters and reject changed retries.
  • Enforce uniqueness in PostgreSQL.
  • Commit intent before attempting delivery.
  • Hash tokens and redact them from logs.
  • Make expiry and resend policy explicit.
  • Correlate test messages with an intent ID or run ID.

Idempotent verification turns a fragile email side effect into a recoverable workflow. The provider may still be delayed, and a worker may still fail, but a retry will have a known meaning. That is the boundary an authentication service needs to stay correct under ordinary network failures.

title: Three owners of one token: how my AuthContext, my axios client, and localStorage split auth state
description:
In my starter kit, the Sanctum token has exactly one name and exactly two modules that touch it. That was a deliberate decision, and it is the reason I can change my auth storage strategy in an afternoon instead of a week.

The name is saas_token. It lives in localStorage. Here is everyone who is allowed to know that.

Owner one: the axios client. Every request passes through a request interceptor that reads the key and attaches the header:

client.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('saas_token');
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

And a response interceptor owns the "token died" path. On a 401, it clears the key and sends the user to login, unless they are already on the login or register page (redirecting someone off the login page because their non-existent token is invalid would be a special kind of bug):

client.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,
  (error) => {
    const status = error?.response?.status;
    const path = window.location.pathname;
    if (status === 401 && path !== '/login' && path !== '/register') {
      localStorage.removeItem('saas_token');
      window.location.href = '/login';
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

Note this happens at the network layer, outside React. No component, no context, no state update involved. An expired token redirects you before React has an opinion about it. And the interceptor still rejects the promise, so a form that triggered the 401 can still show its error state if it wants to.

Owner two: the AuthContext. It holds the token in React state, initialised from the same key, and it is the only place that writes it:

const [token, setToken] = useState(() => localStorage.getItem('saas_token'));

const login = useCallback(async (email, password) => {
  const res = await client.post('/auth/login', { email, password });
  localStorage.setItem('saas_token', res.data.token);
  setToken(res.data.token);
  setUser(res.data.user);
  return res.data;
}, []);

const logout = useCallback(async () => {
  // Best-effort: the session is cleared locally no matter what.
  try {
    await client.post('/auth/logout');
  } catch {
    // Ignore — token is being discarded either way.
  }
  localStorage.removeItem('saas_token');
  setToken(null);
  setUser(null);
}, []);

Login and register write both localStorage and state in the same breath. Logout tries the server first (revoking the token server-side is polite) but clears locally regardless. The session dies on the client even if the server call fails, because a logout that depends on a healthy network is a logout that fails exactly when the user needs it most.

On mount, the context restores the session: read the key, call GET /auth/me, and if that fails, remove the key and settle into logged-out. One code path for "returning visitor" and "dead token".

Owner three: nobody. That is the point. No component reads localStorage directly. No page checks the token itself. Every component goes through useAuth(), which exposes exactly six things: user, token, loading, login, register, logout. And useAuth throws if you call it outside the provider, so forgetting the wrapper fails loudly in development instead of silently shipping undefined auth everywhere:

export function useAuth() {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useAuth must be used within an AuthProvider');
  return ctx;
}

The payoff: if I ever move from localStorage to httpOnly cookies, the change surface is two files, client.js and AuthContext.jsx. Every consumer keeps working because they never knew where the token lived. Ownership is a contract: one name, two modules, and a public API of six values. Everything else just asks.

This is the auth layer of the starter kit I maintain and sell. The full thing, with the Sanctum backend and this exact frontend, is here: Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit

title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4
description:
arXiv:2610.26942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.

title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
description:
arXiv:2610.27030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

title: Securing Agentic Commerce Through Behavior-Aware Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity for Trusted AI-Agent Payment Authorization
description:
arXiv:2610.27483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing use of autonomous artificial intelligence agents in digital commerce creates new security concerns involving agent impersonation, unauthorized payments, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. This research introduces the Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System (ACAGS), a cybersecurity framework combining supervised machine learning, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and explainable AI. The framework was evaluated using synthetic financial transaction data augmented with simulated agent characteristics and five adversarial scenarios. XGBoost was selected following comparisons with alternative classifiers. Across ten experimental runs, behavioral features improved mean F1-score from 52.12% to 67.49%, with agent-specific features increasing performance to 69.46%. The framework achieved detection rates of 99.77% for abnormal agent behavior, 99.73% for impersonation, and 100% for malicious delegation and authorization-scope violations. Compromised-agent detection reached 72.27%. ACAGS also supported APPROVE, REVIEW, and REJECT authorization outcomes, with SHAP explanations providing model interpretability. The results demonstrate the potential of combining behavioral intelligence and delegated authorization controls to strengthen simulated agentic-commerce payment security, while highlighting the need for validation using real-world transactions.

title: Unified Sharp Bounds on Probabilities of Causation
description:
arXiv:2610.27398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) have developed steadily, from the binary measures first introduced by Pearl to the non-binary setting recently studied by Shu et al. As the theory has matured, PoCs have found applications in a growing range of areas, including personalized medicine, marketing and legal attribution. Shu et al. proposed closed-form bounds for multi-valued treatments and outcomes and proved them valid, but left their sharpness in high dimensions open. We close this gap with a mathematical proof. We further show that $\PNS$, $\PSub$, $\PRep$ and $\PN$ are all special cases of a single, more general formula. Combined with their equivalence classes, this settles the question of sharp bounds for discrete PoCs from experimental and observational data: in every dimension, they are given in closed form by a single theorem.

title: CaMeWM: A Causal Medical World Model for Generative Tumor Evolution and Treatment Planning
description:
arXiv:2610.26923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Treatment planning is intrinsically counterfactual: clinicians must compare how a patient's tumor and survival would evolve under competing regimens, whereas a retrospective cohort records only the regimen received and one follow-up scan. A treatment-conditioned generator trained on such data can therefore reproduce historical treatment allocation rather than simulate the interventional disease dynamics needed to rank regimens. We introduce \textbf{CaMeWM}, a causal medical world model for supported post-TACE tumor evolution and treatment planning. CaMeWM implements one intervention-to-decision loop rather than three independent prediction tasks: it first admits a queried regimen only for clinically comparable histories with empirical treatment support; it then generates a distribution of lesion-local follow-up worlds through an action-conditioned response descriptor, deterministic anchor, and residual 3D diffusion transition; and it finally maps sampled worlds to restricted mean survival time (RMST) with a response-Cox utility model. Under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, this loop estimates a prespecified, support-restricted g-formula target; all selection and nuisance estimation are fold-local, and the induced policy is evaluated by cross-fitted, censoring-adjusted doubly robust estimation. Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, CaMeWM achieves 0.618 SSIM and 0.528 change-map SSIM for follow-up CT transition, while its generated-world survival pathway attains a 0.615 C-index; factual-only AIPW estimates a 9.60-week RMST gain (95\% CI 0.61--18.13) for the frozen policy. CaMeWM provides an inspectable basis for retrospective, support-restricted treatment planning.
