title: An LLM-Based Agent for Legal Compliance Assessment: Architecture, Memory, and Evaluation in a Canadian and Quebec Context
description:
arXiv:2610.27347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivi\`eres. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.

title: ORBIT: Autoregressive Time Series Generation via Next Frequency-Band Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.27000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep generative models provide an effective modern solution to alleviating the problem of data scarcity by synthesizing realistic time series. However, despite the considerable progress achieved by existing deep time series generators, two key challenges remain: (1) learning hierarchical representations for heterogeneous temporal patterns; and (2) coordinating the generation process of heterogeneous temporal dynamics. To address these key bottlenecks, in this work, we propose ORBIT, a unified deep generative framework for time series. Specifically, we develop two key components: the Frequency-Hierarchical VQ-VAE (FH-VQ-VAE) and the Frequency-Band Autoregressive Transformer (FBAR). The former learns hierarchical representations by decomposing latent temporal representations into different frequency bands and applying residual quantization with increasing token budgets. The latter establishes a novel low-to-high frequency autoregressive direction, yielding a time series generation process that first constructs global temporal structures and then incrementally incorporates fine-grained temporal details. These compact designs not only disentangle heterogeneous temporal patterns for more effective representation learning but also mitigate potential interference among different temporal dynamics during generation. Extensive experiments on multiple challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that ORBIT achieves state-of-the-art overall performance while exhibiting superior inference efficiency compared with advanced baselines.

title: What Building an LLM-Offloaded Query Layer Taught Me
description:
Last month, we were working on a feature for one of our projects. The requirement was to build a natural-language interface that would allow users to query a fairly large MySQL dataset without having to know anything about the underlying database structure.

The idea was simple enough. A user asks a question in plain English, the application understands what information they're looking for, and the corresponding records or analytics are returned.

Now, as most crash courses and quick development reels would suggest, we could simply pass the database schema and the user's question to an LLM, ask it to generate SQL, execute the query and return the result.

And for a POC, that would probably be enough to demonstrate the concept.

But there's always been a striking difference between validating an idea through a POC and making sure the same feature continues to behave reliably when it becomes part of an application used by different people.

We were looking at a similar situation. The underlying data was changing regularly, users had different access scopes, and the questions themselves could vary considerably. Some users might only need an aggregate count, while others might want to inspect records across different operational units.

Before moving towards wider usage, we wanted to understand how we could approach this without making every database interaction completely dependent on the LLM.

Understanding what we were trying to solve

Before getting into the implementation, I want to clarify something.

We weren't trying to discover a faster way to retrieve records from MySQL. Database indexing, query planners, pagination, caching and application-level data access are already established approaches. We would need those regardless of whether an LLM was involved.

What interested us was the additional layer introduced by natural language.

Consider a conventional API. The frontend might send a request containing a region identifier, a status filter and a date range. The backend knows what those parameters mean and can construct a corresponding query.

With a natural-language interface, the user might write something like, "How many requests were pending by the end of last month?"

There are no predefined query parameters being supplied by the user. The application now has to understand the requested metric, interpret the time period, determine the appropriate data scope and prepare an execution request.

We can look at the overall application flow like this:

Once we isolated this part of the application, the discussion became less about which LLM to use and more about how much responsibility we should give it.

Looking into NL-to-SQL

We started exploring existing natural-language-to-SQL approaches to understand how similar requirements were being addressed.

The basic idea behind NL-to-SQL is straightforward: translate a question expressed in natural language into a SQL query that can retrieve the requested information.

The interesting part comes when we start thinking about what the model needs in order to generate that query.

An LLM understands language reasonably well, but it doesn't automatically understand our database. It needs context about available tables, columns, relationships and sometimes the business meaning behind those structures.

Take a question such as:

"Show me the requests updated this week that are still pending review."

A model could generate syntactically valid SQL for this. But which table should it use? What does pending review mean in this application? Which timestamp represents the last update? Does the user have access to every operational unit represented in that table?

These questions can't be answered reliably just by asking the model to write better SQL.

One approach would be to provide the entire database schema with every request. But for a large relational database, this introduces its own problems. Most of that schema may be irrelevant to the user's question, and the model still has to identify the appropriate tables and relationships from a much larger context.

This led us towards a more controlled approach using a schema card.

We built a schema-card layer to give the LLM only the database context relevant to the question. Instead of passing the entire schema, we used our baseline schema definition to identify role-permitted tables and rank them based on their relevance to the user's question.

The card included column information, saved query examples, and metadata identifying protected fields and scope-related columns. We also kept live database records out of this step, since the model only needed enough context to propose SQL.

The current selection uses lexical matching, which works with known terminology but can struggle when users describe the same business concept differently. Since the card also depends on a baseline schema, keeping it aligned with database changes is another area we have to account for.

What happens after the LLM generates SQL?

Suppose the model successfully generates a query. What should happen next?

In a simple demonstration, we might execute the generated SQL immediately and display the results.

But for our feature, we had to consider more than whether the statement was syntactically correct.

A SQL statement can be perfectly valid and still reference a restricted table, return sensitive information or perform an operation that the interface was never supposed to allow.

For this reason, we limited the model's responsibility to proposing the query.

The proposal followed a structured output contract. Instead of returning arbitrary text containing SQL somewhere in the response, the model was expected to produce JSON identifying the response type and, where appropriate, containing a SQL statement.

We then parsed that response and evaluated the generated SQL using a SQL parser and classifier.

The classifier inspected the statement's structure, determined its operation category and applied restrictions around permitted database operations. The surrounding policy checks also considered the tables referenced by the query and limits on query complexity.

We used sqlglot for these checks, which allowed us to inspect the SQL structurally rather than relying on string matching.

There is a practical difference between checking whether a string starts with SELECT and parsing the statement to understand what it contains. SQL can include nested expressions, common table expressions, functions and multiple kinds of statements. A parser gives the application a better foundation for enforcing the supported query contract.

Of course, passing those checks doesn't prove that the model selected the correct business records or interpreted every filter correctly. Structural SQL validation and semantic correctness are separate concerns, and the latter still needs evaluation.

Once the proposed query passed the initial checks, we showed it to the user.

The user could review the statement and explicitly choose to run it. The application then reclassified and rechecked the stored SQL before sending it through our existing governed read-execution path.

That path already applied execution controls such as result limits, a statement watchdog, response masking and audit records.

I think the separation between proposing SQL and executing SQL deserves a little attention.

From a frontend perspective, we can still make the interaction feel like a single chat conversation. The user asks a question, sees the proposed query and chooses whether to execute it.

But internally, proposal and execution are separate operations.

That gives the application an opportunity to persist the proposal, retain an audit record and recheck the statement when execution is requested. The model doesn't have to remain active while the user is deciding.

It also doesn't necessarily mean that the model is called twice. The LLM may be involved only in generating the SQL, after which the application handles execution and presents the returned data.

We still need the backend restrictions even with human review. A user approving a query shouldn't become a substitute for proper access control.

Where the grammar layer became useful

While exploring the NL-to-SQL approach, we also had another category of questions to deal with.

Consider:

"How many requests are pending in this region?"

The question is written in natural language, but the requested information is something the application may already understand as a supported metric.

We don't necessarily need the model to construct arbitrary SQL for that.

We built a deterministic grammar layer backed by controlled vocabulary to interpret supported analytics questions and convert them into structured intents containing the required metric, dimensions, scope and time information.

Once an intent was resolved and validated, the analytics service could identify the relevant data partitions and read the corresponding snapshot aggregates.

This is where we began separating natural-language analytics from flexible NL-to-SQL.

For known analytics questions, the system could resolve the request without calling an LLM. If grammar couldn't understand an otherwise permitted request, a configured model provider could be used as a fallback to propose the structured intent.

That proposal still passed through vocabulary, scope and permission validation before execution. A permission refusal wasn't supposed to become an opportunity to try the question again through the model.

The grammar layer naturally has its limitations. It can only interpret questions covered by the supported vocabulary and expressions. Maintaining that vocabulary also becomes part of the application work.

So we weren't attempting to handle every possible question through deterministic rules. We were using them for questions whose meaning and execution contract were already known.

There was also a difference in how results came back.

For analytics, the service returned structured aggregate values from the database rather than passing the result into another model call for narration. It could also include information about the contributing data partitions and errors encountered during retrieval.

This was particularly relevant because the analytics service could retrieve information from more than one backend partition. If one target failed, the response could preserve the available result along with information about the failure rather than silently presenting it as a complete answer.

We also had to consider questions that belonged outside structured database querying. A question about an operational procedure, for example, would be better suited to document retrieval and possibly RAG than SQL generation over operational records. That distinction helped us think about where the natural-language querying feature should have its boundaries.

What we learned from the implementation review

After understanding the query flow, we also looked at what happened further downstream.

One observation was that our natural-language analytics path queried its backend partitions sequentially. The NL-to-SQL execution path already had a concurrent multi-target read mechanism, but the deterministic analytics path hadn't adopted the same approach.

This raised a practical performance question.

Even if grammar resolution avoids an LLM call, the total response time still depends on everything that happens after the intent has been resolved. Multiple database connections, sequential reads and network latency can contribute significantly to the overall request duration.

We already had functional tests covering grammar resolution, generated SQL classification and the successful execution paths. However, we hadn't yet measured how the complete interface would behave under higher concurrency or across a larger number of backend partitions.

Another area worth examining was the absence of a request-wide deadline. Individual database statements had timeout controls, but a request involving multiple operations could still spend considerable time progressing through those individually bounded calls.

These observations gave us a better picture of the work beyond the model interaction itself.

Understanding the performance of this feature would require measurements around grammar resolution rates, model fallback frequency, database execution time and partial failures.

We didn't have a clean benchmark that would let us claim a particular latency or cost improvement from the design, so I'd rather leave those numbers out than estimate them.

Where this leaves me

Looking at the completed query flow, I found it interesting how little of the overall execution actually needed to depend on the LLM. The model still helped us handle flexible questions, but we had enough information within the application to manage known analytics, SQL validation and database execution separately.

There's still more to understand about how this behaves under load, particularly across multiple data partitions. title: How to Give Claude & Cursor Safe Database Access Without Crashing Production (Zero-Trust MCP Guard in Python)
description:
How to Give Claude & Cursor Safe Database Access Without Crashing Production (Zero-Trust MCP Guard in Python)

Giving an AI assistant or autonomous agent access to a live database is one of the most powerful workflows for modern software teams: Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Windsurf can write complex analytics queries, optimize slow joins, and inspect schemas in seconds.

However, granting raw database credentials to an LLM is dangerous:

  • Accidental Disasters: One misaligned prompt or prompt injection can lead the agent to execute DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, or unconstrained UPDATE / DELETE queries.
  • Production Freezes: A query missing a WHERE clause or missing an index on a million-row table can trigger a full sequential table scan, consuming 100% CPU and locking transactions.
  • PII Exposure: Raw customer records (plaintext emails, password hashes, credit cards) get pulled into prompt contexts and third-party LLM server logs.

The modern, standardized solution is to place a Zero-Trust Model Context Protocol (MCP) guard between your agent and the database engine.

In this guide, we will walk through how PgSafe MCP was engineered in Python to provide secure, read-only database exploration, forced LIMIT injection, real-time PII redaction, and dry-run mutation simulation.

The Zero-Trust MCP Architecture

Rather than connecting Claude directly to Postgres or SQLite with an unrestricted superuser connection, the MCP server acts as an intelligent firewall:

[ AI Agent: Claude / Cursor / Antigravity ]
                      │  JSON-RPC 2.0 (stdio)
                      ▼
             [ PgSafe MCP Server ]
                      │
           [ ReadOnlyGuard (AST Analysis) ]
           ├─ Blocks DROP, TRUNCATE, DELETE, ALTER
           └─ Blocks Semicolon Chaining
                      │
           [ CostAnalyzer (LIMIT Guard) ]
           ├─ Forces max 1,000 row limits
           └─ Warns on missing WHERE clauses
                      │
            [ Database Connection ]
            (PostgreSQL / SQLite / MySQL)
                      │
             [ Real-Time PII Masker ]
           ├─ Redacts emails (u***@domain.com)
           ├─ Masks credit cards (****-****-****-1234)
           └─ Redacts password hashes
                      │
                      ▼
[ Clean, Safe JSON-RPC Output to Agent ]

1. Enforcing Read-Only SQL Lexical Validation

A secure read-only guard must inspect every statement before it ever reaches the database cursor, stripping comments and blocking destructive keywords:

import re

BLOCKED_KEYWORDS = [
    r"\bDROP\b", r"\bTRUNCATE\b", r"\bDELETE\b",
    r"\bUPDATE\b", r"\bINSERT\b", r"\bALTER\b",
    r"\bCREATE\b", r"\bGRANT\b", r"\bREVOKE\b"
]

class ReadOnlyGuard:
    @staticmethod
    def validate(sql: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
        # Disallow multi-statement injection (semicolon chaining)
        statements = [s.strip() for s in sql.split(";") if s.strip()]
        if len(statements) > 1:
            return False, "Semicolon chaining disallowed."

        # Verify query begins with read-only keyword
        first_word = statements[0].split()[0].upper()
        if first_word not in {"SELECT", "EXPLAIN", "WITH", "PRAGMA", "SHOW"}:
            return False, f"Statement '{first_word}' is forbidden."

        for pattern in BLOCKED_KEYWORDS:
            if re.search(pattern, sql, re.IGNORECASE):
                return False, "Destructive SQL operation detected."

        return True, "Query verified safe."

2. Dynamic LIMIT Injection

Runaway SELECT * FROM audit_logs queries can crash your client's memory. PgSafe intercepts every query and caps row limits:

import re

def enforce_limit(sql: str, default_limit: int = 100, max_limit: int = 1000) -> str:
    cleaned = sql.strip().rstrip(";")
    match = re.search(r"\bLIMIT\s+(\d+)\b", cleaned, re.IGNORECASE)
    if match:
        limit_val = int(match.group(1))
        if limit_val > max_limit:
            return re.sub(r"\bLIMIT\s+\d+\b", f"LIMIT {max_limit}", cleaned, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
        return cleaned
    return f"{cleaned} LIMIT {default_limit}"

3. Real-Time PII Redaction Before Agent Ingestion

When the query returns data, sensitive columns (password_hash, ssn, token) and customer PII are redacted on the fly:

import re

EMAIL_REGEX = re.compile(r"\b([A-Za-z0-9._%+-])[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]*@([A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,})\b")
CARD_REGEX = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{4}[-\s]?){3}(\d{4})\b")

def redact_pii(text: str) -> str:
    text = CARD_REGEX.sub(r"****-****-****-\1", text)
    text = EMAIL_REGEX.sub(r"\1***@\2", text)
    return text

4. Configuring Claude Desktop & Cursor

Add the server to your claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pgsafe": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "pgsafe.server"],
      "cwd": "/path/to/pgsafe-mcp",
      "env": {
        "DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/my_db"
      }
    }
  }
}

Now you can prompt Claude:

"Inspect the orders table, find the top 5 customers with pending invoices, and suggest indexes to speed up this query."

Enterprise Edition: Dry-Run Mutation Simulation Harness

When agents need to draft data mutations or migrations, the Enterprise Pro edition includes an isolated simulation harness:

  • Executes INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE queries within an isolated transaction.
  • Returns row diffs, affected count, and execution time.
  • Guarantees auto-ROLLBACK: changes are never committed to your database.
  • Includes automatic index recommendation advisors and Docker Compose setups.

  • Lite Version (Open Source): Read-only guard and SQLite/Postgres schema inspection.
  • Enterprise Pro Edition ($14.99): PII masking, dry-run mutation simulation, index advisor, Docker Compose, and automated test suite.

title: From DevSecOps to Operational Resilience: 26 Engineering Improvements Across Cloud, Kubernetes and ML Infrastructure
description:
*From Security Scanning to Operational Resilience: Engineering Improvements Across DevSecOps, Cloud and ML Infrastructure *

Lessons from integrating security into CI/CD, strengthening observability, automating recovery, modernising API gateways and improving production operations.

Modern platform engineering is not just about deploying applications faster. It is about building secure, reliable, recoverable and maintainable systems while reducing manual operational effort.

In a multi-cloud environment supporting pharmaceutical SaaS applications, API platforms, Kubernetes clusters and machine learning services, operational excellence requires a combination of DevSecOps, observability, automation, capacity management and disciplined change control.

Over time, I have worked on a series of engineering improvements across CI/CD pipelines, on-premises infrastructure, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), API gateways, databases, monitoring platforms and ML workloads.

These improvements share a common objective: shift operational practices from reactive troubleshooting towards proactive controls, repeatable automation and evidence-based engineering decisions.

This article explores the key improvements, the engineering considerations behind them and the operational value they bring.

1. Integrating Gitleaks with CI/CD: Bringing Secret Detection into the Development Workflow

Security vulnerabilities can enter a production environment long before deployment. Hard-coded credentials, API tokens, passwords and private keys committed to source control are examples of risks that should be detected as early as possible.

To address this, I integrated Gitleaks into the CI/CD workflow to identify potential secrets in source code and related repository content.

Why this matters

When credentials are committed to a repository, the risk extends beyond the immediate application. Credentials may be copied into build logs, cached artifacts, cloned repositories or downstream environments. Removing the secret from the latest commit does not necessarily remove it from the repository's history or eliminate the need to rotate it.

Engineering approach

The integration introduces secret scanning into the software delivery process, allowing findings to be identified closer to the point where code changes are introduced.

A mature implementation should include:

  • Scanning code changes and, where appropriate, repository history.
  • Reviewing findings to distinguish genuine secrets from false positives.
  • Assigning ownership for remediation.
  • Rotating exposed credentials rather than relying solely on deleting them from source code.
  • Defining severity-based handling and exception procedures.
  • Retaining scan results and remediation evidence according to policy.

The next level of maturity is to enforce pipeline failure for confirmed policy violations, subject to an agreed exception process. Detection and build-blocking enforcement are separate controls and should be implemented and verified independently.

Operational value: Earlier detection of credential exposure, improved security awareness in development workflows and a foundation for policy-driven DevSecOps.

2. Strengthening Security Visibility with Wazuh Across On-Premises Servers

Security controls are more effective when infrastructure events can be observed centrally.

I worked on installing Wazuh across on-premises servers to improve security monitoring and centralise visibility into relevant host events.

Key considerations

A successful deployment involves more than installing an agent. It requires attention to:

  • Agent connectivity and health.
  • Collection of relevant security events.
  • Alert rules and severity classification.
  • Investigation and escalation procedures.
  • Ownership of findings and remediation.
  • Monitoring of agent coverage and reporting gaps.

The operational objective is to make security events visible to the appropriate teams and provide a consistent basis for investigation.

A useful follow-up measure is coverage: the number of in-scope servers reporting successfully compared with the total number of servers that should be monitored. Additional measures can include alert investigation time and the age of unresolved high-priority findings.

Operational value: Improved security visibility across the on-premises server estate and a stronger basis for operational risk monitoring.

3. Evaluating Root-Access Changes Through a Proof of Concept

Privileged access is one of the most sensitive areas of infrastructure administration. Excessive or poorly controlled root access can increase the impact of accidental changes, compromised credentials and unauthorised activity.

I worked on a proof of concept for changing root-access practices, with broader rollout identified as a subsequent step.

A controlled approach to privileged access should consider:

  • Whether administrative access can be performed through named accounts and approved privilege elevation.
  • Authentication and authorisation requirements.
  • Audit logging for privileged commands and sessions.
  • Emergency access procedures.
  • Service dependencies that may require special treatment.
  • A tested rollback and recovery approach.

A proof of concept should validate compatibility with existing administration procedures before wider deployment. Production rollout should include a staged migration, clear ownership, exception handling and a method to recover access if the new controls fail.

Operational value: A structured path towards stronger privileged-access governance without introducing avoidable operational disruption.

4. Upgrading Trivy to Improve Vulnerability-Scanning Currency

Container and infrastructure security scanning must evolve alongside the tools, libraries and vulnerabilities they are intended to detect.

I upgraded Trivy from version 0.58.1 to 0.64.1 as part of maintaining the security tooling used in the engineering environment.

Tool upgrades are an important operational activity, but the upgrade alone does not establish that vulnerabilities have been eliminated.

A sound upgrade process should include:

  1. Reviewing release notes and compatibility considerations.
  2. Testing the new version against representative images and repositories.
  3. Validating vulnerability database access and scan output.
  4. Comparing findings and investigating material differences.
  5. Confirming that CI/CD integrations continue to operate correctly.
  6. Documenting the deployed version and the upgrade outcome.

The broader objective is to ensure that scanning remains a dependable part of the delivery process and that findings can be prioritised and remediated.

Operational value: Updated vulnerability-scanning tooling and a stronger foundation for maintaining consistent container security checks.

5. Resolving Certificate Trust Issues Between On-Premises Containers and OCI OpenSearch

Secure communication between distributed systems depends on correct certificate trust configuration.

An SSL connectivity issue was encountered when on-premises containers communicated with OCI OpenSearch. The issue was resolved by adding the required CA certificate to the operating system on the OCI server.

This illustrates an important troubleshooting principle: TLS failures are not always caused by application code or network connectivity. They can arise from certificate chains, trust stores, hostname verification, certificate expiry or configuration differences between environments.

A systematic investigation should validate:

  • The certificate presented by the remote endpoint.
  • The certificate chain and relevant CA certificates.
  • The trust store used by the client process.
  • Hostname and certificate validity checks.
  • Certificate expiry and renewal procedures.
  • Connectivity and TLS negotiation using approved diagnostic tools.

The durable fix should also be documented and incorporated into configuration management where appropriate, rather than relying on manual changes that may be lost during rebuilds.

Operational value: Restored secure connectivity and a clearer understanding of certificate trust dependencies between environments.

6. Improving Cloud Hygiene by Removing Unused Route 53 Records

Cloud resources and DNS records can remain after services are migrated, retired or replaced. Unused records create unnecessary configuration complexity and may introduce security, ownership or troubleshooting risks.

I removed unused Route 53 URLs after identifying records that were no longer required.

DNS cleanup should be performed carefully because a record that appears unused may still support a legacy integration, scheduled job, external client or certificate-validation workflow.

A controlled cleanup process should include:

  • Identifying the record owner and associated service.
  • Reviewing traffic and dependency evidence where available.
  • Confirming that the target service has been decommissioned or migrated.
  • Checking certificate, redirect and integration dependencies.
  • Recording the change and retaining a recovery path where appropriate.
  • Validating service behaviour after removal.

Operational value: Reduced DNS clutter and improved configuration maintainability, provided that dependency checks and post-change validation are completed.

7. API Gateway Modernisation: WSO2, Kong, Azure API Management and OCI API Gateway

API gateways are critical infrastructure components because they sit on the path between clients and backend services. Their configuration, availability and migration strategy can directly affect application connectivity.

My API gateway improvement work included WSO2-to-Kong migration activities, Kong failover-related implementation, API migration from Azure API Management to OCI API Gateway and work involving migration of services to Standard API Manager from Basic SKU.

Addressing OCI API Gateway service limits

During the migration to OCI API Gateway, a service configuration constraint involving the limit of 50 APIs per service required attention. The engineering team reduced the number of APIs configured per service to remain below that limit.

This is an example of adapting API architecture to the constraints of the target platform instead of treating migration as a direct copy of the source configuration.

Resolving Jasper API compatibility issues

Jasper APIs that were invoked from Azure did not function as expected after the move to OCI API Gateway. OCI Functions were used to address the integration issue.

The broader engineering lesson is that API migration requires functional validation, not just successful deployment. Differences in request handling, authentication, integration behaviour, routing and platform capabilities can affect API compatibility.

Reliability and failover

Kong failover implementation and related proof-of-concept activities were also part of the improvement work.

A robust failover implementation should verify:

  • Health detection and failure thresholds.
  • Routing to the correct healthy endpoint.
  • Connection and session behaviour.
  • Authentication, rate limiting and TLS configuration.
  • Recovery when the original node becomes healthy again.
  • Logging, alerting and operational ownership.

A failover design should be tested under controlled failure scenarios before it is treated as production-ready.

Operational value: Improved migration readiness, more deliberate gateway architecture and a structured approach to API availability and failover.

8. Automating Kong API Manager Administration

Manual API management can become difficult to maintain as the number of services, configurations and environments grows.

I developed an automated script for managing Kong API Manager activities.

Automation is especially useful for repeatable administrative tasks when it reduces configuration inconsistency and improves execution speed. However, API-management automation must also protect against accidental changes to routes, credentials, upstream services or access policies.

A reliable automation workflow should include:

  • Validated inputs and environment selection.
  • Authentication using appropriately protected credentials.
  • Pre-change checks and configuration validation.
  • Logging of actions and results.
  • Error handling and safe failure behaviour.
  • Change traceability and controlled permissions.
  • Post-change verification.

Operational value: A foundation for more repeatable API administration and reduced reliance on manual configuration steps.

9. Building a More Reliable Backup and Recovery Practice

Backups are only useful when they are available, consistent and recoverable when required.

I implemented automated backup processes across several infrastructure and data platforms, including:

  • Zabbix
  • Kong
  • Grafana
  • Prometheus
  • Weaviate
  • Dgraph
  • Legal-Elastic
  • Redis
  • PostgreSQL
  • MLflow

Additional work included automated PostgreSQL database backups and the use of an NFS server on separate box to receive backups from the five-node Elasticsearch cluster on Master Node.

The objective was to make backup execution more repeatable and reduce dependence on manual intervention.

Backup automation is only the first step

A production-ready backup process should also monitor completion, validate backup integrity, control access, manage retention and verify that the recovery process works.

Key questions include:

  • Did the backup complete?
  • Does the backup contain the expected data?
  • Is it protected from accidental or unauthorised deletion?
  • Can it be restored independently of the production failure?
  • Can the service be recovered within its agreed RTO?
  • Is the amount of data lost within the agreed RPO?

These checks are essential because a successful backup job is not proof of recoverability.

Operational value: More repeatable backup execution across a diverse technology stack and a foundation for better recovery readiness.

10. Restoring Legal-Elastic and Weaviate Data

Backup processes become more meaningful when recovery is demonstrated.

As part of the operational work, I restored Legal-Elastic on Backup Server and restored Weaviate data on Master node.

These activities provided practical experience with data restoration and the operational dependencies involved in bringing data services back into service.

A restoration procedure should validate more than whether a process starts. Depending on the platform, verification may include:

  • Database or index health.
  • Expected collections, indices or records.
  • Data consistency and application connectivity.
  • Authentication and access controls.
  • Application-level queries.
  • Evidence that the restored service is fit for its intended use.

The next maturity step is to formalise recurring restore tests, record the duration and results, and compare them against recovery objectives.

Operational value: Demonstrated restoration capability for the specific systems involved and a basis for improving recovery procedures.

11. Recovering a 2 TB Disk Snapshot for a UAT Environment

A disk recovery activity involved using a 2 TB disk snapshot to create and mount a disk on the UAT virtual machine on Azure. The restored data was checked with Ayan, after which the original 2 TB disk was depleted and decommissioned.

This activity highlights the importance of managing the complete lifecycle of recovered storage—not just creating the disk.

A controlled process should confirm:

  1. The correct snapshot and recovery point were selected.
  2. The restored disk was attached and mounted safely.
  3. The expected data was available and validated by the relevant owner.
  4. The UAT environment could access the required data.
  5. The original disk was no longer required before decommissioning.
  6. The storage change and decommissioning were documented.

The principle is simple: validate the recovery target and data before retiring the original resource.

Operational value: Recovered storage and validated data availability for the UAT environment, followed by the removal of the original disk after confirmation.

12. Expanding Elasticsearch Cluster Capacity

I added Node 4 and Node 5 as Elasticsearch nodes to an existing cluster having 3 nodes.

Adding nodes can increase available capacity and provide more flexibility in distributing data and workload. However, node addition must be accompanied by cluster-health and capacity validation.

Important checks include:

  • Cluster health before and after the change.
  • Node discovery and membership.
  • Shard allocation and rebalancing.
  • Disk utilisation and storage watermarks.
  • Heap utilisation, CPU and query latency.
  • Replication and recovery activity.
  • Any application impact during rebalancing.

Operational value: Expanded the cluster's node footprint, creating additional capacity potential. The actual performance or capacity improvement should be established from before-and-after metrics.

13. Resource Optimisation Through Pod and Docker Profiling

Infrastructure capacity decisions should be based on observed workloads rather than assumptions.

I carried out proof-of-concept work for pod profiling and then profiled pods across Development, QA, Sales and UAT Kubernetes clusters. I also performed Docker profiling for ML services.

Profiling helps identify:

  • CPU and memory utilisation patterns.
  • Workloads with excessive or insufficient resource requests.
  • Potential memory leaks or unexpected growth.
  • Containers that frequently restart or encounter OOM termination.
  • Opportunities for resource right-sizing.
  • Workloads that may benefit from isolation or separate scaling policies.

This is particularly important for ML workloads, where resource demand can vary significantly between model types and execution patterns.

Profiling should cover normal usage as well as peak periods. Reducing resource allocations based only on average usage can introduce instability during traffic spikes or concurrent workloads.

Operational value: Better evidence for capacity planning and resource optimisation across Kubernetes and containerised ML services.

14. ML Service Rationalisation and Ollama Configuration

I worked on ML service deprecation activities, Ollama configuration changes for ML services and Ollama model availability on GPU hosts.

These activities relate to managing an evolving ML infrastructure footprint and aligning deployed services and models with operational requirements.

For service deprecation, a controlled process should verify service ownership, consumer dependencies, traffic usage, replacement availability and rollback requirements before a service is retired.

For model and GPU-host configuration, important operational considerations include:

  • GPU and memory utilisation.
  • Model compatibility and loading behaviour.
  • Concurrent request capacity.
  • Model-serving latency and error rates.
  • Process health and recovery.
  • Version consistency and configuration management.

The objective is to maintain a service footprint that is operationally supportable while ensuring that active workloads continue to meet their functional requirements.

Operational value: Improved management of ML service and model configurations. Quantified resource savings or inference-performance improvements should be reported only after measurement.

15. Automating ML Service Deployment

I completed proof-of-concept work for ML service deployment automation, with broader automation across all ML services identified as a next step.

ML deployment automation can reduce manual configuration, improve repeatability and help maintain consistency across multiple environments.

A mature workflow should cover:

  1. Versioned deployment configuration.
  2. Validation of required secrets and environment variables.
  3. Image and dependency checks.
  4. Resource configuration and health probes.
  5. Deployment execution with appropriate permissions.
  6. Post-deployment smoke tests and service validation.
  7. Failure handling and rollback.
  8. Audit-friendly records of what was deployed and when.

The important distinction is between a working proof of concept and a fully operationalised deployment framework. Broader rollout should include testing, documentation, ownership and support procedures.

Operational value: A foundation for consistent ML deployment and a path towards reducing manual deployment effort.

16. Operational Resilience Through Swap Configuration

Swap configuration was standardised based on available host memory:

  • Hosts with 8 GB RAM: 4 GB swap.
  • Hosts with 16 GB RAM: 8 GB swap.
  • Hosts with 32 GB RAM: 8 GB swap.

Swap can provide a buffer during memory pressure, but it is not a replacement for adequate physical memory. Excessive swapping can also degrade application performance, especially for latency-sensitive services.

A production implementation should monitor swap usage, memory pressure, OOM events and application response times. It should also consider workload characteristics and the performance implications of swapping.

Operational value: More consistent swap configuration across the specified host sizes, with the actual reliability benefit dependent on workload behaviour and monitoring evidence.

17. Safer Service Isolation and Environment Segregation

I worked on separating the vigilance data service by deploying vigilance-qa in the QA cluster and vigilance-prod in the Prod cluster. I also worked on service-ner environment segregation.

Separating services by environment can improve operational isolation, reduce the risk of accidental cross-environment interaction and make deployment ownership clearer.

However, segregation requires more than separate deployment names. It should also consider:

  • Namespace and cluster boundaries.
  • Service accounts and permissions.
  • Network access.
  • Environment-specific secrets and configuration.
  • Database and external-service connectivity.
  • Monitoring, logging and alert routing.
  • Deployment and rollback procedures.

Operational value: Clearer environment separation and a more controlled foundation for managing service configurations across QA and Sales.

18. Improving Kubernetes Deployment Safety with Health Probes and Strategies

I updated deployment.yaml configurations with liveness probes, readiness probes and deployment strategies for backend services across Development, QA and Prod environments.

These controls address different aspects of application availability.

  • Readiness probes help prevent traffic from reaching pods that are not ready to serve requests.
  • Liveness probes help detect applications that need to be restarted.
  • Deployment strategies control how application versions are rolled out and how old and new instances coexist during a change.

Correct configuration is critical. A liveness probe that is too aggressive can cause restart loops, while an inadequate readiness probe can expose users to an application that has started but is not ready.

Deployment validation should cover normal startup, slow startup, dependency failures, rolling updates and rollback scenarios.

Operational value: Stronger deployment-level health controls and a more structured approach to managing backend service updates.

19. Liquibase CI/CD for Database Changes

Database changes require a controlled approach because schema modifications can affect application compatibility, data integrity and recovery.

I worked on Liquibase CI/CD for database delivery.

A well-designed database deployment pipeline should include:

  • Version-controlled migration scripts.
  • Review and approval of changes.
  • Validation against the target database.
  • Controlled execution in the appropriate environment.
  • Compatibility checks between application and schema versions.
  • Verification after migration.
  • A documented recovery or forward-fix strategy.

Database rollback requires special consideration. Not every schema or data transformation can be safely reversed, so the recovery strategy must be designed for the specific change.

Operational value: A foundation for repeatable, traceable database changes and closer integration between application and database delivery processes.

20. Jenkins Upgrade and Deployment Hygiene

I upgraded Jenkins from version 2.479.2 to 2.504.3.

CI/CD infrastructure is itself a critical production dependency. An upgrade should therefore include plugin compatibility checks, configuration and job validation, backup verification, access-control review and post-upgrade testing.

I also updated deployment scripts to automatically delete TAR files from 52 hosts after deployment, and backed up deployment scripts from those hosts to Bitbucket.

These activities address two operational concerns: managing deployment artefacts after use and retaining version-controlled copies of operational scripts.

A strong implementation should verify that:

  • The artefact is no longer needed by the running application or rollback process.
  • Cleanup only targets the intended files and directories.
  • Script failures are logged and surfaced.
  • The deployment outcome is not reported as successful when required cleanup or validation fails.
  • The version-controlled script is accessible to authorised maintainers.

Operational value: More consistent deployment cleanup and improved version-control coverage for deployment scripts.

21. Standardising the Linux Operating-System Baseline

I worked on upgrading Ubuntu from version 20.04 to 22.04.

Operating-system upgrades require a balance between security maintenance, application compatibility and service availability. A safe upgrade process should include dependency assessment, testing, backup validation, change approval, rollback planning and post-upgrade health checks.

For production systems, I would also verify monitoring-agent compatibility, service startup behaviour, network configuration, scheduled jobs and application dependencies.

Operational value: Progress towards a more current operating-system baseline for the systems included in the upgrade.

22. Managing ML Automation with Locking Controls

I worked on a lock script for ML automation.

Concurrent automation can create conflicts when multiple jobs attempt to modify the same resource, deploy the same service or run an operation that should only have one active execution.

Locking controls can help prevent duplicate execution, but they must handle stale locks, abnormal termination, ownership and safe release.

A production-ready implementation should define:

  • What resource is protected.
  • How lock ownership is established.
  • How stale locks are detected and recovered.
  • How concurrent execution attempts are handled.
  • What happens when a job fails midway.
  • How execution is logged and monitored.

Operational value: A mechanism for controlling concurrent ML automation and reducing the risk of conflicting operations, subject to the lock implementation and its failure handling.

23. Infrastructure Connectivity and Network Resilience

Network availability is a fundamental dependency for monitoring, application connectivity and operational support.

I changed the primary ISP from ACT to TATA after the ACT Fair Usage Policy threshold was exceeded and firewall bandwidth dropped to 3 Mbps.

The change addressed an operational connectivity constraint. It also illustrates why network-provider performance should be evaluated against actual business requirements rather than assumed service capacity.

Useful follow-up measurements include:

  • Available bandwidth and utilisation.
  • Packet loss and latency.
  • Connection stability.
  • VPN and remote-access performance.
  • Incident frequency and duration.
  • Failover capability and recovery time.

Where possible, network changes should be validated against representative workloads and documented alongside the associated firewall and routing configuration.

Operational value: A change in primary ISP to address a bandwidth limitation affecting operational connectivity.

24. Observability with OpenTelemetry

I worked on introducing an OpenTelemetry pod in AKS.

OpenTelemetry provides a common approach for collecting telemetry such as traces, metrics and logs through supported instrumentation and collectors. Its value comes from making it easier to correlate application behaviour across distributed components.

For a production rollout, I would validate:

  • Which telemetry signals are collected.
  • Whether the instrumentation covers the required services.
  • Exporter and collector configuration.
  • Access controls and protection of sensitive telemetry.
  • Sampling, retention and data-volume implications.
  • Collector health and telemetry delivery.
  • Integration with the organisation's observability platform.

Operational value: A foundation for more consistent telemetry collection and cross-service troubleshooting, with the actual observability improvement depending on instrumentation coverage and integration.

25. Resolving an Infrastructure Capacity Constraint in the Network Path

The network-provider change from ACT to TATA also illustrates a broader operational principle: infrastructure capacity issues can originate outside the application or server layer.

When firewall throughput falls, application symptoms can resemble a backend problem—slow requests, timeouts, unstable remote sessions or delayed monitoring data.

A layered investigation should therefore examine the full service path, including the local network, firewall, ISP, VPN, routing and remote endpoint.

Operational value: A practical reminder to correlate application symptoms with network performance before making unnecessary changes to application infrastructure.

26. Bringing the Improvements Together

The individual changes become more valuable when managed as part of a coherent operational improvement programme.

I group this work into six engineering themes:

Security and control

  • Gitleaks integration with CI/CD.
  • Wazuh deployment across on-premises servers.
  • Trivy upgrade.
  • Root-access change proof of concept.
  • Certificate trust remediation.
  • DNS hygiene.

Reliability and recovery

  • Automated backups across multiple platforms.
  • Legal-Elastic and Weaviate restoration.
  • Disk snapshot recovery for UAT.
  • Elasticsearch cluster expansion.
  • Kong failover-related implementation.
  • Kubernetes health probes and deployment strategies.

Automation and engineering consistency

  • Kong API Manager automation.
  • Liquibase CI/CD.
  • Jenkins upgrade.
  • ML deployment automation proof of concept.
  • ML automation locking.
  • Deployment-script cleanup and version control.

Cloud and API modernisation

  • WSO2-to-Kong migration work.
  • Azure API Management to OCI API Gateway migration.
  • OCI API configuration-limit remediation.
  • Jasper API integration remediation using OCI Functions.
  • API migration work involving Standard API Manager.

Capacity and platform optimisation

  • Pod and Docker profiling.
  • ML service rationalisation.
  • Ollama configuration and GPU model management.
  • Swap configuration.
  • Elasticsearch node expansion.

Operational hygiene and environment management

  • Linux OS upgrades.
  • Service segregation across environments.
  • Removal of unused DNS records.
  • Network-provider change to address bandwidth constraints.
  • OpenTelemetry deployment work.

27. Measuring Operational Improvement

Engineering changes should ultimately be evaluated using evidence. For this programme, I would track a focused set of measures.

Improvement area Useful measure
Secret scanning Repositories covered, findings triaged and remediation time
Security monitoring Server coverage, agent health and high-priority finding age
Vulnerability scanning Scan coverage, finding severity and remediation status
Backup and recovery Backup success, restore-test success, RPO and RTO
API gateway reliability Availability, request errors, latency and failover test results
Kubernetes operations Pod restarts, OOM events, deployment failures and readiness failures
Capacity optimisation Resource utilisation, headroom and cost per workload
Automation Manual effort avoided, automation failures and repeat-ticket reduction
Database delivery Migration success, rollback or forward-fix events and post-deployment validation
Network performance Latency, packet loss, throughput and connectivity incidents

I would establish a baseline before claiming a percentage improvement. Where measurements are unavailable, the correct approach is to describe the engineering change and its intended benefit without inventing an outcome.

Conclusion: Engineering Operations as a Continuous Improvement Discipline

These improvements demonstrate how DevSecOps, observability, automation, infrastructure management and recovery planning work together.

Security scanning helps identify risks earlier. Monitoring makes operational behaviour visible. Backup and restoration processes support recovery. Kubernetes health controls improve deployment management. API gateway and infrastructure changes address platform constraints. Automation reduces repetitive work, while capacity profiling provides evidence for optimisation.

The next level of maturity is to connect these activities to measurable operational outcomes: fewer recurring incidents, faster and safer recovery, more reliable deployments, stronger security-control coverage and better use of infrastructure resources.

For me, the central principle is straightforward:

Operational excellence is not the absence of incidents. It is the ability to detect problems early, recover safely, learn systematically and engineer the conditions that make the next incident less likely.

That is the direction I continue to pursue across DevSecOps, cloud platforms, API infrastructure and ML operations.

title: I built a 30 MB API client with Tauri and Rust (Postman is 214 MB)
description:
use an API client every single day. And for a long time, every single day it was the heaviest app on my machine.

So I built my own. It's called Elisa, it's free, and its Windows installer is 30 MB.

Client Windows installer
Elisa 30 MB
Bruno 122 MB
Postman 214 MB
Insomnia 525 MB

Official installers of each stable version as of October 19, 2026.

This post is about how it gets there, and what I learned building it.

Why not Electron?

Almost every API client is built on Electron. That's not a bad choice: it's mature and it lets you ship one codebase everywhere. But every Electron app ships its own full copy of Chromium, plus Node.js. That's where most of those megabytes go, and it's why five Electron apps open at once feel like five browsers.

Tauri takes the opposite approach: it uses the web engine your OS already has (WebView2 on Windows), and the backend is Rust instead of Node.

For Elisa that means:

  • A much smaller download.
  • It opens faster and uses less memory, so it can sit next to your editor, your browser and Docker without your laptop complaining.
  • A real native backend for the heavy lifting.

The frontend is plain React 19, built with Rsbuild. The same frontend also runs as a web app, so you can try it in the browser with nothing to install.

What Rust does under the hood

The fun part of Tauri is that the Rust side isn't just a wrapper. In Elisa it does real work:

Requests go out from Rust. On desktop, requests are sent with reqwest, not from the browser. That means no CORS, real cookie handling, multipart uploads, timeouts and custom certificates. If you've ever had to tell someone "it works in curl but not in the browser", you know why this matters for an API client.

Scripts run in a sandbox. Pre-request and test scripts run in QuickJS through rquickjs, with a pm.*-style API. Postman collections with scripts can come along when you import them.

Load tests stream live. The load tester runs in Rust with Tokio and streams progress to the UI through a Tauri Channel, so the chart updates while the test runs instead of waiting for the end.

A mock server, for real. You can serve any collection as a local API. It's a small hyper server that answers with your saved examples. A browser can't open a port on your machine, so this one is desktop only.

A real terminal. The built-in terminal uses portable-pty (ConPTY on Windows), the same idea VS Code uses.

Local-first, not cloud-first

The other thing I cared about: your collections are yours.

Everything is stored on your machine first, in IndexedDB. Elisa works with no account and no internet. If you want to work with your team, you can sign in and sync to the cloud in real time, but that's optional, not the price of opening the app.

When you're offline, changes go into a queue and sync on their own when the connection comes back.

What else it does

Lightweight doesn't have to mean basic:

  • REST, GraphQL and MCP. You can test MCP servers with auto-generated forms, or turn on "Elisa for agents" so Claude Code or Cursor can read your collections (every change asks for your permission).
  • Flows: drag requests onto a canvas and chain them. Capture the login token once and the rest of the flow uses it.
  • Code and types from any response: TypeScript, Zod, Go, Rust, Python, C#, Java, Kotlin, Swift and Dart.
  • Import from Postman, Insomnia, OpenAPI, HAR or a cURL command.
  • Git: save a collection to a folder and commit, branch and push from the app.

What I learned

  • Tauri is not "free" size. You give up a bundled browser, so you have to respect the system web engine. Testing on the real WebView matters.
  • Moving work to Rust pays off twice: it's faster, and it removes whole classes of bugs, like CORS, that a pure web app can't fix.
  • Local-first changes how you design everything. Every feature has to answer "what happens offline?" before it ships.

Try it

Elisa is free, with no account needed:

👉 elisa.develoops.dev

You can import your Postman collection in seconds and see the difference on your own machine.

I'm building it on my own, end to end: the app, the Rust engine and even the little mascot. So feedback means a lot. What's the one thing that annoys you most about your current API client? Let me know in the comments 🙂

title: Running Claude Code with Ollama and Local Models
description:
Claude Code + Ollama: Coding with a Local Model

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads your project, edits files, and runs commands from the terminal. With Ollama, you can run it on a model hosted on your own machine instead of in the cloud.

Why local models?

  • Your code never leaves your machine
  • No API costs
  • Works offline

In this guide, you'll install Claude Code, run it inside IntelliJ IDEA, connect it to Ollama, and test it on a small Java project.

Step 1: Install Claude Code

Install it globally with npm:

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

Then open a terminal and run:

claude

If the Claude Code prompt appears, the installation worked.

Step 2: Run It Inside IntelliJ IDEA

You don't need to leave your IDE. Open your project in IntelliJ, open the built-in terminal (View → Tool Windows → Terminal), and run:

claude

Claude Code now has access to your project files and works right next to your code.

Step 3: Connect It to Ollama

Ollama exposes an Anthropic-compatible API, so Claude Code can talk to a local model.

1. Install Ollama
Ollama lets you download and run language models on your own machine. Your code never leaves your computer and there is no per-request cost.

On https://ollama.com you can create a free account. The dashboard shows your free quota for cloud models. For the rest of this tutorial (100% local), it isn't required.

2. Pull a coding model:

ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

3. Point Claude Code at Ollama:

export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
claude --model qwen3.5:9b

On Windows PowerShell, use $env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="ollama" and $env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434" instead of export.

Alternatively, let Ollama handle the setup with one command, using --model

ollama launch claude --model qwen3.5:9b

Step 4: Build a Demo Project

Let's test the setup with a small Java project: a console task manager.

Create an empty Java project in IntelliJ, open the terminal, start Claude Code, and give it this prompt:

Create a simple Java console app: a task manager. Users can add,
list, complete and delete tasks. Save tasks to a text file so they
persist. Keep it to 2-3 classes.

Claude Code will plan the work, create the files, fix the errors, and ask for your permission before making changes. Approve the actions and watch it work.

Then run the app and try it out:

Notice that it doesn't only generate code. It also creates the files, runs the program, and fixes its own errors.

Cloud vs Local: Quick Comparison

Cloud Claude Local model (Ollama)
Privacy Code is sent to the API Stays on your machine
Cost Subscription / API Free
Speed Fast Depends on your hardware
Quality Highest Good for small tasks

Conclusion

Claude Code with Ollama is a practical way to try agentic coding without sending your code anywhere, as long as your machine can handle the model. Start with a small project like this one, then try it on your own code.

Thanks for reading!

title: Mastering Flexbox: The Ultimate Stress-Free Guide to Modern Web Layouts
description:
Mastering Flexbox: The Ultimate Stress-Free Guide to Modern Web Layouts

When you start learning HTML, everything makes complete sense until you try to position elements on a screen. For years, beginners struggled with floats, display: inline-block, and complex margin calculations just to put a sidebar next to a main content column. It was messy, unpredictable, and caused massive styling ling stress.

Enter Flexbox (The Flexible Box Layout). Flexbox is a modern CSS layout system designed to align items dynamically, distribute space evenly, and make responsive design completely effortless.

In this guide, we will look at how Flexbox works and the only 4 properties you need to master to build stunning layouts on your phone or computer.

**The Core Concept: Parent vs. Child

Before writing Flexbox code, you must understand its golden rule: Flexbox is applied to the container (the Parent), but it controls the layout of the elements inside it (the Children).

Imagine a standard HTML structure like this:

Box 1 Box 2

Box 3

By default, block elements like

stack vertically on top of each other. To activate Flexbox and tum them into an automatic horizontal row, you only need one magic line of CSS on the parent class:

.container

display: flex;

As soon as you type display: flex;, the child boxes instantly jump to line up side-by-side in a horizontal row.

The 4 Properties You Need to Know

Once Flexbox is activated, you use these 4 core properties on the parent container to control exactly how the child elements move and stretch.

⚫ flex-direction (Controlling the Layout Track): By default, Flexbox aligns items horizontally. You can change the main axis instantly using flex-direction: row; (side-by-side) or flex-direction: column; (stacked vertically).

⚫ justify-content (Horizontal Alignment): This property controls how space is distributed along the horizontal axis. It features configurations like center (packs everything in the middle), space-between (pushes items to far edges), and space-around (equal space on both sides).

⚫ align-items (Vertical Alignment): Centering items vertically used to require massive layout hacks. Flexbox solves this completely with align-items: center;, which aligns elements to the vertical midpoint of the parent.

⚫ flex-wrap (Handling Overflows): If you run out of space on a row, Flexbox defaults to shrinking your items until they look squished. Adding flex-wrap: wrap; allows items to automatically wrap cleanly onto new lines.

The Ultimate Cheat Sheet to Center Anything

.center-box {

If you ever need to center a button, text, or a login form perfectly dead-center on a page, copy and paste this

universal 3-line Flexbox setup onto the parent container:

display: flex: justify-content: center; align-items: center;

}

Conclusion

Flexbox eliminates the guesswork and stress from CSS layouts. By applying display: flex to a container and adjusting how its children align, you can create fully responsive, professional mobile layouts with minimal lines of code.

title: How to get the best and fairest performance out of your ASR system using activation steering
description:
arXiv:2610.26994v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering for ASR systems is an underexplored technique in improving both ASR performance and demographic fairness. We investigate two forms of activation steering: paired activation subtraction, and supervised optimization. We find the former to be ineffective at ameliorating ASR performance whatsoever, while the latter is quite effective at deriving steering vectors (SVs) that improve at once overall ASR performance and demographic fairness along such diverse axes as gender, age, and dialect. We also explore what types of data---from the most to the least personal---are necessary for calculating or training SVs. First, we show significant performance in performance from training SVs using an eclectic group of speakers from the same dataset. Furthermore, we find that vectors trained using acoustically similar speakers leads to ASR performances that are competitive or superior to vectors trained on the same speaker, or speakers from the same labeled demographic group. This finding shows that we can harness activation steering for few-shot adaptation given access to a speaker's demography, or zero-shot adaptation to unseen speakers without the need for any labels at all.

title: Dynamic System Inspired Continuous Large Language Model for AI4Science Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.26959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific foundation models increasingly operate on continuous phenomena, yet still use discrete residual computation. We ask whether pretrained residual transformations can support additional latent computation without expanding the backbone. To test this possibility, we introduce Continuum-LM, which reuses these transformations as dynamical operators in a continuous-depth language model. Its hidden states evolve through an ordinary differential equation evaluated by higher-order numerical integration, with solver order and step size controlling computation. Across eight scientific tasks, Continuum-LM trains stably and improves mean exact-match accuracy by 7.77 and 10.96 percentage points over discrete counterparts at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales, respectively. At 0.6B, it also outperforms an Ouro-style recurrent control under matched parameter and residual-function evaluation budgets. Together, these results support extensible computational depth through parameter reuse, identifying continuous hidden-state evolution as a practical design dimension for scientific language models beyond parameter scaling.
