title: System Design: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
description:
Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking

A practical guide to concurrent updates: version checks, database row locks, conflict aware forms, inventory reservations, deadlocks, and choosing the right strategy.

The problem in one minute

Alice and Bob open the same product editing page. Both see the price as USD 50.

  • Alice changes it to USD 55 and saves.
  • Bob still sees the old page, changes it to USD 48, and saves.
  • A normal "replace the price" request can silently overwrite Alice's change.

Both requests were valid. The problem is that Bob made his decision using an old copy of the data.

Optimistic locking says:

"Save my change only if the data has not changed since I read it."

The server checks a version as part of the write. If someone already changed the record, it rejects the stale write instead of silently replacing newer data.

Think of editing a shared paper form. You photocopy revision 7, make changes, and return it. The clerk accepts it only if revision 7 is still current.

Now consider two shoppers trying to buy the last book. A short transaction can instead lock the inventory row before checking and reserving it. That is pessimistic locking.

Think of one key to a storeroom. The next person waits for the key, then inspects the room as it is now.

Strategy Simple rule Typical example
Optimistic "Save only if my version is still current" A person editing a product price
Pessimistic "Coordinate access before making this database decision" Reserving the last item in a short transaction

Both protect decisions made from shared data. They differ in when they coordinate competing work, not in whether correctness matters.

This guide explains optimistic locking first, pessimistic locking second, then compares them using the same shopping app scenarios.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Concurrent Updates Lose Data
  2. What Optimistic Locking Actually Means
  3. The Version Check Flow
  4. The Atomic Database Write
  5. Try It With Two Database Sessions
  6. Carry the Version Through HTTP
  7. Frontend Conflict Handling
  8. Retry, Reload, or Merge
  9. Inventory and Atomic Business Conditions
  10. What a Row Version Does Not Protect
  11. Optimistic Locking vs Optimistic UI
  12. What Pessimistic Locking Means
  13. The Last Item Checkout Flow
  14. Transaction and Lock Lifetimes
  15. Try It With Two Locking Sessions
  16. A Short Reservation Transaction
  17. What Readers and Writers Experience
  18. Wait, Fail Fast, or Skip
  19. Deadlocks and Consistent Lock Order
  20. Do Not Hold Locks During Payment
  21. Database Locks vs Other Locks
  22. Comparison and Decision Guide
  23. Production Rules and Common Mistakes
  24. Testing and Observability
  25. Interview Questions and Answers
  26. Summary and Further Reading

The Mermaid diagrams render on GitHub and in Mermaid enabled Markdown previews. SQL examples use PostgreSQL, with Read Committed isolation unless stated otherwise. They are learning examples, not a complete API implementation. Other engines have different lock modes, defaults, and range lock behavior.

Reading shortcuts: start with version checks for stale edit screens, row locks for short database decisions, or the comparison for choosing a design.

1. Why Concurrent Updates Lose Data

What is a lost update?

A lost update happens when one successful write overwrites another person's change without detecting that it used stale data.

Consider an inventory count:

Step Request A Request B Stored stock
1 Reads 10 10
2 Reads 10 10
3 Computes 10 - 1 10
4 Computes 10 - 1 10
5 Writes 9 9
6 Writes 9 9

Two purchases happened, but stock fell by only one. The second write replaced the first result.

The risky pattern is read, calculate in application memory, then write an absolute value without checking what changed.

-- Unsafe when this value was calculated from an earlier, unchecked read.
UPDATE inventory
SET available = 9
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100';

Why doesn't a transaction automatically fix this?

A transaction provides an all or nothing boundary. It does not automatically encode the rule "the value I read must still be current."

At PostgreSQL Read Committed isolation, placing a normal SELECT and a later absolute value UPDATE inside a transaction can still allow this stale read modify write pattern.

Higher isolation levels can detect additional anomalies, but they have their own behavior and retry requirements. You must choose the concurrency rule explicitly.

Back to Top

2. What Optimistic Locking Actually Means

What is optimistic about it?

The approach assumes conflicts are uncommon enough that it is better to let people read and work independently, then check at save time.

It does not assume conflicts are impossible.

Three steps define the pattern:

  1. Read the data and its version.
  2. Prepare a change without holding a database lock during that preparation.
  3. Write only if the stored version still matches, then advance the version.
Term Plain language meaning Product example
Version Which saved revision you read Revision 7
Expected version The revision your edit is based on "I edited revision 7"
Conditional write Save only if a condition still holds WHERE version = 7
Conflict Another change invalidated your expectation Database is now revision 8
Compare and swap Compare the current value, then replace atomically if it matches Check version and save together

Despite the name, optimistic locking is usually validation, not a long lived lock placed when the user opens the page.

The database can still take short lived row locks while executing the write. "Optimistic" does not mean "the database never locks anything."

Why is this useful for web forms?

A person may keep an edit screen open for ten minutes. Holding a database transaction open for those ten minutes would waste resources and block competing writes.

With a version, the browser can keep its draft without holding database resources. The server validates freshness when the user finally saves.

Back to Top

3. The Version Check Flow

Initial product:

{
  "id": "P-100",
  "priceCents": 5000,
  "version": "7"
}

The version is shown as a string because large database counters may exceed JavaScript's safe integer range. Clients can treat it as an opaque token.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Alice
    participant API as Product API
    participant DB as Database
    participant B as Bob
    A->>API: Read product
    API-->>A: Price 5000, version 7
    B->>API: Read product
    API-->>B: Price 5000, version 7
    A->>API: Set price 5500, expected version 7
    API->>DB: Update if version equals 7
    DB-->>API: One row updated, version 8
    API-->>A: Saved
    B->>API: Set price 4800, expected version 7
    API->>DB: Update if version equals 7
    DB-->>API: Zero rows updated
    API-->>B: Conflict - current data must be reviewed

The database does not decide whose price is better. It only prevents Bob from accidentally pretending he edited the latest version.

Bob can deliberately apply USD 48 after reviewing revision 8, but that is a new decision based on current data, not a blind retry.

Back to Top

4. The Atomic Database Write

Example table 

CREATE TABLE products (
  id text PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL,
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
  version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (version > 0)
);

INSERT INTO products (id, name, price_cents, version)
VALUES ('P-100', 'System Design Book', 5000, 7);

Safe conditional update 

UPDATE products
SET price_cents = 5500,
    version = version + 1
WHERE id = 'P-100'
  AND version = 7
RETURNING id, price_cents, version;

The version comparison, field update, and version increment happen in one database statement.

Result Meaning
One returned row This write matched the expected version and succeeded
No returned rows No row matched both the identifier and expected version
Database error The write did not succeed normally - handle the actual error

No returned rows does not universally mean a version conflict. The row may have been deleted, may not exist, or may be excluded by authorization predicates. The API must apply its resource visibility policy before exposing details.

Why must the check and write stay together?

This is unsafe:

SELECT version
If version is 7:
    UPDATE products SET price_cents = 5500 WHERE id = 'P-100'

Another writer can change the row between the check and the write. This is a time of check/time of use race.

Put the condition inside the write, not only in application code.

At Read Committed, if two conditional updates target version 7 concurrently, one may wait for the other writer. If the first commits version 8, PostgreSQL rechecks the waiting update's condition against the updated row, and version 7 no longer matches.

What about deletes?

Deletes can carry the same precondition:

DELETE FROM products
WHERE id = 'P-100'
  AND version = 8
RETURNING id;

Otherwise, a stale screen might delete a product that someone else has substantially changed.

5. Try It With Two Database Sessions

Use a disposable local PostgreSQL database. Run the table setup from Section 4 once.

Open two database sessions and read the product in both:

SELECT id, price_cents, version
FROM products
WHERE id = 'P-100';

Both should see price 5000, version 7.

Session A:

UPDATE products
SET price_cents = 5500,
    version = version + 1
WHERE id = 'P-100' AND version = 7
RETURNING price_cents, version;

Expected: one row, price 5500, version 8.

Session B, still using its earlier version:

UPDATE products
SET price_cents = 4800,
    version = version + 1
WHERE id = 'P-100' AND version = 7
RETURNING price_cents, version;

Expected: zero rows. The price remains 5500, version 8.

This first experiment demonstrates a stale edit. To observe actual contention, begin a transaction in A, run its update without committing, and run B's update. B waits. After A commits, B returns zero rows.

If A rolls back instead, version 7 remains current and B can succeed. The deciding fact is the committed state, not which browser clicked first.

6. Carry the Version Through HTTP

The browser needs a way to say which representation it edited.

Two common API contracts are:

Contract Read response Write request Typical conflict response
Explicit application version JSON includes version JSON includes expectedVersion 409 Conflict
HTTP precondition Response includes a strong ETag Request includes If-Match 412 Precondition Failed

Do not mix these meanings accidentally. A failed If-Match precondition normally produces 412, not an arbitrary success response.

Example with ETag and If-Match 

GET /products/P-100

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "product-P-100-v7"
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"P-100","priceCents":5000}

The browser preserves the ETag exactly, including the quotes:

PATCH /products/P-100
If-Match: "product-P-100-v7"
Content-Type: application/json

{"priceCents":5500}

The server maps that precondition to an atomic conditional database update. Merely checking the ETag before an unconditional update has the same race as checking a version separately.

If this API requires a precondition and none is supplied, it can return 428 Precondition Required rather than permit an unprotected write.

ETag details that matter

  • If-Match uses strong comparison. A weak ETag such as W/"v7" is not suitable for this write precondition pattern.
  • A strong ETag must change when the selected representation changes. A row version is suitable only when it tracks every field/dependency represented by that ETag.
  • A client treats the ETag as opaque. The server must correctly handle the HTTP field syntax rather than blindly trusting a string as a database version.
  • If-Match: * checks that a current representation exists. It does not protect a particular revision from stale replacement.
  • Cross origin browser clients need appropriate CORS configuration for the If-Match request header and access to the ETag response header.
  • Authentication, authorization, and payload validation are still required. A version is not permission to edit.

7. Frontend Conflict Handling

Keep three things separate

An edit screen should know:

  1. Base: the data originally loaded.
  2. Draft: the user's unsaved changes.
  3. Latest: current server data fetched after a conflict.

Do not overwrite the draft as soon as a conflict occurs. That would prevent database data loss by causing user input loss instead.

flowchart TD
    A["Load data and ETag"] --> B["User edits a local draft"]
    B --> C["Save with If-Match"]
    C --> D{"Response"}
    D -->|"Saved"| E["Show confirmed result"]
    D -->|"412"| F["Keep draft and load latest data"]
    F --> G["Compare base, draft and latest"]
    G --> H["User resolves overlapping changes"]
    H --> C
    D -->|"Network failure"| I["Outcome unknown - reconcile before retry"]

A small browser request helper

This helper implements an API contract where a successful save returns JSON. It does not decide how your UI displays or merges a conflict.

async function saveProduct(productId, draft, etag) {
  if (typeof etag !== 'string' || etag.length === 0) {
    throw new Error('Load the product version before saving.');
  }

  const response = await fetch(
    `/products/${encodeURIComponent(productId)}`,
    {
      method: 'PATCH',
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'If-Match': etag,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ priceCents: draft.priceCents }),
    }
  );

  if (response.status === 412) {
    return { status: 'conflict' };
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Product save failed with HTTP ${response.status}.`);
  }

  return {
    status: 'saved',
    product: await response.json(),
    etag: response.headers.get('ETag'),
  };
}

The caller must preserve the draft on conflict, load the latest authorized representation, and show a comparison. A network rejection is propagated so the UI can show an unknown outcome, not silently label it a conflict.

An absent ETag on success means this helper has no validator for the next edit. Re fetch before another protected save, or enforce an API response contract that always supplies a fresh validator.

For successful PATCH responses, return a strong ETag only when it correctly identifies the resulting representation. For a transforming PUT, HTTP imposes additional restrictions on returning validators; a subsequent GET can obtain the current representation and validator.

Back to Top

8. Retry, Reload, or Merge

Why not automatically retry with the newest version?

Because that can turn a detected conflict back into a silent overwrite.

Bob's draft says USD 48 based on revision 7. Replacing its token with revision 8 and resending without review erases the meaning of the check.

Choose based on the operation:

Operation Sensible response
Human edits a price or legal document Preserve draft and ask for review
User sets a preference Explicitly define whether latest user intent should win
System increments a counter Prefer an atomic increment when that is the business intent
Background recomputation Re read, recompute, and retry within a bounded budget
Collaborative text editing Consider OT/CRDT rather than repeated whole document conflicts

A three way merge example

Field Base revision 7 Alice's saved revision 8 Bob's draft
Name Book Advanced Book Book
Price 5000 5000 4800

Alice changed the name; Bob changed the price. A three way comparison can propose combining both changes.

If both changed the price differently, that is an overlapping conflict requiring an explicit rule or user choice.

After a merge, submit against the latest version. Another writer might win before that save too, so even a merged write still needs a precondition.

A timeout is not a version conflict

The server might have committed a save whose response was lost. A retry with the original version can then fail because your own first request advanced the version.

Reconcile with current state or an operation status endpoint. For commands with side effects, use an idempotency key in addition to concurrency control.

9. Inventory and Atomic Business Conditions

Not every safe write needs a client read version.

If the business operation is "reserve one item if stock exists," express that condition directly:

UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - 1
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
  AND available >= 1
RETURNING sku, available;

The database checks stock and decrements it in one statement. If two requests compete for the last item, only one can consume it under these semantics.

This is a conditional atomic update, not necessarily a version based stale edit check. It protects a stock invariant rather than detecting whether a person saw an old screen.

flowchart TD
    A["What is the operation?"] --> B{"Replace data based on an earlier read?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["Require the expected version"]
    B -->|"No"| D{"Simple atomic business condition?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Put the condition in the UPDATE"]
    D -->|"No"| F["Consider a transaction and appropriate coordination"]

If the inventory row also participates in a versioning protocol, advance its version on this path too. All writers must agree on how changes become visible to version based clients.

Creating an order and consuming inventory may require a transaction. A guarded decrement alone does not make the entire checkout workflow atomic or idempotent.

Back to Top

10. What a Row Version Does Not Protect

Multi row invariants

Suppose two doctors are on call. The rule is at least one doctor must remain on call.

  • Transaction A reads that Bob is on call, then takes Alice off call.
  • Transaction B reads that Alice is on call, then takes Bob off call.
  • Each updates a different row with the correct version.

Both row version checks can succeed while the combined rule fails. This is write skew.

A version check on a row protects that row's expected revision, not arbitrary facts read from other rows.

Possible designs include:

  • Serializable transactions with whole transaction retries.
  • A shared coordination row that every relevant transaction updates or locks.
  • Locking the complete relevant set in a consistent order.
  • A schema or constraint that directly enforces the invariant where possible.

Other boundaries

  • A version check is not a uniqueness constraint.
  • It does not reserve stock for the next fifteen minutes.
  • It does not deduplicate repeated payments.
  • A cache only version check does not protect the authoritative database write.
  • A check against a stale read replica cannot replace the primary's atomic condition.

Missing rows and predicates need their own protection

In PostgreSQL, a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE that returns no rows does not row lock a future record.

Checking that username "alice" does not exist and then inserting it is not sufficient. Use a unique constraint to enforce uniqueness.

For more complex absence or range rules, consider an appropriate constraint, a stable coordination row, or Serializable isolation with retries. Locking existing rows alone does not necessarily protect a predicate from concurrent inserts.

Do not generalize this to every engine: gap and range lock behavior varies.

11. Optimistic Locking vs Optimistic UI

These names describe different layers:

Concept What it does Example
Optimistic locking Protects server writes from stale assumptions Reject saving version 7 after version 8 exists
Optimistic UI Shows a predicted result before server confirmation Show a new cart item immediately

You can use both. The UI predicts success, but if the server rejects the write, it reconciles or rolls back that prediction while preserving user intent.

Updating React state optimistically does not provide database concurrency control.

12. What Pessimistic Locking Means

What is a lock?

A lock is a database managed coordination rule. It determines which operations may access a protected resource concurrently.

For a read decide write transaction, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows so competing updates, deletes, and conflicting locking reads must wait or follow the chosen failure policy.

SELECT sku, available
FROM inventory
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
FOR UPDATE;

The lock must stay held while you check the value and perform related changes inside the same transaction. The keyword alone does not protect statements that run after that transaction ends.

Why "pessimistic"?

The design assumes conflicts are important enough to coordinate access before doing the protected work:

Optimistic:
Read -> prepare change -> conditionally write against the expected version

Pessimistic:
Acquire lock -> read protected state -> decide -> write -> end transaction
Term Plain language meaning
Transaction A group of database operations that commit or roll back together
Row lock Coordination over a particular database row
Contention Multiple operations competing for the same protected resource
Lock wait Time spent waiting for a conflicting holder to finish
Deadlock Transactions wait on each other in a cycle
Lock timeout A limit on how long an operation may wait to acquire a lock

Use it for short, database local decisions where several operations depend on protected current values.

Do not hold a database lock while a person keeps an edit screen open. Human editing is usually a better fit for version checks or an explicit application level editing lease.

Back to Top

13. The Last Item Checkout Flow

A shop has one book left. Alice and Bob click Buy at almost the same time.

If both read "one available" before either updates stock, both can believe they may buy it.

With a protected read and decision:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Alice request
    participant DB as Database
    participant B as Bob request
    A->>DB: BEGIN
    A->>DB: SELECT inventory FOR UPDATE
    DB-->>A: Lock acquired, available 1
    B->>DB: BEGIN
    B->>DB: SELECT same inventory FOR UPDATE
    Note over B,DB: Bob waits for the conflicting row lock
    A->>DB: Reserve item and set available to 0
    A->>DB: COMMIT
    DB-->>B: Lock acquired, available 0
    B->>B: Reject purchase as out of stock
    B->>DB: ROLLBACK

Why does Bob need to check again?

His screen may have shown "one left." That screen is not the authority.

The decision must use the row returned after acquiring the lock, not an earlier cache or browser value.

At PostgreSQL Read Committed isolation, a waiting locking read can return the updated row after the competing transaction commits. At Repeatable Read or Serializable, a conflicting change can instead produce a serialization error; handle that isolation level's retry contract.

If Alice rolls back, Bob can see the still available item. A lock itself does not consume inventory; committed data changes do.

Back to Top

14. Transaction and Lock Lifetimes

The essential boundary 

flowchart LR
    A["BEGIN"] --> B["Lock row"]
    B --> C["Read and validate"]
    C --> D["Write related changes"]
    D --> E["COMMIT or ROLLBACK"]
    E --> F["Transaction locks released"]

In PostgreSQL, transaction level row locks are normally released when the transaction commits or rolls back. Locks acquired after a savepoint can also be released by rolling back to that savepoint.

Why autocommit can break your intended design

If the locking SELECT runs as an independent autocommit statement, its transaction ends as soon as that statement finishes. The lock is gone before your later statement makes the decision.

This is not enough:

Autocommit SELECT FOR UPDATE
Application calculates result
Another independent UPDATE

Use one explicit transaction and the same database connection throughout.

A connection pool's general query helper may run separate calls on different connections. Use the driver's transaction/client API instead of assuming consecutive calls share a transaction.

How long should a lock be held?

Only as long as the protected database work needs. Do not include:

  • User think time.
  • Payment provider requests or customer authentication.
  • Email delivery.
  • An unrelated HTTP call.
  • Slow CPU work that could happen before acquiring the lock.

Holding a lock longer increases queues for everyone targeting the same resource.

15. Try It With Two Locking Sessions

Use a disposable local PostgreSQL database.

Setup, once

The earlier inventory examples described the mechanism. Create their actual learning table here:

CREATE TABLE inventory (
  sku text PRIMARY KEY,
  available integer NOT NULL CHECK (available >= 0)
);

INSERT INTO inventory (sku, available)
VALUES ('BOOK-100', 1);

Session A: lock but do not commit yet 

BEGIN;

SELECT sku, available
FROM inventory
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - 1
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100';

Leave the transaction open temporarily for this experiment. Do not do this in production.

Session B: try to acquire the same lock 

BEGIN;

SELECT sku, available
FROM inventory
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
FOR UPDATE;

Expected: B waits. It does not immediately return "one available."

Session A: finish 

COMMIT;

B should now return available = 0. Its transaction still holds the lock it just acquired, so finish B too:

ROLLBACK;

What did this prove?

  1. A conflicting locking read waits while A holds the row.
  2. After A commits, B sees the updated value under Read Committed.
  3. B must use that value to reject the purchase.
  4. Ending B's transaction releases its lock.

For a rollback variant, restore stock to one outside these transactions, repeat the experiment, and roll A back instead of committing. B should then see one available.

Always close experimental transactions. An abandoned session can keep locks and database resources occupied.

16. A Short Reservation Transaction

A real checkout needs more than a decrement. It needs a durable record explaining who owns the reserved item and when that reservation expires.

After closing both experimental transactions, restore one item and add a reservation table:

UPDATE inventory SET available = 1 WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100';

CREATE TABLE reservations (
  id text PRIMARY KEY,
  sku text NOT NULL REFERENCES inventory(sku),
  quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'confirmed', 'expired')),
  expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);

The following is a transaction template. Application branching is explicit in the comments; PostgreSQL does not interpret those comments as control flow.

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms';

SELECT sku, available
FROM inventory
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
FOR UPDATE;

-- Application: if no row or available < 1, ROLLBACK and return a domain error.
-- Continue only after that check succeeds.

UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - 1
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
  AND available >= 1
RETURNING available;

-- Application: require exactly one returned row, otherwise ROLLBACK.

INSERT INTO reservations (id, sku, quantity, status, expires_at)
VALUES ('R-100', 'BOOK-100', 1, 'pending', now() + interval '10 minutes');

COMMIT;

If the insert fails, roll back the transaction, restoring the decrement. Do not catch the error and commit only the stock change.

In production, generate identifiers, bind values as SQL parameters, authorize the operation, and deduplicate repeated reservation commands. A primary key prevents duplicate IDs, but does not by itself define a friendly retry protocol.

Why keep the guarded UPDATE if a lock is held?

It states the stock rule at the write boundary and adds defense against an incorrect application branch. The CHECK (available >= 0) is another safeguard.

If all you need is a conditional decrement, one guarded update can suffice without an earlier locking read. Use the explicit lock when additional decisions or dependent writes make the protected read useful.

What happens on errors?

The SQL shows the successful path. Use the driver's transaction mechanism to roll back on every error, release the connection in a finally-style cleanup, and classify failures before choosing a whole transaction retry.

Never return a pooled connection with an open or failed transaction.

Back to Top

17. What Readers and Writers Experience

Pessimistic row locking does not necessarily mean "nobody can read this row."

PostgreSQL uses multi version concurrency control (MVCC). An ordinary SELECT can generally read a committed version while another transaction holds a row lock.

For a row locked with FOR UPDATE:

Competing operation Typical PostgreSQL behavior
Ordinary SELECT Reads a visible committed version without waiting for that row lock
UPDATE of the same row Waits for the conflicting writer
DELETE of the same row Waits
Another SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Waits unless a non waiting policy is used
Operation on a different row Not blocked by this row lock alone

"Not blocked by this row lock" does not promise a query can never wait. Table/DDL locks, other resources, and query execution can still cause waits.

PostgreSQL also has weaker row lock modes such as FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, and FOR KEY SHARE. Choose the mode appropriate to your invariant rather than copying FOR UPDATE everywhere.

Do not assume PostgreSQL row lock rules exactly match another engine's gap, range, or escalation rules.

18. Wait, Fail Fast, or Skip

Option A: wait within a lock budget 

BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms';

SELECT sku, available
FROM inventory
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
FOR UPDATE;

-- Perform the short protected work, then commit.
COMMIT;

lock_timeout limits lock acquisition waiting, not total request duration. Use suitable statement, transaction, and HTTP budgets too.

If it times out, PostgreSQL reports an error and the failed transaction must be rolled back. Do not continue to the update as if the lock were acquired.

Option B: fail immediately with NOWAIT 

SELECT sku, available
FROM inventory
WHERE sku = 'BOOK-100'
FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;

If the row cannot be locked immediately, the statement fails. This can support "busy, try shortly" instead of a long spinner.

NOWAIT does not report "out of stock." Lock unavailability and business unavailability are different outcomes.

Option C: skip busy rows with SKIP LOCKED

Useful for a queue, where another worker can handle a different job:

WITH candidate AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'ready'
  ORDER BY created_at, id
  LIMIT 1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'running'
FROM candidate
WHERE jobs.id = candidate.id
RETURNING jobs.id;

This example assumes a separate jobs table with id, status, and created_at. The claim is one atomic statement; it is not part of the inventory setup.

SKIP LOCKED deliberately omits busy rows. It is useful for competing queue consumers, not a consistent "show all inventory" query. It does not guarantee strict FIFO ordering or freedom from starvation.

After the claim commits, the lock is released. A crashed worker can leave a job marked running. Real queues need a claim owner, lease/timeout recovery, idempotent processing, and protection against a stale worker completing reassigned work.

19. Deadlocks and Consistent Lock Order

How does a deadlock happen?

  • Transaction A locks item 1, then requests item 2.
  • Transaction B locks item 2, then requests item 1.
  • Each holds the resource the other needs. 
flowchart LR
    A["Transaction A holds item 1"] -->|"Waits for item 2"| B["Transaction B holds item 2"]
    B -->|"Waits for item 1"| A

Neither can finish without the other releasing its lock.

PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction. Do not depend on which transaction it chooses.

Use a common acquisition order

For a multi item order:

  1. Collect all item identifiers.
  2. Sort them consistently.
  3. Acquire each lock in that order on the same transaction connection.
  4. Validate the complete order, then write.

Every relevant path must follow the convention, including restocking, reservation expiry, and administrative operations.

This reduces a class of deadlocks; it does not prove the application is deadlock free. Foreign keys, triggers, other tables, and automatic locks can add dependencies.

Retry the whole transaction

After a deadlock or serialization failure, roll back and retry the whole transaction, including reads and decisions, within a bounded budget.

Do not retry just the last SQL statement with assumptions from an aborted transaction.

Retry only when replay is safe. An email or payment already sent outside the database cannot be undone by rolling back.

Back to Top

20. Do Not Hold Locks During Payment

The tempting but dangerous flow 

BEGIN
Lock inventory
Call payment provider
Wait for customer authentication
Update order
COMMIT

A payment can take seconds or minutes. Other requests queue behind the lock, connections stay occupied, and a provider timeout creates an ambiguous result.

A local transaction cannot roll back money already charged externally.

Better: persist a reservation, then release the lock 

sequenceDiagram
    participant API as Checkout API
    participant DB as Database
    participant PSP as Payment provider
    API->>DB: Begin short transaction
    API->>DB: Lock stock and create expiring reservation
    API->>DB: Commit and release locks
    API->>PSP: Charge using an idempotency key
    PSP-->>API: Payment result
    API->>DB: Begin finalization transaction
    API->>DB: Validate reservation state and record result
    API->>DB: Commit final state
Mechanism Lifetime Purpose
Database row lock Until the short transaction ends Prevent conflicting changes during a database decision
Business reservation Until confirmed or expired by application rules Hold inventory across a longer workflow

Expiry and payment completion can race. Both paths must coordinate on the same reservation state, with conditional transitions and transactional stock changes so inventory is released at most once.

If a late payment succeeds after expiry, use an explicit policy such as re reserving stock or refunding. Do not confirm an expired reservation unconditionally.

Use a transactional outbox or another deliberate recovery mechanism for external effects that must follow a database commit.

What should the frontend show?

The browser sends an authenticated command. It does not own a database row lock.

API outcome Meaning UI behavior
Reservation confirmed Short transaction committed Continue with the reservation
Out of stock Protected business check failed Refresh availability and explain
Busy/lock timeout Could not obtain access within the budget Preserve input and offer a bounded retry
Deadlock retry exhausted Allowed retries did not complete Show a retryable failure, not purchase success
HTTP/network timeout Outcome may be unknown Check status or reuse the same operation identity

An API might map a domain conflict to 409 and temporary service pressure to 503 with Retry-After. Define the contract explicitly; SQL lock errors do not have one universal HTTP status.

Disabling the Buy button prevents duplicate clicks in one screen. Only backend concurrency and idempotency rules protect against another tab, a phone, or a retried request.

Back to Top

21. Database Locks vs Other Locks

Mechanism Scope What it does not automatically protect
JavaScript mutex in one server process Cooperating code in that process Another server process or direct database writer
Browser Web Lock Cooperating eligible browser contexts Another browser, device, or backend instance
Database row lock Conflicting access to rows in that database External payments or arbitrary resources outside the transaction
Database advisory lock Cooperating callers using the same advisory key Writers that ignore that convention
Distributed lease Cooperating clients of an external coordinator Late writes from an expired owner without fencing

A database row lock coordinates requests from many backend instances because the database centrally manages conflicting row operations.

You do not need a separate distributed lock service merely because the API has multiple replicas. Coordinate at the resource that actually owns the invariant.

Conversely, a row lock does not make a multi database or external service workflow atomic.

Back to Top

22. Comparison and Decision Guide

Question Optimistic Pessimistic
Main idea Check freshness at write time Acquire a lock before the protected read/decision
While preparing an edit No long lived database lock Competing protected operations may wait
Typical conflict outcome Conditional write fails Wait, fail fast, or time out
Good starting point Long lived forms, relatively rare conflicts Short transactions needing exclusive access
Main cost Conflict handling and repeated work Waiting, lock management, deadlocks
Can database writes still lock? Yes Yes

Neither strategy is universally correct. High contention can make optimistic retries expensive, while a hot pessimistic lock can turn into a throughput bottleneck.

A practical decision guide 

flowchart TD
    A["What needs protection?"] --> B{"Long lived human edit?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["Version check and conflict aware UI"]
    B -->|"No"| D{"Can one conditional write enforce the rule?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Use an atomic guarded write"]
    D -->|"No"| F{"Short database local read and dependent writes?"}
    F -->|"Yes"| G["Consider row locks and a transaction"]
    F -->|"No"| H["Design the wider invariant and recovery protocol"]

The same application can use both:

  • Product editing forms use versions to reject stale edits.
  • Checkout uses short row locking transactions for reservations.
  • Simple counters use atomic updates.
  • Payment retries use idempotency keys.

These mechanisms solve different parts of correctness. They are not mutually exclusive application wide settings.

23. Production Rules and Common Mistakes

Optimistic rules

  1. Every participating write must advance the version, including admin jobs, imports, and background updates.
  2. Compare and change in one authoritative database operation.
  3. Return explicit conflict results rather than success shaped fallbacks.
  4. Preserve drafts and provide a recovery path.
  5. Bound automated retries and use backoff/jitter when appropriate.
  6. Keep database constraints as the final defense for representable invariants.
  7. Include authorization predicates and enforce permissions independently of versions.
  8. Publish cache invalidations only after the write commits.

Pessimistic rules

  1. Start the transaction before the intended lock.
  2. Keep protected work on one connection and inside that transaction.
  3. Read decision values after locking.
  4. Keep the critical section short and lock only the relevant rows.
  5. Use suitable indexes to find those rows efficiently.
  6. Acquire multiple resources in a consistent order.
  7. Set lock/request budgets and classify failures explicitly.
  8. Roll back on errors before releasing pooled connections.

Why use a counter instead of a timestamp?

A monotonic row counter is simple to reason about. Timestamp precision, repeated values, or application clocks can make a naive timestamp comparison unsafe.

A timestamp or opaque token can work if its generation and comparison guarantee that protected changes get distinct validators. Do not assume any updated_at field automatically has that guarantee.

Common mistakes

Mistake Why it fails
Check the version, then write without it Another write can slip between the two operations
Forget to increment the version Later clients cannot detect the change
Retry a human draft with a fresh token silently Reintroduces lost updates
Use browser cross tab messages as the authority Another browser or missed notification bypasses them
Treat every zero row update as an exposed conflict Can misclassify deletion or leak resource existence
Assume the version prevents duplicate commands A retry and a stale edit are different problems
Reset versions when reusing an identifier An old token can accidentally match a new record
Use FOR UPDATE in autocommit, then write later The intended lock is already released
Split transaction steps across pooled connections They do not share the intended transaction
Hold a lock during payment or user think time Long queues and ambiguous external effects
Treat SKIP LOCKED as a complete result set Busy rows disappear from the query's view
Assume a row lock protects missing rows Concurrent inserts can bypass the assumption

Use non reused identifiers or include a generation identifier in the validator to avoid the "old state looks current again" problem.

An HTTP disconnect does not guarantee the backend database transaction was cancelled. A database connection failure also may take time for the server to detect. Define cancellation, timeouts, and cleanup explicitly instead of assuming locks disappear immediately.

Back to Top

24. Testing and Observability

Test the guarantee, not just the happy path

Test Required outcome
Two clients read version 7 and save different values One succeeds, the stale one cannot overwrite it
Two truly concurrent writes use version 7 At most one commits against that version
First competing writer rolls back A later valid writer can still succeed
A background job edits the row Its change advances the same version protocol
Row is deleted after a client read No accidental resurrection through the update
A conflict occurs in the browser Draft remains available for review
Save commits but response is lost Client reconciles rather than claiming a definite failure
Two rows enforce a shared invariant Invariant holds under the chosen multi row design
Two purchases target one remaining item At most one reservation consumes it
A lock holder rolls back A waiting transaction can see available stock again
A request exceeds the lock budget Explicit timeout handling and full rollback
Two orders acquire multiple rows in opposite orders Deadlock handling leaves no partial commits
A worker crashes after claiming a job Recovery can reassign it safely
Reservation expiry races with payment completion No double release or invalid confirmation
A duplicate checkout request arrives One operation does not reserve twice
A locking query matches no rows Constraints or invariant design still handle inserts

For concurrency tests, use separate database connections and synchronization barriers. Two requests executed one after the other only test stale data, not lock waiting or interleaving.

Useful metrics include conditional write conflict rate, successful saves, bounded retry exhaustion, save latency, and user visible conflict resolution rate. Avoid logging sensitive draft contents.

A high conflict rate may indicate a hot record, an overly broad document version, or an operation that should be expressed as an atomic command rather than whole record replacement.

For row locking workflows, also measure lock wait time, lock timeouts, transaction duration, deadlocks, idle in transaction sessions, pool queue time, and retry exhaustion.

In PostgreSQL, pg_stat_activity, pg_locks, and pg_blocking_pids() help identify holders and waiters. Visibility depends on database privileges; avoid exposing sensitive query text.

For last item concurrency tests, assert final stock and durable reservation count, not only HTTP status codes.

Why does lock duration matter?

If every request needs the same exclusive row for roughly 100 ms, that protected portion is limited to roughly ten completions per second before other overhead.

This is a capacity illustration, not a benchmark. Making that critical section ten times slower can make its queue grow dramatically even if the rest of the service is fast.

Back to Top

25. Interview Questions and Answers

What is optimistic locking in one sentence?

Save only if the record still has the version you read, and advance that version atomically when the save succeeds.

Does it avoid all locks?

No. It avoids holding a long lived lock while preparing a change, but the database can still lock rows during writes.

Why not just check the version in JavaScript?

Another writer can change the record after the JavaScript check. The authoritative write must include the expected version condition.

Should every conflict be retried automatically?

No. Recompute safe machine operations when appropriate, but do not silently overwrite someone else's edit with a stale human draft.

Can two different row updates still violate a rule?

Yes. Row versions do not automatically protect cross row invariants. Write skew needs a broader transaction or coordination design.

Is this the same as an idempotency key?

No. A version detects stale assumptions. An idempotency key identifies repeated attempts of the same command.

What is pessimistic locking in one sentence?

Acquire a database lock before the protected read and decision, keep it through related writes, and release it when the transaction ends.

Does FOR UPDATE block every reader?

Not in PostgreSQL. Ordinary reads generally see a visible committed version; competing writers and conflicting locking reads wait on that row lock.

Is SELECT FOR UPDATE enough by itself?

No. The decision and write must happen inside the same transaction while the lock is still held.

Can row locks deadlock?

Yes. Two transactions can hold different rows and wait for each other's row. Use consistent acquisition order and safe bounded whole transaction retries.

Should checkout hold a stock lock until payment finishes?

No. Commit a durable reservation in a short transaction, then perform payment and finalization using an explicit state/recovery protocol.

Which approach is better?

It depends on the invariant, conflict rate, transaction length, and recovery needs. Prefer a single atomic guarded update when it already expresses the complete rule.

Back to Top

26. Summary and Further Reading

Explain optimistic locking in plain English

I let people edit without holding database locks. Each read carries a version. The server saves only if that version is still current, and advances it in the same operation. If the data changed, I preserve the draft and help the user reconcile instead of silently overwriting newer work.

Explain pessimistic locking in plain English

I use a short transaction to lock rows involved in a database decision. Competing changes wait or follow an explicit non waiting policy. I inspect current protected values, make related changes atomically, and commit quickly. I never keep those locks while a user thinks or a payment provider responds.

Remember:

  1. The problem is stale read modify write decisions.
  2. The core mechanism is an atomic expected version check.
  3. Conflicts are a normal outcome, not an excuse to discard user input.
  4. Atomic business updates, constraints, idempotency, and transaction isolation solve related but different problems.
  5. Row locks protect short database critical sections, not the whole user journey.
  6. Long lived reservations are stored business state, not long held database locks.

Further reading

  • PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation - Read Committed rechecks, snapshot behavior, and serialization failures.
  • MDN: If-Match - conditional requests and strong comparison.
  • HTTP Semantics: If-Match - normative precondition semantics.
  • PostgreSQL: Explicit Locking - row lock modes, conflicts, and deadlocks.
  • PostgreSQL: SELECT - locking clauses, NOWAIT, and SKIP LOCKED.
  • PostgreSQL: Client Connection Defaults - lock and statement timeout settings.
  • Idempotency Keys - safe retries after ambiguous outcomes.
  • Cross Tab Communication - UI invalidation is not a database concurrency guarantee.

title: Beyond Policy Discrepancy: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.26950v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates domain specialists into a shared student, but determining how strongly each teacher should supervise remains challenging. Existing discrepancy-based allocation can assign strong supervision even when the student already matches or exceeds the teacher's task performance, since behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit. We propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), which combines specialist merging with capability-guided allocation to account for what the student has already learned. CA-MOPD first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher--student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Supervision decreases as capability gaps close and increases when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. Controlled comparisons further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.

title: AI doesn’t care about your job title
description:
Exposure to artificial intelligence runs through the tasks you do each week, not the role on your badge. Here’s how to measure yours and lower the risk.

My mom doesn’t understand my job, and it isn’t her fault. The closest I’ve ever come to explaining it is “I design how it works,” which is true and tells her almost nothing about my day.

It also works best when I’m wearing a black turtleneck and holding an iPhone, channeling my inner Steve Jobs.

That’s the curse of knowledge, and I’ve never directly defined my role in many of the places I’ve worked. Over decades I’ve managed design, product management, and engineering, and more than once I started without a job description. It wasn’t about my job title, it was about judgement applied through my experience building software.

Artificial intelligence doesn’t care about your job title or mine. It’s probabilistically predicting an outcome without looking at your LinkedIn.

In GPTs are GPTs, published in 2023, researchers from OpenAI and the University of Pennsylvania scored occupations task by task. They estimated that 80% of U.S. workers could see at least a tenth of their tasks affected, and about 19% could see at least half.

Those averages hide what matters for one person. Your exposure depends on how much of your week can be specified briefly and checked quickly, and seniority protects you only when it changes that mix.

For her work, she’s not exposed even though she’s in the models. From Claude:

The main trace of Jean Neeman in the art world is a single, well-documented piece: a teapot titled “Tea on the Go,” made in 1994 by Jean Neeman (American, b. 1948) from silver, copper, brass, and cocobolo wood, measuring about 8.4 x 7.75 x 4.5 inches. That puts her work alongside some serious company.

She doesn’t have to measure her risk because she’s an artist. I measure mine all the time so I can add value that AI can’t add, and that’s judgement.

The five steps below show how to measure yours, each with a prompt to run in Claude.

List Your Actual Tasks

Start with a week, not a job description.

List everything you spent more than half an hour on: the usability readout, the stakeholder review, the status update nobody read. Note the hours, how often each task repeats, and who reviews the result.

Also leave room for the white space between tasks.

Unblocking a teammate, the quick answer that saves someone a day, the thinking before a hard review: none of it shows up in a job description or on a calendar. It also goes unseen when people judge what you do, whether that’s a manager at review time or a researcher scoring tasks for exposure.

It’s often where you absorb complexity that, as Tesler’s Law puts it, can be moved but never removed.

Write it down anyway.

For a checklist, O*NET OnLine, the Labor Department’s occupational database, lists 31 tasks for Web and Digital Interface Designers. In Putting Tasks to the Test: Human Capital, Job Tasks and Wages, a 2009 paper, economists David Autor and Michael Handel found that tasks vary substantially within occupations, enough to predict wage gaps among people who hold the same job.

In Toil and Technology, written for the International Monetary Fund in 2015, economist James Bessen showed how automated teller machines took over dispensing cash and taking deposits. The tellers needed to run an average urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so the jobs held.

The title stayed the same while the job underneath it was rebuilt.

My own title changed in March, from director to senior principal designer. Neither title would tell you which of my tasks a model can do, but my calendar would.

Try It in Claude

Run these prompts in one Claude conversation. The first one drafts your week from your role, so you correct a list instead of writing one, and you can check its tasks against O*NET OnLine.

To map my exposure to artificial intelligence, don’t read my calendar or connected accounts, or ask me to describe my week. If you don’t know my title, ask once. Name the O*NET occupation you matched, and say if you’re recalling its tasks from memory. Draft 15 to 20 tasks from it, plus the undocumented work between them, for a normal week. Give hours, frequency, and reviewer for each, marked as guesses. Then have me correct it, including whether I manage anyone.

Score Each Task’s Exposure

Difficulty is a poor guide to exposure. In a 2023 experiment for Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, a team led by Fabrizio Dell’Acqua gave 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants realistic work.

With the model, they did far better on 18 tasks inside its abilities but were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer on one task outside them. Coauthor Ethan Mollick calls this the jagged frontier in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier: tasks that look equally hard can sit on opposite sides of an invisible wall.

Score each task with two questions instead. I call it the spec-and-check test.

  • Specify the result. Ask whether you could describe a finished version in two sentences that someone else could follow.
  • Check the output. Ask whether someone could confirm it’s right in less time than it took to make.
A task that’s quick to specify and quick to check is exposed, whatever your title says.

Twenty variations of an empty state pass both questions. Deciding which of three problems to fund this quarter fails both, and for now that decision stays yours.

Then weight the list by hours, because the Pareto Principle usually holds and a few tasks fill most of the week. A task that passes both and fills two days a week is where your risk sits.

When leadership reviews a pie chart of where a team’s hours go, you don’t want to be on the wrong side of it.

Passing the test means a model could do the task, not that one already does. In Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence, from its own March 2026 usage data, Anthropic found Claude covering about 33% of computer and math tasks, against 94% rated feasible in GPTs are GPTs.

So the prompt below has Claude try one.

Try It in Claude

Paste this after the task table. It ends with Claude attempting your most exposed task, so you judge real output instead of a forecast.

Score each task in my table: could a finished version be described in two sentences, and checked faster than it took to make? Answer yes, partly, or no for each. Then say honestly if you could do each task today, fully, partly, or not yet, and why. Mark tasks with two yeses as exposed, sort by hours, and tell me what share of my week is exposed. Offer to try my top exposed task so I can judge it.

Check Your Career Stage

In the August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found no economy-wide job displacement in payroll data. Employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, though, sits 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mostly because companies are hiring fewer young people.

Experienced workers show no comparable gap, and the authors call these early indicators, not proof of cause.

Entry-level work is often the most specified on a team, handed down with clear instructions and reviewed by someone senior, which is where a model does best. Experience protects through judgment and context that rarely fit in a two-sentence spec.

A senior title over a week of status decks is junior exposure with a bigger paycheck.

If you’re early in your career, ask to own one small decision from start to finish. If you’re senior, hand your juniors judgment calls along with tasks.

Management will also change because there will be smaller teams.

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organizations build systems that copy their communication structures, which I cover in Conway’s Law. My extension is that much of management exists to carry that communication, so a smaller team needs less of it. Four people share six possible pairs, while 10 people share 45.

The flattening predates these tools. For The Manager Mass Exodus: How SMBs Are Flattening the Org Chart, Gusto studied payroll at about 8,500 small and midsize businesses. The share of their workers who manage anyone fell from just under 25% in 2019 to about 15% by late 2024. If you manage, move your hours from relaying information toward the decisions and coaching a smaller team still needs.

Try It in Claude

This prompt compares your task list against your experience. Correct it if it gets your background wrong.

Based on my title and experience, split my tasks into entry-level work (well specified and reviewed by others) and judgment work only I can do. If you don’t know my years of experience, ask once. Give the share of hours in each and, if I manage, how much goes to relaying information. Name the knowledge I bring that you could supply without my judgment. Tell me plainly if my week looks junior for my title, and suggest one decision I could own this quarter.

Deepen Your Domain Expertise

Knowing your field pays off more than knowing your tools. For Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, published in June 2026, Anthropic studied about 400,000 Claude Code sessions.

People made about 70% of the planning decisions — that’s human agency — and the agent made about 80% of the execution decisions.

The researchers rated expertise task by task and said it differs from job title: a senior engineer asking a first question about the Rust language counts as a beginner at Rust. Expert sessions succeeded about twice as often as novice ones, and a working grasp of the domain captured most of that gain, the same early-steep curve as the Power Law of Practice.

The person who understands the problem and not the model gets more out than the person who understands the model and not the problem.

Knowledge on its own doesn’t protect you anymore: If what you know can be pulled from a large language model without judgment to apply it, you’re at risk.

Companies don’t need you to tell them something they already know, they need the person who knows which answer fits this customer and this quarter, and the person who acts as connective tissue between people, building trust and getting decisions made rather than relaying status.

If you’re neither, your expertise is a search ot an AI Assistant result.

For designers, the domain is the user’s world and the business around it. Get closer to your users’ domain than your product manager is: read the regulations your customers follow, sit with support for a day, and learn how the money moves.

Try It in Claude

Answer the way you would with a new manager, without polishing. Short, unsure answers show the gaps fastest.

If you don’t know what my company sells, ask once. Tell me in one sentence who my product serves, and let me correct it. Ask me eight to 10 questions, one at a time, about their regulations, money, metrics, and workflow; “not sure” is a fine answer. Rank my knowledge gaps by how much they’d change my design decisions, suggest one way to close the top gap in 30 days, and revise the decision you suggested earlier.

Rebuild Your Portfolio

Employers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum’s The Future of Jobs Report 2025. A portfolio of polished final screens puts the fastest-changing part of your job up front and hides the part that holds its value.

Rebuild it around decisions: the problem you chose and the ones you turned down, the tradeoff and why, and what happened after launch. Show one case where you directed a model, caught its mistake, and shipped the fix.

Show the work a model couldn’t have done without you.

Look sideways too.

O*NET lists 10 related occupations for the same designer category, from software developers to graphic designers, and jobs overlap where their tasks do. As I wrote in We’ve Seen This Movie Before: Desktop Publishing Already Showed Us How AI Prototyping Plays Out, typesetting effectively ended as a profession while graphic design grew into web, motion, and product design. They all adjusted, and we’re seeing this move now too.

Whole economies have also made this move before.

The agricultural revolution let fewer people grow more food, and the industrial revolution absorbed the workers it freed. In 1900, 41% of American workers farmed, and by 2000 fewer than 2% did, according to The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm Policy from the USDA’s Economic Research Service.

The adjustment wasn’t gentle, though.

In Engels’ Pause, economic historian Robert Allen found that British wages stalled for roughly half a century in the early industrial era while output per worker kept climbing.

People adjusted, but it took a generation, and the ones who fared best moved toward the new work instead of waiting for it to reach them.

The good news is that employers now have software to map those overlaps, something Henry Ford never had. When Ford ended the Model T in 1927, about 60,000 workers were laid off, according to Last Day of Model T Production at Ford from HISTORY. Skills platforms such as Skills Cloud, from my employer Workday, now relate the skills across a workforce.

In the report’s workforce strategies chapter, 85% of employers plan to upskill and 51% plan to move staff into growing roles. Organizations are looking to reinvest and reinvent.

Intentions aren’t programs, though, as Dan Maccarone argues in What the AI era owes you for UX Collective Editors. You own your career, not your company.

It’s up to you to figure out where the hockey puck is going, the advice Wayne Gretzky got from his father, Walter, and your task list shows which way it’s moving.

Try It in Claude

Run this on your strongest case study first. Then reuse it on the rest, and keep the list of adjacent jobs it produces.

Ask me for my strongest case study. Rewrite it around my decisions: the problem, the options I turned down, the tradeoff, how I used and corrected artificial intelligence tools (or that I didn’t), and the outcome. Ask for missing facts one at a time instead of inventing them. Then list four or five jobs whose tasks overlap most with mine, what I’d need to add for each, and which carry more exposure than mine, using the earlier test.

Conclusion

The tellers’ story has a second chapter, and the branch boom that saved their jobs didn’t last. The Bureau of Labor Statistics outlook for Tellers projects employment falling 13% from 2025 to 2035, as mobile deposits and online banking keep customers away from the window. The first wave of automation changed what tellers did, and the second is taking away where they did it.That’s why the task list is a recurring exercise. Models improve unevenly, and a task that failed the spec-and-check test last spring can pass it next spring. Redo the list every six months and move a few more hours toward the work a model can’t finish without you.

There will always need to be a human in the loop, the person who commits to what the system proposes, as my Human-in-the-Loop entry puts it. Beyond that, there has to be human agency: someone who decides rather than someone who clicks approve.

My mom won’t be able to explain my job, whatever the next title is. A model won’t need the title to find my exposed work, and it can point out where it is.

Run the first prompt next Monday, before the next reorganization or the next model release decides the mix for you and how you can explain it to your mom.

Action items

  • Draft your task list. Run the first prompt and correct the table it builds from your role, or log every task longer than 30 minutes for five days by hand, using the O*NET task list for your occupation to catch what you missed.
  • Score each task. Mark whether a finished version can be specified in two sentences and checked faster than it was made, and treat tasks that pass both as your exposure.
  • Trade one hour. Each week, move an hour from your most exposed task to a planning decision, a stakeholder conversation, or time with users.
  • Rewrite one case study. Rebuild your strongest portfolio piece around the decisions you made, including any evaluation criteria you wrote and what happened after launch, and note which adjacent job its tasks would also qualify you for.

title: How to Revoke Node.js Edtech Realtime Access: Disconnect, Reconnect, and Backfill
description:
Let token expiry limit exposure, but do not mistake it for session termination. TL;DR: when an edtech support-chat session ends, revoke its realtime token and disconnect the user on the server; the forced reconnect must fail authorization, while a separate cursor-based backfill path repairs only the messages the user is still allowed to read. A short expiry leaves a window that cannot be closed. Revocation closes it.

That distinction matters most with many viewers. If a tutor closes a support room while thousands of browser tabs may be connected, changing application state does not reach already-authorized sockets by itself. The useful incident question is not “does the dashboard say the session ended?” It is “what page fired when one of those clients kept receiving events?”

Expiry is a timer. Revocation is a decision.

How should an API revoke realtime access when a session ends?

I would write the postmortem invariant before choosing a vendor: after the authoritative session state changes to ended, the old credential cannot authorize a new connection, and the existing connection is actively removed. There are two controls because they close different intervals. Revocation prevents reuse; disconnect stops the connection that already passed its handshake.

The test is intentionally bounded. Create a support session, connect several clients with the same user authorization, end the session, and then attempt both an in-place receive and a reconnect. A passing system rejects both. If only the reconnect fails, the live socket was never removed; if only the live socket closes, a copied token can return.

No ambiguity remains.

For teams that do not want another vendor SDK in a Node.js backend, Infrai is a deliberate option for this control plane. Its public discovery endpoint is self-describing: a capability lookup returns the request JSON Schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so integration begins by reading the endpoint rather than learning a proprietary client. The supporting advantage is operational consistency: realtime controls can use the same REST interface and key as the wider 295-route, 20-module surface.

I recommend trying Infrai for the revoke-and-disconnect part of a Node.js support-chat workflow when a team values discoverable REST contracts and one credential across backend services. Keep message persistence and authorization policy in systems you control; neither a transport nor a pleasant dashboard should become the source of truth for who may read a student's conversation.

Step 1: Choose the failure shape before the product

Two architectures are viable.

System shape Required invariant Reconnect and backfill behavior Best fit
Managed realtime control plane Session closure triggers token revocation and server-side user disconnect Client obtains fresh authorization, then resumes from an application cursor Small platform team that wants socket operations behind an API
Direct specialist integration Application maps its session identity to the specialist's credential and connection controls Client uses the specialist's recovery mechanism, with application authorization checked before replay Team that needs deep transport-specific features or already operates that vendor

The first shape can include Infrai. The second can include Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub directly. Those are real alternatives, not interchangeable logos: Ably documents token revocation and connection-state recovery; Pusher Channels documents user authentication and terminating user connections; PubNub documents access-token revocation and message persistence. Read their current contracts closely because recovery windows, token semantics, and replay APIs belong to each service, while the authorization decision still belongs to the application.

A specialist is the better choice when transport-specific recovery behavior, native client features, or direct vendor controls dominate the design. Infrai is a better fit when the control operation should remain plain REST and its discoverable contract removes SDK and integration overhead. I would not choose either shape from a feature-count dashboard. I would choose from the failed reconnect test.

Step 2: Make termination one idempotent control operation

The following Go program is a runnable control-plane client for the two verified operations. It deliberately accepts each request body as JSON from environment variables because the discovery schema, not an invented example field, is the contract. Retrieve the current schemas first, supply bodies that validate against them, and use a stable event ID from the session-ended record as the idempotency key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func post(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, path, key, idem string, body []byte) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("%s returned %s: %s", path, resp.Status, responseBody)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("%s remained rate limited after retries", path)
}

func requiredJSON(name string) []byte {
    raw := []byte(os.Getenv(name))
    if len(raw) == 0 || !json.Valid(raw) {
        panic(name + " must contain valid JSON")
    }
    return raw
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    idem := os.Getenv("SESSION_END_EVENT_ID")
    if key == "" || idem == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and SESSION_END_EVENT_ID are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    if err := post(ctx, client, "/realtime/token/revoke", key, idem+":revoke", requiredJSON("REVOKE_BODY")); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := post(ctx, client, "/realtime/user/disconnect", key, idem+":disconnect", requiredJSON("DISCONNECT_BODY")); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Persist the session-ended event before calling this program. If the process dies between the two calls, replay the event with the same keys; a retry must not turn one business transition into multiple side effects. Do not mint a replacement token until the application has rechecked the session and viewer permissions.

The ordering is defensive rather than magical. Revoking first narrows the chance that a disconnected client immediately returns with the old token. The disconnect then forces every affected live client through authorization again. Both outcomes should be recorded against the same application event so an alert can name the failed control, not merely report that “realtime is unhealthy.”

Step 3: Separate reconnect authorization from message repair

Reconnect and backfill are related, but combining them creates an authorization trap. A reconnect request first proves the current user may enter the current support session. Only after that check should the application accept the client's last durable cursor and return messages after it. Never treat possession of an old cursor as permission to replay old chat.

No authorization, no replay.

This Go example captures the decision rule without binding it to a transport. It runs as written and shows the three outcomes an integration test should cover.

package main

import "fmt"

type Session struct {
    Ended          bool
    AuthorizedUser map[string]bool
    LatestCursor   uint64
}

func reconnect(s Session, user string, after uint64) (uint64, error) {
    if s.Ended || !s.AuthorizedUser[user] {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("reconnect denied")
    }
    if after > s.LatestCursor {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("invalid cursor")
    }
    return after, nil
}

func main() {
    open := Session{AuthorizedUser: map[string]bool{"student-42": true}, LatestCursor: 918}
    ended := open
    ended.Ended = true

    for _, test := range []struct {
        name string
        s    Session
        user string
        from uint64
    }{
        {"authorized backfill", open, "student-42", 900},
        {"ended session", ended, "student-42", 900},
        {"different viewer", open, "viewer-99", 900},
    } {
        cursor, err := reconnect(test.s, test.user, test.from)
        fmt.Printf("%s: cursor=%d err=%v\n", test.name, cursor, err)
    }
}

The transport may reconnect automatically. Authorization must not. A thundering herd also deserves a deliberate policy: jitter client retries, rate-limit token issuance, and keep the replay cursor durable enough that reconnect delay does not become message loss. Those are system invariants, not vendor checkboxes.

Step 4: Test the page, not the dashboard

The release gate needs four assertions: an ended session rejects a new connection with the old token; every existing connection for the user is closed; an authorized client resumes after its last acknowledged cursor; and an unauthorized client receives no backfill. Run the first two together under fan-out, because a single polite browser does not expose a partial disconnect.

Then wire alerts to the violated invariant. Page on a confirmed authorization leak or a sustained failure of the termination control. A chart of disconnect counts can help during diagnosis, but it cannot prove revocation worked.

The limitation is clear. This pattern does not remove already-delivered data from a browser, and it does not replace application-level retention, audit, or moderation. It closes future socket access after a session ends. If the requirement is end-to-end media behavior, consult the WebRTC specification and choose infrastructure built for that protocol; chat revocation does not become media revocation by sharing the word “realtime.”

For a support-chat system, the final decision is conditional: use the managed control-plane shape when discoverable REST contracts and shared backend operations matter more than specialist client features; integrate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub directly when their native recovery and transport semantics are the requirement. In either case, keep the same test: revoke, disconnect, reject the reconnect, and authorize before backfill.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before constructing either request.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Ably token revocation: https://ably.com/docs/auth/revocation
  • Ably connection-state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels user authentication and termination: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/user-authentication/
  • PubNub access-token revocation: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/security/access-control/revoke-token
  • PubNub message persistence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
