title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
description:
arXiv:2610.27323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. We first show that this contextually appropriate granularity is recoverable from pre-generation hidden states, even when generated responses are misaligned, with disclosure levels exhibiting an ordered structure along a common hidden-state direction. Motivated by this, we propose an inference-time route-and-steer framework: an ordinal granularity router maps visual-contextual privacy representations to a disclosure route, and a disclosure-level-conditioned steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. Across four VLM backbones, our method improves visual-context-aware disclosure alignment, better balances over- and under-disclosure, and incurs only modest changes on general capability benchmarks. It further transfers to another dataset with a distinct data distribution and privacy-risk taxonomy.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: Encapsulation and Visibility in Java: Protecting Your Objects
description:
When writing Java code, it’s easy to focus on making a program work. But good object-oriented design is also about controlling how that program can be used.

That’s where encapsulation and visibility come in.
What Is Encapsulation?
Encapsulation means protecting an object’s internal state and providing controlled ways to interact with it.
Instead of allowing other classes to change a field directly, we can make it private and expose methods that enforce the object’s rules.



public class BankAccount {
    // Private state: cannot be changed directly from outside the class.
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        if (initialBalance < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Balance cannot be negative");
        }
        this.balance = initialBalance;
    }

    // Public API: exposes only the information callers need.
    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    // Public behavior: validates changes and protects the object's rules.
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit must be positive");
        }
        balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0 || amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid withdrawal");
        }
        balance -= amount;
    }

    // Package-private: available only to classes in the same package.
    void applyMonthlyFee(double fee) {
        if (fee < 0 || fee > balance) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid fee");
        }
        balance -= fee;
    }

    // Protected: available to subclasses and classes in the same package.
    protected boolean hasMinimumBalance(double minimum) {
        return balance >= minimum;
    }

    // Private: internal implementation detail.
    private void resetBalance() {
        balance = 0;
    }
}

title: Day 13/90: Interfaces fundamentals - Go Backend Engineering
description:
Day 13/90: Interfaces fundamentals

90 Day Go Challenge: Zero to Production

Today I focused on making interfaces fundamentals feel like concrete data modeling and control flow, not syntax trivia. The strongest checkpoints were make values, structs, and interfaces say one clear thing about the state they represent, use control flow and method choices to make valid transitions obvious, and prefer small explicit data shapes over clever abstractions that hide the real meaning.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was using broad or vague types until the data model stops explaining itself. The day felt better once the service boundary stayed visible and each component had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next service still feels related to the same design idea. I also want to keep tracing one request path end to end because it exposes weak assumptions faster than a larger demo.

title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?
description:
arXiv:2610.27592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aiming to modify textual content while preserving the original style, Scene Text Editing (STE) has significant practical value in many applications. STE typically requires paired images before and after editing for training. However, recent approaches rely heavily on synthetic paired data and complex disentanglement strategies. They struggle to faithfully capture the diversity and complexity of natural scenes, often producing artifacts or hallucinations. In this work, we challenge the common practice and investigate whether STE can be driven by turning each real sample into its own paired supervision. Concretely, we explore multiple ways to disrupt the original image (e.g., Crop, Shuffle, Mask) to construct self-paired training data, and build a strong baseline (TextRIRO}) upon a conditional diffusion architecture. Our experiments show that combining character-column shuffling with image cropping (Shuffle&Crop) effectively destroys text semantics while preserving key style cues, enabling the model to learn editing behaviors directly from the real text image. With this concise yet real-oriented design, TextRIRO achieves promising performance in both accuracy and visual realism across real-world benchmarks, substantially mitigating the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Furthermore, we leverage TextRIRO to build TextRIRO-3M, a large-scale realistic dataset for long-text recognition by concatenating edited and original images. Experimental results show that training recognition models with TextRIRO-3M significantly improves recognition accuracy, demonstrating that TextRIRO provides highly useful training resources for downstream tasks. Overall, TextRIRO lifts STE to realistic, reliable, and widely applicable new levels. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextRIRO.

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: The 13% Penalty: Why Synchronous APIs Still Scale Better Than You Think"
description:
When I built a lightweight framework to act as a data marshal for my decoupled single page apps, I didn’t intend to write an architectural thesis, but along the way, the data forced me to confront three pervasive myths in modern web development. First, PHP is inherently slow, second that synchronous APIs can’t scale to modern demand, and finally that you must trade developer experience for raw performance. I confronted these assumptions the only way that matters, by building. I created a framework called mouse-php, created CLI tooling that eliminated micro-framework friction, and stress tested said framework to failure. What the benchmarking revealed was illuminating. The industry consensus around these three ideas aren’t built on hard engineering limits but misattribution, vendor marketing, cargo-culting, and outdated assumptions. Here’s the story of that build, the benchmark data behind it, and why low-level simplicity routinely beats over-engineered complexity.

When I set out to build mouse-php, my goal was to create a lightweight API that acted strictly as a data marshal for decoupled single page applications. Some choices were obvious, like stripping out framework bloat and keeping execution linear. However, I quickly realized that most lightweight solutions sacrifice developer velocity in the name of absolute performance. This exposes a false dichotomy in modern web development: the belief that developer conveniences must always come at the expense of runtime performance. Because I built mouse-php to solve my own production friction, I focused on creating low overhead pipelines that preserve developer ergonomics, this led to three distinct architectural choices.

1. The Inverse-MVC Pattern & Thin PDO Data Marshals

Traditional MVC frameworks push heavy ORMs and deep object graphs into giant models. In mouse-php, I inverted this relationship and completely ditched the ORM in favor of a clean, structured PDO wrapper. My primary motivation for dropping the ORM wasn’t raw performance, it was Developer Experience. The idea that ORMs deliver a superior DX is a shallow illusion. ORMs make trivial queries like User::find(1) look convenient, but simple requests were never difficult to manage in the first place. The moment an API requires real world database operations requiring complex JOINs, aggregations, or precise index targeting the ORM becomes a hindrance rather than helpful. Developers end up having to fight method chains, specific esoteric syntax, and performance killing abstractions just to perform queries that could have been written in three lines of SQL. By replacing ORM with an easy to parse PDO wrapper, mouse-php models act as bare metal data marshals executing raw, prepared SQL statements while still being easy to maintain.

  • Better DX: Developers write clear, explicit SQL without fighting dynamic query builders or dynamic relation tracking.
  • Zero Hydration Tax: Bypasses object instantiation and reflection entirely, fetching database results directly into native arrays at C-speed.
  • High Reusability: Because models are reduced to simple data pipes rather than stateful domain objects, a single query model can be applied across multiple controllers or background jobs without instantiating heavy object trees.

The performance boost of keeping database overhead under 1ms is simply the natural byproduct of choosing a cleaner developer interface.

2. Associative Array First Routing

Industry standard routers rely heavily on complex regex engines to parse dynamic URIs on every incoming request. In mouse-php, the routing engine uses associative array hash lookup first. Because decoupled SPAs communicate most efficiently via explicit RPC-style endpoints, direct match routes can be resolved instantly at C-speed using PHP’s native array key lookups. While dynamic URIs are still supported for standard REST compatibility, they are treated as secondary paths. Bypassing regex route parsing for the majority of API traffic eliminates a massive chunk of per-request CPU tax.

3. One Way Middleware (Abandoning the Onion Model)

Most modern frameworks use an “onion model” where middleware wraps both the incoming request and outgoing response in nested closure. I always hated dealing with onion middleware in heavy frameworks, debugging nested execution stacks across response boundaries was a constant source of friction as well as trying to just figure out how to use it in some cases. I moved mouse-php to a strict one way pipeline simply to make middleware easier to write, manage, and debug. But just as with the PDO wrapper, simplifying the DX revealed a blueprint built for high-throughput performance. In this linear model, middleware has only two jobs: guarding the application and injecting context.

  • Fast Escapes: If an authentication check fails, the pipeline immediately triggers an escape hatch and terminates the request early, preventing the request from controller instantiation entirely.
  • Direct Context Injection: For example if an auth check queries user details, it injects that data directly into the request payload. The downstream controller receives pre-hydrated context without making a second query.

Middleware never touches outgoing responses. Any final response formatting happens predictably in the controller layer via lightweight utilities. By replacing wrapped stack frames with a simple, unidirectional pipeline, we gain total debugging clarity and linear execution speed.

Once mouse-php was running, I needed empirical data to verify its throughput limits. Benchmarking modern HTTP APIs accurately is surprisingly nuanced; preliminary tests with closed loop tools like autocannon produced inconsistent, warped latency figures, likely due to Coordinated Omission. To get accurate, un-skewed latency profiles, I migrated the test bench to wrk2, an open loop benchmarking tool that maintains a fixed, constant throughput rate.

The Test Environment

All benchmarks were executed locally on bare-metal hardware to isolate the stack’s raw execution capability:

  • Hardware: Lenovo IdeaPad 5 2-in-1 (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, 16GB LPDDR5)
  • Operating System: Arch Linux (Kernel 7.2.8, KDE Plasma, non-essential background processes terminated)
  • CGI & Web Server: Apache httpd paired with PHP 8.5 PHP-FPM
  • PHP Runtime Tuning: OPcache enabled with aggressive timestamp checking disabled, JIT compiler active.

Test Parameters & Sweeps

  • Load Profile: wrk2 was configured with 4 threads, 100 concurrent connections, and a 60-second duration per run.
  • Rate Sweeps: Tests began at a 100 Req/s baseline and scaled up in increments to locate the framework's saturation knee.
  • Averaging & Outliers: Each target request rate was executed in three 60 second rounds and averaged together. If an anomalous system hiccup occurred, a 4th validation run was conducted to eliminate system jitter.
  • Thermal Mitigation: Because mobile SoCs aggressively thermal-throttle under sustained multi-core loads, a mandatory 5 minute system idle break was enforced between every run above 10,000 Req/s to prevent thermal soak from skewing tail-latency measurements.
  • Middleware Context Disclosures: Test endpoints were assigned to the native global_bypass middleware group. This bypassed client facing rate limiters and payload formatting guards that would otherwise reject standard synthetic wrk2 traffic, while mirroring how high throughput public endpoints are configured in production.

Using these test parameters, our control run targeted a route that returned a static JSON payload, isolating mouse-php’s routing request handling, and output pipeline from external I/O bound dependencies.

Static Endpoint Results

Req/S Average Latency(ms) P99 Latency(ms) Max Latency(ms)
100 1.6 3.75 4.69
500 1.58 3.58 4.64
1000 1.43 2.49 3.29
2000 1.41 2.12 2.75
5000 1.7 2.82 14.74
10,000 3.08 4.59 45.18
12,000 1.66 3.13 37.12
14,000 1.78 4.81 51.7
15,000 1.79 4.53 52.73
15,500 2 11.88 74.94
16,000 1.93 13.61 68.73
17,000 1.99 12.4 57.15
17,500 2.27 19.4 72.04
18,000 3550 6843.33 7446.67

Analyzing this dataset reveals clear systems level behaviors regarding where the stack excels and precisely where hardware limits force it to break:

  1. The 2000 Req/s Efficiency Sweet Spot:

    Across the entire test suite, 2000 Req/s represents the optimal operational state. At this rate, latency hits its absolute minimum across all metrics : 1.41ms Average, 2.12ms P99, and a tight 2.75ms Max Latency. This is where request frequency perfectly aligns with CPU governor frequency scaling, worker process scheduling, and L1/L2 cache retention without triggering thread contention or queue accumulation.

  2. The 15,000 Req/s P99 stability Zone:

    While Max Latency tail drift begins decoupling after 2000 Req/s as individual process scheduling delays occur, the Average and P99 latency curves remain tightly locked together all the way to 15,000 Req/s. P99 latency does not break 5ms across a 15x increase in load. This proves that under normal operating conditions, 99% of requests pass through the framework’s array routing and one-way pipeline nearly instantaneously.

  3. The Warning Sign (15,500 Req/s):

    At 15,500 Req/s, P99 jumps from 4.53ms to 11.88ms. This decoupling between Average Latency(~2.0ms) and P99 marks the inflection point where OS socket backlogs and FastCGI worker queues begin running near capacity.

  4. The 17,500 Req/s Saturation Knee:

    The system maintains stability up to 17,500 Req/s with a 2.27ms average response time. Pushing the load to 18,000 Req/s causes the latency to explode immediately to 3.55 seconds.

This vertical wall isn’t an application level framework crash, it is classic FastCGI socket backlog exhaustion. When incoming connection rates exceed available PHP-FPM process slots, the OS TCP backlog fills up, incoming requests queue in kernel space, and the system hits its absolute physical CGI throughput ceiling on this hardware.

With the static baseline established, the next phase of stress-testing targeted an API endpoint that executes a live database query on every request, simulating a realistic application workload.

Database Endpoint Results

Req/S Average Latency(ms) P99 Latency(ms) Max Latency(ms)
100 2.2 4.94 5.59
500 1.66 3.8 5.04
1000 1.52 2.64 3.46
2000 1.63 2.63 4.03
5000 1.96 3.2 15.48
10,000 3.43 5.83 55.38
12,000 1.69 3.29 37.42
13,000 1.93 6.02 56.91
14,000 1.98 11.38 59.11
15,000 2.26 13.71 60.84
15,250 2.27 16.4 58.37
16,000 3380 6755 7280

Comparing this dataset directly against our static control run reveals a great deal about mouse-php's execution efficiency under real-world I/O pressure:

  1. The Remarkable 13% Delta:

    The standout takeaway from these benchmarks is how little performance degrades when introducing a database query. Moving from a static JSON response to a live MariaDB lookup shifts our maximum stable throughput ceiling from 17,500 Req/s down to 15,250 Req/s is a mere 13% reduction. In typical web frameworks, the ORM and object hydration layer create a massive performance cliff. Here, because mouse-php uses a thin PDO wrapper that bypasses hydration overhead entirely, the database roundtrip adds less than 1ms of average latency across the board.

  2. The Persistent 2,000 Req/s Sweet Spot:

    Just like the static control run, 2,000 Req/s remains the absolute peak efficiency zone. Even with database reads executing on every single request, the system hits its tightest latency alignment (1.63ms Average, 2.63ms P99) right at this threshold. This confirms that CPU cache locality and process scheduling dynamics dominate the profile long before database I/O becomes the bottleneck.

  3. Predictable P99 Coupling & Early Decoupling:

    The P99 latency behavior mirrors the static control curve, though it begins its upward drift slightly earlier (~13,000 to 14,000 Req/s). This minor variance makes complete sense: as concurrent requests climb, the local MariaDB connection pool and socket buffers absorb additional load, causing occasional tail-latency stretching just before the saturation threshold.

  4. The 15,250 Req/s Saturation Wall:

    At 15,250 Req/s, the system holds the line with a sub-3ms average latency (2.27ms). Pushing past this edge to 16,000 Req/s triggers an immediate system blowout, with average latency jumping to 3.38 seconds. Just like the static run, this wall represents the physical concurrency limit of our local FastCGI and database socket queues on mobile hardware, rather than an application-layer failure.

The parallel behavior of these two charts tells a definitive story. mouse-php is bounded primarily by operating system socket limits, CGI throughput, and local hardware constraints, not by the application code or data-fetching pipeline. When your database backed endpoints can sustain over 15,000 requests per second with sub 2.5ms latency on a laptop, the argument that "synchronous PHP can't scale" completely falls apart.

Now with the data we have from our benchmarks we can more closely examine and determine the validity of pervasive myths and popular beliefs that dictate many of the design choices in web development. The numbers show us that the limitations that are often attributed to entire programming languages or execution models are almost always the result of something more specific that became an artificial dependency.

Myth 1: “PHP is Inherently Slow”

For over a decade, “PHP is slow” has permeated the zeitgeist of web developers through the industry. This is usually cited as a reason to justify migrating simple applications to heavier enterprise run times or microservices. However, this myth is the product of two sources that this data shows are both incorrect now or assigning the blame to the wrong source. The first source of this was likely from bad experiences from old versions of PHP, and the other misattribution: blaming the language runtime for the sins of the framework.

PHP a decade ago when this argument started was a much different beat then what we have now, and part of the problem is these critics of PHP have not been paying attention to that fact. As shown with these benchmarks PHP 8.2+, PHP-FPM, and optimizations like OPcache can make even synchronous PHP extremely fast and reliable while still letting you have the advantages of synchronous operations. There are also operations in PHP that are just faster than anything else with the same accessibility as PHP, like database operations and encryption. One of the things I learned building mouse-php and mRPC/colby-jack was how to implement HMAC for both PHP and Javascript, and not only was PHP’s implementation more performant but far easier which means more secure as there are less chances for me as a developer to make an error.

The other source of this becomes obvious because mouse-php makes engineering choices that removes many of the sources of bloat that come from typical frameworks. As a result the performance uplift over a typical batteries included framework is obvious. I wasn’t the first to notice this naturally, microframeworks like slim exist to address this same bloat but this remains a source of this myth because typically people bench marking PHP reach for Laravel or Symfony as that’s what most people outside the PHP ecosystem think of for PHP backends. What our benchmarks show just like the outdated idea of PHP that the framework tax and the abstraction baggage that comes with the massive frameworks is the true performance killer and not the language runtime.

Myth 2: "Synchronous APIs Can’t Scale to Modern Demand”

The modern cloud-native ecosystem is built on the premise that synchronous execution models hit a hard wall under real world load, necessitating complex asynchronous event loops, reactive streams, or Kubernetes-orchestrated microservices.

Our MariaDB benchmark challenges this assumption. By pushing a database backed endpoint to 15,250 requests per second with sub 2.5ms baseline latencies we showed that a simple synchronous request response model can absorb massive production traffic. To put this number in perspective 15,250 requests per second equates to 1.3 billion requests a day running on a laptop not built for web hosting. For 99% of web applications, microservice splits and async complexity solves problems they will simply never have and just introduces operation overhead, or latency taxes that definitely don’t need.

This does reveal the source of this myth however, cargo-culting and vendor marketing, the idea that these complex solutions are the best practice primarily comes from people seeing FAANG companies use these solutions in their own stacks. The problem with this is the colossal delta in traffic and developers between even a decently high traffic application and Google. The scale that a FAANG corporation’s infrastructure is working at means that the economics and what makes something efficient change drastically meaning that trying to copy their infrastructure leads to unnecessary complexity or even worse performance in certain areas then the simpler solution.

Myth 3: “Performance vs. DX is a Zero-Sum Game”

Perhaps the most damaging myth in web development and one I began to be frustrated with the trade off narrative: the belief that if you want high performance, you must write low level, tedious boilerplate; and if you want great Developer Experience(DX), you must accept a heavy runtime tax.

Building mouse-php showed me that not only was this not true, but many features touted as making things easier for developers are shallow making the performance trade offs bad deals for the convenience, actually make things more difficult when you actually try building something, are just a development tool and don’t need to affect the performance of the production runtime. The interesting part of the performance uplift shown in this post was that it wasn’t the direct target of the choices made, removing ORMs and simplifying middleware management and flow was all done to just make it easier to understand and work with. These benchmarks are particularly interesting because this API was created from a blank directory. From that blank directory I created and configured the endpoints in around ten minutes, which was a great demonstration that performance doesn’t need to be hard.

Good developer experience isn’t about hiding complexity behind magic abstraction, it's about making the complexity easier to understand or removing redundant work. True DX is about clarity, predictability, and getting out of an engineer’s way. When tools are simple to reason about, high performance isn’t something you have to explicitly aim for; good engineering choices become obvious as a natural byproduct of clean design.
When we strip away industry dogma, cargo-culted microservices, and multilayered abstraction taxes, web architecture becomes remarkably clear. The benchmarks suggest to us: simplicity scales, hardware is rarely the real bottleneck, and high performance is simply the natural byproduct of clean design.
For 99% of web applications, the push toward "cloud complex" architecture solves a scaling problem they will never face, while saddling them with operational overhead they definitely don't need. You don't need a thousand dollar auto scaling cluster to build something fast.
What all of this has shown me is that respecting developer velocity and application performance are not mutually exclusive. When you look past industry assumptions and focus on building well reasoned solutions to immediate problems, you can create outcomes that defy expectations.
This approach gave me a tool that not only delivered sub 3ms latencies on database backed requests, but did so with a backend that took ten minutes to build from an empty directory, all without the added complexity of managing asynchronous loops, explicit state lifecycles, or heavy framework abstractions.
Sometimes, all it takes is stepping back, cutting out the bloat, and letting the metal do what it was built to do.

title: Learning-Theoretic Foundation for General Coded Computing: The Adversarial Setting
description:
arXiv:2610.27440v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial workers pose a severe challenge in distributed computing systems by returning corrupted outputs that can substantially distort the recovered computations. Coded computing addresses this threat by introducing redundancy across worker assignments. Existing exact and approximate coded-computing methods typically handle adversarial outputs by explicitly locating and correcting or removing erroneous evaluations, which adds significant computational overhead at the master node. Moreover, existing analyses do not characterize how the recovery error scales with the number of workers and the adversarial budget.
  In this paper, we develop an adversarially robust extension of general coded computing (GCC), a learning-theoretic approximate coded-computing framework that designs the encoder and decoder by minimizing an upper bound on the end-to-end recovery error. Rather than identifying corrupted workers, the proposed method uses smoothness regularization to limit the influence of their outputs. The resulting encoder and decoder can be implemented using smoothing splines with linear master-side complexity. We derive a non-asymptotic bound on the worst-case end-to-end approximation error by decomposing it into three components: (1) the encoder approximation error, (2) the decoder reconstruction error under fully honest results, and (3) the adversarial perturbation error. For maximum of $q\geq 1$ adversarial workers among $N$ workers results in a worst-case error of order $\mathcal{O}((q/N)^{6/5})$ with appropriate selection of smoothness parameter, demonstrating that the approximation error vanishes asymptotically whenever the number of adversaries grows sublinearly with the network size. Experiments on scalar computation and neural-network inference are consistent with the predicted convergence behavior.

description:
Day 17/75: Binary search in Java

75 Day DSA in Java Challenge

Today I focused on protecting the search interval in binary search in java so every bound update stays justified. The strongest checkpoints were state what the active interval still allows before the first loop iteration, move left and right only when the predicate proves one side is impossible, and test the smallest failing boundary because off-by-one errors hide there first.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was moving left and right without a precise definition of what they still allow. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. That is the bar I want from this track: code that stays readable when requirements move, not just code that compiles today.

title: Autonomous LLM Agents as Dynamic Decision Nodes in Temporal Sagas
description:
Modern core banking platforms are increasingly adopting generative AI and Large Language Model (LLM) agents to handle complex operational reasoning—such as assessing unstructured trade finance documents, triaging complex fraud cases, and resolving cross-border exception processing. However, introducing autonomous AI agents into core banking workflows presents a fundamental architectural contradiction: Temporal Sagas demand absolute determinism, whereas LLM reasoning is inherently non-deterministic.

Temporal workflows achieve fault tolerance through event-sourced execution replay. If a workflow definition behaves non-deterministically during history replay, execution drifts, state corruption occurs, and replay validation fails. Conversely, LLMs generate probabilistic outcomes influenced by temperature settings, floating-point variance across hardware inference clusters, and model version shifts.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, core banking platforms resolve this tension by encapsulating autonomous LLM agents inside isolated Temporal Activities bounded by strict JSON schema contracts, formal validation guardrails, and deterministic fallback paths. This paper evaluates the operational boundaries, dynamic task planning topologies, mathematical reliability models, and compensation patterns required to deploy autonomous LLM agents as dynamic decision nodes in distributed core banking Sagas.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

Architectural Boundaries across BIAN Service Domains

Not all decision nodes within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) ecosystem require LLM autonomy. Integrating AI agents into deterministic Sagas must be strictly categorized by domain risk and exception frequency.

BIAN Service Domain Capability Mapped to LLM Node Autonomy Level Primary Risk Boundary Fallback Mechanism
Trade Positioning LC (Letter of Credit) document clause verification Semi-Autonomous Operational Exception Human-in-the-Loop Approval
Fraud Evaluation Suspicious transaction triage & contextual analysis Autonomous Decision False Positive Risk Default Deterministic Rule Engine
Customer Onboarding Unstructured Identity Exception Handling Semi-Autonomous Compliance / Regulatory Re-route to Compliance Officer Task
Payment Execution Automated Payment Clearing & ISO20022 Routing Strict Deterministic (No LLM) High Financial Risk N/A (Hardcoded / DMN Engine Only)
Position Keeping Double-Entry Ledger Posting Strict Deterministic (No LLM) Balance Integrity Risk N/A (Static Microservice Logic)

The Determinism Isolation Pattern

To prevent non-deterministic LLM behavior from corrupting Temporal's execution history, LLM agent reasoning must never execute directly within a Temporal Workflow Definition. Instead, the workflow definition maintains absolute determinism, while the LLM execution logic is fully encapsulated inside a Temporal Activity.

                  THE DETERMINISM ISOLATION ARCHITECTURE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TEMPORAL WORKFLOW ENGINE (100% Deterministic Event History Execution)          |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [Start Workflow] ---> [Execute Activity: RunAgentActivity] ---> [Branch Logic] |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------^-----------+
                                      |                                 |
                           1. Invoke Activity Payload        4. Return Deterministic
                              (Structured Context)              Structured JSON Output
                                      |                                 |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------+
  | TEMPORAL ACTIVITY WORKER LAYER    v                                 |           |
  | (Non-Deterministic Sandbox)                                         |           |
  |                                                                     |           |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------+  |           |
  |  | LLM AGENT REASONING LOOP                                      |  |           |
  |  |                                                               |  |           |
  |  |  [Construct Prompt] ---> [LLM Inference Engine (OpenAI/Ollama)]|  |           |
  |  |                                  │                            |  |           |
  |  |                                  ▼                            |  |           |
  |  |  [JSON Guardrail Validation] ◄── [Tool Call / Re-Act Loop]     |  |           |
  |  +----------------------------------│----------------------------+  |           |
  |                                     |                               |           |
  |                          2. Return Output Schema                    |           |
  |                             (Passed or Rejected)                    |           |
  +-------------------------------------│-------------------------------+-----------+
                                        v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | IMMUTABLE EVENT STORE & STATE AUDIT                                             |
  |  [ Persists Prompt Hash, Token Cost, Confidence Score, and Decision Payload ]  |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key Architectural Rules

  1. Replay Immutability: Temporal records the activity output payload (the LLM's final structured JSON decision) into the workflow's Event History. During workflow replay, Temporal does not re-invoke the LLM activity; it simply reads the recorded decision payload from history.
  2. Deterministic Branching: The workflow evaluates the structured decision payload using standard deterministic logic (if/else or switch statements) to dispatch downstream machine Sagas or human tasks.
  3. Idempotency & Retry Safety: LLM activities must implement strict idempotency keys (derived from WorkflowID + RunID + ActivityTaskID) to prevent duplicate inference costs or repeated side effects during network retries.

Mathematical Model: Agent Decision Reliability & Guardrail Probability

The reliability of an LLM agent operating as a dynamic decision node within a distributed financial Saga depends on schema adherence, hallucination rates, and downstream transaction commitment.

The probability of a successful autonomous decision node commit Pnode-success​ across an agentic execution path is defined as:

Pnode-success​=Pschema-valid​×(1−Phallucination​)×Psaga-commit​

Where:

  • Pschema-valid​ is the probability that the LLM output conforms strictly to the target JSON schema on attempt k (where k≤MaxRetries ).
  • Phallucination​ is the probability that the agent generates a factually incorrect decision despite schema validity.
  • Psaga-commit​ is the probability that the downstream distributed machine Saga succeeds without compensation.

If the agent's confidence score falls below a pre-configured threshold θconfidence​ , or if Pschema-valid​=0 after maximum retries, the system triggers a Deterministic Fallback Override, shifting control to a standard rule engine or human user task.

Technical Implementation: Agentic Activity & Temporal Workflow

1. Structured Output Decision Schema (Java DTOs) 

package com.xenon.banking.ai.model;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.util.List;

public record TradeExceptionDecision(
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String decisionOutcome, // "APPROVE_EXEMPTION", "REJECT_EXEMPTION", "ESCALATE_HUMAN"
    @JsonProperty(required = true) double confidenceScore, // 0.0 to 1.0
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String reasoningSummary,
    @JsonProperty(required = true) List<String> verifiedClauseIdentifiers,
    @JsonProperty(required = true) String recommendedCompensatingAction
) {}

2. Temporal Activity Encapsulating the LLM Reasoning Loop

This Java activity executes an agentic reasoning loop using structured function calling. If the LLM generates invalid JSON or fails validation constraints, the activity retries locally up to a bounded threshold before returning an explicit failure state.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.activity;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.xenon.banking.ai.model.TradeExceptionDecision;
import io.temporal.activity.Activity;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityExecutionContext;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.util.Map;

@Component("tradeAgentActivity")
public class TradeAgentActivityImpl implements TradeAgentActivity {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Override
    public TradeExceptionDecision evaluateTradeException(String documentText, String exceptionCode, double transactionAmount) {
        ActivityExecutionContext ctx = Activity.getExecutionContext();
        String workflowId = ctx.getInfo().getWorkflowId();

        System.out.println("Executing Agentic Decision Node for Workflow: " + workflowId);

        // Construct System & User Prompt for Structured Function Calling
        String promptPayload = buildPromptJson(documentText, exceptionCode, transactionAmount);

        int attempts = 0;
        int maxRetries = 3;

        while (attempts < maxRetries) {
            attempts++;
            try {
                // Call LLM Inference Endpoint (OpenAI / Internal Enterprise Model API)
                HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create("https://ai-gateway.internal.xenon/v1/chat/completions"))
                        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("AI_GATEWAY_KEY"))
                        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(promptPayload))
                        .build();

                HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

                // Parse Structured Output Response
                String rawJsonResponse = extractStructuredJsonFromResponse(response.body());
                TradeExceptionDecision decision = objectMapper.readValue(rawJsonResponse, TradeExceptionDecision.class);

                // Validation Guardrail: Enforce minimum confidence threshold
                if (decision.confidenceScore() < 0.85) {
                    System.out.println("Agent confidence score (" + decision.confidenceScore() + ") below threshold. Escalating.");
                    return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", decision.confidenceScore(), 
                            "Low confidence score in automated evaluation.", decision.verifiedClauseIdentifiers(), "NONE");
                }

                return decision; // Successfully evaluated and validated

            } catch (Exception e) {
                System.err.println("Attempt " + attempts + " failed to parse LLM structured decision: " + e.getMessage());
                if (attempts >= maxRetries) {
                    // Fail-safe default returned to Workflow
                    return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", 0.0, 
                            "LLM execution failed structural validation after retries.", List.of(), "NONE");
                }
            }
        }

        return new TradeExceptionDecision("ESCALATE_HUMAN", 0.0, "Execution exhausted retries.", List.of(), "NONE");
    }

    private String buildPromptJson(String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount) {
        // Formats prompt enforcing JSON Schema output constraints
        return """
            {
              "model": "xenon-financial-agent-v2",
              "messages": [
                {"role": "system", "content": "You are a specialized risk evaluation agent. You must output JSON conforming strictly to the TradeExceptionDecision schema."},
                {"role": "user", "content": "Evaluate document: %s under exception code: %s for amount: %.2f"}
              ],
              "response_format": {"type": "json_object"},
              "temperature": 0.0
            }
            """.formatted(escapeJson(documentText), exceptionCode, amount);
    }

    private String extractStructuredJsonFromResponse(String responseBody) throws Exception {
        var node = objectMapper.readTree(responseBody);
        return node.path("choices").get(0).path("message").path("content").asText();
    }

    private String escapeJson(String input) {
        return input.replace("\"", "\\\"").replace("\n", " ");
    }
}

3. Temporal Workflow Definition (Deterministic Branching)

The workflow invokes the agent activity. Depending on the agent's structured decision, it deterministically dispatches an automated downstream machine Saga or suspends for human review.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.ai.activity.TradeAgentActivity;
import com.xenon.banking.ai.model.TradeExceptionDecision;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface TradeResolutionWorkflow {
    @WorkflowMethod
    void processTradeException(String tradeId, String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount);
}

public class TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl implements TradeResolutionWorkflow {

    private final TradeAgentActivity agentActivity = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            TradeAgentActivity.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder()
                    .setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
                    .setRetryOptions(io.temporal.common.RetryOptions.newBuilder()
                            .setMaximumAttempts(3)
                            .build())
                    .build()
    );

    @Override
    public void processTradeException(String tradeId, String documentText, String exceptionCode, double amount) {

        // 1. Invoke Isolated LLM Agent Activity (Non-deterministic code runs safely inside activity)
        TradeExceptionDecision agentDecision = agentActivity.evaluateTradeException(documentText, exceptionCode, amount);

        // 2. Deterministic Workflow Execution Path based on Activity Event History
        switch (agentDecision.decisionOutcome()) {
            case "APPROVE_EXEMPTION" -> {
                // Trigger automated machine Saga step (e.g., Ledger Release)
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).info("Agent approved exception. Executing release Saga.");
                executeAutomatedReleaseSaga(tradeId, amount);
            }
            case "REJECT_EXEMPTION" -> {
                // Trigger automated cancellation & compensation Saga
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).info("Agent rejected exception. Executing compensation Saga.");
                executeCompensatingCancellationSaga(tradeId);
            }
            case "ESCALATE_HUMAN" -> {
                // Halt workflow deterministically and await Human-in-the-Loop Signal
                Workflow.getLogger(TradeResolutionWorkflowImpl.class).warn("Agent requested human escalation. Awaiting signal.");
                awaitHumanReviewSignal(tradeId, agentDecision.reasoningSummary());
            }
            default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unexpected agent decision outcome: " + agentDecision.decisionOutcome());
        }
    }

    private void executeAutomatedReleaseSaga(String tradeId, double amount) {
        // Standard deterministic machine Activity calls
    }

    private void executeCompensatingCancellationSaga(String tradeId) {
        // Standard deterministic compensating Activity calls
    }

    private void awaitHumanReviewSignal(String tradeId, String reasoning) {
        // Suspend workflow execution until human approval signal arrives
    }
}

Transactional Consistency and Saga Compensation Scenarios

When an autonomous LLM agent decides to approve an operational exception, it triggers forward transactions (e.g., balance holds or ledger postings). If a downstream microservice fails after an LLM agent decision has been rendered, the Temporal orchestrator automatically executes standard Compensating Actions.

  AGENT DECISION SAGA COMPENSATION FLOW

  +-----------------------+        1. Approve Exception        +-----------------------+
  |  LLM Agent Activity   | ---------------------------------> | Temporal Saga Manager |
  | (Evaluates Document)  |                                    | (Workflow History)    |
  +-----------------------+                                    +-----------+-----------+
                                                                           |
                                   2. Execute Step 1 (Ledger Debit)        |
                                                                           v
  +-----------------------+        3. Step 2 Fails (API Timeout) +-----------------------+
  | Downstream Services   | <----------------------------------| Executing Machine     |
  | (Ledger / Risk Engine)| ---------------------------------> | Activities            |
  +-----------------------+        4. Trigger Compensation     +-----------+-----------+
                                                                           |
                                   5. Execute Rollback Activity            |
                                      (Revert Ledger Debit)                v
                                                               +-----------------------+
                                                               | Audit Log & Escalate  |
                                                               | to Human Desk         |
                                                               +-----------------------+

Compensation Safety Rules

  1. Non-Reversible Actions: An LLM agent must never execute uncompensable real-world actions (such as dispatching an external Fedwire SWIFT MT103 message) directly from within its reasoning loop.
  2. Two-Stage Authorization: The agent activity may only modify internal staging state or emit execution intents. The actual final settlement step must be gated by a secondary deterministic activity or a human approval check if the transaction value exceeds strict monetary limits.

Observability, Prompt Lineage, and Auditability

Financial regulators (such as OCC, EBA, and MAS) require complete lineage for AI-assisted operational decisions. Storing only the final decision payload is insufficient; the system must retain full cryptographic lineage of the agent's context.

Audit Metadata Record Structure

For every LLM decision node invocation, the activity writes an immutable audit record to the centralized log storage layer, linked to the Temporal WorkflowID and RunID:

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-2026-902183",
  "temporalWorkflowId": "TradeResolution-TR-9902",
  "temporalRunId": "b182f4e8-421d-405a-a309-88f2b7190012",
  "bianDomain": "TradePositioning",
  "llmProvider": "Azure-OpenAI-Internal",
  "modelDeployment": "gpt-4o-financial-v2",
  "promptHash": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "inputTokenCount": 1420,
  "outputTokenCount": 185,
  "rawOutput": "{\"decisionOutcome\":\"APPROVE_EXEMPTION\",\"confidenceScore\":0.94,\"reasoningSummary\":\"Clause 4b matches standard ICC UCP 600 rules.\",\"verifiedClauseIdentifiers\":[\"CLAUSE-4B\"],\"recommendedCompensatingAction\":\"NONE\"}",
  "confidenceScore": 0.94,
  "schemaValidationPassed": true,
  "executionTimestamp": "2026-09-16T11:56:28Z"
}

Integrating autonomous LLM agents into Temporal Sagas bridges the gap between flexible AI-driven reasoning and rigid financial reliability. By strict application of the Determinism Isolation Pattern—confining non-deterministic LLM execution inside structured Temporal Activities while keeping the orchestration workflow fully deterministic—core banking platforms achieve intelligent operational automation without sacrificing transactional integrity, fault tolerance, or regulatory auditability across BIAN service domains.
