title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System
description:
arXiv:2610.26948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. However, extending these methods to many product domains faces a dilemma: deploying a separately adapted VLM per domain scales cost linearly with the number of domains and requires routing each dialogue to the right model, while naively merging all domains into a single VLM degrades accuracy because product characteristics vary widely across categories. We propose LightCRS, a lightweight, query-conditioned framework for unified multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations once offline with frozen encoders. Online, a compact 5.3M-parameter module fuses this evidence for each dialogue via query-conditioned cross-attention, whose parameters are shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing natural Reddit recommendation-seeking conversations with Amazon product listings. LightCRS achieves state-of-the-art average HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, improving HR@1 by 35.4\% over the strongest baseline while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. Joint multi-domain training itself improves HR@1 by 15.2\% over separately trained single-domain models.

title: Mistral Large 4 Benchmark for Coding vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
description:
Mistral Large 4 scored 0.5462 on our Gauntlet benchmark, 28th of 44. About a third of what it lost came from a check of ours that read its table the wrong way round. All 12 amounts it put on screen were correct. I went in expecting to write about a slow, expensive model, and on our Forge benchmark that part holds up.

If you pay for a coding agent, this model is pitched at your budget. Mistral released Large 4 on 6 October as a Public Preview, 1.05 trillion parameters with 52 billion active and a 1M-token context, at half its list price for the first two weeks. Their launch post puts it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro on their own Coding Agent Index (49.8%), which is the kind of claim that moves a budget, so we ran it through both of our agentic coding benchmarks. The Gauntlet has an agent build a payments console with two services and a 3D view inside 150 model calls, then scores it on 99 checks. Forge 2.0 asks for a v2 upgrade of a working Jira Forge app inside 300 calls and scores it on 105 checks against three seeded Jira sites.

Getting a Gauntlet score took four attempts. The first, on 9 October, ended after 49 calls on OpenRouter's "Upstream idle timeout exceeded". On 18 October the second was ended by Mistral's servers. Early on 19 October the third was ended by a bug in goose, the open-source coding agent we run (our own fork), and the fourth finished that afternoon. Its Forge 2.0 pair scored 0.1086 and 0.3304 for at least $10.95. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 did better on the same Forge task. It's the 17 October snapshot I wrote about in my DeepSeek piece, and it scored 0.2422 and 0.6618 for at least $0.62 in about a quarter of the time.

On the Gauntlet the low score is mostly our scorer's fault. On Forge the code losses were Mistral's own. Our harness also gave it a smaller context window than DeepSeek. The build trees show where each loss came from. This is one scored Gauntlet run and one Forge pair, in our setup, on a model whose vendor says it can change silently while it's in preview.

Mistral Large 4 benchmark results: Gauntlet 0.5462, Forge 2.0 median 0.2195

Mistral Large 4 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
Gauntlet 7.2 0.5462, 144 min, $4.93 0.6957, 23 min, $0.21
Forge 2.0 build 1 0.1086, 118 min, at least $5.40 0.2422, 28 min, $0.30
Forge 2.0 build 2 0.3304, 106 min, $5.55 0.6618, 30 min, at least $0.32
Unscored Gauntlet attempts 9 Oct: idle timeout after 49 calls, at least $1.43. 18 Oct: Mistral 503 after 30 calls, at least $1.18. 19 Oct: our 400 after 97 calls, $3.04 none

I checked these on the live boards on 21 October; if a run page says something else now, trust the run page. All six Mistral runs together cost at least $21.53, with three of the bills only lower bounds.

Six things we found in the Mistral Large 4 builds

  1. The x0.6 "wrong money" critical on the Gauntlet is our bug. Our money check compares the amounts on screen with the oldest 50 payments, and Mistral's table opens on the newest.
  2. Mistral's money formatter works on integer digits with a per-currency decimals table, the same approach as DeepSeek's.
  3. Forge build 1, by my reading, lost most of its gap to build 2 to a throttle it wrote itself: it booked 25 to 34 times the real cost of a list call and paused its own scheduled work each hour, before its v1 migration could run.
  4. Neither Forge build ever displayed its admin page, and neither ran a browser self-test.
  5. The 18 October attempt opened with one 37,853-word thought that ran 18 minutes, hit a 65,536-token output limit and was thrown away.
  6. Mistral's API refused a message order that three other providers' endpoints had answered, through OpenRouter, in our runs two weeks earlier.

Mistral Large 4 on our Gauntlet: 0.5462, about 0.70 without a check of ours that misread its table

Most Gauntlet checks just add to a weighted average, but a handful are critical, and when one of those fails it multiplies the whole score down, by as much as x0.6. Wrong money in a payments console is one of those. The money check is called b_money_rendered. A browser probe reads the amount cell of the first 12 rows of the payments table. Then the scorer checks that the digits match a stored amount and that the decimals match the currency, because amounts are stored as integers in the currency's smallest unit (cents, or fils for the Kuwaiti dinar). A correct cell shows two decimals for EUR and USD, none for yen and three for dinars. Mistral's run scored 0.00 on it, with the detail line "0.00 of 12 cells exponent-correct; JPY/KWD traps 0.00", and the multiplier took the whole run from 0.9104 down to 0.5462.

What Mistral rendered

These are the 12 cells the probe read, verbatim: KWD 111.000, ¥594, ¥199, $4.47, ¥809, €224.00, KWD 82.400, €33.10, KWD 2.420, ¥1,060, $1,840.00, KWD 72.400. Our probe also records each row's id, and joined to the fixture, pay_12287 is stored as KWD 111000, so 111.000 dinars is right, and pay_12286 is JPY 594, which needs no decimals. All 12 are right. So are the probe's 12 extra rows.

Its formatter in web/app.js (lines 7 to 25, with the source's \u escapes shown as characters) never touches a float:

const CUR = {
  EUR: { sym: '€', exp: 2 },
  USD: { sym: '$', exp: 2 },
  JPY: { sym: '¥', exp: 0 },
  KWD: { sym: 'KWD ', exp: 3 },
};
...
const s = String(a).padStart(exp + 1, '0');
const int = s.slice(0, s.length - exp) || '0';
const frac = exp > 0 ? s.slice(s.length - exp) : '';

It planned this before writing it. At 10:58 our time (EEST), 27 minutes in, it checked the contract's example and two real payments in its thinking: "129900 EUR → €1,299.00 ✓; JPY 8564 → ¥8,564 ✓; KWD 8263000 → KWD 8,263.000 ✓". Our scorer's own screenshot of the inspector shows that dinar payment as KWD 8,263.000, and the inspector check (q_payment_context) passed.

Why the check said zero

Here is the scorer, score_sb7.py around line 973:

first_page = c.pack.payments[:50]
by_cur: Dict[str, set] = {}
for row in first_page:
    by_cur.setdefault(row["currency"], set()).add(row["amount_minor"])

payments is stored in date order, so payments[:50] is pay_00000 to pay_00049, the oldest fifty. A rendered cell only passes if its digits equal one of those fifty amounts, so the check assumes, without saying it, that the table opens oldest first. Mistral's opens newest first (sort: '-created_at', web/app.js:49). None of its 12 cells could ever match. Our probe even collects the row ids "so the scorer can join against fixtures", in its own comment. No scorer file reads them.

I re-graded the run with the scorer's own _money_ok function, copied unchanged. It gives 0.0 as written, 1.0 against the 50 rows actually on screen, and 24 of 24 when each cell is joined to its payment by row id.

Was opening newest first a mistake by Mistral? Its contract fixes the API's default order ("created_at (default, ascending by INSTANT)") and says the Date header toggles, but it never says which way the table starts. Mistral saw the gap and decided, at 11:48 our time: "The grader might check the first page shows specific rows? Unlikely to assume an order. I'll default to '-created_at' (newest first) — most console-like." It bet that the grader would not assume an order, and the grader did. You can argue the UI should inherit the API's default. I'd listen. Even then it's a sort-order quibble. The check charged it as wrong money.

Who did better at money

All five models I compared passed with 1.0: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol (the model behind Jev Router's top Forge score), GPT-6.1 Sol Pro and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. All of them open their table with sort: 'created_at', and so does our own reference app, which is why our release validation never met a descending default. Grade those five tables against the newest 50 payments and four score 0.0, Sol 0.05.

DeepSeek's formatter is close to a copy of Mistral's:

let digits = String(Math.abs(minor));
if (exponent > 0) digits = digits.padStart(exponent + 1, '0');
const whole = exponent > 0 ? digits.slice(0, digits.length - exponent) : digits;

Same idea, same output. It got 1.0 and Mistral got 0.0. Sol and Sol Pro call Intl.NumberFormat and divide the integer by 10**exp first, and Sonnet does the same with Math.pow, which is fine for amounts this size. So on money code it's a tie between Mistral and DeepSeek. The sort order made the difference.

Mistral did leave one real money bug, in its own test. Its browser self-test checks the first amount against /^[€$¥]\d[\d,]*\.\d{2}$|^KWD [\d,]+\.\d{3}$/, which would reject a correct ¥594 because it demands two decimals after a yen sign. It printed "PASS money formatted" four times, and my guess is that its own first row was never a yen payment. I can't see which row it was.

Without our false critical: about 0.70 and 11th of 44

The score path for this run goes like this. Its checks earned 0.9104. Our false critical multiplied that by 0.6, to 0.5462. Separately, a run that fails some of the 3D checks gets a ceiling on its score, and Mistral's partial failures on picking, the coasting camera and the overview's legibility set it at 0.709. The ceiling formula keeps a score just under the cap, so without the false critical the run would come out at about 0.7048. That's my arithmetic, not a re-score. The board still says 0.5462. It would sit 11th of 44, two places above DeepSeek 1017's 0.6957. The 3D failures, which are Mistral's own, cost it about 0.2 on top.

My audit of that check turned up a second flaw. The yen and dinar "traps" score 0 when no yen or no dinar row happens to be among the cells the probe reads (up to 12). A run whose visible amounts are all right can still pay x0.92. Four ranked runs paid it that way: Elorian Glimpse, Step 5 Preview, Qwen3.8 Omni Flash and GLM-5.3. Across every Gauntlet 7.2 build I could reach, Mistral is the only one the sort assumption hit.

Is Mistral Large 4 good for coding? Forge 2.0 builds of 0.1086 and 0.3304

Forge 2.0 tests the same habits harder: the agent reads a long spec, upgrades a working Forge app under a Jira rate model, and has to prove it all in a local sandbox (our Forge emulator kit) before the calls run out. My piece on the September DeepSeek V4.1 Flash covered this same task, with medians of 0.33 for it and 0.67 for Opus 5.5 in an earlier comparison group. Both Mistral builds and DeepSeek 1017's pair are in the same comparison group on our board. That means the same task, seeds, scorer and engine build. All four asked for the same effort setting.

A Forge 2.0 score is the earned score times a critical multiplier times a reliability factor, where reliability starts at 1 and loses up to 10% for each group of checks whose worst check failed, with a floor of 0.25. Build 1 sat on that floor (its unfloored product was 0.2194) and build 2 came out at 0.4718. Neither triggered a critical. My reading is that most of the 0.22 gap comes from build 1's throttle and the order it ran its migration in.

Build 1 throttled itself and never migrated

The task gives each Jira site a rate budget of 2,400 points an hour, and background work may use 70% of it, so 1,680. Build 1 wrote a gate for that in src/dose.js (lines 76 to 88):

if (dose.bg + estimatedCost > limit) {
  const untilMs = hourStartOf(now) + 3600000;
  await kvs.set(PAUSE_KEY, { untilMs });
  throw new QuotaPaused(untilMs);

The gate is fine. The estimates feeding it were not. With no points header from the site, it charged its own counter from guesses. It booked 51 points for a board or sprint list page (src/config.js:43, cost: 1 + 50), 105 for a search and 260 for a changelog bulk fetch. On the scoring site its first scheduled run had counted 1,567 points after 21 seconds. The next estimated call would have taken it past 1,680. So it paused for the rest of the hour. Yet the site's own ledger for that run says it had spent 715 points over 27 requests, with list pages costing 1.5 to 2 points each.

That would only have been a nuisance if the migration ran first. It ran last. reconcile() in src/index.js calls reconcileAll, then saveClosed, then migrateV1Rows, and the pause in the first step skipped the rest. Its rescan had no cursor. Each hour it started over and paused in the same place. Our scorer's verdict reads "0/130 historical changes v1 never recorded" and "h2: 0 of 59 v1 rows in scope-ledger", and it traces 15 checks to that one root cause.

On the development site, which our spec gives the same shape on another seed, the gate tripped too, twice. At 21:19 our time it wrote "The reconcile hit my own dose gate". After a reset one run got through and it reported "migration complete (88/88)".

Build 2 got the same thing right. I think it was more luck than design. Its cost counter under-counted instead (its own words near the end: "my costOf under-counts returned records"). It ran over the background share in 4 of 31 hours, and on our scoring sites it never paused early. In its last minutes its own dev run did pause early. At call 300 of 300 it spotted the ordering problem: "I'm at the call budget (300/300) — this is my final turn". Then it moved the migration to the top with the comment "it is the graded deliverable and needs the fewest points". It never ran that version. It still scored 59 of 59 migrated and 130 of 130 backfilled. DeepSeek 1017's build 2 had that ordering from the start (src/sync.js:409, "Migrate v1's rows first").

Neither build displayed its admin page

Both Mistral builds score 0.00 on the admin panel tier. That one failure takes down the panel labels, the CI web trigger (no secret can exist before the panel's Rotate button creates one) and the admin boot check with it. Build 1's src/frontend/admin.jsx ends with export default AdminPage; and never calls ForgeReconciler.render, so UI Kit had nothing to draw. It found that out at 21:39, on the 298th of its 300 calls, when its only admin-page test printed "(nothing rendered)". Build 2 does call ForgeReconciler.render(<App />) at line 197, and the non-admin view displayed its permission message, but the admin view came back as an empty tree. The probe recorded no error that explains it. And build 2 never ran the kit's UI Kit check on that page.

DeepSeek 1017's build 2 renders the same way (admin.jsx:186) and ran that UI Kit check 14 times before it finished. The habit shows in the counts too: DeepSeek's two builds invoked their resolvers in the sandbox 45 and 30 times, Mistral's 3 and 4, and neither Mistral build ran a browser self-test at all. Build 1 also sent 37 of its 355 tool calls, about one in ten, to a bash tool that doesn't exist (goose's is called shell), and build 2 sent 19 of 344.

Build 2 had good moments. It had the highest UI-function (0.9957) and reconcile (0.9974) tiers of the four builds in this comparison group. Both are small tiers. Both also beat an Opus 5.5 build from an earlier group. In its last ten minutes it noticed that v1's React bundles were 244 KB against a 150 KB boot budget. It rewrote all three Custom UI pages in plain DOM, to between 102 and 106 KB each.

Mistral Large 4 vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017: 27 minutes to the first file against 2

Time is where the two models differ most. Mistral's first app-code write came 32, 35 and 27 minutes into its three Gauntlet attempts of 18 and 19 October, and about 49 and 55 minutes into its Forge builds. DeepSeek 1017 wrote its first app file 2.4 minutes into its Gauntlet run and about 4.5 minutes into each Forge build, and it finished both Forge builds with 29 to 37 calls to spare. Mistral ran out of calls in both.

Its median call took 4.5 to 4.8 seconds on Forge against DeepSeek's 4.0. The typical call barely differs. The slow tail is what costs it. Each Mistral run had calls that took 11 to 18 minutes, and in the Gauntlet attempts the calls over five minutes add up to more than half of all the time the model spent answering. DeepSeek's slowest call in any of its three runs took 71 seconds, and across our runs Mistral generated between 55 and 70 tokens a second while DeepSeek managed 108 to 155.

The 18-minute thought that was thrown away

The 18 October attempt that Mistral's servers later ended opened with one thinking call of 37,853 words that ran 1,081 seconds. It was coherent (under 1% of its 12-word sequences repeat). It covered the money rule, the 3D tower heights and the order of the services. Then it stopped at exactly 65,536 output tokens. goose marked the reply as cut off, and nothing in it was carried out. Its next thought: "Let me continue. I was planning extensively. Time to write code." goose sent no max_tokens and our model limits list 262,144 output tokens, so the 65,536 cap came from the serving side. Whether that's OpenRouter or Mistral, our logs don't show.

Reasoning was 57% to 81% of everything it generated, depending on the run. On Forge both builds also compacted their context three times, once the prompt had grown to between about 170,000 and 210,000 tokens. After most compactions it re-read files it had already read ("I need to re-read the v1 sources and my v2 files"). Build 2's own compaction summary says it plainly: "I've spent ~66% of context on exploration; no code".

Those compactions are partly ours. goose gave Mistral a usable window of 262,144 tokens. It took the smallest Mistral endpoint's 524,288 (the EU one) and reserved half of it for output, on a model whose card says 1M, while DeepSeek got 655,360. At about 200,000 tokens a call, DeepSeek would have compacted too under Mistral's limit, and under its own it never did. The summary calls ran about 9 to 11 minutes per Forge build, inside the times charged to Mistral.

What did the long thinking buy? On the Gauntlet, quite a lot: its plans got the money rule right, and its decisions file is careful (a rejected draft is terminal, and any further action on it answers 409 invalid_state). On Forge it bought almost nothing the tests could see. A build that reads for 50 minutes and finds its admin bug on call 298 has no calls left to fix it.

Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user': the 400 that was our bug

The third Gauntlet attempt ended at 02:05 our time on 19 October, 97 calls in, on this answer from Mistral's API, passed through OpenRouter:

{"object":"error","message":"Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user'","type":"invalid_request_message_order","param":null,"code":"3230","raw_status_code":400}

Mistral had asked for two tools in parallel, read_image on a screenshot and shell. OpenAI's chat format only accepts text in a tool message ("For tool messages, only type text is supported", in OpenAI's API spec). So since goose 1.0 the formatter has put a placeholder in the tool result and sent the picture as a separate user message right after it. With one tool call, or when the image comes back last, that's harmless. When an image result comes back before another tool result, the request goes out as assistant (two tool calls), tool result, user message holding the image, tool result. Mistral refused the second tool result because a user message stood between it and its call.

Who is right? Mistral's function-calling docs show the order only as a table ("assistant fc.1, fc.2 → tool r.1 → tool r.2 → assistant"), and the error type invalid_request_message_order isn't in their error glossary. Anthropic states the rule in words: "You cannot include any messages between the assistant's tool use message and the user's tool result message." Our request broke the documented order. I count this one as ours.

Three of our runs from 3 and 4 October sent the same order, and all three were answered and scored: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (served by Claude on AWS), GPT-6.1 Sol Pro (OpenAI) and MiMo V2.6 Flash (Xiaomi). All three went through OpenRouter, and I only see what goose sent to OpenRouter, so whether OpenRouter reordered anything for those hosts our logs can't tell. Mistral refused it the first time. Mistral's own coding CLI has an open pull request for the same failure, where a steered user message ends up between a tool call and its result.

We fixed goose 17 minutes after the 400 (commit a0247fffc2, "keep parallel tool results contiguous when one carries an image"). Inside each run of tool results the image messages now move to after the last result, merged into one user message, and a test replays the exact refused request. It shipped in Goose Swarm 3.0.119, our desktop app, on 19 October. The scored fourth attempt most likely ran on 3.0.119, and it never called read_image, so the fix wasn't exercised in a Mistral run.

The second attempt's ending wasn't ours. At 19:40 our time on 18 October Mistral returned "Internal server error" (type unreachable_backend, a 503). goose resent three times with backoff, the last one failed the same way, and the run ended after 30 answered calls and at least $1.18. The 9 October attempt ended on OpenRouter's side. Three times, while it was writing its main service file, OpenRouter dropped the reply with "Upstream idle timeout exceeded", and goose gave up after the third resend. Our harness refuses to score a session the provider ended, because grading a half-built tree would publish an outage as the model's score.

What a Mistral Large 4 build costs: about 18 times DeepSeek's, at sale prices

Its Forge pair billed at least $10.95 for a median of 0.2195. DeepSeek 1017's pair billed at least $0.62 for 0.452, which works out at about $50 per median point against $1.36.

Those Mistral prices are the launch sale: Mistral's changelog says "Launch pricing: 50% off for 2 weeks" from 6 October, which by my arithmetic runs out around the 20th, though OpenRouter still showed the sale prices on the 20th. Its model page lists the regular rates as $1.36 in, $4.18 out and $0.14 cached, and at those rates the same pair would cost roughly twice as much, around $22, or about 35 times DeepSeek's at the off-peak rate it ran at.

Where Mistral's money went:

Mistral b2 DeepSeek 1017 b2
Requests 305 271
Prompt tokens per request 99,182 201,619
Share of prompt served from cache 84.6% 99.7%
Cache-read price per million (OpenRouter list; DeepSeek at the off-peak rate it ran at on Sunday 18 Oct, double at weekday peak) $0.07 $0.003
Uncached prompt price per million $0.68 $0.15
Bill $5.55 at least $0.32

DeepSeek carried twice the context into each call, inside a window two and a half times larger. Nearly all of it was billed as cache reads at a price 23 times lower than Mistral's. At list prices, fresh prompt tokens make up about half of each Mistral Forge bill, though they're only 13% to 15% of its prompt tokens. My guess is that the three compactions per build and the re-reads after them are a large part of that uncached slice. On the Forge builds the compaction summaries also ran on Mistral itself, because our host pin caught the helper calls meant for a small Gemini model. We fixed that while build 2 was still running. It shipped in 3.0.119, after the pair. The fourth Gauntlet attempt's four Gemini helper calls are inside its $4.93.

What the architecture might explain

Mistral publishes less than I'd like. The model card says "a granular Mixture-of-Experts architecture" with "52B active parameters and 1.05T total parameters, and a 1.6B vision encoder", a 1M context and "Status: Public Preview". The Hugging Face placeholder says 49 billion active per token, 52 billion counting embeddings and output layers, with weights expected on 31 October. The launch post defers the architecture, "additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology" to the weights release, and says "the reinforcement learning run behind this preview is still in flight". Expert counts, the attention design and a licence aren't published. There is no tech report yet.

On reasoning, Mistral's reasoning guide documents two values for this model, high and none. We sent medium. We do that for all our cloud runs. It's a valid value in Mistral's API schema, OpenRouter lists only high and none and defaults to high, and nobody documents what medium becomes. The 57% to 81% reasoning share suggests it was not thinking minimally, but that's an inference from our token counts.

I have two guesses about the behaviour. A preview whose RL run is "still in flight" may not yet be tuned for long agentic loops, where a long think costs calls and minutes. Our Forge logs look like that. Thorough reading, late writing, no time left to test. And 49B active parameters per token (52B with embeddings) is about three times the 16B at decode on the V4.1 Flash card, which the 1017 snapshot updates. That fits the gap in tokens per second we measured, though serving hardware and load matter as much, and our numbers can't separate them. Nothing in the cards explains the admin page or the throttle. Those are decisions in the code. I'd judge it on the code.

Mistral's own lifecycle page adds one more caveat: Public Preview models "allow silent updates". A pinned mistral-large-4-0 today may not be the model we measured on 18 and 19 October.

Where we were wrong

  1. Our Gauntlet money check assumed the table opens oldest first and charged Mistral x0.6 for correct money. Joining each cell to its payment by row id fixes it; it isn't shipped, and the board still shows 0.5462.
  2. The same check scores a currency that isn't on screen as a failed test. Four other ranked runs paid x0.92 for it.
  3. We capped Mistral's context at 262,144 tokens on a 1M model, against 655,360 for DeepSeek, so its six Forge compactions and their minutes and dollars are partly ours.
  4. goose put a user message between two tool results whenever an image came back before another result. Mistral refused it, and that ended a run. Fixed in 3.0.119.
  5. Under a Mistral host pin our helper calls went to Mistral too, so its Forge bills include summary work meant for a cheaper model. Fixed in 3.0.119.
  6. We asked for reasoning effort medium, which Mistral doesn't document for this model, so the effort it really ran at was the provider's choice.

Should you put Mistral Large 4 behind your agent?

From these runs, not yet for long agentic builds like our Forge task. It read for close to an hour and ran out of calls. It also cost about 18 times DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at sale prices. On the Gauntlet, once our check is fixed, it sits around 11th of 44, which is respectable for a preview that's still in training. I'd look again when the weights and the architecture write-up land (Mistral says 31 October), with the effort set to high or none and a full context window.

If you try it in your own setup, test four things. First, check whether your agent ever puts a user message between tool results (images, steering, injected reminders), because Mistral rejects that request outright. Through OpenRouter, the hosts behind three of our earlier runs answered it. Set the reasoning effort to a value Mistral documents. Watch the time to first write and the slowest calls rather than the median, since the 11- to 18-minute calls are where its time went. And read the failing check before you believe a critical, ours included.

Goose Swarm isn't production-ready yet. We run these boards with it because we know what it's made of. I'd like to hear from anyone running Large 4 in a real agent loop: did you get the long first thought too, and did none make it usable, or just cheaper? Tell me in the comments.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: Day 13/60: HashSet patterns - Rust DSA
description:
Day 13/60: HashSet patterns

60 Day Rust DSA Challenge

Today I focused on using Rust hash-based collections deliberately instead of treating them like magic storage. The strongest checkpoints were make the key and the stored meaning explicit before the map starts growing, update the hash state in the right order so the answer check stays correct, and use HashMap and HashSet for a defined reason instead of by reflex.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was building the right map but updating it in the wrong order. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests. title: Reconstruction-Optimized Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse expert activation, but deployment still requires storing a large number of expert parameters. We study post-training expert pruning using task-domain calibration data as a subset-selection problem: given a pretrained MoE layer, select a fixed number of experts that best reconstruct its original output. Exact subset search is combinatorial and becomes intractable for modern MoE models with many experts per layer. We develop OptEP, a scalable continuous relaxation that directly optimizes differentiable expert-selection variables, followed by a lightweight reconstruction-based update of the retained expert weights. Across multiple MoE architectures and tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approach improves over the strongest existing expert-pruning baselines, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 15.05% on Qwen3-30B-A3B, 14.55% on Qwen3-235B-A22B, 11.06% on GLM-4.5-Air, and 16.20% on Mixtral-8x7B. The improvements are particularly pronounced under aggressive pruning, demonstrating that reconstruction-driven expert selection and weight adaptation can preserve substantially more of the original model's performance while reducing the number of retained experts.

title: When Does an Added Planning Capability Create Operational Value? An Observable Evidence Standard
description:
arXiv:2610.27305v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial artificial intelligence (AI) planning systems combine predictive models, optimization logic, controls, and governance rules, but improvement in the complete policy does not show whether one addition made an independent contribution or whether that contribution justifies its burden. We address this attribution problem with an observable evidence standard that separates opportunity to act, executed-plan change, operational consequence, equivalence, uncertainty, and operating scope. Using forecast-to-plan replay on Favorita, M5, and Walmart data, we apply the standard to heterogeneous planning additions. Three limits of single-indicator evaluation emerge. First, a composite policy can conceal negligible component contribution: one control changed only 15 of 681 executed plans. Second, changing execution does not guarantee stable benefit: the evaluated multi-period capability helped in several long-lead settings but was 7.6% more costly under tight capacity. Third, indirect evidence can prioritize review but cannot complete attribution. Independent runs produced different paths in 19 of 599 cases that a rule-based check predicted would be unchanged. Although a lower-cost diagnostic matched the full-evaluation winner in only 55.0% of cases, it selected an option within the $10^{-6}$ cost-equivalence tolerance in 79.5%; the remaining cases prevented the proxy from authorizing acceptance. These experiments establish capability-level contribution evidence; the organization completes the value decision by weighing it against implementation and sustaining burden. The resulting capability evidence record links the observations to validation, deployment scope, fallback, monitoring, redesign, and retirement decisions.

title: Day 13/60: GORM basics - Go Backend Engineering
description:
Day 13/60: GORM basics

60 Day Go Backend Engineering Challenge

Today I focused on keeping gorm basics honest about query boundaries, transactions, and data ownership. The strongest checkpoints were decide where transactions begin and end before mixing reads and writes together, make query shape, connection usage, and migration ownership explicit, and separate storage models from transport models so schema changes stay contained.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was letting transaction scope grow until failures become impossible to reason about. The day felt better once the service boundary stayed visible and each component had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next service still feels related to the same design idea. I also want to keep tracing one request path end to end because it exposes weak assumptions faster than a larger demo. title: Vulnerability Analysis for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement
description:
arXiv:2610.27293v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (SMARL) aims to learn cooperative control policies under prescribed safety constraints. Al- though existing SMARL methods focus on enforcing safety during policy optimization, their vulnerability remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates inference-time observation attacks against SMARL, where an adversary perturbs the observations of a subset of agents, thereby altering the actions produced by their policies. We propose MinMax Attack, an attack framework that jointly selects adversarial target actions for compromised agents while accounting for the Cooperative Resistance of benign agents. We further derive a bound on the induced safety cost and characterize its relation- ship with the Compromised-Agent Budget and the Perturbation Budget. Experiments across multiple safety-critical multi-agent benchmarks and representative state-of-the-art SMARL algorithms show that MinMax Attack induces substantially higher safety costs than existing attack baselines while preserving task reward, thereby reducing its detectability and achieving both attack effectiveness and stealthiness.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: 5 quick checks to make a website load faster
description:
A slow website loses visitors before they read a single word. Here are five checks I run on almost every site, in the order I do them. None need special tools.

1. Measure before you change anything

Open Chrome DevTools, go to the Lighthouse tab and run a mobile report. Note the scores for Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Total Blocking Time. Without a starting number you can't tell whether a change helped.

2. Compress and resize images

Images are usually the heaviest part of a page.

  • Convert photos to WebP or AVIF.
  • Resize them to the size they are actually shown at. A 4000px photo in a 600px box wastes bandwidth.
  • Add loading="lazy" to images below the fold: 
<img src="team.webp" width="600" height="400" alt="Our team" loading="lazy">

Setting width and height also stops the page from jumping around as it loads.

3. Cut unused CSS and JavaScript

Open DevTools → Coverage and reload. It shows how much of each file is never used on that page. Remove unused libraries and load scripts that aren't needed immediately with defer:

<script src="app.js" defer></script>

4. Turn on caching and compression

  • Enable gzip or Brotli on the server.
  • Send Cache-Control headers so returning visitors don't re-download files that haven't changed.

5. Check your fonts

Every font weight is a separate file. Use only the weights you need, and add font-display: swap so text shows straight away instead of staying blank:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
}

Recheck

Run Lighthouse again and compare it with your first result. Most sites improve a lot from just the image and script steps.

What is the biggest speed problem you've run into? Let me know in the comments.

title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.27450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

Anti Money Laundering AI

v1.16.11

On October 14, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.11.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.16.11.

Application Integration

Security

An Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the AuthConfig validation and integration execution runtime in Application Integration versions prior to August 27, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Issue

Generally available: When you reserve capacity by using future reservation requests, you can specify that Compute Engine delivers your reserved capacity as specifically targeted reservations. Specifically targeted reservations help you track and control which Compute Engine instances consume your reserved capacity. For more information, see About future reservation requests.

Feature

Generally available: You can increase the size of a Google Cloud Hyperdisk volume that's in multi-writer mode while the volume is attached to multiple instances. Previously, you had to detach the volume from all instances before you could resize it.

For more information, see Share disks between instances and Change the size or provisioned performance of a Hyperdisk volume.

You can automatically preserve BigQuery data policies and data governance tags (Preview) applied to tables across Dataform executions by enabling the preserveGovernanceControls option in your table or workflow configuration. Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in the United Kingdom

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in the United Kingdom.

  • Location availability: Supported in the UK (europe-west2) in-country region with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).
  • App availability: Turned on by default in the web app for the UK region. Administrators can manage access with the Gemini 3.8 Flash toggle under Model availability.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in Workflow Builder

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for Workflow Builder. Gemini 4 Argon is also available in Workflow Builder workflow agents. Updates take up to a day to appear in workflow agents.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.

For more information, see Workflow Builder.

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Enhanced SARIF 2.1.0 reporting: Updated cm report SARIF output with standardized rule descriptors, severity properties, and repository-relative artifact locations for improved GitHub Code Scanning compatibility.
  • Model invocation metrics: Added model invocation tracking to cm stats --json, providing total, per-session, and per-turn invocation counts.
  • Bug fixes:

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is available in Public Preview

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from DeepSeek is available as a fully managed model (MaaS) in Model Garden. The model accepts text and image input, targets agentic and coding tasks, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens.

For more information, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Performance of the Cloud Storage Sink connector has been improved. The improvements include reduced out-of-memory errors, higher maximum throughput, and avoiding creating a large number of small files.

title: Deploying an AI Stack for a Call-Led Business: Checklist, Smoke Test and Adoption Tracking in Python
description:
If the agency becomes a deployment, then deploying the growth stack for a call-led firm is an engineering problem. This post sketches the steps in Python: an onboarding checklist as data, an integration smoke test, and a training tracker. It is an illustration, not a customer story, and I have no results to share.

The premise comes from watching traditional, call-led businesses fail to self-serve AI tools, and from public writing by BCG and Google on why adoption is about people and process, not software alone.

1. The deployment plan as data 

DEPLOYMENT_STEPS = [
    {"step": "crm_import",      "desc": "Import existing leads into the CRM"},
    {"step": "telephony",       "desc": "Route calls through the dialer, log outcomes"},
    {"step": "whatsapp",        "desc": "Connect WhatsApp business number for follow-ups"},
    {"step": "ad_reporting",    "desc": "Send lead-source data back to the ad platform"},
    {"step": "team_training",   "desc": "Train the sales team on the daily workflow"},
]

2. A smoke test before go-live 

def smoke_test(integrations: dict) -> list[str]:
    failures = []
    if not integrations.get("crm", {}).get("lead_count", 0):
        failures.append("CRM has no leads - import failed or empty")
    if not integrations.get("telephony", {}).get("test_call_logged"):
        failures.append("test call was not logged")
    if not integrations.get("whatsapp", {}).get("message_sent"):
        failures.append("WhatsApp send failed")
    if not integrations.get("ads", {}).get("last_sync_ok"):
        failures.append("ad platform sync failing")
    return failures

3. Track adoption, not setup 

def adoption_report(weeks: list[dict]) -> dict:
    # weeks: [{"calls_in_dialer": 40, "calls_total": 45, ...}, ...]
    latest = weeks[-1]
    return {
        "dialer_usage": latest["calls_in_dialer"] / max(latest["calls_total"], 1),
        "followups_on_time": latest["followups_done"] / max(latest["followups_due"], 1),
        "crm_records_touched": latest["records_updated"] / max(latest["records_total"], 1),
    }

What this shows

The code is simple on purpose. The hard parts are steps 2 and 3: verifying each integration actually works for this client, and measuring whether the team uses it after you leave. Public guidance from Google says the same thing in different words - measure whether the tool helps the business, not how busy it is.

Limits

Real deployments have per-client quirks this sketch ignores: number porting, consent rules for messaging, and data cleanup. Treat this as a scaffold.

Tej Pandya, founder of GrowEasy.ai.

title: Day 17/60: Matrix operations in Rust - Rust DSA
description:
Day 17/60: Matrix operations in Rust

60 Day Rust DSA Challenge

Today I focused on making matrix operations in rust work with Rust slices, strings, and indices without losing correctness. The strongest checkpoints were decide early whether bytes, chars, or slices are the right representation in Rust, keep the transformation or scan state explicit instead of mixing index tricks together, and use iterators and owned buffers deliberately so UTF-8 handling does not become accidental.

The mistake I wanted to avoid was mixing byte indexing and character assumptions in UTF-8 text. The day felt better once the invariant stayed visible and each update had one job.

The goal for tomorrow is simple: keep the rule clear enough that the next variation still feels related to the same idea. I also want to keep tracing tiny examples because they expose weak assumptions faster than large random tests.

title: REM: What to Store, When to Recall, What to Forget in Experience Memory for Coding Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27377v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. Retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether the agent needs an experience, at which point, or for how long. We introduce REM (Reusable Experience Memory), a framework that manages the memory lifecycle from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions. What to store: each completed trajectory is consolidated into a phase-structured document, two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory. When to recall: the document is injected at the start of the task; the costlier implementation record is withheld until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling. What to forget: the record is evicted after a single exposure. On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM retrieves the related trajectory more accurately than every state-of-the-art memory system (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and improves, in every replicate, end-task resolution (27.6% vs. 24.9%) at 17% lower cost. Injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory, even when oracle-retrieved, does not. Ablating any of the three decisions reduces resolution. Altogether, these results demonstrate that the bottleneck in experience reuse is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, opening a control-theoretic perspective on agent memory.

title: Modeling Authentic Research Trajectories: A Graph View of Research Ideation
description:
arXiv:2610.27337v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The research idea in a published paper is rarely the project's initial idea. Between the two lies a closed-loop process in which researchers run experiments, derive insights, identify challenges, explore the literature, and revise the idea, with each step motivated by evidence and reasoning they can articulate. We call the path one idea takes through this process, with the evidence and reasoning behind each step, its authentic research trajectory. Although it underlies every scientific contribution, it is rarely recorded. Existing LLM-based research agents generate an idea once, refine it against reviews, literature, or their own experimental results, or search over candidate ideas and experiments. In all of them the text of the idea evolves, while the evidence and reasoning that connected one version to the next are discarded. We propose the Research Progress Graph (RPG), a representation of authentic and complete research trajectories. An RPG records the evolution of an idea as typed research states connected by cognitive transitions, each annotated with a temporal index and the reasoning behind it, which makes this evolution an explicit object of study. We ground the representation in authentic trajectories whose steps their authors justify in annotations and papers. Comparing the representations of thirty-five research agents with the RPG, we find that each is an incomplete RPG; none keeps the state that changed, the evidence that changed it, and the reasoning connecting them as one evolving record. Modeling ideation with the RPG changes how research agents should be designed, evaluated, and trained. Agents predict the next research state instead of a complete idea, ideas are evaluated as trajectories instead of final texts, and authentic trajectories serve as training data. These directions shift research agents from generating static ideas to modeling how ideas evolve.

title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.26904v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.

title: Retries Are a Distributed Systems Bug Waiting to Happen: Designing Idempotent APIs
description:
Every network call can fail in three ways: it fails, it succeeds, or it succeeds and you never find out. The third case is where most production incidents live.

Junior instinct: "Request timed out, retry it."
Senior question: "What if the first one actually went through?"

The core problem 

Client                 Server                  DB
  | --- POST /charge --> |                      |
  |                      | --- INSERT charge -> |
  |                      | <------- OK -------- |
  |   X (response lost)  |                      |
  | --- POST /charge --> |   (retry)            |
  |                      | --- INSERT charge -> |   <- duplicate

The client can't tell "never arrived" from "arrived, reply lost." Retrying blindly means double charges, duplicate orders, double emails.

Fix 1: Idempotency keys

The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it on every attempt. The server stores the result and replays it.

Client                       Server
  | POST /charge                |
  | Idempotency-Key: abc-123 -> | not seen: process, store result
  |  X (response lost)          |
  | POST /charge                |
  | Idempotency-Key: abc-123 -> | seen: return stored result, no new charge

app.post("/charge", async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.get("Idempotency-Key");
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Idempotency-Key required" });

  // Atomic claim: unique constraint on key
  const claimed = await db.idempotency.insertIfAbsent({
    key, status: "in_progress", requestHash: hash(req.body),
  });

  if (!claimed) {
    const existing = await db.idempotency.get(key);
    if (existing.requestHash !== hash(req.body))
      return res.status(422).json({ error: "Key reused with different payload" });
    if (existing.status === "in_progress")
      return res.status(409).json({ error: "Request in progress" });
    return res.status(existing.code).json(existing.response); // replay
  }

  const result = await chargeCard(req.body);
  await db.idempotency.complete(key, 200, result);
  res.json(result);
});

Details that matter:

  • Make the claim atomic (unique constraint, not check-then-insert).
  • Hash the payload. Same key with a different body is a client bug, so reject it.
  • Handle the in-progress state so concurrent retries don't race.
  • Set a TTL (24-72h is common).

Fix 2: Retry correctly

Retries without backoff turn a blip into an outage (the retry storm).

Attempt:  1    2      3         4              5
Wait:     0 -> 1s -> 2s ------> 4s -----------> 8s   (exponential)
               +-jitter: random within each window

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function retry(fn, { retries = 5, base = 200, cap = 10_000 } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (err) {
      if (i >= retries || !isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      const backoff = Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** i);
      await sleep(Math.random() * backoff); // full jitter
    }
  }
}
  • Jitter is not optional. Without it, every client retries in lockstep.
  • Only retry transient errors (timeouts, 429, 503), never 400/401/404.
  • Respect Retry-After. Put a retry budget at the service level.

Fix 3: The dual-write problem 

await db.save(order);        // succeeds
await queue.publish(event);  // crashes here -> DB and queue disagree

You can't make two systems commit atomically. Use the transactional outbox:

+---------- one DB transaction ----------+
|  INSERT order       INSERT outbox_event |
+-----------------------------------------+
              |
     relay polls outbox -> publishes to queue -> marks sent

This gives at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent too (dedupe by event ID).

What I'd standardize on

Layer Rule
Write endpoints Require Idempotency-Key
Clients Exponential backoff + full jitter + cap
Messaging Outbox + idempotent consumers
Semantics Assume at-least-once, design for it

Takeaway

"Exactly-once" is mostly a myth. What you actually build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which behaves like exactly-once from the outside.

Design every write as if it will be sent twice, because eventually it will be.

How does your team handle idempotency? Keys, natural dedupe, or hope? Let me know in the comments. 👇

title: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates
description:
arXiv:2610.26899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.

title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
description:
arXiv:2610.27438v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce \textbf{MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing)}, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$--$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$--$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.
