title: Code Got Cheap. Your Attention Didn't.
description:
Andrej Karpathy hasn't written a line of code by hand since December 2025. His workflow flipped from 80% manual coding to 80% agent-driven, with the remaining 20% spent on oversight. "I'm still the bottleneck," he said -- not because the agents are slow, but because he can only review so fast.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn →

That one sentence contains the entire economics of the agent era: code generation is approaching zero marginal cost, but human attention remains fixed. The binding constraint on your agent fleet isn't compute, API spend, or model capability. It's the operator sitting between generated output and production, deciding what to trust.

And most teams are treating that constraint like it doesn't exist.

The Numbers That Should Scare You

Faros AI analyzed 22,000 developers across 4,000 teams in March 2026. The data is sobering:

  • Code churn up 861%. Agents rewrite code that was just written -- often their own.
  • Incidents-to-PR ratio up 242.7%. More code, more bugs, proportionally more bugs.
  • PRs merged with zero review: 31.3%. Almost a third of changes ship with nobody looking.
  • Per-developer defect rate: 9% to 54%. Six times more bugs per person.
  • Median review duration up 441.5%. Reviews take 4.4x longer when agents write the code.

Read Addy Osmani's full analysis on agentic code review ->

Meanwhile, a study of 25,264 agentic pull requests found that 42.27% of projects had participation ratios below 5%. The overwhelming majority of agent-authored PRs are overseen by a single human. One person, standing between an arbitrarily large output stream and production.

The community is feeling the pain. On Hacker News, developers are building tools specifically to triage which agent PRs deserve human eyes and which can ship:

View discussion on Hacker News ->

The numbers tell a consistent story: individual throughput is up, team delivery is flat or worse, and the review queue is where velocity goes to die. A Harvard study confirmed the pattern -- agents increased code volume by 30% without a matching gain in resolved issues. Review times jumped 49%. Revision requests nearly doubled.

The core problem in one line: Agents produce code at machine speed. Humans verify it at human speed. The queue between those two speeds is where your entire engineering org lives now.

The Attention Economy of Agent Fleets

Here's what nobody is saying clearly enough: you need an attention budget, not just an API budget.

Addy Osmani, formerly of Google Chrome and now author of the most-cited practitioner writing on agent management, frames it this way: the bottleneck has shifted from "can this agent write code" to "should we build this" and "can I manage multiple agents doing so effectively." His operating setup: 4-5 background agents on bounded tasks (tests, docs, dependency bumps) plus 3-5 local sessions for architecture and product work. Boris Cherny, Claude Code's creator, reportedly runs 5 local plus 5-10 browser sessions. Greg Isenberg described running 5-10 concurrent cloud sessions producing 22-25 PRs per day.

Read the full piece: Your AI coding agents need a manager ->

But there's a catch. Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report found that developers fully delegate only 0-20% of tasks to agents while actively supervising 80-100% of what they delegate. If you're running 10 agents but supervising 80% of their output, you haven't saved attention -- you've multiplied the demand on it.

The uncomfortable math: attention doesn't scale linearly with agent count. Each additional agent doesn't add a fixed oversight cost. It adds a variable cost that depends on the trust level you've established, the reversibility of the change, and the blast radius if something goes wrong. Most teams ignore this entirely and discover it when the incident count spikes.

Practitioners are already asking this question in the open. One Ask HN thread captures the tension directly -- how do you harden AI-generated changes to a million-line legacy SaaS before review?

View discussion on Hacker News ->

The Three Attention Allocation Patterns That Work

After reviewing every practitioner framework published this year -- from Osmani's operating loop to Somasundaram Sekar's five-layer review model to Semgrep's risk classification -- three patterns emerge that actually survive contact with production.

Read the full article on Substack ->

Pattern 1: Trust Tiers (Not Uniform Review)

Stop reviewing everything the same way. Classify your agent output into tiers:

Tier 0 -- Auto-merge. Formatting, dependency bumps, documentation fixes, test additions that pass CI. These are reversible, low-blast-radius changes. Set up automated gates (lint, typecheck, SAST, test suite) and let them ship. Semgrep's data shows this class covers roughly 40% of agent output.

Tier 1 -- Batch review. Feature additions in well-tested areas, refactors with high test coverage, infrastructure changes with rollback plans. Review these in blocks -- not one at a time as they arrive, but in a daily 30-minute review session. A reviewer can meaningfully assess roughly 200-400 lines per hour. Batch them into digestible chunks.

Tier 2 -- Deep review. Auth changes, payment flows, data migrations, API contracts, anything touching shared interfaces. These get the full human review: intent verification, structural analysis, edge-case probing, and the knowledge-transfer check ("can the author explain the agent's approach?"). If they can't, the code doesn't merge.

Tier 3 -- Human-only zones. Architecture decisions, security-sensitive design, product strategy expressed in code. No agent touches these without a human co-piloting from the start. Osmani calls this the "own" category -- work you keep, not delegate.

Read Semgrep's take on risk-based code review ->

Contrarian Corner: Some teams are pushing for full auto-review -- AI reviewing AI at every tier. Monperrus's June 2026 paper argues human review is "neither meaningful assurance nor scalable" and should be replaced entirely. But CodeRabbit's data shows AI-coauthored changes had 1.7x more issues than human-only code, and a 146-PR study found 93.4% of flagged issues were caught by only one of four AI reviewers -- none caught them all. AI review has correlated blind spots. Use it as a first pass, not the final word.

Pattern 2: The Review Sandwich

This is the pattern emerging from Osmani's agentic code review framework, refined through GitHub's internal data: AI first pass, human middle, author verification.

  1. AI pre-screen: Run 2+ different AI review tools (their blind spots don't overlap). This catches surface issues -- style, known anti-patterns, obvious bugs -- and generates a risk score for triage.
  2. Human judgment layer: Humans review intent (does this match the ticket?), risk tier (what breaks if this is wrong?), and structure (are the abstractions right?). This is the irreducible human work.
  3. Author verification: Before merge, the human who requested the change must explain the agent's approach. If they can't articulate why the code works this way, it doesn't ship.

GitHub reports this pattern reduced human review time by 30-50% internally -- not by removing human attention, but by focusing it on the decisions only humans can make.

Pattern 3: WIP Limits for Agent Streams

This one comes straight from manufacturing theory, and it's the most underused pattern in agent fleet management.

Cap the number of active agent streams to your review capacity, not your compute capacity. If you can meaningfully review 4-5 PRs per session, don't run 15 agents producing 25 PRs. You'll spend the day context-switching between review queues instead of actually reviewing.

Osmani recommends explicit WIP limits:

  • Define kill criteria before starting a feature (what counts as "stop and ask")
  • Set time limits ("stop and report blockers after 15 minutes without progress")
  • Cap the number of concurrent agent PRs waiting for review at a number your team can clear in a day
  • Use git worktrees to isolate agent work -- one agent per PR, no merge conflicts

Read Wavect's analysis on focus as the bottleneck ->

The Wavect analysis argues there's no evidence-based universal ceiling on agents per operator, but recommends measuring accepted outcomes rather than activity, and reducing concurrency when review queues grow. The right number of agents isn't "as many as possible" -- it's "as many as you can verify."

The delegation brief: Before spawning any agent task, Osmani's framework requires a written brief covering: outcome, context, constraints, non-goals, acceptance criteria, integration notes, and a verification plan. This costs 5 minutes up front and saves 30 minutes of confused review downstream. The four-forms-of-oversight study (17 developer interviews) found that two of the four oversight forms happen before the agent writes any code -- a priori control and co-planning. Front-loading intent is cheaper than back-loading review.

Measuring Oversight Cost

You can't budget what you don't measure. Here are the metrics that matter for attention allocation:

Ready-to-accepted time. How long between an agent finishing a PR and a human accepting it? If this grows faster than your agent count, your attention budget is overdrawn.

Review queue age. If PRs wait more than 2 days for first response, you have a capacity problem, not a velocity problem. Target 4-hour first response, 24-hour resolution.

First-pass acceptance rate. What percentage of agent PRs merge without revision requests? If it's below 60%, your agents need better briefs -- the problem is upstream, not in review.

Cost per accepted outcome. Track API spend + compute + human review hours per merged, incident-free change. Not per PR, not per line of code -- per outcome that worked. This is the number that tells you whether your fleet is actually productive or just busy.

Oversight-to-output ratio. What percentage of your engineering hours go to reviewing agent output vs. doing work agents can't? If review consumes more than 40% of senior engineer time, you're spending your scarcest resource on verification instead of judgment. That's a staffing problem, not a tooling problem.

The Community Is Split

The developer community hasn't converged on a single answer. HN threads show a spectrum from "just review the agent's approach, not every line" to "I still read every diff":

View discussion on Hacker News ->

And the broader question of how to use LLMs effectively in established codebases -- where the stakes and blast radius are highest -- continues to generate heated debate:

View discussion on Hacker News ->

The Skill Atrophy Problem Nobody Wants to Talk About

There's a darker side to the attention allocation question. A position paper from Dhanorkar et al. (2026) interviewed 17 professional developers and found early signs that supervising agents erodes hands-on programming skill. One participant said they had shipped Go code they didn't know how to write a month earlier.

This creates a vicious cycle: as developers spend more time reviewing and less time writing, their ability to catch subtle bugs in agent-generated code degrades. The reviewer atrophies into an approver.

The atrophy trap: Laurie Voss's data from WeAreDevelopers World Congress shows coders using LLM assistance wrote 700% more code but released only 30% more actual software. The gap isn't laziness -- it's the review and integration capacity that doesn't scale with output. And the more you outsource the writing, the less qualified you become to do the reviewing.

The fix isn't to avoid delegation. It's to keep humans writing code in high-judgment areas (Tier 3) while delegating bounded tasks (Tier 0-1). The Pragmatic Engineer's conversation with Osmani frames this as "mutual amplification" -- using agents to handle volume while keeping humans sharp on the work that matters.

What This Means for You

If you're running an agent fleet today -- or planning to -- here's the playbook:

  1. Audit your current oversight spend. How many hours per week do your senior engineers spend reviewing agent output? If you don't know, start measuring. The number will surprise you.

  2. Implement trust tiers. Not every change deserves the same attention. Auto-merge formatting and test additions. Batch-review feature work. Deep-review anything touching auth, payments, or shared interfaces. Keep architecture human-only.

  3. Set WIP limits based on review capacity, not compute capacity. If your team can review 15 PRs per day, don't let agents produce 40. The excess just rots in the queue and creates merge conflicts.

  4. Front-load intent. Write delegation briefs. Define acceptance criteria before the agent starts. Two of four oversight forms happen before any code is written -- invest there.

  5. Measure outcomes, not output. Lines of code and PR count are vanity metrics. Track cost per accepted, incident-free change. That's your real productivity number.

  6. Protect review capacity like you protect compute. When you cut headcount because agents made coding faster, you're cutting the one resource that doesn't scale with AI: human judgment under load.

The teams that figure out attention allocation will ship 10x more than the teams that just add more agents. The constraint was never code. It was always the human in the loop -- and now we need to treat that human's attention like the scarce, expensive, non-renewable resource it is.

For the verification side of this problem -- how to build trust gates that actually work -- see Lean Is Becoming AI's Trust Layer. For fleet orchestration patterns, see The Agent-of-Agents Problem. For why the model isn't the bottleneck, see Your AI Agent's Bottleneck Isn't the Model. And for the PR-volume data that kicked off this entire conversation, see 10x PRs, 1x Reviewers.

Originally published at AgentConn

title: VampPrior Unleashed
description:
arXiv:2610.27322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep latent variable models (DLVMs) underpin many modern analysis pipelines, for example in single-cell genomics, yet their prior distributions have received markedly little attention. The VampPrior approximates the optimal prior (the aggregate posterior) and often attains high model evidence. Here, we identify two key limitations of the VampPrior: it ties prior and posterior uncertainty to a single amortized covariance and clusters poorly due to its fixed uniform mixture weights. We unleash the VampPrior by decoupling its prior and posterior covariances, resolving the conflict of generating high prior and low posterior entropy with the same shared parameters and substantially improving model evidence. We then replace the uniform mixture with a Dirichlet process. When combined, our proposals provide higher model evidence than the VampPrior and robust non-parametric clustering. Augmenting single cell Variational Inference (scVI) with our prior improves single-cell integration and clustering across six atlases while significantly raising model evidence. Our approach changes only the prior and thus can be applied to any DLVM with a continuous latent space.

title: LoRASpace: A Pool-Wide Shared Substrate for Static and Dynamic Multi-LoRA Composition
description:
arXiv:2610.27444v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories host many LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept or task. Combining several LoRAs in one generation forces a trade-off. Merging their weights into one update needs a single forward pass, but LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere and quality drops. Running each LoRA in its own forward pass (composite) preserves quality, but inference time grows linearly with the number of active LoRAs. We study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi-LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low-rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that keeps 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the summed LoRA ranks is needed, and the subspace grows sub-linearly with pool size. A 48-LoRA sub-pool of LoRA-Hub on FLAN-T5 tasks shows comparable overlap (62%), while the diversity-curated LoRA-Retriever benchmark sits near the no-overlap baseline (96%), so pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We build on this overlap with LoRASpace, a training-free method that computes the subspace once per pool and reuses it in two inference modes, a static mode at merge cost and a dynamic mode for input-dependent routing. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace is more than 6x faster than composite with six active LoRAs on a 17-LoRA pool, mainly because it runs one backbone pass instead of six. In an ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace, so the quality gain does not depend on the pool-wide basis. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever benchmark, compression is small and gains come from coupling with external retrieval.

title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
description:
arXiv:2610.26979v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

title: Deep Auxiliary Learning via Bilevel Feature Optimization for Label-Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.26954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Auxiliary learning (AL), which can improve the performance of a primary task by leveraging related auxiliary tasks, is commonly regarded as a special case of multi-task learning. Existing AL approaches typically require manually annotated auxiliary labels, increasing annotation costs, particularly in medical imaging where expert labeling is expensive. In this work, we investigate whether segmentation performance can be improved using auxiliary tasks whose labels are automatically derived from existing segmentation annotations, requiring no additional manual labeling. To address this, we propose a novel auxiliary learning framework, formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. Our method enables effective knowledge transfer between tasks via a feature communication module, enhancing the primary segmentation task. We evaluate the method on three medical image segmentation benchmarks under limited-label settings. The results demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior label efficiency. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/FupingWu90/ALBO.

title: Selling time, not files: hosts, multi-host carts and a 10-minute Join window
description:
A course is a file you can sell a thousand times. An appointment is an hour that can only be sold once. That one difference shapes most of the booking system in VeloxonHub. The 30-second reel shows the flow from the outside. Here's what happens inside.

1. An appointment is a product with booking rules

The host creates an appointment in a 5-step drawer: details, type and host, availability, booking rules and pricing. Under the hood it's a scheduling product with appointment settings: duration, buffers, an advance-booking window, booking, cancellation and reschedule cutoffs, capacity per slot, an approval flag, whether multiple slots can be selected, and the Join window.

2. Free or paid is decided by the price, not a flag

If the appointment has no active price, the booking page shows a plain "Confirm Booking" action and calls the booking endpoint directly. Several slots are booked one by one, and on a partial failure the UI keeps only the slots that still need booking and says exactly which failed. Package appointments use pre-paid credits and go through a batch endpoint instead.

If there is a price, the selection goes into the same cart and checkout as every other product.

3. Slots belong to hosts

Each host has weekly availability rules plus exceptions (extra hours, blocked days, vacations) and site-wide holidays. The booking page loads a month of slots, and every slot carries its host_id. Choosing a host filters the calendar to that host's slots, so the client only sees times that host can actually take. Times are stored in UTC and shown in the visitor's time zone.

4. Multi-host selections are priced per slot

When multiple selection is on, a client can mix hosts: Monday with one host, Thursday with another. Pricing doesn't apply one rate to the whole selection. Each slot is resolved through its own host:

  • if the host has active prices of their own, those win;
  • otherwise the product's default price applies;
  • only active prices count, so an archived host price never sets the total.

The result is a list of lines (time, host, amount) plus a total, and a flag if the selection mixes currencies. The server resolves the final amounts again at checkout, so the browser never decides what anyone pays. There's also a conflict check, so one person can't put two overlapping slots in the cart.

5. Join is a 10-minute window, decided by the backend

After booking, the call shows up in the client's schedule. What the main button does depends on the delivery method (join a room, get directions, check in, wait for a call), and the backend sends that as joining_details.action.

For a virtual call, Join only becomes active join_available_minutes_before the start. The default is 10 minutes (COALESCE(join_available_minutes_before, 10)), and the host can change it. A small ticker on the client re-checks every 15 seconds, so the button turns on without a reload.

What we'd tell someone building the same thing

  • Let "free" fall out of the price data instead of a separate flag.
  • Attach every slot to a host, and price every slot through its host.
  • Never trust a price from the browser, and check for overlapping slots before checkout.
  • Treat "join" as a window with a status check, not a link you hand out at booking time.

Try it with a free trial: https://veloxonhub.com. Happy to go deeper into availability exceptions or multi-host pricing in the comments.

title: When Does Hate Transfer? A Large-Scale Study of Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27285v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective detection of hate content is essential for maintaining healthy online communities, yet performance can vary substantially across languages. This work investigates a core practical question: Can training data from one language support hate-speech detection in another language with comparable performance? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale study across 14 languages. \change{We observe consistent patterns in which certain language pairs transfer more effectively than others. Among the factors we measure, linguistic similarity is the strongest predictor of these patterns, with temporal overlap and dataset-size difference playing smaller roles. These measurable factors do not fully explain the observed patterns; a complementary qualitative analysis suggests that shared cultural cues and communicative norms may be associated with some of the remaining cases, particularly within several clusters. We present this cultural interpretation as a hypothesis from qualitative inspection rather than a measured cause.}{} Our analysis includes low-resource languages, offering practical insights into when cross-lingual transfer can support them and where its limitations emerge. These findings inform the design of more reliable multilingual hate-detection systems.

title: A GitHub Actions Security Gate for Node.js: Block Leaked Keys
description:
A GitHub Actions security gate for Node.js is a single workflow that runs on every pull request. It scans the new commits for leaked API keys, checks new dependencies for known vulnerabilities and confirms the lockfile is honest. If any of those checks finds something real, it blocks the merge. You can build it in an afternoon with free tools, and most of that afternoon goes into tuning, not setup.

You may have found a live Stripe key in a commit from three weeks ago. Or you may have a Dependabot tab full of alerts that nobody has opened since spring. Either way, this walkthrough is for you.

Why do leaked keys and vulnerable packages get past code review?

Code review happens on diffs, and people reviewing a diff read the logic, not the config. A key pasted into a test fixture looks like noise. A risky transitive dependency hardly shows up at all. It sits somewhere in a 2,000-line lockfile change that nobody scrolls through.

AI coding assistants make both problems worse. To get an example working, they hardcode credentials, and they add packages without a second thought. The code runs, the reviewer approves, and the key goes into history.

What does it cost when one slips through?

Deleting a leaked key in a later commit does not remove it. Git history keeps it, and so does every clone and fork. Bots scan public pushes for credential patterns all the time. The only real fix is rotation: you find every service and environment that uses the key, issue a new one and redeploy without breaking production.

A vulnerable dependency costs you differently. You end up doing an emergency upgrade across major versions, under pressure, on code you didn't write.

The hidden cost is a noisy gate. If the check fails on things that don't matter, people stop reading it. They re-run it, or an admin turns on bypass. Then the one real finding goes straight through.

Do you actually need a custom gate?

Maybe not. A solo side project with no paying users and no production credentials may only need what GitHub already gives you: secret scanning with push protection and Dependabot alerts, both free on public repositories. Turn those on and stop there.

You need the gate when several people merge code, when the app holds customer data or payment keys, or when part of the codebase came from an AI builder and nobody has reviewed it line by line.

The workflow

Save this as .github/workflows/security-gate.yml:

name: security-gate
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Scan PR commits for secrets
        uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main # pin a release tag or SHA
        with:
          extra_args: --results=verified,unknown

  dependencies:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/dependency-review-action@v4
        with:
          fail-on-severity: high
          fail-on-scopes: runtime

  lockfile:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - name: Lockfile matches package.json
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - name: Lockfile only pulls from the npm registry over https
        run: npx --yes lockfile-lint --path package-lock.json --type npm --allowed-hosts npm --validate-https

Here is what each job does and why it is set up this way.

Secrets. TruffleHog scans only the commits between the PR base and head, so it stays fast. fetch-depth: 0 gives it that history. --results=verified,unknown means it fails on keys it confirmed are live, plus keys it couldn't check. It ignores ones it proved are dead.

Dependencies. Dependency review looks only at packages this PR adds or changes. That one choice keeps old debt from blocking unrelated work. fail-on-scopes: runtime ignores dev-only tooling. On private repositories this action needs GitHub's paid code security add-on.

Lockfile. npm ci fails when package.json and package-lock.json disagree, which catches the classic "I edited package.json by hand" PR. --ignore-scripts stops install scripts from running inside your gate. lockfile-lint fails if a resolved URL points to an unknown host or plain http, which is a common way to sneak in a tampered package.

If dependency review isn't available to you, swap that job for npx --yes audit-ci@7 --config audit-ci.jsonc with a config like this:

{
  "high": true,
  "skip-dev": true,
  "allowlist": [
    // Only reachable from an internal admin script. Review by 2026-12-01. Owner: backend lead
    "GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx"
  ]
}

How do you tune it so the team doesn't learn to ignore it?

Only fail on findings someone would actually fix today. Everything else goes into a report, not a red X.

  • Start with verified secrets only. Run TruffleHog with --results=verified for the first two weeks, then add unknown. The team's first experience should be a real catch, not ten false alarms.
  • Gate on high and critical in runtime code. Moderate issues in a test runner are real, but they are not merge blockers. Handle them in a scheduled job.
  • Run a nightly full audit separately. A schedule: workflow running npm audit --omit=dev across the whole tree catches newly disclosed issues in old packages. It opens an issue instead of blocking someone's unrelated PR.
  • Every exception needs a reason, an owner and a review date. An allowlist entry with no comment becomes permanent. The allow-ghsas input on dependency review and the audit-ci allowlist both work for this. Read through them once a month.
  • Keep the gate under three minutes. Slow checks get skipped. The three jobs run in parallel for that reason.
  • Make the failure tell people what to do. Add a short note to your PR template: if the secrets job fails, rotate the key first, then remove it from the code. Removing it alone fixes nothing.

How do you make sure nobody can skip it?

In your repository settings, add a branch protection rule (or ruleset) on main and mark secrets, dependencies and lockfile as required status checks. Turn on "Do not allow bypassing" for admins too. A gate that the most senior person can quietly skip only trains everyone else to ask that person.

One honest limit: this gate stops new problems. It doesn't find the key that was committed eight months ago. Run a full history scan once (trufflehog git file://. --results=verified) and rotate whatever it finds before you trust the clean green checks.

If your app started life in Lovable, Bolt, Cursor or a similar tool, the exposure is usually bigger than one pipeline. The vibe coding security guide covers what to check beyond CI. Or send your repo or pipeline to Geminate Solutions for a free review, under NDA, with a reply within 24 hours.

title: I built a browser for AI agents, then benchmarked it against Playwright MCP and browser-use
description:
Every agent I tried on the web had the same problem: it was reading too much. A browser tool hands the model a page snapshot, the model clicks, and then gets a fresh snapshot of the whole page again. Most of the tokens go on re-reading things that didn't change.

So I built AgentGo, a Chromium browser for Windows (Rust, on CEF) made to be driven by an agent over MCP. Then I measured it against the two tools most people use today.

The result

Same model (gpt-6-luna, medium reasoning), same 24 BrowserGym MiniWoB++ tasks, a fresh agent session for every task, only that browser's MCP tools, and the page's own reward decides.

Setup Solved Median time Input tokens Agent turns
AgentGo 0.1.5 22/24 32 s 94.7k 7.7
browser-use 0.13.11 19/24 92 s 209.9k 13.2
Playwright MCP 0.0.83 18/24 42 s 178.4k 13.0

About half the tokens, roughly half the turns, and the fastest median per task.

Why it uses fewer tokens

Three design choices do most of the work:

  1. A compact outline instead of a snapshot. browser_open returns headings plus the things you can act on, one per line, as [ref] role "name". The refs stay stable while the page changes.
  2. Only what changed. After browser_act, the reply is the diff: + for new elements, - for removed ones, ~ for changed values. The model doesn't re-read the page to find out whether its click worked.
  3. The browser waits, not the model. Each action waits for the page to settle before answering, so the agent doesn't spend turns calling "wait" and reading again.

It's also a real browser rather than a test harness: its own pointer and keyboard (so date pickers, sliders and key-listening widgets behave), the agent can have its own signed-in accounts, and payments or final submissions pause until the person approves them in the browser window.

What it got wrong

Two tasks beat every setup, AgentGo included:

  • form-sequence-2: the instruction never says to press Submit, and no agent did.
  • click-pie: every agent opened the pie menu and clicked the item, and the page didn't count the click.

And the limits of the test itself: one machine, one run per task and setup, one model. MiniWoB++ pages are small; a different model or another run will move single tasks. The full method, every task's result, and a separate check on 20 real websites are in the benchmark write-up.

GoMini

AgentGo also ships GoMini, a small model (322M parameters) that runs on your own GPU and takes routine steps, like filling the values you supplied, so the big model doesn't have to read every page. On 13 held-out task types it went from 15 to 39 of 65 subgoals between versions. It's still in development: with it on, AgentGo solved the same 22/24, at slightly more tokens.

Try it

  • AgentGo (Windows 11, free): https://github.com/Moha2005269/agentgo
  • Claude Code: /plugin install agentgo --marketplace Moha2005269/agentgo-mcp
  • Other MCP clients: the installer connects Claude Code, Codex or Droid, or run agentgo mcp. It's also on the official MCP Registry as io.github.Moha2005269/agentgo.

I built this solo. I'd love to hear what breaks, and which sites you want me to try next.

title: Give your coding assistant a design brief, not just a screenshot
description:
A screenshot can show a coding assistant the shape of a design. A short brief with actual colors, typography and spacing gives it values it can work with. You can collect those values with browser DevTools; a CSS inspection extension can reduce some of the clicking.

Disclosure: I'm working on Stylegrab, the extension used in the accompanying demo. The workflow below also works manually.

Editorial disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance. The examples and product demo use our own sample page; the extension does not call an AI model.

Choose the part of the reference that matters

Start with a page you own or have permission to reuse. Pick one component and a small set of visual rules: a page background, text and accent colors, body and heading type, common spacing and corner radii. Keep your own product's content and identity.

Read rendered values as well as source rules

The declaration with the highest selector specificity doesn't always win. Cascade layers, importance and other parts of the cascade come first. In DevTools, use the Computed panel to check the final value before copying it. For a tool, this is a useful regression test:

@layer base, overrides;
@layer base { #example { color: red; } }
@layer overrides { .example { color: blue; } }

For <div id="example" class="example">, the normal declaration in the later layer wins: blue. A copier that sorts only by selector specificity will give you the wrong starting point.

Write a compact brief 

Use these reference values for our settings panel:
Background #0E1016; surface #171B24.
Text #E7E9EE; secondary text #A6ACBA; accent #7C6CFF.
Body: system sans-serif, 16px, line-height 1.5.
Heading: 28px, weight 700.
Spacing: 8px / 16px / 24px. Cards: 12px radius.
Keep our own copy and product identity.
Verify contrast and keyboard focus.
Check the result at 390px and 1280px widths.

These are illustrative values. Replace them with the values you actually need, and compare them with your project's existing design tokens.

Export a component as a starting point

A static HTML/CSS export can help with a button or card. It doesn't bring along the application's state, JavaScript interactions or all responsive rules. Check asymmetric borders and radii too: four different corners cannot be represented by one uniform rounded class.

Verify in the destination page

Check the narrow layout, focus and hover states, text contrast, and the influence of your own theme. With Tailwind, make sure the generated classes are included in your build and that your theme hasn't changed the meaning of a named utility.

The Stylegrab guide includes the workflow and demo. Its free inspection tools and Pro trials are being prepared for the Chrome Web Store release; the page shows the current installation and payment availability.

title: Sharp Degree Bounds for Putinar Certificates in Terms of the Positivity Margin via Analytic Sums of Squares
description:
arXiv:2610.26976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We establish sharp degree bounds for Putinar sum-of-squares (SOS) certificates in terms of the positivity margin $\delta$. For any fixed Archimedean quadratic module with prescribed generators and any fixed bound on the degree of the objective, we prove a uniform certificate-degree upper bound of $O(\delta^{-1/2}\log^2(2/\delta))$ for normalized polynomial objectives. We show that this bound is sharp by constructing a matching lower-bound example in three variables, thereby establishing that the dependence on $\delta$ is optimal. These matching bounds also yield sharp worst-case convergence rates for the Lasserre hierarchy.

title: CEFR-oriented Russian Text Simplification Using Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27237v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a study on controlled automatic simplification of Russian texts using preference-based optimization algorithms with a focus on adapting texts to the A1, A2 and B1 proficiency levels. We fine-tune YandexGPT using Rejection Sampling and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) methods to improve control over the complexity of the generated text. We compare several training configurations that differ in dataset composition, text type and the strategy used to construct preference pairs for DPO. For automatic evaluation we train a regression model based on ruRoBERTa-large to predict continuous complexity scores corresponding to CEFR levels. We also consider semantic similarity, lexical coverage and quantitative readability metrics. Human evaluation assesses simplicity, fluency and adequacy. Our best model achieves 87.15\% target level accuracy, an MAE of 0.35 CEFR levels and a target interval MAE of 0.11. Manual assessment shows that 75% of the evaluated simplifications match the target morphological and syntactic level, and fluency and adequacy scores are especially high for A2 and B1. Although A1 remains the most challenging level, the model significantly reduces the proportion of vocabulary and grammatical constructions beyond the target level while generally preserving meaning. Our model is freely available on $\href{https://huggingface.co/kmustakova/RuSimplifier_DPO}{HuggingFace}$.

title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.27233v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

title: Detecting Errors in Large Language Model Responses: The Incremental Predictive Value of Hidden States
description:
arXiv:2610.27455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although large language models support a wide range of tasks, hallucinations remain a major obstacle to user trust. When a model generates an answer, both its internal processing and final output vary with the question. Internal states are often expected to offer richer signals for hallucination detection. However, studies using these states typically report their standalone discrimination performance, while output-side comparisons often use simple baselines with weaker modeling capacity. We integrate output-side information available at inference time into a combined baseline and compare detection performance before and after adding hidden states under identical data splits and evaluation rules. Experiments cover open-ended generation and constrained multiple-choice tasks across different models. Adding hidden states improves AUROC by approximately 0.004 and 0.039 on the two tasks, respectively. Hidden states thus provide additional predictive information, but strong standalone detection performance can still yield only limited additional gains.

title: Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support disassociating replicas
description:
Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support disassociating a replica without deleting its table or data. Global tables provide fully managed, multi-Region, multi-active replication. You can now stop replication to and from a replica and continue using the same table as a single-Region table.

An account can leave a shared multi-account global table and continue using its table independently. You can also stop replication to a Region while keeping its table for local workloads, validation, or audit, without creating a replacement table or copying data.

DynamoDB supports disassociating replicas in all AWS Regions for same-account and multi-account global tables that use multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC).

To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, DynamoDB API, or AWS CloudFormation. For more information, see Disassociating replicas in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide.

title: Trail-Weighted Influence Scores for Approximate Outcome Prediction in Bayesian Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.27366v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction. A traversal enumerates the active trails from each evidence node to the outcome, scores each trail by the product of its edge strengths, and drops evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, we show that the trail score equals the exact correlation between a trail's endpoints, that a chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, and that the pruned posterior is within a computable sum of per-trail terms of the exact posterior when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node. We prove this bound, check it exhaustively on all small trees, and show that it fails when dropped trails share a branch. In simulations on random trees, thresholding trail scores gives 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. We also apply the score, as an unproven heuristic, to seven bnlearn networks with colliders and loops. Keeping the top half of the active evidence by trail score gives lower error than random pruning on all seven, but it is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven, so we show no speedup. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on networks they never saw do not beat the trail score or mutual information, but trail features carry most of what they use and clearly outperform generic graph features. A bound for general networks is left to future work.

title: Top 5 Ways to Humanize ChatGPT Responses in Your App (2026): System Prompts, Post-Processing and Tools
description:
Updated October 2026.

If you've shipped an LLM feature, you've probably had this feedback: "It works, but it sounds like a robot." Users notice the bullet-point reflex, the "Great question!" opener and the closing "Let me know if you have any other questions!" These patterns make a support bot feel scripted and a writing assistant feel generic.

This is a practical list of fixes, from cheapest to most involved, for developers who want LLM responses that sound like their product rather than like a default assistant.

First, define "human" for your product

Nielsen Norman Group describes tone of voice along four dimensions: funny vs. serious, formal vs. casual, respectful vs. irreverent, and enthusiastic vs. matter-of-fact. Pick a point on each before you touch a prompt. "Casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact" is a spec. "Friendly" isn't.

1. Rewrite the system prompt with rules and examples

This fixes the most for the least effort. OpenAI's prompt engineering guide recommends specific instructions and examples of desired output, and that applies to voice as much as to format.

Voice: casual, serious, respectful, matter-of-fact.
- Answer in the first sentence. No greeting, no "Great question".
- Use bullets only for 3+ parallel items. Otherwise, prose.
- Max 3 short paragraphs unless the user asks for detail.
- Never end with an offer of further help.

Good example:
User: can I change my plan mid-month?
Assistant: Yes. You'll be charged the difference for the rest of the
month, and the new limits apply right away.

Honest note: the biggest single win, but long conversations drift; re-inject the rules.

2. Post-process with a deterministic filter

Some phrases survive any prompt. A small regex pass strips them before display:

const STRIP = [
  /^(great|good|excellent) question[!.]?\s*/i,
  /\s*(let me know|feel free to ask) if you have any (other|more) questions[.!]?$/i,
  /^certainly[!,.]?\s*/i,
];
export const tidy = (s) => STRIP.reduce((t, re) => t.replace(re, ""), s).trim();

Honest note: cheap and reliable for openers and sign-offs; don't use it to rewrite the middle of answers.

3. Run long-form output through a humanizer before publishing

For features that produce content (email drafts, product descriptions, blog sections) rather than chat replies, a dedicated humanizer is worth adding to the review step. UnAIMyText is a free AI humanizer that rewrites at the sentence level, varying rhythm and replacing stock phrasing while keeping meaning. Free runs handle 500 words each with no total cap and no account, and you can set formality and emotional tone first, which maps neatly onto the voice spec above.

Honest note: it's a web tool with no public API documented on the site, so it fits a human review step for generated content, not a real-time chat pipeline.

4. Use QuillBot or Grammarly for in-browser review

If a person reviews generated content before it goes out, the extensions they already have can help. QuillBot's free humanizer works in five languages and runs inside ChatGPT and Gemini; Grammarly's humanizer covers six languages and can learn a custom voice.

Honest note: great for reviewers, irrelevant for automated replies, and QuillBot's free requests are short (around 100 words).

5. Fine-tune or few-shot with real transcripts

If you have a corpus of excellent human support replies, few-shot examples (or fine-tuning, where available) teach the model your actual voice better than any adjective.

Honest note: the most effective long-term fix and the most work: you need clean, consented data and an eval set.

How to test it

Keep a fixed set of 30 representative user messages. For each change, generate responses and score:

  • Does the first sentence answer the question?
  • Any banned phrases left?
  • Average response length vs. target.
  • A blind human rating: "sounds like us" on a 1-to-5 scale.

Automate the first three; do the fourth weekly with two teammates.

FAQ

How do I stop ChatGPT starting every answer with "Great question"?
Ban it in the system prompt, give a counter-example, and strip it with a regex as a backstop.

Should my chatbot use bullet points?
Only for genuinely parallel items. Prose reads as more human for short answers.

What's the best way to humanize long generated content in an app?
Prompt for structure, then run each section through a humanizer during human review, then edit.

Common mistakes

  • Over-casual voice in serious contexts. A billing or security answer shouldn't joke. Let tone vary by intent: route sensitive intents to a stricter prompt.
  • Stripping all structure. Steps in a how-to should stay numbered. "Human" doesn't mean "no formatting."
  • Faking empathy. "I completely understand how frustrating that must be" on every turn reads as scripted. Acknowledge once, then solve.
  • Shipping without evals. Voice changes can quietly hurt accuracy. Re-run your factual eval set after every prompt change, not just the tone checks. A friendlier answer that is wrong is still a wrong answer, and users forgive stiffness far more readily than errors.

Verdict

System prompts and a regex filter will fix most chat replies, and few-shot examples fix the rest over time. QuillBot and Grammarly help human reviewers working in the browser. Overall, UnAIMyText is the best option for humanizing long-form generated content during review for free, because each run takes 500 words with no total cap and its tone settings line up with a voice spec you've already written.

Disclosure: written by the team behind UnAIMyText, one of the tools listed. Competitor details come from vendor pages as of October 2026.

title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
description:
arXiv:2610.27032v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.27047v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

title: The Twenty Minute Review That Keeps My Agent Honest
description:
I do a short review every Friday. Twenty minutes, sometimes less. It is the only maintenance ritual I have kept for more than two months, and it is the reason the setup has not quietly rotted.

What I look at

Five things, in this order:

  1. The refusals. Every task the agent declined or escalated. Not to fix them, just to check whether the reason still holds. Half of them were right last week and wrong now.
  2. Tasks that took more than twice my estimate. Either the estimate was wrong or the task is not automatable yet. Both are worth knowing.
  3. The retries. Any task run more than once this week. The reason for the retry is the bug, not the retry.
  4. One log, read end to end. Not skimmed. One, chosen at random. Skimming ten tells you less than reading one.
  5. Things I approved without reading. If the list is long, my approval gate has become a rubber stamp, and the gate is now decoration.

What I do with the output

Usually two or three lines of change. A pre-flight check gets added, a task file gets a better finish condition, a note gets written to the notes file so the same thing does not happen next month.

Most weeks there is nothing dramatic. That is the point - the review is not for finding incidents, it is for catching drift before it becomes one.

Why twenty minutes and not an hour

An hour-long review becomes a project, and projects get postponed. Twenty minutes fits between other things on a Friday, so it actually happens. The value is in the repetition, not the depth.

The failure mode of an agent setup is not a dramatic break. It is a slow accumulation of exceptions that everyone remembers exists but nobody wrote down, until one day the automation is a fragile museum piece that only its author can operate.

I have run that setup before, in other forms. The review is cheap insurance against building it again.

If you do something similar, I would like to know what you look at that I do not. Mine has stayed the same for two months, which probably means it is missing something.

title: Announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a managed ingress solution for your ECS services
description:
AWS announces Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Gateway, a new resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized applications by dynamically provisioning and managing Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and their supporting resources directly in your account.

With ECS Gateway, platform teams define organizational networking standards once on a gateway and associate it with one or more clusters, giving organizations a centralized way to govern how traffic reaches their ECS services. Application teams simply opt in to inherit those standards without requiring networking expertise. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing, allows up to 25 services to share an ALB to optimize infrastructure costs, and gives each service a unique Domain Name System (DNS) hostname. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs when capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. You can inspect these resources and the gateway route to each service to see exactly how requests reach your applications. For traffic and health monitoring, you can use standard ALB metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and target health information from Elastic Load Balancing.

To get started, create an ECS Gateway, associate it with a cluster, and opt in your ECS service by adding the gateway connector parameter using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the awsvpc network mode across all launch types. It is available now in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when your services connect to the gateway. To learn more, refer to the AWS News blog and our documentation page.

title: BUMP: Body-driven Unified Multi-object Physics for HOI Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.27066v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating human-object interactions (HOIs) with multiple objects is challenging because the resulting motions arise from different underlying causes. Human motion reflects semantic intent, intentionally manipulated objects must remain coordinated with the human, while surrounding objects move primarily as physical consequences of contact and collision. We present BUMP, a text-driven framework for multi-object HOI generation based on a simple principle: learn intentional motion and simulate physical consequences. Our method first generates full-body human motion from text and scene context, then predicts trajectories for a small number of intentionally manipulated driver objects conditioned on the human motion. We then obtain responder object motions through physics simulation, allowing the framework to handle varying numbers and configurations of surrounding objects without expanding the learned trajectory output space. To address the scarcity of paired full-body multi-object HOI data, we combine heterogeneous supervision from human-only motion, full-body HOI, and hand-centric manipulation data augmented with plausible body motion. We further introduce outcome-conditioned interaction editing, which infers a local modification of the causal driver object trajectory from a desired responder object behavior without requiring an explicit target driver object trajectory. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both single-object and multi-object HOI benchmarks. Qualitative results showcase diverse scenarios involving inter-object relationships and edits, highlighting the advantage of our unified model formulation.

title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.26995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.

title: How to Coordinate Role-Based CLI Seats & Session Handovers for AI Agents: A Governance MCP Server
description:
How to Coordinate Role-Based CLI Seats & Session Handovers for AI Agents: A Governance MCP Server in Python

In 2026, multi-agent software engineering swarms (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, Roo-Code, AutoGen) frequently operate directly on local repositories and shell environments. Teams deploy autonomous agents to build features, fix bugs, run test suites, and execute deployments.

However, operating multiple agent sessions in the same terminal environment quickly exposes three critical concurrency and governance hazards:

  1. Race Conditions & Write Collisions: When two agent sessions attempt to run git commands, build artifacts, or modify configuration files simultaneously, uncoordinated processes overwrite each other, producing corrupt states or broken builds.
  2. Session Handover Amnesia: When an agent session terminates—whether reaching its context window limit, hitting a timeout, or concluding its turn—the successor agent starts blind. Without an auditable session handover ledger, the new agent doesn't know what commands ran, what uncommitted changes exist, or what steps remain pending.
  3. Out-of-Domain Execution: An agent tasked with CLI scaffolding (domain:cli) accidentally runs destructive database or cloud infrastructure commands without boundary enforcement.

To eliminate these hazards, we built CliSeat: an open Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that enforces role-based single-writer seat locks, logs cryptographically hashed session handover briefs to an immutable SQLite WAL ledger, automatically reaps abandoned seats via heartbeats, and redacts sensitive credentials from command I/O.

🏗️ The System Architecture

CliSeat acts as an authoritative governance sidecar between your AI assistants and the host shell:

           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |            CliSeat Pro MCP Server             |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   | Single-Writer Seat|  | Handover Ledger   |  | Command Governor  |
   | Lock (domain:cli) |  | (SQLite WAL SHA256|  | & Secret Masking  |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      |   Governed Shell I/O    |
                      +-------------------------+

1. Single-Writer Seat Dispatch: Enforcing Mutual Exclusion

Only one agent session should hold mutation rights over a specific architectural domain at any given moment.

CliSeat manages domain seats (domain:cli, domain:db, domain:infra):

class SeatManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seats = {}

    def claim_seat(self, seat_id: str, holder_session_id: str, lease_ttl_sec: int = 180):
        seat = self.get_or_create(seat_id)
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        # Reject if held by an active session
        if seat.status == "occupied" and not seat.is_expired():
            if seat.holder != holder_session_id:
                return {
                    "status": "rejected",
                    "error": f"Seat '{seat_id}' is already held by '{seat.holder}'.",
                    "seat": seat.to_dict()
                }
            # Renew lease if already held
            seat.last_active = now
            return {"status": "renewed", "seat": seat.to_dict()}

        # Grant exclusive lock
        seat.holder = holder_session_id
        seat.status = "occupied"
        seat.claimed_at = now
        seat.last_active = now
        return {"status": "claimed", "seat": seat.to_dict()}

If another session attempts to mutate the repository while domain:cli is occupied, the claim is rejected immediately with the current holder's session ID and remaining lease time.

2. Preventing Context Amnesia: The Handover Ledger

When an agent finishes its task or reaches token budget exhaustion, it must produce a structured sign-off brief.

CliSeat persists every handover to an atomic SQLite WAL database sealed with a SHA-256 state hash:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class HandoverLedger:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "ledger.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def record_handover(self, seat_id: str, event_type: str, session_id: str, brief: str):
        entry_id = f"hnd_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        # Generate tamper-evident cryptographic hash
        hash_payload = f"{entry_id}:{seat_id}:{event_type}:{session_id}:{brief}:{now}"
        state_hash = hashlib.sha256(hash_payload.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("""
                INSERT INTO handover_ledger (entry_id, seat_id, event_type, session_id, brief, state_hash, created_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?);
            """, (entry_id, seat_id, event_type, session_id, brief, state_hash, now))

        return {"entry_id": entry_id, "state_hash": state_hash[:16], "timestamp": now}

When the next agent takes the seat, it simply calls get_handover_history(seat_id="domain:cli") to see:

  • What previous agents completed
  • Unfinished branch names
  • Known issues or test failures
  • Pending pull request links

3. Boundary Enforcement & Secret Masking

To prevent accidents and credential leaks, CliSeat intercepts terminal commands:

  1. Domain Whitelists: An agent on domain:cli is allowed git, npm, pip, pytest, and cargo, but blocked from executing database or infrastructure mutations.
  2. Credential Redactor: Masks GitHub PATs, AWS secret keys, Bearer tokens, and passwords from command arguments and output logs. 
SECRET_PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{15,}", re.IGNORECASE), "Bearer [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?:ghp|gho|ghu|github_pat)_[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}", re.IGNORECASE), "[REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]"),
]

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    for pattern, replacement in SECRET_PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(replacement, text)
    return text

4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

Adding CliSeat to your local AI environment takes seconds. Add the following to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cliseat": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "cliseat.server"]
    }
  }
}

Available MCP tools:

  • claim_seat(seat_id, holder_session_id)
  • heartbeat(seat_id, holder_session_id)
  • release_seat(seat_id, holder_session_id, handover_notes)
  • get_seat_status(seat_id)
  • execute_domain_command(seat_id, holder_session_id, command_line)
  • get_handover_history(seat_id, limit)
  • reap_expired_leases()

🚀 Get Started: Open-Source & Enterprise

The open-source CliSeat Lite is available immediately on GitHub under the MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/cliseat-mcp

For enterprise development teams requiring the persistent SQLite WAL handover ledger, automatic heartbeat reapers for crashed sessions, credential masking, and complete container manifests:

title: The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era
description:
title: "The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-29T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [architecture, devops, softwareengineering, cloud]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of software engineering architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Examining Each Factor (Config In Environment: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Stateless Processes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Port Binding: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how The 12-Factor App Methodology in the Cloud-Native Era functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Software engineering Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Examining each factor (Config in environment, Stateless processes, Port binding, Concurrency, Disposability) through modern containerized application architectures."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.
