title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
description:
arXiv:2610.26866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.

title: AWS KMS Key Policies: The Access Model That Trips Up Everyone
description:
Day 13/60 -- AWS KMS key policies.

The single most important thing to understand: KMS key policies override IAM policies. If the key policy does not grant access, IAM cannot grant it. This is different from S3, Lambda, and most other AWS services.

Every customer managed key needs this in the policy:

# Create a KMS key with a policy that separates admin from usage
KEY_ID=$(aws kms create-key \
  --description "app-encryption-key" \
  --query 'KeyMetadata.KeyId' \
  --output text)

# Grant encrypt/decrypt to the app role only
aws kms create-grant \
  --key-id $KEY_ID \
  --grantee-principal arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/app-service \
  --operations Encrypt Decrypt GenerateDataKey

# Add an alias for human-readable reference
aws kms create-alias \
  --alias-name alias/app-encryption \
  --target-key-id $KEY_ID

# Verify key rotation is enabled
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id $KEY_ID
aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id $KEY_ID

Without it, IAM policies in your account have zero effect on that key. Miss it and you call AWS Support.

Practical tip: Use kms:ViaService conditions to restrict which AWS services can use a key:

{
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "kms:ViaService": "rds.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"
    }
  }
}

This ensures your database encryption key can only be used through RDS, not directly by someone with Decrypt permissions.

Audit your existing keys with:

for key in $(aws kms list-keys --query 'Keys[].KeyId' --output text); do
  echo "=== $key ==="
  aws kms get-key-policy --key-id $key --policy-name default
done

Check that every key has the root statement and that admin/user roles are separated. This is Day 13 of the 60 Day Cloud Security Challenge.

title: Your dependencies will break. Your CI will leak. Probably not today.
description:
Your dependencies will break. Your CI will leak. Probably not today.

The day the platform removes the API you depend on, or the tag you
pinned to gets moved, is the day you find out. I wanted to find out
earlier — so I built breakcheck, a zero-dependency Node.js CLI that
scans a project for things that will break or leak before they do.

Why now? Three things happened in the same week:

  • Chrome and Edge are removing XSLT. Python removed imp and distutils in 3.12. Platforms remove things with short notice, and a vendor can halve a shutdown notice and break your migration plan.
  • A workflow pinned to @v4 trusts that the tag still points where it did yesterday. Tags move. Commit SHAs don't.
  • A recent wave hijacked ~1,900 GitHub accounts and reached ~30,000 repos — most of the damage ran through over-privileged automation, not zero-days.

breakcheck doesn't fix any of this for you. It tells you exactly
where it is, with a fix for each finding, so the next breakage is a
planned migration instead of a fire drill.

What it checks

Plain Node.js, no network, no telemetry. It scans locally:

File Rules
package.json Deprecated deps (request, node-sass, tslint, …), moment maintenance-mode warning, floating versions (*, latest, >=), engines.node on an EOL Node
requirements.txt Deprecated Python packages (pycrypto, nose), unpinned requirements
pyproject.toml requires-python allowing EOL Python
.github/workflows/*.yml Actions pinned to a mutable tag instead of a full commit SHA, permissions: write-all, broad contents: write, pull_request_target, hardcoded token-shaped secrets
Dockerfile Base image with no tag, :latest, or a major-only tag
Code (.js/.ts/.py) Removed APIs: browser XSLTProcessor, Python imp, collections.Mapping-style aliases, distutils

Demo

The bundled examples/broken/ project is broken on purpose — one of
almost everything:

$ node bin/breakcheck.js check --path examples/broken
[ERROR] broad-permissions: 'permissions: write-all' grants every permission to the workflow
       fix: Grant only the permissions each job needs, e.g. 'permissions: { contents: read }'
[ERROR] unpinned-action: Action 'actions/checkout@v4' is pinned to mutable ref 'v4'
       fix: Pin the action to a full commit SHA
[ERROR] unpinned-base: Docker base image 'node:latest' uses the mutable ':latest' tag
       fix: Pin the base image, e.g. 'node:22-alpine'
[ERROR] removed-api: XSLT in the browser is being removed from Chrome and Edge
       fix: Move the transform to the server, or pre-render at build time
[ERROR] deprecated-dep: 'request' is deprecated since 2020 and unmaintained
       fix: Replace with node:http / undici, axios, or node-fetch
[ERROR] eol-runtime: engines.node '14' targets Node 14, which is end-of-life
       fix: Move engines.node to '>=18' (20 LTS recommended)
Summary: 10 error(s), 3 warning(s), 7 file(s) scanned.

examples/clean/ passes with Summary: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 6 file(s) scanned.

Use it in CI 

# Scan a project (exit 1 if any error-level finding)
breakcheck check --path ./my-project

# JSON output for CI / scripts
breakcheck check --path ./my-project --format json

# Also fail on warnings (strict mode)
breakcheck check --path ./my-project --fail-on warn

Warnings don't fail the run by default, so you can adopt it without
breaking existing builds. Turn on --fail-on warn once the warnings
are down to zero.

What it deliberately does not do

The deprecation list is small on purpose: every entry is a removal or
deprecation that is public and settled, not a popularity contest. And
the tool never phones home, so it can't check live advisories — pair it
with your package manager's audit for CVEs.

One more deliberate choice: there is no --fix yet, and pinning
:latest to an explicit tag will intentionally never be auto-fixed —
picking the version is a decision, not a chore.

Repo: https://github.com/techdevfun/breakcheck — MIT, zero dependencies,
Node.js 18+.

title: Exploring Recurrent-Depth Language Models for Multitask Clinical Text Processing
description:
arXiv:2610.27559v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical natural language processing includes diverse tasks such as information extraction, classification, and question answering. Developing one model for all tasks could simplify deployment and improve knowledge transfer. We evaluated whether small recurrent-depth language models can meet this need through joint fine-tuning and compared their performance with standard transformers. We fine-tuned Ouro1.4B-Thinking, Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, HRM-Text-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-8B on 9 datasets covering information extraction, classification, inference, and question answering, and evaluated them on four additional datasets excluded from training. Across these 13 datasets, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking achieved higher performances than Qwen3-1.7B on 11 datasets; Ouro-2.6BThinking was competitive with Qwen3-8B on most tasks. Ouro models showed the largest gains on inference and question answering, whereas HRM-Text-1B showed mixed results. These findings support further study of recurrent-depth models for clinical tasks through controlled experiments to isolate architectural effects and investigate how recurrent computation influences reasoning, knowledge acquisition, and generalization.

title: Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Logs Said 1970-01-21 (and the Seconds vs Milliseconds Fix)
description:
Unix Timestamp Converter: Why My Logs Said 1970-01-21 (and the Seconds vs Milliseconds Fix)

I spent a solid forty minutes last Tuesday staring at a billing page that claimed every subscription in our system had expired on 1970-01-21.

Not 1970-01-01, the date everyone learns to recognize instantly. 1970-01-21, a much more specific flavour of wrong. That particular wrongness has exactly one cause: a millisecond timestamp got handed to code that expected seconds.

The API was fine. My frontend was not.

If you have ever debugged a date that landed in 1970, or a "today" that showed up eight hours early, this is the checklist I wish I had taped to my monitor. Three ways to convert a Unix timestamp, then three traps I keep stepping in.

Method 1: Python 3.11.1

Server side, datetime.fromtimestamp() is the whole job. The one argument that matters is the second one.

# Python 3.11.1
import datetime

ts = 1761000000

utc = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, datetime.timezone.utc)
print(utc.isoformat())
# 2025-10-20T22:40:00+00:00

print(datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts).isoformat())
# 2025-10-21T06:40:00   <- same instant, my laptop is UTC+8

Skip the timezone argument and you get a naive datetime silently rendered in local time. That is where off-by-eight-hours bugs are born.

Going the other direction, build an aware datetime and read .timestamp():

# Python 3.11.1
import datetime

d = datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
print(int(d.timestamp()))
# 1792540800

print(datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat())
# 2026-10-21T01:47:19.575814+00:00

I always store UTC and format at the edge. The Python datetime docs spell out the naive-vs-aware rules better than I can, and they are worth reading once.

Method 2: Node.js 22.13.1

JavaScript's Date constructor takes milliseconds. Full stop. It does not guess, and it does not warn.

// Node.js 22.13.1
const seconds = 1761000000;

console.log(new Date(seconds).toISOString());
// 1970-01-21T09:10:00.000Z   <- wrong, this is my bug from Tuesday

console.log(new Date(seconds * 1000).toISOString());
// 2025-10-20T22:40:00.000Z   <- correct

Backwards is Date.now() (milliseconds) or Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) when the backend wants seconds:

// Node.js 22.13.1
console.log(Date.now());
// 1792547248983

console.log(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000));
// 1792547248

MDN's Date page is the reference I keep open, especially the section on date-string parsing, which never behaves the way people assume.

When I am already in a terminal, GNU date is faster than opening an editor:

TZ=UTC date -d @1761000000 '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z'
# 2025-10-20 22:40:00 UTC

TZ=UTC date -d "2026-10-21 01:47:19" +%s
# 1792547239

Method 3: paste it into a browser

Sometimes I am reading a stranger's log line and do not want to boot anything. A free online Unix timestamp converter handles both directions in one input box, and shows UTC and local time side by side, which is the part I actually care about when the number came from a server in another region.

I keep this browser-based timestamp converter bookmarked for exactly that. Nothing is uploaded, the arithmetic happens in the page, and I can hand the link to a support engineer who has never opened a REPL.

Three traps worth memorizing

1. Seconds versus milliseconds. Symptoms: a date in January 1970, or a year around 57000. In Node, new Date(1761000000) returns 1970-01-21T09:10:00.000Z. In Python, passing the millisecond value straight in does not degrade gracefully, it throws:

>>> datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(1761000000000)
ValueError: year 57773 is out of range

That traceback is a gift. It means milliseconds, and the fix is to divide by 1000.

2. Timezone drift on round trips. A date-only string is parsed as UTC, but a date-time string without an offset is parsed as local. On Node 22.13.1 with TZ unset on a UTC+8 box:

new Date('2026-10-21').toISOString()
// 2026-10-21T00:00:00.000Z
new Date('2026-10-21T00:00:00').toISOString()
// 2026-10-20T16:00:00.000Z

Python mirrors the trap in reverse. datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0).timestamp() returned 1792512000.0 on my machine, while the same value marked UTC returned 1792540800.0. Eight hours apart, because a naive datetime is interpreted in local time. Set TZ explicitly in CI, or your tests pass locally and fail in the container.

3. The 2038 ceiling and 32-bit storage. 2147483647 is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. Store timestamps in a 64-bit column or as bigint, because a signed 32-bit int wraps one second later. Postgres integer and legacy MySQL INT columns are the usual offenders, and they will not complain until they do.

I also stopped trusting shell date syntax across machines. GNU wants date -d @1761000000; macOS and BSD want date -r 1761000000. Run the GNU form on a BSD box and you get:

date: 1761000000: No such file or directory

Same command, same number, completely different parsing. Any script that might run on a laptop needs the branch.

Task Python 3.11.1 Node.js 22.13.1 Shell
Epoch to UTC datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, timezone.utc) new Date(ts * 1000) TZ=UTC date -d @$ts
Date to epoch int(aware_dt.timestamp()) Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) TZ=UTC date -d "$str" +%s
Unit seconds, float milliseconds seconds
Main trap naive datetime reads local seconds treated as ms BSD date -r vs GNU date -d

Two habits fixed this class of bug for me: I name every timestamp field with its unit (expires_at_s, created_ms), and I never let a naive datetime cross a function boundary. When I do need to eyeball a number fast, the timestamp converter at utilvy shows both directions at once, which is usually enough to confirm whether I am off by a factor of 1000.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com

Announcement

Beginning October 5, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) instances running Looker 26.18. Feature enablement for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Feature

Looker now includes built-in support for the Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) dialect. The Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) uses the bundled Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver, so that you don't have to install unpackaged custom JDBC driver JAR files. See the Dremio documentation page for more information.

Feature

The AI-Assisted Quick Starts feature, called Starter questions in the new Explore experience, is now generally available.

Feature

The new Diagnose & Repair tool evaluates your LookML project repository across eight diagnostic test checks in either your personal development environment or the shared production environment. When issues are found, Looker can automatically perform repairs (such as removing stale lock files, fixing file permissions, or repairing corrupted object indexes) or rebuild damaged repositories while safeguarding uncommitted changes on a dedicated recovery branch.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now includes the Style Validator, which enforces LookML coding standards, naming conventions, and structural best practices across your LookML project. You can run the Style Validator with the default built-in ruleset or customize rule severities, file exclusions, path overrides, and custom rules by adding an lkmlstyle.yaml configuration file to your project repository.

Feature

Now available in preview, Conversational Analytics agentic workflows support scheduled agentic workflows in addition to triggered agentic workflows. You can use scheduled agentic workflows to schedule recurring deliveries of AI-generated insights summaries, data tables, visualizations, and PDF reports to email or Slack by using natural language. Recipients can select Investigate in a workflow notification to open a private, persistent conversation with the data agent.

Users and admins can manage workflows on the updated Manage Workflows user page and Manage Workflows admin page, respectively, and Looker admins can monitor scheduled workflow runs and troubleshoot errors on the new Workflow Executions admin page.

Workflows that were created in versions earlier than Looker 26.14 appear on the Legacy Workflows tab and must be recreated.

Feature

Now available in preview, Looker Data Apps are freeform canvas dashboards that are built by local AI coding agents, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or Cursor, from natural-language prompts. Data Apps give you complete visual layout control (including absolute positioning, overlapping elements, and custom web components) while remaining bound to Looker's governed LookML semantic layer and user permissions.

Change

In Conversational Analytics, the default question mode is now Fast rather than Thinking. Fast mode is intended for answering quickly, and it directly maps your query to underlying LookML definitions without generating reasoning steps. You can still select Thinking mode from the question mode drop-down menu when asking complex, multi-step analytical questions about Explores or dashboards.

Change

The Modern User Interface preview feature toggle now defaults to ON.

Change

The Modern visualization theme now supports map charts (static map points and regions), word cloud charts, and donut multiples. While support for donut multiples was previously documented, it is now officially available with this release. These additions expand the range of visualization options that are available with the modern theme.

Feature

Looker now supports connections to the ClickHouse 26+ dialect. ClickHouse 26+ uses modernized JDBC drivers and introduces support for symmetric aggregates. See the ClickHouse documentation page for more information.

Feature

With global access, you can route your outbound traffic through specific regions to meet regulatory compliance or cost requirements. You can also use this option to simplify your network administration by managing outbound traffic from a centralized location.

This feature is available in Preview.

Feature

Using gcloud CLI, the securitycenter REST API, or client libraries, you can configure Pub/Sub and BigQuery continuous export to receive notifications when findings are deleted from Security Command Center due to data retention policies.

Apigee X

Announcement

On October 20th, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-6, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-6 within the next seven to 21 days. A notification containing the expected date of upgrade will be sent within the next two business days.

Note: Instances that meet either of the following two criteria will not be updated:
  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud SDK

Breaking

590.0.0 (2026-10-20)

  • (App Engine) Removed the app-engine-grpc component from the Google Cloud CLI.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Fixed

A security issue in GKE fleet management that could have allowed unauthorized configuration changes to clusters registered to a fleet has been resolved. The fixes are rolled out to all regions, and no action is required.

Fixed

This is an update to the release note regarding the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver issue published on October 2, 2026.

This issue has been resolved. You can upgrade your cluster control plane to the following versions to fix the issue for ubuntu_containerd and older cos_containerd node pools:

  • 1.37.1-gke.1552000 or later

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

For more information, see approximate aggregate functions (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL), HyperLogLog++ functions, and Sketches.

title: Uncertainty Gates the Gradient: Adaptive Updates for Generalized Few-Shot 3D Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.26909v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones. Complementing this, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) to enforce learning from high-confidence dense signals. On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ (1-/5-shot), UGA sets new state of the art with an average +3.08 HM IoU over the strongest prior baseline.

Abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.
